Ehh, bought it after watching some youtube videos, but unfortunately after just a few play throughs I feel I experienced everything the game has to offer me and for a $15.00 price point I wish I was able to refund the game. There is a nice learning experience and exploration feel to the game at the start, but it is short lived.
I wish the game was better and more fleshed out. I wish it wasn't just Dorah the Explorer meets Binding of Isaac. I wish it was more like an RPG strategy game instead of a Rogue-like experience. And when I say Rogue-like, it is probably further away than most titles, but man does it feel like I am playing one the majority of the time; so, I will stand by that thought.
For about $5.00 I would feel better about my purchase, but anything higher just doesnt seem reasonable to me.

"I remember the day I saw her first, the lovely Tatanu'kki, a warrior female from a jungle tribe. I remember her helping us sneak by horrors in the jungle, as other teammates came and left our expedition she stayed. Her, me, our persian translator, a wonderful young english writer, and a determined sailor. We also had a dog courtesy of the writer.
I remembered how she had fallen in love as we entered the strangest land explored yet, a land of mushrooms and lizard men, and she begged me to stay with her beloved. This... is not a happy story, I knew we needed her, but against my will and own affections I left her with them. My team thought great of me for it.
Now its been 5 months, I am on my way to my destination. After learning the pyramid we seeked was locked behind 3 totems, we had trekked to each, the tribes had given us a Tricerotops and I had adopted an orphaned raptor on our journeys. My persian translator... was killed by a massive, horrifying bird in a fit of combat that would have been easy had our writer not lost our only rifle. As he died, our sailor scot mourned him, strange I thought, those two had hated eachother when the expeditions began, but now they were close friends... were... it was only days later that the sailor gave up on life, telling me to take care of his wife with all the power I could muster. Now alone with the writer, his dog, and my pack dinosaurs, we set back to the temple after completing the ritual to reveal it. In our stupor and lack of sanity.. we didnt see the fires coming, our revealing the pyramid had activated volcanic activity around us, and me, being i was riding a fast raptor, along with the dog and tricerotops, were able to flee. My writer, my poor writer who by this time hated me, hated everything, hated the jungle, hated adventure, sat there in the flaming woods screaming, laughing as his fleshed was burned.
Days later, with no food, water, and only the animals left, i came upon the pyramid, I had survived. Me, a dog, a raptor, and a tricerotops. My friends, all gone, and somewhere in this jungle,  Tatanu'kki was sitting happily with her new lover, and in my heart a hatred for her swelled, as if it were her fault! Her fault for leaving! her Sneaking prowess would have led us safely by the bird, if we had escaped the bird then our persian would be alive! if he was alive so would too be our sailor! and with their help we would have made it out together... My one poor choice, my one moment of thoughtless love, killed them all. Theres no room for love out here, in this horrendous heart of darkness."
Every bit of this story is accurate, and it only covers the final of 5 voyages I went on with this team. This game has a massive amount of storytelling ability, your adventures can go anywhere, and random events are everywhere. It's not nice to you, bad planning and mismanagement of inventory, bad choices, will kill you, happily. This is a game that looks cute, but will rip your heart out and doesnt pull any punches, my simple choice to risk a day or two of no sanity and press on resulted in my tired crew losing our weapons, which led to the persian dying, which led to the scot dying, which led to the writer going mad. It all connects, your crew has biases and loyalty is dependant on your choice. Bringing a woman on the expedition can tick off the men in it, etc. This is a poweful and fantastic game.
However, there are a few points of contention i have with it.
The game is heavily randomized, but not entirely. The same people and the same side quests have popped up every single time I played it (Side quests meaning the ones given at the docks, the in-world side quests are random) and the same people offer their services. The game is also very linear, with a story that you are fighting against a few other explorers to get your face on a statue. This is my biggest beef with the game, if you removed that, added more randomization, and gave me different goals or maybe my own chosen goals instead of "Reach pyramid as fast as you can while finding stuff, for 5 adventures, then the game ends" I would enjoy it much more and replay it more often. Also, on any mode but easy, you need "Moonstones" to open the final pyramid, I dislike this mechanic as you dont know its there until the game tells you, and it makes expeditions more taxing because you have to search these stones out to open the pyramid, on hard you also have to go BACK to your ship instead of each ending at the pyramid, I actually enjoy that mechanic, much more than collecting stones. The fact some disasters can also end an expedition entirely gets old, i.e, you need a moonstone from a temple, but taking it will open a chasm that blocks the pyramid permanately, what do you do? fail, simple as that, quit, lose, get over it.
The game has easy to mimic graphics and a super simple system of characters that makes you wonder why they didnt allow us to make custom characters. If you can draw a bad pixel art face and a bad pixel art stickfigure, you can make all you need to have a custom character in this game.
Theres some other things id like to touch on, the dice combat system, yes the one that looks REALLY simple and unappealing, is actually REALLY fun, and its not totally random. as you roll the dice, you get to make combos for your attacks that have different effects, and you get a few rolls so you can plan out your chances to get the best possible attacks for a situation. However the lack of a "Dice library" to show you all combos means you may not realize some of them until you try them, for instance, if you have a rifle and only one "Eye" die, you will likely think its useless because the best you can do is "aimed shot" 4 damage, but if you had a second eye die, you get a "Precision shot" that does a whopping 12 damage, you would never know this until you got to try it by getting another eye die, which when trying to stay alive is not something youd think of, you are likely holding many more attack dies. In this way, a combo library would be tremendously useful.
Some of the random events give your friends weird traits, usually bad ones, like paranoia or phobias. By the end of a single expedition, your whole crew will be a mishmosh of mental disorders. The only way to fix this is to go on an expedition that is guaranteed to have a shaman and have him cure them. This shaman being the only real cure (Despite the fact they get to go home for a while between expeditions) is a black spot on the freedom of the game, maybe spending some funds in civilization to fix them or something of that nature could balance it out.
The tent is a game-breaking item that allows you to recoop sanity anywhere as long as you dont mind the RNG events having a spin everytime you do it (Which would happen regardless if you slept at the tent or in a village or by one of the safe zones). I feel the tent should be a permanant item, but maybe add more consequences or risk to using it to balance that.
And finally, theres some nasty bugs left, the game can tell you to dismiss someone to make room in your party, but wont tell you special cases where dismissing does nothing, so after dismissing 3 party members that didnt fix the problem, as in they are never coming back, you might be a little angry at the game for saying you could do it in the first place.
All in all, great game, I love it and recommend it, though I do hope the devs come back and add another game mode and possibly some other features that could greatly increase the replayability for us. I did put down alot of "Downsides" but they are fairly minor in all honesty, the game is amazing.
One last note, THANK YOU DEVS, for adding Selous to your game. Very few people know of him nowadays, but he is a personal hero of mine, I appreciate you giving him the spotlight.

Ok, before I get picky, this is a Hunt simulator. You will have to find prey, but you can and will become the prey too. As another said, it could use some polishing. If they'd polish and add to this game, I'd pay 3 times what I did... but they didn't and I didn't. It is still worth the price and then some for just the animals though.
Cons: I wasn't liking the game for the first... 15 minutes as it got boring with nothing to cut with my machete and the landscape graphics... need work... there was a wave breaking a long ways from shore and 15 feet high... and plants/objects are often seen floating, the same tree graphics are used over and over. Then the... I think that noise is supposed to be grasshoppers doing the clicking noise when they fly, it sounds like a glitching object does in other games. Needs work there too. No jumping or swimming was a let down, but wasn't really needed. I did not encounter any game breaking glitches so all that said, not a problem.
Pros: Now the up side is, the way these animals act is awesome and to me seems like they put a lot of thought into it. A T-Rex would look at me around a tree like my sisters dog does her snack toy. *I know the tasty snack is in there, but why can't I get it??* haha That said, it sucks cuz you know you are doomed without a better weapon. Then those raptors! A pack of 4 hunted me for 10 minutes. I made a mistake and ran for it. lol Like with dogs, not a good idea. The triceratops is what you'd expect, nice until you get too close or poke one with an arrow. Could use a few more types of animals, especially herbavores. I can't say that I
recommend this game, but that doesn't mean that I don't recommend it at all. For those who are interested in hunting, tracking, dinosaurs, and cooperation read on.
The game is far from perfect and at times there are graphical issues that I do feel shouldn't be a part of a 'finished' game. When you use 'x' to free look for example, you can see through your character models body. It isn't a terrible issue that makes the game unplayable by any means, but you can't help but feel like that was something that the developers just decided to leave as is, instead of cleaning up the code and flushing it all out. I've also felt this unfinished feeling when a raptor charges me only to get glitched into a rock or the surrounding environment.
The auto run feature, which you use by pressing 'q', is an amazing implementation and I wish more games would incorporate such (listen up DayZ devs, I'm shouting in your direction).
If you like dinosaurs, the hunting experience and are able to handle some wandering around across a pretty large map this game is exactly what you are looking for. It is difficult, however, so be forewarned that nothing about this game is easy...especially if you are after the queen rex. I spent about 45 minutes hunting my first rex with a buddy of mine and this was both a stressful and satisfying experience that most games don't offer. The actual feeling of accomplishment upon taking down such a large and terrifying creature was worth the pain staking game of peek-a-boo we played while implementing strategical shots to the beasts vitals.

The display chart of where you hit the beast is an exceptionally well done & very rare feature of the shooter genre.
You want to go for the vital organs as headshots on dinos don't do too much damage. Remember how they have tiny brains?
To top off the chart, it shows who did what, how many shots you each hit the dinosaur with and where. (ex: the lungs, the kidneys, the heart, the spine, intestines, liver, body shots, etc.) and then it continues to break up the stats into a nice percentage read out. For example with the t rex we took down, I dealt 88% of the total damage and was able to see my shots highlighted on an x-ray chart of the dino, likewise, my buddies fired shots that hit and overall damage (22%) were displayed. You then get to take a screenshot of your accomplishments for all to see.
You are able to determine your location and meet up with other players via the GPS that you spawn with. Yes, you can place markers on important locations and yes there is a distance displayed on all your squad mates so you can spread out and cover more ground. As you roam, keep the GPS equipped in your left hand and search for others dead bodies and loot spawns. The GPS is also an incredibly valuable tool with which you will be able to track dinosaurs and recieve updated information about them (their species, their sex, etc.) You will also be able to tell how damaged a beast is that you have already wounded, what % of life they have left and where you hit them.
The weapon selection/dino variety is limited (I believe that there are only five dino species at the moment, all of which are aggressive, even the herbivores) and this is something else that makes the game feel slightly unfinished
You can find clothing that increases your ability to hide (ghilly hats, shirt, pants, etc.) but again, there aren't many customization options for your character.
There are a few attatchments you can add to weapons, only optics related: red dot, scope with zoom, etc.  No suppressors or compensators, extended magazines, flashlights, etc. A couple weapons I've used so far include the .308 single shot pistol, the .700, the shotgun with slugs ammo type, the .308 rifle with scope, the riot shotgun, the assault rifle and the anti .308 along with the bow and arrow setup. I know that a .50 cal sniper rifle is in the game, but I've had no interest in using it after having the .700.
There are dinosaur calls used to attract certain breeds and you can use dino eggs to cover your scent. You will find mushrooms littered throughout Eden, but be cautious as they can lead to death!
Two of last things I'd like to touch upon are the graphics and the audio of this game. The vegatation/forestation is epic. The night to day transistions are graceful and seem wonderfully natural. The dinosaur models are quite detailed. The weather effects are something to pay attention to as the rain/fog cuts your vision. It becomes crucial to be able to listen in the distance for the raptors calling to each other and planning their attack(s) or to hear the mild thunder of a Rex off in the distance looking for prey.
Pick the game up when it is on sale, don't expect a "Triple A" experience, and don't play it alone. If you aren't into dinosaurs, hunting, or co-op don't bother.

I will not recommend this game in it's current state.
I love VN, and i generally loves any kind of VN, even with all their unique gameplay twist.
Just Deserts however, made me hate the game, to the point that i haven't touched it again.
Bland at best. It's your usual 'guy get stuck in a situation where only he can do everything and surrounded by only girls'. I wouldn't say it's bad, but i will say that it's not interesting.
Then again, i'm sure most of you (including me) buy VN for the waifus, not the story. In that regard, i'll give credits where it's due. Even if the character is painfully cliche, to the point that the creator possibly just took the most popular VN tropes and used it, each of the character has enough uniqueness to it to make it interesting. The personality is diverse enough to create a unique chemistry between each characters, and their interaction with the MC is also good enough.
At the very least, the characters is interesting enough to make me want to go back, so it's something.
The art is pretty good. Not really really good, but it's above average. There will be time where you question the proportion of certain character in certain poses, but it won't happen too often. The character's design is pretty nice as well, so no complain here.
The background is nothing noteworthy though, and just like the MC of the game, you'll quickly get tired of seeing sands.
I'm not qualified to judge the music, since i tend to not care about the music, but i can at least say that the music is enjoyable. Not too repetitive, fits the mood, but not good enough to leave a lasting impression.
The voice acting however is a bit, disappointing, namely Cornelia's and Cecile's. It's like those voices where the actor/actress tried to give an accent that he/she is not born with. Cornelia's British accent is pretty painful to hear, and this is coming from someone who really love British accent. Cecile's French accent is not that good either, since it really felt like it's made up.
Now i know that hiring VA isn't cheap, and since the other characters actually have likeable voice, at least i can give credit for that. After all, there's an option to turn off certain character's voice.
This is the one reason why i wouldn't recommend this game for now. It's like your usual RPG with social elements, you have a home hub where you buy stuff and interacts with people, then you have the battle section where you do battle and gets money.
The home hub is pretty basic, and i have no complain about it. The battle system however, is a glaring problem for me. It's repetitive, it's boring, it's not balanced properly, and the worst of all, the animations itself took way too long. Everything is animated, from attacking, to the HP dropping, there's almost nothing that's not animated in the battle. It's one thing if the animation is interesting enough, but the animations here is too damn repetitive.
Enemy will just use 1 or 2 attacks, and those 2 attacks always uses the same kind of animations, all the time. There's no differences in animations, and even if there's differences, the animation still took way to long to make it interesting. I can understand giving a long animation for some kind of ultimate attack, since that attack does need to be menacing and memorable, and doesn't get used every turn, but animating a simple attack? Not necessary.
Your action isn't much different either. There's no 'skill' (like magic, spells, or stuff) like many turn based battle offers, since there's no MP bar either. It's replaced by support skill, which can be activated by using money. It's quite costly mind you, so earlier in the game, you won't have much use for it. The only difference in your attack is the weapon you wield, and even then, you wouldn't find much difference, since you're using guns after all.
Worst part is the fact that the whole thing is based on this battle. There's no way to get money outside of battle (aside from selling stuff you found from battle, but then again, you need to battle), and almost everything cost money.
Oh, and you can't skip the animations, no matter what button you press.
As a VN, i'll give it 7/10. It's average, but it's fun enough to ensure people to come back to finish it. The characters is interesting, the art style is nice, the VA is good enough, save from a few, and the music is enjoyable.
As a RPG however, i'll give it 3/10. This is why i said i wouldn't recommend it for the time being, because the whole thing revolves around you doing battle and getting money, but the battle itself is pretty dull and not interesting. It's worse than a chore.
Until the battle system is improved, i suggest wait for a while. If you don't mind the battle system though, or you already fell in love with one of the heroines, feel free to get it.
It's a good VN, but not a good RPG.

Endless Legend seems to think it's a semi-interactive movie being rendered in real time, where every move of a unit results in beautiful gradual reveals of new lands as the grey fog of war rolls away in a manner that is wonderfully polished, but also rather slow. Similarly in battle, you can watch as each of the six little figures in your army draws their bow, nocks an arrow, and goes through an irritatingly long firing animation. Then a number indicating the amount of damage doesn't just appear, oh no, it has to rise up and glow and pulse. Practically everything in this game glows or pulses. Even the borders have pulse animations. Buy this game if you love beautiful graphics and have lots of time to spare to appreciate the loving detail with which every last object has been crafted. Buy it if you can't decide whether you want to play a game or browse a graphic designer's portfolio. But don't buy it if you want an interface that responds faster than a sleepy teenager on a Saturday morning, because you're likely to get sick of how long it takes to go through the most basic actions of a strategy game which thinks every individual unit deserves treatment worthy of an RPG protagonist.
The interface is also dubious in more ways than just the overdone graphics. Early in my playing, I wondered what the "next unit" key was - a common feature of most similar games which ought by now to be standard - so that having exhausted one unit's movement points, I would be able to move the next without having to search for it on the map. Tapping a few guesses like "n" and "Tab", which did nothing, I then attempted to press F1 to look up the hotkeys, but still nothing happened. Fumbling around a bit more, I found that hitting the Escape button presented me with an "archives" button on that menu, unhelpfully labeled "an assemblage of wisdom".
Did you think this might be the help function? It's not. It's a link to an Endless Legend wiki, which isn't even hosted on a professional site, but on the free and ad-infested Wikia network. I'm not sure what exactly lies behind this outsourcing of documentation to the userbase, but among the possibilities are laziness, sloppiness, and crippling overspecialization where everyone was working on the graphics.
As I write, the Wikia for Endless Legend does not have a page describing the hotkeys.

This is a game that has left me very conflicted on whether or not I can recommend this game at all as there are some things that are fairly good and other aspects that are not so good. I don't expect myself to write a very long review of Just Deserts since I normaly don't play Visual Novels very often and I apparently have very bad tastes for them as well. First off, the voice acting is pretty good, especially the fact that they went as far as to give them accents for their respective nationalities. What's a bit awkward is that the voice acting sometimes does not match the text on the screen along with one or two instances where the audio bugs out a bit. For whatever reason, everytime your player name is included in the character's speech, they just stay silent and never talk in a way that they can say the same thing making the conversation feel a bit awkward, but it's possible to talk in a way where they don't have to address the player name to keep the natural flow of their speech, but they never did so there's that.
If you're expecting a deep story behind the alien attacks, you're not gonna get it since the story is just "aliens are invading Earth, don't bother asking any questions and just go exterminate them". With aliens in the picture, there is the combat system to go along with it, but unfortunately the combat in the game is a huge deal breaker for some people because the combat system is extremely basic, flawed, and just plain boring that feels like unnecessary padding, especially the fact that you cannot skip the combat animations and text that constanly pops up every time an action takes place. Getting equipment is outrageously overpriced compared to how much money you earn which is especially problematic in the early game where you only have a pistol and a knife, plus it's completely reliant on RNG in addition to the enemy always having the advantage over you. In fact, most of the equipment available for purchase is completely useless and a waste of money with the only weapons you will find yourself using the majority of the time is the RPG, the shotgun, the smg, and occasionally the knife for cutting though shields. During combat, you can call out for support from any of the heroines you've brought with you during your patrols, but the way it was built makes money even more of an issue since calling in support of any description will siphon a huge sum of cash out of your bank account for whatever reason. There also appears to have an initiative system for whomever has the higher speed stats gets to go first and the game does not give you any information on the enemy's statistics whatsoever other than a generic health bar so there's more RNG on top of your RNG. Lastly, the aliens themselves are not very interesting to look at because they're all just elemental polygons.
There are quests you can partake in to increase your relationship status with the other heroines, but at least half of them is completely dependant on RNG while the other half is to empty your wallets on overpriced tat like say Cornelia asks you to kill X number of X-type aliens, but you could do nothing but patrols for 3 days straight and never reach the amount of kills needed to complete the quest all because X-type aliens never spawned or don't spawn enough to get there.
At the end of the day, Just Deserts is not a bad game per say. It's a light-hearted story with light-hearted characters that apparently goes down a more serious tone when you get to know them I suppose, but then again, the tone of the writing was never consistent to begin with. There's an alien invasion, yet most of the time everything else that happens around you makes you completely forget that there is an invasion in the first place. There are multiple endings, but then you end up asking yourself if you want to deal with the monotonous combat system for several more hours just to see a different variation of the the same ending. I have no idea. Perhaps it depends on how you personaly feel about your first playthough, but if I had to describe all of the mechanics of this game in just a few words, it would be one of those games that has RNG built on top of RNG times seven. To recommend or to not recommend? That is the question I ask myself everyday when it comes down to personal enjoyment vs overall quality. If you can tolerate the questionable mechanics of Just Deserts and enjoy a light-hearted story to boot, then Just Deserts could be for you. Otherwise, I regrettably suggest you look elsewhere for something that's less frustrating to go through.

I very much enjoyed the visual novel parts of the game, including having certain events tied to certain locations and heroines.   As far is a time limited visual novel where you need to raise stats to a certain level by the “end game” to not fail this would be average to above average title (B+).  I found the characters, story, art, and voice acting all very enjoyable.
However, progression to success is locked behind a stat wall that could be hard to overcome.  There are battle stats, money, and relationships in the game.  To beat the game you need to hit non-specific thresholds for all of these.  Relationships open new battle skills.  Money can be used to build relationships (gift buying) or direct combat power (weapons armor).
So here is the biggest negative for me.  I've save scummed more for this game than any other game I've played in the last 5 years because of  failing relationship quests and combats.

Why? Relationship quests are tied to a girl, location, and sometimes an item.  To complete a quest you may need a certain girl to go to a certain zone – it she doesn’t before the quest expires you fail and lose affection.  Sometimes the quest is to kill XXX of some monster or collect a mob drop.  Once again this is random.  This means the simplest way to raise affection  is to simply feed your chosen girl(s) gifts. This is boring and suffers from a poor UI, which will have you sitting in an inventory screen and reading the same “thanks for the gift” text way longer than could ever be enjoyable.

Second grievance:  Combat that you aren’t prepared for can be unbeatable, and if you die you must load your last save.  So save often. If you find yourself outclassed and need more money to buy better equipment your only choice is to buy “repellant”  and earn money at 50% rate (which means you’ll likely never catch up to monsters level as they get harder with time).  Before I got into the habit of saving before every random encounter I was about to quit the game and refund it.
To help ease the money grind (I assume) there is a special (random) item drop from mobs that sells for more money than you would ever earn by farming monsters. The item I am talking about can be given to ONE girl to raise her ONE relationship level, or you can sell it for so much money you can probably max out 2-3 girls with gifts, this just forces the player to grind the through the UI pointlessly.

Developed by Vith Floor and published by Sekai Project on steam. Just Deserts is a sci-fi action dating sim where you play as a soldier who must protect a city from mysterious alien attacks, while at the same time you will also be seeking to capture the heart of your dream girl(s)! It should take you around 6 hours to complete 1 route. For a full completion maybe 30 hours?
Moving onto the story, it is definitely one of the weaker aspects of this game. The overall plot is that the protagonist is immune against the aliens waves that the aliens used to disrupt normal troops brainwaves which in turn may kill them, and you have a month to find and destroy the alien ship. Okay with the plot explained let’s go into some issues with the plot.
The aliens are never explained they felt like they are just there for the sake of the plot which is to oppose the military base in the middle of a desert. Nothing was explained for the aliens they are just there taking on the role as being a obstacle in the story. The story feels “empty” and almost meaningless. For a game that has stat management my actions or anyone else’s actions for the most part did not change anything in between the game everything was predetermined, its only either you date 1 of the heroines or don’t at all. THE END.
In fact the only way you can change some actions is just by choosing which heroine you want to date and train with them, eat lunch or dinner with them, buy them medicine etc etc… It is like playing some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ RPG game where a quest ask you to go to point A to get an item and bring it to point B that has no relation to the story at all while in the middle of the quest you start to question yourself “Why am I doing this? Oh just for the sake of doing it”. Even when the game tries to add in some kind of drama or emotional appeal, it always falls flat because It tries to have humor and pop references while trying to be deep and serious at a very random time hence the pacing of the game does not have any form of synergy. One scene has two characters quite literally killing each other over a game of Monopoly, while a later scene tries to hit home the reality of war and how not everyone can actually be saved. The writing is literally all over the place, from the random events you encounter to the moments leading up to the final boss. Overall the story just falls flat.
Some things I would like to say first is that the combat system feels very badly designed. The enemy always have an advantage over you no matter how small. Okay I get that they want to make the game challenging but the fact that the final boss fight can be affected by your strategy / actions at the front makes it so annoying and unnecessary, because when you make it to the final boss if you want to correct your mistake you have to backtrack an extremely huge amount. Not to mention backtracking will not solve anything if you do not have a plan. Basically to “beat” this game you will provably need some planning and luck. You need money to get gifts for the heroines or to complete a quest so that it can be used to get increase their affection for you.
Looks good so far? Right here comes my explanation of why I did not like it at all
The animation speed in battle is very slow and it cannot be skipped. In order to get money you will have to battle a lot all the little animations for hp decrease and status effects drag out the battle. So with all of this in place it takes out the enjoyment for me and making the game a grindfest and a waste of time looking at HP bars moving up or down.
In terms of my preferences of difficulty. I have played games harder than Just Deserts like kara no shoujo or Pretty x Cation [Note I am comparing them in terms of complexity/challenges only] but they are much more manageable than just deserts. Why?  because i am in full control of the game, there is no randomized events that are just there to screw your plan up or some RNG system that controls your fate. Lets take for example in just deserts I failed 2 hard quests that requires me to eat with a specific heroine for 5 times within 3 – 5 days(?) Seems pretty manageable right? But no..  I failed simply because the heroines just do not appear at the restaurant or camp cafe to eat, I managed to eat with them 4 times and after that for the final time I am required to eat with them time I checked for them to go back to the [eating location] but they just simply do not appear there and hence I have no way of completing the game at all. Basically the quests felt very random even with a plan there is a chance that you will fail. Failing of the quests does not give you a game over but it affects your relationship with the heroine and in turn affect the whole game which is just downright annoying to deal with. [Just like real life 😉]
But the most annoying part is the Money:
Everything is money in this game without money you pretty much can’t get anywhere in the story. Obviously you can earn money in this game but only through “patrols” but the money you earn from successfully completing patrols is pathetic and the items in the game are priced at a ridiculous amount. Those patrols will earn you $40,000 if you use a repellent to lower your chances of encountering aliens but to get the repellent you have to spend $20,000 first so with simple calculation a patrol with a repellent effect only earns you $20,000. Not to mention even with repellent there is still a chance that you will meet aliens and in the event that if you met 1, yup you guessed it.. That hard earned $20,000 is wasted.
So you literally save and reload a patrol until you get one specific item, that has a (ridiculous) high value, just to get some equipment and to do some activities / buy Items for your heroines. This just turns the game from “I just want to enjoy the story” to “I have to save and load to get specific items to enjoy the story”. It literally becomes a task and a game that becomes a task is not fun at all.
Lastly, the actual gameplay of Just Desert it uses a turn-based RPG battle system where you just battle against aliens you meet on your patrols. During your turn, you can attack, use an item, or, if you brought a partner, you can use a special ability. This is basically all of it is in a nutshell, with just a few more mechanics that does not really affect the gameplay in any way. It’s very simple, so simple that I got bored with it just after 5 patrols. It also doesn’t help that you can’t skip the animation for enemy attacks which are so slow. The battle system they use It’s too simple and never rewarding it never evolves it is always the same thing over and over again. To add in extra spice there is also an RNG system which is just there to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off in combat.
Just Desert is a disappointing game to me it just left me bored, confused, and frustrated. I know this isn’t a serious game, but even just the mechanics of the game itself and the writing just did not feel interesting enough to keep me from wanting more as it goes all over the place and never to places that really mattered. Though there’s a lot a replay value, it will be exactly same as your first playthrough and no changes just cut-scene changes and that is it.
If you’re looking for a good RPG experience, a good dating sim or a good VN experience, you won’t find one in Just Deserts.
This was really a hard decision I had to made I honestly wanted to recommend Just Deserts but I just can’t seem to find a good reason to do so, as I went back into my memories of the game bad points just kept on piling up. So I am really sorry even though that effort was put into developing Just Deserts. I just simply can’t recommend this game.

If you're a fan of Dungeon Siege 1 and 2, this game isn't even remotely the same. It was sold by Gas Powered Games (DS1/DS2 creators) by Chris Taylor and Square Enix were the buyers.
Obsidian Entertainment butchered the style of Dungeon Siege entirely, but they obviously couldn't have been trying to use anything more than a similar lore basis.
Ignoring the relation to the previous two games, this isn't actually a bad game in it's own right. It's got a decent story and a decent combat system, though it's entirely designed for consoles and simply given a decent PC port.
While it doesn't re-invent anything, it's a solid title if you get it on a Steam sale for under 7$. It gives roughly 20 hours of gameplay, and the DLC adds another 2 hours or so as well. More gameplay if you replay it to try out each character, as you can only play that one character, even though you recruit all 4 throughout the game. All 4 character clears would be around 60+ Hours of gameplay.

I really hated this game and Europa Universalis when I first got them.  I wanted to jump in, murder all of the nonbelievers and create the world under my iron fist.  This is not that type of game.  Even though Civ and Total War pretend they've made improvements in diplomacy, they still really only come down to killing everyone else.
You will not jump into this game and eradicate the lesser countries.  What you can do... is subjugate them under your nation, push your influence, and try and form the nations of Italy, Germany, etc... out of the smaller city states.  Or if your citizens live in a state owned by another nation (such as Greece and the Aegis Islands being owned by the Ottomans), you can through some sneakery diplomacy take them with no bloodshed, or even get the major world powers to do the dirty work for you if you need some early weak undeveloped nations to colonize but lack the resources to mobilize yourself.
There's a definite learning curve, but luckily there's Youtube to show you what the heck you're doing.
Now that I've given it a second chance and know better what to expect from it, I definitely see what everyone meant about this being the 'big boy game' that you move to when you grow up from Civ (not that I dislike Civ at all).

The perfect period. The perfect setting.
By far my favorite (grand) strategy game of all time.
Paradox games are not cheap, primary school strategy, as Civilization. But I suppose you are already aware of that.
What I love of this game is the close period to ours, so the historical digression would not be as shocking as having Japan colonizing Brazil. Whether Prussia succeeds unifying Germany and the equilibrium of power created in Europe World Wars may never happen or will develop in a different path. Plus, the exploration of Africa may develop different amid this power struggle.
I love the “Great Power” scenery. If you are a Great Power your weight in the game is stronger. You may lose this status if you don’t play well enough. Or you can begin with a small, remote, forbidden kingdom and make of it a new Great Power. There you can see a “Japanese Africa”, well plausible by the 19th century if a lot of effort is put on it; maybe instead of focusing on Indonesia or Manchuria.
Economics is extremely complex. You can easily ruin or thwart your country’s development. This is good, so you don’t think strategy is just about building armies and send them to conquer.
Graphics are getting old, but I prefer it to new games like Europa Universalis IV. It’s just what is needed in the World Map. Even seems like a big parchment extended over the table of the General.
Longer period setting than Hearts of Iron, not so much as in Europa Universalis. Playtime: you can end a play in a weekend.
If you love strategy, I recommend this 100%.
PS: I played way much longer before adding the game to steam.

This game is concrete evidence that Steam reviews need a "meh" option instead of an up or down recommendation. The 10-12 hours it takes to learn the mechanics and memorize the encounters and actually win your first game are pretty fun, and the game is unforgiving enough that it feels satisfying to beat. But it's billed as a highly replayable FTL-style roguelike and the replayability just isn't there: the differences between the explorers are marginal, the variety of encounters is frankly pathetic, and the "procedural generation" just shuffles the map a bit without any significant effect. So I'm giving it a thumbs down for not delivering on what was promised, but if you can wait for a sale it's not the worst thing I've ever spent $10 on.

Originally I was not expecting to like this game. However, I ended up finding myself sucked in quite easily to the game overall and I feel that I will be playing this game to completion... which is a rarity with Indie titles for me. Feel free to check out my review here:

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
A surprisingly good adventure brawler with plenty of charm, action and classy artstyle. In Cross of the Dutchman, you play as Pier, the farmer who turned into the commander of a Frisian army, an example for all people who were oppressed by the Saxon invaders. While leading the rebellion you will get to meet and befriend historical characters and let them join your cause for freedom!
You will explore the Frisian landscape as it was during the 16th century and experience first hand how people struggled to survive during these times of conflict. Travel to villages, farms, forests and other landmarks and collect and find the treasures and gold that is hidden all over Frisia.
Lead by example with your formidable sword which inspires fear and respect with even the toughest of enemies. The legend says that Pier was able to cut down multiple Saxon mercenaries with a single blow! (The sword is nowadays displayed in a museum in the Netherlands)
During the game, you will be able to help Pier by improving his abilities and making him even more powerful. Using your sword and fists you will make your enemies tremble!  - Highly Recommended!

Cross of the Dutchman puts you in the boots of Pier, a simple farmer until the Saxon's decided to turn up and cause problems for the locals in the nearby villages. At this point you become tasked with repelling the invaders and rallying people to help fight for your cause to become the Legend you were born to be. This is based on hisotical events and while I might not know anything about them I do feel like it's telling a good story for the most part, I just wish there was more to the story since without spoiling anything it just ends and you feel like there should be more to the tale.
Gameplay is pretty much a simple hack and slash, you have two attacks "Basic" and "Special". Your basic attack is a simple punch (or sword when you aquire that), the special attacks can purchased and swapped as you progress and find coins that drop from barrels/chests. You also have a Health upgrade/stamina upgrade vendor that can give you a boost to stats. My only beef is the combat doesn't feel good and you can't block, if enemies overwhelm you it might be best to run away and recharge health. Controls feel a bit stiff to do (I used a pad) and moving wasn't a problem but lining up my aim to an enemy became a bit hard to do.
Enemy variety is basically two types of enemies (the melee ones and the ranged ones), I feel like it's a wasted opportunity to add some more enemies to the game and perhaps even add some boss fights to mix things up a little. Since there is only one path to the story there is no side questing to be done and that's something I'd have enjoyed. You do have Stealth sections that require you to move without being detected but it feels a bit easy and doesn't bring much to the game overall.
Art style is really great, I do like the cutscenes but wish they had some voice acting to go with them as they feel would benefit from the dialogue of a narrator at least. Video options are pretty limited, you have Very Low, Low, Medium, High and Very High to select from so it would be nice if they allowed more settings there to pick from (especially resolution options).
Length of the game is not great, I managed to finish in 2.7 hours and that's doing 27/31 achievements with a couple of the collection achievements being missed it might have taken me over 3 hours in total and I wasn't speeding or anything. It's apparently a 6-8 hour game to do everything according to the devs but I have to question that with what I played.
Would I say yes to the game? It depends, if you're someone that enjoys a casual little hack and slash adventure then it might be the game for you but at the price I feel maybe it's too much for what you're getting. Perhaps a DLC or sequel might be able to fix some of the problems I felt were lacking.

Cross of the Dutchman is a third person rpg beat 'em up that tells the story of Pier Gerlofs Donia, a Dutch folk hero who was later known as Pier the great. Pier is a hulk of a man, but happily assumes the role of a gentle farmer and family man.
Unless you set foot on his land. Then he'll punch you and nobody will ever see you again.
In Cross of the dutchman you control Pier as he gets deeply enmeshed in the conflict between his people (the residents of 16th century Fresia) and Saxon invaders because he wants some fish for dinner. After whalloping some guards into what must be a near comatose state, the angered saxons attack the farm belonging to Jon, one of Pier's neighbors and steal Jon's wife.
This leads to one of the first stealth segments, but not the last, as you have to get Jon's wife back. Then you just have to fight the guards you had to sneak past, making the entire exercise pointless.
Stealth segments aside, the dialogue, both written and spoken is interesting ,or well acted and the art direction of the game is colorful with bold lines and I enjoyed it. I feel that the cutscenes could do with some narration and submitted that to the developers, so I hope that is addressed.
Overall, the game is a bit short (About six hours) and ends very abruptly but is a fun play, and a refreshing look back at old punch 'em ups. I also see a lot of comments about the controls, but I didn't have much trouble with them at all with a controller.

Only If is a short indie/puzzle game set in a surreal environment. (Running off the Unity engine I believe?) It offers interesting puzzles that all seem untraditional. These puzzles range from cryptic clues to perplexing platforming. The environments are interesting and occasionally they're quite beautiful to look at. The voice acting in this game is great, but it's saddening that the volume correction is not. Some voices will sound like a whisper while others are more relative to yelling in the player's ear. Characters will also talk over eachother from time to time making some dialog inaudible. Sadly, the story is also lacking. I ended the game desiring so much more, but I was left unsatisfied. Overall, the puzzles and environments stand out, while the story and hard-to-hear dialog fall behind.
7/10  (It's free, so why not give it a shot? It seems most people giving this game a negative review have never played a puzzle game before.)

So, I finally decided to write a review for this amazing game, even though there are plenty already and I'm not very good at this. But here we go anyway.
Unsurprisingly, I first played Skyrim, and loved it greatly. Because of that I always wanted to check out other parts, but was always delaying it for million reasons. Then, a friend of mine just started talking about it, and I thought "Damn, that sounds so cool, I have to play it". So I bought it, and played it. And, man, I love it! This game can be both dramatic and absurd, and that's so cool! I also loved noticing things that were referenced in Skyrim, but I've never noticed before, because I haven't played Oblivion before. I'm sure, if I decide to replay Skyrim now, I'll find even more. As I said, Skyrim is great, and I love it, but Oblivion managed to get me even more excited. Some of the quest lines are so much better! For example, Dark Brotherhood in Oblivion got me much more emotional than in Skyrim, as well as the Main quest. Thieves guild, which was always my favourite in Skyrim - so much better in Oblivion, in my opinion. Well, Fighters guild kinda suсks. The rest are very interesting to play. Oh, and characters... From what I think, there is much more lovable characters in Oblivion than in Skyrim. (I spent way too much time visiting Anvil and just following Hieronymus Lex... And breaking into Skingrad castle to have a chat with Janus Hassildor... And calling Haskill for no reason at all...) Oh, and of course, the random conversations between NPCs? They are beautiful.
Seriously, this game brought me so much joy. If you have doubts like I did, I assure you, this game is worth playing.

An interesting and rather "hardcore" hunting game. I picked this game up on sale and must admit ive found it well worth the price. The graphics are not top shelf, but they are decent. Gameplay works similar to most survival games in that you will spawn at a seemingly random location.
You start with a gadget similar to a phone. This is you lifeline, use it all times until you know what you are doing, even then you will still need it as it helps locate any threats within range.
Basically you will travel to find loot containers, which can  contain weapons, ammo, health, cammo gear and other useful items. You can choose to hunt as soon as you have a weapon but it is advised that you find some decent weapons and ammo, health. Then hunt.
The rest of the game is all hiding and hunting dino's. This is NOT for everyone obviously.
3 Essensial tips to all new players.
Tip 1 DO NOT RUN
There are certain parts in game in which you can run for short periods but beware and as a rookie i suggest avoiding the sprint button until you have sufficiently have an idea of what you are doing.
Tip 2 Sound Is just as important as visuals, so pay attention.
Have a good headset, my 7.1 surround does a perfect job at enhancing certain sounds the dinos make and also gives a good sense as to the direction of danger. (Any survivalist, fps fan should already know this)
Tip 3 Use rocks
Rocks are vital for distracting enemies. Especially raptors who i consider a major pain in the butt when in large packs. The packs are random and range from 1-2 raptors to from what i have seen 6-8 raptors. Kill one and the others will be top of you unless you use rocks.
PROS
- Graphics are decent.
- Fantastic atmosphere, dynamic weather, 24 hr day/night cycle.
- Difficult (more so at first) but you will see that other hunting games are childs play in
comparison.
- Co-op good to play with friends, you can host your own servers.
- Hunting dinosaurs.
- Runs smooth on a decent rig.
CONS
- Ai attack animations could be better
- Ai path finding could be better, sometimes they get stuck on things.
- More weapons? There are about 8-10 but in a hunting game a few more would be nice.
- Ai realism, as they will not attack eachother, feed or drink water
(from what i have seen     anyways) Although they do poo.
- More dinosaurs. Only 4 out the 5 are hostile, some more would be nice.
All in all though i would recommend this game ONLY to people who would enjoy a hardcore "Hunting game"
This is not a survival game in regards to the fact that you do not eat, drink water to survive.

One of the most detailed modern civilization simulators available, Victoria II is all about economics and European "balance of power" politics. A big part of the game is guiding your nation through its industrial revolution and transitioning from an economy that relies on skilled craftsmen to one that can sustain huge factories. The game does a good job of creating a dynamic interaction between the economy, politics, and society. Don't expect too much of an overt narrative though - as in Europa Universalis, the story of your nation will be created through numbers, charts, and events. How you frame the story relies mostly on your own imagination - kind of like making your own head canon. Notable challenges include recreating Japan's rise to power through the Meiji Restoration, weathering the American Civil War, and building the British Empire. There's plenty of room to break history too! Fans of the Crusader Kings or Europa Univeralis series will know that Paradox is really good at creating systems that allow you to have fun rewriting history. You can create a communist United Kingdom, fight for Indian or Southeast Asian independence and industrial power, or build an empire to resist the Western colonization of Africa. Some histories are harder to rewrite than others - but this is a game that rewards practice and experience, and with enough of those almost anything is possible.
Victoria II comes with a "brick wall" style learning curve - if you've played Europa Universalis before and can remember what it was like to first learn how to be good at that game, expect to experience that again. I'm still not very good at this game with only 14 hours registered, but it's fun (despite the frustration) to learn a new system. If you don't like feeling frustrated, I suggest looking up tutorials online because this game's systems are very complex for a newcomer. On the other hand, if you like learning new things and don't mind feeling like a total idiot, or if you don't mind having to scrap whole games' worth of progress to start over, then just dive in and experiment. Trust me, the game will let you know when you've lost. The huge variety of settings and the specific challenges that different nations face ensure that you'll never be lacking inspiration for a new game.
Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm off to create a Romanian superpower to unite the Balkan states.
Like all the grand strategy paradox games will continue being the best (By far!) of its kind, giving you the feeling of control of any country between 1840 and 1930 until Victoria 3 is released

This shares a similiar theme (explorers) and gameplay to Renowned Explorers:International Society. That being said I feel like there is likely some cross-over apeal between the two games and if your a fan of the former it may well be worth your time to give this game and exteneded look.
For me (I would give RE:IS a 6.0) and everyone else I would recommend giving this one a pass. It's a "rougelike" game that fails to capitlize on making each playthrough feel unique. Sure each run will inevitably be slightly different but there are not nearly enough variety in quests, objectives, and variations between playstyles to ward of the feeling that your just wearing a different belt buckle but showing up at the same pub every night.
Positives-
The pixel art defintely gets that retro nostalgia feeling of the good old times fired up when your playing and that's a pretty cool trick that will get my nod of approval everytime. Additionally the combat/event system is a somewhat inovative (or at least rarely seen) dice combo system that was fun for the first few hours of gameplay. However it quickly lost it's luster as once you have a good feel for which combos your trying to line up and how to acquire more dice of a particular sort (combat, magic, etc.) making the decisions as to how you should proceed became rudimentary. There is an RNG element to this game (beyond just the obvios dice) that I felt was fairly well balanced in that making informed decisions and calculated risks in exploration is generally rewarded.
But not so Positives....
The game killer for me here is that his is a rougelike game intended for multiple playthroughs and the variety is lacking. Yes, there are unlockable characters, maps, etc. as you continue to play and meet certain objectives with each run. Unfortunately they do very little to alter the overall feel and even when you setup for a fundementally different build (combat vs non-combat for instance) you will wind up having requiring the same strategy with some name changes to find success. There is not much difference in the design of maps and though they may be procedurely generated I felt like I was going back to the same jungle more than a few times while playing. As a result you do not get much in the way of personal story to puncuate each run and there is not real narrative plotline to help hold your interest. Overall I felt this game was tad too shallow if your a strategy lover but it may be catered to a more casual audience.
Overall Rating 4/10

Basically, it's a hybrid of Team Fortress 2 and Call of Duty, given a DC license and the mind of a 14-year-old.
Playercount averages around 100 people nowadays, so it's nearly-dead I guess. You can still easily find a TDM game (at least in the US). F2P model, but it's pretty fair and you can unlock everything but certain cosmetics without using money. Being an older game, you can run it easily on modern machines, though the hosting system requires either messing with settings or a strong internet connection.
Everything that can be described is basically summarized by the line up top. The weapons mix together conventional stuff like assault rifles with rocket launchers made of PVC and the like. There are passive perks and killstreaks but also gadgets and weird movement options. The aesthetic is both gritty and exaggerated. The tone is dark, but in execution it's lighthearted and pretty tame. The balance is suprisingly good, but there are still some cheap strats abound. Endless contradictions that end up with a bizzare but unique and enjoyable game.
As a note, being an older game it has some older-game stuff to deal with like the cheap graphics (which is usually fine), the weapons being unpolished (I'm spoiled by Battlefield), and the fact that you can't cancel reloads, shotgun pumps, gadget use, etc. by sprinting (again, BF1 has spoiled me). Basically the game can feel a bit clunky if you're used to more modern stuff, but it's pretty easy to train yourself to do it properly. It's pretty much deprecated, but stuff usually still works (apart from unpatched out-of-bounds exploits and an abortive gang-war territory system that nobody cared about). Better than PS3, which is unplayable now, so I guess we're lucky.
Overall it's a decent game, it's free, and it's easy to run. If you're bored, this is worth your time.

Cross of the Dutchman is an isometric adventurer that features a story based off of the real life figure of Pier Gerlofs Donia, a Dutch historical hero. The game is played in an isometric view where you'll be running around completing tasks as you explore the world and help save the people who you love.
Cross of the Dutchman is a pretty simple game mechanically. Combat only has 2 buttons. A basic swing, and a special attack that takes stamina to use. Upgrading is just as simple, with only health or stamina to increase, and you'll also be given the opportunity to purchase new special attacks as well. The basic swing is faster but weaker, but the special attack not only is stronger, but can send multiple enemies around you flying into the air, which is pretty satisfying. Out side of combat the game is pretty linear in it's structure. Though the world may look expansive on first impressions, many areas are gated off until the game want you to reach said area. There are also stealth segments sprinkled in between to add some variety.
Cross of the Dutchman is a game that looks promising judging from trailers and screenshots, but after finishing the game in about three hours, the game shows a lot of flaws. As mentioned above the combat is very simple. This would be fine, except for the fact that it also feels sluggish, and it's the main activity besides running around. Since that's the case, it needed to be polished, it needed depth, but has none of the two. At no time did I ever switch to another special attack, or switch from sword to fist. Once I attained the sword and a special attack I liked it was all I used for the entire game. The adventuring in Cross of the Dutchman is also lacking. It being linear isn't an issue to me, but it demanding that I retread the same grounds three, four, or even five times over is ridiculous. There is a lot of running around in this game, A LOT of it. The game tries to break the monotony of either fighting or running with some stealth segments, but unfortunately the stealth is probably the poorest aspect of the game. It makes no sense why I can take on tens of soldiers at once one minute, then the next, I'm sneaking around just a couple of soldiers armed with lanterns! It makes no sense in the context of the mechanics, or the story, and is an obvious attempt at breaking up the flow in the game (which admittedly, does desperately need).
The game's also short, clocking in at three hours on my first play through, with a story that disappointed me. It's not that the story or characters are necessarily bad, it just wasn't memorable for me. Maybe because I'm Canadian and not Dutch, so I don't feel that historical connection, but there were no part of the game where I felt any emotions, or care for the characters.... except at the end. With out spoilers, the ending of the game was abrupt and felt cut off. The game's narrative finally reaches a point where something interesting happens. Where emotions and character development finally start to take place, then ROLL THE CREDITS! WUT?! Again, I don't want to spoil anything, but the game's ending feels more like the story only just started.
So I've mentioned a ton of things I took issues with, is there anything redeeming about Cross of the Dutchman? Though I've mentioned that I didn't like the combat much, the sense of impact when you hit an enemy, or especially when you use a special attack is really satisfying. Seeing a half dozen men go flying in the air, with some pretty good rag dolling and physics attached is actually pretty fun to see. The game also features some pretty good visual and audio design as well. The cut scenes are done in a still illustration format, but the illustrations are quite nice with a digital comic book look to them. The in game graphics, though low-poly, is quite charming, with colorful environments and characters, some nice particle and lighting effects, complimented with some pretty decent music. The game was also stable and optimized well for me. It never crashed nor did I encounter any major bugs, with it running at over 60 FPS the entire time.
Overall Cross of the Dutchman was a disappointment to me, as I am a fan of Triangle Studio's other game "It came from space, and ate our brains". From the screenshots, trailers, and based off of their previous work, I had high hopes for this game. Ultimately it lacks variety, depth, and it's further mired by an abrupt ending to it's story.
Pros:
- Visual and audio are charming
- Great sense of visual and audio impact as you hit enemies
- Cool style to it's illustrative cut scenes
Cons:
- no replay value
- Basic and sluggish combat
- Poor stealth mechanics
- Too much running
- Abrupt ending to the story

Robert from Triangle Studios was kind enough to give me a key to review this game in exchange for a review on the gaming website I write for.  That review is forthcoming (I'll update this when it's done), but I wanted to play more before I wrote something longer.
So far, I really like this game.  The story is simple, quests are easy to follow thanks to the minimap, the graphics are colorful, the cutscene art is vibrant, and the controller works well for this game.  Combat, upgrades, and maps are all relatively straightforward, so if you're looking for something complex and involved, this might not be the game for you.  I like this more casual game, though.
I only have two "cons" so far:  Firstly, I experienced some lag in two spots during character dialogue, but it cleared up quickly.  Secondly, punching is hard to aim sometimes, and like another reviewer said, I find myself punching air a lot.
I'll be back with a longer review after I finish the game, but so far, so good!
EDIT!  After playing more, here is my full review:

A fantastic story driven game, The humour is great and the jokes are funny, Combat can seem slow at first but once you get a certain item from a blacksmith the fighting speeds up and feels like a more traditional ARPG feel to it.
You can't choose dialogue options when speaking to characters as the game has a fixed storyline based on the folk legend 'Pier Gerlofs Donia'.
The game play style is linear but you can explore to find items/locations to examine to get a piece of dialogue or characters to talk to, there is an assortment of hidden chests in each level to help raise your money and to grab some achievements.
The game has a good length considering its price and have plenty of achievements to grab up.
The art style is largely unique and full of colour, textures seem to be of high quality and the characters have a lot of graphical personality, animations are smooth and plentiful.
The minimap is easy to use and has a waypoint marker to help get around easily.
Stealth elements are there and can be challenging at times, not a Metal gear solid level of stealth but this isn't what the game is about.
You can buy several upgrades and potions from shopkeepers spread around the map, which is another good reason to find the hidden chests.

Aside from that, it was enjoyable, and they hit the price point perfectly for this game.  It's more of a storyline game than an RPG, but it could be a good way to kill a couple hours.
I still get a kick out of the whole "true story based on a folk legend" :P

TL:DR
If you are a freakishly obsessed dinosaur enthusiast, don't buy this game
If you like realism, don't buy this game.
If you like hilariously broken dinosaurs, and dying to invisible forces, and feeling useless you may be in luck.
Firstly the '
'
(This is my own estimation, going on evidence gathered whilst 'playing') You are a random prisoner (who I will refer to as Bob for the purpose of this review), who has been dropped down to the uncharted surface of a planet known as Primal Eden, which from satellite scans appears to be home to
dumb (but dangerous) dinosaurs. Bob is lucky, as he is the prisoner that has been chosen for today to try and terraform and populate the surface of primal eden on his own. Now, if you were a fancy space-age civilisation of humans, you would send down someone well equipped to deal with any dangers that may be present on the surface of the possibly inhospitable planet, wouldn't you think?
No, your standard starting Bob is equipped with a crude machete and white trainers. You know, to kill all those triceratops and T-Rex?
Onto the subject of actual game play
The A.I is pretty 'mediocre' to put it lightly (the dinosaurs frequently rotate on the spot, don't aknowledge eachothers existence and sometimes randomly run of when they attempt to 'attack you' they come back later by emerging out of the ground.)
The weakest spot on a 'Utahraptors' body is its♥♥♥♥♥♥ and not its apparently missing brain or heart.
Jesus the tyrannosaurus has also been witnessed, walking across the surface of the 'sea' only to smite my character down with an invisible attack that caused me to fall out of the world and into the hellish recesses of the low-res skybox.
Also, watch out for the angry chicken dinosaurs that hover a few centimeters above the ground.
The game has potential, but it definitely needs more content. I hope the devs do not abandon the game.

This game was one of the many adventure games I played as a child. I decided to venture into the depths of the ocean once again to revisit a happy part of my childhood, and dare I say it was quite awesome.
Being a mystery adventure game there are of course puzzles that are quite simple and not exactly challanging. It took me one hour to complete this game and that's because I took my sweet time to interact with everything and have a nostalgia overload. The puzzles mainly consist of you talking to different sea creatures and desiphering their clues. The dialoges are charming and well written, and it never feels like a chore to talk to anyone. There are also some special features in this game that is quite classic with older adventure games. For one thing you can interact with everything. If there is a rock  somewhere on the level you can click it and a small crab orchester begins to play, or a shark dances for you, or a hula dancer takes the rock and does indescribable things to it.
I recommend this game for those of you that played this as a child and want to have a rush of nostalgia visit for approximately an hour. It's one of the games that still live up to its name despite you being 20 years older and isn't just tedious with bad humour and lousy gameplay. And although I am very nostalgic about the game, I think it could be played by somebody that didn't have this as a child.

Relic Hunter Zero is a surprising free entry to Steam because it is really really good. It's a 2d shooter rogue lite, meaning that later in the game is really difficult. Your character across runs gets guns as you play through the stages, and at the end of each stage there's a chance to find a piece of a relic that upgrades your character. Along with that you can get bounty, the in game money, to get things in your ship before you begin.
The shooting and movement mechanics go hand in hand. You are really floaty in movement, you can dash and sprint around, and dashing makes you invincible to weapons. The guns are very fun as well. There's three types of guns with their own ammo like Destiny, light, medium, and heavy ammo. It has a mechanic where putting your crosshair over the enemy instead of behind and in front does more damage.
The game has huge potential as far as other features go. I would like to see an online multiplayer along with the couch co op (however controllers aren't really the best way to play this game) and some sort of multiplayer. The balance would be an easy change, as the enemy AI in singleplayer is about as hard other people get.

Even though it was free to play, I feel robbed by having played this game. The first few minutes of the game setup a cruel masquarade, giving the player an expectation of clever puzzle solving intertwined with interesting level design and an engrossing story. I promise that none of these elements come to fruition.
The game very quickly abandons any hopes of requiring any thinking skills after the first quarter of the game, instead forgoing any oppurtunity for player exploration and problem solving in favor of arbitrary direct instructions on how to proceed. There is no point in playing any of the levels, as the game invariably tells the player exactly how to proceed, as if to make sure they complete the story it wishes to show off, thus removing the player's satisfaction of completing the level and killing their motivation to continue.
Additionally, the game is simply not fun to play. Level design is boring and overly complicated, and the game boasts no interesting mechanics aside from the standard "walk, jump, look, shoot" level of interaction.
As for the story, while initially promising, it quickly becomes frustrating and uninteresting, mainly due to the abysmal voice acting used to deliver it. At first, it's forgivable for an independent project, but it quickly becomes annoying and even embarassing to listen to. Since the game has no subtitles, muting the VOs eliminates the story of the game, which, frankly, isn't neccesarily a bad thing. The story is a pretentious mess either attempting to mirror the piecewise story-telling of Gone Home or Dear Esther, or attempting to mock it (given the ending). If the latter is true, it presents a better outlook on the game, but fails to redeem it from utilizing the poor design choices it is attempting to parody. In the end, it is revealed the story doesn't matter, which establishes the biggest shortcoming of the game: it has absolutely no redeeming qualities. No gameplay, no story, nothing interesting, overall a total failure.
While the game tempts the player with replayability, as it utilizes player choice in proceeding, a quick replay reveals the choice changes essentially nothing, and exists soley to entrap the player once more.
If you wish to recieve any enjoyment out of this game at all, play for the first ten minutes, then stop and never pick it up again. Aside from a promising start, this game is an utter failure that is not fit for anyone's consumption.

This is my new favorite game ! It has all the elements of games that I love ... Rogue-like randomness, pixel style graphics and just .. being an explorer ! It reminds me a lot of a very old game I had on the Atari 800 called 'Seven cities of gold'.
Where do you even start to explain why this is such a good game ? The first time you play the game, so much is unknown about the mechanics and what is generally possible .. It's true exploration in every sense of the word. But the little tutorial gets you going very quickly and after that most of the stuff in the game has information if you hover over it with the mouse. The pixel graphics are really well done, everything looks like it is done in the same 'theme' and just fits really well together. The music is also quite fitting, reminded me a little of the music in Pirates! on the Amiga. (Which is another great game with some similar elements to TCE).
Gameplay .. You can't save the game without quiting, so there are no 'do-overs'. You have to make a lot of calculated guesses and very often there are ... not so great results. You are bound to lose a crew member here and there or have to abort a mission (by exiting with a hot air balloon) which will cause you to lose a bunch of equipment and not earn fame for that trip. So far I have found it quite challenging, but not too difficult to enjoy. In fact it's this difficulty which makes it super enjoyable to me.
I feel this will be a game that I will return a lot to in the future. I'm hoping some more cool features will be added in the future like expeditions under water or in arctic areas. But even without that, the replayability is so damn high, I don't think it will ever get boring.

This game I see has got alot of negativity, mostly from those who havent played the game more than a few hours and rage quit after getting killed a few times. There is no doubt that this game takes a while to get used to, even I used to get extremely frustrated at not being able to locate settlements with weapons. But once you start to learn thestructure of the map and the mechanics of the game, and you start to learn new skills and stratagies, this is an extremely fun and exiting game to play solo and with friends. The concept of theHunter: Primal is great, the graphics and enviroment is breathtaking and overall this game truly does deserve more attention. I highly reccomend this game to anyone who loves survival, dinosaurs, action and of course having a great time.
For those who are just starting out, here are some useful tips:
Survival:

The Hunter Primal is all about killing dinosaurs, finding gear and most importantly, survival. You may find the best gear but if you don’t know how to survive and keep it, it’s pointless. If you come across a dinosaur that you are not equipped to fight, you must hide. The best way to stay undetected is by crouching instead of walking if you hear something, and lying in thick bushes if something gets too close… Around the map, you can find health canisters which you can use if you are struggling for health. So if you have one and you need it, don’t save it, use it! When you come across a cliff or steep drop, you should never take the chance of just walking off to get where you want to go, you will most likely just fall to your death…


Killing Dinosaurs:

Utahraptors:

To kill these vicious beasts, it’s all about hitting them in the heart. You can hit them as many times as you like anywhere else and pretty much nothing will happen. To hit their heart, you must hit them directly in the front center of the body. Hits such as in the back of the spine or in the lungs (which are in the center of the side body) are effective too. It is recommended to use a weapon such as a pistol or shotgun against these.

Velociraptors:

These turkey sized predators can really mow you down if you are not careful, there is no set way to kill these, all you have to do it hit them and they will die… Using a machete or axe is by far the best option when fighting these things, although be prepared as they can come in packs of up to 12…

Tyrannosaurus Rex:

I reccomend NOT attacking this alone! You should always bring a friend along. (by playing online) If you choose to take on one, be sure to bring powerful guns and plenty of ammo. You need guns with at least the power of a 308 Rifle but a 700 Rifle or .50 Cal is recommended. When firing at this beast, you want to be hitting the heart which is located in-between its small arms.

Triceratops:

When taking on a Triceratops, you need to have a decent weapon with plenty of ammo, it is unlikely to attack you but you never know. When trying to hit it, go for the lungs, spine and heart. It is recommended to use a 700 Rifle or a 308 Rifle with plenty of ammo.
Quetzalcoatlus:
This flying dino can be annoying considering it can be hard to hit, the best way to take one down, is to shoot at its body as it attacks by swooping down on you. They are quite fragile creatures and can be taken down with as little as two hits from almost any gun.

Settlements & Gear:

Finding Settlements:

It may seem hart at first, but finding settlements is very easy. When you start the game, you will get a “Map fragment” when you use that, you will be revealed a settlement on the map, all you have to fo is set a waypoint there by going on the map and clicking a point and go for it!

Finding Weapons/Ammo:

Weapons and ammo spawn at places called "settlements" these are marked by little symbols on your map. The best place to go is the settlement at the top of the volcano in the center of the map. This is the ony place you can find the .50 cal rifle, however it is still extremely rare. At this settlement you are likley to find shotguns and good camoflauge equipment.
