Hello, my name is Blackmagix95, and this is my review on TheHunter: Primal. I been playing this game ever since it was early access, and judging from my experience with the game, I recommend this game ONLY to people with a lot of patience and a sense of intelligence. Besides, most of the bad reviews on this game were made by players who played less than 30 hours or gave up on the game because the developers were barely adding content, even though they were working on new games like Mad Max or Just Cause 3. TheHunter: Primal is also nowhere near a survival game. It is more of a hunting stimulator, but with dinosaurs. If you really want a dinosaur survival game, go to freakin ARK. Last thing I want to see on the game's community discussions is more ARK favoritism and hateful rants.
Anyway, when I played the game at launch, I did had some terrible experiences with TheHunter Primal, but eventually I managed to learn from my mistakes and applied them to my skills.
It is true, this is game is hard for new players but it is part of the learning process and requires patience. Once you begin the game, it is recommended that you find a group of people to hunt with, especially if one of them has experience with the game, but ASK FIRST. It is also important to put time into the game in order to have a basic idea on the game's mechanics and to understand the strengths/weaknesses of certain guns/weapons, the dinosaurs and their AI functions/behaviors, the hunting advantages/disadvantages in certain environments, and what parts of a dinosaur's body is best to shoot at. And lastly, do expect to walk a lot; the map layout is pretty big and there are some momemts where you don't run into many dinosaurs. That is where patience and intelligence is needed.
If you can't dedicate the time to learn from the game, too impatient, or lack basic common sense, DON'T BUY THIS GAME. I used to join groups when I was a noob, but now I can solo-hunt with just a bow, a .44 magmum revolver and a machete/hatchet.
Also, there are a lot of guides made to help new players out, and most of us pro-players are willing to provide tips/tricks for the game. Take advantage of them. Who knows... perhaps someday I may run into one of you new players. Do expect me to hunt naked since I got rid of all of my noble clothing to get more inventory space for stuff. DON'T DO THIS STUNT UNLESS YOU UNDERSTAND THE DINOSAURS. YOU WILL BE DINNER!

TL;DR
Awesomenauts is a fantastic game, and worth a try.  Most of the reviews from 1,000+ hour guys that are bad are probably because they are salty about a nerf or the game "isn't like it used to be".  If something seems unfair, it's probably lack of knowledge or  lack of teamwork. (there are still moments that are unfair, but that usually isn't because of the game)
A lot of the reviews complain about high ping having an advantage, but from my experience it can be either. Some matches  the high ping player just can't be touched, and other matches the lowest ping player is impossible to dodge, but most matches it's all just fine.
Like any MOBA, most of the bad reviews from high hour players is probably from salt because their favorite character was nerfed, or the game, "Just isn't the same anymore".
I've rarely noticed being put into matches against people that are way better than me, but it usually comes down to the other team working as a team (not as well as a premade. There is quite a noticeable difference) while my team is doing whatever they want instead of working together. However, when a new season starts, you might run into the issue of super good players for a few days, but it is usually fine the rest of the season.
MOBA community so there is that toxic "YOU GUYS SUCK I QUIT, NOOBS PLEASE KILL SELF." guy in about 25% of matches (he's the guy that runs into a 3v1 and then complains about his team sucking when everyone else is pushing a turret), but I usually encounter friendly people.  A lot of people I've come across are willing to teach people how to be better.
I will say that some moments can  be unfair, but I haven't played a multiplayer game in my life that is 100% fair 100% of the time.  There will definitely be moments where you will say, "Dang, if we had this character on our team, this character on the other team wouldn't be 11-0 right now." but that encourages you to think of a solution with what you have.  There are some strategies that seem ridiculously broken at first, but if you can convince your team to work together, those strategies (from what I've encountered) will not hold up.
Awesomenauts is a fantastic game and is my favorite MOBA.  I don't know if it has something to do with my childhood growing up with platformers, and my interest in strategy games, but I have a blast even when I go 0-6 on a day (I still rage, but I still have fun).  It has its flaws, some of which have existed for too long without cause, but like with life: If you focus on all the bad, you'll never have time to see the good and you'll end up in despair (except in this case missing out on a great game).

I LURV VICTORIA II.
Quite a neat politics-simulator.  Even better with mods.
In the game, you get to take the reigns of a country in the Industial Era and help modernize it as you enact successive layers of liberal (in the classical sense) and socialist reforms.  It can be fun to try and work out which combinations of reforms work best.
Religion and culture factor into the game, but only minorly; and there's no way to change your religion or culture unless there's a specific event that's been written for it.  Also, sometimes religion is a little buggy; it's set per country, but this can cause issues if, say, you start as Sokoto, form the Toucouleur Empire, and then form the Mali Empire, then you'll end up Catholic, because the Mali Empire is coded as Catholic in the game, even though Sokoto was a Sunni state.  No big deal, though; just edit your save, and change yourself back to the correct religion.
The game is no longer developed, so if you encounter any bugs, you'll have to either fix them yourself, or work around them (often using a combination of cheats and savegame editing).  It can be fun to edit the configs, though.
In fact, the game is so old now, that most mods are no longer developed.  So, I highly recommend playing the game with a mod from the beginning; that way, any tweaks you make to the game's files won't be lost when you inevitably do decide to use a mod.
Also, I've got it running perfectly in Wine.  In fact, once you've gotten it set up in Wine, you don't even need Steam to be installed, which is great.
It's a really good game. Probably in my top 5 games, A LOT of replayablity.

Paradox Interactive must be the masters of Strategy games. This is one of their finest. Victoria II is set in the Victorian Era in the 19th and early 20th century. From 1836 to 1936, you have 100 years to lead a nation to triumph. There are no official goals in the game. You make the goals. But the de-facto prospect is making a country into an economic or military superpower. Some nations like Great Britain are already big at the start, but playing a small nation like Greece can give you the opportunity to give it a time it never saw. That's right. You're not playing history. You're re-writing it. Every little thing you do in the game can have big, unintentional outcomes. Doing something in North America might somehow cause a war in Europe. You never know.
This is just how fun Victoria II is for history buffs. You can play unlikely countries and turn them into a colonial superpowers. I played Ireland and gave it African colonies. I claimed the island of Hawaii for Mexico, preventing the USA from annexing it in actual history. I played the Confederate States of America and fought hard for it's independence and giving it colonies around the world. There is just so much you can do. So many opportunities.
But while that sounds like a lot of fun, you're going to have to work hard to achieve your goals. This game has a huge learning curve. In fact, I was almost turned off by the game when playing it for the first time because of how complex it was. But learning is the fun part. I didn't spend a lot of time with the tutorial. I just played around and learned as played. Right now, I know how this game works. But I'm still learning. As I said before, you have to work hard. There's a lot of things to do when managing a country. Here are those things.
- You have to manage taxes and government spending. Some countries might have to rely on heavy taxing on the poor, middle and rich if the government lacks a lot of money in their bank. You might also have to cut down on military and infastructure spending to rake in cash. If you are in serious decline of money, you can borrow funds from the bank. But you will have to repay those debts. Some nations have the population and profits to not worry about funding. But other small nations will.
-Economy management. You might have to open factories to gain profits. Depending on your country's economic policy. You can open factories or let the AI capitalists do them for you. These factories needs craftsmen and whatever resources the factories need. And let's talk about that next.
-Resources. This is the fun part. Let's face it. Some nations don't have everything they need. A small country like Texas (which lacks a big population and resources) might have to go to war and conquer weaker nations to prosper. Colonies help boost the resources and pops you need.
-War. It's not the primary focus of the game, but it's a whole lot of fun. War is not the goal. War helps your goals. As mentioned before, you might need to start a war to conquer a nation/colony for more resources. Or you might go to war to establish a puppet-state which acts like a permanent alliance. Whatever suits your agenda, War can help you.
-Diplomacy. Okay, it's not really the intriguing part but politics and international relations is what makes things more interesting in Vic 2. If you want to survive, you might need to make a few friends when making more enemies.
- Technological advancement. You got a century to run a country and while years go by, new technologies will be available for you to develop. This is how a country will improve and become stronger. Military, Naval, Commerce, Culture and Industry are the 5 tech trees you can develop on the way. Culture, industry and Commerce might be important for nations that are just sitting around, but warmongers might like Military and Naval much more better. All 5 of the trees are important however, so don't try and pick the military ones only.
-Politics. Oh man, sometimes the hardest part of running the nation is how to deal with your citizens. If you're a democracy, people are gonna have vote for their favorite political party. And each political party that could be in power, will affect your nation. Hell, if you're population manages to vote the Communist Party in, you might accidently have caused your country to be a dictatorship. If you're not managing your country well, rebellions can happen and if you can't fight off the rebellions with your military, you might be running a new government soon. You can also make political and social reforms like voting policies or whether or not the minimum wage should be lower.
-Colonization. This is the best part of Victoria II. There are several uncolonized parts of the world. Not that they lack populations but that there are no established nations there. Australia & New Zealand are mostly uncolonized with the exception of a few provinces. But most likely, Britain will do inevitably colonize them. North America will be the only continent to be fully colonized quickly. There are unclaimed land that the United States, Mexico or Britain will grab before the 1850's. But the glory of colonization occurs in Africa. Most of the continent is unclaimed. There's only a few nations and small colonial settlements that exist.
-Modernization. Europe, in this time period has the technology that is top of the line. So most of the world is somewhat behind compared to Europe. So if you're playing a country in Africa or Asia, you will want to spend some time modernizing. Japan is the pretty much the only country in the game that modernizes so quickly. But not only that, you get to turn Japan into a colonial superpower faster than any other country that hasn't westernized.
While I did not mention everything, there is just so much you can do. Key historical events like the American Civil War can occur when the time is ready. You can also install mods that improve the gameplay experience. The New Nations Mod adds countries that the developers should have added before.
I definitely recommend Victoria II for anyone who is into strategy games and history in general.

First playthrough review:
Took about 5 hours.
+ The voice acting is generally pretty solid with one notable exception.
+ The music fits the scenes well, but there isn't much variety and it becomes repetitive.
+ The dialogue is generally entertaining, both dramatic and comedic. A tad juvenile for my tastes.
+/- No autosave. Manually save often or you'll regret it!
- The combat mechanics are easy to pick up, but extremely repetitive and often tedious.
- The story was lacking. It has a great premise, but didn't feel fleshed out. At the end I was left feeling like "Is that it?"
- There are 5 romanceable characters, but it didn't feel like there was enough time to interact with them and also prepare for the final battle at the end of the month.
A similar but better experience in my opinion is
.
The Long Version:
You have thirty days to prepare for an all out assault on the alien base. During each of those days you will have to chose how to spend your time, either by getting to know your squad better, or training for combat, or in fighting the aliens to earn money.
You need money to romance the ladies, but you also need money to upgrade your weapons and armor and use special abilities in combat. You only get money by fighting the aliens, and the difficulty ramps up fairly quickly even if you upgrade your weapons and armor. This is where things broke down for me.
Stronger weapons are very expensive, plus I wanted to spend my money to get to know the women in my squad, which meant that when I was in combat it was a miserable experience. Enemy lifebars ticked down slowly, and every time they healed themselves it made me want to rip my hair out.
I'd love to play this game again to get to know my squadmates better, because I think I missed out on a lot by spending my time training for the coming attack. The problem is, I don't think I can subject myself to the tedius combat for a second time. If I do come back to Just Deserts it will be a long time from now when I've forgotten just how painful it is.

Characters are lovely even when they're swearing. Also trying to min-max schedule in a limited 30-days timeframe gives moderate challenge and pressure, which is always a good thing. I think a casual gamer would easily top 15+ hours of gameplay from this.
One minor con factor are endings. I've checked 4 endings (harem ending not included, and they are all abrupt, short and not quite believable. One character's ending was merely a few lines of text that had next to 0 implications of characters' future. If you put high value to endings in dating genre, don't buy this game (or at least wait for 50% sale).

This game is not what is seems to be.
It claims to be a game about exploring and discovery with some RPG elements, it mentions being rogue-like.
What it really is another RNG fueled disaster where you're supposed to glean some kind of fun out of while every action you make burns down the world around you, none of your actions seem carry any consequence/reward of note, and you're flooded with pointlessly cruel and illogical events based on your 'sanity' - which is only recoverable very situationally, and often times at the cost of driving your expedition to insanity itself (through drugs, alcohol, and other ailments).
The 'point' is to find the 'golden pyramid' on each expedition - but there's no hint as to which direction one has to go from the start to find it, ultimately resulting the player ping-ponging from point of interest to point of interest - marked with an innovative '?' on a map hex - or seeking high ground to find more '?'s to bounce off of.
The greatest enemy you're fighting is 'sanity' - a pink bar which drops every time you move and increases only when you consume mind-altering substances (this seems very flawed to me) or sleep - which you're only allowed to do at villages or in random 'natural camp sites', unless you somehow managed to buy/find a tent (worth more than most 'gold' artifacts, yet still only provides barely more sanity than a jug of booze, and provides lovely event oppurtunities like 'this guy lost a photograph of his wife' or 'this person lost a charm bracelet' which, if failed [random dice roll], leads to more sanity loss and people getting upset, completely negating the rare item you just wasted).
Which leads us to the real flaw: there is no opportunity to restock the supplies that matter, and expedition size & inventory space is cripplingly restrictive.  Before you leave for each expedition, you can buy supplies, but they're all supplies which make movement easier, and given the limited space for supplies, I'd rather maintain my group's sanity.  But I cannot buy booze, tents, or any other sanity restoring substances/items while 'restocking' for the next expedition.
It's like 2 or 3 people made the game, working independently on different parts of the game to deliver on - but in the end none of them actually finished their part and they threw it all together with some RNG and called it "rogue-like", and now they want $15....

Cross of the Dutchman is an RPG about a true story but it unfortunately fell way short of my expectations. The game features a terribly lackluster combat system and is only carried forward by having a gripping story.
This combat system is one of the most boring I have ever seen in a game. You have 2 buttons to press. Left and right mouse button. Left does a standard attack and right does a power attack. The power attack can only be used when your stamina bar is charged to max. Apart from gaining a sword instead of your fist the combat doesn't change dramatically throughout the entire game. It basically consists of click, click, click, click, power attack, click click... and so on. No kind of innovation in that whatsoever.
There are a few things you can upgrade to make your combat slightly better. You basically have 3 upgrades that you can buy for both your fists and your sword. They each increase stamina, damage and range differently. They also give your attack a slightly different asthetic attack to it which I was unsure whether that actually made a difference. One problem I came across with this system is that it seems only your most recently purchased upgrade shows the asthetic animation. Which was annoying because the first upgrade I bought for my fist was the most expensive one. So I lost this after buying the previous upgrades later on. You can also buy a few health upgrades and stamina upgrades. These are the only purchasables and isn't enough to improve the combat system.
Dutchmans enemy variety doesn't help it either. Basicaly there are only 2 different enemies. These are an archer and a soldier. There are varients of each of these with differing amounts of armour. Though only have these 2 different enemies to fight gets boring really fast.
What would be nice for them to do with the combat system is to have combos. This instantly makes a games combat way more fun. It makes it actually require a bit of skill. Constant spam clicking isn't fun by anyones opinion I wouldn't have thought.
What about gameplay? Is there any other types of gameplay instead of combat? Well there is one other. You also have a stealth mode which happens a few times throughout the game. This involves you trying to avoid patrolling enemies and hide from them. They have lamps so you can clearly see the zone you have to stay out of. This adds a bit to the gameplay to get away from the boring combat.
The thing is though is the way in the which the game includes these different activities is just in a cycle. The basic cycle of the game is this: Go to an area to an area to fight an enemy, get ambushed, fight the enemies in the area you was going to, go to another area, get ambushed, fight enemies, sleep, do stealth mission in dark... repeat. Not much variety there. The biggest problem is that the areas you have to go to always seem to be the other side of the map to you.
So what exactly is it that redeems this game from a negative review into a positive? Well the only thing really is the story. Cross of the Dutchman is said to be based on a true story. It follows the story of a land where the towns are being taken over by saxons and they are putting horrible taxes and such on the people. They won't stand for this and the main character, Pier, decides to start a revolution to stop this. This is the basics of the story but within it there is a lot of twists and sadness. Each of the characters works together to build of the story and each of them have their own unique personality.
In itself this story might seem rather basic. What I really like about the story is the cutscenes. After an event instead of telling the rest of the story through dialog they use cutscenes. The beauty of this is how amazingly they are styled. I love it! A fantastic soundtrack plays in the background of these cutscenes.
The only other thing that impressed me with the game is the graphics. I do really love the cartoony style of the game. Everything seems to follow this art style and nothing is missed out from it.
Although I loved the story I had a bit of an issue with it. The ending seemed very abrupt. Just when I was getting into the story it just seemed to kind of end. The story is resolved a little in a custcene after it and then it just ends. I was literally sitting there at the end staring at the credits like "Is that it?". It only took me just over 3 hours to complete as well. I definitely expected a longer game that that.
I also had a few other small bugs. A few times I got stuck in areas. Most of the times it just took a bit of a wiggle of the mouse or attacking of the sword to get out. But once it required me to restart the game. These aren't common so it shouldn't be a big deal. The other problem I had was with chests. Chests are went to know when you've already opened them and not let you open the same chest again. However on one of the times booting up the game I noticed the game had forgotton this. So I found I could open all the chests i've already opened again. Effectively this made it so I could double my money.
Honestly I was very dissapointed with this release. The only thing that keeps me recommending the game instead of putting it as a negative seems to be a story. If only they could have put as much effort into the combat and actual gameplay as they did with that story then it would have been a great release. I would say the price point is quite reasonable though. £5.99 isn't too expensive.
Disclaimer: I was provided a free review key by the developer to make this review.

If I were to describe Only If in one sentence, I would say it's like Penumbra, Myst, Alice rolled up into a single adventure directed by the Coen Brothers. Cross of the Dutchman’s controls are relatively intuitive and simple and the game comes with full controller support. The mouse is used for everything and the left mouse button is used for both movement and attacking which is odd at first. You most hold down the mouse button over the enemy you wish to start attacking however should they move your attack will stop leading to clunky fights, mind you keys are rebindable which does help. Movement is better with the controller however there is one major drawback with the controller with the controls which is input speed which directly relates to the character animations. On a controller if your moving with the thumb stick, you cannot instantly attack instead you have to wait for Pier to come to a complete stop before the attack will initiate which often means getting hit by an enemy. It’s infuriating.
Pier has both a health and stamina bar and can must a basic attack combo that never changes as well as a powerful attack that uses up stamina. Pier will have access to hand to hand combat as well as the use of a 7ft sword. In historical text it was said that pier was so proficient with a great sword that he could decapitate several men in one swing.
In the first part of the game you don’t have access to the sword meaning that all combat is done via fist fighting. This coupled with multiple enemies dealing a heavy amount of damage leads you to kite enemies around the map while your health regenerates as there are no heath and stamina pickups. After some progress in the game you’ll not only gain access to your sword but several purchasable upgrades that will increase your health and stamina allowing you to take a lot more punishment before ducking out.
While the combat is passable and indeed sometimes fairly enjoyable, it’s so basic that it leaves me wondering how great it could have been with a couple of core design changes. The implementation of combos and a blocking mechanic would have work wonders for the combat. It would have given it depth, stopped it becoming repetitive and ultimately stopped the kiting issue. While Pier can change out his power up ability via purchasable upgrades it doesn’t change much in terms of the combat. The enemy variety in the game is also non existent with just melee fighters and arches in varying degrees of armor denoting health.
Triangle studios in the past have developed games for mobile devices and this clearly shows in their approach to cross of the Dutchman. In fact everything from the UI design to the combat reeks of touch screen friendly meaning a mobile port of this game is pretty much on the cards and while that’s all well and good for the developers, what it leaves PC gamers with is a husk of what the game could have been. Not to mention the game is incredibly short taking just about three hours to complete. In fact the game only really tells half of Pier’s story and just as things are heating up the game ends which was both a disappointment from a story perpective and a relief from a mechanical one.
At a 9 dollar price points it’s a difficult one to recommend simply because there just isn’t that much there. The game is not bad by any stretch but I don’t think it meets the standards it could have. I think that it will appeal to history buffs, younger teens and people who just need a quick hack and slash experience but other than that I cannot see many walking away completely satisfied from what the game has to offer.

Quite easily one of the best games I have ever played, it is truly a timeless masterpiece.
The premise is typical of Bethesda, you create your own character, customize it and escape from a prison, from there on you do what The Elder Scrolls does best, just live your life your own way, do the main quest, serve the Daedra, help folks out there, or be a nuisance to all, your options are only limited by essential characters not dying this time.
As a product of 2006, this game is known for not aging exactly gracefully, but the whacky dialogue, funny faces and weird bugs add to the charm this game infected me with when I was young, I'm still playing it as a 20 year old!
The factions this time can all be joined without consequence unlike earlier games, if you want to be a Dark Brotherhood leader while also helping the emperor light the Dragon Flame, feel free! There are no consequences outside of killing a few people, but you won't miss out on anything, and every faction has its own fun story to do, each one giving at least several hours to the experienced player, a new player will find many hours of fun, anger and reward for being a master thief, or a devoted necromancer killer.
The main story itself was well written, even includes figures like Patrick Stewart and Sean Bean, as well as other memorable voice actors (RIP Jauffrey, you had the best voice actor) It's your typical Bethesda story, start in a dark prison, rise to becoming a legendary and beloved hero, bringing salvaation from a destructive army, with Sean Bean right by your side.
I must also point out the DLC is a MUST to try, especially Shivering Isles, objectively the most clever and well done DLC to date, I would have to make a separate review just to go into detail with that, that's how big it is! But other DLC includes the infamous horse armor (Shadowmere didn't look bad in iron plates though) several house DLCs such as running a pirate crew, owning a castle, a wizard's tower in the far north or a vile lair made for the darkest citizens. Mehrunes' Razor is another great DLC, the largest dungeon in the game and your reward is a powerful blade that can kill in one hit, it's an amazing quest that really takes time, and worth your money, Knights of the Nine is the last one, and again a large, amazing story, it's tough though because you have to remain absolutely perfect to keep certain powers in check, you'll find out.
All in all I must give my favorite childhood game an 11/10, it's simply that good, despite it's age, it's a funny, timeless classic that won't be easily forgotten, especially how in recent years it's faced the meme effect, bringing more people to a game they will spend hundreds of hours on, you have to play this game at least once before you die, you will never, ever regret going through the first dungeon, all the way to the final battle.

This review is meant for any new player joining the fray of Crusader Kings but also contains some remarks about the future of the platform. Crusader Kings is a grand strategy game slash feudalism simulator focussing on dynasty mechanics and the intricacies of realm inheritance. In this simulation, thousands of feudal lords and overlords interact with each other, all with different personalities and different interests. Your goal: to make sure your dynasty survives the Middle Ages and becomes as powerful as possible. You do this by managing your vassals and your dynasty members (your main task) and waging war (your secondary task).
Want your dynasty to control the throne of France? Murder the king of France, marry his wife (which will make you king but will not give your dynasty a right to the throne) and finally get a son with the French wench who will have a right to wield the standard of Saint Denis! You'd rather want to stay a vassal of the king of France and coerce his royal highness into strengthening your interests? That's even more enjoyable! Keep up your levy strength, get a seat on his council and murder off anyone who opposes you. This more or less is what makes the game tick and also what makes it fun. Because every dynasty member has his strength and weaknesses, you are constantly battling the odds.
To put it simply. The game is loads of fun and extremely entertaining. It will take you definitely dozens of hours to learn and appreciate the complexity of the mechanics that are working underneath the hood of this magnificent feudalism simulator, but it is worth it. Power through it! PLEASE!
But what about the dozens of DLC that are available for this title, you might ask. Do I need them? The answer is "sort of". They make the game deeper and more enjoyable. Especially the ones that introduce more mechanics like the Early Middle Ages start, the Vikings expansion, the brotherhoods and the Way of Life mechanics.
But I would also like to make the point here that the "platform" format that Paradox Games, the developer and producer of the series, are using in almost all of their grand strategy games (CK2, EU4 and HOI4) is getting problematic. Ever more and more DLC's are piled on top of code that is getting dated and does not take advantage of new and better ways of simulation and calculation. Crusader Kings II came out in 2012. We are now almost in 2018.
It will be very hard for both Paradox and the players of Crusader Kings to switch over to a sequel. Players have invested hundreds of euro's/dollars in the old platform and will be anxious about starting with a new "empty" Crusader title. Paradox will want to maximize profit and squeeze every penny out of the old platform for as long as it can. The longer it goes on, the harder the switch to Crusader Kings III will be.My opinion? We need a platform switch now! We need a better and quicker simulation! We need a better UI. We need to bring Crusader kings into 2018 and 2019 as quickly as possible.

A superb game with excellent role play mechanics, a beautiful OST, and a lot of potential playstyles & strategies that are neither too forced upon you nor too complex to understand. Compared to Europa Universalis IV, this game is superior, and not just for the setting. EUIV to me always felt like playing catch-up due to the over-reliance on Ideas & Technology, and how the combat & ruler mechanics just felt completely out of your control due to the obscenely random nature. CK2 in contrast offers you much more control, letting you take responsibility if things go well or horribly. It also allows you to disable certain features & events you find distasteful, like the mongol invasion, aztec invasion (no you didn't read that wrong), plagues, and much more. Control & Strategy are really the key words here.
So why am I giving this a thumbs down?
Simple, you have to buy the game in parts. If you buy just the base game, no DLC, it will be objectively inferior, which makes sense in theory, but in practice, all the DLC would be able to buy you the base game around 6 times over, at £200, around $250, for the whole package, and there is zero indication that that's as high as they'll go. Even if we assume 1/4 of all the DLC is just e-books and ahistorical music that you do not need, that's still £150, £180 with the base game. However, if ye do decide to just purchase the base game with yer doubloons, there ARR other ways to get the DLC, me hearties, but I'm too much of a landlubber to tell ye where X marks the spot on yer map.

This game is definitely a gem. I'd love to see a revival or something, this game has a lot of character. The humor isn't even for me but I still find the game very charming. The weapons, perks, killstreaks, deathstreaks, etc are all very unique and fun. I'd play it more but not many people are playing it anymore. Any gamemode that isn't team deathmatch is pretty much empty for the most part, so I'd just stick to team deathmatch.
Progression though is similar to CoD. You level up and unlock things like playercards, skins, emblems, goofy outfits for your character, etc. It feels good to earn coins and unlock things for your own character. The gameplay itself is also solid and pretty smooth. The guns feel responsive and fun, and they all have their own things that make certain people attracted to them. Same with the perks and other things you can add to your loadouts.
Speaking of loadouts, it's definitely the best thing about the game. This game is technically a "hero" shooter. But here you make your own hero / villain type character and play as them. They have different body types that give you different stats. And like other team based hero shooters, while the game is about the objective, you can play whatever the hell you want. There is no "pick tank or i throw" here. Your character can be whatever you want them to be. You could roll around on skates and cheer up your team with a megaphone, dive bomb people, blow people up, freeze them, whip out a sword or shuriken and get to slicing, whatever the hell you want. I even made my own loadouts similar to standard hero shooter characters.
It's a lot of fun. Just watch out for higher level players though.

PC controls have been long since patched but the controller implementation is near perfect.

During the late 90’s/early 2000’s Humongous Entertainment released an absolutely fantastic stream of “edutainment” point and click adventures for children. These titles focus on a range of light academics including basic geography, basic to upper elementary level mathematics, logical thinking, critical thinking and puzzle solving, topped off with reinforcement of good manners and polite social etiquette. At the lower end of the age spectrum, they may require some adult supervision and supportive guidance, but there is no better series of games for a child’s first venture into PC gaming.
If I recall correctly, I didn’t get into Freddi Fish until I had already become fairly invested in Putt-Putt. Because of this, I don’t have the same nostalgic tie to the franchise. That being said, there are still scenes of this game that upon replaying, were as vivid in my mind as the day I first played them. The Missing Kelp Seeds was the first Freddi Fish game I played and I enjoyed it immensely. The change in scenery helped keep me engaged and also broadened my academic interests as a child.

Sound: 10/10 -- Game is fully voice acted in Japanese with a beautiful backing soundtrack. I don't mind that it's repetitive in nature, it's a studio-quality soundtrack. Atmospheric and easy on the ears.
Art: 8/10 -- I personally enjoy the blurry, hand-drawn look of the backgrounds for each scene, but I know not everybody would agree. Also the outfits on the boys take me to the lawlacaust.

Toma and Ukyo both felt out-of-touch for me, because their characters were a bit outlandish. Toma felt far more troubled than he let on and Ukyo had lost his ♥♥♥♥ing marbles. It's not often that you'll hear me, of all people, make a statement like this, but I genuinely feel bad that I got this game at such a high discount. I bought Amnesia when it was 90% off for the winter sale, and it's certainly one of the best visual novels I've ever played.
For one thing, this game is just incredibly well-made. Now, a good 90% of the visual novels I've played have been freeware ones I've found online across various forums. None of them have had particularly high production values or anything like that; at most they've feature a couple of CGs and a bonus scene or some questions answered by the creator about their game, but besides that they're pretty basic. To get a game with so many CGs, which are remarkably well-drawn and colored; voice acting; an awesome soundtrack (I may or may not have gotten about 60-65% of my playing hours for this game by just leaving it open while I did other stuff on my computer in different windows, just because I really liked the music); mini-games (albeit ones with rather poor controls in several cases, though that may be due to my mouse being particularly terrible);  and over 20 different endings is a completely new experience for me. It's been somewhat hard for me to go back to playing games without most of these nice features, or at least where these features aren't as well done as they are in Amnesia. I feel like I stole something by getting a game this nice for only three dollars.
But speaking of all of those endings I mentioned, let me discuss the actual routes and characters, since they make up a bulk of the game's experience. The routes are set in different alternate 'worlds', each of which is named after suits on playing cards. Please note that you should probably play the routes in the order they're listed as choices; I made the mistake of playing Toma's route first, since he was the only character I was curious about going in, and I can't help but feel like I would've enjoyed the game that much more if I had just chosen his route last. (In Shin's route, at least, things become a *lot* more predictable once you know the sort of stunts Toma's capable of pulling.) Each route has a good end, a normal end, and several bad ends. Note: there's 5 routes to play, not 4, but the fifth is only unlockable after you've done the others.
Now onto the characters themselves. For the most part, I thought all the romanceable guys were pretty likeable and well-portrayed. Not all of them strike me as 'boyfriend' material, but nonetheless, every one of them was quite interesting in his own right. While the guys are essentially stock otome love interests- we have a blunt tsundere with a heart of gold, a chivalrous playboy whose only *sincere* romantic interest is in you (the heroine), a logical and seemingly cold (but entirely adorkable) nerd, and a yandere willing to do anything to protect you- they're all either played to perfection or with an interesting twist on the usual 'type'.
My personal favorite character is Ikki, which says a lot, since I typically dislike the 'playboy' type (if I don't ignore them as an option altogether). But Ikki was sweet and had quite a bit more depth to his character than I was expecting, and several times I really wanted to hug him because I felt so badly for him. That said, I don't think I actually disliked any of the love interests, at least not in retrospect. Some of them made me very frustrated, and some of the routes were outright morally compromising (I'm looking at you, Toma), but they were really enjoyable overall. Hell, Toma's route was the first one I wanted to replay- I don't like him as a love interest, particularly, but he was damn entertaining.
And while I haven't said anything about Ukyo, he was a different sort of character than I've dealt with in any otome game before. I'm still not quite sure what to make of his route. I will once again offer a bit of advice and say this: DO NOT LOOK UP ANYTHING RELATED TO UKYO UNTIL YOU'VE PLAYED THROUGH HIS ROUTE AT LEAST ONCE. Once again, I made the mistake of spoiling the twist with him before I even unlocked his route, which took away a lot of his charm for me. Instead, playing through his route was something of a drag because I didn't have to piece together any of his cryptic statements or anything.
This whole review has turned into one long TL;DR, so I'll say this in conclusion: Amnesia was a thoroughly enjoyable game. Even the characters who I didn't particularly like as love interests were quite entertaining regardless, and this is certainly the most professional, well-presented otome game- or visual novel in general- that I've ever played. I probably would've liked it even more had I not spoiled some major aspects of the story for myself, but even given that, Amnesia totally won me over. I'd love to see more on Steam from Idea Factory in the future.

After around 160 hours of straight playing, Victoria 2 has been my favourite grand strategy game, I love it more than CK2, HOI3 and EU3. It's been very enjoyable, it has a lot of hidden mechanics, while not being as confusing as HOI3, or as bare bones as CK2. The game has a massive choice of countries, most of which you will be able to succeed with. Whether you are playing Japan or Bavaria, if you're good enough you will be able to play it. The game does have a few lag spikes, but that may just be the five year old or so computer I play it on.

The game has some glitches which can be annoying, but not a lot of them are game breaking. One rather annoying thing is the fact that once you install the expansion, everything is a bit less crazy. I play Paradox games for alternate history,  not to see a bunch of AI gobble up helpless Asiaa Minorites.
Still, after that, the game is still absolutely fantastic, and if you are a fan of Paradox Strategy games, you should already own this.

It's still a good game and if I would rate this game I would give it a 7.5/10, but as the devs still try to improve it and use aspects from the community, I wold say its more like a 8.5 or a 9/10 when its fully finished

Cross of the Dutchman is a historically accurate hack n' slash adventure where you play as Pier Gerlofs Donia; a 16th century hero that helped defend Fresia against Saxon invaders. Pier is also a huge bad♥♥♥♥♥and the best person ever.
It's a lighthearted and very accessible action game that gamers of all ages (Well, maybe not under 8?) would appreciate. With very light RPG elements like skill, health and stamina upgrades and mouse based click and kill combat you are able to enjoy the story instead of drowning in stats.
There are both straight up combat and stealthy missions as you run around the Frisian countryside. I liked the combat better.  NPC friends with join you as you fight Saxon swordsmen and archers. Combat isn't anything new but it performs very well aside from being a bit sluggish at times. Getting the sword is a big bonus! It's massive and feels authentic.
The length of the game is a tad on the short side (I beat it in under 5 hours) so don't expect a non-linear Skyrim experience. You'll progress through the story as scripted with a little free time to look for hidden treasure chests. Still, it is a great romp and I had a lot of fun playing through it!
Also, I hope you enjoy breaking crates and barrels.
Disclosure: I was provided a press copy of this game for review purposes. My opinions and endorsements are my own and I was not compensated any other way!

Pier Gerlofs Donia is a farmer living a quiet life with his family until, one fateful day, Saxon legions start making trouble in the nearby lands: Pier decides to take matters into his own hands and Cross of the Dutchman is an action adventure game letting us experience how this man turned into a folk hero.
An original setting, so far from the usual fantasy stuff one finds around, interesting story and good soundtrack are sadly paired with clunky combat, simple and linear quest design and underdeveloped characters.
-the historical setting is real, interesting and very original
-I appreciated how the devs went out to portray medieval Europe in a believable way as seen in the various building, clothes, armor etc..
-decent soundtrack turns great in the final chapters
-said final chapters (8 and 9) have a good momentum and feel suitably epic
-while nothing to write home about the graphics are decent, clean and work well enough: the cartoonish art during cutscenes is also likeable
-with such a rich setting and a folk hero to match I feel the game'd have benefitted from giving us more info on them: historical screens and collectibles- like those on Valiant Hearts- would have gone a long way into making us more invested in the game and character
-even for an action adventure game the character upgrades are very streamlined (2 stamina and health upgrades, 6 special moves divided between fists and sword): I personally find it too skimpy even for the genre but your mileage may vary depending on your taste
-combat is very simple and quite clunky, you have a basic spammable attack plus one (or more, if you buy them) special attack that uses stamina. It's a bit difficult to properly aim your blows and the fact Pier moves forward while attacking makes things even harder: there were a few times when I found myself punching air. A controller makes things somewhat easier though
-combat design per se is, once again, very simple since you don't have any sprint, dodge or parry buttons and are sometimes faced with quite many enemies that can surround you and quickly drop you if you're not careful. A good solution until you get a sword or upgrade your health is to use a special move, run away while your health recharges and do it over again but it isn't fun nor it feels epic: cutting down the number of enemies and/ or giving us more defensive options'd have helped
-stealth sections, while generally easy, add nothing to the game and lack any fun factor: it's also aggravating that, if one gets caught, you have to start over from scratch (in chapter 7 this meant replaying about 4 minutes stealthing through the previous areas again)
-UI is disappointing in some aspects as in it lacks a clear way to know when a special move is available again ( either a tick on the stamina bar or the ability glowing when ready'd have been great) and the special moves you can buy lack a description apart from some very vague bars regarding their stamina cost, range and damage
-the various characters, including Pier's family, are generally paper thin and little more than a portrait and some dialogue lines: since they have little background and we don't really have time to form an attachment to them during the game I sadly didn't really care much for their fate
-you only have 6 areas to explore (your farm, a couple of surrounding villages and the roads connecting them), they're quite small and tend to all look quite alike
-very linear with no extra quests and also short, I've finished it (opening about 3/4 of the secret chests) in less than three hours
Reviewing Cross of the Dutchman feels a bit weird since this'll be, at the time I'm writing, the only negative review it's getting: I want to point out this is NOT a bad game per se but, in the end, it just feels too generic and bland in its gameplay to warrant a recommendation. I know this isn't an AAA title and the price is low to match the fact, but there's no denying it'd have used either a better narrative or a more engaging and complex combat system to distinguish itself in a genre that's been done countless times before...as things stand the only thing making it stand out is its, admittedly good, setting but that's- imho- not enough.

I'm not going to try to write a "real" review for Freddi Fish and The Case of the Missing Kelp Seeds, because at this point it seems rather unnecessary. Originally released almost two decades ago as an easy, semi-edutainment children's adventure game, it was among the very first PC games I ever played and I still have quite a few fond memories of the numerous hours I spent trying to solve the mystery which now seems so utterly simple.
Flash forward to today and I'm once again joining Freddi and Luther, only this time I'm not playing in accompany with my three year old niece, who can barely use a mouse but found the colorful world of one of Humongous Entertainment's most enduring games utterly engrossing. I wouldn't have expected it to hold up in modern day, nor hold any interest for kids anymore, but to my surprise it became a great moment of uncle/niece bonding that has now renewed my fond memories of the game and added some new ones.
If you have no nostalgia for Freddi Fish and are just looking for a decent adventure game you probably won't get much out of the experience, but personally I was pleasantly surprised just how entertaining it still was for new and old audiences alike. I also discovered it was headed by Ron Gilbert of all people, a fun fact that just makes me love the game all the more.

Victoria II is a grand strategy game from Paradox Interactive, the same company that created Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, and Hearts of Iron. The game is easy to learn to play, but challenging to master. It features very complex inner-workings that can take a very long time to fully understand, but players willing to tackle the challnges this game brings will be entertained for hundreds of hours.
In a nutshell, Victoria II gives the player command of any country on earth in the century from 1836 to 1936. It is a game based on history, but it is not an historical simulation. Expect weird things to occur, like a communist revolution in Texas, a globe-spanning Greek Empire, or a fascist Brunei launching devastating wars of conquest in every continent.
The player's role in the game is to ensure their country's success or dominance. Like other Paradox games, you cannot "win" or "lose". There are no standardized goals, like "Conquer 50 provinces" or "Destroy Such-And-Such". Rather, you  do whatever you want to see your country and its population thrive (or collapse into total anarchy and civil war, if that's your thing). You can use any number of tools to see your country grow, from cajoling other states into joining your "sphere of influence", to forcing them in at the tip of your sword; from encouraging immigration to your lands, to conquering more populated lands; from building titanic industrial machines, to dispersing protesting strikers dragging down your titanic industrial machine. Warfare forms the core of the game, with economic and political concerns filling in the peacetime. You'll often find yourself invading other territories to secure access to an important resource your factories need, otherwise those factories will go out of business and uppity, hungry workers will insist on throwing your Absolutely-Monarchical♥♥♥♥♥out on the street to watch in the cold while they establish a Dictatorship of the Proletariat.
The game is intricate and difficult to master, but the online community will help you overcome most of the impediments. There is also still something of a modding community, impressive after 4 years. The existing mods are quite fun to play, greatly enhancing aspects of the game or setting it in different eras. All in all, 9/10.

I always felt that platforming games were the default genre of gaming. With games like these, it's easy to see why.

Super Ubie Island REMIX is a platformer made by Notion Games that was originally kickstarted in 2012 (as Super Ubi Island, but the name had to take the change because of Ubisoft).
You control a small cute alien that has crashed to a planet with classic biomes like forests, deserts, or tundras. Speaking of cute stuff, that's something the game deserves praise for - nice cutscenes (between zones) and overall sweet drawn graphics and good character animation (for a platformer). The successful presentation is also followed with funny sounds and fine soundtrack.
As for the gameplay talk, there isn't much innovation, developers followed the classic formula known since Super Mario World. Besides jumping and double-jumping, you can also glide which will be most frequently used, as level design is built a lot around it. Attacking NPCs is done by classic jumping on head. The controls are overall responsive without any lags, it was nice to play with Xbox 360 controller. (Though there are some bugs, as once I've seen webkit debug popup.)
There isn't an overwhelming amount levels and if you don't want to complete the game on 100%, don't expect many hours of playtime. Still, it'll depend on your skill, as even though the levels are short-ish, there aren't any checkpoints and since the first levels there are places that instantly kills you, making you starting the level from beginning (and losing collectable items from specific level).

I feel bad giving this a Thumbs Down. I really wanted to like it. I feel as if i SHOULD like it. I mean, it even has Aleister  Crowley and Lovecraft as playable characters. I should love it. But....i feel like it just barely misses the mark.
It's not necessarily a bad game, and I can definitely see it being beloved by a certain group of people. Your enjoyment will probably depend upon just how much you expect from it.
I honestly expected to enjoy this more than Renowned Explorers, which is the obvious point of comparison for CE. However, that did not end up being the case. This game is basically a crapshoot. There is (seemingly) no strategy or depth to the combat. In the early rounds, at least, you stand little to no chance in a fight against the wildlife. Unless you have a lot of companions, mayhaps... but you wont have many, because chances are that at least one person in your party has already gone crazy and started murdering everybody else by the time you even reach a fight.
Each of my playthroughs went the same way: trudge to a question mark, steal some loot/recruit some villagers, trudge towards a second question mark, get interrupted by a message that one of my crew had gone mad and murdered a villager, try to head back to ship to regain sanity, have a few more crew members murdered upon the way, eventually get attacked by an animal with no crew remaining because they all killed each other, die. (Although i did actually reach the temple twice, both times by myself because my entire crew had been killed. *shrug*)
I don't know, maybe i was missing something. But after a few runs, i didn't really have any interest in exploring it further.
Elements had already started repeating, i was already seeing the same places and events, after just 2 or 3 runs.
The emergent storylines can be fun/interesting. The characters that you can choose from are great. I actually like the graphics and the writing. But the gameplay itself ultimately ended up boring and frustrating me, and felt largely shallow.
I would recommend RE if you want a similarly themed game with some more depth, and with a more proactive role for the player. You have many more choices in combat, exploration and events are more interactive, and you feel as if youre playing a much more active role in the success or failure of your expedition.
Curious Expedition (in my opinion) is much more random, and you're basically at the mercy of the randomly generated environment.
If you would rather play a more casual game and just roll with the punches/dice and sort of just passively sit back and watch the expedition unfold, this may actually be a better choice (rather than RE). Otherwise, i would recommend RE.

Gotham City Imposters is easily one of the best multiplayer competitive shooters I have ever played. It's genuinely fun, and addictively so. Given it's free you should download and try it for yourself.
The strength of the game is the variety it offers for any playstyle. While games like Overwatch, TF2 etc. offer character classes for you to play that feel different from each other Gotham City allows you to build your own.
The game allows you to spec your character with a variety of options outside of the normal choice of guns most games offer - though the list of guns, and weapons is extensive (almost exhaustively so given all the mod configurations available for each weapon). In addition there are multiple 'gadgets' that vary the type of movement or ability you have ingame (gliding, skating, grappling, cloaking etc). You also select bonus abilities that act as buffs to your character ingame, a personality type that does the same, a side item (which can be offensive or defensive like a pipe bomb or armor plating), as well as a body type. The body types offer various degrees of health at a cost to your speed. All of these options combine together in your 'loadout' to offer a unique approach to how you want to play and move through the game.
The game's maps themselves are solidly balanced and without fault. They are just small enough to keep the action going but large enough, with enough idiosyncracies to provide sniping spots. The point being they accomodate both active and passive approaches to gameplay.
As for game modes the only populated mode is Team Deathmatch and hey if it's good enough for the new Doom to be primarily focused on that as its multiplayer mode then it can't be counted as much of a fault here. It would be nice if the game were more popular to allow the other modes some viability but Team Deathmatch is so much fun in itself I've never had any feeling of loss for the other modes.
You accrue experience by playing which enables you to unlock more weapons, mods, gadgets, body types, cosmetic items etc. There is really no reason to spend any money on this game unless you want some of the costume (cosmetic) items that are only available for purchase. Gameplay wise you will unlock whatever you want at a fairly quick rate. You should be able to play the game normally, find what you like and unlock it without feeling any sense of grind. What leveling grind there is exists purely for 'call sign' cards that appear whenever you kill an opposing player and cosmetic skins for your weapons.
The only downsides to the game are negligible and I can't say should dissuade anyone from playing it:

Crusader Kings II is my favourite Paradox Game at the moment. Not because I have the most playtime on it, that award goes to EU4, but because for some reason, CK2 just has a way better DLC model than any other paradox game.
Most DLC are focused, and you can exclude a lot of them on your first playthrough (notably: Sword of Islam, Sunset Invasion, Horselords, Sons of Abraham, The Republic, Rajas of India and The Old Gods), the game will not be as fleshed out, but you can manage just fine.
However, I must admit that to get the full experience, you need all the DLC. My advice would be to buy the cheap base-game, and then play with a mate who has all the DLC, since multiplayer lobbies always share DLC with the host. CK2 is an amazingly deep and fleshed out game mechanically when you have all the DLC, and it's amazing how it has evolved from an almost exclusively warfare based game, to a game where the intrigue and courtly shenanigans sometimes run so deep you lose track of it.
CK2 multiplayer is just generally a blast too, it's a shame that so few people play it compared to EU4.

Steam sorely needed another otome game made by a studio that's been in this business for years.  Since Steam's change in discount policy, Amnesia has been on sale for $3 after 90% discount.  That alone should be enough to invest at least 3 hours of your time in a guy you're interested in.
It's $3 worth of silly writing, romance, and good-looking guys.  Now... Reasons why $3 is worth your time...
1.  Character and CG art are done well.  The artist does a good enough job with mixing up different viewing angles of the scene, but the placement of hair or other parts of the characters makes the viewing angles of their faces look weird (i.e. their noses seem to disappear).  Similarly to CG viewing angles, it was a nice touch to have character sprites facing the player in order to convey a sense of direction.  Likewise, these additions add to some imagination that two characters are directly looking at each other.  There's also lip movement when characters talk so the player isn't staring at stiff mouths all the time.
2.  Plots for 4/5 guys are done well in the sense that it's not romance-focused, but more mystery-focused as the player pieces together what happened before the heroine lost her memories.  At the same time, the player has to take care to not max out the suspicion parameter lest that triggers bad endings or characters may take advantage of that.
3.  Each guy has a distinct archetype so the player can freely pick any to start.  Overall, Shin and Toma are the childhood friends (i.e. romantically aggressive and romantically a doormat, in that order); Ikki, Kent, and Ukyo (<- unlocked after playing the other 4) are the older guys roughly ages 21-26 (i.e. not-typical-playboy; stoic, logical guy; and aloof romanticist).
: Don't pick Toma's route (Diamond world) if you're not familiar with an archetype made popular with Mirai Nikki.
1.
.  A lot of people hate hearing Orion, and I agree in that Orion was the weakest link.  Although I appreciated Orion's hinting of how to respond to specific situations, his role as the heroine's voice and partner-in-crime was horrible.  The game's rated T for Teens, but Orion's regurgitation of really obvious information and constant attempts to get you to doubt everything were patronizing at best, and very insulting at worst to the average 13-19 yr old's reading and problem-solving skills (or am I giving teens too much credit?).  Furthermore, taking his advice seriously in Ikki's route(Spade) can get you the bad ending quickly.  Likewise, Orion forgot to remind the heroine to read her diary in Toma's route (Diamond) which would've saved a lot of headache.
2.  Beyond Orion, writing is
in Toma's route and a bit in Ikki's route.  Logic was missing and anyone who understood dramatic irony can piece together the mysteries quickly, which makes Orion's remarks even more irritating.  Overall, the heroine is written so then she only has more lines
.  Before she gets all of her memories back, she is practically silent except when picking dialogue choices.  I'm sure people don't stay silent all the time just because some memories are missing, especially if it's a survival issue of not letting others know they have amnesia.  Something to keep in mind is that the almost-silent heroine exists
(e.g. Persona 3 and 4's silent protagonists... except they had personalities too...).  While I wouldn't mind it in an otome game, this storytelling device was done poorly and if you want a voiced otome heroine, look to
.  The wording of the dialogue choices can be frustrating sometimes, because there are the obvious ones and the less obvious ones that boost the trust and affection parameters.
3.  A minor dislike in the backgrounds.  Although stylistic and doesn't clash with character art, the resolution was noticeably awful when zoomed in for the purpose of perspective.  Not only was the resolution bad, but the backgrounds don't look like they were manually drawn and look like filtered photos.
4.  Getting the air hockey achievement wouldn't be so bad if the devs just optimized the friggin' game.  The lag is intense and there has already been a major thread providing self-taught solutions to minimizing the lag so the mini-game can be tolerable.
For $3, you can't go wrong with purchasing this game if you're into the otome visual novel genre.  Just think of it as a discounted game that can provide you with a light story and some laughs along the way.  Be aware that this game was released a couple of years ago by the Japanese company, Otomate.  Why emphasize the "Japanese" part?  Because there are plenty of non-Japanese gamers who were instantly turned off by a silent heroine and some of the things the guys say (e.g. "Watch your surroundings full of guys oogling your bikini", "Don't you know it's dangerous to invite a guy to your room when living alone?", "I don't know if I can control my urges" etc) because part of the writing is influenced by Japanese storytelling targeted at Japanese women.

Victoria II is a grand strategy game from Paradox Interactive, the same company that created Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, and Hearts of Iron. The game is easy to learn to play, but challenging to master. It features very complex inner-workings that can take a very long time to fully understand, but players willing to tackle the challnges this game brings will be entertained for hundreds of hours.
In a nutshell, Victoria II gives the player command of any country on earth in the century from 1836 to 1936. It is a game based on history, but it is not an historical simulation. Expect weird things to occur, like a communist revolution in Texas, a globe-spanning Greek Empire, or a fascist Brunei launching devastating wars of conquest in every continent.
The player's role in the game is to ensure their country's success or dominance. Like other Paradox games, you cannot "win" or "lose". There are no standardized goals, like "Conquer 50 provinces" or "Destroy Such-And-Such". Rather, you  do whatever you want to see your country and its population thrive (or collapse into total anarchy and civil war, if that's your thing). You can use any number of tools to see your country grow, from cajoling other states into joining your "sphere of influence", to forcing them in at the tip of your sword; from encouraging immigration to your lands, to conquering more populated lands; from building titanic industrial machines, to dispersing protesting strikers dragging down your titanic industrial machine. Warfare forms the core of the game, with economic and political concerns filling in the peacetime. You'll often find yourself invading other territories to secure access to an important resource your factories need, otherwise those factories will go out of business and uppity, hungry workers will insist on throwing your Absolutely-Monarchical♥♥♥♥♥out on the street to watch in the cold while they establish a Dictatorship of the Proletariat.
The game is intricate and difficult to master, but the online community will help you overcome most of the impediments. There is also still something of a modding community, impressive after 4 years. The existing mods are quite fun to play, greatly enhancing aspects of the game or setting it in different eras. All in all, 9/10.

*This review is for the full collection.*
It's a slow and number-filled grand strategy game for the most patient of players with an interest in the time period (1836-1936). Same as other Paradox games, it's real-time but you'd be mad to play it without frequently pausing unless you already know what you're doing. Every Paradox game can be said to specialize in one aspect or another of grand strategy. Victoria II does politcs and technology best, but other aspects are generally well-done too.
The period is a time of great powers flexing their muscle across the globe, vying for influence, territory and resources, and not usually through war but through diplomatic influence, alliances and colonization. Great powers ingame have special mechanics that allow them to add lesser counties to their Sphere of influence, giving them first dibs on resources and safety from invasion. That's not to say other countries are not worth playing, but the couple dozen of countries that have potential to be GPs have more flavor to them and really have disproportionate power thanks to a variety of bonuses that GPs enjoy. Much of the dynamic of the game comes not from painting the map (which is harder to do than other Paradox games if you stick to the recommended level of Infamy) but rather from trying to overtake other countries in Prestige, Industrial Power and Military Power for that coveted GP status.
This is where the technology system helps even the odds for some countries, and it is good. Every technology has juicy bonuses as well as possible inventions (which have  a chance of occurring each month), which means that every tech brings big progress, giving you lots of freedom to focus on whatever playstyle you want, and making sure there is a great sense of progress all throughout the game. In fact, that sense of progress is done extremely well as different eras go by. You'll see armies and navies becoming faster, population increasing rapidly, industrialization progressing at an exponential rate, and battles becoming ever more bloody and longer, with an emphasis on defense. The scramble for Africa takes place in the 1870s and there's a couple of points where you will need to reorganize and rethink your army composition to account for the new nature of warfare, including new unit types.
The combat in Victoria II is comparable to Europa Universalis - armies face each other with a vanguard and rearguard each, with a variety of bonuses and maluses affecting how much they hurt each other every day. The armies here tend to be large and the combat attrition-based. You're expected to swap armies to and from the meat grinder to ensure that your army's Organization lasts longer than the enemy's. Early on you'll have to worry about supply limits but with technology this becomes less of an issue, as battles in rough terrain accomodate fewer soldiers at a time anyway. This is definitely a game where you want to pause every day or two on large wars. Civilized countries can conscript part of their poor population, making for even larger armies. But later in the game these are pretty much just cannon-fodder unless you have some professional support waiting for them to help them overcome enemy defenses when attacking.
The military AI of the enemy is actually somewhat competent. It'll at least know to avoid dubious battles, even when it outnumbers you but you have other advantages. It'll also use appropriate generals for what each army is doing (the generals have their own randomized bonuses). Still, the player's intellect is a force multiplier and you should be able to win any evenly-matched war. Specifically, the AI neglects to really rotate its reserves like a player would, and pull them back to be reinforced at the start of the month.
Your country's ruling party affects a variety of things, most notably the level of involvement you have in the economy. Monarchies can appoint whichever party they want, except unwashed radicals of course. Many factors will affect which parties your population supports, including events, the standard of living, and Militancy and Consciousness levels. Consciousness reflects how much your population will press for reforms, either political or social. This has the double-bladed effect of boosting your research over time, but leading to rebellions if you fail to pass popular reforms. Which just might happen if your Upper House is not as keen on reforms as the general populace. Still, some countries like Russia can pretty much remain a monarchy throughout the game if you make sure your people are content. Every GP and Secondary Power has a slightly different experience, which is strongly influenced by how you manage the country. Absolute monarchies are much more smooth-sailing overall, but usually come with low literacy. China, Japan and the USA stand out from the rest, each with its own challenges and potential.
There are many tradegoods, but trading and most of the economy usually work on autopilot, especially later in the game when in most types of government, capitalists are allowed a free hand in building up industries. Usually in not a very clever way as they will often just derp out and build a bunch of telephone factories that are just destined to close soon after. But it's the same for the AI countries, so hey. And if you want to micro everything yourself, you can go with State Capitalism or Central Planning policies, found at your local Reactionary, Socialist, Communist or Fascist party, and do everything yourself. At the expense of some efficiency, however. And lots of time, as you will have hundreds of factories by the late game. Still, the freedom is there and a whole different playstyle is available for those who want it.
The diplomacy is fairly standard for a grand-strategy game, there's nothing too outstanding here. You make alliances, with a Prestige hit if you refuse to join a defensive war. If relations are bad enough between two countries, you can fabricate a Casus Belli, but be prepared to take a likely Infamy hit. This is actually the main way of getting aggressive wars started. There are random events that will give you a Casus Belli for no Infamy, but these are pure chance. Take too much Infamy, and everyone gets to fight you for free. The interesting bit is Crises - when a region gets 'hot' enough due to the presence of a Liberation Movement or other cause, the Great Powers will take sides and, if no compromise is met, will go to war. These are major and will change the face of the map in a different way every time. Here, I just wish the same hotspots wouldn't get hot so often, like in one of my games, Greece kept sparking a crisis every year for a while, with few exceptions as it just got hot faster than anyplace else. Still, it's a great system for keeping things fresh and interesting for GPs especially.
So compared to other Paradox games, I would say it's more deterministic in that, short of some really gamey behavior, you're unlikely to paint the map the color of Peru or some other minor country. The focus is on GPs and SPs, expansionist warfare is rather limited except against uncivilized countries. You can only choose from two start dates - 1836 or 1861. The type of freedom and variety here is different from other Paradox games, it comes from the amount of control you have over politics and the economy, as well as how you meddle in world affairs. Instead of grabbing land from your civilized neighbors, you're supposed to humilate them, beat them down, leave them open to rebellion, take their allies away and in some cases fracture them into smaller nations.The game's timeframe is relatively short - though it still takes dozens of hours for a normal playthrough - but every game is guaranteed to be different thanks to the crisis system, rebels and other factors.
Allows you to live out your fantasy of being a ruthless imperialist.  10/10 would subjugate the godless Orients again.

When I explain this game to friends, I always call it the Otto von Bismark simulator. I think this is perhaps the best way to sum up the role of the player in this simulation of the period between 1836-1936.
In contrast with other titles from Paradox that people may have played, this game has a much lighter focus on war, and a far greater and deeper focus on internal politics and social movements than any other Paradox title. Detailed data on industry, demographics, trade, and government policies are all there to be manipulated for the advancement of the goals of your people, or alternatively, the goals of their ruler. The player truly is the arbiter between a ruler and his people, and decides the political outcome for any state in the whole wide world, by the end of the session. This makes up greatly for the notable fact that this is the shortest of true Paradox "grand campaign" games (since I don't consider Hearts of Iron to be one). The fact that only 100 years is playable is far outshone by the amount of activities to partake in as you play them.
Now, I should note, for players of newer Paradox titles (as I myself was when I picked up V2), that the war AI is quite inferior to that of the more recent titles (particularly the fantastic EU IV AI), and graphics are also much less immersive. However, in my opinion, the sheer volume of social and political management you have access to during "downtime" completely demolishes a sole reliance on good graphics and war gameplay. In fact, if you couple the fact that V2 is a fully developed game that is not undergoing constant mechanical reinvention and the fact that it does not suffer from the great DLC bloat of those newer titles, you, like me, might come to find that Victoria 2 is the greatest Paradox grand strategy title.
Highly recommended.

Super Ubie Island Remix is a cartoon-like platformer game that draws heavy inspiration from classic platformer games (think Mario, Sonic, etc). You control an alien who has crashed onto a planet after being attacked by an evil floating head. To fix your ship and get home you need to collect parts located at the end of each world. Each world has a short hub world that allows you to access all of the levels within.
The game handles very well with both keyboard and controller. I played through the first world with both and found the experience to be fairly comparable.
The strongest part of the game has to go to the soundtrack. This game is full of well produced music that fits it's aesthetic style very well. As you play the game you collect coins which can then later be exchanged for additional music tracks.
The game's art style is reminiscent of the bygone era of flash games. This would have been right at home on Newgrounds or Miniclip back in the day. Despite that this game certainly holds its own. It's quite a fun platformer and I've enjoyed my time with it so far.
Not too bad, def worth a small purchase gameplay and review video attached!
