Now, I'm updating my review after many more hours on the game that might be more helpful to those who are deciding to purchase it or not.
General Gist:
Amnesia: Memories is an otome game, meaning it is directed at a female audience, with the style of a dating sim. However, this is not your average VN because of its dynamic complex plot where a "spirit" named Orion bumps into you and you get the option to choose between worlds to enter and live. In addition, you remember nothing other than your name and are doing your best not to raise suspicions among co-workers and friends. Your family are who-knows-where.
Needless to say, you start each world with a different boyfriend and different realities or personas between characters. Take "Manager" for example, the guy changes his behavior between each world.
There is a hidden theme in the game (spade...clover...Diamond...Heart... and I'm not sure what was the fifth one they made represent the fifth / Ukyo )
Coming from Con Vs. Pros.
Pro:
-Somewhat unique storyline -- I mean you still have amnesia throughout all of it, but the boys have different backgrounds you will have to go through and learn about. (( (Slight spoiler) There is a yandere & someone with split psycho behavioral disorder amongst the five. ))
-Voiced -- Not everyday will you get a completely Japanese voiced Otome game for a reasonable price based on the quality of the game given.
-Beautiful Illustrations -- Many of us know that this is as high quality as it gets. / Hot as hell. / Even the simply backgrounds give a sense of professionalism
-Five Long Routes & multiple endings. It does have some replay value if you don't get the good ending on the first try, but if you are like me and after doing four rounds of Ukyo and not doing so hot, you'll have to rely on guides. It's impossible unless you have a million hours to spend crashing and burning. However, if you're also like me, I fear bad endings so it's been a tough ride. The endings are also satisfying to an extent. I mean, no one has babies or anything too drastic, but you do get a peek into their future. I highly recommend Kent because well, he's simply cute, but many tend to like Ikki or Shin (no matter how mysterious that guy is.) If you look at my hours now, which should surpass around a day's worth (I took breaks in between routes) , that is how long it'll take to finish four routes (depending if you don't get short bad endings) & by looking at the guide, it feels like I'm just going to constantly get spooked by Ukyo for an eternity. It has taken me about a night and evening to finish a route so I'd say about 5-7 hours per route on good ending, but it really depends on your speed. I like to immerse myself and understand the storyline before continuing panels so I might be one of the slower readers.
*Trading cards
*Cute CC's / Wallpapers
*Minigames
Con:
-Price I think the hardest choice for me was judging whether the price was worth it. As mentioned above, the quality states that is definitely worth it, but I bought it on a really high sale. I believe it is a definitely good buy.

I own 200 steam games but have never before written a review for a game that I liked, mainly because I'm lazy.
If I can be bothered to say this game is good, then you can be sure it is. The game is in the vein of FTL, and other party based roguelikes. You have a central character who starts with one of the game's many skills and a set of items choosen from one of the game's many items. In addition you will have a couple of starting followers. Each of the possible main characters has a skill, followers, and items that form a complementary set. The objective of the game is to survive 6 expeditions across the world in a race against a collection of AIs also choosen from the main character pool. As you work your way across the landscape in pursuit of the 'Golden Pyramid' each action either costs (or replenishes) your party's Sanity. Beware, if you run out of Sanity it shalln't be long before your party members go mad, desert, or even begin to kill each other (This can be hilarious).
The art to this game is the careful balancing of your limited inventory, each expedition you are forced to chose between the items that form the means of survival and the items that are coverted by the people back home which you need in order to gain both prestige and the cash that you absolutely need for the next expedition.
There are various routes to victory and I personally had heaps of fun with the trial and error acquistion of knowledge on how the means on how to play the game.
This game IS challenging, you can assemble a party based around rooting out culutral pieces from the temples of the land, around peaceful cooperation with the natives and trading your way to success, or, just plain bloodbathing your way to glory. I've won in each way. I'd say my success rate is 1/10 beaten runs, and on average I would get to the 3rd trek before giving up.
The game has several randomisation different mechanisms, each with many different options, such that it's almost impossible to repeat the exact same expedition twice, although you may begin to recognize each of the possible outcomes for each mechanism.
Overall the game is rewardingly difficult.
Finally, the soundtrack is amazeballs, I love it.
As far as negatives go, I'd say that the game has a couple of minor balance issues with some paths to victory being a little easier than others, although nothing is guaranteed. Really though, I'm struggling to come up with negatives. Read the haters for bad things, but overall, great game, love it.
Replaced my pack mule with a dinosaur which unlocked a new character who can command animals. Spent my next expedition goring enemies with a water buffalo. 10/10 would explore again.

Oblivion is rich in story and detail.
Before buying this game off steam, I have played tons of hours of other versions of Oblivon very thoroughly.
The characters are diverse and interesting to talk with, more books can be found around Cyrodil that expand the lore of Tamriel and further. Combat is smart and makes the player think which tactic to use when in combat.
All voiced dialogue is a plus, but there was a small variety of voice actors for such a large number of npcs.
The npcs personalities however are very eccentric and witty, which bring a lovely colorful flavor to the Elder Scrolls IV.
Oblivion brings similar elements that the former game Morrowind brought to the player which were very successful and have adapted these elements to better enhance the players game experience. With a ton of replayablity!
I give Oblivion a 9.5/10.
Overall The Elder Scrolls IV Oblivion was a piece of fine art in The Elder Scrolls series. There were a couple things Bethesda could have done better though, a bigger number of voice actors, a more lore friendly Cyrodil where there should have been a more diverse set of colovian cultures shown, to name a few. This is certainly one of my favorite Elder Scrolls games in the franchise. If you haven't played it before, you're really missing out!

Awesomenauts is a very fun MOBA game in the style of League of Legends or Dota, but with a twist: it's a side-scroller. This might seem a little weird, until you actually play the game. Everything is executed perfectly, and I can honestly say this is more fun than either of those games. The side-scrolling format works very well for this kind of game, and the lanes are vertical: you have to jump up and fall down through platforms to traverse the map. There is a "jungle" of sorts where you can kill creeps for health, which adds an interesting level of strategy as you jump away from threats, only to heal quickly by killing a couple of jungle mobs and jumping right back into the fray. I've only played this game for an hour or two so far, but I can tell this is going to be the perfect time-waster. The voice acting is hilarious, the graphics are superb, and everything about this game just flows perfectly. Definitely a must-play for any fans of the MOBA or fighting genres.

Basically, it's a mix between a simplified Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic.
You place one city per region, exploit and develop the region while expanding into neighbouring regions via the methods you know from Civ while building one or more heroes (skills and gear).
The good thing here, is that each of the "races" have very distinct units and capabilities as well as quest lines which feel much more complete than Civ's quests.
For example; one of the races doesn't consume food, but instead only purchase their citizens using dust (gold). Another race (insects) don't use any dimplomacy or diplomatic tech, but instead gain food for all units which die during combat.
I also like the fact that you can upgrade your units with the same gear you would give your heroes.
...I didn't care to play the tutorial, so I didn't notice this until at the end of my first game on classic difficulty(!)... which reminds me. If you're a Civ expert, then your second game in Endless Legend should be on one of the hardest difficulty settings, otherwise you'll probably never break a sweat.

In a busy field of 4x and strategic, turn-based games, Eternal Legend stands out. The user interface is functional once understood, but will take some getting used to. The art is gorgeous, and is reminiscent of the art of Moebius and other continental European sci-fi and fantasy. The aspect of the game that really sets it apart is the asymmetry of the factions. The game plays radically differently depending on the faction played. If you do dive in, take some time to get to know the game. When in doubt, look up the way the mechanics of the game work on the Internet. This is a complex, serious 4x strategy game, and requires some time to break the learning curve at moderate difficulties.

It's very rare that an overall good game is ruined by only one or two bad design choices, unfortunately that's the case here.
It becomes clear early in the game that, for some reason, the devs thought it would be fitting to lay out clear paths to walk which do nothing but start levels over, with seemingly arbitrary paths leading to level completion.  This creates frustration that is further exacerbated by long lead ups to those confusing paths.  The result is a trail and error system that is more punishing than rewarding;  And nothing is more annoying than having to play the same sequence multiple times over when you don't know what the devs intended for you to do.
I hate to give this game a bad review, because there is genuine quality here and it's all free.  However, when stumbling blocks turn into outright roadblocks of confusion, an entire game can be ruined in an instant, which what happens here unfortunately.

General Overview: You play as an amnesiac heroine thrown into a world with established relationships. It's up to you, with the help of a spirit called Orion to navigate and try not to get yourself thrown into the explosions of Bad Ends.
If you're expecting full-on fluff and all, this VN won't be for you. There're some fluffy moments, mixed with slight comedy but otherwise you're on the mystery/thriller/emotional rollercoaster train. This VN explores some dark elements in terms of human nature, as well as the struggles between doing what feels right and what doesn't, whether to follow your heart or your mind.
All the routes differ from one another, but overall there's actually a hidden connection between all of them which makes it all the more fascinating.

Special Tactics Online is a tactical/ strategy shooter with addictive gameplay.
This game now in Early Access, but in this stage its also can keep your mind for couple hours.
The gameplay is turn based you sent orders for your squad what contain a four member, after that when you end own turn your opponent do same. In a multiplayer the players have 50 second in each turn, in other modes time is not limited. In a game you can found five different classes, all has different features. You also can use in every round one type of booster (from four available) and you can use three different grenades types. At the moment game has 7 maps, but this amount will be grow up in the future. Also you can change a weapons of your squad members.  You can buy weapons, on the store, what you can earn playing, survival mode, and multiplayer.
Control is well solved, you can lean this enough fast with basic tactic elements in well complected tutorial.
Game have a three modes: campaign, survival and multiplayer. In a campaign you should try complete the current missions , the missions are various, for example your main objective can be a kill a target, save hostage etc.
In a survival mode, your objective is to defuse a bomb in so many rounds how you can and hit bigger points. In every round the enemies number grooving and they improve their tactic. Also if you complete extra challenge you can earn more points.
In a multiplayer you play with another player, in this mode one player main objective is to plant the bomb, in this time the other player should try defuse it.
The graphic is  well designed and looks good. Sounds are good, and music to. Game also have a leaderboards and replay saving feature.
So my verdict
+Deep tutorial
+Leaderboards
+Addictive gameplay
+Cross-Platform multiplayer
+Deep tactical system
+However its a Early Access, it have enough content right now
-At the moment is hard to find an opponent in multiplayer
-Only one game mode in multiplayer
-No steam achievements and trading cards
I think this game is very promising, its in Early Access, but from the start have enough content what in future be even more. The gameplay is interesting, can keep you mind for longer time. The biggest minus in the moment maybe that, game is less know, so in a multiplayer is very hard to find a opponent, but the developers today released the demo where a multiplayer is available, so this probably resolve the problem with active online players.

Mr.President! is a politically comedic Unity game based on the likeness of yours truly. The aim of the game is to defend "Ronald Rump" from terrorists, most commonly snipers, with a bulletproof bodyguard, the player. It should be known that it is also a Physics game involving thrown objects and "Ragdolling" yourself in order to clear specific tasks.
Each level serves as a "Scene" with Rump about to get killed and the bodyguard player spawning in a position. You must race and overcome obstacles in order to push Rump out of the way before he gets sniped, or falling into another form of death occasionally. The game spans 10 chapters each with 4-8 scenes in them. What I really like about each chapter is the different settings and themes they went for. You have areas like the Mexican Border, a meeting with a Putin counterpart (Named "Rutin"), and even a KKK rally.
Now for nitpicking, you can see the game appears rushed and/or buggy, as there are many things wrong with it. Especially when it comes to Physics games seeing how the physics tend to be pretty wonky at times. Also some of the level designs are pretty annoying, requiring precision and sometimes heavy luck. Perhaps the worst part of the game is one later scene from the Russia chapter. Another thing too is a performance issue. Even at lowest graphics settings, my laptop overheated until I realize I could set to Power Saver and play the game from there.
However, most of the frustration in the game is snubbed by the entertainment this game offers. In most cases you have something you find so hilarious that you don't mind resetting over and over just to see it again, or for me at least. I'm sure a few others will see it that way too.
There are also other minigames to go with it, but I haven't played them yet, as I only passed the full main game. I'm pretty sure it won't need any major explanation anyway.
Overall, the game is *just* okay. The concept is awesome, but half of gameplay isn't really. It would've been better if it was polished more and if the graphics issue was more optimized, but still, okay. 6/10

At first, Endless Legend looks like Civ 5 put into a fantasy world. While they have several things in common, mostly building an empire through diplomacy, conquest, and expansion, Endless Legend has several features that separates it from Civ 5.
First is how different each of the factions feel and how they are played. In Civ 5, the difference between playing different
factions generally boils down to small percentages. While these can drastically affect the game, you will mostly play the way everyone else does. In Endless Legend, each faction has its own distinctive traits as well as playstyles. One faction can force peace on other factions while another can teleport their units to cities. These differences become even more interesting as you start creating your own factions. In short, if you find yourself playing the Roving Clans after finishing a game with the Necrophages, you probably won't be using the same strategy.
Second is the winter season. Periodically, winter rolls around and generally makes the game harder. Exactly what it does varies from game to game, which can provide a whole new set of challenges with each individual game. It also adds a good bit of difficulty. In Civ 5, the only thing that usually keeps your armies at bay are mountains and other rough terrain. While rough terrain is also in Endless Legend, winter will drastically slow an army down and effectively make combat a fairly rare occurence during winters (at least until the mid to late game as you find ways to become immune to winter's effects). As the winters get longer, the game becomes more difficult, with the actions you take during the summer becoming much more important when the next winter rolls around.
Third is unit customization. In Civ 5, your units become better as you advance through the research tree and they are generally static throughout save for the upgrades they get when they level up. In Endless Legend, your units each have their own equipment set that you can customize to your liking. If you're looking to make your ranged unit zip across the map while hitting hard, you can give them the equipment they need to do that (after you research it, anyway). Unit customization also allows your army to adapt to the situation at hand. If you find that your army is equipped to handle flyers while the enemy sent in melee and ranged units, you can retrofit your army accordingly (provided they weren't killed off before you got the chance).
These are only a handful of the differences between Civ 5 and Endless Legend. Ultimately, if you're looking for a 4X game with some fresh ideas, you'll probably find it in Endless Legend.

The closest thing I've found to solving my Civilization and Age of Wonders cravings at the same time. Absolutely beautiful game, great empire building, and entertaining gameplay.
Pros:
+ The game looks incredible
+ Very fun empire building (none of the empire building aspects are terribly deep, but overall theres a lot of things which lends it depth).
+ Interesting array of units.
+ Resources and diplomacy are easy to understand.
+ Map is somewhat self ordering (its actually a challenge to find and place cities in optimal ways).
+ Quest system is interesting, and for the most part entertaining.
+ Game is very smooth and streamlined if you desire it to be.
+ Improvement system for units is interesting.
Cons:
+ Not a lot of unit diversity. You can recruit units from minor tribes, but in reality its somewhat of a letdown that each empires armies boils down to 3 different units. The game would really benefit from a larger roster of empire specific units (at least one for each type of role) or more units opening up when you recruit a minor faction (the haunts give both flying ghosts and infantry ghouls for example).
+ Combat is a mixed bag. It looks pretty, can be fun at times, and is relatively simple - but by and large is something I mostly skip over.
+ Hero trees are flat out boring.
Neutral:
+ Game sometimes feels like it plays itself at times. Its not a con, because you can always find ways to occupy yourself, but the feeling is still there.
Overall great game. Mostly a empire simulator to be honest.

I really wanted to like this game. A futuristic RPG about two warring nations who have populated a planet after being driven from the Earth. Sounds like a decent plot to base a game off of. So why did this game fail to entertain? There are a number of reasons which I think it just isn't up to snuff.
First off, lets talk about the main character. Ugh, Rick, is our typical angsty teenage boy trying to "find himself". He's always so depressed because people are always fighting but does he really do anything about it? No, he says he won't fight, but then doesn't want to disappoint his parents. Then he has this elder friend who asks him to fight, and he has this whole inner struggle that is just plainly boring to watch. He makes me long for the days of the silent protagonist. Do you remember Chrono from Chrono Trigger? Never said a word the ENTIRE game. Still had more personality than Rick.
Second would it be too much to add a RUN button? It might be one of the lesser annoyances of this game but I feel like if you're going to have me travel to the forest a half a dozen times the least the developer could have done was add a run feature. Instead I'm trudging through the same dungeon at a leisurely pace for the 10th time I'm sent there for something.
Third, the plot. I feel like this game wants to give that whole moral dilemma type of vibe with the dialogue. But it's constantly hammering this idea into you with long winded diatribes from Rick and Co. about who's side is right about the war. And as much as he seems to dislike his people for killing animals and whatnot he defends his nation every chance he gets. And to make matters worse is there's one flashback that the characters all seem to play every time they reminisce about the past. This flashback of ONE event happens literally half a dozen times. If you're going to use life defining moments in time use them sparingly for maximum effect. Not every time a character has some inner conflict. It loses it's effect if you're showing the same flashback scene several times in one section.
I could go on ad hominum about the things wrong with this game including the boring battle system. The one thing I appreciate is that it's just the first episode. I can't express how disappointed I'd be if this was supposed to be some 50 hr rpg in one shot. I probably won't bother with the second episode if it's going to be more of the same as the first.

Amensia memories is a great otome game thanks to the beautiful art, developed characters, decent voice acting, and the good writing. But more importantly, this game really shines as a whole. A lot of visual novels try just go with the different routes being unconnected so that you get a different experience with each, but not too much of a whole story. Amensia memories is able to provide the unique experience of multiple, separate routes while all braiding back together into a beautiful story.
The characters are also incredibly well done. While it is true your boys have this tendency to monologue at you, I rarely found myself wanting to skip through it. Often, I would say man, I wish there was a route for the girls in this game just because they too are well done and I would love to see more of them.
The final detail that makes Amesia Memories unique is the story telling is refreshing because of one lovable spirit. Orion takes the role of the narrator, guide, and friend so while the protagonist is not entirely robbed of her own voice and personality, it puts her on the back burner from having to forcibly describe every scenario and feeling. Often, visual novels get into an awkward form of story telling where the protagonist fails at "show, not tell" and painfully details every thought and feeling. Instead, we have Orion asking your opinion and formulating plans that show how the protagonist, and subsequently the player, feel about it.
You will laugh, you will cry, you will spend the night in a dog cage, and you will die plenty of times. It's a wild ride, but it really is worth it. I highly recommend finishing each possible ending to get the full extent of its value. Like I said, this visual novel is at its best as a whole, so if you pick it up, be prepared to devote some time to getting the big picture. It will be worth it.

This used to be one of my most favorite games of all time, and the only reason that's no longer the case is because I basically played it to death (the 132 hours recorded on Steam are only after I got a Steam key for the game and don't include the hours I put in before with my retail copy). Basically it’s exactly what it says on the tin; you pick a country and play through a very loosely-defined era (despite the game being called Victoria, the game ends well past the OTL ending of Queen Victoria’s rule) that includes a bit of the Texas Revolution, the American Civil War, the Scramble for Africa, the Great Game (though in mechanic only), and World War I. However, unlike this game’s predecessors Europa Universalis III and Hearts of Iron III, the focus isn’t as much on territorial conquest as it is on diplomatic intrigue and the economy. Speaking of the economy, this game has one of the most detailed economies in any strategy game, along with one of the most detailed population simulations in any strategy game (every third person in the world is represented in the game and the amount that their demands are fulfilled influences the likelihood of revolts happening in your country). Of course, learning how to utilize such complex systems requires a lot of time compared to other games, but that’s one of the draws of this game: you learn something new about its mechanics almost every time you play it. Many great mods for the game also exist, including the obligatory modern day mod as well as overhaul mods that add more historical events to the game. And of course there’s some “Dwarf Fortress-style” RNG-based fun to be had with this game, as with any other historical game that tends to get ahistorical very quickly once the computer-controlled countries decide to experiment with unusual decisions.
Obviously there are cons to this game as well. The biggest for a new buyer would have to be the game’s (and Paradox’s) DLC policy. In recent years, Paradox has become infamous for its DLC policy of shipping out small, frequent expansions alongside patches to the vanilla versions of the games that make it semi-mandatory to keep having to buy the new expansions to keep having a good time with the games. Since this policy began with Crusader Kings II which came out in 2012, one would think that Victoria II, which came out in 2010, would not have these DLC-related problems. Unfortunately, at the time when Victoria II came out Paradox had an
DLC policy where new patches for the game would only work with the latest expansions, so you’d have to get every expansion in order to have every bug fix. Thankfully, Victoria II only has two major expansions (“A House Divided” which adds an extra start date so that the player can jump into the American Civil War right away, and “Heart of Darkness” which revamps the mechanics for colonial expansion), so getting the mandatory whole experience isn’t too expensive, but be prepared to spend an additional 150% of the base game’s price to max out the expansions that you need to have the latest patches (which most of the mods will need to work). Another negative for the game is its age; the last update was the “unofficial” Christmas update in 2015. Some people will perceive this as a negative; a game that is no longer being updated no longer has the hype from the community in a lot of cases, and any new bugs would have to be worked around rather than being repaired in patches. However, people exhausted with Paradox’s current rapid-fire DLC policy might find a “dead” game like Victoria II more comfortable (which is definitely the case for me; I still play Europa Universalis III occasionally, but as of me writing this review I don’t have plans to get EUIV because of how frequently the game changes). I’ve heard that the multiplayer for this game is a bit more clunky than the post CK2 titles’, however I’ve never played multiplayer with any of the newer Paradox games, so I can’t say for sure.
Overall I’d recommend this game. People tired of EUIV’s frequent updates who still want the EUIV diplomatic shenanigans and colonization will find something here, people who want something more complex and deep than HOI4 will find something here, and newcomers to the grand strategy genre will definitely find something here like how I did when I picked this up as a rougher introduction to the genre. First, a warning: This game is NOTHING like DS1 or 2. Nothing at all. If you were expecting a party-based Diablolike, you won't find it. Obsidian took DS3 in a totally different direction. The random loot/mobs has been watered down, the control over your party's development has been watered down, your ability to control your party itself has been limited, and your progression and potential has been reworked into linear specialization of your basic skills.
When you get over the shock of realizing you're playing a game that's NOT really a DS title, you realize the game stands well on its own. It has a certain charm in the combat, the characters are credible and engaging, and the story is interesting. DS3 should be approached more like The Last Remnant and less like Diablo. Play it for the story and you won't be disappointed... even if the lack of character customization and the limited progression choices hamper replay value.
Worth checking out the demo before hitting the Buy button.

Taken on it's own merits the story is interesting, the playable characters are fun, and the combat handles well while keeping the fights difficult.
But do NOT expect Dungeon Siege 3 to be like 1 and 2. I am highly annoyed that this is a console port, and would be a great game if not for my expectation of what a Dungeon Siege title should be.
The multiplayer is more like Fable 2 than your typical dungeon crawler. You could even compare it to Hunter: The Reckoning or Marvel Ultimate Alliance. The biggest weakness here is really that the camera locks your team into a small area of movement on screen while enemies will spawn and attack outside of it. You need to move together, while still blocking and dodging, in order to engage targets.
It's no wonder why you only get the single player versions of DS1 and 2 when you buy this, LAN either of those 2 games and you will have a vastly improved multiplayer experience...

After playing this game for  quite some time, its time for me to update my review of it.
The graphics and evniroment in the game are very very nice, in fact so much so that I have logged in at times just to get screenshots to use as desktop wallpapers. If you have a machine capable of reliably running this at the hightest settings, do so, its amazing!
The gameplay is a mixed bag, there are issues like very low stamina and  lack of being able to swim for even a few feet or climb anything that put a lot of undue hardships on the player and kills what is otherwise a really nice immersion factor.
The search for better gear is a bit tedious too and could have been handled a bit better.
The actual hunting part of the game is quite enjoyable and is a nice mix of  fun and fear. The multiplayer modes are what you'd expect, PvP and PvE are both playable altho the hosting setup can be a bit buggy at times.
The dinosaurs models are all very nice, altho the developers seem to have a feather fetish, and put them on damn near everything.
The Dinosaur AI is.....well, OK at best and notably arfy at worst. At their best, the dinosaurs act like you would expect them to, nd its sometimes fun watching them from afar. I've seen a T-Rex seemingly following a heard of Trikes, and watched Utah raptors interacting with each other in a manner that seemed realistc. I would LOVE to see some actual dinosaur on dinosaur predation though, that would add immensly to the gameplay.
On the other paw though, the dinosaurs seem to have senses and abilities that defy physics at times, able to climb terrain that they should not be able too, and detect things that they simply should not be able too see/smell/hear at times and be totaly blind to things they should be able to see/smell/hear at others. An animal the size of the quetzalcoatlus (as modeled ingame) should not be able to fly with a man sized object in its claws.
They also have supernatural stamina, unlike the player, and can and will run clean across the damn island when wounded. Any animal that bleeds out to a noted point of say below 20% health should not be able to run for any notable distance....EVER!
On the whole its still a fun game to play but the asking price is way too high. this is at best, a $20.00 us dollar game. Get it on sale, or part of a bundle and then its worth it.
I would reccomend it conditionally, get it on sale, just don't pay full price for it.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

I have played The Elder Scrolls series since the first game released years ago.
The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion was by far my favorite one.
It has an immersive combat type, with magic, archery, and melee for those who like to choose between the combat triangle or even master the combat triangle as a whole.
There are many types of weapons you can use for each combat type, with many types of armor to choose from. The skills that are available are unlike The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, where each skill level up factors into your level, but instead you choose 7 major skills that your character will use through their lifetime and each level up in those major skills factors your level. There are also character statistics that are much like Bethsda's Fallout series, where each one has a different effect.
The story itself is interesting, though you can kind of call it short-lived. The side-stories are immersive and have deep lore to them - people who enjoy learning about the history of Tamriel will enjoy playing through each side-story and listening to every word that every NPC has to say.
Gameplay 8/10

Visuals 7/10
Diversity 10/10
I definitely recommend this game to anyone who loves an RPG based game.

The point is the writing just feels fresher here than Skyrim overall,  I think after I finish with this I will check out what all the hub-bub about Morrowind is all about.

You know those fun little european resource/exploration board games? Well imagine if one of those magically became a video game, and a good one to boot. That's Curious Expidition.
It's an exploration game where you go to visit a foreign land in search of riches and adventure, while at the same time competing with other explorers for fame. First place gets a golden statue made for them in their honor (and a golden border around that explorer in the character select screen). It's a blast to play, and they did a really good job at making almost every single decision important. Do you rest at a spring or push forward? should you attack that pack of velociraptors or sneak by? Do you go to the desert or the jungle? The game really gives you liberty on how you would act in each scenario, but it's not as oppresive as games like say Darkest Dungeon.
I have been playing this game since around beta 21. It has hands down the best developer involvement I have ever seen in a video game. That is not an exaggeration. They promised to ship an update every month, and sure enough every singe month they have either updated the game, or provided an explination for the delay. Every update they upload a video explaining the changes and hint at the content to come.
They really listen to the community too. In the earlier versions, you could talk with slave camps but not attack them. Many people that played the game asked for that to be a feature. Sure enough, as of now you can attack slave camps. It means so much to see such dedication to a project.
Next time you see this game on a sale, I highly reccomend picking it up.

Ok so first I'd like to tell you that my number of hours played are a bit lying, since I bought this game a few days ago, and I litteraly spent my whole weekend playing this game when it was free on Internet.
So first, I wanna give you what I think of positive in this game. I'll begin with the play life of this game, and you have to know that it is barely infinite : you can already replay this game as much as you want, and even if the expeditions are "limited" to 6 per save (which means you end the game after 6 trips, with leaderboards and everything) you can play again when you feel like it ! Everything changes and is set back to 0, so you are totally free to do what you want.
Then, the randomness of this game makes it very interesting. Indeed, since every land you visit is generated randomly at the beginning of each trip, there is no chance that you play twice on a similar land.
Also, the diversity of territories available makes the choice of the destination at the start difficult : even though you don't have the choice before your first trip, you will soon be able to judge by yourself which land you feel like exploring, weighting the pros and the cons of each : do I really feel like taking 60 waters because I'm going to the desert just to avoid the burried pyramid's land ? The choice is, in fact, crucial even before you have arrived at your exploration site. And I'm not talking about the huge amount of "grounds" there are, between the forests, the deserts, the mountains, the hills, the lakes, the swamps...
This leads me to my third point : the free and total gestion of your equipment, your expedition members, your standing (how well the natives consider you), your path, your time... You are litteraly able to influence your trip not only in the good way, but also in the bad one : you can decide randomly to dismiss all your followers and to drop everything you have. This makes the game interesting, especially if one of your follower dies or if you dismiss him. Your relations with the natives are an important point too in the gestion of your trip : do I really wanna steal this idol in the middle of the village, risking a fight if I get caught ? What happened if I steal those gifts to their gods ? The villages are so important in this game you better give everything you have just to make sure you will be able to sleep in every village you reach. The inventory is a crucial aspect of the game too : the choice of the equipment you leave at the ship, what you wanna buy before leaving, what you wanna trade with natives or traders, what you will need for sure and what you can drop. The path you wanna take is then not only given by the relief, but also by what you can use to reach certain areas, and by the animals that can attack you. Because yes, the combat aspect of this game is interesting too; knowing that your followers are really low on health will make you doubt about whether you can try to run in front of those tigers, gorillas, panthers, raptors (yes there are raptors in this game :D )... Personally I really like how the combat are set up : you have your dices, which give the ability you can use (shield, escape, attack, ...) and you can use them as you want, which makes it essential to understand the combat mode.
To get back to the randomness, I have consciously avoided the true enemy in this game : the sanity. Basically every move you do costs you some sanity, which represent the state of mind of your followers and yourself. It is EXTREMELY IMPORTANT to manage to use your sanity well : let it reach 0 and watch your followers getting paranoia, claustrophobia, cannibalism, disappear... How many times did I watch powerless my followers dying one after the other because a f*cking expedition member discovered the great taste of human flesh ? Of course, you can gain sanity, by different ways : resting in waterfalls or under a rock if you are lucky, sleeping in a village, or using alcohol or coke leaves at last chance, praying none of your followers will turned alcoholic or drug addict. This sanity bar will soon become your worst nightmare, forcing you to come back after 20 days to the ship to sleep freely and surely.
And this will be my last point : the feelings I have playing this game. I'm pretty sure I had never prayed to find something useful as much in any other games I played as in this one. Simply because everything relies on luck, randomness and the choices you're making all the way long from the beginning to the end, this game will surely makes you sweat more than a horror game, or a 20 kilometers run. This game is not only allowing you to play a story, you are litteraly writing your story, and this is the best aspect of it.
To sum it up (sorry I love to write a lot about things I love) :
PROS :
-great duration of life
-very interesting and unique
-total control of your expedition, inventory, followers, and so on
-22$ is a very good price
-makes you feel the story
-many ways to finish the game and the expeditions
CONS :
-luck is an important factor
-very "precise" type of game, not any similar ones (FTL, Minecraft, 80 days)
-Tim Timster always turns into a cannibal D:
CONCLUSION
Buy this game, it is 10 times worth his price, very interesting and fun game to play, with free control over your gameplay.

A game of exploration, equiping your party, hiring people, finding lost temples, trading with natives/traders/slavers.  At the end of an adventure choosing to sell the goods or donate them for fame.  Walking takes sanity points, which can be replenished by rest locations of consumables - but run out of sanity points and people in the party may act in odd ways.
When you get in combat, you have dice to roll and different characters offer different dice.  You put dice together to make attack or defence combos.
I was initially a bit nervous about the graphics looking rather basic, but the interesting story text and strategy helps you forget about the graphics issue.
A key positive point about this game is the many ways you can choose to play - focusing on combat and hunting animals, focusing on trade skills, focus on science comes with later characters unlocked I guess (by some unusuable science items on sale) etc.  It feels like the game gives you a fair amount of freedom.
A very enjoyable game - and the developer has said although it's approaching launch that they will add more content.
I like the way you can unlock new characters as you play the game, but I would have preferred a much greater focus on unlocks to keep my motivation.
The current game is a system of playing 6 maps to try for the best score.  I would prefer if it was just 1 map per game, but that you can spend your fame/money points on permanent upgrades for characters or unlocking new characters - and playing harder maps allows you to shop for different permanent upgrades or unlocks.  A bit like Lost Castle / Rogue Legacy systems.  As your explorer gets more powerful you can penetrate further into the map and get more points for buying increasingly expensive unlocks.  Then unlocking a new character you are back to being quite weak but with interesting new future options.  For me this would be a lot more addictive and satisfying.  I hope the developer can notice this comment and consider adding it as an additional separate game mode.

Gifted this out of the blue, I wasn't exactly sure what to expect. What I got though was very pleasant.
This is casual at its purest form for me. I hardly even think about winning, I find it more of a platform to socialize with friends than a raw, gameplay experience, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
There is a disappointing amount of content gated behind paywalls and timesinks, but as somebody who purchased a couple of character packs (granted, this is primarily because I received the game for free) I suppose I can't really criticize too heavily in that regard. It's hard to show somebody this game in good faith knowing how much of it is unavailable to them from the get-go, but I think that presented as a cute board game meant to pass the time a la Candyland or Chutes and Ladders, it retains much of its charm.
Speaking of which, the game is adorable. Wonderfully sweet pastel art stretches from corner to corner, and the music, voice acting, and sound design all contribute seamlessly to the bubbly atmosphere. With so much to offer aesthetically, it only makes me wish even more that the brunt of its content were more easily accessible. If I'm to understand correctly, this game is sort of the "crossover" of the companies' many other games, with characters being drawn from other products of theirs. I suppose that makes this a compliment to each of those games more than this one specifically, but the designs of each of them are really great and there is no doubt that a lot of creative love went into crafting each aspect of this experience on a production level.
While the paper thin gameplay will not attract anybody looking to get serious with this game, the production qualities of this game and its casual appeal make it something that is certainly worth a look. Unfortunately, just like that shiny new pair of shoes, it may lose some of its luster when the price tag is flipped over. Even still, I find myself
leaning towards recommending it, if only because I think it offers a uniquely therapeautic gameplay experience that is difficult to come across within the medium.

This game is very enjoyable! It's basically a 4x-strategy game like Sid Meier's Civilization franchise but set in a fantasy world. I also believe "the story" is a prequel of sorts to this games predecessor: Endless Space - which is worth picking up aswell if your into the whole space thing. Overall however I like Endless Legend more.
It is a very enjoyable game with what I think is one of the best user interfaces to date. It's just so clean - every game should have this. Unlike Civ where you can build cities everywhere and are technically not limited (well only through the map size) to have as many cities as you want, you are here limited to one city per region, which I think is a good thing. Since you can expand your cities later on, you'll think twice on where to put them strategically - especially since there are height differences on the map providing bonuses and maluses in fights.
The battles are enjoyable although the animations can get quite repetitive. However unlike the newer Civs you do have multiple units in one army. Going into battle on the battlefield you'll fight on several tiles which are part of the region your fighting in - overall I think fighting is better done than in the newer Civs.
The factions you are able to play (and play against) are all very unique and will extremely affect your playstyle and strategy since every faction has it's own backstory (and story/questline!) and special mechanic. The replayability value is huge here since your way of playing will also be affected by the ennemy you are fighting (different armies, with different equipment for different ennemies).
TL;DR:
pros:
- UI
- unique factions
- replayability
- interesting economy with different ressources and types of ressources (for equipping your armies and providing stat bonuses to your empire)
cons:
- one annoying reappearing bug, where i'll have to reload the last turn or it would break my savegame file - might very well have been fixed by now
I feel like I'm in a new world in this game, the music and gameplay just blend very well for me.

First off, I do like the artistic side of the game and the story line is a more new one to me so it was good to feel like you are engaging in some new. But the game itself kinda ruined that with the playability of it. There was numerous things that I didn't like:
1st: Event processing. Half the time I wanted to explore the map after an event, but then its like, "nope, teleport back to town".
2nd: The level system & Equipment. Played for 2 hours, am level 20's, and have not gotten any new weapons or armor (I bought the tunic and bandana at the start). The only weapon that is of use costs 15000$ and you will never be able to afford that for quite some time. I had like 6k or so when I stopped. There is no "cool new weapons or armors", your strength is only from leveling up, so you never feel like you are actually becoming powerful. It feels more gringfest then anythhing else.
3rd: Skills. Super unoriginal skills. Each person has their own keyword for their skill (as far as I got there was God, Metal, and Angel). So for example your first couple skills for the main character is "God Sword, God Focus, God Blast". Also with that, everyone has the same skills. Each person has a heal, a KI restore, and a Power attack. Since everyone's health and KI grows at the same rate and everyone basically has the same skills it feels like all the party members are the same. It's like playing with duplicates of the main character.
4th: There were some holes in the story as well. The biggest one for me is the part where you have to go recieve a canister and then you have to go get a special KI crystal to trade (which was a huge pain to walk back and forth with). The leader tells you that he will pass you for the graduation exam for doing it and you don't have to kill any KI creatures. This is where the problem happens with story. It is basically nearly impossible to avoid enemies. They have sporadic pathing and some are really fast. So you know, you kill like 100 KI creatures with the amount of traveling you have to do. I tried avoiding them at first thinking that if you killed one it might affect the story, but nope, apparenlty you can just slaughter them all, and still be crying about how you are trying to be peaceful and not kill them.
5th: Health & Items: Basically you only level up to face the bosses. All enemies once you level up enough you will be able to 2 hit them with normal attacks only. They only deal 20-30 (this is being level 20 range) damage and you have 1106 health. You want to just ignore them all, but then its like, "oh this boss might actually kill me because he deals 200" You basically gring to fight bosses. You also collect KI crystals to use to restore health and what not. They heal by 10% 25% and 100%, (from what I have seen) and you get an abundance of them. I do a long sidequest and he is like here is 3 10% health crystals. With your health pool and how fast you level up, your health will never get low enough to actually start using them. All they do is just sit in your inventory.
So all in all with story and artwork I would give it a 4/10.

When push comes to shove, It's nothing that special. If you like otome games and gorgeous art, you’ll enjoy this game. The translation has its flaws, but it’s much better than most of the otome games you can buy on mobile nowadays. It’s also less expensive, since you don’t have to spend $2.99 to buy each chapter. If you want to play this game but have no prior knowledge of visual novels, I would definitely recommend playing some low-key, less intense games before buying this one. I can’t imagine going into this game without being familiar with anime tropes and the culture behind its gameplay, since some of the characters and places can come off as odd or unsettling. The key is to not overthink the story flaws (even though they’re in abundance) and just play it for the romance routes. Pros:
1. Endless Legend is gorgeous to look at, plain and simple. From the terrain to various info and quest pages, it all looks great. A lot of care went into making this game look good.
2. There is more to a good 4X than killing the other guy, and Endless Legend delivers with complex Empire Management. From tweaking production, to long term tech planning, you can control in detail more than just where your armies are going.
3. Usually, combat tends to be a chore, but no with Endless Legend. With Auto-Resolve for the "easy" battles, you can focus on the important ones instead. The Tactical battle is a hybrid of Disciples and Age of Wonders, where you control your troops, but not everything they do. Also, new techs allow you to upgrade your armies with better equipment, and you can pick different bonuses as well, but all of it done in a non-time consuming way.
4. Factions do not just look different, but they actually feel different, and not in just subtle ways. At the same time, they feel balanced against one another, so every game never feels like one faction will always win. This extends to victory conditions, as each faction features their own unique quest line for victory!
Cons:
1. The A.I. can be a bit bi-polar sometimes, but it is by no means stupid (usually). The A.I. can and will kick your sorry hide if you let it, so for those looking for a single player only experience, you will find the A.I. to be more challenging than the A.I. in Civilization (which I have hundreds of hours in, including Deity wins).
2. Digging for information can be a minor chore, as some things are not really well explained, or obviously laid out. However, there is a lot of information and guides done by the community that are readily accessible to help you out.
Summary:
I strongly recommend Endless Legend to anyone that is a 4X fan looking for their next fix. I play both Multi-player and Single-player, so this will easily continue to be one of the games I will be pouring many hours into. It takes all of what makes a good classic 4X strategy, and adds in some refreshing twists that will not disappoint.
tl;dr If you are familiar with losing an hour or more when you said "just one more turn", then Endless Legend will not be kind to your sleep habits!

Endless Legend is a nice take on the 4X genre, and I could summarize it as the child of the Civilization and Age of Wonders series. It's focused on tech research and city building and administration like Civilization but still has the very interesting tactical aspect of combat of AoW; moreover, you still have the possibility to upgrade your current units and heroes with the latest weapons, armor and artifacts you have researched -- a bit like what you can do in Stardock's Fallen Enchantress or in the classic Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.
A novel aspect of EL with respect of all the games I've mentioned is that the game map is divided into regions and each region can host upto one town only; this makes things a bit more interesting as the town has to be placed strategically in accordance with which resources the single region has to offer.
The graphics style is really appealing to me, and the music (that you get also in MP3 format bundled with the game download for free) really nails the mood and tempo of the game.
The only bad thing that I can say about EL is that the AI isn't very challenging at all; sometimes it could just stay idle in its initial territory for the most part of the match -- that's what happened to the Mezari in my first ever game. If this one issue is fixed, EL can become a true classic gem of the genre.
My vote: 8.5/10

I've owned this game for quite a while now, and have almost all the DLCs except for Reaper's Due and Jade Dragon. Being a fan of RTS and grand strategy games, I got hooked up on CK2 fast, by the end of my first session I was already craving for more. Why? Well, the RNG aspect of the game creates some quite funny situations (and a few infuriating ones), the balance between the micro and the macro is good, you don't need to keep rushing back to check on your demesne during a war, and in times of peace you can develop your country without too many interruptions. But the part that really caught me were the mods. The modding community has created an astounding amount of content, creating new experiences every time. Every gameplay is different, even if you start with the same character over and over. The bad side is: amount and price of DLCs. Before TRD and MNM every DLC was split into 2 or 3 different packs, which then had to be purchased to fully enable it. Paradox has remedied it somewhat, but the DLCs are still quite pricey and are best acquired during sales. You can play without any expansions, but to have the best experience you need quite a few.

This is THE BEST GAME I have played in years. It is a unique specimen, clearly influenced by such early games as The Oregon Trail, and very heavilly influenced by the Roguelikes of old. It has an incredible depth of gameplay, uniquely implimented and engaging, and a strong sense of atmosphere and narrative. After staying up all night playing this game the first night I purchased it, I sat back and pondered the adventure my party had had, and although the narrative was one essentially driven by my decisions, rather than by any pre-written storyline, it felt worthy of any film or novel. And even though my four hour session had ended ultimately in disaster, with my party running out of supplies in the depths of the jungle, slowly losing our minds and dying off one by one in varied and disturbing ways, I felt very satisfied, as if I had just read a very good but tragic novel.
Yes, it is quite difficult at times, but it is not the rage-quit worthy, seizure inducing difficulty that comes with twitch reflex games such as Volgarr the Viking, or the early Mega Man games. Every expedition, whether successful or horrificly failed, will have a unique story to tell, and you will learn valuable skills as a player that allow you to progress that much farther the next time you play, as any Roguelike should. DO NOT PASS THIS GAME UP. You will be missing something very special. **also, at the time of writing this is in early access, but I would never have known this if not for it being displayed on the game's steam page. It is deep, bug-free as far as I have seen, and exceptionally replayable.

TLDR: I really love this game, it's probably one of my all time tops.
Curious Expedition is a seemingly simple take on a seemingly common genre: a survival exploration game with 2D pixel art. But as much as that sounds horrible and generic and flavor of the month, it's not at all.
There is a quote on the store page from a Rock Paper Shotgun article, that the game already has a lot to offer the player, even as an Early Access title. That's true, but that quote is from 2014 and currently
.
Curious Expedition's first great success is that it's actually an *exploration* game. So many games featuring exploring are all about clicking nodes or collecting some sort of points or resources or whatever. Curious Expedition pushes you to explore, punishes you for exploring poorly and rewards you for exploring well. You also will want to gather supplies and loot as you go, of course, but you can beat a map without food or loot, but not without exploring. Using sight lines, clearings in the forest or gazing across a lake all quickly become habitual.
Curious Expedition's second great success is it's use of the setting. The Age of Exploration is fairly seldom seen in games, and the use of real people for the character names gives a fantastic effect similar to the Civ games: "how is Harriet Tubman still ahead of me I hate her!!" or whatever the case may be, it's more memorable and engaging than the alternative. But the setting also extends to the way race relations work in the game, or the various side effects of consumables or the way male and female characters may be received. None of it is done with a heavy hand and if anything many fine touches may be easy for some gamers to miss, but they're there and they're fantastic.
The music is fantastic, and changes dynamically based on how your expedition is faring. The pixel art is very well done and while some of the early placeholder art was very ugly, the final versions of things have all been fantastic. The character models are very simple but when you see yourself riding a raptor, it won't matter too much.
BUGS: There are a few, but the devs are very active on the Steam forums and will be happy to see your screenshots. I have never had a single crash type error ever, only things like typos or quest glitches.
PRICE: It's not going under $11 until after it has been fully finished and released, which is not going to be super soon. You get a lot of great game for the price so either grab it the next time it's marked down or just give them three extra bucks.

So I got Alpha Kimori in a recent RPG Humble Bundle, so my first point of contention is pretty irrelevant to me, but geez, this game is not worth 10 bucks. I mean, I don't want to sound cheap here, but see those 3.5 hours? I beat the game in those 3.5 hours. Yes, I understand that the game is short because it's being released episodically, but I'm pretty sure I'd have to buy episode 2 if I wanted it. Which I don't. And not because of the length.
The first blaring flaw in the game is translation. Sometimes translation issues give a game character. Other times they feel lazy. This falls into the latter. The translation is stiff at the best of times and grating at the worst. This doesn't help the fact that all the characters are stock, dusted off from the JRPG bin. The whole thing is pretty tired. Even trope characters can be interesting and fun if they're presented in an interesting way, but you're not going to get that here.
AK plays as a linear jog from point A to B, with the only mix ups being thrown in are honest to god fetch quests. If you're going to send me on a fetch quest, at least try to pretend like it's something important. Rather than deliver 50 ethers to a guy with the most stilted sense of logic I've ever run across.
The battle system is boring. It's RPGMaker's stock battle system. That's it. You can attack. You can use a special attack. The main character had a whopping 4 special attacks by the time I finished.
For as much as I disliked this game, I feel like there should be more for me to complain about, but there isn't, because the game is 4 hours long. There's just nothing to it, and it's definitely not worth buying.
Pros: Some of the artwork is decent.
Cons: Poor Translation, Irritating Soundtrack, Bad plot, bad characters, boring battle system, some of the rendering on the art slides is grainy for evidently no reason, no real choices to make in a game about morality, I could probably go on but I think everyone gets it.
0/5

Football Manager has been made great again. Because Football Manager is fun again.
Some of the "modern" aspects of the game have been scraped away (mainly the psychological management) in favor of 2012-like more balanced system.
Instructions you give to players finally make a difference. Since dropping the sliders in favor of roles & instructions, it was very frustrating to have your team play the same every single game, no matter what you say. NO MORE! It's not 100% perfect, but it's much much better.
AI transfer policies seem better and random highly unlikely things (1 year injuries) aren't common any more.
Press conferences are still bland af. Everything present was in 2011.
There isn't much pressure to make your tactics detailed. You can live with default settings and adjusting roles.
Player search results aren't cached, so when you want to go through a list by looking at player profiles, every time you press back, it has to re-process.
Most criticism in Steam reviews is about lack of Chinese language and unrealistic match simulations. I can't/don't want to comment on the first point, but it's kinda unbelievable people still expect *realistic* matches. Sure, every year SI says it's going to be realistic, but come on! There was never a realistic CM/FM game and it won't be in forseeable future. It's, at least, fun again.
FM17 is a well-rounded game, unlike last editions. People who criticise the game about its gameplay are probably oversaturnated. This franchise is evolutionary by a for-profit company, not revolutionary. It's basically *only* an improved older version. If improved isn't good enough for you because you've played enough of 14/15/16, you're gonna be frustrated. If it is, ignore the mixed reviews and buy it.

Endless Legend is a nice take on the 4X genre, and I could summarize it as the child of the Civilization and Age of Wonders series. It's focused on tech research and city building and administration like Civilization but still has the very interesting tactical aspect of combat of AoW; moreover, you still have the possibility to upgrade your current units and heroes with the latest weapons, armor and artifacts you have researched -- a bit like what you can do in Stardock's Fallen Enchantress or in the classic Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.
A novel aspect of EL with respect of all the games I've mentioned is that the game map is divided into regions and each region can host upto one town only; this makes things a bit more interesting as the town has to be placed strategically in accordance with which resources the single region has to offer.
The graphics style is really appealing to me, and the music (that you get also in MP3 format bundled with the game download for free) really nails the mood and tempo of the game.
The only bad thing that I can say about EL is that the AI isn't very challenging at all; sometimes it could just stay idle in its initial territory for the most part of the match -- that's what happened to the Mezari in my first ever game. If this one issue is fixed, EL can become a true classic gem of the genre.
My vote: 8.5/10
PS: I'm still waiting for the Linux release!

Attention long time Civilization fans, prepare your wallets for battle!
Do you long for the good ol days of Civ IV? Before our beloved friends at Firaxis decided that we did not enjoy the near-tedious level of management and detail in their flagship title; and long before they began the process of streamlining (aka watering down) all of those aspects? The time when playing a single turn of a 4X strategy game could take 10, 20 even 30 minutes? Well look no further for your next strategy fix.
It may sound as though I am being sarcastic, but for those of you who truly enjoy the long, slow and deliberate game style the older Firaxis used to offer us, then Endless Legend is worth a hard look.  EL is molded from the standard 4X format we are used to but with a heavy layer of originality and flavor thrown on top, not to mention some fantastic novel gameplay mechanisms.  If you are ready to take full control, and I mean FULL control over every aspect of your sprawling population, right down to the weapons each individual unit carries, then its time to pickup Endless Legend.
Overall: 8.5/10
Suggested Maximum Purchase Price: $20-25 (US)
PS: I am not hating on Civ 5, I love that game.  But in my opionion, it did not fill the painfully intricate shoes of its older sibling, and left much to be desired.  I was finally able to fufilled that desire with a heavy dose of Endless Legend.

You have very little control over actual fighting, which can be annoying, but if one army is much stronger than the other, you can just auto-resolve the fight to save time.

Crusader Kings is one of those games where you are given endless choices and apportunities, a chance to live the great life of an emperor and to enforce the power you have to stay in such a position. This is a game about people and your goal is to make as many babies as possible to ensure your line does not die.

You always imagined that you would be a decent ruler, a fair and benevolent man or woman of the people.
You swore that you would never abuse power for personal gain, that there is a noble, pure, and divine vision to follow... but yet every event or message that pops up on your screen just pulls at you a little, doesn't it? Just nags a tiny bit - at the strings of your soul.
It's just a light tickle at first, barely noticeable as you look at your options and choose the way ahead. But then only a little while later you're sweating. Surely assassinating your rival's child isn't a bad thing, right? I mean you're doing it for the greater good aren't you?... and imprisoning your ever faithful adoring wife isn't wrong, right? I mean... you suspect she's plotting against you without any evidence - but if she was that good at winning your trust -of course there wouldn't be any evidence, would there? Hmm... maybe you should execute her as soon as she arrives there, just to be sure... Your Secret Society friends didn't like her anyway...
Playing this game will reveal the darkness hidden in the deep reaches of your soul.
You will do evil, depraved, despicable things to good people and you'll love every moment of it.

First, let me tell you a story - a story about a nun. She accompanied me from the very beginning. Why? I have no clue. But I let her stay. On my second mission, I came across an unknown fluid in a temple. I didn't like my nun very much since she was sexist, a nun, and pretty useless for the most part, so I told her to drink it. She didn't even hesitate and gulped it down. Her hands then transformed into claws - and although she probably didn't like it, it was the best thing that could have happened. With her beast claws she tore apart panthers, gorillas and even a tiger for me. She was a walking menace, following my orders. She also became an alcoholic because of all the whiskey I forced her to drink in my effort to keep her sane. By the end of the fifth mission she was the most important member of my team, next to the water buffalo. On my last mission I went into a cave without a torch. It was pitch black. Suddenly the nun was gone and in her place was an abomination. Did she transform? Was she eaten? We weren't sure. The abomination was still cool since it also followed us around and was a good fighter, too. But one night, it started eating my soldier and I had to put it down. We had to go home without the nun. She almost made it to the end. We only got as far as we did because of her. This is for the nun whom I disrespected, whose name I've already forgotten, but whose claws I'll never forget. You rocked.
Okay, storytime's over. This game is an almost accurate representation of the British Museum's history. It's the 1800's, archeology and exploration are en vogue. You are a famous person of your choice, you travel to a wild, unexplored part of the planet and then proceed to rob the people there of as much cultural property as you can - and hope you'll get away with it. Steal from temples, kill wildlife, trade with villagers and/or slavers, catch butterflies; all that and more for fame, money and the British Museum.
The maps and events are randomly generated to guarantee a high replay value. You can manage your party and your inventory, both with solid mechanics and lots of choices. The battles are dice-based and strike a very nice balance between strategy and luck. Even though the game is still in early access, it feels pretty finished for the most part and the devs have delivered a good amount of updates over the last couple of months.
Verdict: A good game, definitely worth a try.

"So Hashbrick do you recommend Alpha Kimori Episode 1?"
"Absolutely!" is what I would have said if it didn't have so many things wrong with it.  At this point it is nothing more than a "Well if you like RPGs and don't mind a huge let down...be my guest"
Let's go down the list of everything that just makes this a disappointment in any regard.
CONS
Short - 5-7hrs depending on how hard you grind there isn't much going for it.  The story has a hard time taking off and when you are done you are still wondering what exactly went on in that short time frame.  This is exactly why RPGs were never made in episode form originally, it is hard to tell a meaningful story in a short period of time.
Soundtrack - Get ready to hear the same damn music over and over.  One of the songs actually sounds like watching a citcom where it hits the high notes and out comes the actors running down the stairs with their names appearing.  It is a very odd taste of music and you will groan everytime you hear it even with the short episode.
Lack of Strategy - The only time you will ever use "skills" is on boss fights to quickly defeat them, other than that the whole game is cruise control of spamming just attack and watching♥♥♥♥♥♥die.  There is no weaknesses or status effects just a minor attack up, attack down system.
Redone & Overused Areas - Get ready to go to the same damn areas you go through in the beginning of the game with the exception of the final area that is new everything is rehashed for every quest and side quest.  You litteraly do not venture more than a woods right next to your town and nothing more.  There is times where you wish they'd just wipe the enemies clean and just let you run instead of running into lvl 1♥♥♥♥♥♥at lvl 32 just cause its the very first area but you need to do quest X here for the 10th time.
Story - Extremely weak story of a love triangle (or lack there of) between a brain dead, can't think for myself female that is obbsessed with the main character to the point it makes you sick.  Then this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ likes the chick you could care less about while you hunt for another chick on the other faction to realize that you could care less about your own morals that were forced on you by your crazy♥♥♥♥♥parents who have no problem to just kill you off if you fail your exam?!?!  Oh ya and something about some alpha ship that came from Earth to this planet, with two factions; one that wants to get back to Earth and one that wants to just stay and make the best of it, who then made these Kimori human like things but not considered humans who consider themselves gods, while 7 souls of angels that turn into some kinda gem thing implanted in 7 different characters that can call these angel things in battle, while the other faction can turn into enemies and the reason to kill monsters on the planet is to harness their ki energy for....reasons.  Confused yet?  Good don't expect anything else when it ends there is nothing if anything explained in this crazy mindless plot. (It is suppose to sound like a run-on because of how short the episode is and how much they jam in your throat)
Items That Don't Matter - Throw your items in the garbage, you will never use them if you are on par with the levels you should be.  As for weapons and armor you will get hand outs during the story no point of ever using the stores ever...
Lack of world building - There is no detail in most the areas you will travel through, just plain grass, caves, one town and a small one with little to nothing in it.
Cutscenes - Not only will you see the same cutscene cut up in different places over 10 times in different points in the game as they ram it home that "this is the defining moment of change!"  You will also be greeted to ingame cutscenes that require npc movement that takes so long and you can't move until its complete.  The graduation ceremony you watch 3 npcs walk up take their document and go back to their place, for what, what point is there making the player wait a long♥♥♥♥♥time for no gain, no dialog, just movement...  Seems like they just did one flash back and cut it up cause it was too much work.
PROS
Graphics - looks good for a 2D RPG, models are nicely detailed.
Battle Engine - While not having to actually use it much, it is overall a well built battle engine turn based menu system.
Character Building - While being short it does a ok job at detailing some of the characters and giving them a background, this is probably the shining moment in the game and the only shining moment.  There are some cliched character of course but for the most part the reasons and ambitions are clearly detailed throughout the short episode.
FINAL THOUGHTS
If you like a RPG with a meaty story, look elsewhere.  If you don't mind grinding mindlessly and go through the same areas over and over again for a little piece of pie (the story or lack thereof) then by all means take the plunge.  I can't recommend this game based on the obvious issues with this game there is no meat for the lover of RPGs and in retrospect if I had known it was going to be what it was I probably would have not pushed myself through the entire episode.
2/10 - extremely average run of the mill RPG with little to no reason to actually need to experience it.

I stumbled onto this game while looking for an RPG to put some time into. Normally I never play 4x strategy games because I find them slow and requiring more time to learn than I have the patience for. Endless Legend hits a sweet spot I hadn't experienced before! The story of th factions are actually interesting and the systems are complex, but not to the point of being a daunting research-fest. The game also looks gorgeous and that music....so good! The additional quests from ruins or minor factions definitely help keep the game moving. Combat is fun, and you have to remember to equip better gear as your hero characters and armies gain experience. I did find that combat can be a little odd at times; like selecting a character to attack, but the minion runs to the other side of the board instead. Difficulty wise, as a 4x newbie, I keep getting my butt kicked by the AI on normal (darn Cultists). Overall, Endless Legend is a fantastic game with a great melding of turn-based RPG/ character building, strategy, and open-world exploration...and good faction stories to boot! Each game takes a few hours to play through and with something like 7 or 8 factions, that's a whole lot of replay value! Do yourself a favor and add this game to your collection!
