The ugly: No matter what you do in battle, if you're scripted to lose, you're going to lose.  Even if you one shot the enemy, once the battle is done it'll pretend like you lost the battle, making it feel like there's no point to winning them.  The finale brings up an interesting aspect of the story, namely the ability to (DON'T READ THIS IF YOU DON'T WANT SPOILERS) harvest the gems of enemies and add their strength to your own (DON'T READ THIS IF YOU DON'T WANT SPOILERS) but there is no mechanic in game to do that.  You're also greeted with a strength +100 gem, but it's the only one you get and it's impossible to get more.
All in all, this game is worth $5 or even $10, but for a five hour game it's not really worth $15.  Get it on sale if you can, because there's a part 2 that steam needs to add (and a part 3 they need to make supposedly) that will eat your money away if you buy it at full price.  It's not worth $45 ($30 for both parts for a 12 hour game) for however many hours, but it's a fun game for a one and done.

Alpha Kimori is a game I have some tough love for. It lusts to be a better game, and while what is at its base is decent, the episodic nature that can be healthy for most forms of gaming just doesn't click with this sort of game. Just when some character development is made, the game ends, and the sequence of events leading to the "climax" feels hurried and poorly explained, leaving us with a cliffhanger of sorts that feels more like a transition than an ending to a product.
To give credit where its due, the ability to avoid most encounters thanks to their corporealLater on they make the enemies track you, which gets a bit comical once you get a good conga-line of enemies following behind you. Thankfully the battles themselves are quick and harmless, and while there is no autobattle feature, rapidly tapping enter until everything is dead seemed highly effective in every situation except boss battles.
The mythology is interesting enough, and while the core story concept seems to have some depth, we only gather so much before we are booted to the credits. For the length of the game, flashbacks occur far too often, encircling the same scene from different perspectives. While this idea could work well in a different context, the scene they use is a bit too boring, and gets further ridiculous as they show the amount of people tied into this one fairly mundane encounter. One flashback was enough for this bit, but it occurs at least 6 more times, JUST to make sure you get the picture. The heavy-handed plot is definitely worth the watch however, as I got a good chuckle once I realized what they were going for, but don't expect any real thought-provoking moments. The protagonist in particular is a classic case of insensitive prick with a harem complex, and the dissonance of "I don't want to hurt any innocent creatures" combined with him and his constantly changing female companion slaughtering thousands of said creatures is just silly, especially given that his "reluctance" is the main driving point of this first chapter.
When it comes to pacing the game is sporadic, as the lack of fast travel has you going through the same enviornments and encounters without adding anything to pad out the repitition. It would be okay if there was a variety of locations, but almost every mission objective is a little farther than the last within the same four areas, and there are no shortcuts that are always open to you. The shortcuts they do provide are often story specific, and while they usually teleport you back to save time, they aren't always a two way street, which had me flinching every time I found out I had to go through that same forest with the stupid purple bunnies for the 10th time.
Ultimately, Alpha Kimori is a b-tier RPG with a lot of camp to it that keeps its charm even after it outstays its welcome. The effort is genuine, and I will honestly consider picking up the rest of the episodes once they're released, for there is something at the core of this that I can't help but admire. I enjoyed my time with it, and while my attention was mainly focused on the show I had playing in the background, I've found myself thinking about it well after finishing and I couldn't tell you why. Definitely worth the pickup if you can look past the flaws and enjoy the heart that it has.

Paradox Studios grand strategy games span the history of the world in a more-or-less continuous order; at time of writing, I consider the main series to be...
Crusader Kings II (769 - 1453)
Europa Universalis IV (1444 - 1821)
Victoria II (1836 - 1936)
Hearts of Iron III (1936 - 1948)
So Victoria II sits near the end of that progression, covering the fall of the Ottoman Empire, the American Civil War, the growth of Japan (and industrialisation in general), and notably, the First World War (if it happens!). It's a period where huge political shifts occur in the power structure of the world, the first major colonisation pushes are made, and eventually, the scramble for Africa. You can take control of LITERALLY any country and pilot them through this period, building railroads, factories, battleships, and influencing policies, political parties, and social movements. You can grow your country into one of the Great Powers of the world, and establish protectorates, bring other countries into your sphere of influence, and found colonies.
This one game, with its incredible scope, is really many different games in one; playing America (initially a slave state) will be a largely different experience to playing, say, China, which will yet again be different to playing a tiny country like Panama. I've had most fun playing the 'middle' states, like Persia, Japan, and Australia (after devolving it from the British Empire). While it's hard to rock the boat at the top of the great powers list, I've also had fun playing France, making major in-roads into the nascent Germany, and conquering Switzerland. Alliances can bring about amusing consequences (like, in my France game, Equadorian Sardinia??), and national decisions can create large diversions from history.
All this aside, bear in mind this is a Paradox strategy game. Which means, if you haven't played one before, be prepared for a LONG game, with potentially a lot of waiting. Colonisation, a really key part of the game for great powers, isn't possible until over 20 hours in, at least. The menus are many, and the choices opaque. I highly recommend watching a Let's Play for this game before you attempt it. Once you've learnt to play it, however, it's a very rewarding experience.
It's not for everyone, but if you like long, deep Grand Strategy games, give a try.

Originally a lovingly crafted although sometimes rough simulator focusing on managing a feudal dynasty in medieval Europe, the game has since grown so dramatically in both scope and vision to be virtually unrecognizable. It is wonderfully complex but it is based on a series of core fundamentals that are relatively easy to learn and operate. It has humor and a quirky charm, while still having a vast array of historical and quasi-historical data with which to play in a sandbox of “what if” history. Even if that sandbox is still largely limited to Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and parts of Asia including a shrunk down, slightly deformed India. Can you conquer your little corner of the world? Absolutely. Can you scheme and plot and destroy your enemies? Sure. Can you advance your family dynasty by fair means and foul to secure a place in the history books? Check. Can you go insane, worship dark gods, slay a Lovecraftian horror, add the necronomicon to your library, raise the spawn of the devil, appoint a horse to your council and take advantage of loop holes in the games systems to get a court full of horses to spread throughout the world? Of course, what’s the point of getting up in the morning otherwise? You can also build up a kingdom or an empire from a lowly county or dukedom, navigate political alliances and marriages, build and develop your holdings, appease your vassals, bribe council members, influence your liege lord, build vast armies, write a magnum opus, build an observatory, throw wonderful parties, organize great hunts, play chess with Death, the sky is seemingly the limit and with every dlc the sky seems to get a little broader and a little crazier. Although the game engine is showing its age a little and some of the dlc is decidedly fanciful and not to everyone’s taste, the game is a solid experience and a ton of fun, and very open to being whatever you want to make of it.

I have no grand strategy experience prior to picking up this game. I do however have experience with titles from Paradox and it was the reason I trusted them enough to try this title. I love every other Paradox game I've played.
Pros
Sound effects are on point. I really like the background sounds when you click on different things. Coins clinking around, horses, people talking. It feels right.

So much potential for potitical intrigue, I've already had 3 family members try to kill me and even have my sister in prison right now. She's being tortured for plotting to kill me. (This is so far the most memorable part in my game)
Zero issues with bugs/crashes or the like.
No set storyline it develops as you make choices and it feels like things go on around you that are randomized depending on what stats the npcs get. This is really coo because you never know what might happen in a given play through and for that the replayablity value is probably off the chain.
Cons
It has been an extremely slow process learnig how to opperate the UI in this game. Almost nothing has been intuitvie for me so far. Even though this is a con I wouldn't say this doesn't have its merits though. I do like a challenge and so I appriciate a game that doesn't hand-hold.
DLC. The business model for this game seems pretty greedy. Things that seem like they should have been added in the standard game you have to purchase via DLC. This isn't CKII specific really, it's all of Paradox's games. I love their games, hate their business model. Even so, I will say this game is worth picking up on sale. It might be worth the full price but I just don't have the time and experience to support that claim yet. I have a suspicion it will be though.
That's all I got for now.

The Hunter Primal. After reading dozens of reviews, and playing it for a few dozen hours myself I have come to some conclusions about the game. First off this is NOT a game for EVERYONE. Are you patient? This is arguably the most expensive tramping simulator out there... No kidding! There have been times when I've tramped for over an hour and not seen a Dino or anything of real interest except very beautiful scenery, but even that can get old. Or, you can load the game up and stumble across several T-Rex or half a dozen Raptors that tear you to shreds and cause you to lose all your gear that you've spent over ten hours collecting.
A lot of people review the game negatively based upon the fact the game "isn't finished". The game is perfectly playable and enjoyable as it is, and is indeed "finished" it isn't however very "polished" and a few areas of the game could do with vast improvement, in fact a lot of areas could. If you need a slick, styled, polished game, this probably isn't for you. This game however is extremely immersive, and also very lonely.
One of the great reasons for this game is the sense of abandonment, the aloneness, even with other players in the game. It's a harsh environment, there's big creatures out to kill and eat you, weapons are scarce and ammo is scarcer. It really does get the adrenaline going, which is a definite pro.
Some say the game is easy, some say the game is hard. The game is both and neither. The difficulty is based on serveral variable factors, your skill at FPS, your gear (guns, ammo level, camo), your environment (jungle, plains, hills etc..), and the ammount and type of dinos around at the time. Sometimes it's near impossible to even stay alive, other times you're tramping around shooting things without a worry or care in the world. This is enjoyable as at times you can relax at times you need to focus more.
All in all I enjoy this game very much, I wish there were more types of dinosaurs, and some parts were more polished but I very happily recommend it to people who fit the criteria above. Load up! Lets go hunting!

Heroes of Might and Magic III and Civilization V had a baby and called it Endless Legend. Friends had this game before me and were kind enough to buy it for me (thank you!). First off, I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game. At first it was difficult to get the hang of, the UI and all the buttons needing to be pressed was a bit overwhelming at first. Then I got into the groove of it all and begun to love this majestic and sexy game. The factions/races are all interesting and scary in their own way. I love the Drakken but I am terrified of the Necrophages and Cultists.
It takes the resources (strategic and luxury) per turn from Heroes, the unit, city and building creation from Civilization while set in a fantasy world consumed with cold war and distrust. The races have their own unique style to how they progress in the world and all seem to be rather balanced. For every downside there is a plus like the Roving Clans, cannot declare war and lose movement/money when winter comes. But played right can make you still earn a profit and even more in summer. At times it seems that a race sucks as you conquer them without effort, till you try them and see how dangerously powerful (or controlling) they can be. It has the RPG elements in it that you have heroes to upgrade and there are quests to fulfil. Doesn't really count as a plot but it explains more about the factions. Like Civ land ownership is VITAL.
Expanding a lot will make your people unhappy, but each land will have something useful, whether it is the minor factions, strategic resources or the many luxuries that can boost you like steroids. Like Civ there are a lot of things to increase the happiness of your cities. There is a marketplace that has every resource available in the game you are currently playing (some luxuries can’t be mined sometimes and will be not available in the market then) allowing you to sell and buy the things you need when the time comes to it. This includes units and heroes (the main way to get heroes).
Every race’s heroes have their own faction bonuses; it encourages you to buy other faction’s heroes to be assigned in your cities to provide food, production, science or dust (money) to enhance its overall growth. I am rambling too much but I am just saying this game is pretty damn good. It needs more content but I hope the devs are already thinking about that. 9.5/10
Best alternative if you didnt like the new Civ game.

If you are a fan of otome games this is a good one. Though not as good as Hakuoki which is by the same creaters, it still is a beautiful game. When I tried the anime I felt like it was missing something and that the game was probably better. I was right. I like that you can get different endings depending on your choices. Plus the art is gorgeous.

TL;dr: For an otome, it is quite dark. So things get crazy pretty quick. You have many hours that you can put into the game, depending on how fast you read, it may vary. The characters are all unique in their own way, some more unexpected than others. The Art is very beautiful, followed along with very well chosen voice actors. The stories all can get you very involved and wanting more. Only bleh is some achievements suck and Orion constantly yappin'.
Recommend: To those who like Visual Novels, unique characters, romance, engaging stories, and pretty art.
-----------------------------------------------
Game: There are lots of hours that can be put into this game which is good when seeing the price on this game. You get also a lot of unlockable additional content which makes it more worthwhile.  Such as memories and short stories in the boys' perspectives. Oh and mini-games which are pretty fun if you aren't in the mood for reading. Good amount of save slots, but in the end, I was wishing for more for Ukyo ~ n ~  Also is great that you can choose how it is read. You can turn on and off the V.A.'s, put it on Auto, Speed through text, show text and previous text all together, etc... Made it definitely a good experience. AND to make things better, if you're trying to get a different ending and playing through again, if you speed through, it will stop and play if there is text that you have previously not read in your other playthroughs! And it will highlight which answers you've already inputed. No trying to remember now :3
Achievements: Some of these achievemnts are literally so annoying I just gave up -.- One is where you have to click the image multiple times just for the guy to say a couple things. Looked up where to click and it still does absolutely nothing.  Everyone, but Kent's, I have had difficulty getting one part of their picture to work, It is seriously the dumbest thing ever. >_> The others are easy to obtain.
Anime VS. Otome: I found out about the anime first then the otome. I'm happy I came across the otome because now I realize how BAD the anime is. The anime doesn't cover really anything, Like the first 5-10 mins of the boys' story in the otome, so it was nice to really get to delve into these boys stories way more than the anime ever did.  Only thing is I kind of liked in the anime that Orion wasn't there 24/7. The otome he just literally drove me bonkers @ n @
Art: The art is very beautiful and definitely draws you in.  Their character design is actually very well thought out and you see a bunch of tiny things that really bring everything together, Also with their personalities, it ties in with the design. They have different poses which are good as well. The only weird thing for me is how large some of their hands were... But the style and coloring is very pretty. The gallery has lots of pretty images that are saved from your specific route and you can even move around the picture and check out different areas of it. There was a lot of variety and ones you unlock just from completing certain acheivements. Though that stupid ctrl-left click thing for their "hidden" message things were annoying. I'd click and it would end up going to the next image instead. I had an immensley hard time trying to get parts of an image to register. No matter how many times I clicked Toma's fist in the 2nd variation nothing happened, Shin and Heroine picture variation 2, her face would not react at all, Ikki and the heroine at the theatre, the hand wouldn't register. I've looked this stuff up to see if I'm just clicking slightly off, but I am clicking where I need it. So that part gets a 0 in my book because it was just frustrating.
Music: The music wasn't distracting and pretty good for the most part.
Characters: The characters all had variety and interesting endings, though some just seemed completely random at times. I wish there could have been more choices to choose from and Orion would STOP making decisions for me -.- I'm looking at Toma's route heavily when Orion becomes really annoying. Speaking of Toma,
I liked the guy characters because they all had their set personality making it fresh when you go to a different route. And many of the stories were very interesting to go into. I don't want to go into too much detail so this will be spoiler free.
Shin-> He is such a tsun tsun but  a sweetie ^ u ^ Oh and suprisingly the smartest guy out of the bunch in the end. I guess seemed a bit more realistic to me than the other boys.
Toma-> I personally really liked his character, he's definietly not for everyone. I just liked he was really out there compared to the other characters.
Kent-> He starts off a total meanie-poo but like Shin he really isn't that bad. He goes off onto a lot of tangents of things like math and what not. But he was an amusing character.
Ikki-> The "playboy" or "pretty boy" character but reading his story, there is so much more to him than on the surface.
Ukyo-> Prepare for the feels! His story is so bittersweet. You can't help but like this guy T w T
Based on the characters themselves and how much I liked them:
Based on stories I found the most interesting are in the order:
. Ikki and Kent's story didn't interest me as much, I guess they just felt, I guess more like slice-of-life, while the others seemed to be a bit crazier with their stories, drawing me in more. (However, this is just a personal preference)
Story itself: I found it a quite interesting premise, though I wish you could voice up more, Orion ends up taking the brunt of everything, which kind of ruins the effect for me. But
Voices: The characters' voice acting is very good @ w @ I really enjoyed them. I especially liked Shins. Haha. But I think they all fit the characters very well.
~Overall. I really enjoyed the story and the characters in  it.  It was an enjoyable experience overall and would recommened to anyone who likes visual novels and an interesting set of characters.

If you are the berseker kind, you will learn that the best approach for hack and slash depends on enemy positioning. Alpha Kimori is a game with an interesting story. The gameplay itself is that of a simple RPG. The difficulty isn't high and in general you won't find any great challenge in this game. The main point of the game IS the story, resulting in a short game with characters you can still really care about.
If I had to describe it, I'd say it feels the most like a visual novel with RPG elements. All in all, the game is for a somewhat niche group, but it's awesome all the same. If you're looking for a good story, be sure to check this game out!

It's good, but I believe you have to have an affinity for classic JRPGs from the 16-bit era to really enjoy it, otherwise it'll just feel tedious a lot of the time.
The story isn't bad, the characters have a bit of depth and development to them, and the sprite work and art design looks nice.  As an RPG, its battle system is just standard basic attack, magic, and item commands selected from a menu, with an option to defend and recover HP/MP, but doesn't offer anything beyond that.  Enemies show up in the field and battles can be avoided for the most part, which is a step up from having to deal with completely random battles.
The game could have stood to have a wider variety of music tracks.  You'll be hearing the same upbeat town theme a lot of the time, which will sometimes end up clashing with the tone of the story when things take on a more serious mood.  The first episode is also really short.  Taking my time with it and walking away from it every so often, I still managed to get through it in under 10 hours, and a good portion of the game has a lot of padding from battling and backtracking.
Overall, it offers enough where I could recommend it if you really like older console RPGs and can get it for cheap during a sale.

Overall, I generally like the game and will eventually pick up the 2nd one, but I will only slightly recommend this game for the following reasons:
1. You end up going through the same areas over and over again on different quests thoughout the story line.  There is a whole built world map that you can see the few times you get outside of one of the 'dungeon' forests, but each exit leads only to the next area on the quest, so you will be going through the same areas over and over killing the same monsters over and over.
2. Near the end, some of the areas are mixed up by adding some extra monsters that you fight, they are about 10x stronger than the other monsters in the area (that were a little bit of a challenge at the beginning of the game) but give the same or in some areas less experience and treasure than the original monsters.
3. There is a weapon in the weapon shop that seems to have no use whatsoever during the game, it's the most expensive item there, but the main character, nor any of the people that can join the party (and stick around longer than a fight) seem to be able to use it.
4. Some things in the game seem to have weak story line, for example at one point you get the giant robots, use them then 'give them back' in the middle of a forest, who you took them from, and why you gave them back at all, considering how the story line is progressing at that point seems a mystery.
5. You are pretty much on a rail throughout the entire game, sure you can run around in the area and kill all of the monsters in each area if you wish, but if you try to backtrack, your companion scolds you, tells you where you need to go and then you have to follow the rail to the next event.
6. Some of the spell effects seem over the top and just take too long to show on the screen, When it comes to the big final fight, multiple large spell effects happen, which really makes the combat rounds last a while
7. Very little in the way of equipment upgrades during the game, except through scripted events.  Yes it's a short game, but still.
It however is a nice game, and was fun while it lasted, but it did get a bit old with the constant backtracking.  So I do recommend it.

Welcome to Curious Expedition, a game where you pick from several historical figures to explore the untamed lands of the world.  Gather loot and fame, but don't vex the natives too much or they may hunt you down and take your head.  Survive by eating chocolate and drinking whiskey and if you need,  hunt Raptors for their meat.  Run out of food, become insane and some of your traveling mates may even try to eat you or each other.
Object of the game is to become the most famous explorer, which is accomplished over six missions by finding precious artifacts and the golden pyramid.  Top your high score or unlock more explorers by accomplishing certain goals.
Game mechanics and combat is governed by RNG, but most decisions are in your hands, such as leveling up, what equipment you bring on an expedition, where you explore.  Do you steal every artifact you find only to anger the natives or do play nice with natives to help you find the golden pyramid?
The choice is yours.  Highly recommend buying the game.  Already played for 26 hours and plan to play some more.
Developer is very responsive to the community.

Victoria II is a very niche game in my opinion. This is not for everyone. The combat is basically a combination of luck and stats and is very frustrating so don't come into this game expecting anything like StarCraft.
As an avid lover of history though this is basically my wet dream come true. Victoria II focuses on the Post Napoleon Era of the world. This game allows you to play as basically everything country that existed between the early 19th century and the 1920s. I have never seen a game that allowed me to play as Belgium or Colombia or Hawaii. The point is to take your country from an early industrial state to being an imperial empire.
You have to build your nation, your economy, your foreign relations, and your military. Either hope to be one of the eight main superpowers or pray to at least maintain your independence. What it most interesting is that there doesn't seem to be a way to actually "lose". When my government was overthrown I thought I lost, but the game kept going. Except we were communists and new social policies were in place and my ecomony was wrecked from the civil war. Which is interesting mechanic. The objective is to be the top great power and you are competing with over a 100 other nations that may come and go. Mods add even more.
Victoria II works for me because I like the management aspect and it focuses on my favorite era of history and allows me to play anywhere in the world. I have to plan my economy and expansion and go to war carefully since it can cost you prestige, cost you a portion of your workforce if they get slaughtered, and drain your economy (like a real nation).
It's not a perfect game, but I have fun and maybe you will too.

At one point in time GCI was one of my two favorite FPS games and I easily considered it one of the best ever made.  Having played every major FPS since the original Doom on a 486 that's no short story.  It was wholly unique, immediately and immensly enjoyable, never grew stale, and best of all was downright hilarious.
Now, it's just a runny poop stain on FPS history.
GCI (on every platform) had issues from the very beginning.  PC wasn't the worst- that was outclassed in awful by the horrendous PS3 version- but to say it had a rocky start would outshine the kindness of St. Hammish, the Patron saint of cleaning Scottish pub washrooms.
It didn't work with most graphics cards, the servers were laggy and spotty (if you could even get in a game), and crashes/glitches were more numerous than matches completed.  If memory serves- I was an alpha/beta tester for GCI- there was an interesting friends list bug that would soft lock the lobby and never load the game for any of the players, the only way out was to force close and restart.  Also, GFWL.
Still, people tried their hardest to enjoy and play it because it was just *fun*.  Over time- far too late most would say- GFWL was removed and the majority of major crash issues were patched out before going F2P on Steam.  There was a brief period after that in GCI reigned in as much glory as it could muster...
But now that glory is long gone.  There are still a handful of people playing it but everything that wasn't solved on the technical side of the game is what reigns now: terrible P2P connections, graphic card compatibility issues (new ones), and good 'ol crashes, bugs, and disconnects.
If you missed your chance and tried to see what it was all about now, it wouldn't seem like much of anything.  Ugly, strange, barely working... it would appear as just another downloadable CoD clone.

This was my first 4x game so I can't really compare it to other games like Civilization. After the 30-minute tutorial (atleast for me), I instantly fell inlove with it.
If you haven't played a 4x game ( like I was before I bought this) , then the gameplay mechanics will be very confusing unless you play the tutorial. They made a nifty feature where you can just close a window by right clicking which is very useful. You could play the game with just your mouse. There are also keyboard shortcuts.
The battle mechanics are like a game within a game. You can manually chose how your army will fight. Also, you can customize each of your troops and heroes. Also, HEROES! You can buy heroes from the marketplace which can be a Governer or a General.
Factions have diversity! No factions are alike ( except for the reskin of the Vaulters faction from the Emperor Edition but they mentioned that it was just a reskin). Each will play out differently. Each has its own unique advantages and disadvantages.
The graphics and music are amazing. Not too bright nor too dark.
The only downside for me is that there are barely any online games (atleast where I live). The bots are fine and dandy but sometimes I want some soul to feel the defeat , you know?

Honestly, if you claim yourself a 4X strategy fan and don't own this game, people are going to wonder if you're lying to them.
This game does something I've had criticisms about Civilization over the years.  Each faction is very starkly unique from one another and very fun to play since they all require different core strategies in the long-game.  I always felt that Civilization didn't do enough to make different empires feel interesting and varied, but now I can wipe my hands of the franchise altogether because Endless Legend does it right.
Secondly, I LOVE the hero mechanic.  Having Heroes of Might and Magic-esque quests that help you learn about the lore and the world is brilliant. Secondly, the strategy in developing these Hero units and recruiting more opens up an extra layer of depth.  Outside of the tech trees for each era, leveling the Hero via combat, garrisoning, and quests can help you in even things like city-planning as they can grant bonuses to cities that they govern.
There is too much to talk about, so go get this game and find out for yourself how awesome it is! DO IT NOW!  (You won't regret it)

A damn fine game, the best yet from Amplitude, which is saying something.
I played Endless Space since beta, solid game.  Skipped Dungeon of the Endless, it might be good, just not my thing.  Endless Legend shows that Amplitude has been actively learning from past mistakes and pushing themselves to improve.  It's weird, normally I prefer sci-fi to fantasy (though EL has elements of sci fi), but Endless Legend is done well enough that it really doesn't matter.  I had actually been eagerly awaiting Civ Beyond Earth, but when that turned out to be a bland 'meh' (seriously Firaxis, a simple redo of Alpha Centauri in a 3d engine would be miles ahead of BE, what the hell), Endless Legend came along and took its place.
Innovative city building and expansion system, clever use of territories on the strategic map similar to Total War style, seasonal changes which add both flavor and very different gameplay, and polished tactical combat although unit selection is a bit lacking--WITHIN factions I should note, different factions have very different units and play styles.  Fundamentally a very well done game which offers loads of replayability and works across all sorts of play styles, from tech to build to war.  I can't wait to see what Amplitude does next.

Sometimes faces of the heroine was a bit awkward, but it didn't detract from anything.
The only disappointing thing about the art in this game is the how little effort was spent on the backgrounds. The backgrounds are basically nonexistent. While the game was good enough in every other area for me to overlook it, I think some fully realized background art would have greatly helped in the immersion of the story for the player. I can't decide if backgrounds were done in the strange minimal way they did because of budget, laziness or somehow to fit their theme of needing to remember their past/
.
When I went into this game, I kind of just expected something fairly cheesy and while it was certainly cheesy, it was also a mystery/psycho-thriller of sorts! Most of the routes revolve around a bit of a mystery and puts the heroine in dangerous situations. I felt like I was often doubting the truth of the situation and who to trust. I actually played Ikki's route first without knowing anything about who I was picking in the hub world and was it certainly a shock when
.
Each character route is pretty much its own contained story and all of them were engaging in their own way. I played Ken's route last and that was a nice break from all the craziness of the other routes.
You don't really get to know the 'real' story behind the game until you play the hidden route, but it reveals some fun things that explain more about the heroine's situation and all the strange things going on in her life.
Individual character routes can be hit or miss depending on what you like in a story. I haven't gotten all the endings for all the characters, but the replayability of this game is pretty high and I will probably try to tackle that at some point in the future.
The writing was generally good. I don't remember any glaring typos or grammatical mistakes. There were a few lines here or there that were a bit strange, but the translation overall seemed sound and very readable.
All the characters were pretty likeable - some moreso than others. As you change routes, your relationships to and with certain characters may shift a bit and this changes how they act towards you as well. The 4 main bachelors were all interesting in their own regard and I won't go too much detail into what each are like, but here are a few sort descriptions:
Shin - Your childhood friend in most routes and is one year your junior. He is pretty loyal and kind of hotheaded. He really,
wants to prove himself to you.
Ikki - Super flirty and has his own fanclub of girls. He was the first route I played and I pretty much loved him, even if
!
Kent - Highly intelligent and socially stunted, Kent doesn't really understand how to vocalize emotions and ends up just appearing to people a bit like a robot. It's up to ~you~ to help him out of his shell.
Toma - Toma is the "older brother" figure. He's overprotective
and does everything in his power to keep the heroine 'safe'. I hates his route the most, but it was also the weirdest and most surprising route? If you like
, you'll love Toma.
Hidden Route - You'll know who it is when you play the game! This will unlock after you get the good endings for all the other guys.
Side Characters -
All the side characters were fun and added things to the story. Orion, the stand-in for the heroine, as the heroine is more or less mute in this game, was also pretty great! He brought a lot of comedic relief to an otherwise dark story. Orion also was pretty much the voice of reason when the heroine made stupid decisions (I know, I know, I made them
her, but the game gives me no choice in the matter if I want a certain ending!). It was fun having some sort of company on this strange, wonderful journey of trying to remember if you were in love with a certain boy or not!
Unlike some other otome games (which I have been obsessively playing after playing
), you can pick your character route right away from a hub world. You aren't told who you are picking per se, but are given a choice between worlds named after card suits. Each suit is affiliated with one of the guys and you just pick a world and boom, you're already on your way to woo the guy of your choice.
Once you are put on a route, you can see some affections meters. There are a few meters you need to keep your eye on and the choices in the game really made a difference. I think I got two variations of Ikki's bad endings before looking up a walkthrough and getting his good ending! With at least 3 endings for each bachelor and little variations in between, I felt like your choices did have an impact, even if you didn't necessarily see it straight away. The deviations in how a story concludes isn't too different between the endings but I think they are different enough to merit seeing all of them.
As there are so many endings, the replayability is pretty high for this game! Like it said at the beginning, I will probably end up replaying this at some point to get all the endings. I only have the bad endings and normal endings left though so I will probably feel a bit said when I reach them.
This is a pretty fun game to spend a good chunk of time on. Using a walkthrough will definitely help speed up the process of getting the route you want. The art is gorgeous and the story is engaging! If you haven't tried playing an otome game before, I would definitely pick this up. It is 100% worth the full price of the game, but it often goes on sale for a few dollars on Steam. If you're unsure about the game, pick it up then, but I still think it's be worth it if you like visual novel type games with a good chunk of mystery and suspense.
Suggested route orders I've seen end up being a variation of:
Kent > Ikki > Shin > Toma > Hidden Route
With Kent being first as it is the leasty spoilery.
My route order (as this was before I knew there might be spoilers in one route for another) went:
Ikki > Shin > Kent > Toma > Hidden Route
Shin and Toma's routes kind of spoil each other's I'd say. I played Shin's route before Toma's and I kind of knew what would inevitably go wrong in Toma's route! I played Toma's route last because I knew I would be freaked out by it!

Alpha Kimori (ep1) is a fun little RPG (in JRPG-style) that while not perfect does prove that with effort a small group of people can use RPG Maker to put something together worth your money. RPG Maker has a seedy reputation due to some people abusing it but it’s far from a bad piece of software, and in the right hands can be used to everyone’s benefit. Alpha Kimori is one such product that stands as testament to this.
That said the game doesn’t try to be anything more than it appears to be, a very traditional RPG in the style of old SNES classics. Characters have HP/MP that you use in the usual turn-based format to launch your staple attack/magic/healing commands (given different names in this case, but still the same), and you run around from place-to-place viewing events. So if you’re looking for something that stretches boundaries you’ll be disappointed. But, if you can enjoy that style of old-school gameplay then Alpha Kimori is a very polished version of those styles. I should mention here that battles are not random but instead initiated by contacting enemy sprites on the field.
Story-wise things are interesting but feel a little scatter-brained, as if not all the dialogue is in the correct order. For instance our main characters occasionally have drastic shifts in their points of view within the very same discussion, rather than seeming like a solid progression from one view to the next over the course of several discussions. Still the story it’s trying to tell is interesting enough, there are plenty of tropes but it’s still trying to be its own property despite that. Similarly most of the characters are likable, the above mentioned shifting back-and-forth on positions sometimes detracts from them but in the end they’re mostly solid.
Some blatantly not so great points include there being a little too much backtracking for its own good as you revisit a small set of locations many times, it could have stood to have a few more songs for world locations and events (for instance it continues playing the bubbly, upbeat city theme even when events get serious which detracts from the scene taking place), and it’s very easy to begin with and even simpler if you spend more than a few minutes grinding with nothing coming close to beating you.
So make no mistake, if you don’t like this style of game then Alpha Kimori will NOT change your opinion on them. But if you do then this is a well-polished game that clearly has intent to go somewhere and should keep you content for the 5-7 hour playtime the first episode purports.

At first I went into this with some high expectations, but that turned out to be a bad way to enter this game. I can say the music is very much memorable and the mood of the game is never at a low point due to the colorfulness. However, the events were unfolding in a rather rushed manner at the start and some things made me think "this feels like something an elementary schooler would write". The characters weren't exactly weak but their development could have been handled better. I don't know anything about the development of this game but it wouldn't surprise me if this was a rather rushed job or just geared towards a younger audience in general. But on that note, Miku singing the theme song is supportive of the latter thought.
However I did enjoy the nostalgic turn based system, though with the large stat increases between levels I never really felt challenged until the very end, and it still wasn't that much of a challenge. Then again, that may have been intentional either because of the shortness of this entry (which I do hope isn't going to end up to be the last of this title) or a desire to minimize the tediousness of level grinding as can be experienced in other JRPG's or other RPG's in general.
Though as I progressed through the game it felt like things were improving, noticeably, in these areas I've mentioned. In the beginning some of the grammar and speech of the characters wasn't well written but became nearly natural closer to the end, and this is something that will be hard to miss when one plays for themself. Something about the very end of the game was rather strong, though I can't pinpoint what it was as some of the same mistakes could be spotted. I feel that the developers have the potential to do better in the next entry after seeing the end and I hope to see episode 2 in the future to see if my hopes aren't for naught.
Ultimately, try not to go in with high expectations like I did. This game is fun and worth the price if you're willing to get used to it as I did. It's short length (about 5 hours at my pace) was a bit of a letdown, but not crushingly so. I found myself satisfied with this game and don't regret taking the time out of my day to give it a try.

Alpha Kimori is a sci-fi Japanese-style RPG set on a planet that humans have colonized and fled to, and home to two warring factions: one that wants to reclaim Earth, and one that wants to live in peace on their new home.
This game is really bad.
In a good RPG, combat requires some tactical decisions and creative use of skills and abilities to beat tougher enemies. In Alpha Kimori, combat is purely a grind, with 99% of fights requiring nothing more than mashing Attack, 1% requiring the occasional Defend command to heal, and 0% of the fights requiring the use of a skill. The sole exception to this rule is the final battle, which is the game's only interesting fight. I highly recommend using JoyToKey and setting up a turbo controller so that it will do the button mashing for you.
In a good RPG, characters are deep and memorable, live in an interesting world, and take part in a grand story. In Alpha Kimori, the plot is dumb and predictable, the heroes have no interesting qualities, and the world is shallow.
Here's the plot: one faction likes to kill animals and people to drain their energy. Our heroes are the only few people that think that rampant murder might be wrong. So, after murdering a few hundred bunnies and birds, the heroes decide to abandon their home for another faction that is only a little less bloodthirsty. A few times, they remember the one defining moment in their lives (the one time someone said that killing was mean) in the form of about ten flashbacks to the same event. There's supposedly a romance in there too, but our leads have less chemistry than oil and water.
I should also mention that the quest design is awful. It mostly consists of running through the same dungeons over and over again, sometimes taking the long way around just to stretch out the game.
The graphics look decent, except that the character won't stay anywhere near the center of the screen. The music is upbeat but not at all memorable. The controls are sub-par, and the game is in desperate need of a sprint button.
I really only continued this game out of a morbid curiosity to see how bad it would get. The bad news is that this game really just isn't even entertaining. For most of my playtime with Alpha Kimori, I was actually playing Mario Golf and letting the turbo controller do all the heavy lifting. This game is a tedious mess, and I can't recommend it to anyone, even if you get it free.
The developer needs to get the first game right before continuing with this "trilogy".

An spoiler-free example:
Someone mentions, that this girl wants a word with you, so you head to her home.
The girl isn't there but you can talk to some stranger in her house, who tells you that she is in the flat of that dude upstairs.

Gladly, another random person tells you they are both at a top secret place, and because he's a nice guy he will tell you where it is.
IF you bring him this stone, which is unfortunately at the end of a place you already been three times.

Another example:
There is this super important tower which you have to get to immediately.

This basically the gameplay.
Someone tells you to grind through those three zones, you go back, to another port of your hometown, only to get told to go through the damn three zones again.

Alpha Kimori™ 1 is an RPG where the goal is to reclaim the Earth after an alien attack. Like usual, your character is super special and can help to save to world. You can harness power from Ki crystals, and control a large robot exoskeleton to assist you in your attacks.
Gameplay consists of the normal RPG maker fare. Click to select attack, click enemy to target, repeat. You can explore a few towns, including the large starting town, and encounter many battles in the overworld map. You can see the enemies on the map, so avoid them if you are tired of grinding.
The story did not really grip me in the beginning, and I quickly found myself clicking through dialogue to get to the next scene. The graphics are not much beyond the royalty free inclusions in RPG Maker. The music was ok, but could have been royalty free for all I know.
I must admit that JRPGs are not really my preferred game, beyond a select few. There really must be a good story behind them, and I really found it lacking here. I experienced as much as I could before I lost total interest, but sadly that time came very quickly. I can not recommend this unless you are desperately looking for a new JRPG to play, and you have exhausted all other options.

Critics of this game lament that the game is not orthodox enough and lacks solid object-oriented puzzles, but they are barking up the wrong tree and/or trying to fit a square into something that requires a circle. This game is not designed to tell you a story or test your IQ by presenting challenging puzzles. This game is about having fun -- loads and loads of it. I can't believe it's a free game, and if I had had to pay ~$5 for this game, I wouldn't have regretted it.

Game crashes right after instalation, giving and error of: File exception 622.
The solution is to do the following:
1. Go to the folder /Steam/SteamApps/common/Victoria 2/map/cache/
2. Delete all of the contents of this folder, but NOT the folder itself.
3. Go to the folder /Steam/SteamApps/common/Victoria 2/
4. Run v2game.exe
5. Your map cache should now be reconfigured. Exit the game.
6. You should now be able to run Victoria 2 normally, using the Victoria 2 launcher (victoria2.exe) or Steam.

Im so sorry Civ 5, Endless Legend is just better. Thats not easy for me to say, as i love Civ 5 more than any other game ive ever played. For years ive come back for one more turn, endlessly, never tiring of the game. Untill i bought Endless Legend after seeing it win 2014 game of the year on Rock Paper Shotgun. I bought it, and stumbled through the first few turns of a Drakken playthrough, and realized in those few turns that i was suddenly tired of Civ 5. I have said, "man i wish that feature was in here" or "they should but this and that in Civ BE (which they didnt) or "this needs to change in Civ 6" a million times. And all those changes i ever wanted were already there in endless legend. Entire armies of only unique units. Truly fully cusumizable units. Cities can expand in physical size on the map and encompass more tiles, till the planet looks like Coruscant. Truly unique factions, not just a weak bonus and one unique unit, i mean the factions are unreacognizable from each other. I mean one faction can even MOVE its cities somewhere else. Or this other one can literaly trick other players into siging and agreement that they dont want. another action quite literary feeds on the flesh of the other factions for growth. They are all truly disticnt, unlike civ 5 and BE's stale factions and units. If you were whatching a game were you couldnt see the name of a factions cities and could not see there factions color on civ 5, you probly couldnt tell two factions arpart, untill one of them builds there only unique unit. That will never be a problem in EL. Not only is every unit unique, but the city art is so lovingly crafted, a glance at a city and you know what faction owns it. Each faction has radically diferent architechture from the others. But enough on the aesthetic part of the game. The gameplay is something to behold. Because gameplay is different for all factions, ill just cover the basics. There are regions. Only one city cam be built in a region, and that city is named after the region its constructed in. Once a cities constructed, a farm or any other tile improvement (called exploitations) are automatically built on the tiles surrounding a city. As your population grows, you gain workers. Workers dont roam the map, but instead are assigned in cities to work a specific type of tile, not an individual tile. Cities expand to new tiles by building districts, which expands  the size of the city by adding a new bock. Coin is replaced by dust, which is money, and has magical purposes as well. Luxary resoursces are used to create empire boost, which cost a amount of resource, so having large quanities of the smae luxary is very beneficial. Ifluence is used to make deals, and assimilate villages, which are a mix of barbarians and city states. There are so many diferent systems in this game i cant possilby cover them all. Just buy the game and play it.

A fun alternative to Civilization.  The factions are quite varied in their aesthetic and play-style, the setting is interesting and the core 4X functionality is well realised.  It also does a better job than its peers in making non-combat win scenarios possible and (generally) fun to achieve.  The game generally flows at a good pace, with minimal periods where you are either overwhelmed with things to do or bored with nothing to do but press 'next turn'.
The game is not without its flaws.  Many units are currently underpowered, resulting in combat being more mono-dimensional than it is supposed to be.  The quest system needs work too, with the randomness making some quests either pointlessly easy (eg do something you are already one turn from completing) or near-enough to impossible (eg get to a point on the far side of the world, past the territory of multiple enemy factions, in X turns).  Similarly, quest rewards are so random they can either be utterly useless (sometimes even awarding technologies you already possess) or nigh game-breaking (eg technology that makes your army dramatically more powerful than anyone else can possibly field).

Endless Legend took me by surprise. I have been a huge Civilization 5 player, with 263 hours on file at the moment, and my heart had always belonged with that game. I recently found interest in Endless Legend and purchased it and I think its a game that every fan of the 4x genre should play or at least look into.
Pros:
1. Beautiful, intriguing world. Tons of inventive lore infused throughout the game.
2. Emphasis on effective empire management. City-building, economy balancing, and researching the tech-circles are really fun. There is also a great emphasis on resource management, each worker you unlock can be placed in different points of emphasis for more resource gain. If you are play a science victory you may want more workers placed in science production to research quickly. If you are playing a supremacy race you may be more interested in placing your workers in industry so you can build units/city expansions quicker, etc...
3. Combat is done nicely. You can choose to tactically face your opponent in a way that sort of reminds me of Heroes of Might and Magic. It is turn-based and there may be some strategy. If you don't like that you can choose to spectate and watch the computer make your moves for you or you can just auto-resolve and move on. If you auto-resolve or spectate, you can choose for the computer to be aggressive or passive as well. You can also upgrade units with new weapons that you can craft through the research tree, or find in quests.
4. Different factions that actually play quite differently. Some factions just simply cannot do certain things. Such as the necrophage, they can't create peace treaties. They are simply a faction that is meant to kill everything. Playing as the necrophage you may want to push all your workers into industry in order to build your improvements/milita quicker. Playing as the ardent mages you may want to move your workers into science production so that you can rush through the research tree and race to a science victory. There is even a faction that relies solely upon Dust (the games gold currency).
4. Some innovative features that haven't been seen in 4x genre. For example: race-specific quest lines that actually serve as a unique victory condition, seasonal effects (summer/winter), the concept of regions limiting city placement, reinforcements, how heroes are handled (as generals or governors), etc., etc.
5. The seasonal affects may actually impact some factions play. I know that whenever I enter the winter my production slows greatly. I end up losing roughly 60 gold per turn and most of the units can only move 1 space or so.
6. You can assimilate with minor factions and build/upgrade their units once you acquire them. They also have bonuses that they will provide to your city once you control them.
7. The artstyle is very intriguing.
8. It isn't like other 4x titles. In fact it does a very good job at seperating itself from other 4x titles (civ 5, age of wonders, etc..)
9. You can create your own factions with all the different perks and army units that are provided in the base game. So if you don't like the factions that are in the game you can customize your own from the bottom up.
Cons:
1. A.I. is kind of bad with certain factions. With the Drakken they are really strong but with some of the other factions they act kind of stupid. This is the game's greatest downfall. But with the modding community helping this out and patches still being worked on (i think) this will come to an end hopefully.
2. It would be cool if there were more factions. I'm sure there are other factions you can download through mods but it would've been cool to see more than just 9 factions in the base game.
3. To some this is a con: The game is not as easily learned as something like Civ 5. Each turn you have to remember where your units were, you have to remember which direction they were heading, and what they were doing. There is more micromanaging in this game with emphasis on what workers produce which things. There are some things you may even have to wiki as well. There is a lot of things you will just learn the more you play considering the game doesn't really hold your hand at all. Even the tutorial is very basic and doesn't quite go over everything you will face in the game itself.
Summary:
When i play this game i instantly compare this game to an RPG. There are very many RPG like elements that are fused with the 4x style and this game does it VERY well. The artstyle is very unique and the way it plays is somewhat similar to what HeroScape was like back in the day. In my opinion it is more smooth that Civ 5 and there is more thought that is required within each turn. There aren't many situtations where you will just sit there and continuously hit the end-turn button. There is always a goal in each turn whether it is working towards the factions quests, trying to parley and assimilate with a minor faction, or expand. Yes, the AI needs improvement, but overall I think this is a great game. I wouldn't even say that the AIs mistakes are as noticeable as some of the other strategy games that exist. Playing on higher difficulties even create a loss more often than not so I think that creates a nice challenge sometimes.

I bought the game in late 2014, before it came to steam,  and it's a game I've come back to at least once every couple of weeks since then. It's got great replay value, and each update has brought more and more things to explore.
I am a particular fan of the writings of H.P. Lovecraft, and the game evokes a strong lovecraftian sense of horror, brought out even further by the text being presented in the style of a first person journal.
The theme of the game really draws you in and, from reading interviews, I saw that it was influenced by Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, which I decided to pick up. It has a lot of powerful imagery, particularly in conjuring the sense of being utterly alone in the jungle, with just a thin barrier of trees between you and the incomprehensibly vast wilderness. That detachment from civilisation comes through incredibly well in The Curious Expedition, especially in the descriptions of the campsite at night - the alien sounds, the foreign smells, the endless darkness - it all serves to immerse you in that unfamiliar world.
I highly recommend this game to all who will listen, and I look forward to discovering all the secrets in the updates to come.

After almost 20 hours I realize what this game is trying to do, it's a fine game, but not more than 5 dollars in fines.
You're Roland in jurassic park 2, a hunter that got so bored with deer he became bald and decided to hunt dinosaurs.
A dinosaur shooter can have you replace the dinosaurs with pokemons, or zombies, it won't feel much different, you shoot the small once, the big twice.
However this is a hunting game, with dinosaurs. Hunting games have its roots in realism, covering mechanics of smell, wind, weather, anatomy, bullet calibres, camouflage. These features all play a part in your success of hunting the prey. In other words, shooting everything in the face won't work out when your'e facing an animal with the skull thickness of armor plating on a T51 tank and the capability kill you before you finish reloading a magazine.
The game doesn't give many tools, because it wants to be a survival game, they expect people to come in, know how hunting games work, and apply that to survivalism and dinosaurs, when most people think this is killing floor with dinosaurs, myself included.
A big realization of the difference of this game is, how your prey will almost always outrun you when its health gets low. This occurs almost all the time, provided that everyone spawns with a knife at level 1, they run faster, hit harder, and have more bodies than you.
So what do you do to succeed, you run, you hide, you scavenge other players bodies, and abandoned outposts for weapons.
Because in this game, access to weapons doesn't mean it gets easier, it just allows you to make more mistakes. A player can use a bow and one shot a triceratops if you aim for its heart and because ammo is limited, it is encouraged to do so.
You hide in the woods, listen for the noise and stalk the pack, finding one triceratops by itself muching grass, by watching the foliage you figure out the wind direction, staying downwind, so it can't detect you by smell, you crouch up to its side of the belly, drawing the bow, aiming for the spot behind the joint of the foreleg, a direct hit pierces its heart and kills it instantly, while the kid that plays call of duty is shooting it with a 50 cal, 11 times on the crown of its skull doing 1% total damage.

If you miss, you aim for its lungs, then its intestines, because it won't run as far without proper respirations, and it will bleed out if you shoot it in the intestines.
I hope this helps you understand this game better.

Part of the reason I played Amnesia: Memories - my first Otome game - is because of an early GameCenter DX episode. Shinya Arino was challenged to win somebody's heart in
, an entry in a highly-regarded Otome series. Despite spending 13 hours, following guides, and doing seemingly everything right, his confession of love to Seiran was met with: "It's 1000 years too soon for you to make fun of me. Wash your face and try again." Working so hard only to fail has to be absolutely heart-wrenching, and yet...strangely exciting.
The strength of a game is in its ability to engage everyone outside of its target audience. On the surface, an Otome game involves romancing attractive men, which to a straight male gamer like myself, doesn't sound all that enticing. However, by utilizing a compelling narrative and/or intriguing game-play elements, I'll find myself immersed in every aspect of the game. Despite my inexperience with the genre, I believe Amnesia: Memories is a fantastic game. It couples a strong plot with great characters, and the few game-play elements bring everything together.
Due to the meddling of a strange kid named Orion, you've lost your memories. As pay-back for the mess he's put you in, Orion offers to guide you through five parallel worlds. In each world, you meet the same characters, but their personalities - as well as yours - are different. Moreover, the world you choose determines which man you could have a serious relationship with. There are other events that can occur, some funny, some dangerous, but all worth experiencing. Whether you find true love, see the story to its conclusion, or even meet a miserable end, is all determined by what you say and the actions that you perform.
As in real life, the lack of communication can ruin any relationship. Due to your amnesia, you won't know the right thing to say, so you'll have to pay attention to conversations and keep track of the details. While it would be very easy to use a guide and guarantee the best endings, I think actually putting in the effort to know someone is far more rewarding. On the other hand, my initial play-throughs mostly resulted in failure, so maybe I'm not cut out for videogame relationships. The point is that the less hints you have to work with, the more likely you'll become attached to the person you're interested in.
As your story progresses, a handy chart tracks your relationship with the male lead, as well as suspicions due to your lack of memories. It's amusing that one of the few distinctly "game-like" elements actually isn't all that effective. For one, it isn't always clear whenever you say the right or wrong thing. Orion or one of the other characters may chime in, but sometimes you're left in the dark. The charts are more likely to shift when your attention is elsewhere, not when you're saving, reloading, and looking for the slightest change in your "does he love me?" gauge. Furthermore, this is all the more reason to not refer to a guide early on. After all, real relationships aren't forged through the use of cheat-sheets.
As for the guys themselves, I think the writers did a fantastic job giving them plenty of depth. I mean sure, they're attractive enough, but that's to be expected. The most appealing aspect is finding out what they're really all about, and discovering just how much they care. These guys know exactly what to say and when to say it, so those special moments really have a lot of impact. The average story takes about 4-5 hours to complete, and if you're really into someone, there's going to be those few times where he'll really turn up the charm. I'll admit, I get a little light-headed whenever Shin blushes. On the other hand, a couple of the storylines are more intriguing and disturbing than they are romantic. If you've browsed the community hub, or read some of the other reviews, you'll know exactly what I'm talking about. If not, then my advice is to play through the stories from top to bottom, exactly as they're listed in the game. In any case, there are more than enough dark and mysterious elements that make for very compelling entertainment.
This game also benefits from having high production values. Aside from the heroine, everyone is fully-voiced, and the acting is more than serviceable. The CG scenes are very nicely drawn, and the soundtrack is decent enough for setting the mood. The fast-forward system makes replays a breeze, and the mini-games are an amusing diversion. The backgrounds are a little washed-out and bland, but they're the last thing you'll notice when playing the game. Again, this is my very first experience with the genre, but I can tell that the developers really cared to deliver an appealing product. Although, I did notice a few typos in this localization. It's nothing major, especially considering the size of the game, but all the same it's worth mentioning.
All in all, Amnesia: Memories is a superb example of an Otome Visual Novel. Not only are the stories well-told, but the characters are endearing, and everything looks and sounds wonderful.. It'll take 25+ hours to experience all of the content, so anyone out there wondering if they'll get their money's worth doesn't need to be concerned. Still, I have to admit that I'm a little frustrated with myself. I played through all of the stories and not once was I able to get a good ending without a guide. There was always that one moment where I treated the guy I was dating as a third wheel, or didn't appreciate his gestures of affection, or failed his math test. Ahh...if only relationships were as easy to understand as
.

As like many Otome games, there is obviously a lack of realism. However, trudging through some of the weird premise that all the boys love you without any memories, you'll find a pretty intricate foundation for the world of Amnesia. I found it pretty fascinating in the aspect for world building. I've always been interested in a visual novel that basically goes backwards (due to amnesia).  Story-wise, it's a lot deeper than it appears. It may seem shallow at first, but once added together it has some depth and darkness. It's eerily dark and convoluted for an otome, actually.
A note: Unfortunately, I wouldn't recommend it to a male audience. I imagine it would be well welcomed by girls (because it's made for girls). The game is also based on Japanese culture, so some parts may not relatable to a Western audience(?).
Game-wise, while I enjoyed the routes to some degree, half of the characters lacked the development they needed/deserved in their respective routes. A lot of issues especially with Toma and Ukyo are shoved under the rug rather than resolved in a constructive and healthy way. I'm assuming that this may be addressed in the sequel games (Amnesia Later).
I really like the characters themselves! Possibly the only reason I continued to read. Their relationship web, aside from the MC, made them a lot more likable. I'm also a sucker for reminiscing in any medium.

Very unbalanced, seemingly unfinished even for an episode.  You could grind and buy the weapons and armor in the stores like I did, but nearly everything but the shields are given to you just by wandering around. Everything else in the shops is priced at nearly 1/10 of that.  Lots of artificially forcing you to walk everywhere, with tight corners to force you to battle monsters.  Oddly inserted fetch quests, having to randomly grab 50 of an item, which I conveniently had through grinding.
Near the end of episode 1, I was Level 37 with all the equipment upgrades and could crash through scores of enemies without really needing to heal (even outside of battles). But the last boss fight of the episode nearly slaughtered me.
Supposedly your character wants to live without killing or hurting, but you can't help but slaughter the local wildlife.
.  There were several battles where I'd defeat the super-powerful boss and then the plot would still show me defeated.  I was death on RPG rails and everyone called me lazy and under-achieving.  It doesn't seem like your performance affects the plot much.  In fact, only 3-4 skills per character at Level 37.  Pretty vanilla for the understated town badass. I don't think I'd try it on the minimum specs.  Maybe it was the AMD drivers, but more visually impressive games are smoother and less demanding.  It's probably RPGMaker, which never seems to be smooth in full screen mode.  The game didn't seem like it would run in windowed mode, though (Alt+Enter).  It would show a window, but only display 1/4 of the screen in it.
It has potential, but because of the plot on rails it seems more like I'm playing a visual novel with a high encounter rate than an RPG.  Seriously, one weapon upgrade.  It
be worth $5 (half the price), but I'd look around and catch it in a bundle or on sale, rather than paying full price.  2D JRPGs are nostalgic, but it's not like they're uncommon, even today. - The Meiji Restoration of Japan

Endless Legend took me by surprise. I have been a huge Civilization 5 player, with 263 hours on file at the moment, and my heart had always belonged with that game. I recently found interest in Endless Legend and purchased it and I think its a game that every fan of the 4x genre should play or at least look into.
Pros:
1. Beautiful, intriguing world. Tons of inventive lore infused throughout the game.
2. Emphasis on effective empire management. City-building, economy balancing, and researching the tech-circles are really fun. There is also a great emphasis on resource management, each worker you unlock can be placed in different points of emphasis for more resource gain. If you are play a science victory you may want more workers placed in science production to research quickly. If you are playing a supremacy race you may be more interested in placing your workers in industry so you can build units/city expansions quicker, etc...
3. Combat is done nicely. You can choose to tactically face your opponent in a way that sort of reminds me of Heroes of Might and Magic. It is turn-based and there may be some strategy. If you don't like that you can choose to spectate and watch the computer make your moves for you or you can just auto-resolve and move on. If you auto-resolve or spectate, you can choose for the computer to be aggressive or passive as well. You can also upgrade units with new weapons that you can craft through the research tree, or find in quests.
4. Different factions that actually play quite differently. Some factions just simply cannot do certain things. Such as the necrophage, they can't create peace treaties. They are simply a faction that is meant to kill everything. Playing as the necrophage you may want to push all your workers into industry in order to build your improvements/milita quicker. Playing as the ardent mages you may want to move your workers into science production so that you can rush through the research tree and race to a science victory. There is even a faction that relies solely upon Dust (the games gold currency).
4. Some innovative features that haven't been seen in 4x genre. For example: race-specific quest lines that actually serve as a unique victory condition, seasonal effects (summer/winter), the concept of regions limiting city placement, reinforcements, how heroes are handled (as generals or governors), etc., etc.
5. The seasonal affects may actually impact some factions play. I know that whenever I enter the winter my production slows greatly. I end up losing roughly 60 gold per turn and most of the units can only move 1 space or so.
6. You can assimilate with minor factions and build/upgrade their units once you acquire them. They also have bonuses that they will provide to your city once you control them.
7. The artstyle is very intriguing.
8. It isn't like other 4x titles. In fact it does a very good job at seperating itself from other 4x titles (civ 5, age of wonders, etc..)
9. You can create your own factions with all the different perks and army units that are provided in the base game. So if you don't like the factions that are in the game you can customize your own from the bottom up.
Cons:
1. A.I. is kind of bad with certain factions. With the Drakken they are really strong but with some of the other factions they act kind of stupid. This is the game's greatest downfall. But with the modding community helping this out and patches still being worked on (i think) this will come to an end hopefully.
2. It would be cool if there were more factions. I'm sure there are other factions you can download through mods but it would've been cool to see more than just 9 factions in the base game.
3. To some this is a con: The game is not as easily learned as something like Civ 5. Each turn you have to remember where your units were, you have to remember which direction they were heading, and what they were doing. There is more micromanaging in this game with emphasis on what workers produce which things. There are some things you may even have to wiki as well. There is a lot of things you will just learn the more you play considering the game doesn't really hold your hand at all. Even the tutorial is very basic and doesn't quite go over everything you will face in the game itself.
Summary:
When i play this game i instantly compare this game to an RPG. There are very many RPG like elements that are fused with the 4x style and this game does it VERY well. The artstyle is very unique and the way it plays is somewhat similar to what HeroScape was like back in the day. In my opinion it is more smooth that Civ 5 and there is more thought that is required within each turn. There aren't many situtations where you will just sit there and continuously hit the end-turn button. There is always a goal in each turn whether it is working towards the factions quests, trying to parley and assimilate with a minor faction, or expand. Yes, the AI needs improvement, but overall I think this is a great game. I wouldn't even say that the AIs mistakes are as noticeable as some of the other strategy games that exist. Playing on higher difficulties even create a loss more often than not so I think that creates a nice challenge sometimes.

I am not big into writing reviews, however, after seeing how many "Positive" reviews there are of this game, I thought I would put in my two cents as to why I believe that this game should be removed from the store, even though its free, and either be re-worked by the developer or scraped.
1) Dialogue / Voice Acting: The diagloge throughout the game has no quote worhty lines and I ended up muting it on my second playthrough because once you play through the game and know where to go and when, the dialogue and voice acting serve only to detract from the gameplay.
2) Level Design: The levels are short and sweet, which is something I appreciate, however despite the small levels there seems to have been very little work put in to their development and they are bland/uninteresting. Also, if steps aren't followed in a precise order, the level has to be restarted, and can be very frustrating.
3) UI / Menu Navigation: There is no UI. Which is fine, however even the menu has horrible navigation. The only options available are to quit or continue. No subtitles are available. Volume within the game is unadjustable. The only options within the game are found at launch, which is the screen resolution, graphic quality, and controls.
4) Plot: Interesting concept. Horribly executed. Plot is developed entirely through dialogue and my comments on that can be found above.
All in all, I don't think this game should be offered on the store, even for free. I can appreciate that it may be hard to develop a game as a one-man/woman development team, however, that leaves no excuse for poor execution and if you are debating on creating a game by yourself, please keep an idea of what a good game requires in your mind.
