This game is hilarious, beautifully-crafted, and addictive. It's wonderful in its simplicity, infinitely replayable, and every patch improves the game significantly. I've been playing for nearly a year now, and have no intention of stopping -- what is more, playing a single game has successfully turned several of my friends into committed players too. Heck, it'd be an excellent party game, where a room full of people vote on the decisions the expedition should make. I paid $13.99 for this last year, and I don't regret one cent of that.
A special note of thanks should be made towards the Germans who've made this. The makers of the game are so dedicated to their craft and to their customers that when I bought it last year in its earliest Alpha stages, it was better than most triple-A games at release. They are so dedicated that when they released a fun Halloween patch last year that nearly broke the game, they immediately released a patch to fix every single problem. They are so dedicated that, even though they added some truly odd characters (Harriet Tubman? Marcus Garvey I get, but...Harriet Tubman?!), they actually make all the characters WORK in the context of the game: Nikola Tesla has a death ray! Sir Richard Francis Burton can speak to all natives! Charles Darwin gains Sanity by collecting butterflies! They are so dedicated that when they added H.P. Lovecraft to the game, they programmed him with a secret, unique code that will only make sense to people familiar with his personal life. They are so dedicated that I keep forgetting that this game is STILL in Alpha! They could easily release it now without changing a thing! But they care so much, they are keeping it in Alpha until it fits their exacting standards.
UPDATE: This game has officially launched, is better than ever, and just keeps getting better! Also, fans of Lovecraft will especially love the new Arctic regions... Even the new explorers are awesome! I'm just sad they haven't added some ancient explorers from Egypt, Greece or Persia.

This is actually my first review of a game (I believe), so I'll try to be very honest.
I got this game in a bundle, and was thinking that this would be similar to Savage Lands, or Rust or any other game like that. Instead, I got very happy when I found out your main objective is to HUNT DINOSSAURS, which sounds and should be extremely awesome and fun. Instead what you get is a barely playable piece of garbageware.
There are several things wrong with this game, but I'll start with the few that ARE good:
- For the size of the island and the amount of things it renders, it runs very smoothly compared to other similar games, that are usually terribly optimized for PC;
- The dinossaur models look really nice. They did an awesome job modeling these creatures;
- The sound plays a very important role, which is always nice;
- Multiplayer hosting is very easy and straight forward;
And that's basicly all there is good to it.
Everything else is pretty bad:
- You can't run 50 metres without running out of stamina. Remember that you are playing a game where you fight dinossaurs, often bigger and faster than you, and you cannot run enough to dodge their attacks. I read the forums, some people view this as CHALLENGE, where I just view it being abnoxious, because the very moment you find yourself at the wrong end of a dinossaur, you're done for.
- Did I mention that the stamina you use for running is also the same stamina used for attacking? That makes a hit & run strategy completely out of the question. you either hit and die or run and die a little bit later.
- The fact that you can't run makes playing with friends extremely annoying, since when you die, you respawn nearly a mile away from a friend, and
- Your initial weapons are pretty much useless. Regardles of how much you manage to dodge the dinossaurs and attack, the moment the dinossaurs feel like they're getting too hurt, they run away instantly. This makes sense, and I can imagine it would lead to extremely fun moments where you'd race against the dinossaur or stalk him to his nest if, you know,
- Regardless of the dinossaur's difficulty, they're pretty dumb. If you circle them by the tail they'll just endlessly turn with you. Ocasionally they'll try to run forward and turn around to gain some space, but if you go after them you'll get them by the tails again.
- There are smaller dinossaurs in the island that are actually killable. I figured they'd be for early-game, for people to hunt down these easier dinossaurs until you progress and unlock better stuff to kill the big dinossaurs with. Big F-ing nope. They attack you, take life easily from you if they're in a group, and give you nothing at all if you kill every single one of them. Not a single G.
- The game is very undecisive when it comes to movement in various terrains. You aren't allowed to jump, but you can take fall damage from very small falls. You can climb up mountains that almost make 90 degrees with the ground at regular speed as if it were nothing, but good luck trying to go back down. Yeah, apparently all the dinossaur dung on top of the mountain made your feet slippery, and as soon as you touch the ground to climb down again you'll instantly slip and fall to your death.
I could go on for several more points, but I feel like these are the main decisive points on why I recommend people to avoid buying this game. I have played bad games on Steam and never wrote a review on them, but I had to for this game, for the simple reason that it had everything needed to be a great game, and in the end it feels more like a slap in the face for ever buying it.

In Amnesia: Memories, you first open your eyes to a vast empty space which - you soon learn - is the gateway to many parallel realities. You then meet a spirit (Orion) who basically tells you that he's stuck inside your consciousness; his collision being the cause of your memory loss. The first major choice you make in the game is to pick which reality/world you came from: Heart, Spade, Clover or Diamond, i.e. according to the motifs associated with each of your love interests. There's also an unlockable world (Joker) you can only get after achieving good endings in the other realities.
(5/5)

General Review:
As someone who plays countless of Otome Visual Novel style games, this one was absolutely beautiful and I would recommend this game if you love otome games that have bad endings or if you're a crazy person that loves getting 100 percent achievements out of a VN/Otome. This one isn't quite as amazing bad ending wise, as other Otome games but - There still were many bad ends with several CG's, and it allows for further interactions later.
1) Music: 8/10. The music Looped really well, and I didn't get annoyed with it despite playing the game continually from start to finish.
2) Voice/Translation: 10/10. The voices came out really well and I actually liked all of the male actor's voices in this. In the story, and the "extras" which I won't spoil. There were no bugs or typos in the translated to English version.
3) Artwork: 10/10. This was beautiful. All of the CG's/Artwork was impeccable with this. I didn't find any weird looking scenes or anything off with any of them. All of the characters looked like themselves, and MC looked pretty in any of them where you see her.
4) Characters: 8/10. There's a few things I didn't like which I'll place in spoilers, ordered by who I liked best (A), to who I didn't like much.(E)
A. Toma
B. Shin
C. Secret Path
D. Kent
E. Ikki
5) Story: I haven't watched the Anime Entirely yet, so I'm not certain how much of this comes from the Anime or if the Anime was made based on this game, BUT - The storylines here get pretty deep and they all have at least one or two things in common. I do think that overall the story was really good, but it had a few places where the story seemed to be a little slow, or a few extra days where they weren't really adding much to the story. I also want to say that some of the bad ends I would have prefered to see CG's on. They didn't really seem to have much "closure" and the fade to red thing seemed a bit cheap, given how hard some of those ends are to find.
Things I liked:
*CG Menu.
I liked the fact that you have the cg with ability to scroll over and see the whole image as some of the cg images are rather huge. I also liked that they're organized by the character's name, as it makes it easier to browse though.
*Extra stories/Minigames:
I liked the extra stories that you can unlock, as well as the minigames. At first you don't realise that some of the things are only unlocked by playing these.
*Bonus True Ending: TL;DR: That path ties everything together and makes the game make sense.
Things I didn't like:
* No ability to Replay Endings from the Endings menu.
I didn't like this because while it is fine to replay a game, It's really hard to remember what the right choices were if you have "already seen" answers highlighted.
Advice on what I would do differently:  If you could have the ability to re-watch the full story with an ending that you already unlocked. Then have the game just let you click/confirm the choices for you since you've already unlocked the path. That's something I haven't seen in any other otome game.
*MC wasn't voiced. I don't like this because in auto mode, if MC says something, it skips over it instantly.
*Spoiler for CG's:
Bonus:

This game is a perfect example of why plataformers were so popular in the 90s. It will test your skill and reflexes, and will also deliver scenarios where you'll need to be clever to continue, which makes progress very rewarding. You control a humanoid creature called Abe who has no fighting skills at all, you only means to attack will be whatever the environment provides you (most notably mind control, but also grenades or even explosive farts :D).
The objective of the game is to save your fellow mudokons (creatures similar to you), who you guide by talking to them and telling them what to do; while staying out of the many dangers presented to you and them. It is a difficult game by today's standards, but the learning curve is balanced enough to let you learn the mechanics before becoming really challenging (secret areas are challenging from the very begging tho, so beware). Also the presence of a quicksave feature will make the journey less tedious.
The game is not very long (long enough for its price tag tho), but its packed with secret areas that are more challenging than the main game and will extend the playthrough time. Sadly there's little replay value (except maybe for saving them all / killing them all), but i enjoy playing it over again from time to time.
Runs perfect in my low end pc, I haven't had any issue so far.
A timeless classic, a sequel that improves its predecessor, and a must-have if you even remotely like plataforming or stealth games.

One of my favourite games of all time. I replay this game and its prequel every year or so.
Abe has tight and weighty movement controls. Some might take a while to get use to it, but it is very intentional and they are better implimented than many other cinematic platformers.
The game is full of fanastically designed enviomental puzzles. Requiring stealth, timing, problem solving, possession of enemies and of course gamespeak, which is a mechanic that allows Abe to communicate with his fellow slaves to attempt to rescue them. "Hello" "Hello" "Follow Me" "Okay".
Fanastic visual art design all around. Character design and animation, background art, and the atmosphere and mood of oddworld are all absurdly well crafted, especially for the time of release.
The sound design and music is top notch. Nice psuedo-industrial, ambient pieces that add so much to the atmosphere.
Also your money goes straight to Oddworld Inhabitants to help develop more Oddworld games in the future (minus what goes to Valve of course), no publisher taking major cuts.
Highly recommended, along with Abes Oddysee.

So, I am one of the fans that buys the game each year no matter what, but I am not biased. This is only the beta version (the full release will be launched in 4th November) .
1.  There is more information than ever, which is easy to access in the panels. Before and after each game you receive a report from your analyst in which you can find every information about the opponent. Yes, in the editions before you could only have a report about the next opponent, but not one after the match. Now, in FM 17 your analyst will compile a summary of the match after it's finished and you can see what went good / wrong. This saves you time of analysing each stat after a game. In my opinion this is one of the most powerful features of FM 17.
2. The game runs on 64-bits if you have a 64-bit OS and CPU. This is great because you can feel how fast and responsive the game is.
3. This might be a minor change / addition, but the new skin (the green one) is excellent. Easy on the eye, easy to read and pleasant even at night.
4. I've played about 20-30 games so far and I can really say that this match engine is good. No more overpowered crosses to the back / near post. No more unmarked fullbacks and ultra-concentrated game in the middle. I tried 4-5 different tactics (4-4-2 diamond narrow, 4-4-2 flat, 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1 wide and a strikerless one). Each of these tactics worked as you would expect it too.
5. Scouting not has a new option when you want to get information about a new player (Scout until full knowledge). Not a big deal, but it's a welcome addition.
6. The pre-season takes longer then before because you recieve more information and therefor, you access more information. Also, signing a player take a tidy bit longer because of the negociations and so is when offering a new contract to one of your players (in most cases).
When FM 16 came out I was very excited because I loved the interface, the responsiveness of the game, even the way the font popped out on the background itself. In short, I loved it. The problem was in the match engine and I have to say that it was the biggest dissapointment I ever had in FM. The opponent was defending so narrow that it would leave acres of space down the flanks so your fullbacks were always unmarked. It was almost pointless to play an AMC because you would NEVER take advantage if his creativity since he will 90% of the situations just pass it down the flanks where were your unmarked fullbacks. The second issue was the overpowered crosses.  Because of these 2 big problems I felt compelled to revert back to FM15 (which I loved). Now, FM 17 looks even better than FM16 and the match engine is very good (given the fact that it's only a beta). By the way, I haven't seen any major or big bugs in the game so far. FM15 was a very good edition which provided great functionality, a more than decent match engine, but it felt a bit laggy overall.
1. The player models in 3D on the pitch and the ball itself need some tweaking, minor touches. The ball looks a bit too bright and the player's jerseys seem a bit unclear if you use a distant camera (elevated).
2. The colors in Football Manager Light Skin need serious improvement. It has very bad contrast in every aspect. However, the dark skin and the new one (green) look very good.
Honestly, I am trying hard to think of "bad things" in FM17. After the backlash they got for FM16 match engine, the developers corrected their mistakes big time and they added a lot of new things upon that. Regarding the match engine, I think the progression has stalled because of the setback in FM16, but the good news is that now it's playable and really enjoyable. I hope you find this review useful.

Don't let the "Mostly Negative" fool you it seems to just be more than a few disgruntled Chinese players who are annoyed there's still no Chinese language feature. Now for my review.
My first 3 hours have been great and have reminded me why this is the only game series I bother pre-ordering. The new UI looks a lot sharper and cleaner but will still be familiar to players of the series. The new social media feature is also pretty cool as well in my opinion. So far in the beta I've encountered no game breaking bugs or any bugs for that matter, and the fact that in my Arsenal save (COYG) I lost a first team player for 2 months to injury during a damn intrasquad friendly tells me the game is working well. I will keep updating this review throughout the beta but for now this game is looking like money well spent.
EDIT: I do often wonder at times in FM games how much of an effect your tactics truly have. You can set up a high class team against some distinctly lower level opposition to play control but rarely will you ever feel like you've truly dominated a match and had a one sided outing as does happen in real life. Of course large teams don't always have their way but they do more often than not. Also, and this was the case in 16 as well, it seems that as soon as you score the opposition will always fire back almost immediately, regardless of your defensive setup or how the match was going beforehand. I'd like to know if the rest of you are having the same gripes as I am though I am happy to report that I have yet to encounter any really game breaking bugs only one instance where my manager avatar got deleted for some reason.
EDIT: It's gotten to a point where I genuinely believe that the match engine will just ♥♥♥♥ with you whether or not it makes sense. I've had matches where I concede within two minutes despite having my world class defenders against much lesser opposition. After maybe 40 minutes we'll bounce back, not two minutes later the opposition has the lead again and this happens no matter who you're playing against. I also feel my tactical instructions will be ignored, I set my team up to clear the ball to flanks but all balls go straight down the middle, shorter passing never works and the team constantly loses the ball with hopeless overhead through ball attempts. At this point I'm not sure whether or not selecting "Retain Possession" even does anything. For better or worse though this is the closest thing to football management and as such I will still reccomend it but oh my it seems the same old flaws keep repeating, making the game force feed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to players does not constitute balanced difficulty in the slightest. Veterans of the series will encounter the same issues in a prettier engine and new players will have to steel themselves and prepare for inevitable rage quits. Is FM the Dark Souls of football sims? Seems like it's trying to be.

So, you think you're pretty good with a controller, do you? Here's your chance to prove it. "TorqueL" is a "controller ONLY" game, and while it's a simple game for anyone to play successfully, to exceed one must be a controller MASTER!
The goal is simple, and common, enough. Move yourself, a figure in a small, box, from point A to point B. (I haven't played much over an hour or so, and I presume the game becomes far more complex that what I will have the experience to describe.) The box can roll by means of the left stick. But the box can also be launched in any direction. And not just four directions, but conceivable ANY of 360 degrees. Each side of the box has a color which corresponds to a controller button. Pressing that button rapidly shoots out a "rod", sending the box in the opposite direction. But should you desire, any combination or number of the four buttons can be pressed. This allows an average (or less) player such as myself the option to suspend the box in space in potentially dangerous locations, allowing me to plan and act slowly and with caution.
Dangerous, I said? Yes, since every "pool" (maybe not, since they can also be on the ceiling) of red is deadly, and any contact will cause instant death, and make the level restart automatically. Fortunately, the button-generated rods can be held, freezing them in an extended position. A Controller Master can no doubt FLY across a layout, never pressing any but THE perfect button as they roll and fly. I can't, so I'll press all buttons as necessary, and carefully control the buttons and the stick to slowly move the box into the best, next position. But apparently time is tracked, cumulatively, so speed is very much a factor.
But there's more to "TorqueL"! There are also areas that change the direction of gravity (more like "Super Goo Goo" than "Gravity Error", both very worthwhile games.) Not necessarily just up and down reversals, but horizontal as well. And several of these areas can be alongside each other, creating a situation requiring great skill indeed!
I notice on the Store Page trailer that at a further point a family element is added to the box, so I presume some form of story may be involved. The Store Page references 50 levels, seven basic routes and one secret route.
TorqueL IS a fun game, and I learn something about control on pretty much every level. Once I gain comfort with the controller (which I intend to) I should be better able to play other controller games as well. I got TorqueL at discount, about $7US, and even that was a bit high. As much fun as this game is, I fear most players would feel $10US is quite high, compared to similar arcade/puzzle games. (I say "similar, but nothing is "comparable".) The choice is yours.

Disclaimer: review copy received from the developer.
TorqueL is unique because player movement within the game is unlike that of any other game. That makes it a new kind of challenge; a level design which would be simple beyond belief in a regular platformer isn't so simple in TorqueL. If you like platformers that break the mold... this one really does.
As I write this, the game has no other positive reviews because there are no checkpoints and no saves and the developers did that on purpose. When I asked the developer why, he said that he didn't want people starting from the middle without the muscle memory developed in the earlier levels, since getting through later levels depends on techniques mastered in earlier levels. He also said that players who are really good at the game can get through the earlier levels in short order anyway. The game is designed around mastering the systems and getting better and better at the game through repetition.
In short, this game is aimed at the kind of person who enjoys speed runs and skill mastery rather than the casual platformer player.

I'm pretty torn on this game.  You're thrown into a new world through an escape pod and left with a machete and a map chip to help guide you through an expansive world.  Your apparent objective is to hunt down as many dinosaurs before succumbing to your inevitable demise.  Once you die, your equipment and your body is left to be eaten while a "family member" is spawned at a random place nearby.  If you want that equipment back, you basically have to trek through the jungles and mountains to regain your possessions or search for more boxes of goodies scattered throughout the lands.
The pros of this game are that you get to walk around with dinosaurs, enjoying the view, and taking the time to learn the long-lost art of tracking down game.  You can spend hours doing this.
The cons are plentiful.  There aren't many dinosaurs.  You'll only get the 5 types of dinosaurs advertised.  It can get pretty repetitive hunting down the same dinosaurs over and over.  There's not much variety in that sense.  To make matters worse, the AI for the dinosaurs are pretty bad.  They each have their own way to move, which of course makes sense, but they tend to move directly towards a waypoint.  If you run out of the way, they will not change their path.  They'll arive at the waypoint, then turn around to recalculate.  This doesn't make the game any easier, because the T-Rex will kill you, but the realism takes a hit in that sense.
To add to the cons, the game is not fun when you're playing it alone.  It's all fine and dandy while learning how to do things, but once you figure out the main aspect of the game it gets pretty boring.  I can only play long enough until I die, and then I shut the game off.
There are no missions or no primary objectives.  You just kill dinosaurs and hope to harvest them for points.  You collect the same objects over and over, and then go out and use them against only a few of the dinosaurs.  The rest of the time, you're tracking for hours looking for the one that you wounded while avoiding the ones that are just too hard to kill or more likely to kill you in one blow.  You need multiplayer to make this game enjoyable.
And my biggest buzz kill is no controller support.  I never liked keyboard/mouse games, especially when I have a perfectly good controller that can execute all of the small list of tasks available to the player.  Your guy can't even climb, jump, or swim, so there's nothing complex behind slapping on a few instructions for a controller.
Overall, I say it's a well made game that I enjoyed for some time and would recommend for others to play, but like the dinosaurs it doesn't stand the test of time.

I actually really liked this game.
It's a rouge-like adventure game set at a time between 1880-1910. You chose a famous person from that time era (usually not even an explorer) and help them discover 6 golden pyramids so they have have a statue made of them.
The game is mostly resource and perk management, but despite that, it never really gets old. Combat is totally optional and is a completely unique engine which stands out from all others and is generally fun once you understand it.
As you move through the world, you take sanity damage (recieving more based on harsher environments). To refill your sanity, you need to eat, drink, or rest. This is merely one aspect of the resource management and you must always be prepared.
Additionally, you need to fund your next expedition and to do that, you need to come back with treasures and decide if you will gift them to a museum, sell them for funds, or trade them with natives. Be careful though, because each time you steal from a sacred temple, it makes the natives in that region angry at you. This is a really good risk/reward system. Especially since your treasures share inventory space with your guns, food, torches, and other equipment.
Also, you can train a velociraptor or triceratops as your pet, so that's pretty schanzzzy

I enjoy permadeath games. As a professional game developer, I think very hard about how it relates to game design and whether or not it benefits my own works. With that said: I am disappointed that some of these talented developers have such massive flaws in their thinking.
However, I'm very tired of these idiotic permadeath developers who feel the need to, like a religious fundamentalist, force their irrational playstyle down other's throats. Why not make it merely an option? Why even delete from the HDD when you could simply remove it from the game only? It's even worse when their incompetent programming results in consistent bugs that delete your files or their lazy programming fails to write a solid save system from the start.
Guess what? It's a singleplayer game, and a game where progress is important- ESPECIALLY since it is permadeath. Having bugs that delete your save for no reason or hiding the save file from the user is anti-consumer, anti-player, and pro-idiot-developer.
As a professional programmer, changing this to be an option or simply not deleting the file on the system is elementary. It would take a few minutes to fix. A complex solution to backup old files (in case of bugs or the desire to scum save) is also elementary. Even clearing them out after a week to prevent the hard drive from filling up (which is unnecessary since these save files are so insignificantly tiny) is an elementary thing.
As a game designer, there is absolutely no reason not to make this an option. We're just lucky these guys are fanatical permadeath devs, maybe big nerds, but nothing else.)
In other words: MAKE IT AN OPTION. How hard is that to grasp? Why deny the player that control in a singleplayer game? There is NO reason to deny them. There is NO excuse, technically. You are without excuse to not empower players rather than try to force them to play in your misguided way.

There are good strategy games, there are great strategy games, there are strategy games you won't be forgetting anytime soon. And then, there's Victoria II.
Set between 1836 and 1936, Victoria II is a grand strategy game that allows you to take control of any (yes, ANY) nation in the world that existed in the 1836 or in the 1861 start dates (the latter only available if you own the A House Divided expansion) and experience the Industrial Age and the beginning of the 20th Century in a most vibrant, colourful and enthralling fashion. At a first glance the game may very well look like other grand strategy games, even like other Paradox titles, such as Europa Universalis IV or Crusader Kings II, but don't let the looks deceive you: this is one of their most complex and finest titles to date, if not the one.
Essentially, you are in control of the nation's every aspect: from taxes, tariffs and social reforms to diplomacy, war, technology and the military. Yet, the game's unique twist comes from the fact that you're somewhat powerless to do as you please with your nation, rather steering it - or doing your best to - towards the course you wish it to take. It is not for you to decide, say, that you want to be a Communist Dictatorship, or a Fascist, for that matter. You need lots of conditions, the most important of which is an angry populace that may crave the former if they don't have their life needs met, or the latter if their revanchism desire is high and they want lost national territories back. Essentially, you end up doing what the majority of the populace wants you to do, and what you try to do in turn is to steer said majority's preferences.
And that's where the game truly shines: you truly feel that your country IS alive. Each and every group in even the tiniest of provinces, clerks, labourers, clergymen, aristocrats and whatnot have their own agenda, worries and interests. Even in wars, when your people die, they truly do. So, if you fight a prolonged war, chances are that you won't be replenishing those soldiers from the regiment's province anytime soon - as regiments are reinforced with men from the province in which they were raised. Also, if you mobilise your nation and send your factory workers to war and they die, expect your economy to take a hit and even have areas having a shortage of male population. There's also factories and the economy, which each nation having RGOs (Resource Gathering Operations) that yield raw materials which you may sell to the rest of the world, or you can industrialise and sell finished goods - the smart move. The economy system is deftly crafted, and is incredibly complex, yet it's neatly automated that you can leave it to the AI to figure it out while you do the rest.
Also, the game has a neat diplomacy system, that has nations in different tiers: the Big Eight, "the Great Powers" are the greatest of them all, capable of having a Sphere of Influence of their own, affecting with their decisions and will many other lands and fighting for supremacy with the other great powers. Then, there are the "Secondary Powers", which is made up of the next eight countries. These countries, while not capable of having a Sphere of Influence of their own, are major players and may engage in some minor activities as the Great Powers do, such as colonising. Finally, the rest of the world is made up of Civilised Nations and Uncivilised/Primitive Nations, which strive to become westernised and make for a great game on their own - Meiji Japan is awesome. Speaking of which, there are tons of events and decisions for every country, with anything ranging from the Unification of Germany and Italy (and even Scandinavia) to the Boxer Rebellions and the First to the Pole expedition. Usually, the big players have the best events and decisions, but even the smallest of countries have a bit of flavour.
It is worth noting that the two expansions add so many neat features that they are truly a must have: A House Divided adds tons of events and decisions for the US and the Civil War, as well as some additions to the westernisation process, and the much needed National Focus mechanic. Then, Heart of Darkness completely revamps the colonisation system and introduces the crisis system, which pits the Big Eight as they take sides in international crisis over the fate of territories in the world, in a virtual representation of the various european congress that took place in the late 19th Century. When war erupts between two or more Great Powers on each side in the latter half of the game, this may lead to a World War, in which nations fight to the death and in which demands are cheaper to ask for in terms of badboy - the ingame value tha represents warmongering.
Sound-wise, the game is GREAT. The soundtrack is awesome, especially if you get the Songs of the Civil War DLC. Then, there's the graphics deparment, which is serviceable, having a very 19th century looking interface and some cool unit sprites. There was a DLC, called Old Vic that truly rendered the UI beautiful, but it doesn't work in A House Divided and Heart of Darkness. Still, the game is alright in the visual department.
All in all, the game's awesome. A word of warning, though: it is complex and not for the faint-hearted, having one of the steepest learning curves of all time. But once you get past it, this game will reward you with limitless hours of unparalelled joy and fun. If you like grand strategy games, then look no further, for this is the best game you shall ever play.

This game needs major balance changes and other improvements before it's worth anywhere near $15.
- The tutorials are totally inadequate. They don't even explain how the (very unintuitive) combat works, and what they do explain isn't explained well.  I completed an entire playthrough of six expeditions, but I still don't understand how characters level up. I know it has something to do with exploring new sections of the map, but that's it.
- The game is just BRUTAL for newbies because the player isn't shown basic information. The game doesn't warn you that your explorer can only have four other helper characters before you recruit a fifth, forcing you to dismiss one (angering the others). In combat, each heart stupidly represents TWO health. Countless other examples.
- Competing against other explorers to steal the most treasure from natives around the world is a great premise, but it's mostly wasted. After choosing who to play as, you don't interact with the other explorers AT ALL - you don't talk to them (who doesn't want to talk smack to Harriet Tubman?), you never get to explore the same area of the world as them, you don't even compete with them for supplies or helper characters! Harriet Tubman may as well just be
- a stranger's high score on an arcade game that you're trying to beat.
- The dice system is a MESS.
The basic premise of combat is that all of your party's dice are rolled, and then you combine the symbols rolled to do damage to enemies, or to block damage that turn. While you can do a little damage with just the symbols from your characters' basic dice, most explorers start with a gun (the game seems to make it almost impossible to get a second gun), and combos that involve a gun are MUCH more powerful. More to the point, because it's so dangerous to let enemies have even a single turn in combat, either you will have to avoid combat entirely (by using up special items to do so) or your choice of party members will be almost totally dictated by choosing people who have the right color dice to use your gun properly to burst down the enemies in a turn or two. This really screws up the theme of the game! If you choose the explorer who starts with the rifle, soldiers are largely useless to you because they have red dice, while the rifle only combos with the symbols from blue dice. Oh, and did I mention that the game doesn't tell you what symbols a gun needs to combo? They leave it up to you to "experiment" - i.e. to get mauled to death by beasts and natives until you look up everything on the wiki. (Every armed explorer seems to start with the wrong characters to combo with his gun...
).
- The game talks about a "weight" limit, but the system is that you have a certain number of inventory slots, each of which can hold a stack of up to 10 of the same item. Yes, old school gamers, that's right - the terrible inventory system from the original Jagged Alliance is back!
- There are TOO many items that are very similar, and the game doesn't handle them properly. Rope and "climbing gear" are separate items (even though the image for climbing gear includes rope) but you have to use ROPE to CLIMB up a shrine, NOT climbing gear). During an expedition where I was looking for musical instruments to bring back to someone in England, a native asked to see my bongo drums, and when I handed them over he tuned them to sound better, increasing their value... but when I got back to England, the stupid buggy quest didn't recognize the improved bongos as a musical instrument.
- Interface problems! You only get to visit the store ONCE after each expedition - click carefully! Haggling doesn't reduce prices... instead haggling appears as an item with negative value in the inventory of whomever you're trading with - that sounds like the worst possible way to implement haggling because IT IS. When you unlock a new explorer, the game doesn't tell you HOW you unlocked him (although you can check the conditions to unlock new explorers by clicking their blank portraits). If you have two animals in your party, you can't directly mount the second one - you have to dismount the original one first. When mousing over items in inventory, their tooltip is shown in the OPPOSITE DIAGONAL CORNER OF THE SCREEN.
- Every successful expedition ends with you following your compass to find a golden pyramid. The compass mechanic is TERRIBLE. It gets more accurate as you discover more areas, meaning you have to watch is sllloowwwwllly swing back and forth at first to get even a rough idea of what direction to head in. The game NEEDS a better way to show you roughly what direction the pyramid is.

An absolutely brilliant concept, that has been implemented very well. Lead a team of intrepid explorers on increasingly difficult expeditions, as they battle everything from giant gorillas to mummies. Their greatest adversary, however, is not the beasts, but their own sanity. As they penetrate ever deeper into the dense jungles or barren deserts, their minds deteriorate. When you run out of water, machetes, and similar tools required to cope with the climate and terrain, the process accelerates. This is when hilarity ensues as the dark humour starts to shine through in earnest. Redcoats with drinking problems may turn into paranoid cannibals, reckless use of ancient spells may transform the most trusty follower into a flesh-eating abomination, and one by one your expedition will succumb to the madness.
Anyone with even a vague appreciation for tongue-in-cheek 19th century-style exploration (i.e. plundering), the Indiana Jones movies and/or Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (or Coppola's Apocalypse Now for that matter) will find plenty of amusing references to chuckle over.
In gameplay terms, it's a pretty classic roguelike, with plenty of similarities with FTL. The combat system is easy enough to grasp once you've learned the basics (combos are key, as are balancing defensive and offensive moves), but deep enough to keep you entertained. It's challenging, but not absurdly difficult (unlike many other roguelikes), with a high replayability value.
I tip my jungle helmet to the devs, and thrust myself into the jungle once more. Just one more expedition...

100% Orange Juice is a board game, wherein the player must travel across a board, obtaining stars (the game's currency) and killing enemies to earn points, and prevent the other 3 players from doing the same. The graphics, music, interface, etc. are all very well done, albeit I imagine most would have preferred an in-game tutorial over having to read an instruction manual. Additionally, the player must obtain cards to try and obtain an advantage, with some ranging from simple things like restoring health or getting an additional dice roll, to the simply unfair, and this is where my mine gripe with the game begins. The only reliable way of obtaining more cards and characters (as well as other cosmetic things) is to play through campaign. The problem with this is the fact that the AI has such an absurd RNG advantage it simply isn't fun to play at all. They will always land high rolls when it's convenient, and low ones when it's not. Never do they seem to find bad cards. Whenever they desperately need to obtain a certain variable to win a battle/get a star, they will. Thereby, I found myself in a Catch 22 of sorts. I can't do well because I don't have good characters or cards, and so, I can't advance in the campaign to earn these cards or characters to allow me to win. Not too fond of the announcer or character DLC, but right now, that's not as bad as it could be, and it ultimately isn't too bad.
Overall I do recommend this game, albeit I think its progression system is a flawed one. A solid 8/10.

After playing through this game twice, through both "white pawn" and "black pawn" scnenerios, I have to say I really did enjoy this game a ♥♥♥♥ ton. The game is challenging, but oftenly not THAT challenging. However, it makes you think and keeps you on yout toes a bit as well. There is a lot of trial and error involved, and some places where I died a ton as well. There are subtle clues all over the place, some of which display to you only once. Look around everywhere when you can, because that can help you a ton as there are clues hidden about.
Sometimes you have to think about the conversations you have with Vinnie, but don't over do it with the puzzles. I got hung up once in "white pawn" scenerio, but ONLY because I WAY over thought it. If you get hung up at all, just remember the clue from when Vinnie goes to shoot you in his riddle (behind where you first come into the room to your left). I personally loved it, and I liked the things I noticed during certain scenes or by looking around. I honestly loved this game, and considering my 2nd play through was the next day that kind of says a lot for me. Granted, it is a short game, like an hour and a halfish for white pawn, and a little over two hours for black pawn.
In all though, I'd deffinitely recomend this game to anyone. It's fun, some of the altercations between the two guys bring a decent laugh or two, and the ending was just a blast. I liked the music that played, which I felt fitting. and while it feels like "Oh, this is the end of the game...", but it really isn't. There's a few more things to do, and then you get the ending where you find out something that I totally didn't expect. Just how it ends is enough to make me want to come back and play it again. If I were to rate this game, I'd give it an 8/10. It might be short, but it's also a free game with what I feel to be replay value to be had for sure. The puzzles can be simple, or they can be hard. The two paths are enjoyable, and I really enjoyed the ending and the whole surreal aspect that the game had. Granted, it can use some work in a few place, but I think it's pretty good as it stands now. As I said before, definitely recoment this game, and have even done so to a couple of friends.

It's 2D League of Legends with a fraction of the community. If you enjoy competitive PVP oriented games, then Awesomenauts will suit you well.
As other reviews before me have said, the matchmaking is awful. At first I didn't realize I was going up against "premades" (a group of 3 players who queue together) and I would get completely stomped all game. Unfortunately I'm too stubborn and competitive to give up. For those who aren't like me, it's a huge turn off and most likely a large contributor to the low playerbase.
The queue system has a 3 minute timer to allow players to join. If there aren't enough players and the timer runs out, you're given the option to "force start". This immediately starts the match and fills any empty slots with bots. The bots are terrible and you never want one on your team. Running that 3 minute timer out is not uncommon and, on occassion, I've found myself the be the only one in the queue. Unlike LoL, players can join mid-game and replace the remaining bots.
This is the kind of game I wish would do better but falls short in a lot of categories. There are other MOBAs that do their job much better. I enjoyed most of my time spent with the game although it's caused it's share of frustration too.

Victoria II is a game that starts in 1836 and ends in 1936. So 100 years of gameplay. This is one of Paradox's faster paced games, as years can go by very quickly depending on the speed and how you manage that time. In my case, I only play as challenging nations like: Texas, Hawaii, Bali, Nejd, Ionian Islands, Mecklenburg, and Cuba. I find joy in trying to turn a small nation into a successful empire. This usually takes many years to do, however.
- Population: The main difference I can list right off the bat, compared to other Paradox titles, is that this game focuses on your population. Your population is comprised of: Farmers, labourers, craftsmen, soldiers, officers, clerks, slaves, and other professions. Naturally, if you want armies, you need soldiers. If you want to become rich, you must employ more workers into your factories, and more labourers into the fields. It's very important to keep your population content with your government, or they may revolt. Many may find revolts tedious and annoying, but I for one believe that revolts are one of the most crucial parts to the game. And I will explain why momentarily.
- Politics: While a game like Hearts of Iron III has politics, there isn't much depth to it. You really have little control over what political party rises in Hearts of Iron III. In Victoria 2, your population plays a major role in what political party is elected (assuming that they are allowed to vote!) This game contains 7 different political factions: Liberals, conservatives, anarcho-liberals, reactionaries, socialists, communists, and fascists. Of the 7, I always go socialist--as I am very familiar with this system. Along with the political parties, you can combine this with different types of governments. There are monarchies, democracies, dictatorships (and proletarian dictatorships for the communists.) The best part about government changes, is that the flag of a nation will change as well. For example; if Germany turned into a proletarian dictatorship, they would receive the flag of the DDR. While if they turned into a fascist dictatorship, they acquire the flag of the Third Reich (Kind of...) I love the political aspect of this game, and it is likely the one reason I constantly play this game.
- Revolts: As I said, these are usually annoying to you in two ways. 1. They may be attacking your country. 2. They may be attacking a puppet/ally, and thus will tear your ties with that nation if overthrown. Now, on the other hand, rebels are truly what makes the game interesting. The Russians are defeated BADLY in a war, and communist rebels rise. They overthrow the Russian Empire and form the Soviet Union. If you ask me, that's pretty damn interesting! After 80 years of seeing the same old Russian Empire, it's nice seeing them throw out the red color and put on the classic hammer and sickle. How about Scottish rebels? Is it not interesting to see Scotland gain independence from the United Kingdom through violent means? There's both pros and cons to rebels. I personally have NO PROBLEM with rebels, ever. I just choose the socialist party loyalty national focus on my nation, let my nation turn more red, and I seem to be in good hands. Otherwise, if the rebels want to fight, I will go Rocky IV on them. So in other words... I love rebels.
- The scramble for Africa: This is such a fun part of the game, but I feel that it mainly improved with the addition of the Heart of Darkness DLC. Throughout your game, you will notice that Africa is a mere wasteland of uncolonized land. There is generally nothing interesting that surrounds Africa until the 1870s, when the doors are unlocked and all great and secondary powers are given the green light to begin colonization. It's nothing short of a big race. Everyone wants to get their hands on the most land, and if you plan things out accordingly (like perhaps annexing Liberia before 1870) you can form a massive African empire. What you choose to do with your newly acquired African land is up to you. Use it for its resources, or release it all into one giant satellite nation. Overall, this is always an exciting event of any campaign.
- Technological advancements: In 1870, everyone but the primitive nations essentially start off with the option to build infantry or cavalry, and that's about it. As for navy, you can build anything as simple as a clipper transport or frigate. As time goes on, however, and you research more, you will acquire much more advanced types of infantry and warships. I am personally a big fan of the tanks that are available in the early 20th century. More than tanks, however, I love the battleships. Nothing is more satisfying than having a battleship and spotting an enemy fleet of mere commerce raiders. It's simply too funny of a battle. Unfortunately, technology is not my favorite aspect of this game. I much prefer Hearts of Iron's system and I really wish they had implemented something similar in this game. While Victoria II has a wide variety of technology branches, I simply wish the decisions I make for research was as dynamic as it was in Hearts of Iron. I'm crossing my fingers that next time around, Victoria III (Not announced YET) will give you the option to completely focus on a specific part of the game. Considering I'm pro-navy, I would love if I could continue to improve the strengths of my battleships.
In conclusion, I love this game so much. Whenever I look at all of the other grand strategy games on Steam, I contemplate, and I cry. I leap into bed and soak my pillow with tears, understanding that there will never be another day where such a worthy game will hit the stores. ...but I'm just kidding. I love Europa Universalis IV a lot too.

Victoria II is one of the lesser dreadnaughts of the Paradox Interactive fleet of grand strategy games. It builds on the concepts of Europa Universalis, allowing you to take control of a nation in 1836 and see if you can't create a place in the sun for your nation before the games end date, 1936.
Now, Victoria 2 has its issues. It's immensely complex to master, but easy enough to play. You have access to more charts, sliders, and government oriented features than any other Paradox games, and rivals Hearts of Iron on that note. But there's so much more to the game than that.
You have to manage your political stability; ensure all ideologies are pleased. Or you can oppress your opposition, and create a one-party state if you wish. The game features several political ideologies, each with their own style and restrictions. Each nation has its own distinct parties, all of whom have different goals and policies tailored to that nation.
You also have access to large amounts of information in regards to your nation's population. You can see how many capitalists, aristocrats, soldiers(enlisted and un-enlisted), farmers, etc. you have living in your nation.
A House Divided adds a new starting point in 1861, and lets you justify wars by manufacturing a reason. It also adds several new features that help non-western nations be more entertaining.
Heart of Darkness focuses on warfare and the geopolitical game, adding Crisis that can escalate into world wars if not resolved, and newspapers that give you a summary of important world events.
All in all? An excellent game, if you enjoy Europa Universalis, or Hearts of Iron, you're bound to find a few hours of enjoyment in Victoria 2*
* That's an understatement.

A hidden gem of a fantasy business roleplay game. I paid 49p in the Steam Winter Sale for this game, a price even including trading cards. It feels like a steal at this price. The full price is a very fair £1.99, I would personally pay around £4.99 for this game so the developer is being extremely fair here with the pricing which I hope rewards them with more customers – thank you!
The game looks simple and I was conscious of some reviews saying it is a “short story” – but that all depends how quick you skip / read the text and mull over the strategic options. I finished my first game (52 turns is the time limit) in 2 hours but can see me playing this many times over to both win the game and collect the achievements.  For 49p (or even full price £1.99) this represents excellent value.
The game reminds me of the art style and era of Merchants of Kaidan.  Where as in the excellent game Merchants of Kaidan you were travelling the World to make a profit as a merchant in a text based RPG, in this game you focus on running one Tavern business. But in both games the art style and characters you meet is fantastic. The options for running the Tavern “appear” simple at first but they more you play the more the game expands out with new options, for example introducing a magic ability for your character at one point.
The basics of the game is there are initially 4 factions to make happy, but strategy means you should focus on 1 faction at the expense of others. You prepare meals for your tavern and choose music to attract the right sort of client.  Decorate your inn, expand your inn. In each turn you have to deal with an interaction that occurs and your choices dictate the outcome – gain/lose money, gain/lose customers, lose magic mana, etc. Your decisions also affect whether your tavern is seen as “cool” or more business like (and if so save on taxes). By the end game there are quite a few things to manage.
Alongside the business aspect is a core political story which develops, the first time round I was not successful in that so will try again.
For the money, this is a 8.5/10 game: 85% Must Buy. I don’t usually write reviews after 2 hours but I feel I already have my moneys worth and it is fun and I can tell this is a long term winner. If you like the idea of running a business in a fantasy setting in a light text/art based RPG, this is for you.

Victoria 2 has a lot of issues that will be a turn off for many people. For instance, it has a fairly steep learning curve. More importantly, however, is that there are too many restrictions on the player. For example, your hand is often tied by the policies of the ruling political party in your country. If a laissez faire party is running things then you’ll have to pray that your country’s capitalists think a tank factory would be profitable because you won’t be able to order one yourself. If the ruling party is pacifists then you won’t be able to pile on extra demands in your peace treaties. Also, there are too many restrictions to prevent warmongering which I disapprove of. Let us act like Napoleon or Hitler and watch the world come together to destroy us.
That being said I really like it because it handles internal politics very well and you can play as any country that existed between 1836 and 1936 (even Texas). So consider this a recommendation if you like grand strategy games.

"Tintin and the Golden Pyramid"
Tintin is approached by a explorer who wants to find the legendary golden pyramid.
He enlists Tintin and Captain Haddock to come along with him.
The group travels to a far away corner of the earth and journey through the wilderness.
You find a remote village and barter with the natives for supplies, explore some ruins, fight dangerous wildlife, the Captain drinks some Whiskey and there are some funny antics,
You know fairly common "Tintin-adventur stuff".

The group discovers a cave and the Captain explores a crack and doesn´t return. After waiting for several hours they search for him but turn up empty handed.
Moral hits rock bottom and their supplies run out.
Suddently Tintin demands that they kill and cook one of the animals.
The only animal there is Snowy, so they butcher, cook and eat Snowy!
Then the duo comes to another cave that turns out to be a tunnel that might lead to the hidden golden pyramid. They wander through although they don´t have any torches left.
And when they come out Tintin is gone and replaced by a horrible disfigured monster dressed in Tintins rags that follows the trek now.
Later they make a camp and the Captain returns. He has found some whiskey and got lost in the cave.
They celebrate and later that night the explorer wakes up to some horrible sounds and finds that the Tintin monster has strangled and eaten the Captain. The explorer flees in horror and runs into the night. While doing that he knocks over the lamp what starts a wildfire that kills the Tintin monster.
In the last panel you see the explorer running towards a looming golden pyramid through a burning forest and the comic ends there.

(Tl,dr)
The game is a funny and macabre adventure where you walk the thin line between sucsess and failure.
You have to balance your short term goals (survival) against long term aims (more money and fame).
To get this right is very hard and more often than not you die horribly because the golden idol you looted triggered a cataclysmic trap.
There are some rough edges that need to be balanced out better, i.e. sometimes you have to take the treasure from a shrine with horrible unavoidable consequences to be able to enter the golden pyramid.
But overall very entertaining, quirky game with nice retro graphics for the wannabe Indiana Jones adventurer.

So my most recent campaign something amazing happened: I found a dinosaur skull on my third expedition! When I returned to London that unlocked a special area for my fourth expedition: an area secreted in a volcano shell in North America! I had been mercilessly hunting every wild animal in sight and was loaded with funds from selling the pelts, so I stocked up and ventured forth!
A few days into the journey my expedition came upon 2 Raptors! They proved no match for my guns and advanced tactics and I harvested their skins and feasted on their meat. It was delicious. A month later I found a raptor hatching ground, with a live egg! I took it with me, expecting to sell it back in London for a fortune. Shortly after this something strange happened, even by the standards of a prehistoric expedition! I found a village, not of humans, but of Lizard People! Luckily I was skilled with languages and was able to communicate with the natives. When I asked if any would wish to accompany me I was offered the service of a dinosaur! The Chasmosaur put my Donkey to shame with it's ability to carry my gear, so I left the Donkey to find its way in this strange land and continued on. After several fights with other Raptors and Giant Birds my egg hatched, a tiny Velociraptor had emerged! Of course I kept the little thing with us and carried on. Shortly after that we found the Golden Temple and made our triumphant return to England.
With the treasures I had accumulated in that wonderful land I became famous and wealthy beyond imagining! I upgraded the already impressive carrying capacity of my Chasmosaur, stocked up on tons of supplies, and decided to explore another prehistoric location. This time I was in Australia and everything proceeded as before, when my Raptor was fully grown I dismissed my Sailor, over the protestations of my Cook and Soldier, and made room for my new scaly friend. Mounted upon his back we progressed! Everything seemed to be going so well, until I came to a Shrine. I was familiar with the normal traps in these structures and foolishly decided to loot it before sufficiently exploring the area. We barely managed to outrun the lake that spread across the entire region, but worst of all when the dust cleared I was stranded! Barely a few parcels of land surrounded by impassable mountains and depthless lakes! I was forced to construct a balloon and leave most of the treasure, including what I had looted from the shrine, behind as my companions and I escaped back to London. My rivals successful expeditions allowed them catch up, and in some cases surpass, my fame.
Undaunted I prepared for the sixth, and final, expedition. There was only one choice that could cement my victory, a primeval location in Africa. Having spent most of my funds on the previous expedition I was forced to make do with what little I could still afford, although I was lucky to retain the services of all my companions. We set sail, more determined than ever. After the voyage we immediately saw a pair of Raptor packs patrolling the area, and decided that the best course of action was to stock up on food and trade supplies by righting these creatures. We were successful and had begun to rebuild our stock of supplies. After several months of adventuring, finding keystones and activating mysterious shrines, we had a good stock of supplies, having encountered a brave, wandering merchant several weeks past. Eventually we came upon another shrine, having been unsuccessful in my previous expedition I knew that to truly win this competition I needed the golden treasures, valued greatly by the Explorer's Society, hidden within. I put more effort into preparing this time, clearing out all I needed from the surrounding area before venturing into the forbidden shrine. Inside we went, and two gold idols were inside! I grabbed them and we ran, a vast chasm opened up behind us, yet still we ran, until a mountain showed my lack of planning, slowing us down. The chasm opened beneath our feet and that was the last anyone saw of us.
...
10/10 Would die again.
A thoroughly challenging and amazingly fun game. The above was my fourth campaign (although I have watched several LPs of earlier builds), and despite my last minute death, with victory tauntingly close, I was still enthralled. The last game I felt this way about was FTL, and in many ways Curious Expedition reminds me of FTL. You build up your expedition crew, manage inventories, decide how to proceed. If you like rogue-likes, enjoyed FTL, or just have 15$ to spare, I HIHGLY recommend this game.
Even though it says Early Access the game is very polished, only a few small bugs, and some balance issues, remain. Honestly I would be happy with the game if they stopped development now, so if they keep improving it (and they've said they plan to!) then I will be one happy camper.
Fun game, reminds me very much of the game "Seven Cities of Gold" for the Commodore 64 (and later MS-DOS)

Only If is not a good game, it's not even a coherent, satisfiying narative experience. What Only If is a glimpse into the future of video games, where the boundaries between the strict game genres are cast aside, and new forms of storytelling are forged.
Similar to the vein of Gone Home, Only If tells a short story of a young man that is at the crossroad of personal, emotional changes. But the thing is that someone or something is pushing him to make a choice, forcing him to change.
On the plus side, the game has a delightful voiceover work, with snappy and vibrant dialogues, and for the most part it's a good-looking game considering this was made by a very small independent team with some very interesting ideas. On the negative side, the story is a mess, with a theme that was not appealling to me. While some levels look gorgeous, such as the "Park" level, most of them are not visual stunners and aren't designed well. The game struggles to communicate with the player, it has a poor way of teaching the player the basic use of commands, or hinting them what are they supposed to do next. It shows that it's creators have an interesting vision but still lack the experience to share it with others.
Then why am I giving Only If a thumbs up? Because behind all the things that don't work, you can feel that the guys who made it have a potential to make a great game. It's like an unknown little movie that you accidentally stumble upon, or an experimental, concept album you find at the market: they are not great works of art, far from it actually; but they show signs that in time people who created them can make a truly stellar piece of work.
Only If is a glimpse into the future of games, where everyone can create and share interactive stories and experiences. There will be a lot of blunders and failures along the way, but with every such game that tries to achieve greatness, we are one step closer to making the Citizen Kane of games.

This game is one of the classic RPGs that you constantly hear about. There are many amazing moments and plenty of quests to keep players entertained.
The Good:
- Quests: The Quests of Oblivion have been hailed as some of the most interesting and fun quests in the elder scrolls series, and for the most part, they're right. The quests know when to be serious, but keep a fun atmosphere throughout.
- The World: Oblivion takes place in Cyrodil, the heart of the Septim Empire, and home of the Empirial City. Unlike Skyrim and most other RPGs today, Oblivion's world is colorful and vibrant. It has the classical RPG elements in the world, and pulls them off without many faults.
- RPG: Oblivion is an RPG, far more in the sense, than Skyrim. Oblivion can be complex and have a lot of equations the player doesn't notice, but it's also simple enough for those who do not care about such complicated systems. This truly feels like an RPG, with the ability to do so much.
-DLC: This version of Oblivion comes with the DLC. Most of the DLC is great and worth your time. (Except that infamous horse armor) The plots of both big DLCs are interesting and fun.
The Bad:
-Graphics: This game originally came out in 2006, of course the graphics aren't going to be great. Still though, once you're a few hours in, they stop being so hard to notice. Although still ugly, the animated style makes the game look better the longer you play it.
-Combat: The combat is extremely clunky. There's no pause between strikes and everything feels too light, as if it doesn't have weight. Still though, like the graphics, you stop noticing this once you get used to it.
Overall, I'd have to give Oblivion an 8/10, and claim it to be one of those games you have to play before you die. Definitely reccomend.

Okay, so I never like writing bad reviews/responses for things. Positivity is very important to me. But this was a complete waste of my time. Look, I'm familiar with the "masculine, vaguely threatening dude gives mysterious and inscrutable tasks to you through a radio while shouting obscenities at you" and "bizarre lateral-thinking puzzle type gameplay revolving around vague keywords" cliches of modern gaming (which I totally unironically love), but they have to lead to something. This was completely pointless. The annoying banter with your captor is utterly meaningless and the ending resolves nothing. I guess the gameplay is pretty surreal, but it's never interesting. On top of that, I was expecting a story-based type of game experience (at least for a generous definition of "story"), but this is definitely not that. Near-constant, terribly voice-acted cursing, drug references, memes (yes, actual memes), and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ "twist ending" that had no relevance to anything previously established do not make a compelling story. This may honestly be one of the worst games I've ever engaged with. Please don't bother playing it.
And I know some people will say "oh, but it's free!" Time is more valuable than money. I'm not criticizing it on the grounds of the engine or the limitations of a small-scale game (although the bizarrely antiquated save system did raise an eyebrow). I'm not complaining about spending money on it. I just think that all of the effort put into this game was clearly spent in the totally wrong direction.

It is a creative game which does a good job of evoking the sense of adventure that is appropriate for  the setting. You can choose both the companions you want to take with you, and the perks  you gain each expedition, making for many different play-styles. The most important thing in an early access game is a good core concept, which this game has. Some more options would be welcome, such as more FTL-style "special" options when you have the right companion, perk or item. There are some, but this aspect could be expanded on. Also, there should be a doctor companion, both for practical reasons, and as it would be fitting to the setting.
The biggest criticisms at this point are game breaking bugs, and that the difficulty level can sometimes be obnoxious. Sanity seems to drop too fast, and when it's out, the companions start killing each other too quickly.  As for the combat, most enemies seem to  be able to wipe out the party alarmingly quickly, although I may need more practice. On that note, the tutorial seems quite anemic, with most aspects of the game unexplained.
The core game play is solid though. A little expansion, balancing and debugging, and this will be a great game,  well worth supporting.

When going on an expedition, you'd normally expect the story to start off with hardened adventurers off to explore new lands. You probably don't expect someone like Marie Curie, Harriett Tubman or Nikola Tesla going on these expeditions, but this isn't any expedition; it's an expedition in the game The Curious Expedition. Published and developed by Maschinen-Mensch, The Curious Expedition is a pixel art-styled exploration game with dice rolling combat and RPG elements, and it's now on Steam Early Access. It's an odd little game that can't be recommended to everyone, but for those who enjoy quirky little strategy games, this game is for you.
A curious thing about The Curious Expedition is the fact that there is no real “good guys” or “bad guys” like you'd see in something like, say, Tomb Raider or The Uncharted series. Yes, you do need to beat your competition, but they aren't necessarily bad people, they're just people you're competing against to make the most money. The game is rather amoral, which is a delightful change of pace considering how black and white a game like this could potentially be if given in the hands of the wrong developer. However, The Curious Expedition takes it to a different level and makes your actions affect your party members in different ways, making their general rapport with you, however basic a few lines of dialogue can be, completely different.

A mild thumbs up for interesting and friendly concept, and low price ($2.99) at my time of purchase. However, I finished my playtest wanting the game to be more than it is. I would be giving a neutral rating if this were possible.
- The music is great; the art a sort of pencil-sketch style that does a good job. The English wasn't written by a native speaker, however. The grammar is generally okay, but you consistently encounter words that are completely inappropriate. For example, "the right SPRINKLES are what makes a people come and go" (referring to extras that improve the tavern; I believe the word they wanted was "touches"). Other times, the game refers to the "cave" when I believe it means "cellar".
- It makes excessive use of anachronisms (your bard can play rock music, for example) and fourth wall breaking (in one weekly event, I have too much to drink and see my beer floating before me. My choices are to grab it or "press the space bar". I chose the latter, and
- Something about the core game mechanic is unfulfilling; there just isn't enough to do in the tavern management, and no real sense of story in the choose your own adventure part. You have four types of customers (guards, rogues, wanderers, etc) and can change the menu, music and decorations to draw more of one or another; your one "choose your own adventure" choice each week inevitably changes your reputation with one or more groups. These A / B choices do not give a sense of story so much as they simply move sliders around. The management part feels similarly unfulfilling; you're given a money dump at the end of each week, which happens as soon as you make your "choose your own adventure" choice. The money seems to pour in no matter what, and the net at the end of the week doesn't really feel like it has much to do with my choices so much as like I've been given an allowance by Mom and Dad.
The game would probably do better if it were re-tooled into a real-time mode (like the old SIM series) with a more rapid-fire series of events to respond to and the ability to pause. It would probably be better if there were some micro-management to do in real time, and the events occurring more than once per week.

Endless legends is a game unlike any I have played before. It begins much in the way a game of civilizaiton would, you place a capital and branch out to new cities through the use of settlers, conquests, bribes, and even an intriguing quest system. If you enjoy games like civilization revolution then you will love this unique twist and style that endless legends brings to the genre.
While this game is one of the best games of the genre it does have its draw backs. Throughout my play through I began to notice a few irritating things that I feel are necessary to understand about this game before purchase. My first point would be to say that this game is not one that encourages variety. Every faction has three basic units that are unlocked fairly early on, and then they are allowed to assimilate a few minor factions along the way in order to broaden their unit scope. While this may not seem like a big deal to many people it does put certain factions at a major disadvantage against experienced players. My most recent encounter with this is that the Mezari start the game with ranged units that are able to move and shoot all in the same turn, this allows them to kite early game fights and put almost all other factions into the dirt early game. While this may seem like something that many people see as counterable you have to realize that certain factions such as the drakken and the broken lords have no way of countering a ranged unit as they have no late game ranged units of their own without using a valuable assimilation slot.
While this game does have its flaws, it is almost impossible to pass up. Its unique quest system sets it apart from the other titles in this genre, as you now no longer have to build a final building but instead with each faction you are encouraged to follow a specific path that will also allow you win the game. Knowing these paths for each faction you are offered a very interesting way of now denying your allies victory, without having to declare war. We also see the hero system in this game help to further its path to the top of my list of most played games. This game rewards those who use its heroes correctly, offering multiple skill tree paths and roles for heroes. A fully leveled hero in this game could be the difference maker in a battle, as a support hero might be what is needed to keep one militia group alive against multiple titans.
I strongly recommend this game to any lovers of the civilization series, it sticks to the basic city building aspect of the civ series, all the while giving a unique spin on the battle system and diplomacy system.

This game is one of the most fun 4x games I've ever played. Where the Civ series has an advantage of using historical figures to make their game interesting, Endless Legend uses unique fantasy-based creatures and worlds each with their own unique playstyle and pros/cons. It differs from Civ in plenty of ways that make it far from just another Civ rip-off and I can't wait to see where the game progresses in the future.
I'd recommend the game to anyone who's enjoyed the Civ series and is looking for a fantasy-based Civ game.

I can see myself ending up putting a lot of time into this game. After being disappointed by Civilization: Beyond Earth, I feel like Endless Legend scratches all the itches that Beyond Earth should have. It borrows a lot of the good things from Civilization V, and fixes a lot of the bad things. Combat consists of tactical battles between two armies of multiple units and possible reinforcement from other units in the area. Where Civ 5's combat is cramped and tight, Endless Legend has found a decent compromise between "one unit per tile" and the ridiculous stacked armies of Civ IV. At the same time, walls and cliffs between tiles adds more tactical variation to the maps.
The world is beautiful. Where Civ:BE all feels a little bland and samey, this game has individual regions which each have their own visually spectacular biome. Also unlike Civ:BE, the factions in Endless Legend all feel distinct and interesting. Leader portraits are animated in this really cool oil painting style. Even the hexes have variance to them, looking like randomized, striking geographical shapes rather than identical hexagonal tiles. This game may not have the greatest graphics of all time, but the excellent art direction and attention to detail more than make up for it.
It does seem a little barebones compared to games like Civ in terms of sheer numbers of factions, units, and technologies. In the end though, everything combines to create quite a deep experience. My only real complaints are that a few parts of the user interface are counter-intuitive, and that it can be difficult to find your units in the clutter sometimes. It can be annoying, but I've mostly gotten used to it. I recommend Endless Legend for anybody who enjoyed Civ V. Just play the tutorial and it'll be simple to figure this game out.
