Platformer, where six Players in two Teams of three, try to push their creeps into the enemy Main base.
Turrets block the entrances into the Base which need to be destroyed.
Its pretty standard MOBA in that regard, comparable to League of Legends or DOTA.
But as its a Platformer/JumpnRun , and not top down like usual Mobas, Lanes are essential Levels/ Floors.
Which adds a Ton of new Gamplay elements, like Jumppads ,Fall through Floors, Jumping,Flying,Gravity (Falling Objects like Mines/Acid) etc. to the Moba genre.
The only Resource in Game is "Solars" which is essentially Gold.
You collect it from fallen Foes/Creeps or in smaller amounts by collecting it at certain Points.
It is only used to buy/Extend Your Skills.
You essentially have several Skillrows ,with 3 being dedicated to you three active skills and the rest to general /Utility/ Defense.in each skillrow you can pick and upgrade up to 3 Abilities.
This allows you to customize you character to a Degree.
For example Voltar ( a support / Healer) , can upgrade his standard healray to get piercing,More Damage,More Range, making him a decent Harasser, and preventing him from buying more for his Main Attack (3 max Upgrades per Ability).
Or he could go with Heal over Time,Range, and knockback (if he charges his heal to Maximum),making him the Cavalry, with less Fire power , but great Healing/Rescue Ability.
The Characters are pretty Diverse, and differ in Tactics, Movement speed *and* Modes (Flying, teleporting,hovering , Doublejump,dash etc),attacks , Momentum etc.
There are around half a dozen Maps each with a unique Twist like instant kill Trapdoors, Antigravity Zones,Extensive jungles,Teleporting Wormholes.
In Comparison , to other Mobas its far less about Number Crunching and that "perfect Build" and more Action/skill oriented.
Players are constantly evaluated and rise or fall through the Leagues, of which there about i think 8. Matchmaking usually tries to pair Players from the same league against each other.
Playing against Bots is available,which are not Stellar on Higher Difficilty,but acceptable on lower Levels.
It also has Playback where you can not only watch almost every Game you have ever played,
but also export/save it to Harddrive, only view killscenes, Track single players , or freecam, and a lot of other Stuff.
Gameplay/Graphics are fluid Exception the occasional Lagger, the Screenshots and Video above are representing the In game Experience.
Soundeffects are good, each Character has his own Soundtrack ( Main Theme/ Kill streak Music etc.)
****** TLDR: ******
Awesomenauts is a well designed Moba Variant, it does not waste your Time,  not perfect but acceptable matchmaking , a living Community,constant Updates.Easy to learn hard to Master Action Gameplay with Tactical Depth.

Update 9/2-ish: Game is still good. Development has progressed well, and I'm still more than happy to reccomend The Curious Expedition to any roguelike fans. It's a unique blend of exploration, chance, and one-more-life design loops that make the game well worth the price. This game is worth your money.
Update 6/18: The developers have added more stuff, tuned other stuff, and balanced all of the previous stuff. It's a neat game. Some of my previous complaints still stand, however, as the event content seems to be a bit lacking. With that said, however, I can still wholly reccomend this neat take on the roguelike experience.
A fun roguelike with events that (at the time of this early-access review) get to be a little too predictable after repeat playthroughs. With that in mind, I'd say that this is one of the few roguelites that actually understand the design principles behind permadeath/procedural generation in games.
Every experience, both positive and negative, preps you for your next playthrough. Most importantly, however, is the fact that I never feel like the game left me in an unwinnable scenario. I'm happy to report that my expedition team has died because of my own stupid mistakes rather than anything that the game has thrown at me.
It's worth an impulse buy for a few hours of entertainment, but I'm going to hold off on playing it again until the full product is released because the events can get (again, at this point in time) a little samey.

Football Manager 2017. Well where do I start? Honestly I was a little apprehensive when even considering purchasing it, simply because I've been disappointed by the lack of innovation or progression by the past versions, namely 2014 and 2015. Soo did this version manage to finally meet expectations? Yes.
Okay, aside from the standard database updates, there are quite a few things to note about the new series.
I for one can say that this new overlay of FM17, definitely looks significantly crisper and cleaner than its predecessors. The simple white background looks significantly better than the cluttered and messy overlay used in the previous generations. Definitely a plus point.
Also glad they kept the layout of the buttons, though it took time to get used to in the past, it is definitely more streamlined and organised than those of the 2011 and 2012 versions.
Okay I know the video that SI posted up looked as though there was absolutely no difference whatsoever in the 3D engine, however rest assured, it is definitely far from it. The movement does look smoother, and yes I do agree the AI is definitely smarter as well (though wish they could be even smarter, sometimes stupid things still happen). Couple of new moves and celebrations have been added, but nothing overall groundbreaking. Just a nicer feel to the overall gameplay experience.
Well this one is a nice touch, but it lacks features, significantly. It's a nice idea, but that's about it. Simple a nice idea. That hasn't been executed that well. Lack of options to customise the character is disappointing. Seems to have no choice in some cases. Personally I think this is a totally pointless feature. But maybe it's still beta soo for all I know maybe there will be more options on full release.
Same old story. Nothing much to say here. Just some new questions and more ways to answer. Nothing much. (Still gonna skip most press conference unless its a big match).
Well well who would have thought SI would include this in the game? BIG BIG PLUS POINT. Absolutely love it, it makes things more realistic. Though it runs on the presumption of the regulations that may be put in place its a nice idea. I like it. But it be nice to have an option to disable it for those that don't want it. Nice touch, I like!
I like the new input of the way in which the agent can speak with you in terms of promises to the player that will be transfered. This gives you greater freedom to see what the player himself wants from joining your club. Also gives you a good idea if you will be able to accomodate him hence further impact on your decision to purchase him. Thumbs up!
Okay, soo many of us heard SI banging on about the introduction of "Sport Scientist" etc as staff members, now personally i've left the recruitment side of it to my board members. Hence nothing much to comment about there, though I have signed MANY sport scientists apparently. Anyways, what delights me more is the scouting regime that is in placed. My scouts pick up significantly more players than ever before, finding many and giving much more indepth analysis.
Well here's the touchy subject. Many people often complain that their team has too many injuries and claim it is the game's problem. Well infact, it's not. If you explored deeper into the game mechanics, you will realise that the way inwhich you do your training (team) affects their overall fitness. Next up the individual trainining regimes you put players on, also affect it as well! If you overwork your player, there is a significantly higher chance of them getting injured! Gonna try to make this review as short and informative as I can.
theHunter: Primal is an amazing and fun prehistoric hunting game.
The Lore:
You are an intergalactic prisoner or something, who gets sent to an alien planet, inhabited by dinosaurs. Your goal is to kill everything you see, so that an intergalactic coorporation can settle and build cities and stuff on it or something.
The Gameplay
The gameplay is based around stealth and hunting teqnicues. Don't make sound, and don't be downwind for a creature etc. if you don't have powerful weapons or a shelter, you are gonna find yourself crawling amid the foliage from time to time. Sometimes you get eaten, sometimes you don't! There are a wide selection of weapons and camoflague clothing in this game. Each item being different and useful for certain situations. You will spend most of your time searching for lootcrates and settlements. The walk from each settlement/lootcrate can be long, so grab a snack while you're at it!
Some people may find this aspect boring, but I quite enjoy it. It's peaceful and calming to take a stroll through the world of TheHunter: Primal. My main issue with the gameplay, however, is the low stamina. You run out of stamina pretty fast in TheHunter: primal.
Hunting

Awesomenauts, is a sidescrolling MOBA, with profoundly unique mechanics and gameplay. Under the correct circumstances, this game can be a hell of a lot of fun. Unfortunately, it is severely held back by issues that have gone
unaddressed by the Developers.
Pros-
-Each Character is unique, not just in appearance, but in the way they are played.
-Amazing soundtrack.
-Controls are tight and responsive.
-Decent selection of levels, each with their own quirks.
-Great UI.
Cons-
-Abyssmal matchmaking.*
-Broken Characters (Overpowered) will often not be fixed for months, if ever.
-Host reliant servers, (often extremely laggy)
-Bots in regular games.
*By abyssmal matchmaking, what I mean is that it makes the game nearly unplayable. Often you will join into a 1v3 situation, where the bots on your team, have already fed the enemy 15 kills, which is damn near impossible to recover from by yourself. People queing with friends, have a massive advantage, as team comunication when solo, is very limited. There is also a time limit in the lobby of every match, if it runs out before the match has filled with players, the game can be 'force started', which means that one or both of the teams, will have NPC bots on them. The NPC's are fine late game, as they have some sustainability by then, but early game, when it matters, they are nothing short of fodder. Having one on your team is a massive handicap, much more so then if they were'nt there at all, and you will play with them nearly every single game, and nearly every single game they will feed like hell.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

This game has been a blast, despite being early access the game is fairly fleshed out and does not feel unfinished (
).
It has a very interesting turn based/dice roll combat system, which would normally turn me off the game but they do it very well. With multiple rolls per turn and the ability to keep some dice without using them in a turn while subsequently rolling others, they win me over.
The graphics, while not "next gen", feel like they belong to the game and do not take from the experience in anyway. The simplicity (not to discredit the artists) of the graphics makes in easy to differentiate between land tiles, while also making the game brilliantly colorful.
Gameplay is great! Movement is based on "Sanity" and while you can move with 0 sanity, you'll be in for a surprise if you do (I recommend doing it every so often just for the experience, just don't do it in a game you're trying to win in. :P) The party members all have unique qualities (some good some bad), which make some better defensively, offensively and even gives healing abilities. Additionally they have qualities that improve the overall game, like allowing you to carry more, or give them more health. That said they also can have things like Kleptomaniac or Racist, which can be super harmful for your group.
Currently there is no save function (As of build 0.17.1) so the game plays like a rogue-like which is fine with me. Some may not enjoy that aspect of it, but to me it adds to the suspense of the game. Knowing that one wrong move could be the end of the expedition is thrilling.
Anyway I hope this review was helpful to you!

One of the best platformers ever made, Abe's Exooddus is a direct sequel of Abe's Oddysee and features even more levels than it's predecessor, while also bringing the most requested features of the last game, namely the ability to quicksave, restart levels where you messed up and all-talk.
The game features plenty of mechanics and contains sections of stealth, logic, agility and sometimes observance.
To name one of the mechanics that makes this particular game stand out, you have the ability to posses enemies and use them in your advantage to either destroy their own kind or free your path. Every single type of enemy has different types of abilities and limitations and it's up to you to figure them out. Some levels even prevent you from using your powers so you will have to use your brain to find a way around.
The game also throws a challenge at you. Fellow enslaved people of your race are scattered around levels and it's up to you to talk to and lead them to portals that bring them to their freedom. You can either succeed or get them killed in the process, or even ignore them altogether and continue in your journey. You can command them using the talk system, unless they're mad or depressed, where you'll have to console them first, or smack the crap out of those affected by laughing gas.
I personally think that's a very unique mechanic. Sometimes you'll have to clear a whole level then come back to the very beginning and escort your pals. Blind ones are also present and telling them to stop in their path is mandatory for their survival.
You'll be rewarded for saving many of your kind but punished for refusing to or saving too few.
The atmosphere of this game, like the first, is amazing. The story elements, the setting, the soundtrack and the characters make it up for one of the greatest cinematic experiences I've ever experienced. The graphics and the cutscenes are pre-rendered 3D sequences and they look just great for a game that came two decades ago.
I should probably also mention that this game, unlike other titles on Steam that originally came during the 90's, fully works on both modern and old systems.
I don't really have negative feedback about this game. It's one of the things that made up my childhood and replaying it was a lot of joy. I guess that there were a few annoying levels that felt a bit repetitive(the ones that feature fleeches for instance), but other than that, everything is godlike. I highly recommend this game to anyone.

In my opinion: best of the oddworld series.
It doesn't only improve on abe's oddysse (able to make multiple mudokon follow, quicksave, better voice, ect.), but also features more variety in gameplay.
If you've never heard of the series and are curious about jumping into one of these games, I recommend that you start here. That or you can wait and see how the remake turns out, in which case you should just start from the first one instead.
The game itself is a highly pre-rendered puzzle platformer which takes place in a strange world with weird creatures. You're basically trying to save as many modokons (green aliens) as possible, in various ways. There's 300 mudokons to rescue, you don't have to rescue all of them in order to complete the game, since many of them are hidden in all sorts of sercrets. You have the ability to possess creatures and take control of them, also each of them have their own set of voice commands which can be used to interact with others, it has a unique approach to a dialogue system which is a pretty messy, but it shouldn't get in your way too much.
If you get stuck at some escape levels, don't forget that the X key makes you instantly roll while you're running, also F5 is a shortcut for quicksave and F6 for quickload.

This is my absolute favorite game of all time and my longest played game ever with 712 hours on steam + 100+ hours on other computers. And I'm here today to tell you why you should invest your money into buying this beautiful pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ even at full price.
Note: This review is played with all the expansions "Heart Of Darkness" and "A House Divided", these expansions are absolutely  NECESSARY to get the fully enjoyable Victoria II experience (But don't get the rest of the DLC, waste of money)
For starters, this game is not for the casual player, far off. This game is a part of the very small and obscure genre of Grand Strategy video games which is made by the Swedish Developers of Paradox, but the genre is slowly growing. Grand Strategy games are very much focused on portraying a grander scale of the already existing genre of strategy (for example 4x Civilization), But with this grander scale also comes hard to learn controls, mechanics and A LOT of trial & error if you don't like watching spoonfeeding guides. And adding insult to injury, this is also the most complicated Grand Startegy game of them all, compared to games like Crusader Kings & Europa Universalis. But if you are willing to play a game for several hours just how to learn to play it, watch tutorial videos and get repeatedly ravaged by the AI, proceed reading this review.
A simple rundown of the game: Victoria II is a game about country/empire managing where you play any country  during the time period from 1836 to 1936. You control the economics, build industry, watch your population grow and wage war with the goal of being a dominant power in the world.
Let's start with the content. Put simply: It's endless. You want a game which takes up to 30+ hours just to finish one campaign, and then restart a new one with another of the 200+ playable countries within the game? (Even more if you add mods like HPM, GSG & NNM) There's no goal in the game except surviving from 1836 to 1936, other then that, you set up your own goals . Want to conquer the entirety of Africa as Egypt? Do that. Want slavery to survive and prosper in North America? Do that. Want to turn uncivilized ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s into empires and great powers? Do that. Want to be the dominant world police as Canada? Dude, do that.  It's all up to you.
What I also like with the game is that every country in it's own right is unique and feels different, some less and some more. Great powers contain a lot of flavor and will offer a lot of historical facts, trivia, decisions and events that will both hinder and help you. Some nations lack in these areas, but is easily fixable by mods out there.
The most important mechanic in this game, which is ultimately the extremely unique population system. Every nation (and uncolonized land) have it's dedicated population at the start of the game, and it will day for day to the end of the game grow. This is the most addicting mechanic of the game, trying to make your nation prosper in the best way possible. POP's has they are called, pretty much defines everything in the game. They pay the taxes you need, produce the goods your selling and buying, work in the industry you build and the most important one, they are the soldiers in your army. If every soldier die in one of your divisions, that division dies off with them. There are no imaginary soldiers that appears from nowhere and refills your army here like in CKII & EUIV, Every pop in the game counts, and every death is a casualty for your nation.
The graphics in the game is very simple and really is just a giant map of the world. But considering what kind of game it is, it does the work and even in my opinion, very charming. While the game always start you out in terrain mode, I suggest you always play in Political Mode, which colors every nation in it's unique color.  The game offers many ways to see the game with different kind of modes in the map veiwer. From looking where population density is highest in your country to where you can currently colonize in the world. Mods exist to further improve the graphics with better huds, bloom and textures.
The soundtrack is absolutely phenomenal, with amazing orchestral victorian music which sets up the mood and atmosphere to wage war against your enemies. Even if you are not going to buy the game, you should do yourself a favor and listen to the soundtrack of this game:
And for those who enjoy modding and playing with mods, this is the game for you! I can safely say that this is one of the most easily moddable games out there. Even I during my free time have created custom countries and events for the game. So if you want to spice up the experience, make your own country and scenario! But if you are to lazy to do that, do not worry. Victoria II's mod community is huge and surprisingly keeps this old obscure game alive even to this day.
Want more nations for your game? (150+, more events and more decisions):
Want to play in modern times?
Want the Zombie Apocalypse to hit the world 1836 and then try to rebuild the world?
The modding possibilities are endless, which in my opinion is the games strongest point after the revolutionary POP mechanic. Make your own or play the amazing mods that people make even to this day
And that wraps up my review. Put simply, I goddamn love this game and if you like what you are reading, you should consider buying the Victoria Collection right now, or wait until the game hits a sale.

I started playing this game early February during early access with some friends and we had an absolute blast playing this game. I have had more fun playing this game than I have playing any other game. When we first started out we were crapping ourselves with every noise we heard and were just about crawling from base to base. When we found weapons, the fun exponentially increased as we were able to kill our first raptors and eventually hunt our first T-Rex. But, even though we had weapons we were still at the mercy of the dinosaurs.
We eventually had a shot at the PVP gameplay, with... mixed results. It was incredibly fun to play because the only way you could tell if someone was near you was by physically seeing them or hearing their gunshots. Playing PVP really kept you on the edge of your seat as you never knew if you were in someones sights and you didn't necessarily want to fire your gun in case you alerted people to your prescence. And hearing gunshots was just as terrifying because you can tell people are close, but you had to try and locate them using surround sound and the loudness of the gunshot. Although it was frustrating to lose your equipment, as my friends and I have lost the best gear several times, being killed by players or the dreaded cheater... The PVP experience was another amazing aspect I enjoy to this day.
To complete my review, my feelings toward this game are that it is the best gaming experience I have ever experienced. But due to lack of care and the greed of the developers it has somewhat withered away behind other games such as ARK, (I do not plan to play ARK. Riding dinos? Really?!). Anyway, this game had the potential of becoming something much more that it was initially planned to be, but the developers have seemed to ignore the game and the community which has led to a LOT of flak from the community and players.
My #1 suggestion would be to keep updating the game with patches and more content, but this seems to be out of the question. So I think the BEST option for the continuation of this marvelous game would be for the developers to open the game to modding in the Steam Workshop. This would mean more great content and patches for the game without consuming the time of the developers.

This all would be okay if you could reliably play multiplayer with other human players but playing online is incredibly buggy. I game a lot on my mac and it's usually very reliable however EL will usually crash about once every 100 turns, I'm pretty sure the mac version of the game, not my mac, is significantly bugged because it happens on my housemates mac too. Crashing as the game host means all other players will be kicked but it's unlikely you'd get as far as to crash because usually human players that join your game online timeout, disconnect or fall out of sync within 15 turns.

An extremely impressive game for being in Early Access. That said, there is so much more to be added to the game as well. The Curious Expedition caught my eye while I was looking for a game somewhat similar to Sunless Sea. That is, an adventure game that bases itself primarly on text. What I found was a great mixture of that and old school RPGs.
The game itself is played by selecting a character (based on historical figures) whom has his/her own traits, followers, and starter gear. This selection ultimately determines your playstyle. You will visit various locations while competing with several other adventurers to bring back the most impressive artifacts and native items. There is also a kind of bonus you can complete if agreed upon before leaving.
Ex. 1. A priest asks if you would help him spread the word of God in a certain village.
2. A commander asks you to bring back a soldier who is AWOL.
There are are also many interesting mechanics such as a 'Sanity' Bar which determines your movement across the hex-like board of the land. There are deserts, jungles, mountains, and other terrains to trek across, each with their own dangers and rewards depending on what region you're exploring. When on an expedition, the further into the map you go, the more will be revealed.
Things will can very interesting, very fast once you choose to steal that idol the Natives worship. Sometimes natural or...un-natural disasters can occur sending you scrambling across the board in panic. Your adventure ends when you find the Golden Pyramid in each area you visit. However, you may stay as long as possible if you wish to collect more artifacts and such. These can be sold or donated to the musuem for fame at the end of each expedition.
-

The Curious Expedition is very impressive, especially for an Early Access game. It is fair to say that whatever content is put into this game when its full release occurs will only make the game that much better. Any fans of Adventure games or even RPG fans will find that this is actually a very nice change from the norm. There are many choices and consequences that will affect your story, ranging from minor to catastrophic. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who loved Sunless Sea (although this game is not as dark) or anyone that is seeking an adventure game that is focused mainly on text. The music in the game is also pretty cool.

So I've played Victoria II + expansions (AHD and HOD) for a bit (mostly POP demand mod) and I'm certainly no grand master of strategy or anything, but there are still a ton of things that annoy to no end about this game. They annoy me so much I've decided to write this entire rant about them. My experiences with these kind of games are rather limited, I've played HoI 2 like 70 years ago quite a lot and HoI 3 only for about 10 minutes cause I ♥♥♥♥ing hate sliders. Otherwise I've played some of the older Total War games and Civ games (including Civ 5) but I can't really compare this game to Crusader Kings 2 oder EU 4 or something. I'm just some guy on the internet so I have honestly no idea how to systematically review things so I'll just name things as they come to mind.
So first, what exactly is this game trying to be? It's trying to be rather historically accurate but at the same time... it's not. When compared to the mass of events you have in HoI, the game feels really empty. That is understandable as HoI covers a much shorter time range and allows for a more historical simulation. But did really so little happen during those 100 years that most events you have are just random events during elections and such? I wish there were more events that influence my relations with neighbouring countries and such. But instead, everyone is just sitting there and I'm only increasing or decreasing my relations over the diplomacy screen. Lame. At the same time, it's like the game is discouraging 'unhistorical' conquest. Why do I get a massive hit for administrative effenciency (or whatever it's called) for a state just because it's not a 'core' area of my country? You'd think after 50 years of something, people would get used to being citizens of my country, but nope. You don't even have any way of influencing core areas.
As usual, the tutorials suck. They show you every screen of the game once and that's about it. What is it with these kind of games and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ tutorials? This game was released in 2010, do they still expect players to read through the manual (100 damn pages)? Tell me the most important stuff during the tutorial or have useful tooltips during the game, damn it. It's not like in League of Legends or similar games where most knowledge is meta stuff that you learn as you play, so it's not like it would be entirely impossible to have a decent tutorial. What research should I focus on? What should my army composition look like? What do all the stats a general has mean? Well, good luck finding out.
The AI sucks. They are incredibly hesistant when it comes to alliances but they will allow basically everyone and their mom military access to their country. Yeah right. It's almost as if borders don't particularly matter. They are also incredibly incompetent when it comes to managing an uncivilized country (or unciv as the community calls them). So don't expect anything from AI controlled uncivs in this game. You'd expect them to wage wars against each other and try to become a relevant country in their area. But instead they just sit there, eventually going bankrupt. Would a decent AI for unvics be too much to ask for? The fact that those countries never manage to do anything really takes away from the game.
Also the AI is just so incredibly stupid when it comes to leading wars. Unlike in HoI, you can't just declare war on a country. You always need a casus belli (CB) to declare war on someone and if you don't have one, you gotta make one. But making one risks you getting caught which results in you getting infamy (which gets reduces each month) and a lot of infamy is bad (like unrest in HoI). You'd think the AI uses their infamy wisely to press their advantage, but nope. They often just sit there with 0 infamy. But at the same time, when they do have a CB, they will often go to war even when it's complete suicide. You'd think the AI would be competent enough to calculate whether they can win a war or not, but nope. So Germany goes to war against France and gets their♥♥♥♥♥handed to them for no real reason. Over and over.
Naval units suck. The game only simulates a global market rather than local markets or supply lines so you can't block a country from trading or anything. Hey Paradox, ever heard the term 'Pax Britannica'? Why can't ships support your land units or anything? During that time, a superpower without a strong fleet would have been unthinkable. But according to this game, all you need is a strong land army to beat your neighbours over and over. Also, is a global market really realistic? I mean sure, the superpowers probably had plenty of international trade going on, but did all the backwards Asian countries or small European countries really trade on a global scale? I can't believe that. You'd think a game about a time where a strong fleet was basically the most important thing in the world would concentrate on forcing the player to play along, but nope.
The economy is so hard to follow. Why are the production and trade screen seperate? You know, seeing how much stuff I produce and how much is traded (supply/demand) is sometimes important to know so why not just have it on one screen? Doesn't make any sense. It's also hard to understand why your factories aren't selling all their stuff. What's the problem with not selling everything anyway? You'd think they can just store some of their productions and sell it later when demand is higher. But nope. Apparently furniture unsold gets thrown away or something. If you're wondering "what's the catch?"... well, there is no catch.  It's free.  Really free.  No DLC, deluxe editions, or microtransactions hidden in the game itself.. There's nothing to buy, it's just free.. because I guess the developers felt like it.  And that's really nice of them.  They gave out the source code, too.. so if you know how to mod stuff, you could do almost anything you can imagine with it.
Is it fun, though?  Sure!  It's right up my alley.  It's a top-down action game, where you explore procedurally generated floors, kill all the enemies, and look for pieces of relics to bring back to your home base.  There's a bunch of stuff to unlock, including additional playable characters, weapons to grab before you head into the action, shortcuts to lower floors (similar to spelunky, so you can skip the early floors if you desire), and the relics themselves, which you can equip once you've found all the pieces, for bonuses to your characters' attributes and abilities.
It's challenging, but not unfair.  There's also plenty of strategy to employ.  The dog-like enemies hate the humanoid enemies.. If you can make them fight each other, that makes things easier on you.  Sometimes you'll come across cages of the dog-like enemies, giving you the chance to release them to thin the enemy numbers, just be careful and watch to make sure you don't get caught up in the attack!  I also enjoyed the exploding barrels.. they jettison themselves roughly in the direction opposite from the side you damaged them, so they essentially become missiles that can clear a lot of enemies when used effectively.
Anyway.. I don't know why I'm writing such a lengthy review for something that costs nothing, you should just download it and try it yourself.

is the debut game coming from the French indie developer studio, From the Bard, presenting a tavern management simulation in a fantasy setting. For me it is a brilliant idea, since we rarely take a look on the NPC side of any fantasy story. I've been playing RPG games for years now, both on computer and tabletop. In nearly all those games that I've been to, all player characters voice a dream one time or the other: dealing with the main quest and being able to retire to safety one day to open an inn or a tavern. It's the optimal retirement plan for any medieval adventurer, ask anyone! Now, you can actually do it, yet again another adventure is included for you nonetheless.
Your uncle was a Tavernier before you, and now your time to take the establishment over has come. As he retires, he shows you the basics and leaves for you to handle the management of the tavern in the town. As you start, you'll have guests coming from many different social groups: folks, guards, rogues and wanderer to start with. They all prefer something else on the menu, a different kind of music for the local bard to play, some other treatment coming from the Tavernier, etc. It will be your job to attend them and pick one to favor above others to get a reputation and a social standing for your own self. As you go by though, a mysterious visit from the town mayor occurs. He comes in, picks one of your patrons and no one ever sees that man again... This unsettling occurrence repeats every month and townsfolk are reluctant to talk about it. Only if you manage to earn the trust and acceptance of one group, you may delve into this eerie mystery and uncover the scheme which threatens to destroy the whole town! Enjoy your retirement!
Now that we're done with establishing the base setting, let's hit our other subjects. For the display, nothing is marvelous or spectacular, but all artwork are fitting for the setting as hand drawn characters and environment. I enjoyed different kind of customers and their various outlook in game. There is no voice acting whatsoever, but you are free to choose your background music - folk, metal, jazz, classical, you name it! - fitting for the social group you are trying to impress. All musical numbers are free sample legends, playing on the same piece until you change it.
As for the game mechanics, it all is quite simple: easy to learn, yet hard to master. According to the kind of customers you favor, your complete number of customers for the week and the random encounter you face, your whole income is regularly calculated. You have to deduct your taxes from that though. With your earnings, you are free to garnish your tavern furthermore, to attract more customers. Random events occurring at the end of each week will depend whether you have the right decoration, have appropriate amount of money, whether you are considered a professional or just a cool guy too. Each new group you favor will unlock different random events for you to enjoy, and their outcomes will affect you furthermore.
Each month, an event relevant to the main story will occur, and if you've managed to fulfill its criteria, you'll progress in the main story. If not, you'll try next month. In 52 weeks, your game will come to an end, whether you've managed to solve the plot and face the main villain or not. So, I foresee various trial and error periods before you manage to complete the game with the good ending. Once you get a hold of how the main scenario works, you won't have that much of a trouble though. Then, achievement hunting begins - which is the real challenge. There are 4 main social groups and 4 more that you can unlock in your progression (you have to pick 2 for a single playthrough) according to your choices. They all will present you different abilities like tipping, attracting customers, being able to use magic etc. So, this simple little indie game presents a surprising amount of replay value for you.
Well, at the end of the day,
is obviously not the best thing since sliced bread, but it is a successful indie management game with a good story in store for its value. I do recommend the game for your discovery. Good day, and good gaming to you all!

This is a good indie management game with decent replay value for a low price. You are given
proprietorship of a tavern, and you have 52 weeks to figure out what evil is happening in town, and to make necessary adjustments to your tavern in order to put a stop to this evil before the 52 weeks end. You will want to decide what factions you want your tavern to appeal to (folks, guards, rogues, wanderers, mages, etc.) by having your tavern bard play music that appeals to them, changing tavern decorations, changing menu items, and other changes. You will also be given a randomized moral decision every week that will increase and/or decrease certain attributes of your tavern (percentage of your customers that belong to different factions, how much gold you have, whether you choose to have a "cool" or "pro" tavern alignment, the customer tipping rate, total number of customers, etc.).
Depending on the changes you make to your tavern and the weekly decisions you make, this will affect the path you take and the ending, of which there are several pathways and endings. The first time you play, it may take two or three hours to finish, but every playthrough afterwards will take significantly less time because you will see certain recurring weekly decisions pop up every now and then. There is replay value in that there are different ways you can play depending on what weekly choices you make and what factions you appeal to. Unfortunately, while the weekly choices are randomized, there are not a lot of them in each pathway. Once you get to a third or fourth playthrough, you will start to notice a lot of reoccurring weekly decisions, which can feel repetitious and reduce the time of those playthroughs to around half an hour. However, this isn't an issue with me personally; this is because you still get a significant amount of content for the low price because of the variety of paths that you can take and the endings.
The artstyle is great, the music sets a good mood, and it controls very well. The negatives I have with Tavernier are minuscule. There are some minor spelling/grammar mistakes throughout the storyline and dialogue interactions with characters. Some of the outcomes from your weekly decisions don't make a lick of sense, and there are glaring plot holes in the storyline. Also, I noticed in a couple of my playthroughs that one or two randomized weekly decisions will pop up every single week in the latter half of the 52 weeks for some reason (possible bug?). Despite these shortcomings, I recommend Tavernier for providing good tavern management entertainment and replay value at a budget price.

On the downside, combat is still a little unintuitive, and there may be some balance issues with some of followers - the artist needs a buff to offset all the inventory they take up. Also, some of the events are poorly balanced - right now, exploring caves is completely pointless, because it seems to outright kill max level companions the majority of the time. A bit more variety in the early expeditions would be appreciated too - right now, it's just a case of 100% the first expedition to rush on to something more interesting.
Overall, thoroughly recommended.

The Curious Expedition is an interesting game. First off it is fun, the most important thing for a game to be. The varied environments and random nature of the game means that it has a good replayability. The combat requires you to think about what you're doing and is random enough that it's unpredictable, but not so random that it's ridiculous.
Second, it's challenging. Finding all of the seals, stones or whatever else you need to access the pyramid can have you scrambling across the map. You run out of sanity as you move around and can replenish this with different foods or resting in certain locations. You have to deliberately decide where to move otherwise you will eat through your sanity like mad. The creatures in the game range from weak hyenas, to raptor packs that will anihallate all but the strongest parties. As of the time of me writing this review, I've beaten all 6 expeditions once after 6 hours of playing. My only criticism of difficulty is that deaths can be extremely random.
Third, the game is funny. From alcoholic nuns to cultists that are afraid of butterflies, your party members can be amusing as well as helpful.  I had a party member kill off all the other party members because he was convince they were trying to kill me.... or were they? I sold a nun into slavery to buy a native scout. Ronimo is clearly a team that thinks of concepts first, balance second. 3) When you win, it's extremely satisfying.
I thus say to not start playing Awesomenauts. Once you're in, you're in and you'll do a long stint, just like DotA. It's better thus to avoid it completely and live a relatively carefree life.

But beyond that, there are some massive design flaws with the single player mode. The fact that ending or losing a game kicks you back to the menu and forces you to watch the dialogue exchange again is infuriating. Nominated for the “test of time” award. This was my absolute favourite game when I was a kid and I still love it to this day.
It may be partly because I only owned about 3 games at the time but I must've sunk more hours into this game than any other.
The atmosphere and world are great, a dark story with just the right amount of humour. Abe is the last hope to free his enslaved people, who are forced to work in dangerous conditions by greedy slave traders who care only about profit, but if you get bored of all that you can press a button to make Abe fart, which causes all Mudokons next to him to take step back, and those further away to giggle.
Gameplaywise Abe’s Exoddus is a puzzle-platformer with the emphasis on the platforming over the puzzling. Most of the puzzles are easy to figure out, but actually completing them is another thing. It manages to fall into that elusive sweet spot of “challenging but fair”. You will die a lot but the game rarely resorts to fake-difficult instant-death traps. I remember playing some of these levels for the first time, I almost smashed my keyboard in frustration and yet every time I screwed up I knew it was my own fault. Each failure leaves you even more determined to finally beat this damn level.
This game seems to be less popular than its predecessor, Abe’s Oddysee, (although that may just be my group of friends) but I definitely prefer this one. Partly because I actually played this sequel before the original but also in large part because of the addition of quicksave. There is nothing more frustrating than completing a particularly difficult section and then dying 3 steps from a checkpoint and the quicksave handily eliminates that frustration.
The graphics are somewhat dated but it still looks pretty good for its age, besides it’s only $3 - or even less if you wait for a sale - what more could you want? Highly recommended, especially for any fans of old-school platformers.

Only If is an outstanding flagship of uniqueness. Solving the in-game riddles was enjoyable, and the concept of the story itself was interesting, and I felt it to be well-written.

There was a strange glitch in the mission where you leap from column to column, cracking pots. When I would shoot them, a shadow passed over the player, and I would look up to see what it was. The remnants of the cracked pot were the size of the field of view and raining down on top of me, as if they were instantly enlarged and duplicated above me. I thought that was strange.
I think that at the /very/ least, this game has fantastic potential. I do tend to enjoy this sort of game - there's a bit of management in there, mixed with some visual novel storytelling - but I didn't enjoy Tavernier. This is a game with a lot of glaring issues that pop up constantly.
Firstly, there are grammatical errors. A lot of them. And not simple, forgiveable things like a misplaced comma here or there, but great big flashing misspellings and broken paragraphs that launch me right out of the game, not that that's terribly hard because the story is completely nonsensical. Not to spoil it for those who still wish to play it, but the primary antagonist shows up multiple times throughout the story in disguise to actively help you, and this is never explained. You can also apparently become captain of the guard just from having a lot of coppers drink at your establishment.
Finally, the choices you get given throughout the experience have bizarre outcomes that don't make a lick of sense, including random radical alignment shifts, which can be devastating for a game that flat out requires you to fo all out with your alignment choices. Being anything but abusive to the guards that show up on occasion apparently makes everyone (including the guards) think you're less "cool," while the only way to regain coolness seems to be to do things that actively hurt your business.
It's all rather poorly thought out and irritating, but it also seems to be the very first game from this developer, so this is to be expected. The art is nice, and FromTheBard may go on to make some genuinely good games in the future, but this is not one of them.

I want to preface my review by saying I do appreciate the game, and like it's style...I am not a fan of the game however.
I like the retro-style graphics that seem to be making a resurgence in recent years. For gamers such as myself that have been gaming for 20+ years, it allows a sense of nostalgia from games of my youth. It's a colorful, vibrant appearance that even in the games darker moments, it still has an appealing taste.
I love the idea that the only narration in the game comes from stylized journal entries. It really adds to the immersion that you really are part of the expedition...vaguely reminds me of the older "Oregon Trail" (why are there no oregon trail games on steam?) games, but with a nice, animated scene to help you imagine the scenario at hand.
The open-world, rogue-like gameplay is well thought out. Forcing you to search actively for landmarks and assets in the wilderness, while providing vague clues as to what direction you should follow. My only experience with rogue-likes has been "Neo Scavenger," and I enjoy the style. Again, reminding me of archaic titles I grew up with, and board games I could never get anyone to play as a kid....however this leads me into my grips with the game, and why I really don't play it any more beyond 3 hours.
To me, the inventory system is flawed. A party of a handful of people, and a pack mule ought to be able to carry a vast array of supplies for an expedition...I think at the most, I had like 8-10 slots available (inventory size is relative to # of people and # of animals in party). Only 1 type of item can occupy a slot, but can be stacked in quantity in the same slot - regardless of object size...so an ancient mummy takes up the same space in the inventory as a sack of marbles. I got irritated trying to manage having enough bartering goods on hand, vs enough 'morale food' (whiskey, chocolate, etc. to boost 'sanity,' which gradually drains as you move around the map), vs enough tools (machetes, climbing gear, dynamite, to navigate treacherous terrain) vs relics and souvineirs (to boost my final score) to progress. 8-10 slots is too few for 3 people and their donkey, sorry...The cumulative party inventory size for a crew of that size seems like the inventory for 1-2 people with no animals.
So because I couldn't properly equip myself (in my opinion) I had a hard time with people deserting me, and in one instance, catching my donkey muttering to himself (I'm guessing a coding error, as it is a 'random encounter' intended for a human party member...I got a laugh out of it though). I understand the game is meant to be challenging, I do. My first playthrough on the first round, I finished, and thought to myself 'Wow, I did it in a timely manner, brought everyone home, and even a souvenier! No fights with locals, or wildlife, I'm doing great!" ....No such luck. Not only did I come in last - It was by a HUGE margin. I have no idea how the computer expeditions are scored, but something seems off, since they always recieve enormous amounts of points...maybe it's a union thing, i don't know.
I respect the game however, and maybe I'm doing something wrong. I will continue to follow it, and try again occasionally, I simply don't enjoy it.

This is an absolute gem of a game. A really unique concept and lovingly executed by a very small and dedicated dev team. Even at this stage of development it is very playable with a lot of interesting and different mechanics. It is very heavy on storytelling, and each expedition tells a new tale. The graphics and animations are also very cute. And the devs are very friendly and active in the community, very communicative about their plans, and frequently implement ideas and comments from community discussions - and I've only been following this a couple of weeks. To boot, the game has a darkly humourous streak, while at the same time managing to make incisive commentary on the very negative effects that colonial exploration and expansion had on the rest of the world.
To avoid potential disappointment I should just comment on the Early Access status of the game. Mechanically and structurally there is a whole lot of stuff in there but currently the content isn't anything like as fleshed out within that as it will eventually be. The Early Access period is being extended somewhat indefinitely so long as they can afford to keep adding comment, and the devs have indicated they want to carry on until around the end of the year. So given they are currently releasing pretty feature-packed updates every couple of weeks, there is an absolute ton of stuff still to come.
Finally - Charles Darwin riding a velociraptor, legging it from a tear in the fabric of space-time consuming the entire map, of course not forgetting to continue gathering rare butterflies with his butterfly net on the way. Enough said!

a great 4X game which is well thought out. i love civ and came to endless legend from civ 5. EL plays very differently. there are quite a few core differences which take a little getting used to.
each region can only have one city. think of them as counties/states and county/state capitol.
luxury and strategic resources do not have to be within your city border. only needs to be within your county/state border.
anomalies - special land tiles - have to be within your city borders.
cities can be expanded with burrough streets. if a city tile has 4 other city tiles next to it, it goes up a level and gives more food/science etc.
each major faction only has 3 units + inital hero. more unit types are gained by assimilating minor factions - little towns within a county/state you control.
research pies (for want of a better word) have icons on to show roughly what it does. so a spade icon means new resource extractor.
luxuries are activated via empire screen. must accumilate a stock of them then use them to get happyness.
strategic resources work the same, but seems you can only use one at a time as a "boost".
units can be grouped into armys and army size increased via research.
assimilating a subdued minor faction is done via the empire management screen.
keep upgrading units via the army management screen.
population automatically works all tiles. but you can move the populace about in a city and assign different resouce focus to them. this is done in the city management screen.
winter season - be prepaired for it. it can really hurt.
those are some of the major differences between the two games which had me scratching my head for the first game.
hope that helps!

: I was surprised at how much I enjoyed this one. I wasn't very impressed with the anime (it was gorgeous, but just wasn't that great otherwise) and the initial pre-release reviews for it weren't that exciting. But once I completed it, it became one of my favorite VNs/otome games. I think it's well-worth being a game in your collection, even if you're not normally interested in otome.
: Disturbing themes. As I said in my tl;dr, expect to be murdered a few times. As a minor spoiler, one of the love interests could easily fit under the 'yandere' (sick-love) type. The images never get beyond about PG-13 (for sexiness - you see very little or nothing in terms of violent images). As long as you're prepared for murder and yandere, you should be able to handle what the game throws at you.
I will note that one of the endings was so disturbing I had to walk away for a few minutes. Several of the Bad endings are actually quite disturbing, so while I kind of enjoyed it in the thriller sense, some people might not.
: Seems quite good! I didn't have any issues understanding what was going on and it reads quite well.
: A few minor issues. A few typos here and there, but nothing to really disrupt your enjoyment.
: Really top notch. Plenty of gorgeous CGs, a wide range of character sprites, and a really cool style overall. This is absolutely a game you could buy just for the art and be satisfied by if you like what you see from the screenshots. (Granted, it's not flawless, but it is very high quality.)
: I personally enjoy it quite a lot. It's a shame you don't see the Heroine very much since I really dig her design, but all of the characters are quite nice to look at. (Okay, it's over the top, but it seems to be normal in their worlds, so it works for me!)
: Have you ever had one of those dreams where you're dropped unprepared into a situation? Like, for me, I get dreams where I have to take a test I didn't know about, or I'm given a role in a play right before the curtains rise, or I'm being put on the field for a ColorGuard performance and have to rely on my memories of doing it in high school. Imagine that, but "for real". At least the Heroine has a cute and friendly Orion to help her out a little bit.
You need to figure out what your life is like in the world you choose and what your relationships are like with the people you meet. Eventually, you'll come to understand you're in a relationship with a guy in the world you're dropped into and balance trusting him and giving him the benefit of the doubt with not letting on too much too soon about not being the woman he knew.
This delicate balancing act is the heart of each story and I personally found it interesting every time. The individual stories are a little linear, so the first part of a story route is pretty well the same, but it does branch out towards the end, meaning multiple distinct endings for each hero.
For the most part, I enjoyed each hero's routes. (The "yandere" hero, not so much, but I can't say his route wasn't
, just not one I'd experience for romance purposes.) I think that most otome fans will find at least one hero they'll really enjoy.
: A blank slate - pretty literally, too. She has almost no text dialogue in the game and you have to simply infer she says something. This means a lot of monologuing on the part of the heroes - which is great if you're digging the voice actors (personally - I love them), but it does feel a little awkward sometimes, especially if the other characters point out that the Heroine is silent. It's clear from the flashbacks and comments from the other characters that she
a distinct personality of her own before her amnesia, so I'm willing to give it a bit of a pass. Once she gets most of her memories back (assuming she does, that is), she starts having lines of dialogue, so I infer that means she's in full control of her "self" again, so the lack of real personality of her own before then feels fine to me in a story sense.
I highly recommend the game and hope you enjoy it too!

The main casualty of advancements in online gaming has been local co-op. We all have memories of convening at a friend’s basement or room and playing games together while screaming about screen-peeking, cheat codes, and all other manner of sore loser-isms. Developer Stegersaurus Software Inc. shares those memories and made Mount Your Friends as a callback to the glory days of old. Needless to say, Mount Your Friends is definitely a much more explicit game than anything we played growing up. Never in my life did I expect to write this sentence but the dong physics are second to none.
The first thing you notice about Mount Your Friends is the gang of Speedo-clad, Diglett-looking bodybuilders that you control. The premise of the original mode of the game is simple enough: each player has 60 seconds to climb on top of an ever-growing pile of the other players and get as high as they possibly can, with whoever tops the pile being the winner.
The challenge comes from the control scheme. Like the Assassin’s Creed franchise, each of the four input buttons controls one limb. Hold down a button and move the joystick to swing a limb; once you release the input button, if you are touching a surface, that limb will adhere to that surface and won’t let go until you manually move the limb again.
Climbing the tower of muscular flesh can be easier once you figure out how to fling yourself from limb ledge to limb ledge, but until then you’ll find yourself slowly climbing up with all the grace of a newborn giraffe. However, this method runs the risk of either under- or overshooting your target and finding yourself flopping through the air until you splat onto the ground. While playing this game with friends, you find yourself either cackling like a madman at their ineptitude or malevolently planning on how to smack the controller out of their hands while playing it off as an accident.
In addition to the original race-to-the-top mode, there are a myriad of gameplay modes for both single and multiplayer. You can race to see who can traverse a rocky obstacle course and collect the most coins, make a bridge across a chasm, or even a freestyle mode without a timer to see what flexing muscular shapes you can build.
The music in the game is just as well-designed as every other aspect of the game. While playing a head-to-head game, the music takes on this epic feel, as if climbing this mountain of digital flesh is as grand as traversing Middle-Earth. I half-expected Gandalf to pop up as the next climber I controlled. If you pull off a particularly long climb, you hear your character stretch and strain to get that last bit of height.
As a multiplayer game, Mount Your Friends is as hilarious and entertaining as they come. Unfortunately, the single player mode gets old after a while. It’s not that the game is boring, but without playing against someone to challenge you, the game loses its appeal. Luckily for those without friends nearby, Mount Your Friends is playable online as well as with a local competitive co-op. There are global leaderboards for those who want to push themselves to keep climbing, but most of the fun comes from watching your friends struggle to climb above the human obstacle you put above them.

One of my favorite Paradox titles, Victoria 2 is all about the diplomacy! Shunning the more combat heavy focus of the EU and CK series, Vicky 2 gives players a breadth of new options. However combat is just as great as in other games, and nothing is more satisfying then stackwiping an army. Word of warning however, for people unfamiliar with grand strategy games I recommend trying CK2 first as Vicky 2 requires considerably more from the player. Watch a few online videos to get your feet wet before diving in.

Victoria II is an internal management game with a (slight) military and diplomatic twist. Unlike Hearts of Iron (Warefare-based) and Europa Universalis (colonisation and exploration-based), Victoria II's focus is on domestic politics and industry.  I  like this game a lot. I like how the power structure of Great Power,teh 8 most powerful coountries in the world, Secondary Power, the the 9-16 most powerful countries, Civilized, and Uncivilized Powers, raned on if  they are westernized or not, is set up. Great powers in the game do what you'd expect a top notch colonial power, like the UK or France, to do. They can push around everyone below them. They can do whatever they want at almost any time. The secondary powers, like Mexico or Sardinia-Piedmont, can colonize and compete with the great powers at times, but cant push people around like a great power. A civilized nation, like Bolivia or Parma, are at the bottom of the civilized world. These are the countries that great powers  mostly try to fight for influence over. They may be the weakest, but some can still have a powerfull industrial and military arm compared to their regional rivals. The Uncivilized, like Oman or Siam, nations are the very bottom of the totem pole of the world's geo-political landscape. They have little power and can be pushed around quite easily (except China). Most are very weak compred to everyone else militarily and industrially. Thes countries are also at the mercy of colonization. They are also fought after by great powers.
Another thing i like is how the game makes you use different elements of your population. Each strata (farmers, craftsman, solders, etc) have a different use which are self-explanitory. a couple uses include, craftsman and clerks: they work in your factories, Beurocrats: help administration efficientcy.
The military system n the game is a bit basic, but like I said in the beginning, it's not primarily a wargame. National ideas are another thing i like because they give certain bonuses to the regions you put one in. THis game also has a decent trech tree. Different nations are better at researchng different parts of the tech tree (Prussia gets a bonus with the army and industry trees and a disadvantage with navy and culture trees).
Each game has its own pros and cons. This game, in my opinion, has pros that outway the cons.

Since this game won the "Labor of Love" award on Steam (but still lost to the gambling game on the other Awards), it's a good time to talk about it and how "love" can be twisted and abused upon. I'll start with the good qualities, but sh*t goes down after each starting.
: Large breadth and depth to explore, but unnecessarily grindy to execute.
Instead of following most MMO's recipes where end-game is filled of lots of people doing the exact same thing, Warframe did balance and interesting gameplay right by differentiating choice from decision correctly. On something like WoW, your build is a "decision": you either make the right call, or you fall behind. On Warframe, the frame's and weapons selection are "choices": there are no wrong answers. Even when the weapon you like is underpowered, finding a Riven Mod for it can put it above any other more popular and more balanced weapon.
And this is where Warframe forces you to make decisions instead of choices (rewarding smarts besides skills): Mods. In order to know how to Mod, you must know the game mechanics, understand the weapon stats, and choose the right mods. As you find more Mods, you get more options and can make better builds.
Besides that, you still need to upgrade those mods, and that takes some grinding to get the resources needed, but the cost for anything on the early game is still doable, and can be achieved while not really focusing on getting resources for upgrades, while instead, making your way on the game lengthy questline or startmap.
, as you understand the limitation of the Mod system and how to circumvent it, you start understanding why Formas are important. And you stumble upon the first grind-wall that is a pain. Putting a Forma on a equipment reduces the cost for equipping the Mod (provided you planned your alignment, showing that you understand the game mechanics), but resets the weapon level to 0. And if you need to put a new Forma, you need the weapon on 30 again. Rinse and repeat. And where most piece of equipment require at least 2 to 3 Formas for an end-game build, you are talking about 1 hour of grinding to perfect an equipment, provided you are far enough in the game. If not, increase that to 2 to 3 hours. And where there is so much to choose from, you won't be playing a single frame with the same 3 weapons, so we are talking about way more hours sinked in this.
This game that sets your player level based on the amount of content you explored by awarding you with experience based on how much unique items you trained to max rank, and this is nice. So you would expect that re-leveling something to the max rank wouldn't be a chore because you "already learned about it". But no. It's grinding time again. The reward of selecting the right alignment for that Mod ends up shadowed by the grinding required to get the item to max rank again.
: Really expansive, and mostly well written, even if sometimes "too much to the face", but mixed with RNG-grinding mechanics is simply ridiculous.
The game does hold your hand too much sometimes, and shoves things on your face a lot, but, in the long run, it still gives you freedom to pursue your objectives in your own fashion and speed. There are lots of content that are hidden and not necessary to be pursued, although the game still nudges you in the direction of them, in a way of making sure you aren't just missing them. Seeking the Cephalon Fragments for example reveals
, and when you complete them, the reward is great. It's a pain to scan the fragments several times in all planets, but it's not something that needs to be done, or even needs to be grinded. You can do as you do other things, and just stopping mid-way of a mission to just collect that bit of info. This is great, because it fuses exploration together with the normal gameplay, thus not making it a task.
But then, DE showed how much they are embracing making the players grind over RNG after implementing PoE, and locked a great deal of lore behind the Ghouls event behind an RNG based grindwall, where you have to repeat the event mission and hope you get one of the 52 fragments needed. There were no mechanics that guaranteed a drop under any circumstances, with players doing the even missions over hundreds and hundreds of times without being able to complete the pieces.
: There are some "pay to progress faster" options, but they are overshadowed (although still conflict) by the cosmetic content, which ends up being the main theme.
Some players will joke saying that "endgame is FashionFrame" or "endgame is IkeaFrame", and that actually isn't much of a joke. After getting a new frame and trying a bit, most players will end up customizing it. After looking at your orbiter for so long, you end up at least changing the internal colors. Most of the cosmetic options in Warframe are geared towards being somewhat easy to fiddle with and making that piece of the game feel like your own. The quality of the deluxe skins, in example, is great, and the prices are a bit steep but still worth. Added, there are lots of player made content that make into the game after reviewed by other players and accepted by DE.
A great game, with lots of greatly designed content, with a nice monetization that evaded the F2P-P2W scheme, but that still followed the grind-traps of MMO's that so much rely on players enjoying repetitive brainless tasks that do not increase your skill, most of these dealing with mental health issues that make them embrace that grinding as "I'm becoming a better player" and not as the real "I don't want to deal with my problems, so let's repeat this task with small gratification until I feel good enough".

There are more good things to say about Warframe then I can go into right now, but safe to say that it is the most addictive and pleasant grind based game I've ever played. I'd say that with memorable characters like our beloved Clem and our good friend Excalibro, Warframe has the potential to be a lasting masterpiece in PC gaming.
There are various things that Digital Extremes gets right with Warframe, like how your first battle suit (called a warframe) is never left behind as newbie material but continues to be useful thoughout the game, or how leveling up in the game doesn't just unlock predictably superior weapons and such but actually unlocks new features and ways to play, or how the storyline manages to leave you looking for the next main quest to find out what happens next, but I think the thing that makes Warframe and its producers stand out the most is how they treat their player and customer base.
Digital Extremes kicks trend started by EA games of screwing the players over with innumerable micro transactions and premium paid content or DLCs. NOTHING essential to the Warframe experience costs money! There is no grind so long or tedious that it demands the use of paid boosters. The ONLY things that must be purchase with real money or premium currency are cosmetic items. Even the premium currency can be aquired by trading various in-game items to other players. This actually makes me want to spend money on the game, in fact, I already have and plan to continue.
You have my respect Digital Extremes.

[Updated for current state of the game 10/8/2015]
Okay so I'm marking this negative specifically for the current state of the game.
Currently the game offers very little for people looking for a game to waste a decent chunk of time in.
The class system is setup where you just pick up 1 of 8 current weapon types that allow you a basic attack and secondary.
There is currently no character progression system nor equipment system (ie: there is no actual loot in the game currently)
to break it down a bit:
Currently lootfest doesn't have a plot or point there is no story (early access so I can accept this)
The control is similar to most voxel hack n slash with the exception that due to the map style the camera can be wonky
The feel is non-existent, you are random character A that randomly kills monsters with which ever left or right click attack you want to save random baby A over and over
The play-ability is one time. Until decent changes i don't feel the need to play it again because no matter how much I play it I will always be random character A equipped with random 2 attacks (A B C or D) that walks through a map to collect keys and for some reason kill a boss for a baby. I wont ever become more than that in the current game system and some random character B that just bought the game could walk in and be the exact same as me despite random character A spending way more time in game playing.
You have the ability to make your own stuff through their voxel system which is a good thing, I've seen it be very successful in other games but this one is still very early in its creation so the creating system is not at a point where it can offer much.
The available maps to play are very straight forward and due to no equipment or leveling there is no point in killing anything on the maps except the bosses (which currently drop a random baby followed by you being teleported back to the starter map)
Now I do expect the game to get much better as the devs work out where they're going with it.
If you feel like helping them move along by buying it in early access don't expect to get a lot of enjoyment out of the current version of the game but rather probably bug test the current version a bit and hold onto your early access version until the final version is complete because it should become a pretty good game.

I hacked my way through a dark prehistoric jungle when I was ambushed by a group of bloodthirsty Raptors.  Nikola Tesla and his crew of intrepid explorers were ready for this, their trials and tribulations over 5 brutal expeditions in search of the Golden Pyramids, far out in the uncharted wilds, had honed their skill and teamwork to a paramount.  Nikola whipped out his Tesla Cannon and fired at the first of the three vicious predators, burning and tearing skin from bone with electric fire.  His cook, what's-her-name, a jolly english woman that had been with Nikola since the very first, had survived worse than this.  Her cleaver was death, just like her cooking.  The first raptor fell, and the party knew what would be for dinner this day.
The thought of over-cooked raptor flesh sent Sir Something-or-Other, a kleptomaniac trader with a penchant for drinking too much and whispering to himself by the campire, into a frenzy of slahes, curses and raw, unbridled wrath.  Days it had been since he last ate anything but leaves of the coca plant, and his mind was not his own.  His hunger ruled all, and was equalled only by his fear of butterflies.  The heart of darkness all men must face in these wilds had taken him, but it was the darkness in him they needed now.  The fear.  The anger.  The booze.  He flanked and struck a raptor as it stood dumbfounded by Tesla's blast, but with him was another.
A native scout, skin dark from years of toil in the sun of the slave camp, hurled a spear with such great force the beast howled in pain and blood.  None knew his name, because none could understand a word he said.  Strengthed and raged by the betrayal of his people and his ill treatment at the hands of twisted, cruel slavers, he relished the ground beneath his feet, the view of the mountains from afar, the comraderie of those who had freed him, and eating hallucinogenic mushrooms whenever the shamans would trade them.  His hunger was of a different sort.  A cannibal, he had long ago tasted the flesh of men, but just once of the mule named Ms. Jones that had carried all their golden relics, stolen from shrines far and wide.  Carried once...but no more.  He had seen to that.  His powerful spear was welcome in this dark place of blood and teeth, a place much like where they had found the last, and perhaps strangest, of all their companions.
The last was a lizard, large like a man and walked on two legs.  Savage.  Incomprehensible.  Tended to end all of his sentences with a long series of the letter S.  His motivations were even more of a mystery, though Telsa seemed to believe he simply enjoyed exploring.  After the mysterious disappearance of Ms. Jones, their faithful pack mule, he was welcomed despite his appearance and poor speech habits.  His claws and teeth did work sometimes far more effectively than spear and guns, and he knew how to slip about the jungle without notice.  It was he who fell the second raptor.
Only one was left.  He thrashed and lept, throwing itself at them, but for naught.  Their tactics were too practiced, too precise.  There could be no victory for such a foe, only death and later...nibbles.
As what's-her-name hacked up the beasts into steaks, Tesla stumbled upon a clutch of hatched eggs.  All had been cracked, recently hatched...all but one.  Thinking this a prize indeed, Tesla gently stuffed it into his backpack, thinking of the fame to be gained, only rivaled in its enjoyment by the seething jealousy of Alistair Crowley and Amelia Earhart.  Those two losers would be SOOOO miffed when he brought a raptor egg back to the Exploratorium.
With full bellies and thoughts of further riches somewhere out there in the jungles, or mountains - or perhaps beneath the fires of volcanoes or under the watchful gaze of very poorly carved sacred statues - the interpid explorers set off again into the wilds.  Mere days had passed when, much to the surprise of everyone, that lonely egg - warmed by a spontaneous wildfire and good company - hatched!  Out came a tiny, sharp toothed baby raptor, his adorable foreclaws already reaching for poorly guarded jugular.  Nikola named him Einstein.
And then the game crashed, because this is still in Alpha.  You should buy it anyway.
