At the moment this game has really bad balance. It's way too random, events are almost always negative and the game doesn't really explain itself well at all. There is a tutorial, but it only explains the most pointless things, things you will figure out for yourself in the first few minutes of the game. There are many more important things it could explain, but it's just a waste of time.
Combat is a great example. You need to combine dice, that the game doesn't even explain go together. The only sign is that dice shake when they can be combined. It would be great if there was just a list of things you might be able to do if you had the right dice. Would make taking chances with rolls feel a little less pointless.
The way the game progresses the competition is also ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It feels like arbitrary advances with AI explorers just shooting up points with no explanation. It feels cheap, and it probably is. Why not have the game showcase the AI achievements, what they brought back, what they get for it? Might actually learn something through playing the game eh?
Talking about random bs the game also likes to apply arbitrary restrictions to proceeding. That stone in the "Shadow" shrine you saw? Yeah, gonna need that to unlock the pyramid- like finding the pyramid wasn't even important, no you gotta unlock the stock lock that no mortal could possibly even open. Oh, going back for the stone? Well how how about getting a game ruining party member abomination to join you and never leave because we made it so that it can't die in battle no matter how many tigers you fight and oh if you think about killing it it will become far more powerful then it ever was in your party? Yup, roguelikes aren't about choosing the best alternative, they are just childish godwin simulators because we all love that.
I also wish the game had some level of ingenuity, or more options in events more alternatives, more use of perks and special abilities, but it all boils down to "do you want to loot or fight this?" The results of which are always bad, but sometimes less awful things happen. Oh and this waterfall is good for sleeping, but this one is only good for going into with a torch, makes sense. It's also kind of rediculous that you party up with the same people, and only ever one person might join you, probably a useless cultist. Also why can't your character level up? Why is he so useless- well okay he doesn't develop unhealthy addictions, psychosis or flat out become a cannibal because we were walking in a forest and he didn't want a chocolate bat, mango, or freaking ask the cook to fry up a tiger steak to eat- nope he wanted the cook for dinner.
Overall, could be really cool. A lot more tweaking with the random map generation, a little more in the way of interactivity and this could be a fun game to spend hours in. Right now it's an okay alternative to wasting time, just to see how random a game can be.

Tremendously fun 4X game. Plays similar to Civilisation games, but made a really nice unit system that allows for huge armies that don't clog up like in CIv5 but at the same time you don't have the SoD problem from Civ4.
The main draw of this however is the different playstyle of all these factions. This is further elaborated with each faction's unique victory quest (which is not an auto-win, it unlocks the Wonder you can build to win the game, but you also get very powerful buildings/upgrades/weapons which allow you to further another win condition) and I rarely had a 4x where each faction's personality blends in so well with their gameplay. Nekrophages swarm over the map and take up slaves for work and food, Cult of Eternal End converts everyone to their religion and builds a single gigantic mega-city (and unlike Venice in Civ 5, they don't suck)
Peaceful gameplay has a unique twist with the influence system. You need influence to declare war for example and you can brown-nose people so much that they literally cannot afford to go to war with you. Also you can block people from buying stuff on the market which can be huge.
Technology also finally isn't overpowered in this game due to the era system. All technologies are equally hard to develop, so you cannot rush to, say, Era 3 and use 2-3 turns to develop what you missed in Eras 1-2. Dedication is key here. And even a technological advantage is nothing if you don't dedicate to building an army and get slaughtered by a player who has extremely powerful demons with 14 moves that plow through your militas like lawn.
The amount of cities is also limited by the regions of the game which helps combat the old mass building of cities for more production. In a normal game, even stuff like Nekrophages usually gets stuck at 6-7 cities tops (if you play 6+ players) unless the other players are apathetic about expansion. The way borders work also lead to border tension more easily and by that extend, you rarely have the lonely isolated player who just goes for science/economy victory while everyone else is eating each other alive.
TL;DR: Endless Legend did everything right in their game. Every faction feels unique, but never like a one-trick pony. The non-war victories finally don't feel stale. Every fan of turn-based strategy games should try this game out. Even if you aren't, I would recommend having a look because the AI is easy enough to beat for a casual players and seeing your War Titans roll out and grind cities to ashes is immensely satisfying.

Fidelio Incident is a brief and, for narrative game enthusiasts, interesting title. Set in the an unspecified Icelandic landscape in the early 2000s, the game features two characters, Stanley and Leanore - an Irish couple whose convoluted history unfolds throughout the game.
In many ways, Fidelio Incident is actually a reverse Firewatch. Set in the a harsh winter landscape, fraught with hazards, guilt trips and downright nervous breakdowns, Fidelio is set in a more emotionally turbulent scale than the easy-going nature of Firewtach. For those unfamiliar with the backstory of recent Irish history, a quick Wikipedia search on the Troubles in Northern Ireland may also prove useful, as the plot may appear a bit alien.
Gameplay is simple and it's based on a non-HUD interface, where elemental effects (cold, fire or such things are signified via representations around the edges of the screen (cold creates frost, fire emits flames et cetera). There are no mobile threats like wildlife as in similar survival type games, allowing for a more leisurely pace and awareness.
Fidelio Incident takes about 2-3 hours to complete - not particularly long, and certain parts do feel a bit like rubber-necking. One can go into specific details about its narrative, which could definitely be improved but overall it delivers its promise and concludes its story with a decent twist.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Amnesia : Memories is a wonderful visual novel that I highly recommend. The basic premise is that you as the main character are suffering amnesia, as well as basically a spiritual possession, and are attempting to regain your memories  and free the spirit from your mind.
There are 5 total romanceable characters, all male.  The first 4 are available as soon as you start the game, the fifth one unlocks after finishing the good endings for the first 4 characters.  All of them have 1 good ending, 1 normal ending and between 1 and 7 bad endings.  They are all very well defined characters, with elaborate stories and very very different personalities.  You have a tsundere, a popular/playboy who yearns for real love, an intellectual who's aloof and bad with emotions and socializing, and 2 yandere characters that are on opposite ends of the yandere spectrum.  Each one of their stories take place on alternate dimensions, so even though the basic story premise is the same for each, the stories themselves are completely different and the side characters will sometimes have vastly different personalities in each route. As a fair warning, if you are someone who needs trigger warnings, you may have problems with one of the routes.
Getting the different endings requires making different selections during the story branches.  Each selection will either raise, lower, or leave your attributes in their current level of accumulation.  There is no stat raising or grinding, it's just a matter of selecting conversation options to raise or lower your trust, relationship and suspicion with each character.  There are quite a lot of branches, and it felt like there should have been more save slots available because of how many choices you have available.
The art is absolutely beautiful, the music and voice acting is great and fits in very well, the stories and characters are well written, and the translation is very accurate - though there are a very few spelling and grammar errors, it doesn't stick out horribly or detract from the experience.  After beating all the stories and endings there are also mini games, additional memories and short stories that follow up with the characters, leaving a huge amount of content in this game, it's really surprising how much content the game offers.
Pros:
+5 very different romanceable characters
+so many endings
+mini games
+unlockable bonus content
+art
+music
+story
+a 12 episode anime series you can watch elsewhere if the game isn't enough for you
Slightly Irritating:
~a few spelling/grammatical errors
~no obvious exit option in game
~while you can customize controls, it doesn't tell you what the buttons do
~for some people the achievements aren't working (IF is currently working on fixing it)
~a character who goes too far
~could use more save slots
Cons:
-I can't really think of anything outright negative about this game.  :)
If you like anime and/or visual novels I really recommend you pick up this game, it is definitely worth the money, even at full price!

It looks like this game is an abandoned early access. Technically there are people working on this but apparently they aren't being paid.
However, the number of bugs are limited to a few areas and the game is generally playable and all of the bugs I have found can generally be worked around. I have played this game for 60 hours on steam and probably a lot more out side of steam but just given the steam numbers this has cost me 17p per hour of fun I've had on it.
The bugs I've found in this time:
Pathing: When ever a character makes a choice about what to do it tries to path it's way to that and if there isn't access to area it is trying to get to (like if you bult walls all around your base) then it takes a while to try the next work item. This can take a long time if you have 3 jobs it can do and 20 it can't. Fix: Don't make jobs your people can't access.
Archery Training: There is a function that allows you to equip your units with items. If you equip an archer with a bow and a melee weapon however they don't seem to train at archery targets. Fix: Remove melee weapons when you have someone archery training.
Training: There are a couple of problems with training firstly if you set people to train a targets they won't go there on there own you have to tell them to go and secondly the system doesn't tell you that you can't train when you get to level 11.
Equiping: When you tell a unit to equip items they don't do it immediately they wait until they are going to drop off or pick up items presumably for efficiency. Fix: Switch the characters profession to something else and then switch back once they have got the required items.
Courage: You units have courage levels which go down when they see large numbers of enemies but it doesn't seem to take into account if the unit is safe from the enemy i.e. behind a wall while the enemy units are all melee and also it doesn't seem to take into account when you have a large force at your back. Fix: The way I solve this problem is to try and get to a place where I can see only 1 enemy and shoot it to reduce their numbers. Being behind walls also really helps.
Building: Sometimes you make a build order and it seems like there is no reason that it isn't being completed, I've only had this happen once in probably 100 hours of play. Fix: Delete the surrounding blocks if it is safe to do so and then rebuild a layer at a time.
There are lots of games like this (some of which are also abandoned) Towns, Gnomoria, Stone hearth, Banished and Life is Feudal:Forest Village
Personally I play them all.
Should you buy it?
If you have played any of the above games and like that style of game then your enjoyment will get you past the few work arounds you have to do.

The Curious and Exciting Journal of Johan Huizinga!
Day 1: I set down upon Jayapura with great excitement, knowing that fame and fortune awaited me. Such a beautiful landscape lay before me that I should never see its like. A missionary by the name of Derrick Fry joined us, along with Derrick Richard--a grizzled old tar, and Chalipa Sorabji--a curious Persian lass with a knack for foreign tongues. I'm sure we shall all get along splendidly on this magical voyage.
Day 3: Only 3 days in and we came across an elephant graveyard. After loading up on some guilt-free ivory, we headed out. Chalipa was rather put out by this, however, and babbled on about evil spirts. Silly superstitions do not scare me, however. This is the modern world, after all!
Day 7: Such luck! Underneath an unsightly stone we found a drum and some cocoa leaves, which I shall savour later. Chalipa screamed and pointed at the stone, claiming it was the head of a long-dead heathen god. Bah! Richard asked if he could have the drum, but I wouldn't have him damaging this priceless relic, and had Chalipa carry it instead, despite her protests.
Day 18: We came across the village the Missionary was after. A curious New Guinean tribe of warriors. I was halfway through recording a study on their culture when an older fellow asked to play me a traditional tribal rythmn on the drums. Thinking this invaluable to my studies, I agreed, whereapon he bashed Chalipa in the face with it and began babbling some heathen curse. Chalipa cried herself to sleep as the rest of us slept soundly. We awoke to the happy sound of children's laughter, with them pointing at us--no doubt as some sort of tribal gesture of friendliness. We left as they waved their spears and shook their fists in some primitive sort of goodbye gesture. Such pleasant folk. I hope we see them again.
Day 26: After resting at a leisurely hot spring, a tiger, painted in white swirls for some reason, attacked us. It was a hard fight, but interestingly, the tiger only seemed interested in attacking Chalipa. We quickly dispatched it, but Chalipa was left with a nasty wound, and we have no medicine with which to treat it. She mumbled about the curse as she passed out.
Day 34: We came across the shrine the chieftan from the previous tribe had told us about, inside which we found a beautiful golden vase. As I picked it up, Chalipa woke long enough to scream some nonsense about the wrath of the gods, but her babble was drowned out by the sudden volcano forming beneath us. My word, New Guinea is such an active place! We bid a hasty, but dignified retreat from the shrine, stopping only long enough to have tea.
Day 41: Times have gotten hard for us. We have run out of both tea and whiskey, and Chalipa simply will not shut up about these ghosts of hers. As if to accentuate the ridiculousness of her claims, a funny little tribesman clutching his chest crawled toward our camp in the middle of the night, his wound looking far worse than hers. "Why, that's no ghost, it's just a silly man." He motioned toward us, and toward his chest. I assured us we loved his people too, and his face screwed up in agony, presumably over the knowledge he could not come with us. He shook his head and repeated the motion, pointing towards our surgical kit, and back to his chest, which appeared to be decorated in blood spatter patterns--a tribal custom I'm sure. "Yes, I know, we love modern medicine too." He then went to sleep right there on the ground. It's amazing how comfortable these people are within their native land! Chalipa began screaming about death again, for some reason. This would prove to be a long night.
Day 52: After backtracking through no small amount of volcanic ash, we finally found the fabled Golden Pyramid! It was a lovely site, and scores of natives poured forth from what was left of the jungles, shouting and waving their spears--no doubt in celebration of our accomplishment. I did not get much chance to study the pyramid, however, nor even to thank our generous hosts, as Richards quite literally scooped me up in his excitement, and made for the boat home. I admonished him on the way back to London, but I gave him a bit of a break after a sudden swell threw Chalipa off the boat and he narrowly rescued her from a school of sharks that had been following us since we left.
Weeks Later: Back home safe in London, my fellow adventurers and I had a jolly good laugh about our adventures back home before the awards ceremony. Afterward, I was keen to get on safari again, and so I gathered up my trusty sailor and translator to settle the logistics. Chalipas face went pale with wonder and she screamed with what I can only assume was excitement all the way back to our next destination. What a fun time this will be!

The Curious Expedition is yet another Kickstarter-spawned entry into the ever-growing field of Rogue-Likes, but with a refreshing new twist. This time around, the player takes on the role of a small party of 19th-Century explorers engaged in a gentleman's wager - to travel the world on six concurrent expeditions, competing to see who can gain the most fame. It's a fairly quick and lethal game, but that's exactly what it's meant to be - a good way to kill a few hours at a time, running expedition after expedition off to their doom.
GRAPHICS: Expedition uses a rather charming 8-bit style, which I personally found very appealing. Trying to make sense of things can be a bit daunting at first, especially once the world map is spread out in front of you, but once you have a few games under your belt it becomes easier and easier to glance at a pixelated hex or crude 8-bit figure and know exactly what you're looking at (ie, the "Dwarf Fortress ASCII Effect").
SOUND: The music for Curious Expedition is likewise done in a retro style, and while the number of tracks are currently rather limited (just three or four), they're all sufficiently catchy. The sound effects are rather crude, but again that matches the 8-Bit style of the game. Nothing ground-breaking, but it gets the job done.
GAMEPLAY: Expedition is still in an Alpha state, but the vast majority of the game mechanics are in place. There are already a fairly impressive number of items and treasures to find during your explorations, the combat system is fully functional (though poorly explained), and I only encountered a single minor bug during my first dozen or so campaigns. The basics of the game are fairly straightforward - you explore randomized regions, attempting to find treasures while simultaneously tending to your expeditions needs (most notably staving off insanity). Honestly, what's there is already an almost complete game, though some might argue that in it's current state it isn't worth the full $15 asking price. There are three main sticking points for many players:
First, the game lacks any significant documentation. There's a basic tutorial that can teach you about the exploration phase of the game, but it skips over several crucial elements of the game (it completely ignores the combat system, for example). Many of the items and abilities you can acquire in the game are poorly explained, and require the player to use trial and error to discover how they work. Proper documentation will likely be provided once the game is further along in development, though, so this is a minor issue.
Second, the game is VERY random. This is to be expected for any rogue-like game, but there are some who will argue that The Curious Expedition takes it too far. I will agree that the game can be very unforgiving, and the RNG can certainly work against the player at times, but proper planning still plays just as much a role in the game as luck does. Still, if you hate games that are "too random", then this is a title to skip.
Third, the combat system is... unique, and rather hard to wrap your head around. Akin to oldschool dice games like Dragon Dice, each character in the party (and certain special weapons) provide one or more dice in your combat "dice pool". Each round of combat, you roll the dice and use the resulting sigils (eyes, heads, swords, shields, etc.) to build combos. A single sword sigil, for example, will allow you to make a basic attack (1 damage). A sword plus an eye sigil will allow you to instead make a precise attack (3 damage). A sword plus a shield sigil will allow you to balance offense and defense with a riposte (2 damage, 2 defense). There are a few dozen possible combinations, some which are only possible with specialized equipment in your inventory (firearms, rayguns, melee weapons, etc.). You can reroll your dice twice a turn in hopes of getting better combinations of sigils, but once you run out of combo moves it's time for the enemy to beat on you for a turn - and they're often very deadly, so it's important to balance out your offense and defense carefully. Some people dislike this system, but I found it rather intriguing.
Ultimately, The Curious Expedition is a game that I would certainly recommend, with the understanding that it is a quick-play rogue-like with a somewhat hefty reliance on both luck AND skill. Even in it's alpha state I've found it quite entertaining, and while the learning (and difficulty) curve is very steep, I've generally learned from each loss to the point where my last two expedition parties were able to complete the game successfully. The average game session is quick and satisfying, with each expedition taking anywhere from five to twenty minutes (once you know what you're doing), and a complete "campaign" consisting of six expeditions (though you'll often die well before reaching the sixth expedition). A basic save and quit feature allows you to stop playing at any given time, and pick up again later - though there's only one save slot, so you can't have more than one campaign in progress at a time.
Given that the game is still in development, I fully expect that it will only get better with time, and look forward to seeing what the devs come up with. While details are sparse, current chatter implies that we can expect to see many new items, characters, and encounters added to the game in the coming months.

-Good writing and story
-Mostly painless multiplayer.  Simultaneous turns are welcome.
-Good new concepts.  Winter is a period of increased cost and slowed movement, injects manageable uncertainty.  It can be thought of as a cyclical global economic depression.  No workers, just city buildings to improve tiles.
Con:
-World location quests need balancing.  Some objectives are much more annoying to fulfill than is justified by the reward.  Some rewards are useless, some are incredibly powerful, and overall the questing system does not reach its potential.  Some quests are tedious micromanagement (I refer to you, quest that requires a level 4 infantry hero to complete)
-Computer difficulty.  The AI is not very challenging,  At higher difficulties, the computer players get resource bonuses.  AI is hard to do well for a strategy game, but this one is noticeably worse than Civ 5.  Games against the computer rarely last to completion: long before any victory conditions are met, the player will have achieved superiority, and a long slog through the remaining provinces remains.  With a large enough resource headstart, the computer will be very challenging in the early game, but can't keep pace with the player.
-Writing and story.  One problem with having a single story-line for each race, even if it is well conceived and written, is that it doesn't give the same satisfaction on future playthroughs.
-Terrain.  Whereas the distribution of resources in Civ 5 dictates expansion and diplomatic relations with other countries, in this game city placement is more of a task of selecting the highest output tiles.
-Auto city governors.  These guys love to build unique buildings, and if you let them run free they will sink all your resources (non-refundable) into starting construction of the unique buildings in each city.
-Research mechanic.  Each tech you research increases the cost of all future techs.  So if you skip over an early tech, going back to research it will effectively slow techs at your higher level.  I see the need to scale requirements with the greater research power of a large late-game empire, but the way it's implemented penalizes a large empire for researching low level techs.
-Inadequate documentation.  The manual is a wiki page, and the developers seem to rely on the community to explain some game mechanics there.  What does the parasite skill do, and why do the slugs cast it on your own units?  (After battle it will spawn a unit from an affected enemy that dies, and nobody has any idea why the slugs cast it on friendlies.)  This is the sort of thing that should be explained.

Endless Legend has taken all the things that made Endless Space unique and worth playing, put it into a fantasy world and improved on all the things that made Endless Space dull. It’s set on one of the many planets once occupied by an ancient race called the Endless (set in the same universe as Endless Space).
You still have your standard resources of food, tech, production, dust (a form of magical currency). But you also have power/influence which is used to give your empire boons or assimilate minor races into yours (a feature which allows you to further customise your empire as you go, granting bonuses and unique units). This addition to the standard 4X formula, along with the others, gives Endless Legend a superb amount of depth and uniqueness.
Wars are generally the thing that prolong turns in 4X games. But Endless Legend has implemented an interesting system where battles can only last for a max of four turns. When two armies meet, all the units separate and you start the battle. If you have other armies in the region or the battle is taking place close to a city, that army or the city militia come a turn or two in as reinforcements. If all of one side is eliminated, than a winner of the battle is declared… how chivalrous.
I have nothing but praise for Endless Legend. The game has complexity not only in its mechanics but in it’s lore, look, content and design. Of course, complexity and depth can also give birth to confusion. Descriptions for abilities or traits aren’t always available and there are sometimes dozens of factors affecting various aspects of your empire. But given enough time, it wouldn’t be hard to figure out what these traits are. I personally can’t wait until I reach that point and I feel that’s when the game will really take off.

Some factions have incredible bonuses to diplomacy so expansion and peace is easy for them. The Broken Lords faction have a win condition of controlling a large portion of the map and almost exclusively use the dust resource. One group actually has a motivation to be at war with as many people as possible (the quintessential strategy horde army). As a result, I'm struggling to defend myself and maintain peace throughout while building up my cities rapidly since that's what the Wild Walkers are best at. Overall, it's an interesting and challenging game that encourages different forms of play and many hours of play time to master. Definitely requires more than one playthrough.

The Fidelio Incident is a walking sim that offers a short but interesting little story about a number of characters, primarily a married couple. It is indeed loosely inspired by Beethoven's opera “Fidelio”, and while I wouldn't label it a thriller, as the description on Steam does, the game is a rather trippy experience throughout.
As with most walking sims, there is little gameplay to be found here. The gameplay generally consists of you walking around in a harsh and freezing environment, scrounging for warmth, lost diary pages and solving a few puzzles along the way. And while the diary pages are integral to the story and character development, unfortunately the same cannot be said for the puzzles. For all intents and purposes, the game would have been better off without these puzzles, as they do nothing more than bore and keep you from becoming completely immersed in the story and the struggle of the main character. Nearly every single one of the puzzles boils down to the player turning steam valves on or off. Exciting stuff, I know. It's a shame this is the case, because given the adult themes of this game, one would hope that the puzzles would offer a bit more substance, ideally in a way where it informs or elaborates on the player character's mental state and/or development. Now to be fair, I did spot a couple moments where this was attempted (albeit, to a very minor degree), but due to the limitation of what a steam valve can accomplish in the game, these moments fell flat as a pancake.
With that said, what doesn't fall flat in this game is its writing, narrative and voice over work. The actors who portray Stanley and Leonore are both wonderful, and the writing is spot on in how it illuminates to the player the personalities of the couple, the history they have with one another and the political climate they are outrunning. The game does this with only audio, as character models are used sparingly, similarly to something like Soma or Firewatch. And like Soma or Firewatch, the dialogue, whether it be the player character talking to himself, speaking to another character, or diary entries, all of it somehow manages to feel natural and unobtrusive. This of course  is a great service to the game's story, one that, as I previously mentioned, attempts to cover some difficult themes, such as grief and the consequences of violence. While I have watched and played plenty of walking sims that have attempted to tell "mature" stories, The Fidelio Incident is one of those rare few that actually succeeds in doing so. I cared for the two individuals and their relationship, and I wanted things to turn out well for the both of them.
Ultimately, if you're a fan of games like Firewatch, Soma or Dear Esther, you may want to check this one out. However, and I do want to stress this, because I know this varies for each person and I feel it's worth bringing up. This game is very short. I finished my first playthrough in 2.3 hours, and that was me taking my sweet time with it. I was able to complete a second playthrough in about 45 minutes, just by bypassing a couple of diary entries and jogging around instead of walking. Personally, I don't mind short experiences like this, but you may want to wait for a sale if you feel the current $10 price tag is a bit much.

This game is, simply put, one of the best strategy games I've ever played, by a long shot. I have since bought Europa Universalis IV, Victoria II and plan to get Hearts of Iron IV in future. This studio has gotten a lot of flak for their... questionable DLC policy, and it is upsetting that you have to get through a paywall of about £100 when on sale to get the "full" game, not counting cosmetic DLC, but even the base game provides hundreds upon hundreds of hours of gameplay, with all the expansions I've bought so far being a tonne of fun, if not completely worth even their sale price. I would HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone looking to break into Grand Strategy, or looking for an amazing roleplaying and storytelling engine. Buy the DLC if you've put a hundred hours in and feel like you want to, but the base game itself is where it's at.

In this game your are not....I repeat, you are NOT the dominant species on this planet...and I for one ENJOY the hell out of that.

Ahh oblivion i remember getting oblivion as a late high school graduation present I had so many great memories playing this game on the Xbox 360.
I am one of the biggest elder scrolls fans there is I mean just look at my profile it is obvious lol I have been playing and enjoying elder scrolls games since 1994 when Arena released when I was just a little girl that barely started 1st grade haha i understand I was quite young to be playing such a game but I LOVED it I LOVED the huge open world (even if it is copy paste lol) and the lore and all of the possibilities of roleplay and murdering goblins was always interesting haha (I was a good girl I promise) point is that I became attached to Bethesdas first ever big title and would follow the development of Daggerfall few years later buying it as soon as I could get my parents to give me allowance for it haha and daggerfall was amazing the land you can explore is the size of great Britain itself and the combat was cool for the time and as I would read about the lore of High Rock and bretons/high elfs I would only grow more interested in elder scrolls then once morrowind came out 15 years ago with it's first ever fully 3D world and realistic beautiful and unique environment and the wonderful lore of the tribunal, Azura, boethiah, the dwemer, chimer, red mountain, lorkhan and the tools of kagrenac, etc... this was a epic change from the rest of the elder scrolls but a change mostly for the better for the story of morrowind during the tribunal was very interesting and detailed and the beautiful 3D world was something to admire especially back then when fully 3D open world games were just starting to come out and it also was a unique world never before did we see guars and giant mushrooms and the many odd shaped plants we would see along with the foggy and mysterious theme of many of vardenfells areas and let's not forget the huge silt strider and the wonderful cliff racers that we all know and love haha  (many times they had killed me lol).
- But then and THEN OBLIVION FINALLY CAME OUT JUST A FEW YEARS LATER and my dad got it for me for a late graduation present! To my surprise! Haha and when you added all the many mods that I was able to access on pc into the mix versus Xbox the possibilities were endless for fun but at the same time oblivion was stable enough to take seriously at least for the time and had a beautiful and rich environment though probably not as big of a change compared to morrowind change from it's predecessor and the story was well a bit lacking I admit although I love some of it the biggest thing that drew me to it was goofing off and just exploring the world doing side quests and joining the many guilds especially the dark brotherhood (which I think oblivion had the best dark brotherhood questline of all es games) and role-playing as a evil sorceress/daedric cultist which was a common interest for me haha (like I said I'm a good girl I promise) and seeing all the parts of the map unlike morrowind oblivion was the first fully 3D and realistic world game of es that allowed you to see a bit of all of the region's of tamriel if you went bit north of the colovian highlands you could see the snowey and mountainous lands moat similar to Skyrim along with all the nords of Bruma then if you went south-east you could see some of the various swamps of black wood like youd see in Argonia the land was huge obviously not compared to arena or daggerfall especially but for being fully 3D and so realistic it felt bigger because copy pasted environments got old quickly after being exposed to morrowind haha (Bethesda has spoiled us now I'm so spoiled I find it hard to play morrowind and daggerfall because of the horrible graphics XD)

Amnesia™: Memories is a fantastic game. Truly an otome game after my own heart, portrayed in a way that's great for those who are not generally fans of the gaming genre or looking to play their first one. Possessing beautiful graphics, an A+ storyline, as well as characters each with their own distinct opinions, feelings and identities, this game was well-worth the time I put into it and hopefully the start of many more otome games to come (to Steam).
I found this game to be unique in it's large cast of characters and the relationship dynamics between them, both romantic and platonic. As well as the heroine there are three other girls, Sawa, Mine, and Rika (plus Ikki's crazy fangirls), who each have unique relationships between eachother and the heroine, and of course Waka, the manager, the authority figure of the group who while his personality might change from world to world, his essence does not. The verisimilitude of this game brought about by these dynamics was truly a breath of fresh air.
Of course, no game is perfect. There seem to be issues with recieving the Steam achievments for this game (hopefully that will be fixed, the game is still quite new), I found Ukyo's good end to be a little anti-climatic (I'd already seen the anime, so that probably had an impact), the backgrounds were somewhat underwhelming (pointed out to me while I was broadcasting this game to a friend, though I think it helps to not distract from the characters), Orion was used a
to portray the characters thoughts and feelings (of course, due to their bond he would know all about them), and I was a little concerned about how in Toma's good end
.
This game does possess some subjects that while horror visual novel fans might love, some might find triggering. This isn't an innocent, cutesy otome game. While there's no sex, there are mentions of it in discussions, as well as gory off-screen deaths involving fire, knives, roofs, etc. Plus
.
So to sum it up;
If this looks like a game you would enjoy and you have money to spare I reccomend you purchase the game, both for the game itself and to show Steam and game developers that otome games have a viable market here.

TL;DNR- Very great VN. 9.5/10 Would forget about life again.
Now for the long version: this is quite possibly my favorite VN that I've played to date. I should start with a disclaimer that I'm fairly unusual in that I'm a straight male who generally prefers otome VNs, but if you can get over being a virtual girl chasing after virtual boys (or rather being a virtual girl being chased by virtual boys, I suppose) then I would recommend this VN to you regardless of your preferences... assuming those preferences didn't exclude VNs themselves, I suppose.
The story is fairly simple- you're a girl who lost her memories because I spirit crashed into your noggin or something and threw them across time and space and you gotta retrieve them by talking to a bunch of cute boys in parallel worlds who knew you before you lost your memories... that's about it (well, for the most part... the final arc has quite a bit more to it, but I'm not gonna spoil). Though this fairly simple setup allows it to focus more on the characters rather than developing a convoluted plot, and it does so very well. The writing is very good, dare I say quite exceptional by most standards, I found myself genuinely laughing and crying many times, it was really quite absorbing.
If I have any criticisms though, the first one would be the character design. Some of the characters look really good: I love the look of the Main Character (henceforth referred to as MC-chan because I'm a weeb and generally a terrible person) and Orion was cute... annoying at first, but he really grew on me; and Toma and Shin are both pretty good looking, but everyone else out of the main cast have outfits that look straight-up ridiculous... I mean, there's a character (Ukyo) who looks like he was a cab driver airlifted straight from the chessboard dimension... another character (Ikki) has what appears to be a tattoo of a spade on his face, which I assume they thought for god knows what reason accented nicely with his spade hairclip... like, what even the..? I mean, the boys themselves look really good, it's just their normal clothing is generally just absurd. I know this seems like a small complaint and it's totally subjective but considering you'll spend the majority of the game staring at them and reading text, if you don't like the way they look it can get pretty grating.
My second criticism is that in almost all of the CGs, MC-chan looks like a deer in headlights, like "OMFG HE'S KISSING ME WHAT DO I DO!?", even when there's no reason for her to do so. I mean I'm not exaggerating when I say that there was an instance in which I (and by proxy, she) asked a boy to hug her, he did, and she looked surprised that he did so in the resulting CG... like, why? Did she suddenly realize she left the stove on back home?
Other than that, there's a minor thing of the talking animations being... kinda lazy, it's basically characters just opening their mouths over and over again in the same robotic way until the speaking audio is done, it reminded me of the Putt-Putt games I played when I was a kid. That's pretty minor though since most of your game is spent looking at the bottom fifth of the screen reading text and listening to japanese voices anyways.

This is the first dating sim and the first visual novel I've ever played.  I bought it entirely on a whim, mostly because it was on sale.
And I LOVED IT.
Pros:
-Amazing art
-Great characters, and not just the main love interests, all the characters
-Compelling storyline with multiple endings
-Relationships feel real and not forced (for the most part)
-Parameter system is quite helpful to find out how you are doing
Cons:
-There is the need to save spam in some instances, or you might die unexpectedly and lose a lot of progress
-Your helper spirit, Orion can be pretty annoying at some parts and is a master of stating the obvious
-Parameter system, while helpful, can't tell you what the boys actually want, leading to some frustration.
(For example, in one route I got a bad ending due to having too much suspicion. After restarting saves, micromanging descisions, and starting the route over again, I had to look up a walkthrough to find out that you have to be super lovey-dovey. but those descisions made him super suspicous so I always rejected those choices, leading to a getting an ending where he was too suspicious of me even though my suspision was as low as possible. Wow that was a long tangent/rant. Anyway.)
-One storyline is a bit fetish specific and may to off putting to everyone else
-The achievments are bit broken, for me at least. Totally did what the achievement told me to, but Steam won't give me it
Conclusion:
The pros massiy outway the cons. I really really enjoyed 4 out of 5 routes (sorry, just not into yanderes). This game is good for hardcore dating sim fans and people with just a passing interest, like me.
More of these games on Steam please.

It was a great start! As I was the great Charles Darwin! My crew of a Scottish soldier, a native translator, A water buffalo and a royal soldier of her majesty. We were beating the lots of them, gaining money and making fame to all the world to see. Each and every time succeeding. exploring the lands and roughing through acres of forest collecting endless supplies of insects. My crew and I were trained in the action of wildlife and survival.
This expedition  seemed too good to be true. The conditions were spot on perfect. A challenger put me on the spot for a 80 day excursion to see I could make it. I accepted and grabbed my supplies before the way out.
The landing spot was perfect as i saw every forest around me. mountains to the right of me and grasslands up north. I could also spot many cave & shrines entrances on the hillsides which meant one thing: Loot and lots of it. We build camp and rest before the scavenging and ran into a raptor and quickly fought hard with our 2 shotguns, rifle, pistol and our wits of course.
After collecting the skin we head to this well-buried shrine, a place that seemed perfect to explore. inside this cast and deep place was an alter that had the trinkets of the forgotten. As we approached this untouched table my heart was pounding with the thrill. I am unsure though of what to get.
With all the weapons, traveling gear and the treasures so far we could only grab two things out of the three valuables:  a golden llama statue, a golden goblet and a stone that glimmered on the shade it was in. My vision said gold as i hurried to grab it and went on our way. But an odd warping sound came about as we exited that shrine, i thought it was just my imagination.
As we continued on our timed journey i thought i was losing our sanity for sure. As we came closer to the forest that would obviously bring us forth towards that golden pyramid of destiny and fame the mountain range that once was there suddenly disappeared and all you could see was another world. It was like looking into the vast reaches of space itself, and it seemed to be growing.
I thought we were just hallucinating from the leaves we had snacked on. We ran towards that end point only to find the pyramid sealed. There was a little nook that a certain stone could fit in to open the gateway back to the queen herself. My mind was stunned as i realized that we had to go back to the shrine. My reality sank even more as the forest and mountains that surrounded us was being engulfed by this darkness.
We make a mad-dash back to the shrine, fleeing from the enraged inhabitants and wildlife that chased us. Only a bit to go and we would be back to that cursed place. But as we approached it there was a flood of nothingness coming straight towards us.
Would I ever see life again? Would I be able to identify more of my innuendo names for butterflies? will i have one last cup of tea at the explorer's lodge if i make it to the other-side? I'm afraid not, we became engulfed by the void and was never to be heard of again....
tl;dr Dont ever forget to pick up that damn moon stone!

Booting up Endless Legend for the first time I knew I was in for something special. I had previously played the 4x Space Civ Simulator, Endless Space, and thoroughly enjoyed it. Both are made by Amplitude Studios and are part of their multiple-game and multiple genre universe spanning series that have been released in rapid succession over the last few years. Endless Space, Endless Legend, and Endless Dungeon, are the three games currently released from Amplitude. All giving their own slightly varied experience.
Endless Legend is the most recent iteration of the endless universe. Starting the game up I was surprised to find a very sparse menu. This is something common between all of the Amplitude games. A minimalistic styled menu that gives you little to do but jump right into their game and get started. That's exactly what I was eager to do.
What the Endless series also excels at is punishing mistakes. The first few times I played I was decimated by nearly every other civilization in the game. Still though, each time I played I made progress. This is one of my favorite parts about civilization builders. Failing and returning to re-build my civilization stronger and more robust. After about 4 times playing through, I finally conquered the world and won. In total this took about 20 hours just to give you an idea of how long it takes to become proficient.
Personally I won by taking the military route after I began falling behind other civilizations in points, however it caused my people endless unhappiness to be ruled by a dictatorial warlord. Still though it was a win even though it wasn't by the conditions I had originally intended. Most of the civilizations have conditions they are better suited to winning with, but every option is always open.
The science "ladder" you climb while playing brings you into several era as you play. Each era increases the power available to units and the technology but also increases the production requirements of each city. This adds a depth that includes time as a measurable resource that must be managed. After playing Civilization games I have to say that this is a small change but makes a large difference in how quickly you may want to uncover new technologies.
This combined with the happiness mechanic makes even advancing in production and technology a balancing act. Destroying facilities and units that require upkeep from previous eras can actually help you in the short run to recover and quickly produce more powerful units. Other regular resources are provided in the same way most are in 4x turn based games. They are however more difficult to balance and utilize properly. Running short on resources is common and so is having to make hard decisions.
The biggest draw that I saw in the game was combat, and the turn based mechanics. As far as I could tell, 2 people would take turns at 1 time. Which means you would be moving units at the same time and so there is at least a bit of real-time attention needed as if you are paying little attention to what your units are doing they can be attacked easily. Prioritizing movement over building can save or ruin opportunities. Combat between units is played out simultaneously on your turn between armies in a tiled strategy turn-based format. I know that this type of combat has gotten a lot of flak in reviews as a negative aspect to the game, but I consider it a positive.
Consider for a moment that the entire "default" game takes place over 300 turns, the combat helps break up the repetition of the turns with something different and stimulating in a different way. Everything Endless Legend does seems fresh even though it utilizes formulas from many previous games. The fusion of turn based civ building and combat works perfectly with the way the game is paced in my opinion.
I for one am eagerly awaiting the further release of games in the endless series. I can't wait to see what Amplitude studios comes up with next.

After the disappointment for me thta was Endless Space, I picked up Endless Legend with a  bit of trepidation: I had picked up a lot of fantasy 4x games recently (Eador, Age of Wonders 3, Warlock 1 and 2, there's been a lot lately...), but I'd heard great things about Endless Legend. Plus it was on sale.
Glad I picked it up. It's easily been the bes tof the lot for me, and a lot of my issues with Endless Space are either not present or solved here.
Endless Legend is a fantasy 4x game where you play as one of 8 distinctly different playing races, trying to complete one of many victory styles (Score, Economic, Diplomatic, Science, Supremacy, Elimination, Expansion, Wonder). Each race has its own array of traits and units, and you can also make Custom Races based on the foundation of one of the main races, creating something you'd enjoy playing the most. The races range from diplomatic Drakken (dragon people who can enforce diplomatic treatises), to fast expanding Zerg style bug-men (unable to use diplomacy, Cold War is the best you cna hope for), to Broken Lords (who dont't use food, instead using Dust [Gold] to create new population and heal units!), to the Cultists of the Eternal End (who are a "Single City Challenge" civ, unable to settle new cities, but can convert minor civs [city-states, for civ 5 players] to their cause, creating more worked tiles and free units.)
The game plays out like most 4x games, on an overworld map, where you deal with thing slike happiness, luxury and strategic resources, making new towns, researching tech, exploring, etc. Endless Legend adds heroes to the mix, which do the usual things you'd expect. They can be made governors of cities, or generals of armies, and will level upa and learn skills to make them better at these things. Endless Legend also uses "Regions" to compartmentalize the map and show where you can place cities. Since only one city can be in a region, you find yourself competing for distinct places on the map, rather than a nebulous "this area by the iron and 2 diamonds". It lends theme to the game. Cities also develop interestingly: Rather than a simple influence array that increases, you build physical additions to your city, Boroughs, that will expand the circle of worked tiles. A larger city actually takes up half a dozen tiles or more on the map, which give sit a pysical presence, both out of combat and in combat (more on this in a bit). Building tightly packed cities also levels up your districts, making your cities happier and even more efficient. You cna also find special ruins around the mpas thta will give you quests to perform, giving direction to your expansion actions, and rewarding you for completing them. Minor civs also give quests as one way to pacify them, the other methods being bribing with money, ror simply defeating them.
Combat in the game plays out like a middle ground of Age of Wonders/HoMM and Civ. Your armies enter battle, you cna give commands, but your units will perform the command sthemselves, moving and positioning how they please and then firing. Their AI takes over via a player-set stance (Aggressive, Defensive, Hold Ground) if your desired action can't be performed.  The AI is competent in this, and generally tries to keep ranged units in cover and uphill, and flanks and surrounds with melee units, buffing with support units. A human can generally do better, of course, but the AI is good enough to where you never feel like you need to really worry, which is nice. Auto-resolve is also there, of course. A neat thing I enjoyed aobut the combat is that the battlemap is actually the overworld map itself, overlaid into a combat grid, meaning a chokepoint or defensible area on the overworldmap is actually a chokepoint in battle.
Talking about combat leads into units... Eahc civilization has three units, but each unit can be equpped with several types of weapon, armor, and accessories, allowing you to customize counter units as needed. Strategic resources are used to create extra-powerful, specialized weapons and armor at the cost of consuming these resources for your elite units.  Minor Civs (city states) can be assimilated into your empire to allow you to create their unit as well, like axe weilding minotaurs, spear using centaurs, chain lightning blasting Haunts, and massive skeletal demons. You can also purchase mercenaries from the marketplace from other civs: Any unit you disband or sell actually oes to the market, where it can be bought by any other player in the game. Unfortunately the marketplace is EXTREMELY expensive for units and heroes, and I found that unless I was playing the trade focused Roving Clans or the money-loving Broken Lords, I mostly ignored the market.
Victory Conditions are hit or miss for me. Most of the non-combat ones feel "boring".
-Score is score. Highest wins.
-Diplomacy simply relies on an invisible "diplomacy points" counter, where you get extra points for being at peace or an alliance. There's no United Nations, no Apostolic Palace, no civs to influence. It falls a bit short.
-Economic victory is much the same - once a player passes a threashhold for total dust gathered across the entire game, they win. Nothing to do with trade routes or global markets or resources.
-Science victory relies on researching 5 of the 6 "super techs" in the game. To be fair, not much else you can do with a science victory, especially when your "space race" victory style is tied up in...
-Wonder victories. This is the hallmark victory of the game. Every race has a unique 8 part questline that,as you complete, gives you special race specific techs, unique buildings, hero items, and in some caes heroes themselves. When you complete the questline, you are able to build a unique Wonder that, when completed, gives you victory. Some questlines seem inherently easier to complete than others, and some come off as contradictory: For example, the Roving Clans, a race thta actually cannot declare war themselves (only defend) must conquer another city, often far away and already held by an opponent. You must then passive aggressively annoy the other civ into finally declaring war on you first. The Drakken, a race of peaceful lorekeepers, must also do the same, although here you cna at leats declare war yourself. These are a few small places where the lore of the game and the mechanics don't quite seem to mesh, and it's a shame, because a LOT of work clearly went into this victory.
-Expansion victories rely on you colonizing a certain percentage of the entire map. I cannot possibly fathom doing this on even the middle sized maps, or rather: Cannot comprehend doing it without already having wiped out the entire rest of the game militarily. Your happiness would plummet so low it hardly seems worth it to expand that much.
-The military victories are the usual lot. Supremacy is being the last civ with a Capital City, and Elimination is the complete destruction of all others.
Things the game does not do well: Aside from the victories above, this game maintains a few of the Endless Space oddities that I dislike. Many diplomatic actions are tied up in the tech tree, taking up valuable science from researching thing slike, say, science boosts, or food, or dust, or strategic resource extractors. The market, both resource and unit (thye are separate techs) are also techs, and I find myself ignoring the market in almost eveyr game that I don't start with it as a free tech. It's a shame, really. I also do not often find myself researching the unique strategic resource weapons and armor techs unless I'm the Vaulters, a race that gets bonuses both to their collection, and for units using the Resource Weapons.
I would, even with these minor complaints, recommend picking up the game for any fan of th 4x genre.

A very good game, but not without its flaws, which are elusive yet substantial enough.  The tactical combat is limited by the approach taken such that you fight on the actual features of the "map board", with very limited control by a player. By itself this is fine - a game whose victories are primarily achieved strategically - but amongst the flaws it hurts the effort overall. Possibly the worst part of the game is the fact that in a cooperative game versus the computer, players cannot participate in the same battle, even though their armies may be **right there**. All of your strategic level efforts lead to the big payoff of a tactical reckoning, and yet you can`t share in combat... in a supposedly cooperative game.
Very good art style, very distinct factions, a terrifically robust strategic layer, soured by an inadequate cooperative implementation. Age Of Wonders still holds the crown.

Sadly I found the music/audio to be somewhat lacking, which is sad for a game that is marketing itself on being inspired by Beethoven's only opera. The soundtrack in itself is good, no question about it, but the occasional mixing and layering of different soundtracks (on purpose or not...) made me feel somewhat lost. Aswell as the game lacking some clear audio effects:
- No footstep or splash sound when walking in water
- Mostly the same footstep sound no matter if walking on dirt or snow
- Some interactibles lacked sound effects which made them feel "hollow" and without weight
Control wise the game clearly is made to be played with a controller and not with mouse and keyboard (although it is possible). Especially noticable is this when the cursor randomly dissapears from the menu or the camera goes into som kind of "hold-and-drag" mode. Another thing that annoyed me was the fact that I as the player never got any control over when I wanted my flash light to be on or off. I understand that there are some points in the game where the player should not get access to something that makes seeing easier but there are better solutions to that than taking the decision entierly away from the player.
My last little nit-picky-critic-point is the lack of some kind of inventory symbols. Overall I do recommend the game to anyone who likes games like Firewatch or any other pussel adventure with a bit of horror mixed into it, especially if it is on sale!

As you may noticed, I spent ample of time in this game, coming back every so often to see what changed. I played until I was max level  / prestige to ensure I was certain how I felt about this game. The last few games I played cemented it. My conclusion: Nope. Not worth it.
Firstly, as you may guess, it's a MOBA-type game on a 2D gaming plane. 2 bases, 2 lanes with a “jungle” somewhere. Thus it's normal there isn't a single player mode. Yes you can play vs bots and you can make them as hard as real people. But the main meat of this game is the multiplayer. You will unlock the 16 characters on 5 maps (4 of them are on a paid DLC)  Unlocking them all is just a matter of playing and acquiring solar, the in-game currency / experience. Gaining solar is easy as it's both in-match currency and experience out of it. Levels are quick and more often than not you will gain 2-4 levels per reasonably normal match. After unlocking characters and maps, you will unlock items to change how your skills are in-game. At 133 levels plus 10 prestige levels, it takes a long time to max out.
The characters themselves are cool  in and of themselves. Each has a backstory into how and why they joined the Awesomenauts and their own personality often reflected in the game. All of them spout off random memes and typical nerd references here and there. Some of the (purchasable) skins they have even refer to other games, movies and tv series. Pretty cool overall.
Graphics, voice over and music are quite good. Several famous youtubers voiced some of the characters, adding a nice familiar touch for those that are fans of said youtubers. The music also does explain why I kept returning : achieving a rampage (3 kills without death) gives you a rampage background song of your character's theme. Only you hear this remixed song and it adds a nice touch of encouragement for your accomplishement. Should your team really steamroll the other, you are awarded with "You are awesome!" text and the intro music will start playing instead. Often I would find myself listening to such and such character's songs on youtube, Skolldir theme being a personal favorite of mine.
Now for the bad : first the characters feel unbalanced. Some were nerfed to near uselessness and others never properly balanced and retain their unfair advantages. And don't expect patches to balance them... They come every 4-6 months. The reason why so long? MOAR SKINS DLC!  Enjoy seeing the same characters winning constantly.
Matchmaking feels completely arbitrary : you often play against or with people that outclass the others (i.e. out of the "league" you play) which leads to steamrolled games. Of course one can explain this as the player base slowly moving on but still hard for new players to even start off. Quitting has no real penalty so players do it left and right. What penalties you ask? No win bonus on your next victory and a "loss of ranking". Read the first phrase of this paragraph if you don't understand how ironic it is.
For the player base, it's a mixed bag. Most of the games, the chat will be unused short of the GGs at the end. In rare occurrences, you might have a bit of a conversation and some laughs when all players chat up. In others, some "player" (I refuse to acknowledge someone that willingly abuses of a system in a game a player)  will decide that spamming all the voice commands is required to fully control the game. 3 out of 4 are team based and the last is a taunt to the opposing team. But said taunt can also be heard by the playing team thus adding more to the spam. As one person starts, others will also start and continue forth resulting into a spam-o-thon. Unfortunately, there are no squelching in this game. Hope you like hearing that audio spam! Oh wait quitting out of the match is still a viable solution. Thank goodness!
All in all,  don't. There are better games both within Steam and even out of it that can satisfy both a MOBA-type of gamers and platformer gamers without resorting to this one. This one looks nice but it's inner layers hide such frustrating flaws that ruin the overall coolness.
Final silly thoughs : I sometimes imagine this game as a Saturday morning cartoon. The settings does make it viable and will the menagerie of quirky characters...

So I’ve noticed that this game has mixed reviews, most of the negative ones being written by people who have played it for a couple of hours and have been eaten alive, chewed up and spat back out only to be able to write  “this game sucks”. Well my fellow steamers, you are in luck! You’re about to get a summary from someone who’s played the game for 87 hours.
I did write a ton about thehunter: Primal, but figured who will want to read a review the same size as The Wall the Nights Watch guard? So I’ve kindly summarised it.
•	thehunter: Primal is an online hunting survival game.
•	There are 5 different types of dinosaur,
•	11 different weapons and many items.
•	There is a shop where you can use in-game currency to buy weapons and items however you need to unlock them by levelling up. (It is not a P2W game)
•	Everything wants to kill you.
•	Hunting is similar to thehunter, you need to shoot the dinosaurs in the right place. But as the dinosaurs are usually trying to find you, you come across them more often.
•	It is hard and challenging, but you get used to it once you've played for a few hours.
•	There are no 24/7 servers and setting up your own can be difficult as you have to open ports.
•	You can be a lone wolf or chose to band together with friends or you can try to make friends. However if playing the PVP mode, only team up with people you trust, as it’s a dog eat dog world out there.
Pros
•	It’s hard to play, but rewarding when you do well.
•	Great game to play with friends.
•	Very big map.
•	PVP is fun.
•	Levelling up system.
•	In-game shop.
•	Updated by devs.
•	At moments you are terrified.
•	Nice to hunt and be hunted.
•	Day and Night.
•	You get immersed in the world.
•	Great dinosaur behaviour.
Cons
•	It’s hard to play, and annoying when you die a lot.
•	PVP can be brutal.
•	No 24/7 Severs and setting up your own can be a pain as you have to open ports.
•	Render distance is similar to thehunter so dinosaurs/humans disappear when they get too far (however they have to be quite far to disappear.)
•	Hit points on humans need to improve.
•	Levelling up system needs something to show hunters how close they are to the next level.
•	Transition from night to day needs to improve.
If you like to be challenged then this is a good game for you, especially the PVP. Hunting dinosaurs is really exciting and something cool is always happening in the game. This is the kind of thing you will expect:
You’ve been tracking a Triceratops you shot for the last 10 minutes, and you’re lead into a forest. Suddenly you hear raptors communicating with each other, then silence and a rush of footsteps. Screams from the U-Raptors fill your ears and you and your hunting party start manically firing at 5 U-Raptors ambushing you.
Whilst PVPing you're making your way up the volcano with your hunting party and are hounded by the flying Quetzalcoatlus,  one of your party is caught by the Quetzalcoatlus and he’s flown into the sky and then dropped to his death. But the rest of you manage to make it to the base at the top. However a rival hunting party is already there and a fire fight ensues. Your team get mascaraed and you lose all your stuff.

Or you’re walking through the open plains and start hearing thud after thud and the ground begins to shake, you realise a T-Rex is coming for you and all you can do is run. But remember you have a high calibre weapon so try to take it on. You begin shooting at it and its getting closer and closer, just as it’s about to rip you to pieces you see an opening to its heart and shoot your .700, killing it instantly.
Short and sweet, interesting story.
I appreciate that this game tried to do something new and interesting, but it's a bit of a mess.  Ultimately, it's not fun to play and it's not rewarding to complete.

I was 3 years old when this game was released, I was 6 years old when I first started playing it, I was 10 years old when I was finally good enough at it to finish it and I was 12 when I was finally good enough at it to get a good ending. A game cannot be bad if it held my attention for that long, it cannot even be just good if it held my attention for 6 years. There are games which I've abandoned a while ago and never tried to finish, Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus is a game I never trully abandoned because it was too good of a game to fully abandon, regardless of how hard I found the Vault sections (which prevented me from making any progress for years), regardless of how disheartening it was to get a bad ending on my first complete playthrough.
Everything about this game is awesome, the story, the gameplay, the graphics, the characters, the voice acting, the social themes, everything. Words cannot do justice to this game, to paraphrase Morpheus: "Nobody can be told what Oddworld is, you'd have to experience it for yourself."
This is the kind of game that I love so much and I've played through so much that I can practically recite it from memory. Every person has that one game that they grew up with, the game that defined their childhood, for some it's Super Mario Bros. or Final Fantasy, for others it's Metal Gear Solid or Baldur's Gate. For me it's this game, I love this game, I love everything about this game, from its amazing stealth and platforming mechanics, to its beautiful environments that put most modern games to shame. If there's any game that I can recommend without any reservations, it's this one.
And please do drop some money for its slightly inferior but still worthwhile predecessor Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee. Both games are really cheap so there's no way you'll be wasting your money.

Graphics – above average but nothing that special, but I like the look overall.
Gameplay – Poor!
It is just another Endless Space where you memorize the correct Tech. tree sequences, you build your cities as fast as possible (The AI is –why?, because that is way the math works out in these games – just look at any game you lost or won and you can clearly see what happen in the summary growth comparison summary).  So really the first 20-40 moves is a massive amount of clicking and collecting resources to prepare for future battles /protect cities.  It is just hours of clicking with very little strategy.
Battles- Poor!
Complete lack of strategy!  You have really only 3 base units you can upgrade (limited) and not really a good balance between races.  Some races for example really have poor defense against poison bugs –but you would think you could upgrade your unit to adjust to the enemy  - no, just the basic tier weapons ( and I always update weapon and shield as they come).  And the actual battle game play is terrible!!  You cannot really control the sequence of the battle, in real strategy games you would use your archers to weaken an enemy first, then attack with other men and save your large units to take down close combat type enemies.  And I find some races have huge advantage – not weighted properly (each race should balance out other races – strength and weaknesses combined), those poison bugs and surround your best hero and take them out quickly – which leads to another point, the units movement on the board seems to be unpredictable.  I found late to use the hold position and force them to move how you want vs. being stupid and having your unit rush into an area and get surrounded or open a hole in your defense so the Poison Bugs can fly in and surround your troops.  The one saving part of this game was going to be the battle strategy, which I found very little strategy!  I have to laugh when people call this a strategy game, it is nothing but click as fast as you can the first 40 moves or you have already lost the game.  I hope they fix the battle portion of the game because this is the one thing that could really flip my view of the game – it would make all the boring parts worth it.  And for you all that will disagree with this – I assure you, give me same size force but give me the ability to pick who on my team fires first, 2nd, etc. and moves exactly where I say and I will win every battle against the AI or other player who cannot do this.  It is like playing Chess where you pick the general idea (red arrows) and then the AI plays your side and makes stupid moves that lose your men quickly because the sequence was wrong.
AI Cheats! – You can see this easily on Tiny Maps (forces you see what is really going on quickly) where the enemy quickly builds cities are a rate you cannot, and builds an army to attack you while you are still trying to get settlers for your 3rd city…. There is absolutely no way an army of 8 stack could happen that fast and build cities that fast when you are hitting all right buttons to build your cities as fast as possible!!  And in battles I find sometimes you can have 5 guys attack 1 and it will barely move in loss strength, while the AI will bring in troops early with huge attack and life strength beyond any options you have.  I had one bug army where they had 400+ life and like 200 attack while all my people had around 100 and 60 with all the upgrades maxed.  I know people use trainers, play the game 50x, replay every move, etc. to finally win games on harder levels, but what fun is that??  That is not strategy that is just memorizing the sequence that works.
This is better than endless space, but still far from what I would call a strategy game!!  You if like just clicking the board 1000x to play a 3.5hour game on tiny map, then have fun – I found it to be extremely repetitive and boring after playing the first few games!  I really do not see why people like games like this?  Maybe Multiplayer is much better since playing against another person and all the AI bug errors are taken out – never understand the fun of playing and game where it is a race in clicking vs. strategy!
PS. For all you guys that you say beating this on hard AI, it is easy, I say you are cheating!  I see people post things with video that they obviously are using a trainer/cheats and they admit they played the same turns over and over again till they won.  I really hate gamers who say things are easy when it is clear they cheated, memorized patterns or found weakness in AI to exploit, this is not strategy or intelligence, this is just cheating so you can say how easy it is!  Seriously what fun is that!  I buy game to have fun, not to cheat to win, or play 200 hours to learn the AI in and out.

The experience itself is extremely linear though, with not too much to explore outside of simple progression.
