Excellent story, graphics, and superb voice acting wrapped in a fairly conventional walking simulator. If you like sad stories and are interested by either Icelandic scenery and/or The Troubles, give this one a try. I personally felt its dealings with terrorism were mature and interesting, but I certainly am no expert.

A competent entry in the walking-sim subgenre, most notable for its superb imagery and emotional content. The puzzles are straightforward and reasonable, if a bit repetitive here and there. The subject matter is an unusual choice from recent history that is both bold and respectful. I found the voice acting to be excellent, which isn't always the case in games developed by small shops.
The overall play is a bit short and the puzzles could have been more challenging. Moreover, the puzzles seem a bit absurd here and there. There's a reason for that, but it comes out late in the game and, until you learn what it is, you may find the absurdity distracting.
If you liked Firewatch but prefer a richer graphic context, more akin to The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, have a look at this one. Where Firewatch held fast to a rigid realism, The Fidelio Incident might remind you here and there of the "Twin Peaks" TV show.  Now, Firewatch, Carter, and "Twin Peaks" all got an "A" from me, while this one earns a respectable "B." If you like walking sims, great imagery, and the enigmatically surreal, that's a "B" you should try yourself.

It was a great start! As I was the great Charles Darwin! My crew of a Scottish soldier, a native translator, A water buffalo and a royal soldier of her majesty. We were beating the lots of them, gaining money and making fame to all the world to see. Each and every time succeeding. exploring the lands and roughing through acres of forest collecting endless supplies of insects. My crew and I were trained in the action of wildlife and survival.
This expedition  seemed too good to be true. The conditions were spot on perfect. A challenger put me on the spot for a 80 day excursion to see I could make it. I accepted and grabbed my supplies before the way out.
The landing spot was perfect as i saw every forest around me. mountains to the right of me and grasslands up north. I could also spot many cave & shrines entrances on the hillsides which meant one thing: Loot and lots of it. We build camp and rest before the scavenging and ran into a raptor and quickly fought hard with our 2 shotguns, rifle, pistol and our wits of course.
After collecting the skin we head to this well-buried shrine, a place that seemed perfect to explore. inside this cast and deep place was an alter that had the trinkets of the forgotten. As we approached this untouched table my heart was pounding with the thrill. I am unsure though of what to get.
With all the weapons, traveling gear and the treasures so far we could only grab two things out of the three valuables:  a golden llama statue, a golden goblet and a stone that glimmered on the shade it was in. My vision said gold as i hurried to grab it and went on our way. But an odd warping sound came about as we exited that shrine, i thought it was just my imagination.
As we continued on our timed journey i thought i was losing our sanity for sure. As we came closer to the forest that would obviously bring us forth towards that golden pyramid of destiny and fame the mountain range that once was there suddenly disappeared and all you could see was another world. It was like looking into the vast reaches of space itself, and it seemed to be growing.
I thought we were just hallucinating from the leaves we had snacked on. We ran towards that end point only to find the pyramid sealed. There was a little nook that a certain stone could fit in to open the gateway back to the queen herself. My mind was stunned as i realized that we had to go back to the shrine. My reality sank even more as the forest and mountains that surrounded us was being engulfed by this darkness.
We make a mad-dash back to the shrine, fleeing from the enraged inhabitants and wildlife that chased us. Only a bit to go and we would be back to that cursed place. But as we approached it there was a flood of nothingness coming straight towards us.
Would I ever see life again? Would I be able to identify more of my innuendo names for butterflies? will i have one last cup of tea at the explorer's lodge if i make it to the other-side? I'm afraid not, we became engulfed by the void and was never to be heard of again....
tl;dr Dont ever forget to pick up that damn moon stone!

A great game that I'd love to see a few things added to to only make it better.
-more randomness in some events to really make every playthrough authentically be unique.
-more goals.  the side-quests like finishing an expedition in under 80 days is cool, but possibly something beyond just finding the golden pyramid each expedition to add more variety and types of gameplay.
-achievements would be really nice for this game.  as would be fame leaderboards.
-a tutorial for combat.  I had 4 tigers absolutely slaughter me before I realized how the dice actually worked.
Those points aside it's a pretty fun game that makes me want to load it up and try again after a few hours.  It's easy to pick up and play any time with no sense of devotion, which is a rarity for me in a lot of games as I tend to hop from game to game constantly and often times never get back to one I had played.
After several failed expeditions you will start to slowly teach yourself what is essential for each leg of your set of expeditions.  Realizing soon that in later expeditions that rope and dynamite are VERY vital to completing expeditions.
This game makes you ask the tough questions. Like: Do you want to go insane or fight raptors so you can cook their delicious meat?

This game is fun and shows a lot of promise.  Randomly generated areas to explore.  Resource management.  Expedition and inventory prioritizing.  A lot of the pieces of a fun exploration roguelike.  Graphics are minimal but sufficient, and should help to lower the needed resources.  I say should because...
This game needs some serious optimization.  I expect a game like this to be able to run on my laptop, not require a hardcore gaming computer.  By expedition 4, the game became nearly unplayable, and then finally shut down after using up all my system resources.  This is with a 2.6 quadcore and 8GB ram.

An individual game of Curious Expedition might last less than a half hour, but it's the sort of game that I keep coming back to over and over.  Every time I lead Amelia Earhart to her untimely and often brutal death in the untamed wilderness (falling prey to things such as starvation, cannibalism, panther attack, volcano, etc. etc. etc.) , I think "that's it!  I'm done!" and go to do something else.  It's not long later that I find myself starting the game back up again.  The Curious Expedition has me in its grasp, and I'm OK with that.

It's one of those games that slowly builds on you. There's a depth that's not readily apparent from the tutorials, so much trial-and-error and exploration is necessary (a good thing in my opinion given the nature of the game). I found myself recounting my failures to others, weaving the story together and then reflecting on how compellingly the game had provide the raw materials.
There's a few elements of the game that could use some polish, notably combat, which I believe was just overhauled. Combat is dice roll + combos, however, the dice symbols are somewhat arcane and there is no reference in-game for the combos. Minor things for now given it's early access.
The music is great, the art lends well to the theme. Tons of characters to play as. Highly recommended.

Ck2 is a very engaging and fun experience marred by overpriced and unnecessary DLC. The game itself is quite fun and attempting to consolidate your power and conquer the medieval world is a blast! Unfortunately the dlc for the game is ridiculous, as many of the dlcs only allow you to play as different types of governents that are already present in the game. That isn't to say the dlcs are poorly made, just that it seems as though it should have already been inlcuded in the game. This isn't so big a problem until to realize there is dlc... for the dlc. Additional content packs, portrait packs, and unit packs exist for most of the dlcs. For example if you bought the Horse Lords dlc and wanted the "whole" experience of playing a steppe nomad you would need to buy not only the additional content pack, but also portrait and unit packs for the Turks and Mongols. This is just unnecessary, you shouldn't have to buy dlc for your dlc. Other than the dlc problems the game is great fun and I would recommend it if either you or your wallet can look past the flaws created by the sea of dlc.
Yes, the DLCs are expensive and often bring not enough content for the price. But the game is good and will take away a few hours from your life, it's worth it !

Victoria II, yet another masterful game from the company that dictates the "Grand Strtegy" genre. This game has many realistic situations and options the allow for countless hours of gameplay. Ofter times, I think to myself "Where did my entire day go" while playing. Granted that overall the game is amazing, it does have some flaws. Rebels are a serious issue that Paradox desperately needs to fix in Victoria III (if we ever get it). I'll go over some general pros and cons of this game:
PROS
-Great gameplay
-Pick any country and guide them through history (or alternate history)
-Great powers have a ton of decisions
-Easy to mod
-TONS of great/fun mods to play
-Mods patch issues with the vanilla game
-Every country offers a different expirience
CONS
-Rebels arouse too often and in way to large numbers (I've had over 3/4 of my population become rebels)
-Populations are unrealistic (China is the only country exceeding 1 million population)
-The warscore is broken (Warscore measures how well you are doing in a war and the higher it is, the better deals you can get during a peaceoffer. I can honestly say that this is my absolute favourite game ever, and I am happy that it's on Steam since my PS1 broke down. I really believe that this game gets heavily overlooked when it comes to naming the top games of its generation. Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee gets mentioned quite a bit, but this one... not so much. Which is a damn shame, and I'll explain why in a minute.
The only downside to this was getting it playable was a little difficult. Resolution issues are the first big problem, though that was easy to fix with a quick download of a program. Now the only minor annoyance is that because its natural resolution was 800x600, stretching that to my 1920x1080 caused it to because a little more pixelated and blurry. You can still see everything perfectly fine, its mostly just distant objects or background things during the cutscenes that may be difficult to make out.
Controller compatibility isn't labelled, but it
there, to a degree. I was prepared to use my Xbox 360 controller, but the default mapped controls for it were a mess (chanting was the 'Back' button of all buttons). Honestly, it's easier and probably better to just stick with the keyboard. Any remapping you deem necessary is much less stressful.
As for the gameplay... If you've played Abe's Oddysee, then everything you saw there was improved on here, and for the better. Extra voice commands, emotions of the Mudokons to deal with, often in hilarious ways (particularly with the laughing gas). Possession of enemies ranges further than sligs (who also now have a flying variation). The wider range of enemies, the much more intimidating puzzles, the fact that the major bad guys are actually a within bits and pieces of the game and become a mechanic themselves rather than just be seen and death with via cutscenes... and at its worst, some areas just require careful timing. The game is incredibly simple for the things you can do.
The backgrounds for the environments are spectacular, the music... isn't the stuff of legends, but I have found myself humming or whistling a couple of the tunes here and there. But otherwise the only other major factor is the story, and it's just as weird and twisted as the original. It kicks off right where Oddysee ended (poor Abe doesn't even get time to rest).
And here's a fun fact. Back in the late 90's when this game originally came out, most of this games cutscenes were turned into a short film. A short film that was nominated for an Oscar. A goddamn
! Technically speaking, the first and (I could be wrong with this one) only game to have achieved that.
Besides the questionable performance issues in getting the game going, majority of which easily fixed, I recommend this game and recommend it hard. While I'm at it, I also recommend Abe's Oddysee (or its HD remake 'New n' Tasty'). While it may be a childhood love of mine, it's been 17 years and I can still call it my favourite.
I'm at a point where I can play at least 30% of it with sound alone, and I'm still not sick of this game. It's just that kind of game that I can pick up and play any day of the year.
- If you liked Oddysee, you'll like Exoddus better. If you haven't played it,

Amplitude Studios did a very good job at bringing several new (and good) ideas to the genre. The most striking to me is that each faction plays very differently, most of them even bring some twists to the game mechanics to make them unique. One example is the Cultists faction, that can only be played with one city but have abilities to use tribes for growth, or the Broken Lords, that require no food but need money to sustain themselves.
The tech tree is actually not a tree at all, and this makes the technology evolution a lot less linear than usual. The idea of regions with only one city per region and local tribes is also welcome, and use of the tribes is quite fun without being time consuming.
Diplomacy and combat are more standard, I like the cold war status that allows for aggression without being at war.

I'm really conflicted about this game. On one hand, while essentially being a walking simulator, it has all the important checkmarks of an engaging game.
It has SOME mechanics, it has a concept it sticks to, it has a structure, it has great voice-overs. The visual design is OK as well (more on that later).
And it did engage me till the end - I finished it after all.
That said, I can't say I had fun with the game, which is why I must, sadly, give it a negative rating. Here's a quick list:
1) while the game makes good use of the Unreal engine, the world isn't nearly as "pretty" enough (the visuals are high-quality, just uninteresting most of the time) for me to want to explore it, yet exploration is "rewarded" with journal pages
2) but said journals, while containing a high-quality voice-over, aren't exactly thrilling
3) while it's nice the game has mechanics to raise it above a "walking simulator", these mechanics are more frustrating than fun
4) the entire backstory wasn't really engaging and it felt like it didn't serve any purpose at all aside from a contrived narration at the end
5) the game dips nicely into "confusion" with a lovely little start, but things go downhill; perhaps it's the backstory mentioned above just didn't grip me enough for me to care about the connections (which felt forced)? ...or perhaps the madness aspect never really kicked into overdrive to make it memorable...
6) the ending also feels hallow - it simplifies the experience and doesn't leave much to think about; again, it may be my disinterest in the backstory that's the reason for this?
Ultimately, I got the game via a Steam sale, so I don't feel cheated or overly angry. With that said, if you're interested in this title, wait for a sale. Otherwise it's way too expensive.

What makes this strategy game different from others is the focus on individuals: as the head of your dynasty work to propel it to greatness, in the meantime deal with your sons trying to kill each other, your uncle mustering support for a rebellion to put HIM in charge, Count Casanova seducing your wife, troublesome vassals or a king who will take away some of your land if he doesn't like you...
A lot of people like to really Role Play it and make decisions based on their character's traits as opposed to the best game decision, e.g. what would my cowardly king do? or my wrathful king would execute his enemy even if that will make people consider him a "tyrant."
As for the DLCs: if you're new to the game the large number of DLCs can seem daunting, but you can just buy basic CK2 and play as characters in Christian Europe. Then, after a few games of that, decide if you might want to get the DLC that allows you to play as a Muslim ruler (Sword of Islam) or as a viking (Old Gods). Also, when there's a sale you can sometimes buy all the old DLCs for the normal price of 1 or 2.

"Only If" is here described as a"Surreal first person adventure-puzzle game." Do not play this game if you like that sort of thing, the description reminded you of other well-made games you enjoyed, and your hoping this game will give you a new but similar experience.
Do play this gamer if you're naturally curious to a fault, you've got time on your hands (and/or you don't much value your time), you're a bit of a masochist, and you want to see what happens when a person tries to make a game similar to other games like "The Stanley Parable," "Amnesia," "Silent Hill," "Dear Esther,"and "Portal", and movies like "Inception," "Vertigo", and the last few scenes in "2001: a Space Odyssey," and that person is an idiot.
This is not much of a puzzle game. Every puzzle is either too easy or hard to figure out for all the wrong reasons. As for surrealism well... while the concept of "surreal" might popularly just invoke surrprising, nightmarish, absurdity, surrealism isn't just random imagery thrown on a canvas. Successful surrealist works rely on intentional symbolism derived from psychology, dreams, folk lore, mythology and even contemporary works of art. For all "Only If"'s evocative, and nonsequitur imagery and events there are very few intentional symbols or motifs in the mix. I also find it telling that the only time the game directly  referenced another work besides itself, it was just the radio guy asking you if you'd seen "Inception" and if you remembered the scene where the entire rooms turns over, and then the same thing immediately happens in the game.
This game is most fun during the trippy transitions between it's trippy scenes. Most moments in the game are ultimaltly inconsequential to any large idea, themes or plot but it did a decent job surprising me and not even too bad a job creating suspense. I also enjoyed the rude GLaDOS inspired Brooklyn mafioso sounding fellow who verbally abuses you over the radio at the beginings and ends of most sections. the voice actor deserves kudos. He chews the scenery to shreds but the guy commits to those lines even when they're truly bafflingly written.
This is a really bad game guys. But it's sort of perversely entertaining. And it's also kind of fascinating to see genres and aesthetics I really like in the hands of someone who has completely no understanding of them.

This is a free game available on Steam. Short and sweet, I really enjoyed it - Only If is a great example of how "free" games should be; a fantastic staple of a fun, exciting journey you "experience" as much as you "play".
If you like exploration, narrative-driven gameplay with a well-written story, and varying/surprising special effects, you should really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are very, very good - the amount of detail in every scene is fantastic; I was pleasantly surprised by the great graphics. The sounds, few music pieces, and ambient noises are appropriate for setting the atmosphere. The execution and design of the levels is extremely well-done - the game is split into two unique paths. The back-and-forth dialogue between the characters is well-scripted and well-executed, and many scenes are full of strong emotion - extremely solid and impressive voice-acting.
The controls are simple and fun to figure out. There is no real tutorial, however, you are given button prompts from time to time. There is really no learning curve, since the game is more of an experience rather than a true challenge. That being said, there are certain parts that may require trial-and-error (and maybe a few retries).
Comparing the two paths - and without spoiling the fun, awesome parts of the game - one is quite obviously more well-developed and full-bodied than the other. If you want to short, sweet, and single playthrough for the game, pick the
. This one is much better (and a lot more fun) than the other option.
Loading requires you to type in the keyword for each level, as there is no saving option.
For achievement hunters, this game has 10 very easy achievements. It should be noted that you may have to "verify game cache" if you exit the game and reload, as there seems to be a slight problem in updating the game. If you are not getting achievements (and you know should have), try verifying, exiting, and restarting. It should work now (although you may have do this a few times - whenever you exit the game and load it up again).
Overall, the game is a really fun experience, good for all types of gamers.
Recommend!

Endless Legend is turn based strategy game very similar to the "Civilization" series. You research technologies using science, build buildings and troops with production, collect currency (called Dust in Endless Legend), use food to increase the population of your cities and ultimately expand your "colony" on the fictional world of Auriga. For those who aren't familar with Civ games, you essentially have a world filled with resource tiles where you must decide where to "settle" depending on the resources available in zone of your city.
What is different are that the factions all play extremely uniquely with their own unique units too. Units are classified as Infantry, Ranged, Flyer, and Cavalry each able to get bonuses against one of another type in a rock, papers, scissors fashion depending on the weapons equipped. This brings me to the next neat feature, equipment. In Endless Legend you are able to recruit heroes, mercenary units from native minor factions (which there are many of), and unique units to your faction. Each of these units can be equipped with different levels of gear that improve their combat ability. Heroes even have gear that boosts the strength of the army as a whole. Units gain experience gradually over time and through battle further increasing their combat skills.
What about battles? Battles are fought manually in a turn based fashion depending on the unit's speed (called iniative). You have to use the counterattack abilities, terrain, and type advantages to your favor to gain the upper hand. If you do not wish to fight manually all the time, an auto resolve feature (similar to Civ) is available.
Overall I highly recommend this game to all fans of strategy games.
I don't think I need to put this into words, but in case I do:

Take long enough to play and learn the language of the game and this is a very enjoyable experience indeed! The truly unique mechanics of the different factions make playing different sides a totally different experience requiring different strategies and tactics (and the game actually include both elements of strategic and tactical combat)
In short, this is miles ahead of other recent releases and whilst a little cumbersome on the AI and with a brutal learning curve that will sadly put a lot of people off trying it long enough to see it’s majesty it’s thoroughly enjoyable and well worth the money.

Probably my game of the year for 2014 (a tough contender against Dark Souls 2, in any case), Endless Legend is a fantastic take on the 4X genre.
Do you like Civ? Do you like fantasy / sci-fi? Do you like incredible production value and a great-running, great-feeling game with a ton of character? If so, you should probably play this game.

If you found Civilization Beyond Earth to be bland and uninspired, get this game, it's just so much better all around. I haven't played Beyond Earth at all since I got this during the Winter Sale.
The design choices are just really good, as they are able to eliminate a lot of the little annoyances that traditionally plague 4x games. There are multiple different ways to play and different strategies to try, just a rich game overall.

Endless Legend improves upon the system that was done in Endless Space and refines it close to perfection.
The battle system is quick and easy to learn.  Empire building is a careful management of resources and approval (very well balanced).  The artwork is just gorgeous.  The tech tree is done in a creative way, with no linear requirements (other than you have to have researched 9 of an era before unlocking the next era's technology).
Like most 4x games, the end game can get a little stale, since you will likely know already if you've won or not with 50 turns left to go.
Overall, a very solid 4x game.  I'd place it up there with the Civilization series.

Seeing that Amnesia: Memories is actually my first Otome game I've purchased and picked up, I really wasn't expecting much. I've played games like the Persona series and Harvest Moon series where there are these type of dating sims, but usually those games focused more on other types of gameplay (RPG and farming sim), but this is my first time picking a otome dating sim game where the main point of the game is to go through a span of 30 days with a chosen character where each answer and choice determines if you will be able to truly unlock the memories you've lost through Amnesia.
I thought that after 1 or 2 routes, I would get bored, but I was wrong. I think the strong element that Amnesia: Memories has is its ability to make you continuously want to know what's going to happen next, if you picked the right choices and what the ending you will get. The plot for each 'world' you choose in order to retrieve your memories is determined by the character you interact with. Every route has its differences and you will see how your chosen character develops through the span of 30 days you are given to unlock your memories. I found myself doing my best to get to the bottom of each conflict in each route and when I successfully got through it and achieved the good ending of a route, I felt rewarded for my efforts. and when I got a bad ending, I'd be screeching at my computer wondering what the heck I did wrong. I never thought I'd be invested so deeply in a game where all I literally do is click buttons.
Amnesia: memories caught my interest primarily because of its art. The CG images that are unlockable with each route and sprites are all so beautifully drawn. I also watched the anime that was revolved around this before I realized the game was coming out a week after I watched it. Watching the anime made me more curious about how the game would be and because of having that background, I was able to see how much more the game developed the characters and plot, something the anime could not (due to the amount of episodes).
The reason I am giving this game a 9/10 and not a full solid 10/10 is because I think that after I have completed and unlocked everything, the game has close to no replay value. I think that if there was additional content or gameplay, there would be a higher chance of this game keeping my interest in the long run if I ever wanted to pick it up and play it again. Unfortunately, after I complete everything, there's not much for me to go back to.  Since this is my first otome game, I'm not sure if that's how otome games are or if there's differences in each one in terms of mini-games and gameplay.
Nevertheless, I have been enjoying this game a lot. I am really happy that Amnesia: Memories was my first otome game. It left a lasting impression and I am eager to look into more otome games. I hope Idea Factory decides to localize the other games in the Amnesia series. I know I'd definitely be picking them up.

Although I like otome games, this is the first one I've played to completion or bought online. It was a very rewarding experience, and I do recommend it to anyone who's into that sort of thing. I read a lot of warnings about this game (which are important to take note of!) before buying, and was almost scared away. I'm glad I ended up buying it, though.
First off: Not all of the characters are nice. I initially thought every character would be trying to sweep me off my feet, but it's not like that at all. You pick a single route to pursue and navigate your relationship with the chosen male character (and your other friends) in each playthrough.
Secondly: There are multiple endings. For some reason, I had been lead to believe there were only the four routes and each had a single conclusion (which is ridiculous in retrospect).  A "bad" character may have multiple sides just as a "good" character does. Keep an open mind.
And finally, some have said this game is too hard. I disagree! Which I think I can do since this is my first time completing an otome game. I just had some fun exploring the options, saving often, and checking each character's reactions to my behaviour. Save often and if you absolutely MUST get the good ending, don't be afraid to consult a guide for some help.

I never thought it was going to be possible, but I can now scratch telling both Harriet Tubman and Aleister Crowley "You're going down!" off my bucket list.  Exploring in a game has never been as fun as it's been in The Curious Expedition.  You never know what you're going to uncover next, whether it be an encounter with some savage wildlife, a new species of butterfly for you to discover, or even a tribe of natives that may or may not be welcoming.  Heck, I've had them seem welcoming at first, only to turn on us as the night went on, with the children mocking us as we woke.  You really never do know what to expect with this game, and that makes it all the better.  The game actually feels you with the senses of wonder and exploration as you play.  And it's not over when the expedition wraps up, either,  I really enjoyed the post expedition segment where I decide if I want to donate my various findings to museums, action them off to private collectors, or to keep it for myself, because you never know just what might come in handy on that next voyage across the globe.  For a game that's only in it's Alpha stage, there's already a plethora of content.  You're going to find yourself constantly surprised by something new each time you play.  I can't wait to see what's still to come!
Many people will tell you to avoid Early Access games, but even at this point, there's enough content crammed into The Curious Expedition to warrant being called a completed game.  This one is well worth the price as it is already.  Pick this one up now.  You won't regret it.

THE FIDELIO INCIDENT
PUBLISHER – Act3 Games, LLC
DEVELOPER – Act3 Games, LLC
GENRE Walking simulator/adventure, Indie
THE BASICS:
A Walking Simulator set on a below-freezing island, with some minor adventure elements. You're the only living creature you ever encounter (save for some stinging jellyfish that just stay put in order to keep you on the path) is yourself. Immersive atmosphere – grand music, solid voice acting, and even the snow/wind/etc effects contribute to the feel of the game.
THE FLOW AND THE STORY:
You (Stanley) and your dear love, Leonore, are flying in a small plane when they suddenly crash on a deserted, frigid island. They're both on the run from their past, and now your wife is trapped in the plane's wreckage up on the top of a nearby mountain; her diary was taken by the four winds, and spread out all across the isle. You need to stay alive – often running from a steam vent to a flaming bit of wreckage, or vice versa, just to stave off the deadly cold for a few more seconds. Crank open steam vents to create a safe space, and seek out Leonore's diary entries so that you can both get off of the island alive, and with no-one else the wiser.
CONTROLS:
Controller or WASD (controller recommended by the devs). Simple, straightforward, streamlined controls. No inventory to bother with; items you find are needed pretty much immediately and used automatically. The game tracks diary entries in the pause menu, and there's nothing else to worry about. E to grab items, left-shift to “sprint” (the effects of which range from decent down to almost unnoticeable, depending on the local terrain, aside from blurring your vision a bit).
GRAPHICS:
Grand vistas and attention to detail – even if they are of ice, snow, and half-frozen bunkers for much of the game. Some parts feel same-y quickly, but that just drives your need to move quickly and get to a new, warm area in order to survive. That being said, the environs are convincing and well-executed. Even if there's a whole lot of white-on-white.
SOUND:
Absolutely gorgeous. The game's plot was inspired by Beethoven's opera “Fidelio,” and the music in the game does not disappoint. The soundtrack is free with purchase of the game, and is more than worth listening to on its own. Your boots crunch scrumptiously in the snow, flames crackle with life, and rusty levers groan as you force them to do their jobs.
OVERALL:
Short but good. 2 hours if you rush, 1 and a half if you take your time or just can't quite make it to the next safe spot. That being said, yeah, it's worth fifteen bucks for an experience that makes you think (you'll understand when you reach the end credits), and the inclusion of the OST for no extra charge makes the price more than fair. After all, how may $50-60 games have you played with only 4 or 5 hours of gameplay needed to beat them?
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
Mid-range. Core i3 2ghz+, 6 GB RAM, Win 7+ 64bit

This is one of the best rng based games I've ever played. There are over 40 cute characters to play as. Each one has unique stats and a special card only they can use called a hyper card. You roll dice for moving, battling, and for deciding how many stars you gain or lose. The goal of the game is to collect 200 stars or 14 wins (which you get by defeating npcs or other players) and get back to a home panel.
Despite most of the game being determined by dice rolls, there's still quite a bit of strategy in the game. For example, when you move around the board sometimes there are forks in the path and you can pick which way you want to go. Another option you have while moving is if you pass by a space with another player on it you can choose to battle them and land on the space they're standing on.
The biggest influence you can have on the game is that you get to choose ten cards to bring with you which will go into a center deck with the other players cards for everyone to use. I like that they did it this way because it means no one has access to certain cards without also giving everyone else a chance to use them. Because it's more likely someone else will use the cards you brought the best kinds of cards to bring are ones with effects that benefit you but not the other players.
The battles are where you'll be gaining and losing most of your stars. This is because when a player dies, they lose half of their stars. You have many options to protect yourself from this though. At the start of every battle each player has the option to use a battle card. Some cards make it easier for the attacker and others make it easier for the defender. When you're defending you also have another choice if you want to defend the enemy attack or evade it. Defending is usually the safer option because the game subtracts damage from the attacker's roll with your defense roll (you always take a minimum of 1 damage however). Evading is riskier because if you fail to roll a higher number than the attacker you take all of the damage from an attack but if you succeed you take no damage at all. It's kind of an all or nothing choice.
The developers regularly update the game and add new content. It also has a pretty active community with some people even having tournaments. What are you waiting for? Go get this game already. It's totally worth the price! Just watch out for Poppo because she always wins.

My current favorite 4X. The art style is quite beautiful and the sound is top notch (something this developer always manages to pull off in my opinion). The gameplay is quite solid and the interface is very clean and easy to use and understand.
Pick one of the premade factions (that all play quite differently) or create your own by picking their race and their passives/perks. Each faction has a story that's progressed by completing quests. There are even side quests you can pick up. These quests help add goals that make the turns a little more interesting than just spamming "Next Turn". You can also assimilate minor factions that are located within your territories. This will allow you to use that faction's special unit in your military.
The world is made up of regions, and there can only be one city per region. This makes you plan your expansions a little more carefully as you hunt down strategic and luxury resources (which you can only extract if they're within your borders) or possibly even look for chokepoints to build your cities in so you always have a terrain advantage. Cities can be expanded tile by tile as your population grows, which in turn increases the amount of land that you're exploiting for resources. Putting a hero in charge of your city will also give that city very nice buffs as the hero levels and you pick new perks.
The combat is quite satisfying if you choose to play it out tactically. You can either auto-resolve, spectate, or manually control your units each battle. You can even watch other players' battles in multiplayer if you're allied with them. The combat isn't as deep as some of the other more war focused 4x games, but it's also a lot less time consuming which is something I appreciate a great deal. You should keep terrain and reinforcements in mind as well. You may be able to take out the small army next to you, but the one a few tiles away might reinforce it mid-battle. You'll also need to outfit your units and heroes as you unlock stronger weapons and armor. This will increase their production cost and, depending on what you outfit them with, add strategic resources to the cost.
As briefly mentioned above, this game has heroes that you can either put in charge of your armies or cities. While with an army, they will fight on the field with them. Whether a general or governor, they will level up. This allows you to pick passives that will help them no matter their situation. For example, if they're a governor, pick passives that will increase food or industry production; if a general, give them passives to buff your units. There are also hero only pieces of equipment that you'll come across and quests requiring a hero (sometime of a specific race).
The diplomacy feels a bit lacking, but I've never been one to try for Diplomatic Victories in any 4X. I mostly use it to get map vision and create temporary alliances while I hunt others down.
The tech tree is quite large, and I like the progression system it uses. Instead of tech directly leading to another, you have to research a certain number of techs from the previous tier to unlock the next tier.
Overall, I'm a huge fan of this game. Great art, sound, music, and interface. The game plays and runs well, and it's backed by an active developer.

I'd just like to start off saying that this is
humble opinion an not anyone elses.
Awesomenauts is a MOBA but not in the general sense of other MOBAs. Its a 3v3 2D platforming MOBA. Its very fast paced an rewards teams who act on quick thinking. It even allows the use of a controller, which works very nicely in this along with 3 player splitscreen that can even go into matchmaking. The game runs on Windows, Mac, an even Linux.
Awesomenauts is what I personally like to describe as an Arcade style MOBA. The reason being is that arcade games are fast, an don't last long. Matches in this game can last from 5-15 mins in a short one an 16-30+ mins for a long one. Some people may like this an many others may very well be turned off by this. If you just don't know how to keep up, then snowballing may end up an issue on your constant mistakes. Its hard to take in, but thats just how it is and you need to get used to it. Which means...theres alot of salty players that have yet to move past the stage of "acceptance" so rage quitting is pretty common in this but that moves onto the next thing.
Drop in matchmaking. This system tries to make sure theres always human players on a team but the issue here is that 90% of the time, its dropped into a match where only one turret is standing or the base is already being attacked. You're thrown into a match thats essentially over. However, on the opposite end, it does work if something goes wrong at the start of the match an this is good. But it all really just boils down to the matchmaking (which i will not go into detail in this because as of this writing, the matchmaking is currently being overhauled. This is because the current system is a little iffy due to the low playerbase an steams matchmaking system.) of having a full match constantly. Which proves a point for the next thing.
This game is ALWAYS changing. Theres always balance tweaks an even sheer meta changes. Sometimes good, sometimes bad, but you always adjust an get used to it an see what actually was bad an what is good. An sometimes some crazy balance ideas end up making it in...which ends up getting changed later yet again~
The content is also updated fairly frequently. Currently every naut, aside from the kickstarter funded starstorm nauts&content, is given into the base game for free. At the moment there is only 4 maps in rotation (5 in custom because a newer version of AI station replaced the older one due to severe imbalance) an steam workshop is also on the way down the line to include a mass variety of maps that may very well make it into matchmaking.
Spectator mode will be added in down the line! It was funded by the starstorm kickstarer although i'm not sure if you need Starstorm to actually use it.
The characters have ALOT of personality. This is really just a major thing in this game, they have great voice lines (which all stem from references pretty much.) and the voice acting is fairly solid (but not all. its mostly opinion anyway.) You'd be hard pressed to not find one that didn't just sing to you.
Lastly, The company Ronimo. They handle support requests seriously, an does an extremely good job at dealing with griefing an harassment, and ESPECIALLY, cheating! Granted, you must submit this information to them if you want something done. It won't just magically happen. But if you do, you will 100% for sure get a response. Solid customer support, ronimo.
So to summarise.
-Arcade like fast paced gameplay on a 2D playing field. People may love or hate this.
-Controller support.
-3 player split screen support that can play in matchmaking.
-Windows/Mac/Linux support.
-Drop in matchmaking attempts to keep a match full but sometimes this backfires at the wrong times.
-Balance changes are extremely frequent. Good an Bad at times.
-Frequent content updates. The game will be supported as long as there is an audience!
-Great characters with solid personalities.
-Steam workshop will come later to add even more content from user creation.
-Solid support from Ronimo.

If you Love MOBAs an also love Platformers, you really should try this game.

I am really conflicted about this game. On one hand, I think some of the plotlines are interesting, and I ended up really wrapped up in what would happen -- Shin and Ikki were my favorites by far. The character art is gorgeous, and I think that the game did an amazing job with the cliche amnesia storyline -- there's a lot you don't know but I felt like characters were suspicious when they should be and not when they shouldn't. There are things about the game that drive me crazy.
The character you play is so passive. Orion ends up being the voice for nearly everything that happens and all the recapping irritated me. Yes, I know what that character just said, Orion, I was there and there's no need to tell me yet again. I have no idea why your character would even listen to what Orion is saying given that you don't know him and he's just a random spirit that invaded your consciousness and pushed out your memories. Honestly, the game would have been a 1000% better by cutting the part Orion plays in the story in half. I never fully get why in the Toma or Shin storylines you shouldn't call the police, other than Orion tells you not to, so it ends up making no sense at all. Not to mention how you spend the games supposedly trying to recover your memories, but in the Toma storyline you find your diary and then proceed not to read it for no good reason. Why even have you find it when you did when the game doesn't allow you to read it? Orion might have forgot, but the diary is my character's person, and she definitely didn't forget.
It seems like a lot of people liked Kurt, but I really didn't, and I was so frustrated when I realized there was no way to break up with him. I would have taken a bad ending death to end their relationship, but I couldn't, and in the end, Orion ended up telling me that Kurt was a nice guy, he cared for my character, and obviously my character had feelings for him. WTF. No, no she did not. Her dialogue throughout the path made that more than clear. You see this again at the end of Shin's storyline when your character is sympathetic and apologetic to Toma who was absolutely terrible. I hate it when games force you to think a way that's completely inconsistent with how you're playing your character. There should have been an option for you to say whether you forgive him or not. (The answer is definitely not.)
I was also a little disturbed by the fact that nearly every storyline but one includes either your love interest physically manhandling you in a way that's scary or uncomfortable, initiating sexual contact without consent, or telling you that something you've said or done is going to get you sexually assaulted. Seriously, game? Whether it's a boy that likes you but you don't like them back, or someone who's sexually interested in you while you're either unsure of your interest in them or don't have any interest at all, the game makes it sound like your character has done something wrong. Also, when the women in the game are jealous, they're crazy and murderous, when the men are, it's just because they love you so much. That's not a good message to send. Jealousy isn't sexy or romantic and shouldn't be portrayed like it is. (And as much as a personally liked Ikki's character, I wish the game had addressed the fact that the members of his fan club were all essentially magically roofied by his eyes. This game had so many consent issues in it, and that's before you get to crazy Toma.)
Also, while this is definitely less important than the other issues I had in the game. I really became sick of some of the repetive background art, particularly during Kurt's storyline where you seem to walk a lot but with no dialogue the repetition is both more obvious and tedious. As negative as I'm being about the game, I didn't hate it. I think it could have been a really amazing game, and I did like playing several of the storylines. But the physical and sexual aggression we see from guys we are supposed to like was a bit too far for me. I get it in Ukyo and Toma's storylines but I hate that it pops up in everyone single one of them.

Everything was going perfectly on the the 5th leg of our expedition. My men were strong and well equipped, and I've collected a stash of treasures that I could either sell for fame or fortune. I was so sure that we'd be able to plow through the 6th and last expedition with this team until... I arrived at the golden pyramid only to find I lacked a key to enter it...
I panicked, but hey, this was my best team. We would just drop by at the tomb in the distance and we'd come back to the pyramid and go home in one piece.
Having planned the journey so that we would arrive at the golden pyramid with minimum supplies, (so that we could stack up on treasures) we were in no way prepared to tackle another journey. Still, we made it to the tomb and retrieved the key without much trouble. It was during the return trip that hell broke out.
Having reached zero sanity a long time ago, it was the cultist, the newest member of our group, that faded into the darkness of the night first. Fine. I was prepared for something like this. A few days later, my best man, the British soldier, murdered the sailor, mumbling something about a conspiracy... Also fine. I never really liked that alchoholic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I bet he really was conspiring to kill us all. But a several more days in, my best man also murdered my second best man, the scout! This time, he didn't even bother making any excuses, partially because he was busy feeding on the murdered scout. God, my best friend had turned into a cannibal right before my eyes... I bet the cultist ran away because he knew about the soldier's peculiar habits... I should have realized he was a complete nut right from the start when he talked to me about all that "Gaining sanity from fighting" nonsense!! Fearing my own safety, I ran for my life, leaving the soldier behind. I half expected to be chased down and murdered like the others, but somehow, I made it back to the pyramid in one piece, with nothing but the key and a few hyena pelts. Oh, I was so relieved I was finally able to return to British soil...
I was alone, poor, traumatized, and I've sworn many many times that I would not ever set foot on foreign soil again, but mysteriously, I found myself heading back to the explorers club. Even certain death could not quench my thirst for adventure and perhaps, such madness. Also, the opportunity to build a statue in your honor doesn't come around so easily, doesn't it?
10/10 Would pit myself into the madness and insurmountable odds again for a statue of myself.

"Oh God! Not ANOTHER walking simulator!" I hear you cry.
"Sit down...shut the ♥♥♥♥ up...and LISTEN," I reply.
Alright, so I've been playing a few of these lately, and all you "this isn't even a game" people are probably getting mighty sick of all these products even existing. Well, y'know, sometimes life is hard. Sometimes, you don't get everything you want in this world. And sometimes, just sometimes, things come along which can defy even the expectations of those who swore black-and-blue that they'd never, ever embrace them.
Let's break it down, shall we?
First up, something these "walking sims" actually DO tend to be praised for: graphics. The Fidelio Incident allows you to choose "Epic" graphics quality, and I have to say, that's exactly what you get: epic graphics, from the get-go. You begin in the cockpit of a plane, and it isn't long before that plane is crashing thanks to a bird selflessly splattering itself across the windshield in high-def. So no, this isn't quite your typical walking sim.
Secondly: sound. Top-rate, highly immersive sound design and very good voice acting. The occasional naff line of dialogue ("Ooh, blimey...so fookin' COLD...need to get warm")...but hey, it IS a video game. Get over it.
Thirdly: danger. Yep, there is some. Quite a bit, actually, mostly due to the harsh and unforgiving icy environments most of the game is set in. You will die. Possibly quite a lot. So again...not your typical walking sim.
Fourthly: gameplay. The path isn't 100% linear, and there are some (granted, reasonably simple) puzzles to solve. So there is some traditional notion of "gameplay", for those of you who are truly fussed about such things. (Poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, haha.)
Fifthly: length. Okay, so it's not "epic" in length. Nor should it be. I'm sick to death of long games for the most part. A game well under five hours might put some hair on yer sac...try it.
And last but definitely not least: story. It's a good'un. A real good'un. Told well. You like stories, don't you? Oh, that's right, you only play Call of Duty. (Sorry, couldn't resist.)
On the whole, it's a bit like Kholat (minus the monsters), with a tiny hint of Tomb Raider and the bit when you first crash-land on the icy planet in Dead Space 3 thrown in. High adventure and epic storytelling at its finest. Heck...with a little luck of the Irish, even avowed haters of walking simulators might find something to love here.
You never do know, eh?
Verdict: 9/10.

Absolutely the best Free to Play game out there at the time of this review. It has a very captivating and appealing art style, especially if you love the sci-fi and fantasy genres for gaming. Even if not, you cannot deny that the art, textures, everything is very, very well detailed. The gameplay is rather slow at first once you finish the game's initial tutorial related quests, leaving you off to explore the rest of the Warframe universe on your own, but once it starts to pick up you will find yourself playing for hours on end. Whether you enjoy exploring the terrain, learning the lore, shooting your enemies in the head with shotguns/rifles/pistols, pinning your enemies to walls with bows, or confusing your enemies by throwing daggers at them from the shadows, you will find some form of enjoyment with the gameplay.
Unfortunately, it is a very grindy game, so if you're super casual about gaming, you may not find yourself reaching the end game content within a month or two like those who will put serious effort into it, but rather a year. No matter what, the effort you put into the game will be worth it.
The lore starts off slow, but gets indefinitely better by the time you reach end game/current content. Your mind will be blown because Digital Extreme's story telling exploded into an epic proportion by the time you reach the Second Dream quest in game. No spoilers, but it will be leaving you thinking "This is a free to play game?!" but the story doesn't end there! It's only just beginning by that point!
As for in game currencies, Warframe has the best system I've encountered so far. You don't have to pay to get platinum (Warframe's premium currency) unless you want to directly support the game's development! In fact, platinum is almost unnecessary except for purchasing cosmetics (for your warframe, ship, companions, etc.), which are completely optional, and slots for extra warframes, weapons, companions, etc, which are only necessary if you want to take the game extra seriously and collect all the warframes and weapons (basically a completionist run, with every item in game maxed and still accessible). Platinum in this game is basically a "pay to speed up", where it is mostly used to rush anything you're crafting or just straight out by it from the market place. Did I forget to mention that if you don't want to pay, all you have to do to get your hands on some platinum outside of the amount you get for playing for the first time is trade with other players? Yeah! It's that easy!
TL:DR; This game is the best free to play game where once you get past it's grindy, won't hold your hand all the way through, nature of the game, it's premium currency is optional, the story will leave you with your jaw on the floor, and you will spend countless hours of exploring all the different combinations of weapons, warframes, and customization options to find the one that suits you the most!

My translator fell in love with the prince of an indigenous tribe. We smuggled the prince out of his village and spent the rest of the expedition running from his kin. He then agreed to come to Europe with his lover, and us.
10/10 would support forbidden love again.

You pick an explorer and roll random encounters on a map. You can pick up equipment and treasure, and measure how well you're doing against four AI parties. The combat uses dice that you can hold or reroll for maneuver combinations. Exploration uses dialogue screens for trait-influenced, semi-random outcomes. You can level-up and switch-out your companions for a variety perks that your main also gets to grab a new one of, after each expedition.
A lot of similar-appearing games try to go for a retro appeal to old computer RPGs. What most developers ignore is that those games being appealed to? They were trying to match a table-top experience. This game takes what would be a great table-top experience and combines with it the ability of a computer to spare you tedious rolls of "what are the six hexes surrounding this one?" This game takes a board-game system and beefs it up with a program that'll roll through the doldrums.
Wholly playable, rewardingly-difficult, and most-of-all engaging: Curious Expedition is wonderful. The devs are calling this an alpha build, and it's a full game from the first day it has been on Steam. Early access came about because, after Minecraft, we all hoped it'd be great games that just got better. And then we all got let down because most were scams. This one isn't. This game is worth twice its price in exactly its current state. If you see the videos and are wondering "but it's Early Access, so is it just going to be another dropped project?" Let me re-assure you that, if you purchase it, you won't care. This is one that, if no additional builds are ever released for, you'll still be glad to have purchased.

First of all, I've been looking forward to this game for a while.
The concept etc is interesting but the gameplay is repetitive.
Eventually I realised I was just grinding for points.
Without leaderboards, I don't really care about the points.
I did not find anything in this game intriguing enough to keep me grinding for fame points.
If you think I'm being harsh, let me explain:
There does not seem to be much difference in the playstyle or gameplay when picking different historical characters, it all comes down to doing the same repetitive thing to get fame.
The Random Number Generator decides how well your AI opponents did regarding fame.
The goal is to have more fame than your opponents.
At the end of the expedition, you gathered items from the shrines and villages.
You sell the acquired items for fame or money.
You pick a skill and buy items for the next expedition.
You start in the middle of a map, you calculate the steps and items involved in the path to take.
When you arrive at a village or similar, you trade, recruit, or sleep.
You explore and find shrines, you either take or don't take what's there.
Sometimes taking something from a shrine will have a negative impact on the rest of the map.
Your Sanity and Standing will decrease if you explore too much or interfere too much.
You can keep the Sanity and Standing high using the items you carry.
The combat is on the border of refreshingly fun and annoyingly dull.
You throw dice with moves instead of numbers, and you can make combo's with them.
Combat is easy to avoid, and not impressive enough to strike fear in me.
When you die, if your fame is higher than the RNG AI fame, you're awesome.
TL:DR
Been there, done that. The grind for points to beat RNG AI is not fun enough.

As a gamer with a vast array of stratagy country controlling games. I loved crushing small countries like Paraguay and Uyraguay with the might of Brazil. I really like this genre of games and to find a multiplayer campaign within this genre which works great is a perfect match for me. Victoria II changes the way country building games work by not using ristricting turns which take forever to wait through and instead using real time (with the exception of a timespeeder).
Although the game is a amazing take on the popular genre of games it is lacking in just a few things:
-Battle simulations-Navial and land (e.g. Empire total war)
-Improved diplomacy
-Quicker elections
-Fixed auto peace treaty bug (explained later)
-More recruiting spaces
-AI armies running away from your armies
As you can see these are mostly miner issueses, but even so a Battle simulation would be ideal. So maybe for next game, please. Although I don't mind this, as I know that this is very hard to do but also that it should stay to the roots from which Victoria I was created.
There is some really anyoing aspects to this game such as silly diplomacy, I understand the "reason to go to war with a country rule" but why can't the reason always be conquest. Also no matter what I do I, as a miner nation, can never seem to find a way to please the superpowers (e.g. England, The USA, France, Spain or Russia).
The game needs to re-imagine the election system. Although this is a very big game and there are so many differant countries to play as, I have noticed that Brazil always has elections, which take so long it is just repetetive options of just stupid things.
Now i'm fairly surten that this is a bug but what happens is whilst am invading a country with miles of men after men, a message pops up saying something like "Denmark has requested a peace treaty". When I exit this it then will start a peace treaty on 'White Peace' meaning all my forces just withdraw from the country they where invading. For some reason it does this after I've said no to the peace treaty, this makes invading some counties almost impossible. Actually thats a overstatement as it is still possible but only the second time you wipe them out.
Also playing as Brazil again but also the USA I found that there are just no places you can recruit troops and once you have it won't let you recruit for about another year or two. I see that this is more present in Brazil then in the USA.
Another anoying problem is that the AI do occosionally just see my armies comming and then run away but then when I know which direction there going, they just run in another direction. This again is very hard to make an attack on a country.
The anoying main thing is how the colonization process only happens if you have 30 population, how do you raise the population so you can colonize it.
I know it seems that I have just been slamming this game, I actually love this game and already have, at the time of review compasition, have 13 hours into the game. This is one of my favorite strategy games of all time. It is fun and addictive and is a very historically accurate game (if you find games like Risk and Civ V long, I don't recommend it). Unlike other Paradox games, however, this one focuses a lot on internal improvements instead of war (thanks to the extra-restrictive infamy system). All land not available for colonization in the EU series is colonizable here. This makes for an even better game if you convert from CKII to EUIV to V2 as you get a near full historical timeline for one country. It is always interesting to see how the scramble for Africa plays out in each game (especially if you're involved in it). This game also characterizes the time period very accurately. It is full of many interlocking alliances/spheres with smaller countries along with great power intervention. The crisis system also demonstrates how many near-wars occured during this time over foreign affairs, but were solved through dipolmacy. You have the great powers oppressing the rest of the world taking over land from Asian and African nations for resources and strategic positions, as well. Also, the industrialization process makes up for the lack of war. However, this game does have some flaws. The infamy system restricts expansion greatly which is not exactly accurate to history. Perhaps if infamy was only gained when waging war against great powers or secondary powers. It really shouldn't cost 22 infamy to annex Haiti, Cuba, or other lesser civs. Also, there shouldn't be infamy for LIBERATING a county, something usually regarded as a moral action. Things like the Spanish-American war can't occur due to large infamy gains. Also, the in game tutorials are awful and teach you very little. It will take a long time to learn. Another thing is that, don't be fooled, unlike most other Paradox games, there are only two start dates. There is no full range of date choice. While this seems really stupid at first, it does make sense as if you could just start the game at any date, you will miss the whole industrialization process which is one of the main features of the game. Despite these flaws, this game is great. If you put the time in to learn it, you will love it.
*This review is for the full game with Heart of Darkness expansion

The Fidelio Incident is an interesting game, slotting into the same category as pieces such as Dear Esther, Firewatch, and even a little bit like Kholat.
Though your time in this game is mainly spent walking to point A-B so on, discovering and reading the numerous journal pages trewn across the icy landscape, and listening to the remarkably well done voice acting, you have a few puzzles to break the monotony of your journey and add a bit more depth to your endeavour.
The graphics are fantastic, the only complaint is forced Chromatic Aberration. It didn't work for Payday 2, it didn't work for Life is Strange, it doesn't work here. It is an awful post-processing effect. That being said, the visuals are otherwise clean and vibrant.
The sound design is equally as good, with crackling fire, howling wind, crunching snow and the like. Voice acting is top-tier and is clear as day. The game features a 12 piece score with the main theme being the most prominent piece. The music fits and integrates itself flawlessly, conveying and emphasising emotions, tones, and underlying themes. The piano sounds fantastic here.
Your only real downside comes from the somewhat tiresome puzzles as you find yourself repeating these quite often. The story is enjoyable and based around a real-world issue, The Troubles, which occurred in Ireland. Wrapping in just under 2 hours, The Fidelio Incident is a nice little adventure with some genuinely enjoyable visuals and premise, it's just let down a little from its puzzle design.
If you enjoy games like the aforementioned, games that are generally a single smooth pace, then this is worth checking out. Otherwise, if you prefer a little more engagement, this may not be to your liking.
Verdict: 7-8/10, recommend purchasing when on sale.

Along the same premise as the first game, the Mudokons you're trying to rescue in Exoddus are much more complex than the original assembly. Besides the occasional drunk, blind, or just generally resistant creature, they all emote like mood rings, showing red skin when angry and an off-color greenish yellow and pale tone when sick. You have to find healing rings from Shaman Mudokons and apologize and shoulder-pat to make angry ones happy again so they'll follow you to safety. And blind Mudokons have a tendency to walk into drills and off of ledges if you don't guide them properly with verbal cues. On a positive note, you can use their blindness to your benefit. For example, if a blind Mudokon is on the level below you, notably the one with the lever you need to pull but can't get to, you can stand on the side of the screen you want the blind guy to walk toward, prompt him to follow you, and then tell him to "work" in order to turn the crank or pull the lever that allows you access to another level. Another excellent function is being able to guide more than one Mudokon at a time. In the first game, you had to rescue one Mudokon, then come back and get the other one. In Exoddus, you have an "All o' ya" command that captures the attention of anyone present. At points, you'll have a gaggle trailing behind you - sneaking, running, or jumping into the bird teleporters.
But perhaps even better than the hammed-up gamespeak is the fact that the developers fixed what could easily be called the number one problem with the first game: the inability to save the game wherever you wanted. Not only was Abe's Oddysee a tough game, you spent a lot of time redoing what you'd done because of the need to learn the hard way. Many of the puzzles in the original required some testing before you made it through, and when you have to go all the way back to the beginning of the path each time you fail, it's hard to stay inspired to push forward. In Exoddus, you have an incredibly welcomed quick-save option that allows you to quickly save your progress, anywhere in the game as many times as you want. And when you're ready to quit playing, you simply save to the memory card instead of a quick save, and you're set. This introduces an interesting dilemma, as the quick save certainly makes Exoddus seem easier, in a sense, but the game itself is actually even more difficult than the first one - it's just that now you finally have hope. And just when you think hope's lost, something wonderful like an invisibility power-up appears when you free Mudokon spirits.
Graphically, Abe's Exoddus is the same 2D visual wonder, much like the original or, moreover, Interplay's Heart of Darkness. Yet the graphics seem much more brilliant, as there are more environments with greater diversity in design. And the cutscenes are not only gorgeous, they're entertaining and (can I say it?) funny. No, really. Besides that, the game is quite large, and the environments are expansive. You'll have to rescue the spirits of Mudokons past; battle the typical, yet enhanced cast of Sligs, Scrabs, and the excruciatingly annoying Fleeches (long live the quick save), among others; as well as roll through the mines in mine carts and such. And sound-wise, you really can't get much better without being downright distracting. The voices of all the characters are incredible, and the effects, from getting blown up by a mine to the echoey sound of falling to your death, really can't be beat.
Abe's Exoddus also has a two-player mode. While the Exoddus mainstay is clearly the single-player game, the two-player co-op mode does have charm, as you and another player take turns working your way through. When you die, your partner picks up where you left off and so forth. A bit of advice? Pick a crummy partner, and you might have some fun with this. Otherwise, the waiting game just doesn't parallel the egocentric fun of keeping this title to yourself. In all, Abe's Exoddus is a great example of how a game can stay true to its conceptual pursuit while still improving upon the original, all while keeping its soul intact. If you loved the first one, you'll like this game more. If you didn't play the first one, you can start here. If you hated the first one, it's likely because of the lack of save points, so you should definitely consider giving this series another try.

Endless Legend is a 4X fantasy turn-based strategy game that does a damn good job of keeping you hooked. The gameplay is both fun and rewarding as you playthrough the game using one of multiple unique factions with their own well crafted lore, units, heroes and in-game quests.
Besides the usual city building, exploration, war mongering and researching your way to a victory condition, where this game stands out for me is with it's Heroes and Quest system. Each faction grants you a hero that gains XP and levels, unlocking skills and governing traits that boosts your army and cities. Heroes can also equip items from plundering loot, quest rewards and researching new resource tech. On top of that, each faction has its own Faction Quest that if followed right till the end, will grant you another victory condition, and the story lines are good. The RPG element of this system works well with its fantasy setting.
Presentation wise, this game has some of the best animated 2D artwork I've seen in a while, and the soundtrack is equally as good.
Overall, fantastic game with excellent replay value. Worth the time and money.

For the first 20 hours of gameplay, I thought I had found a new 4X game to add to my favorites along with Civ and AoW. Unfortunately that feeling did not last. Amplitude did a lot of things right but in the end failed to make the game engaging enough for "endless" replays.  Gameplay features that made me come to this conclusion around the 40-hour mark are as follows:
1.	Winter is a game breaking borefest. If it appeared randomly after 30 to 50 turns and lasted between 5 to 10 turns, it would be an interesting feature… but the way it is implement (where winter occurs more and more often, lasts longer and longer and leads to endless winter by turn 200), it is simply a chore and the opposite of fun. The AI does nothing during winter, productivity comes to a screeching stop, and movement and offensive military action are severely hampered. This equates to a clickfest on the “next turn” button. Few skills and techs help with winter’s onslaught, and even if Amplitude added some, it would affect replay. Good 4X games let you implement your winning strategies, they don’t dictate which techs should be researched in order to compensate for devastating scripted events. This reminds me of Medieval Total War, where after building up your empire, you knew that everything would be laid to waste by the scripted Black Plague and the back-to-back Mongol and Timurid invasions.
2.	City invasions are too easy. Considering that empire building is really engaging in Endless Legend, you end up holding off your armies and then unleashing them in the game’s last "decent length" summer, before the endless winter comes, or otherwise you lose on points. Again, Amplitude is dictating gameplay with their lore. I don’t care for lore in a 4X game, it affects replay.
3.	The Quests are ill-conceived and do not provide enough reward. Almost all of them will ask for some resource only available in the next era, to visit a location in a region controlled by another faction that would require you to declare war just to get to it, or to develop one of your city with Level 2 districts and city centers that would take at least 50 to 100 turns to complete. Same thing applies for assimilating Minor Factions: their requests can either not be fulfilled anytime soon, force your hand into war (which you don’t want to do considering the poor return you get from assimilating Minor Factions) or make you turn to the marketplace to purchase the requested items only to realize that it would be twice as cheap to just bribe them into submission.
Putting aside those issues, I love everything else about this game. AI, combat and diplomacy all need to be improved, but it is not game breaking for me. If they can make winter optional or configurable, perfect city invasions so it is better balanced and change the questing and Minor Factions assimilation features to make them more enjoyable and worthwhile, they will greatly improve the replayability factor. As it is now, I was fun playing through a game, but I doubt I will revisit Endless Legend often.
