My oh my, I have played/read a fair amount of VNs, but the writing of this one is on a whole new abysmal level...
Here's the short version: Bad pacing, too much convenience and a goddamn deus ex machina accompaning you sure ruin a story.
And now a bit of elaboration: This opinion is based on sitting through parts of the heart and spades route and mainly focus on the quality of the writing and to a degree the character design
First of all, in regards to the desgin, if the object (and let's face it it's little more than that) of interest of the spades route has a spade tatooed on his face, and yet somehow argues that sunglasses make the difference when it comes to recognition you know what to expect...
But the bigger issue is the writing.
I already mentioned you being accompanied by an incarnated deus ex machina, otherwise know as Orion and I want him to die. In a fire for example, though I am not too picky, anything should do the job.
As the games premise is you, the protagonist, losing all of her memories, it'd reasonable to expect that you would mainly portray apathy towards all of the people you used to know as they're nothing but strangers to you now. In theory the same would go for Orion, who is some kind of Spirit whose objective is to sever hiw tie to you so he can go his way. Specifying any further would be explicit spoilers, though the information is relayed within the first 10 or so minutes of the game.
However Orion acts as the protagonsit providing both your reactions and your motivation in all situations, with your choices, the only means of interaction you have, usually just change 1 to 3 lines of dialouge. Effectively whatever Orion says is what you say, even though he is supposed to be nonexistent fo ranyone but you, also he gets into it way too much...
Orion winds up being nothing but a bunch of plot convenience, e.g. with no explicit spoilers "Oh this route's guy is in some kind of problematic situation with local authoreties, we know he is innocent, but I'm worried nonetheless, and that means you have to be as well even though the story gave you no reason to."
A story that utilizes amnesia as a story relevant tool has one simple advantage, you can forge all bonds and ties to other characters simulatniously to explaining them to the player, meaning, if used correctly you can combine exposition with story telling. It isn't used correctly though, while the protagonist was portrayed as worried I did nothing but shrug in apathy as the whole "conflict" was not an actual issue and easily debunked/resolved.
The story forces a linear approach on the player, even though the concept doesn't fit that kind of story-telling, causing a huge discrepancy between player and protagonist, having Orion being the actual protagonsit, rather than the player, he makes the calls, influences the interactions between characters and is nothing but a hypocrite in the process and that's putting it lightly...
By extension that also is quite telling in regards to the writer, here's some examples of the hypocracy and how it's bad writing:
1st. Orion thinks that Amnesia is treated by confining the patient to a hospital room or their home, took me about 5 minutes of using google to debunk that, he does however know what a goddamn maid cafe is.
2nd. He bases his opinion of humans on the subjective opinion of one of his acquantances and considers them greedy/egoistic, at the same time he thinks you would consider anything they say to be the truth and obey their every whim, making you little else but a toddler
This creates a fun little problem, you are treated as if, by losing all of your memories, you can not understand concepts such as lies, meaning that you wouldn't have common sense either, leading to apathy, otherwise you'd retain things such a common sense thus being able to do simple things such as saying "No" or debunking someones ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t claims.
Here is a direct quote from Orion to put some of the issues into perspective:
"Hee-hee. I'm pretty knowledgeable about human life, aren't I?"
The writer acknowledges the issue, but doesn't bother to fix it... We are talking about a commercial product here, if you know there is an issue fix it, you don't get a free pass by mentioning it and not giving another♥♥♥♥♥♥
Now here is another fun quote:
"[...] try to actively meet people and investigate what kind of person you used to be."
This represents his initial motivation, as for plot related reasons he wants you to recover your lost memories, shortly afterwards however he ignores this objective in order to waste time on investigating an accident in order to make sure it was an accident.
You as the player get to point  out, that the clues at hand are insufficient to really bother wasting time on this investgation, but not a single ♥♥♥♥ is given by Orion and by extension the writer...
I might not be the actual target group, being male and all, but I sure as hell can tell when a story is written in a bad fashion and the fact that some of the issues are acknowledged within the game is quite telling.
All I can say is: Don't bother if you are expecting quality, if you can just roll with all kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and don't expect good writing, aka looking for a good laugh, this might be worth 20 bucks or less.

When I found myself as liberal Russia fighting the French fascists and communist USA in the kingdom of Mexico, I knew this was a great game.
Victoria 2 might be the only strategy game I would ever recommend to someone who doesn't like armies, navies or wars. While it can and does exist as a war game, the game also painstakingly details the political life of a country, and ties it to scientific discovery, economic growth and turmoil, and ethnic strife. The game begins in 1836--when the world is rural, religious, and disconnected. It ends in 1936, when democracy, communism and fascism are using radio and film to fight for the hearts and minds of millions of people.
Nation-states like Germany and Italy (as well as some that never existed like Scandanavia) can be formed as much by shrewd political maneuvering as by military might. Some countries like Russia, Brazil and China are very difficult to play simply because of their own internal problems, and a new player might spend much of the game fighting reactionaries and revolutionaries that retard economic and scientific growth. Other countries like France, Japan and the USA feel almost too easy, and you wonder why the USA didn't do even better than it did in real life. It also allows you to ponder vastly different (yet ostensibly possible) histories like:
-A democratic Russia
-China as a great power by 1920 with the world's largest economy
-A communist United States
-Austria forming Greater Germany
-Panjab uniting India in the late 1800s under Sikhism
-The Ottomans surviving as a federated multicutural state
...et cetera. I even revamped Liberia's infrastructure and education early on and went on to conquer half of Africa by 1910.
The biggest problem with Victoria 2 is that with so many variables that interact with one another, the game still isn't completely fine tuned. This small amount of error becomes noticeable when you have 90% of your population joining in an Anarcho-Liberal (i.e. Libertarian) uprising. The mods available on Paradox's forums fix a lot of these issues as well as revamping and adding gameplay. If you like simulators like SimCity, strategy games like Civilization, or any developments between 1836 and 1936, buy this game.

CK2 has the advantage of a great intrigue system and EU4 has lovely graphics and GUI, but this Victoria 2 game has depth! It keeps you thinking on your feet all the way through to the late game and so far I have not had any time when I havent had a lot to do.

I usually like this sort of game (Having recently played Dear Esther, Vanishing of Ethan Carter and Everybodys Gone To The Rapture), and do not get me wrong, this is in no way, shape or form, a 'bad' game. Let me explain TL:DR.
When you first play, you realise how beautiful it is, how good the voice acting and sound effects are, and feel really in tune with the atmosphere. For this, I absolutely do applaud the developers. The main reason for playing a game like this, in my eyes, is the story. The story is very intriguing and it got me wanting more until an hour or so in when, despite telling myself otherwise, i'd realised what the ending may be.
SPOILERS AHEAD
My prediction was that the events taking place on the island are all in your mind - that stanley is actually in prison and it would come around to this eventually. I then realised that he was not in prison, that he was just remembering past events and that in fact he was there on the island, just trying to get to the top of a mountain.
This in my opinion is a very anti-climactical ending that could have really been developed upon much further than just turn a valve and that is the end. Nothing new really came of the last 30/40 minutes of the 3 hr experience (less if you don't take in the jaw dropping visuals). I felt a connection to the lady up until I realised that we just get there, turn valve, thats it. It felt premature.
I really wish there was a neutral rating on here rather than just yes/no, because although I dislike what eventually became of the story, I love the rest of the game. I can recommend this for the price, but IMO the developers could have done much more with it.

What a weird experience. TLDR; this isn't a game, and can't be recommended AS a game. It's bizarre enough that the niche experience might be good for some though. More on that below.
So like, in 2003-4 my little brother and sister got into Ragnarok Online after I graduated HS and they were still in middle school. I made an account to stay in touch with them so I'm familiar with the original a fair bit.
This "game" is set up to auto-play through a version of that old game. Basically it's a game where every player has the ability (and it's essentially required) to be a bot at any time. That's the base functionality.
Which in a way . . . is good. As RO was always an especially grind heavy Korean MMO. Since it used pixel graphics and always had a limited assortment of items and weapons, character customization was basically nil unless you spent days and days grinding out cards and mats to get anything that might make your character unique. Bots were everywhere and this version of that game basically levels the playing field in a way so EVERYONE is a bot.
And since the memory usage and bandwidth required is from an MMO that was simple even by 2003 standards, this is very easy to keep on in the background while you do other things all day. I did for the better part of a day to see if I could get to the 2nd job change (and after logging out, I'm almost there, but I doubt I'll return).
Obviously as a FTP game there's a bunch of ads for "VIP status" and money backed currency. You don't have to pay anything though if you just leave this on in the background and slowly grind up though.
But the question is: what's the appeal?
Mostly, I think it's to capture some nostalgia for people who remember RO "back in the day" but also remember that RO was a horrific grindfest and don't want to invest the time into it (because you can STILL download and play that game if you want to).
And if you're exactly that type of person, this might be the game for you. It also might work as a sort of demo for people who want to see what RO is like before taking the dive into one of the other versions of the game that you can still play, I suppose.
But for anyone else, especially if you want to you know . . . PLAY A GAME - it's going to be a hard pass.
Check it out maybe if you want to see why people liked the game in 2003 (it's got a charm with the brightly colored sprites and the BGM and all), but you're going to miss out the most important part of an MMO here, which is the potental for a social experience.
For in a game where everyone's a bot, everyone's shy. Might be good if you frequent /r9k/ I guess?

Let me explain why I bought this game : I was hoping to do multiplayer matches with friends for Civilization V. As it turns out, CivV grows slow the longer you play, and online connection with friends fails over and over again. That's why I started looking for an alternative.
With Endless Legend I've had none of those problems so far. Excellent for multiplayer, never lost any connection, very neat UI, and no slowdown symtoms thus far (and I've put 18+ hours into it already). So far so good.
Gameplay itself : the game does play much like CivV (that was a good thing for me, as I was simply looking for something better). It's refreshing to have diverse factions though, some play very differently from others. Supports different kinds of endings, so not just military ones, and I find the trading & diplomacy a lot more natural. Plays a bit faster too, for example, you can send units through tiles twice as fast. The tutorial sadly enough does not cover everything there is to know (so check out city planning online!) but everything is there. Combat is improved compared to CivV : there's either auto-battle (instant fights) or small Age-of-Wonders like sessions. The wonderful thing about it is that these fights occur on the world map itself : if you can reach through the fog of war you can actually see your neighboor doing these little battles, but all battles are executed asynchronously so there's no rapid switching from one to another (which occurs in civV if you enable animated fights during multiplayer). Combat animations are good enough, nothing too fancy, nothing too short.
Soundtrack is ok, you get the mp3 files with the game, which is very nice. The graphics are very nice (although I did read somewhere they are out-dated, they are not, in 'fantastic' settings they are very beautiful). Which brings me to the conclusion this game is great, I find it better than CivV or CivBE (which did not improve CivV that much alas) so definately recommended!

Its a beautiful game with some unique ideas. It looks gorgeous, has nice music, a great interface which has a lot of improvements over Endless Space (although lacking in keyboard shortcuts), interesting stories and factions. But the gameplay just does not work out.
Normal" AI is insanely easy. I just killed everyone on my first game. "Hard" AI is incredible cheaty. You can only scratch your head at how many cities they construct while you churn out your first settler. Enemy AI seems very weak and just wins with extra resources. No apparent AI strategy is visible.
The battle system is atrocious. You can place your units, set them to offensive, defensive or stationary and give them targets. As soon as you press the turn button they do whatever they want. In fact you can just autoresolve its the same. The same company made Endless Space where you could not control your units as well. But they put in a paper-scissor-rock-like system and made sure, that fleet composition and ship design is important. Here, you just need the expensive equipment, there is really no choice. I suggest Archers on stationary. The rules for reinforcements are completely unclear. I think it is based on movement range but the game will not show you any info about it. Why could they not adapt the system from Endless Space? This is beyond me. The battle system is the greates weakness right after the bad AI.
Diplomacy is quite basic and costs too much "Influence" (something you can "gather" like science or dust points). You need quite a lot of influence to unlock Empire plans. Those a really powerful boosts and a must against the "hard" AI. Exchanging a couple of techs is just prohibitively expensive in influence as to render this option useless.
The market for heroes, mercs and resources is a nice idea but again very very expensive. You won't use it much if at all. This is an excellent grand strategy game, with an ideal balance between complexity and accessibility. Of all the Paradox grand strategy games, Victoria II makes me feel most like a real, historical leader, with more methods of expansion that just military conquest, as other titles such as EU III and EU IV can feel like. The expansions are also great, with Heart of Darkness' Great War mechanic really making wars between Great Powers feel meaty and fulfilling. The game can sometimes be a little ridiculous, (such as Russia demanding Scotland as part of a peace deal with the United Kingdom, and African colonial empires often looking like random, intertwined shapes than chosive colonial territories) but the expansions again fix most of these issues with nations taking huge infamy hits for taking regions they have no claim on, and also requiring a valid reason for delaring war in the first place.
On the whole, this game feels very rewarding. Your decisons feel as though they have real concequences, and no two playthroughs are the same. The learning curve is not too steep (compared to say Hearts of Iron III), meaning a few trial games will allow you to know most of the games mechanics. In conclusion, an excellent game, still being supported by the developers, that I always come back to, despite numerous other Paradox strategy games being released since its initial relsease.

I’m ever the cynic when it comes to early access titles, often to the point of barring me from purchasing one. The setting/genre niche The Curious Expedition filled made me initially change my tune, but alas, perhaps I should have been more discerning. My excitement for the setting clouded my judgment.
As of writing this review, I’ve logged 7-8 hours, and while I enjoy the game, I’ve run across a few bugs and headaches here and there. For about a third or quarter of my games, when the game doesn’t lag, it freezes, and when it doesn’t freeze, it crashes, and occasionally combat will bug where the enemy party or your own will do no damage. New party members can’t be analyzed, forcing the player to remember two dozen die faces and traits or hope for the best with their new compatriots, and certain mechanics, such as a party member fleeing (which often results in the theft of an item), forfeit necessary questing items, rendering maps unwinnable. Combat demands better explanation, I was forced to browse the community hub for a guide I'd call plastic at best. That being said, these, to me, are minor issues, and if the developer is perceptive enough, certain to be remedied in the final launch.
The above are not enough to net the negative review, however. Rather than the alpha state quirks, it seems woefully implemented game features are to blame. The game has no concept of difficulty scaling, with some initial starter expeditions wiping a party while other 4th or 5th expeditions being a 20 day affair (to give you an idea of the pace, a ‘race type mission’ wants you to complete the expedition in 80 days, psshaw). The character line-up is as lacking as its difficulty in more ways than one, insofar as some characters’ equipment and party members are so lacking as to render them nearly unplayable, while others seem carbon-copies with only a utility or two of difference. Additionally, the character line up, while not entirely mechanically-inhibiting, is, dare I say it, curious? The likes of Nikola Tesla and Ada Lovelace populate the roster of an exploration title that hints at the Vernian, so I’m uncertain if this was a developer’s fetishizing some of their personal idols or a vapid attempt to gain so-called ‘geek cred’.
The game needs work, and while it remains a good time kill (each game can probably be completed in under an hour), I wouldn’t have paid what I did, despite the sale, had I watched a let’s play first. I’ll be certain to be more careful in the future. Caveat Emptor.

+ Fairly bugfree, despite this being an Alpha game at the moment of this review!
+ Active devs on forums as well as Twitter.
+ Unlockable characters after you achieve some special prerequisites!
+ Loot. And Gold. Did I mention massive Gold Statues?
+ Choice between turning them in for additional fame upon return towards Civilization or additional cash for future expeditions.

+ Upon ending on successful expedition you can choose one perk to aid in future expeditions.
= Some items in your inventory doesn't stack. This is especially true for loot. So that means you have to make a very weighted decision to drop down items that can be very useful towards you instead of loot. I especially found this a huge constraint during my travels.
= Cannot level up beyond 4. Maybe that is due balancing issues?
= Gameplay is alright for an Alpha, I do expect more features as well as nice things in the future for this game.
= The game could be more clear with dice combinations, although I managed to figure out this myself by experimenting... This could be very frustrating for new players towards the game.
= Would like a bit more information about the location I choose to send an expedition from.
= Maybe a HUD or extended info panel/stash once you return from an expedition would be nice so you can adequately prepare for the next one or drop some things behind.
= Improving standings with the local tribes seems near impossible. I've never in all my playthroughs gotten near 20/20 yet. Highest was however 15/20 which I managed to unlock the last and in my opinion, hardest character with.
- Cannot upgrade pack animals, pets or leader. Unsure if intended feature or not.
- Seems there is no way to stop bleeding once it happens without a medi kit. Reminds me of TF2 when I bleed to death =(
- When you trigger certain events, it will become impossible to get near the Golden Pyramid, thereby with no ending button the only thing you can do is restart the game and start a new expedition.
- There is no way to pass time whilst stuck on one spot. (Dev commented on forum that a fix is pending)
- No additional info from the main expeditioneer's sidekicks when you start a new expedition. You don't know what their character info is therefore you have to jot it down somewhere if you want to make a weighted decision on which party to pick before you forget the info again for a new expedition.
If you value one €1 for every hour played, then this game is definitely worth it during their Alpha Access with plenty of potential and growth space. However there will be probably a long time to go before this game is finished, but this game is quite interesting and there was no moment when I got bored with the events in game and my desire to snatch every single golden statue!

This game has some roguelike randomness, pixel art, and can be completed in about an hour if you know what you are doing.  You play as an explorer from a romanticised nineteenth century, choosing from about a dozen historical names with different special abilities.
You start with a random kit of companions and or donkeys to make a party and set off on an expedition to gain fame and fortune.  You must complete six expeditions and beat an arbitrary fame score of AI rivals who you don't interact with.  Each expedition creates a random map which gets larger and more dangerous with each successful expedition.  There are villages and shrines to discover, wild beasts to dodge or slay and wonders both natural and supernatural.  Of course, all abstracted into some tidy icons and statuses.  Combat is a simple and fun turn based system of dice rolling and re-rolling to create combos a la Yahtzee.  The goal of each expedition is to find and enter the gold pyramid somewhere on the map, but you'll want to be carrying some loot before you enter as the pyramid magically ends the expedition and sends you back to the Explorer's club in England.  You'll be able to pick a new perk for your explorer from a randomised three choices.  Then you can cash in each piece of loot for either Fame points or Funds to finance the next expedition.
You'll receive a random quest and be able to shop from a meagre shop whose stores are you guessed it, randomised.  You'll have to adapt to what the game gives you if you want to steer this this baby through to the final expedition.  But, the game is short.  Mistakes are usually costly and often fatal but you aren't deeply invested because it's not an epic game.  Good fun, but currently lacking depth in this Alpha stage.  Still good enuff that I feel I'm going to get my money's worth.

Game Details:
The Fidelio Incident is a single-player, first-person thriller set off the coast of Iceland. Inspired by Beethoven's only opera Fidelio. After a violent plane crash, Stanley must search a desolate frozen island in search of his wife Leonore while covering up any traces of their identity.

As some of you might already know, walking simulators are a genre I particularly enjoy. I noticed The Fidelio Incident recently and was stoked when the developers decided to slide a copy across the ethereal surface of my existential wooden desk. There were a lot of things in the game's description that seemed like they would elevate the walking simulator experience to a new level. A dramatic story isn't necessarily a revelation, but a walking simulator where you hope to be rescued at the same time that you are trying to avoid anybody knowing who you are is definitely a new twist in this genre, and having the professional voice acting talent to support the project is also a nice feature. Plus, walking simulators in an Arctic, or at least very cold setting aren't exactly frequent either. So, how was The Fidelio Incident?
The story in The Fidelio Incident takes place in a remote island of Iceland. You play as Stanley, who along with your wife Leonore, are flying to Iceland to start a new life together. A key aspect to the story is that they are actually fleeing from somewhere and hope to not only start a new life, but also with new identities. However, mid flight, a bird strikes their plane's window and they end up crashing on a remote island. The plane is torn asunder during the descent and Stanley and Leonore end up separated as their parts of the plane crash in separate areas. After you come to, you must try to find your wife while also surviving freezing temperatures in an unknown location.
The suspense of both the situation and the story as it unfolds makes for a compelling journey. As Stanley tries to find his way to where Leonore is, and as the elements become more extreme and daunting, Stanley starts to withdraw a bit into his mind and so the journey isn't just to save Leonore, but indeed is also a journey of self discovery and awareness. He will also discover pages of Leonore's diary that were strewn about, and which reveal a lot about both Stanley and Leonore, who they were, how their relationship developed, and how things led to where they are now.
I thought the story to be quite engaging and interesting with, at least in the video game world, and unusual twist to the approach the story takes. 8.5 out of 10
The gameplay in The Fidelio Incident, as with most walking simulators, is pretty straight-forward overall. You will largely walk around investigating parts of the plane's wreckage while trying to find your way to your wife. Aside from walking, there are a couple climbing sequences, a couple swimming sequences, and your basic interaction with objects, primarily Leonore's diary pages, but also other object needed to complete puzzles or simply needed to survive under certain circumstance.
Since you landed on a frozen island without the proper protection from the elements, you will need to figure out a way to survive sub freezing conditions. Standing near the fiery pieces of plane wreckage is one way, but you will also encounter steam vents that will warm you up as well. These also function as save points in the game, so if you die from exposure, you will end up at the last fire or steam vent you were standing at.
The puzzles in The Fidelio Incident are typically sequence puzzles, meaning you will have to do a sequence of events in a specific order to progress. Although not particular daunting, a couple of the puzzles will require a little bit of exploration to solve and simply require finding a specific object. The rest are as mentioned: perform actions in a specific sequence to unlock the your ability to progress. Although this can seem like it would get boring, the actual level design makes it never boring and in fact the puzzles allow you to partake a bit in the world around you making it a bit more engaging.
Speaking of level design, instead of random edges of the map, where the edges aren't obvious, there are tons of stinging jellyfish on the shores that prevent you from just wandering off and make for some entertaining dialogue as well. That aside, although you can wander about a bit while outside, overall, this is a fairly linear experience that transitions seamlessly from one area to the next.
The gameplay in The Fidelio Incident was spot on. The controls were tight, performance never dipped under 60 FPS for me, and I encountered zero technical issues at all. I played with a gamepad without issue, and also set F12 to the reset button for easy screenshot taking.
9 out of 10
The graphics in The Fidelio Incident were flat out stunning where they weren't designed to be gloomy, and where they were, the level of detail was spectacular regardless. This is a game that WILL capture your imagination, and the setting also lends itself to a bit of sight-seeing. You will almost definitely take screenshots galore while playing this.
The actual outdoors, in the arctic levels of the game, were simply spectacular. I especially was impressed with the little details, such as the mysterious blue ice known to appear in glaciers and such, the glow from the jellyfish, and the way in which ice, water, and snow interact with each other. The plane wreckage was very cool looking as well. Once you get indoors, the setting changes to exactly how you would think of an underground bunker or facility looking. Dark, grimy, and generally unpleasant as walking amidst tons of concrete slab could be.
Later, as you start to get into the world alteration sequences centered around your self discovery, the set pieces become even more amazing. From swarms of insects to an Irish pub, you will always feel like you are exactly where Stanley is in the game. The appearance really helps serve to transpose yourself into the experience yourself.
Finally, the way the diary sheets are presented also look great. They look like something you would find in a person's diary and are very nicely detailed as well.
9.5 out of 10
As much as the other aspects of The Fidelio Incident shined, they simply could not outdo the amazing voice acting work by Glenn Keogh and Bess Harrison, who truly became their respective characters. Whether Leonore on the phone talking to Stanley while waiting for him to find her (she is trapped, immobile, freezing to death, and yet also at risk of burning to death btw....pretty grim) or reading Leonore's diary sheets, Bess conveyed real emotion and a clear understanding for the depth of the character she was portraying. Likewise, Glenn as Stanley was so completely believable and effective that you really couldn't help but hang on every word of dialogue and hope for a happy conclusion to this even. Basically, they humanized these characters in a way you rarely see in a game and really allowed for the player to connect with them on an emotional level as well.
The soundtrack was also phenomenal. Michael Krikorian did an amazing job of capturing the soul of the game in every moment, with a perfect soundtrack for the experience.
Beyond that, the other audio was also on point, but the voice acting and music put their stamp on The Fidelio Incident and elevated the game to a level that most contemporaries will find difficulty reaching.
10 out of 10

This year has been great for standout titles in the genre, and The Fidelio Incident not only manages to nestle itself firmly into that greatness, but in fact comes out as one of the best of all time.

The game is not as sinister or paranormal as
, but otherwise comparable in many ways, letting you explore massively inhospitable environments through impressively realistic wintry visuals and sounds.
Here, the experience feels less solitary as the main character occasionally receives one-way communications from his unreachable wife, but its story is also mostly delivered through collected bits of evenly scattered diaries and sporadic soliloquy.
Fidelio is also entirely about hypothermia, as the more than revealing signs inform you early on and every step of the way. You have to stay warm, so you'll walk quickly from fire to fire and other occasional heat sources, where the landscape and plot both progressively turn into a surreal guilt trip.
The few items you need are always conveniently located within an easily accessible short range, so there isn't really any reason to divert much from the clear path. Pipes and switches will bring a series of elementary puzzles to solve in order to stay warm or avoid stingy bugs. This is a thoroughly well executed interactive narrative that nevertheless brings absolutely nothing new to the genre's gameplay formula.
It helps to optionally have a basic understanding of Ireland's 1980's political landscape, as the game's underlining setting. Offers around 2-3 hours of icy exploration, a fitting length for a story without filler that doesn't need to be any longer.

If you're a fan of the walking sim genre, I highly recommend this one. One of the best in my opinion, even despite it being fairly short. A great experience that hits all the marks, all for a reasonable, low price.

- Art direction is really nice (the note backgrounds are particularly beautiful).
- Atmosphere really pulls you in. You feel that sense of panic and worry.
- Great VA (I honestly can't remember the last time I heard an Irish accent in a game, so that was cool).
- Unique story that has great pacing throughout. Plot points are revealed as and when they need to be.
- Minor "puzzles" that don't slow the game at all, just add a nice bit of interaction.
- Stellar soundtrack. Really one of my favorites I've heard from any game. Up there with the Firewatch OST, especially in terms of it complimenting the mood and atmosphere of the game itself.
It's weird looking back after playing through it now. It was only a 2 hour experience, but it really managed to immerse me into the world without me even realising it. Few games are able to do that, and even fewer able to do it in such a short amount of time. I found myself actually caring about the characters and their story. Watching the plot unfold over the 2 hours was a nice experience and one I feel was worth the asking price. Overall, well worth the purchase and I hope to see more from A3 Games in the future.

The Fidelio Incident wears its inspirations on it sleeve and wears them proud. Boasting likenesses to Dear Esther and Firewatch, Fidelio sets itself up to fill some big shoes. In the end, it mostly succeeds if not falling a bit short of its lofty goals.
The Fidelio Incident is the newest entry in the burgeoning genre of Walking Simulators. There seem to be more and more coming out, especially by small studios, so it can be a bit hard to stand out from the crowd. One thing that definitely helps Fidelio is that it’s drop dead gorgeous. Made in Unreal 4 (which I’m a sucker for) Fidelio exhibits a high visual fidelity that really makes it stand out from the crowd. I found myself positioning myself for just the right screenshot multiple times.
The story presents itself fairly straightforward, but of course not everything is as it seems. While the inspirations to Dear Esther and Firewatch do ring true on most accounts, Fidelio does continue the quickly tiring trope of document/diary pages to collect. There is nothing inherently wrong with presenting a narrative this way, it would be nice to see progression past this and new vehicles to deliver the story. This is not entirely Fidelio’s fault, but if you’re looking for something you haven’t seen in the genre before, this is not it. Along these lines, the diary pages that you pick up are accompanied by voice over work in addition to text. The VO work is one of the stronger aspects of the game but unfortunately you have to wait with the page open to hear it all. If you close out and continue playing, the VO stops. Now I know that perhaps it makes more sense narratively to only have VO play while the note is open I found myself getting slightly irritated when I had to sit there and wait for it to be over. This is all personal taste, but I would have preferred a Bioshock-like presentation where I could listen to the VO while still exploring since the actors do a great job.
In addition to the voice work, I found the soundtrack to be quite excellent. Inspired Beethoven’s opera, there are obvious classical tones and on overall sober ambience that reminded me some of Radiohead and Nine Inch Nails, two of my favorite groups. The dark soundscape really adds to the oppressive atmosphere and you ascend the mountain.
The gameplay itself is pretty standard fair with the addition of the freezing mechanic – finding heat sources to prevent yourself from succumbing to hypothermia. I found this to be very reminiscent of the 2009 title Cryostasis. Fidelio thankfully implements this to where it’s not a hindrance or annoyance but adds a bit of tension as you explore.
Taking around two hours to finish I found The Fidelio Incident perfectly enjoyable, if not a bit predictable. It doesn’t necessarily bring anything new to the table but what it does, it does well. While it doesn’t ascend to the heights of What Remains of Edith Finch or Gone Home, The Fidelio Incident is still a fine addition to the genre and one that should certainly be played if you’re a fan of its predecessors.

Seeing all these negative reviews written by people who apprently didn't know what they were getting into, here is my attempt at a more objective review.
To start off, lets answer the most important question - is Ragnarok Journey for you?
1. Do you enjoy MMORPGs?
2. Do you hate wasting time by grinding mobs 8 hours a day or finishing similar boring quests like "kill 20 rats"?
3. Do you enjoy everything else that MMORPGs usually offer like dungeon raids, skill and stats planing, guild wars etc?
If yes, then Ragnarok Journey might be for you. If no, then move on to a different game.
The game comes with automation system that lets you focus on other things as you character kills mobs or completes active quests. This means most of your time playing Ragnarok Journey will be spent on planning your character's statistics, skills and equipment. You will have to optimize your available time to maximize possible opportunities. And of course, you will have to party up to challenge powerful World Bosses and dungeons.
Just as in original Ragnarok, so does here your character's build matter. Will you send you character to hunt for a rare card? Or will you team up to take down World Bosses?  Each choice can yield unique benefits, but you can only do so much in a day - pick one over the other and you might find yourself lacking in certain areas, be that PvE or PvP.
This means Ragnarok Journey is closer to strategy games - how well you adapt and what opportunities you seize will determine how well you do in this game. Basically play smart and will you thrive.
Where both games differ is the casual aspect of Ragnarok Journey. The game is significantly smaller than RO and everything is streamlined - you can fast travel from anywhere to anywhere, access crafting, dungeons, World Bosses, and global market, etc. with a signal click.
Speaking of the market, just as about every other casual game out there, so does Ragnarok Journey comes with premium currency. The good news is however, that is possible to get it without paying real money. The market allows you to sell stuff for gems opening another layer of strategy to the game.
To sum up, Ragnarok Journey is the streamlined version of Ragnarok Online. The grind is automated so you can focus on everything else, making the whole game feel more like a strategy than anything else.
Recommended to people that can't invest too much time into playing.

Ragnarok Journey is a generic browser game that basically plays itself with very little required action from the player. Most of the content is locked behind a needlessly long grind or a paywall, and vast majority of eye-catching features require you to sink real money into it. It seems fun and vibrant at first, but it quickly becomes tedious and mind-numblingly boring.
The game has very little depth to it in any way, despite the seemingly large number of different menus and options available. There is very little variety with any activity, and any newly-introduced feature usually gives you one free try of it, and then requires you to pay real money or grind for a very long time. The in-game auction house/market is entirely in the paid currency of Diamonds, as are most of the features that would give this game any redeeming qualities, and I personally found very few redeeming qualities to this title. Many systems within the game are completely unbalanced. I just cannot find many positive aspects to this game, and cannot in good faith recommend it.
There are so many other casual/idle free-to-play titles with considerably more content and much more gamplay value. Save your time and skip this one. If you want to try it (since it's free), then by all means, but I highly advise saving your money for things that are more deserving.

Hey look, otome fans: it’s Amnesia in English on Steam! Those who have been desperately hoping for an English localization of Amnesia (and may even be veterans of the Not-So-Civil Dialoveable-Amnesiac War) will probably get this regardless of reviews. I may just be writing this for my own amusement, but hey, why not? Maybe there's someone on the fence.
...Or in a cage.
Like many of the Japanese games making their way to Steam now, Amnesia: Memories is a port. Unlike most Japanese Steam games’ ports, however, this is Amnesia’s English debut, alongside a simultaneous Vita release. The text is all translated into English with the Japanese voice acting intact.  Fortunately, Amnesia makes a good transition from handheld to PC. Things that may seem like annoyances at first—such as being forced to left-click to progress the text—are easily overcome thanks to the ability to remap keys and controller support.
The game itself looks great in 1080p as well, with easily legible text, though close-ups of characters and backgrounds suffer from minor aliasing. While the character sprites and CGs are beautiful, the backgrounds seem like stock photographs and simple line drawings with your 12-year-old cousin’s favorite “Unicorn Diarrhea” Instagram filter applied. However, my BFF (who normally has good taste) calls them “stylized” and “appropriate” so it could just be my severe unicorn allergy speaking.
Plus there are mini-games, so you get to beat your boyfriend(s) in air hockey and cackle maniacally at the first hint of their sad, sad anime boyfriend tears. Or if they beat you,
There’s also Inexplicably Violent Rock-Paper-Scissors if you prefer. (I would’ve enjoyed seeing additional mini-games, such as Flowerpot-Dodging or Knee-the-Yandere-in-the-Groin, but I understand that this is a visual novel first and foremost.)
Amnesia is a traditional, story-focused visual novel without any stat-raising; endings are determined entirely by the series of choices you make and the parameters those choices affect. Exploring alternate realities and unraveling the mystery of your past(s) is an intriguing approach that takes precedence over the romance in most routes, and completing all five routes is necessary to reveal the full picture. I recommend seeking out the bad endings even if you’re normally averse to your boyfriends hating, stabbing, or dismembering you. Then again, I probably took too much fiendish delight in finding new ways to get what’s-her-face killed.
Each route begins with already well-established relationships, though our heroine has to relearn (and hopefully remember) the exact nature of those relationships over one month. Having amnesia’s rough—even when you regain consciousness and immediately find out you have a hot boyfriend. Ikki’s and Kent’s routes felt like the best introduction to Amnesia’s setting and made the parameters feel especially relevant to the story. There’s no common route at all, so the scenes and events in each guy’s route are unique.
The love interests themselves were diverse and well-written, though how appealing the routes and characters themselves are likely comes down to personal preference. I
one route, enjoyed two very much, plodded through another because I totally already knew whodunit, and then one I fdgsffdgguyuggyhuyghgyuyuyuygugujyguyuyyujuyyhgnugngnnggyhdfrtgdhftrsgfd
Sorry, I must have gotten dizzy after recovering a repressed memory.
If you’re expecting light, breezy romance, this isn’t your best bet, but the feeling that you’re one misstep away from a horrible fate is far stronger in some routes than others. Your adorable giant bug sidekick Orion serves as the game’s main source of comic relief and also doubles as the heroine’s personality, because she apparently lost hers with her memories. I’m not a fan of “blank slate” visual novel protagonists (probably because of my aforementioned rotten personality), and it was off-putting that the MC doesn’t speak, with Orion reacting, thinking, and narrating in her stead. Luckily, Orion is the best. THE BEST.
Even taking my (exaggerated) criticisms into account, I enjoyed Amnesia very much and am thrilled that it got such a fantastic English localization from Idea Factory International. It took me 47 hours total to complete all the routes with their many endings and they were hours very well spent. I hope this is the first of many Otomate releases on Steam and I’d love for Amnesia to help prove that there’s a market for Japanese otome games here.
One last thing—I forgot to make fun of the guys’ outfits, which made them look like they all rolled out of a Hot Topic going-out-of-business sale circa 1995 and woke up in a giant barrel full of rejected Final Fantasy characters’ belts decades later. There, my duty is now fulfilled; it is time for me to leave you. One day (probably today), you will forget ever reading this review…

The only game in recent memory where you have to get senpais to notice you in order to get your memory back.
Amnesia: Memories is a port of a 2011 Playstation Portable visual novel, where the player takes control of a young woman who loses her memories and is forced to retrace her steps (and romance one of five vaguely-androgynous men) in order to get them back. Classified as an "otome" (girl) game, Amnesia is equal parts fascinating and hilarious.
The game starts with your character entering a spirit world, where a being named Orion tells you that he has somehow become lodged in your consciousness, and can't leave until you recover your memories. At that point, you gain the choice of one of four different paths (with one unlockable later), and you have to make decisions over the course of the story in terms how much information you gather and who you choose to romance/hang out with.
The most interesting part of Amnesia is that there's a lot of replay value. There are five distinct storylines, each with a wildly different set of situations and stories that occur. I was part of the beta testing team for this, and was initially struck by how separate each path is. The first storyline I played through (Shin's) had the characters attempting to solve a mystery, while the second was so off-the-wall that it might qualify as a parody of visual novels.
I know the opening line might seem a bit flippant, but that is the crux of the game. You can only trigger your memories by spending as much time as possible with your respective suitor(s), who have a bad habit of not revealing anything important to you until later on in the storyline.
From a plot standpoint, Amnesia is absolutely bonkers. In a good way, of course. The novelty of being a girl trying to collect information about her missing memories is balanced by a set of off-the-wall characters. Depending on which storyline you play, you'll run into a pair of childhood friends competing for your affections (one of whom locks you in a dog cage for half of his storyline), another teen who has somehow been gifted with the ability to be attractive to every woman he sees (thus explaining why he has a harem of girls who harass the player character) and a "Mr. Nice Guy" tutor.
The art style really sets this apart from other visual novels. Characters are expressive, blinking, moving their mouths and speaking in full Japanese. The backgrounds are generally detailed and varied, and there are nice interstitial moments that break up each scene.
There are also a pair of minigames that can be accessed through the main menu, but I didn't spend enough time to have much of an opinion. They're very simple (rock-paper-scissors), but are a neat diversion for anyone who wants to go for high scores.
In the end, Amnesia: Memories is one of the most interesting games I've played this year, and certainly among the best visual novels I've experienced in quite some time. It's well worth a look and offers a lot of value for the money.
Definitely worth a look.

[Disclaimer: In no way, shape, or form was I compensated for the composition or publication of this review. This by my own volition. A review copy of the game was kindly provided by Ideal Factory International.]
Developed by Idea Factory under its Otome game brand Otomate, Amnesia: Memories is among one of the companies pioneering titles that finally gets a western release. And while Otoge or Otome games are meant to cater specifically toward a female audience, a male audience can also partake of them. The story puts players into the shoes of an unnamed female protagonist that has lost her memories after a strange incident. With help of mysterious young boy named Orion, the two work together to help make sense of the heroine’s past life, while trying not raise suspicion from friends and a boyfriend she never knew existed.
With Amnesia: Memories actually being my first Otome game and looking that is from the perspective of a newcomer, I do think that first timers like myself or those completely new to visual novels in general will be able to navigate it easily. For one, before you even start to meet the eligible bachelors, you will be able to choose who you want to interact with from the start by choosing a world – each holding a symbolic card corresponding to that person. You have the aloof Shin of the “Heart” world, playboy Ikki of the “Spade” world, his logical best friend Kent of “Club” world, and the big brother figure Toma of “Diamnond” world. There is a fifth guy and the route that puts all this into perspective, but needs to be unlocked by completing the others. Not only do each the routes play out differently depending on the world, but also changes how certain people will treat you. For instance, Waka, the manager at the place the herione works at is very nice in the “Heart” route, but his personality does shift greatly in others – going from docile to abrasive. This does apply to the other characters you meet as well to varying degrees, and serves as a nice change of pace to see how each route differs despite the feature being nothing new to visual novels.
Even though the main love interest and their personalities play into the typical paradigm most shoujo anime seems to reach for, I did honestly enjoy exploring the backstories of the guys I did go after. My favorite character would have to be the titular Shin, learning the reason behind his distant attitude that stems from a past event with his father. The writing is very simple in many ways and not that great when it comes to giving the story some interesting twist and turns, but still okay in its own right. The individual routes are fine on their own, but overall does fall short of being particularly great. That’s all I can offer on the subject without spoiling it. By the same admission, the characters themselves also aren’t as detailed as they could be, but still found them interesting. Especially in the case of Toma. Yup, very… fascinating personality shift for that guy.
Getting back to gameplay, the same orthodox process of reading text and making decisions at certain points become the norm like most visual novels, with one exception. Keeping with the theme of trying to piece together your life without letting your boyfriend be any wiser, the choices you make do have implications on 3 values: “Affection”, “Trust”, and “Suspicion”. The goal of is to ideally get a “Good” or “Normal” ending by keeping your Affection and Trust values high and Suspicion low. Again, depending on the choices, these values will fluctuate, so it is important to be mindful of what choices you make and keep tabs on your parameter menu frequently. Often or not, it is pretty easy to know how to response, yet can abuse the system by saving your game and seeing how a certain choice goes. In the event that you do have your Suspicion high, the game will continue, but will be able to get a bad ending more easily from making a wrong choice or simply getting the normal ending for that route if you happen to make it through successfully. Since replay value is a big part of games of this nature, it doesn’t hurt and obvious that making multiple saves will offer some assistance.
When you tire of trying to get through the story or even completed the game, besides viewing the CG library for illustrations, listening to tracks, or keeping track of the endings you received, the game does have two mini-games you can play at anytime: Rock-paper-scissors and Air hockey. There not the most interesting thing in the world, but it’s there if you need it as a brief diversion. I would like to detail this section, but since I never actually won a game, I will leave the outcome of what happens (if anything) to be a surprise.
On the aesthetic side of things, the artwork and animation for the game is very impressive. In a lot ways, the color scheme and style used kind of reminds me of that found in Steins;Gate, despite not having the same exact appearance or as drab. Animations are crisp and lively, and actually show off a lot of technical muscle such as changing the characters sprite angles (seeing them from the side or back) that really makes them come alive without having to go toward excess. My favorite animation would have to be of Ikki holding his signature sunglasses and smoothly slipping them on in the same scene almost like it was in one movement. The musical score is very genteel and well-done, piano pieces being the most prominent holding up the sentimental mood – that admittedly, tends get lost at various times. By the time you get through half of the routes it will become droning, yet mildly tolerable.
With visual novels gaining more acceptance and familiarity in the West, I do believe titles like Amnesia: Memories will be great boon for its biggest supporters. It definitely isn’t the cream of crop, especially when it comes to the overall writing, but still fairly remarkable in other areas like presentation and making that presentation work for it during the course of the game. While it won’t be for a couple of months until see Idea Factory’s other Otome offerings, Amnesia is a pretty pleasant harbinger of what to expect and do think this one will keep most fans satisfied for the time being.

The Curious Expedition brings roguelike games to a new setting. You choose to be one out of a number of  19th century "celebrities" leading exploration parties to the unknown corners of the world filled with ancient temples, dangerous creatures and native tribes. All the action is turn-based and your ultimate goal is to finish all 6 expeditions alive and gather the most fame. Travel happens on a hexagonal map slowly revealing the surroundings while you try to gather artifacts and level up your trek members. Items you find or buy (either before the expedition with money or during it by bartering) help you and are needed to keep your parties' sanity.
The different characters make you approach the expeditions differently, with enough fire power you might try to attack every creature to get some loot, with a different group you might want to avoid fights and rather paint pictures of the locations and interact with the locals.
While this is an early access game it already is a lot of fun and has tons of replay value (I already played it a lot before the steam release).

I want to get something out of the way first. I HAVE PLAYED THIS GAME MUCH LONGER THAN THE STEAM PLAYTIME.
Like another reviewer said, this is like a cross between FTL and Jules Verne. Lead a famous explorer (and his/her hired help) through strange new lands to meet (and potentially anger) the natives, battle wild animals and find enough treasure to gain the fame you need to become the greatest explorer the world has ever known.
The map is procedurally so you're going to have a new adventure every time, and the pixel artwork is really charming. In order to survive all six expeditions, you need to make sure you have all the right tools (rope, torches, food, etc) for the job, but you also need room in your inventory to fit all the fabulous treasure you've discovered. It's a fine balancing act between survival and fame/fortune.
Like all rogue-likes, lots of very bad things can happen to you. Shrines that hold the treasures could contain some nasty booby traps, like ever-widening chasms, or the great ball of nothingness, so do you risk getting that sold gold llama statue and thus potentially incur the wrath of the natives/deity/whatever? You won't know what will happen until you take it! Take care of your sanity meter and don't let it get to zero, or bad stuff will definitely happen to you. Crewmembers may fight, turn cannibal or wander off into the dark, never to be seen again.
I've been playing this game since Alpha 10 and even in Alpha status this game is 100% playable and nothing feels 'missing.' The devs have put out numerous additions and bugs every few weeks and this is one of the best rogue-likes I've ever played. It's a very unique spin on the genre, taking place in the 19th century as opposed to generic dungeons and space travels. You're going to feel like you're Indy as you play, except there's no Nazis. Have you got what it takes to become the greatest explorer?

Love this game! The replayability is high because no two expeditions are ever the same. I highly recommend you try this game out if you love the history behind the characters. The music, the sounds, and the art are so well done. The developers are awesome and constantly making improvements, which makes this game well worth the money. Also lady bosses all up in this game!

GIVEAWAY and REVIEW
Curious expedition is crazy Mix of FTL and Julius Verne books like “80 days around the world”. In this game you take part as one of historical explorers add discover forgotten secrets of lost lands. This is an outstanding game. If you like this genre, you'll enjoy this game. Very well presented, interesting setting (not a generic fantasy world), and factions that are genuinely different to one another in terms of how you play as them (not just different lore or superficial differences).
It plays a bit differently to other games of this type. One really nice touch is how you can recruit heroes, and equip both them and the units in your army with different types and levels of equipment, depending on what resources you have. Heroes and units level up, gaining experience from being a governor/garrison, defeating opposing forces etc. Heroes get to pick skills at level up.
Each faction only gets a few unit types, which makes assimilating some of the many minor factions  important for plugging the holes in your own forces - you get to recruit their unit once you've assimilated them. Unit designs can be edited to create new unit types - for example, you might want to have some ranged units using a 2-handed bow, but in other situations you want a one-handed crossbow unit with shields. You also get random quests, often from searching ruins, or as part of your attempts to pacify nearby minor factions (if you don't decide to just raze their villages to convince them to join you). Each faction also has specific, linked quests, which add a nice touch to how you become invested in your faction.
Also the AI seems actually capable of providing a challenge on higher difficulty levels. Minor factions can hurt you if you leave cities or armies undermanned, especially in the early stages - in my second game, I moved a settler with 2 decent infantry units as bodyguard, and had them caught and wiped out by a roaming army, d'oh. I've also had my capital and main army wiped out  by a swarming horde from another, very aggresive faction.
It's not perfect, but the flaws I've noticed are all very minor - nothing frustrating. Seems to be very stable for me; I've had one CTD so far, in 26 hours playtime. I'd like to see more hero options for start-up, and maybe a couple more factions (if they can make them different enough from the already diverse selection). The developers seem to be on the ball with listening to the community (I've only skimmed through forums, so that's just an initial impression). I'd like to see more modding over time as well, to give the game even more legs.
Overall, if you like Civ-style games, I can't see how this game will disappoint. I've logged hundreds of hours in Civ, and I'm finding this game similar enough to be comfortable with, but with plenty of differences and little twists to the format to find it a really pleasant, fun, and engrossing game.

As much as I hate to say it: If you expect a game with frequent updates to its core gameplay or more optimization than there is in the near future, your hope will die faster than you can think.
The Dev who works on the project has written a post about that problem and I think he says it a bit better than I can:
,
Now to my points as to why this game is worth the money anyways.
I have played this game only for a few hours when I started to love this game. But I also kind of hated it. And here is why: When it goes to its core features it basically is minecraft from a different perspective. You have your eight settlers that found themself a place to live. And every settler can be assigned to do different jobs. Over time you will gather ressources that are mainly food, hide and more, loot, wood and stone. Over time you will build up your own little settlement to be a small fortress, castle, village or whatever it may be. It is all up to you. And that is where this game shines as bright as two of the games I dearly love. Minecraft and Terraria.
You can be as creative as you want to be and build what you want to build. Of course you have to rely on ingame features and objects, but that is how the other two games are just as well. Other than that, you can build up your castle with a dungeon below. You can build a village with an escapetunnel within your selfmade Well. Whatever it may be, your settlement can look how you want it to look like.
But this game would be too easy if it was just that. I mean, where does the loot come from? You can get attacked by the wildlife, spiders, skelletons, goblins and probably a few other things as well. And if you dont have your settlers geared and leveled that can mean that your settlement is about to get its *quack* pushed in.
This game, a mix out of AoE and Minecraft, is still worth the money for what you get ingame. It offers alot already and since it aint over in just 2 minutes it can go on for quite a long time. It also offers a lot of replayability. Have you built your castle and you are satisfied? How about a speedrun in which you do everything you just did, but much faster? How about a run where non of your setters die? The possibilities may be limited but they surely wont end after just 5 sessions.
If you really want this game, buy it. I think its worth the money. If you are unsure, then wait until it comes up in a sale.

I had no interest in the game to begin with, and didn't even know the game existed until i checked the wishlist for a longtime friend of mine. Bought the game for the friend, then bought it for myself so he would at least have someone to play with. Good sentiment, horrible financial decision.
Pros:
- Like every other review out there, it's pretty.....as far as turn-based graphics standards go. The unit models are rather interesting as well.
- Good lore, if you're into bothering with reading up any backstory in games.
Cons:
- Abysmally slow-going. Units and actions take their sweet time doing their assigned jobs
- Overcrowded UI. Amplitude seemed convinced that giving you as much detail crammed onto one screen as possible before having to use another was a good idea. It wasn't. Over 3/4th of your playtime will be spent looking for the right menu or icon.
- Steep learning curve. This is not a Strategy game that you can just pick up and play right then and there, especially if you expect it to be as easy to understand as Civ
- Minor issue with crashing and errors. Wasn't as bad as others claim, though the problems were mostly when trying to set up a multiplayer match.
- Tutorial is woefully inept at explaining the various concepts and inner-workings of the game in a clearer manner. I actually found myself becoming more disinterested with the game the longer the tutorial went.
All in all, it looked interesting, but i'd sooner eat my own liver than willingly recommend this game to just anyone. If you have patience, sure give it a try. Personally, the gameplay is too slow and there's far too much information and too little explanation. This game is something id play randomly and only when utterly bored already.
If you're interested, i sincerely suggest you wait until its on a discount sale.

If you like dinosaurs and hunting/adventure games. Then this is for you.

First off, let me clarify: this is NOT a survival game. As long as you don't walk off a cliff or get torn limb from limb by a dinosaur, you'll live forever.
So then what is it? Well I have seen two ways of playing this game.  You can play it as an exploration game, full of emergent narratives and fantastic vistas waiting to be seen by those willing to tread the most dangerous paths. Or, you can play it as a hunting game, full of big things to kill with your big gun and get money and a fancy dead trophy.  I am aware that the game is being designed with the latter in mind. But emergence is one of the truly wondrous elements of the video game as a narrative medium.  New and unanticipated things happen when your audience is also your performer and your performance.
You have probably guessed by now which play style I embrace.  I have ZERO interest in game hunting, dinosaur or otherwise.  I am, however, interested in walking among dinosaurs, as I have dreamed of fondly ever since that childhood  trans-Atlantic flight I spent reading a National Geographic book about them cover to cover, and I apparently was so adorably excited about the whole thing that the pilot gave me his Lufthansa captain's pin and patted me on the head.  More so than any other game I've played, this game allows me to do that.
Luckily you have me to tell you a little bit about what to expect. The very limpid premise to justify your simultaneous existence with dinosaurs is that you are a scout selected to spearhead a colonization effort on this alien "Eden."  Isn't it a little chilling that we are presumably doing this by enacting the mass slaughter of the native fauna? There's some commentary there, intended or otherwise.
Like I said at the beginning, this is not a survival game.  There are no hunger or thirst mechanics.  There's a fairly typical stamina bar depleted by sprinting or melee but quickly recharged.  There is food out there in the wilds to be scavenged, but despite its realistic appearance it's arcade food: eat it to restore health.  Scavenging rather than crafting is your main way of acquiring weapons and equipment.  There are busted colony pods, half-finished bunkers, and the well-supplied bodies of many a less fortunate colonist scattered throughout the landscape.  Early on this will be your only source of gear that *might* protect you when you accidentally cross upwind of that T-Rex you've been tracking.  But more likely you will join the broken bodies of the brave stacked up for carrion (to paraphrase Homer).
Playing as an explorer is indeed punctuated by intense action.  I will shoot a dinosaur to save myself. I will flail my gun around in terror as I hear but can't see the pack of utahraptors close in on me. I will use my machete to hack aside the velociraptor lunging my jugular.  When you kill and catalog a dinosaur you get money and experience based on its rarity, its difficulty to kill, and the integrity of the corpse (prohint: you won't get much for blasting a campysaur with you shotty).  Every time you perish you are brought to a shop screen where you can purchase gear.  The availability of different items is a function of both your xp level and your accumulated capital.  Slowly but surely you get to a point where you can survive most run-ins with smaller dinosaurs on your own.  If you plan to take on a T-Rex or if you want to blast a herd of peaceful triceratops for no reason, hop on a multiplayer server and team up.  Your character is persistent across servers, but taking down a Tyrannosaur (possibly to protect those innocent triceratops) requires well coordinated tactical engagement. Still most of you will die. It's glorious.
I continue to thoroughly enjoy this game.  The crass masculinity infecting the multiplayer chat can be irritating, but it's not game-ruining, and frankly when is it not asserting itself with knuckles dragged and chests bumped in whatever multiplayer chat you find.  The graphics are beautiful, gameplay is challenging and the shooting mechanics are fairly realistic.  The dino AI gets better with every update.  They really will sniff you out if your upwind and enact coordinated assaults complete with feints to draw your attention while they flank.  It's wondrous.
If you are now or ever were a dinosaur nerd, this game is essential.  Highly recommended.

Someone mentioned they didn't like it because they didn't know Irish politics.  I thought what little they touched on had to be public knowledge.  I think most people know about car bombings and violence, even if you don't know why.  Irish Republicans / Catholics want all of Ireland to be free of British rule and the Irish loyalists / Protestants want Northern Ireland to stay part of the UK.  That's really all you need to know for this.  You really didn't even need to know that much, just that there's conflict though the violence has calmed considerable from 30 years ago.  The story is more about remembrance, regret, and resolution.  Both sides had a reason to fight and sometimes good honest civilians turned on their brothers over this issue.  It's really a great subject to reflect on now that the violence is over and scars remain.
As for game play, it was simple.  A couple times I "solved a puzzle" without knowing I did because I likely did things out of order.  Only happened a couple times--got the plane door before I knew why I needed it and I opened the heavy door to get the key card without knowing I needed it or why I was opening the door.  Those are minor things though.  A lot of things happened that I didn't really get until after.
Opening the last value to shoo the bugs from the tree, but it didn't work, the tree sprayed out water the wrong color and a symbol of Stanley's past fell on the ground...  It wasn't until after it hit me why.  In that, I think the developers accomplished what they wanted--to get people talking about all the symbolism in the game.

As a fan of heavily convoluted Lore in games, the Elder Scrolls Series goes deep enough to warrant putting your tinfoil hat on and speculating/uncovering the deep Story of Nirn.
The gameplay is a simplified Morrowind but still has some outstanding writing. The elder scrolls Lore has some fantastic concepts and trying to piece it all together through in game literature is the true mastercraft.
Where the gameplay lacks in its simplified systems (some prefer the simple gameplay) it's still as fun as Morrowind although a little shallow. This theme of simplification/refining seems to follow true to Skyrim. Sure Skyrim is a great game, but it doesn't feel like a succesor to Oblivion. (which I may say Oblivion is the true succesor to Morrowind on such grounds as Mancar Cameron being so prolific for the foreshadowing in Morrowind as aposed to Skyrim basically spelling it out for the player, actual gameplay aside.)
Ideally play Morrowind first (as a scholar) to get a grasp of the state of afairs of the Third Era, Followed by oblivion (as a Philosopher), understanding what is rhetoric and what the Oblivion/Mundus/Aetherius realms are, and finally Skyrim (as a Sage) With a plethora of knowlege that will make the plot weigh much more heavily for the Forth Era.
Overall, buy them all, play them all. If you want an insane (optional) Lore on top of some quality D&D Roleplaying, Oblivion Hits as close to home as any. Morrowind being a game that truly feels like a Home resting place for a fantasy Universe.

Q: is it play by itself?
A: yes it is auto playing, which includes: pathing (auto walk to destination), attack, skill, and potions (can also auto buy potions). we can also choose between auto or manual gameplay.
Q: how is the level?
A: there are 2 types of level, base and job.
Base lv 1 to 50 can be achieved under 2 hours gameplay.
Job lv 1-50 takes 2 day, 1-45 (day 1), 46-50 (day 2), takes 2 days because waiting for "Job Training Ground" reset, located inside "Individual Dungeon" (top right of your screen).
Q: is it true, we have to grind mindlessly 24/7?
A: no, first of all, i'm not a hardcore player. i always do main quests, daily quests, and "Individual Dungeon" which already shows up from Base lv 36.
whenever i run out of quests, i stopped playing and wait for daily quest reset every midnight (UTC -08:00) Pacific Time. you can also type /time in chat for information about server time.
Q: is it a pay 2 win game?
A: of course it is, what do you expect? i mean, well if you're looking for fancy gears. mounts, etc. well yeah, you have to spend some money.
however, i am a F2P player myself, and i think the gameplay and adventure is more important.
Q: what's your opinion?
A: it is a good casual game for spending time, and the size is only around 200 MB.

Experience an in-depth political simulation where every action you take will have various consequences all over the world. The population will react to your decisions based on their political awareness, social class, as well as their willingness to accept or revolt against their government.
This is a wonderfully deep game, and its sandbox nature is much more open than Hearts of Iron III was and so it's much more enjoyable at the beginning.
Saying that it stands head-and-shoulders above all of the scant competition for grand-strategy kingship almost goes without saying...

Vic2 was my second exposure to historical strategy sim games.  EUIII was my first try and it does not trip my trigger.  I usually play in north america.  CSA succeeds in splitting off.  When I first got the game, Great Britain would eventually take territory from USA, but updates seem to have changed that behavior.  The aspects of Vicky that I like are:
1.  rebel uprisings.  They can make you hustle.  But you can beat them by watching the level of unrest and if necessary mobilizing troops.
2. national focus.  What you choose will affect how the game plays out.  Choose to promote immigration and populaton will grow.  Choose a political focus, and you may have fewer rebellions.
3. north america-  this is my home and the states are familiar to me, as is the history.  So I like playing in north america.
4. anti-imperialism - the game is set up for imperialists, since the era was imperialistic.  But you don't have to play it that way.  The ai is imperialistic, so every one of your neighbors will try to eat your lunch, but you can play them  off against each other via alliances.  And of course you need good border defenses.
5.  modding- Big mods are hard but mini-mods are easy.  Just (using the mod folder) change the lua file.  For example, I don't like all the time spent on research, so I changed all research (for all countries) to one day in the lua file. I also cranked up the militancy for captured territories (ha!)  And I changed the end date of the game.

Was looking for a dinosaur-themed game to tide me over until the hype of Jurassic World would get some more dinosaur games going. I liked the premise of this game and finally convinced myself to download it, hoping it would fulfill the dinosaur-hunting void in my life. I played this game for about 6 hours before finally rage-quitting. I found the game very frustrating. At times I would be insta-chomped by a tyrannosaurus or pack of utahraptors without any chance of using my weapons In other lives I would be running away like crazy or staring down at a weak little velociraptor thinking about how nice it would be if I had ammunition and could therefore kill the dinosaur before it killed me. The ability to go back to your death-location and recover your weapons was nice, except that the game's respawn point was so far away from where you needed to go. The five minute walk to recover your weapons felt like an hour.
All I wanted in this game was to kill dinosaurs. I couldn't care less about the "survival" aspect of the game. I finally did kill some utah raptors and velociraptors, but the amount of effort I was putting was not worth the reward. I thought about recruiting my boyfriend to play with me, but with the size of the map and the spawn points and death-respawn and all, there is no way we could have physically gotten close enough to each other to play cooperatively.
If you want a dinosaur-themed game, invest $1 into Orion:Prelude and satisfy your dinosaur-killing urges. And now the trailers for ARK:Survival have come out and I am now in counting down the days until I get to kill dinosaurs AND ride them.
