As someone with over 1000 hours logged on Civilization 5, I think it's fair to say i'm a rather large fan of this genre of game. That being said, once I got this game I haven't been back to Civ yet. There's a lot of aspects about this game that I think Endless Legend does better than Civ 5, for example the tech tree. Instead of a linear tech tree, you have tech eras, and after researching so much from one era you have access to the next era's worth of techs. This means if you're not a militaristic empire, you don't have to waste turns researching needless military techs for example. Another aspect that's nice is the use of armies. Instead of having one unit to a tile, you have as many units on that tile that can fit in your army (starts at 4 + Hero, can get up to 8 + Hero.) And if a fight breaks out near two armies? The second one gets to come in as reinforcements due to their proximity, which is a nice touch as it would be ridiciulous if a nearby army was just ignored.
All in all there's a lot to this game that's great, and very little that isn't. If you're a fan of 4x style games, odds are you'll love this game. The gameplay, the art style and the mechanics all come together perfectly to make an extremely enjoyable game. 10/10 would recommend.

Endless Legend is an interesting 4X. It has alot of elements from their previous title Endless Space (Anomalies, Unit Customization, Approval Mechanic) just to name a few. However, the combat of the game is different and thats subjective really (I like it, but I haven't been in too many bigger battles) its alot less rock paper scissor's now though. Overall though, I like playing the game, the AI is more or less smart to what you expect, but they're pretty aggressive. I never had an AI help me or give me anything just mock me and go to war. But, it itches my (I want to play a 4X real quick) itch. Biggest thing to me that it has going for is how they incorporate the main quest into the game. Its basically a questline you have the option of following in the game or not.
Overall, Endless Legend is a  good 4X that doesn't really take forever to complete, and is generally fun to play against AI. With no real campaign mode though I can see people not really caring for the game, but I like it!
Pros
+Not too lengthy
+Familiar Interface (From Civ and Endless Space)
+Individualizing Units and Heroes are possible
+Alot harder to achieve a Military Victory than other 4X's (in my opinion atleast)

Cons
-Not really for beginners into the genre
-Graphics look pretty, but bog the system down(an example is scrolling from the "world view" to ground level)
-Not a 4X for low end systems(opinion)
-Combat takes a bit getting used to, isn't strait foward(probally just me being an idiot though)
-No actual events to really drive players to do certain things differently(like in endless space)

I just finished this game in one sitting, and the experience is still fresh enough that I can say that I fully understand their inspirations from games such as Dear Esther and Firewatch, and that they are well founded.
As with most walking simulators, the gameplay is pretty minimal, some simplistic puzzle solving and fortunately not too much backtracking. A two hour experience to be sure, but I feel the purchase was well justified for the experience, the story, and the visuals that were presented.
Pros:
=Great atmosphere - The locale and paths were beautiful and fairly well designed, even if it suffered a bit too much linearity, including the occasional invisible wall.
=Beautiful graphical fidelity, photogenic views. (Dear Esther level of shutterbug)
=Great voice acting, nice conviction and some very well conveyed emotion.
=Light gameplay elements that both encourage and discourage appropriately.
=Fantastic parallel story, seasoned with Irish revolutionary history and a loosening sense of what's real.
=Absolutely fantastic musical score, I hope they release an OST!
Cons:
=Story doesn't -totally- wrap up at the end, you're still left wondering why certain things were the way they were, given the explanations at hand.
=Freezing gameplay element encourages rushing through, when the point of a walking simulator is to walk.
Issues:
=Encountered the very occasional clip (carried door clips through the ground, saw through the ground for a brief moment while getting up)
=Had an obvious invisible wall near some pipes in the cave, even though the space was big enough.
=Got stuck in the "among the dead" area because of a lack of a way to jump out of what became my inch-deep death. (between some bones)
TL;DR -- A walking sim that for all intents and purposes, conveys it's message and it's story serenely and almost totally satisfactorily. If you liked Dear Esther or Firewatch, this is right up there with the great interactive narratives.

Only If is a weird game.
As Anthony, you arrive at a party, hosted by your friend Sam(antha). Upon getting to the house, you become unconscious and wake up in a bedroom. No, you didn't have a great night, and you begin bantering with Vinnie, a man you'll only ever hear. As if by magic, he speaks to you via radio, and your journey begins.
Only If is a very short game, and you'll likely finish it in under two hours, but for the price (free!) it's well worth the ride. Your vision of reality will become distorted, things will happen, and your initial confusion with Vinnie eventually becomes swearing at each other. It has some interesting elements, and the puzzles are fun to complete. While not overly difficult, there is barely anything (aside from the first one) to help you, and you really are all on your own.
Creability has done a great job with Only If. The story is great (if a little bit confusing), the graphics are exceptional, and the puzzles intriguing. Even if the game required a purchase, it'd be well worth your money. But since it's free, it is most definitely worth your money.
You shan't be disappointed.

The first thing I noticed in this game is that the graphics are mediocre.  I first spawned in a marshy area and the waves were glitching showing weird visual artifacts.  And things just got worse from there.
At first there's a little tension and excitement walking around wondering when you're going to see your first dinosaur.  My first was a Utah Raptor.  It came up behind me and took a bite.  There were no loud noises, no camera movement, nothing but red around the edge of the screen and a pathetic yelp from my character.  It completely lacked any sense of excitement or realism.
I turned around to see the Utah Raptor that was attacking me.  I moved to the side and watched it as it made a very stiff, robotic move to attack where I had just been.  The animation was weird with completely unnatural movement.
Next I had an odd encounter with a triceratops.  I tried to shoot it with my bow.  It turned and charged at me.  After glitching through some trees I think I ended up sitting inside the triceratops.  After that it trampled me and I died.  Lame.
This game lacks any sense of excitement, seriousness, and gravity.  Many of the times I died I just didn't care because I had a crap weapon and no real equipment to speak of.  The game has no opportunities to invest time and ingenuity to improve your situation.  I think it needs something like crafting or shelter building at least.
The only way to get weapons is to buy them to put on the pod you launch in, find them in drop chests, or from other players (dead or alive).  This is miserable if you're just starting out and/or playing on your own.  You just have to start walking around hoping you run into something before you get noticed by a dinosaur.  I died several times before ever getting a bow.  After  several hours I still have never been able to use anything other than a machete and bow.  I've never even seen any other weapon in game.
This game lacks in variety as well.  After a few hours I've seen all the dinosaurs, seen the one plant that sort of hurts you, and have no interest in playing to see new weapons and equipment.  What's the use of a giant landscape if it's basically the same everywhere?
I paid US $30 for this game.  I feel like I've been completely ripped off.

INFRA is a story/puzzle game in which you play a structural engineer working for a consulting group that's recently taken over control of a city's infrastructure after its government was sacked for corruption.
The gameplay and premise are both equally engaging.  There's no violence here and the main gameplay involves taking pictures of infrastructure damage (and documents related to that damage) and solving simple mechanical/structural puzzles in order to proceed.  You have a flashlight and camera, both of which you'll have to seek out new batteries to keep powered, but the game never really hides these things in devious places, so you shouldn't have to worry too much about it.
Three things to note:
First, the voice acting is...well, it's not great.  I'll just say that it's probably as good as it can be with the budget the development team were working with and leave it at that.
Secondly, the game does NOT have full controller support as is advertised on the store page.  The controller mapping is not configurable, the game does not ever tell you what the controls for a controller are (all menus and gameplay only show keyboard shortcuts) and the gameplay using a controller is fairly janky.
Thirdly, the game does not have a permanent crosshair option.  By default, the game has no crosshair at all, and the crosshair option that is available only makes it appear when your viewpoint moves close to hotspot.  For a game about finding things in the environment, solving puzzles that sometimes consist of small dials and switches and generally being able to keep your bearings, not having a permanent crosshair as an option is frustrating.

Ok first of all, long review, so if you want details and are deciding whether to buy, please read, if not, skip to the bottom for pros/cons.
Before i start also, i do not claim to be amazing at the game (league 3), nor know everything there is on this genre. I have just played the game for a decent amount of time to give a fair review.
SOME INFO ON THE GAME
This is a 2D style MOBA , which is incredibly simple to learn, and very hard to master.
All games are 3V3 with some play variations, online against other people, offline against bots, and i believe if you buy starstorm expansion which i did, you get custom games with friends (have not tried this) You can also play online or offline with friends.
3 or 4 turrets defend a base core drill, first team to destroy the drill, wins. simple concept, whats difficuilt is the character and map match ups. Each character has 2 main core abilities to use, (right click and middle mouse click) a jump (W or space) and an auto attack (left click). A piece of advice for new players, try every character, and see which one plays into your style of play, whether it be a harrasser, assassin, support or a tank, there are a lot to choose from.
20 to be exact with starstorm, 16 without. Soon to be 21 with the next patch and a new character, yes they add new characters.
This game brings so much originality to a very popular genre in gaming atm, the MOBA.
Character designs, style, drawings, effects and sound are very crisp in this game assuming you have reasonable hardware. (even quite low end machines can run it)
So all in all, a very polished looking game.
Balancing in the characters is generally very good give or take a few things. (i will say there is at least 1 awesomenaut that is not really viable as of yet) Updates continually change this so its a hard point to stay clear on.
Games are more often that not short, ranging from about 10 to 25 minutes. However, i have had games last 50 minutes, and also games last 7 minutes, depending on the skill level of the teams playing.
The learning curve on this game is a lot smaller than other games in the genre such as DOTA 2 or LoL. However thats not to say there are not tactics. Lots of crazy 3 on 3 team fights and abilities happening, creeps, collecting money (in this game solar) and buying upgrades to increase your power. Some characters are strong starters, some mid game and some nigh on unbeatable late game.
A lot of good points there to buy the game, so much fun, and the starstorm expansion is certainly worth the extra.
So, bad points.
Unfortunatly if you are a new player (especially to MOBA), the community will hate you, yes, hate you.
You will die and feed the enemy team solar making them stronger, and lose miserably most likely for a while.
This will certainly make your team angry, and cause them to sometimes rage at you, quit the game (leaving you with a bot) or just plain unpleasentries.
My advice -
Practice with bots in this game is essential for begginners, as online games will slaughter you.
You can learn character plays, tactics, and not die all the time against predictable bots.
This brings me on to my next point, the rage quits and people leaving for other reasons.
Playing an online TEAM game requires a lot of coordiation and unfortunatly, bots just do not cut it.
So when you are playing online, and either someone on your team or the enemies quits and leaves, that team is at a significant dissadvantage. It can often take a long time (or not at all) for another player to join the game replacing the bot. I also played a game the other day with 5 bots, for an online game, and no players joined... (perhaps a glitch?)
Match making is also slightly tricky, as i feel it is too wide. If you are in league 3 (as i am) you are matched against everyone 2 leagues away. Which in my case includes league 1. These are not fun games when this happens against a premade team of friends. So solo play drops a notch there as you get to much higher levels.
Make friends, and play together!!
EDIT> Another point to note, the game frequently loses connection to host, and throws right back to main menu. Does not matter if ive been playing for 20 seconds, or 20 minutes, will still do it and drop your rating. Bare this in mind. The devs however have a router connection guide online which i have tried, and also a way of sending a lot of different game logs to them if that does not work. It seems rather long winded however, and should not be something in a paid for online game, considering console versions do not have this issue.
SUMMARY
Pros
- Fantastic artwork, character design, level design and crisp effects and sounds
- Polished game
- Lots of varied, balanced characters to play as
- Short games, between 10 and 25 minutes most often
- Much smaller learning curve than most MOBA's
- Runs on bassically a lunch box, low spec requirements
Cons
- Community is not always great, especially at higher leagues
- Rage quits are frustrating, and well as ruining matches
- Could matchmake to higher league, premade teams, making for a very hard, unfair and frustrating game.
- Occasional connection problems mid game, losing all progress
So all in all i recommend this game, just learn the characters, make friends, and have fun!

While Abe's Oddysee certainly deserves a lot of credit, it is not without fault. The excellent level design, short-but-sweet story, and grand scope of it was hampered predominantly by its checkpoint system. Each portion of a stage would throw three or four challenges at you between each checkpoint, not counting any hidden mudokons. As a result, there were many cases when several parts of a particular stage were easy but fairly slow and time consuming, while later parts were significantly more difficult and led to multiple deaths. Having to replay the earlier, easier parts quickly became very tedious very fast. In some games, this sort of thing doesn't hurt the game, but here, where the gameplay is built around trial and error, and often demands a great deal of patience, it killed the pacing at several points towards the beginning and middle of the game.
I'm mentioning this because Abe's Exoddus included a quicksave feature which circumvented this problem, and for that reason alone could be considered a better game. That's not the only feather in Abe's Exoddus' cap though. The inclusion of such a feature as quicksave can fundamentally change a game like this, and Oddworld Inhabitants clearly kept this in mind. The level design is more challenging than Abe's Oddysee, but more fair. Secrets, previously pretty cryptic and very easy to overlook without the help of a guide, are now found by some out-of-the-box thinking and creative use of the game's mechanics. The core gameplay and overall design have been tweaked to remove tedium. The mechanics have been greatly expanded upon in order to provide much more variety and complexity. The voice acted cutscenes lend the world much more character, and add a great deal of levity to a game that could very easily become quite depressing.
No matter how you look at it, Abe's Exoddus is the better of the two side scrolling games (as of writing this, New 'n' Tasty is still PS4 exclusive, so I can't comment on it yet). It manages to correct the flaws of it's predecessor while also expanding upon everything that was good. It really is what every sequel should strive to be. More of the good, plenty that's new, none of the bad.

Only If is a very surreal experience. You play as an average joe named Anthony. You were invited to a party. You get totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥d at said party. You wake up in a strange house, with a strange man talking to you through a radio. You wander through corridors, abandoned houses, and surreal dreamscapes. The game is very similar to the Stanley Parable gameplay-wise. Only If was constructed entirely on the Unity engine, and it is hands down the best looking game I've ever seen come out of that engine.
Only If's main downside is the lack of replayability. In the Stanley Parable, you have several interesting and varied endings that you can receive, all of which are based on your decisions made during the gameplay. In Only If, there are two endings, and the ending you get is based on one decision made fairly early into the game. I really wish the developers took a more complicated and versatile approach to the game's endings, because one of the endings is, albeit hilarious, really immature.
Overall, Only If is a very good game, and a very interesting experience for a free to play game. I recommend you give it a try.

In infra, you play as Markku, a Structrual Engineer for a company brought into a crumbling city. The story delves deeper and you're embroiled in a conspiracy. First of all, this game was really fun from a standpoint of being a Urbexer. Some of it is city infrastructure, but a lot is off the beaten path, like a Steel Mill where you begin learning of corruption that brought it down, or a system of Minitrains under the city. The voice acting is nothing to write home about, and honestly Mark talking about batteries all the time was a bit annoying. But the rest of it is downright amazing. It feels a bit like HL2 with the puzzles and the decaying infrastructure of Nowhere, Eastern Europe. INFRA makes the best of Source, with the effects pretty breathtaking. There's a sequence where you climb up to the apex of a Steel Mill and it's beautiful. A lot of the areas are open and that can work as a blessing and a curse, you can get lost in some of them. The story of the game is excellent, and the way you find out is excellent. The enviroments are ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful and the puzzles are fun. The game's a walking simulator, sure, but it's a goddamed ♥♥♥♥ing good walking simulator.

Man this one is hard to review. It really breaks my heart to give it a thumbs down. The whole idea and the levels itself are spectacular. The sense of immersion, the atmosphere and mood....just great. The graphics are dated but except for effects it is still visually appealing.
But the gameplay. I am somewhere in middle of the game I just can not continue. I just list some things in no particular order:
- sluggish movement, feels like wading trough water, be prepared to keep shift pressed all the time
- no way to make notes or review your pictures (i so much want to take pictures of the puzzle hints and codes but you can't review them)
- no clear goals what you are supposed to accomplish with a puzzle, sometimes you need to repair a system, sometimes you shut it down to open a door.
- tedious gameplay, there is only one way out every time and you need to search every nook and cranny for objects
- most puzzles are solved by just clicking around with objects, some are pretty illogical
- some timed puzzles are very hard because you do n ot have time to figure them out, you can't pause, you don't know how much time you have left...it is just a mad dash for a solution...expect lots of quickloading.
- story is conveyed trough notes but there is no way to review them and it is too much information to memorize the story
I think the game devs had a great idea but the gameplay itself does not hold my attention any longer. I was especially annoyed by the character controls and the sluggishness of the whole game, because there is a lot of back and forth. I dont know....with a modern engine and some control and UI improvemts the game could have been so much better.

100% Orange Juice serves up emotionally satisfying spectacle, delivered by a writer-director in full command of his craft and brought to life by a gifted ensemble cast that honors the fact-based story.

My goodness, if you like your history, if you have any interest in the 'what if' alternate history genre, or even if you just like creating a good story, then you really should check out this sandbox 'grand strategy' game.
The graphics aren't anything to write home about, but that's really not what this type of game is all about. Unlike many other strategy games, you aren't some abstract nation, and there is no 'win condition' as such. Rather, it's about controlling a succession of characters in a single family dynasty, making key strategic and tactical decisions as the years roll by to enhance the prestige and piety of each of them, and thereby the dynasty as a whole, as at the end of the game you obtain an overall score based on the sum of the piety and prestige of all the characters you played in that game (plus a fraction of the accumulated piety and prestige  of all the other dynasty members not directly controlled by you but who lived during the lifetime of your game).
At times you will likely need to use military force to improve your position, but there are many other ways to succeed and gain territory, primarily through dynastic politics, e.g. clever marriages, followed by either the quick win - but risky - 'removal' of individuals standing between your family members and a juicy inheritance, and/or the longer term attempt to manipulate your bloodline into a position of prominence into as many seats of power as you can.
As well as potentially being great drama, when either you pull this off, or your machinations backfire horribly and your nefarious assassinations are revealed (or maybe you didn't pay enough attention to just how closely related the bride and groom were in that otherwise brilliant dynastic marriage you arranged, and the key heir gains the inbred trait!), there's a strong element of roleplay here, as you can both make choices for your existing character and strongly influence the character development of your wards (which will often include your heir), through the event chains and decision points that pop up for you regularly through each character's life.
Yes, there is a reasonably steep learning curve if you really want to know the full ins and outs of the game, but for the many hours of enjoyment this game can return for you, it's worth investing a few up front to watch the 'How to Play' videos put up by some good YouTubers of this game (I recommend the 'Newbie Ireland' series). Similarly, there is indeed a lot of DLC for this game, but I haven't found it breaks the game or makes it unplayable for those with just the base game: it just means you can't do some of the things some of the AI characters can, and if you do pick them up (especially in one of the regular Steam sales), many of them open up some really interesting new options (e.g. playing as Muslims, pagans, or rulers with Eastern religions), which keeps the game extremely fresh and replayable.
Take a deep breath, be patient in learning the game, and then get stuck in and see what tales of triumph or tragedy your dynasty will forge in the annals of alternate history!

100% Orange Juice is basically a digital anime board game not far off from something like Mario Party. On its surface it is cute and simple and family-friendly; however, the strategies you and others employ from character and card selection to in-game actions as well as being bit by RNG can cause things to become quite deep and ruthless.
Everything from combat to movement is controlled by six-sided dice with cards and random events modifying stats, rules, and so forth. Your objective is to 'level up' five times by amassing increasing amounts of stars and/or wins then returning to a player's starting home tile. Everything is fairly straightforward and easy to learn, yet the limitless combinations and regular updates (free and DLC) make it a game you can come back to time and time again. With a few exceptions it is well-balanced and the online community is enjoyable to play with.
The campaign provides some amusing story as to why characters from various franchises have come together, but most people will likely find the multiplayer the reason to keep playing; knowing those franchises can add extra amusement but is not necessary. The music and visuals fit very well, the music especially being a highlight for me with the visuals providing comedic relief even when the RNG isn't going your way. While there is a fair bit of DLC at this point, you can play without it and still find a great deal of entertainment, the free content providing regular albeit lesser changes; for the price, though, what you get in the DLCs is well worth it and to me feels more like supporting a developer who appreciates their fans rather than any sort of gouging.
The one caveat I would put in is that if you are easily put off by heavy RNG-based games, then save yourself the stress and the money because you can and will do everything right and still lose to a chicken and have victory snatched away one tile away from home (others fear the dreaded seven-gull, but I know it's the sneaky chicken you should worry about; and Poppo, never trust a Poppo).

The mechanics are an absolute mess. However, they were forgivable up until the Green Vase section. Its first problem is that it attempted first person platforming, which is difficult to pull off by exceptional developers. I died over twenty times, most of the time because the game didn't register my jumps. I also fell off the spiral staircase later in the game six times. If your mechanics suck, at least make them forgiving.
What frustrates me is that this game shows potential and I do think the developer should continue making games. There are several instances of it being unorthodox in a good way. However, there are so many things wrong with this game that I can't recommend it to anyone who wants enjoyment. However, I do recommend you play it as a primer on how not to do surreal storytelling.

The Sequel (of sorts) to the Europa Universalis games, Victoria II lets you mess about from 1836 to 1936. While much shorter than EU's massive timeframe, Victoria certainly has alot of stuff happen including the Industrial Revolution, The American Civil War, The Scramble for Africa, the political struggles for democracy and socialism, and lots of other fun stuff. This time period did have some seriously bloody wars (American Civil War, Taiping Rebellion, World War 1), but this really wasn't an age of mass conflict and the game reflects that. This means that politics and economics are much more important than wars. The French Revolution may have been defeated after a quarter-century of war, but the ideals did not die, and they will infect your nation and lead your people to push for reforms and greater equality. Industrial development in turn leads to the rise of the Socialist movement as worker's rights and social welfare become matters of concern. You can ignore both of these forces if you want, but you do so at your own peril. Revolutionary movements can and will rise up to make the changes you won't do.
So basically this is a big pile of political and economic funtimes with occasional violence. It's also an extremely complex and difficult game to learn, so beware of that. If this all sounds interesting to you, then this is a game you may enjoy quite alot. :3

INFRA is one of the most interesting Source puzzle games that I've played in ages. Never would have thought that it would be possible to take something as mundane as being a structural analyst, and turn it into a compelling adventure.
The atmosphere and story are great, and Stalburg feels like a fleshed-out city. The sheer amount of environmental storytelling is staggering, and you'll gladly explore to know more. The game is definitely one of the prettier Source engine games... Except when it comes to the humans. Those fall straight into uncanny valley. Luckily, you don't see too many of them during most of the game. The voice acting pretty amateurish, but I don't know how much you can expect from an independent developer with a tight budget.
The puzzle designs are nicely varied and competent, but there are a few segments where you'll get stuck for hours because you failed to notice one teeny tiny detail, because you were so distracted by the bigger picture, or by things literally exploding around you. Some puzzles you can solve in two different ways or even ignore completely, and these affect the routes you can take and the ending that you get.
As a major negative, the game has really infuriating platforming segments over insta-death floors. These wouldn't be a problem, if your character didn't jump like he was wearing concrete shoes. You're gonna need to quicksave and quickload a LOT. There is also one segment with a super fragile pallet raft that will make you rage hard. The major mechanic of pulling yourself up ledges is insanely picky on when it wants to actually work, so you'll be jumping in front of boxes quite a bit before making progress. This can get pretty frustrating during timed puzzles. Finally, sometimes it's very unclear what water is safe and what isn't. Knee-deep water that was safe in one spot, might be an instant death two steps to the right.
INFRA has a lot more replay value than most other games of its type. There are so many things to photograph, fix and collect, not to mention alternate routes, alternate endings and a plethora of hidden content. As for the moment of writing this, I have only one playthrough and already 30 hours in the game, with plenty more content still left to see. If you like puzzle games and exploring, and have plenty of patience, I highly recommend it.
+ Great atmosphere
+ Pretty for a Source game
+ Good story
+ Nice puzzles
+ Replay value
+ Lots of hidden content
- Bad platforming segments and one bad raft segment
- Picky ledge grabbing
- Inconsistent drowning spots
- Amateurish voice acting

TL:DR This game is hands down amazing i would recommend it regardless of the price, its well put together, has a great enviroment, brilliant story, nice mechanics and can keep you busy for hours at a time if you let it. If your into urban exploring this is for you.
My first run was spent mostly looking at the beautiful sceanery, sometimes you can spend a good deal of time just taking in the view and you only need look at the screenshots for that. This turns out to be quite handy because the aim of the game is finding all the cracks and problems with diffrent structures, buildings, etc. As the game progressed i started realising what i should be looking for, the cracks in the walls, steam leaking from pipes, the massive holes everywhere and it got me more and more involved in looking at everything. Basic rule of thumb is if its broken photograph it.
The puzzle mechanics are nice and break up the corridor sections, often you'll find that you hit a big puzzle area, wander around a bit to solve it and then move onto the next corridor leading to a smaller easier challange so that you keep moving. I admit that some areas can be fustrating but if your really stuck theres generally always instructions nearby plus only so many combinations of switches and valves so you'll get there in the end.
The enviroment in this game soon becomes your enemy, not only because of the above mentioned puzzles but also you will spend half the time wondering "does this count", "should i photograph this" and cleverly enough the camera has a nice mechanic to let you know. Also do not be afraid to use your battery's as this is probably the sole reason that you will miss things as you try to conserve them, generally without any need if your observant.
I fully recommend playing with the headphones on as the sampaling work is pretty amazing and will drag you into the enviroment. The music is great as well and times in at appropriate moments adding to events and milestones.
The story unravels through documents and tapes you find at each site, if you see a piece of paper, book or something written on the wall, read it, so that you understand how everything has come to be the way it is ( then photograph it :P)
Absolutley fascinating way of revealing the story you feel more like a detective rather then a structual engineer.
Once your done with your first play through, your gonna want to run this again just for the fact that there is so much in it that you'll miss first time round. Keep your eyes open as there are some puzzles that link into later parts of the game. However you have 4 save slots and a quicksave option as well so theres plenty of chances to look back at a puzzle if you think you've missed something.
Big congratulations to the guys that made this game its deffinatly one fo my all time favorites, if you happen to get the chance to adapt this for VR headsets at anytime i think it would really push it to the next level. Just as a nit pick i would have really liked an in game count of the documents and repair sites, maybe as a new game plus bonus or something, but thats just me :P

This was the first title I checked out from DEVGRU-P, but they certainly delivered what I was expecting. Two beautiful girls, a tour of Best Korea, and some of the greatest comedy experiences I've seen in ages. If you like the sort of humour the steam page has, then you will love the style the VN has. Stay! Stay! DPRK is amazing at what it does, and a unique experience that can't be replicated.
My breakdown:
PROS:
+Comedy. Some of the funniest satire I've seen, coupled with a great protagonist and an amazing setting, it really makes it an amazingly fun read.
+Character Arcs. Considering I came into this expecting nothing, the characters were rather believable in their own way, and their development was really well done considering one route takes about 6 hours, and that isn't a lot of time to work with when you are trying to deliver a primarily satirical script.
+Unique. Never even considered a VN like this could have existed. Definitely an experience.
+CGs/Sprites. Great art, but there really isn't enough of it to score it higher.
CONS:
-Limited Replayability. Only 4 possible routes (Eunji, Jeong, Neutral and Bad), which can be done in about 12 hours if you take out all the repeat text.
-No Voice Acting. I've been spoiled by a lot of other VNs, so hearing silence when someone is meant to be speaking is kind of immersion breaking.
-Limited Sprites. One of the few repeating characters doesn't even have a sprite, which kind of kills some of the power the final few scenes have.
-Unneccessary Character. The writers added a largely pointless character, with a sprite, who appears in like, two scenes normally. Not only was she pointless and obtrusive to the story, but the money used on her sprite could have been used for the aforementioned spriteless character.
-Scores-
Story: 5
Characters: 7
Art: 6
Music: 5
Enjoyment: 8
Overall: 6/10

PROS:

A gorgeous, uniquely creative fantasy 4x game from the Endless Space studio.
Endless Legend takes all the good bits of Civ, cuts away the extraneous, archaic crap and infuses it with bold new ideas and ingenuity to make a fresh, frankly superior, game. Your military units are content to occupy the same patch of land because, well, we aren't trogloytes here on Auriga. Every city you settle claims a whole region as your territoty, so no scumbag rivals insert themselves between your cities in an effort to screw with you. Nevertheless, you may want to think about making contact with the natives before sitting yourself in their back yard.
And the factions are unique. Utterly unique. They don't just have a unique unit or two and some different stat bonuses, they all have completely different playstlyes. As an example, the Roving Clans are a mercantile faction who can't declare war on anyone and get to move their cities around on giant beetles, whereas the Necrophages are evil bug dudes who can't engage in peace treaties and actually EAT their enemies to get food for their cities! Unit customisation, minor faction mechanics and the handling of quest objectives are all other brilliant ideas that work harmoniously to create a fun gameplay experience.
There are a few bugs with multiplayer still. My friend and I are often unable to reload saved multiplayer games thanks to some unusual desync issues. Despite this we've been trying to get games of Endless Legend in as often as we can.
If you can get past a little lack of polish (they've done remarkably well with so small a team), Endless Legend is a fantastic strategy game that breathes fresh air into an increasingly stale genre. Keep an eye on Amplitude Studios.

Personal, Biased Review:
Whoa.  This is my personal favorite Elder Scrolls game of all time (haters gonna hate).  It is filled with amazing sidequests (such as the Arena, which has appeared in no other Elder Scrolls main series game to date), and a spectacular main quest featuring Sean Bean as one of the main character's voices.  Also, it's the very first game in the series to feature full voice acting, although only 9 people voice over 400 NPCs.  Overall, it's an amazing game, and one I'll be playing off-and-on till the end of time.
Technical Stuff:
Graphics - 8/10
The graphics are much more "curved" compared to the tough characters and rugged landscapes of Skyrim.  However, when it comes to the player animations things begin to take a turn for the worst.  The jump animations are laughable and the swordswing and walk animations feel "claustrophobic" - or, in a better word, "limited."  All that being said, I have got to dock the game for it's poor character animations.  8/10.
Story - 10/10
The entire game has a vast story which, IMO, is the best story in the entire Elder Scrolls universe.  The lore isn't as rich as Morrowind or even Skyrim, but the main questline is exquisite!  The way it blends action in the real-world of Cyrodiil and the hell-world of Oblivion makes it so neither get old (although the way Obliivion is designed is highly repetitive in design; same hallways, same landscape, etc.), and the actual quests, especially the Daedra artifact quests, are amazing and well thought out (THE K'SHARRA IS REAL!!!!  It gets me every time!).
Music/SFX - 8/10
The soundtrack is incredibly atmospheric, and after playing the game every time you hear one of the songs you'll remember that one time you did something really stupid while listening to it.  The SFX can be slightly laggy at times, however, and the voice acting becomes dreadfully annoying after a while, which I have to dock it for.  Overall, though, the game is great for the ears!
Gameplay - 9/10
The controls feel tight and responsive, although the way the attack buttons are mapped (you can change the mapping, though, so don't let this bother you) I sometimes find myself casting a spell when I'm trying to jump!  But, what's worse is the difficulty of quests in relation to other quests in a certain questline.  The first one may be easy whereas the second may be near-impossible, then back to easy on the third.  Overall, 9/10.
Replayability - 10/10
This category is where ALL the Elder Scrolls games excel (if I'm spelling that right. lol).  With over a thousand quests - be it side-quests, side-questlines, or the main quest - the game is extremely replayable!  You can create several characters or just attempt to complete every quest with your massively-overpowered vampire warlord you've strengthened with fifty strength potions! (yes, that's a thing).  The possibilities are endless, and you're the one in control!
Overall - 9/10
Personal Score - 9.9/10

Harvest: Massive Encounter is one of the first steam games I ever bought and one of the few I really regretted. In Harvest you have to micro manage the hell out of everything. There's really only like 3 towers with attacks. There's 0 story, no modding, no interesting scenarios, and for me, very little replayability once you get things figured out.
It does some interesting things and is pretty different from most other tower defense games, but I can't recommend this game to anyone because it has so little depth. The interesting: 1) power management, you have to supply energy to your mines and your towers or they will not work (Creeper World 3 has something like this and I've seen some warcraft 3 custom maps that do this.). This is one of the few places where Harvest shines. 2) chaining of lasers together to make bigger, more powerful weapons. You can end up with an extremely powerful laser weapon and balancing how big you build them vs how many targets you need to hit is the main way you manage your weapons in the game. 3) the creative mode lets you build your base however you like and spawn monsters or waves whenever you want.
Sadly, that's pretty much it. Managing your lasers and your power grid and building some missile weapons is pretty much all you have to work with. In a genre that has everything from poison towers to buffing towers to armor shredders and many other forms of defenses, this one brings very little interesting and new to experience. Once you've played a few hours and survived a couple of onslaughts, you've seen everything the game has to offer. Oh and if you are a tower defense enthusiast who likes mazing, you can forget that. There are no walls in this game, and once a bad guy touches one of your buildings, it's gone. The game is pretty unforgiving in the sense that if you start to lose bits of your base, you've pretty much lost all of your base.
I would *only* recommend it if you are a TD enthusiast (you might find it interesting then) who doesn't mind having a game in their library that they might only ever sink 10 or 20 hours into, or a game developer (to see the unique things it does and the many ways it fails to live up to other games). But it really only has replayability if you are the kind of player that likes to play the same map over and over again to shoot for more efficient times, because that's essentially what the game has: one map (with 3 different skins) and that's it. I was terribly dissapointed in the game and still am, over half a decade later.Sadly, the developer never added anything to the game to give it replayability.
Games that I would recommend over this one:
Creeper World 3 - Arc Eternal (power grid, towers, much deeper gameplay, has a map editor and thousands of maps made by fans to extend gameplay for months or years. It's part tower defense, part real time strategy game (except you can pause) because you can move the towers. The replayability has made this my favorite game on steam since Space Pirates and Zombies (a space ship shooter, not in this genre).)
Gemcraft - Chasing Shadows ( tower defense game with clever upgrade system, something like a hundred maps to play with, and challenge modifiers to make maps as tough as you like. Probably the best pure tower defense game that exists)
Other tower defense worthy mentions: Fieldrunners 2 (great variety of towers, great presentation, good mazing), Sanctum, Sanctum 2, Defender's Quest, Valley of the Forgotten (Great Story!)

Excellent game. The locations are fun to explore, the puzzles complex and varied. The story is interesting and requires you to  search for it. If you have experience of industrial factories, power generation, or water treatment, you will enjoy the acuracy of how they are presented.

Top notch level design, alot of support and new content from the dev's after its initial release.
I enjoyed and still enjoying every bit of this 'different' game.

Plus +:
Graphics: Great environments and, although the character models aren't the best, I feel like it performs well in this feild
Environments: I have always been impressed by industrial environments, and these are no exception.
Story: Makes sense. Corruption fits nicely together.
Puzzles: Clever, forces you to think but are not unmanageable. I would still say they are quite a bit harder than Portal.
Realism: All machines, buttons, power plants, are accurate to real life (they aren't replicas, but my father has worked as an electrical operator and comments on the accuracy of the puzzles)
______________________________________________________
Delta Δ:
Lack of people: Some places are just weirdly empty, there are always reasons though, but they are exhausted.
Difficulty: A minority of puzzles are difficult, recuiring you to explore every nook or cranny you might miss. Many people get stuck, but there are tutorials online.
Glitches: There is a glitch at the beginning of chapter 10, where there is an invisible wall in the storage hangar (as of november 2017). Was not there before, noticed it on my second run. There have been other glitches like this throughout the game, especially for achievements, that hopefully will be fixed.
Gross stuff: Some things (aside from dead bodies) look unessesairly gross. Letters smeared in poo and a trash bag full of body parts you need to carry into a food waste bin are a bit too much.
NOTES:
Length: MUCH LONGER THAN I EXPECTED, about 23 hours to finish without some achievements. The game consists of 10 chapters in 3 parts:
PART 1: Preparations, Just a regular day at work, Heavy industry of the past, Fresh water
PART 2: Public transport, Working overtime
PART 3: Late for a meeting, To save a city, Redemption
Scariness: You aren't fighting zombies or monsters, but there are some scary horror easter eggs and achievements (???, ERROR: BZZZZZZ, and Underground Justice). Aside from this, there are some dead bodies and bags, adrenalin-high collapsing rooms and gas-fire-hallways. It's a subtle version of scariness.
TL;DR: It's a good game

I got timber and stone a while ago and was skeptical about how the game was. I played a little while and I have to say, I really like it. It's a good slow paced game with some action to spice things up. Yes I know the developers hit a standstill and the game it not being updated due to funds. but this game is still really enjoyable. Heres my pros and cons of what I think about it.
Pros:
A good ammount of blocks to build with
A good economy
Able to run in the background (For when it gets a little too boring for you but you want to progress)
Good visuals (Hey the characters arn't minecraft looking!)
tests your resource management skills.
Free camera! (For when you want to see at NPC eye level and explore the houses you created)
Domestication
Good ammount of roles your citizens can fill.
F*CKING BALLISTAS, WHO DOESNT WANT THEM?
A good ammount of craftable resources to keep your citizens buisy.
Enemies to give the game some combat.
Freedom to create whatever kind of building you want.
Randomly generated maps.
Settlers have their own personality (Example like settlers can have good traits like "Brave" or "fast learner" and bad traits like "Lazy" and "bad vision")
Merchants come and go often so you can get whatever seeds you do not have from them or replenish rare supplies even sell some overstock supplies (Like all that quality dirt you have lying about).
When in the background (Or when currently looking at the screen) the game will pause at an event like someone died or a hostile has been spotted and displayed at the bottom of the screen. (It has saved my town many times)
Cons:
The map is a bit shallow when not in mountians. It's only 5 blocks deep including dirt, would love for it to go a bit deeper      and for ores to get richer the deeper you go.
You can (And whill when new to the game) not properly manage resources and fail to be able to create more tools thus practically ending your playthrough early.
One wolf/Goblin/skele/spider is good dame but get 2 or more can and will kill your town. (I have had it where a pack of 3 wolves killed my guards then♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the town soon after)
Getting settlers is a slow process, little too slow in my mind.
Not many terrians. there are supposed to be more than hills/mountians/grasslands/water as said on the big map.
Tutorial is kind of a joke.
Not too many blocks to build with.
Blacksmith and engineer level progression is really low thanks to lack of things for them to do.
music gets annoying, theres very little of it, plus it's very generic.
What I think the game needs when development picks back up on it (If it does):
More blocks.
Dyes and plain blocks to make the town pretty! (Or for you people, create pixel art)
More terrians.
More diversity on how the people look.
children, to grow your town that way.
more modernised weaponry, just like muskets, crossbows, cannons, that kind of stuff.
Overall I enjoy the game.

I've only played a single game to the end, but that's enough to have been won over. Nicely different to the Civ-style of 4X games, Endless Legend provides a compelling playstyle that sinks its hooks in and keeps you going back for One. More. Turn.

I know this game is well-regarded and I purchased it based on high user and critical reviews, but I'm fairly disappointed. A lot of aspects of this simulation are very good - it's not that it doesn't have redeeming qualities. It is, however, a buggy game that confuses pedantry for detail. In particular, the combat system is very, very poor and onerous. Most of the time you'll simply speed up the animation and put it on auto. For a game often touted as a grown up version of Civilzation V, I expected a lot more.
Maybe it gets better if you spend hundreds of hours playing it. I don't think that it's worth it, for that kind of time investment you could be playing EUIV or CK2, and if you did want to keep your job and family you could just play Civilization V instead. The combat and unit placing make little to no sense - for example, you can be in a relatively open area next to an ocean, and if you approach an opponent from a certain tile, only two of his eight units will appear. Since the combat has a hilariously arbitrary 6 turn limit before both sides shake hands and decide to break for tea, this can be an issue if you need to destroy an army racing somewhere important (usually either trying to take a city or trying to escape). You'll often see this happen with minor factions that have 3 or more units built up. You'll get a lonely giant, rather than 3 buddies, and you'll just kill them over 3 times.
The unit "design" system is well intended but often bogs you down. Part of the problem is that when you want to variations of a unit, you can't amalgamate the design at a later date. You might end up with an army with, say, 8 identical units, but they require you to make three different designs for the same unit. For example, if you slap on an accessory that gives your infantry disease immunity because you're fighting bugs on one side of the map, when you bring those anti-bug units over you can't just have them pick up the next infantry upgrade the rest of your army is using.
The tech/city-sim aspect of the game is neat. All and all this has to be the most wildly overrated game on Steam, in part a reflection of the strong desire for a more combat heavy / fiction version of Civilization (which Beyond Earth failed to provide, and I suppose one can say that Endless Legend is at the very least better than Beyond Earth).
I have to say the combat in this game is a flaming train wreck, however. As simplistic as it is in Civilization, it's more sensical and building an army doesn't feel like an awful chore. If you're really into sims, then you'll probably like Endless Legend. Otherwise, stick to Civilization V, and again, if you really want something meaty and time consuming, the Paradox fare is more appetizing.

Probably my second favourite 4x game of all time (Civ2 being the first).
This game has so much to offer, but I would like to talk about Amplitude studios. Great support and devs that actually take player criticism/suggestions in their forums. Other devs do it too, but they are always growing their games and always looking for new ways to improve their games and keep their fans close. They are helpful in their forums and they hold votes for new features from time to time. The game although released has many features that are still in development.
Endless Legend is a fantasy 4x and at first glance it looks like :Civilization 5" or "Civ: BE". What sets it apart are the different elevations and the aesthetic, as well as their creative anomolies, and other fantastical wonders you may encounter. Like the "Age of Wonders" series or "Disciples" series there are many minor fantasy races on the land as well that you always feel excited to encounter you can assimilate up tp 3 races, each race gives a passive boost depending on how many villages you own. Unique to the series(as far as I know) unless you play in the sandbox mode there is the threat of permawinter due to a climate change disaster, each winter is harsher giving you debuffs until summer. slowly winters get longer and summers grow shorter
The major races are all very well thought out, and have something unique about them.
My favourite race the Vaulters, have the ability to teleport troops across cities and are masters of defense. The Cultists only can own one city, but they have the power to convert minor factions in any land and by endgame can easily out compete bigger empires. The Roving clans can rellocate entire cites, and get a portion of market profits making them one of the better multiplayer classes. The other races the Drakken, the Ardent Mages, the Broken Lords, the Necrophages, Mezari(which is founder only and a reskin of the vaulters) and the Windwalkers.
Combat is a mix of 4x tactical turnbased(like Age of Wonders) but happens on the map (like Civ), you can choose targets and stances, you can customize equipment, use terrain to your advantage, and bring powerful heroes into battle. Each battle lasts 6 turns which you can use to your advantage, there is the option to spectate(very cool when you have multiple battles triggered at once), or autobattle which decides the winner which I assume is based on your chance of victory and I imagine RNG. The combat is not too complex, but it serves it's purpose. Naval combat is to be added in future builds
Diplomacy gives all the functional options, trade, declare war, make peace, swap resoruces and tech.
Quests are availible in game which can give you resources, special tech, unique heroes ,and special items. There are also main faction questlines.
Empire building, Each city starts as one hex, over time you can extend your city borders by creating districts. The game makes you focus not only on capturing and expanding to new regions but to expand your already built cities(or city). Every while you have the option to use diplomacy points to give more buffs to your empire.
Tech and research also has character, at the beginning of the game you start at age 1 more tech ages unlock as more tech in unlocked you can research tech from any unlocked age. So this means even if I haven't finished all of my age 1 tech I can get started on my age 2 economy tech and once  age 3 tech unlocks I can skip over some less beneficial tech to give myself some empire passive tech.
Endless Legend is set in a universe full of character. All of the Endless games are in one universe set in different times. This game has very rich lore, which is posted up in the amplitude forums. The Vaulters are a very intersting race to play because they have a place in all 3 Endless games.  The lore is based around an ancient race called the Endless which created an ultimate substance called dust ( dust=gold) which has almost magical properties and renews itself. The game feels very alive, and has great replayability.

Personal, Biased Review:
Whoa.  This is my personal favorite Elder Scrolls game of all time (haters gonna hate).  It is filled with amazing sidequests (such as the Arena, which has appeared in no other Elder Scrolls main series game to date), and a spectacular main quest featuring Sean Bean as one of the main character's voices.  Also, it's the very first game in the series to feature full voice acting, although only 9 people voice over 400 NPCs.  Overall, it's an amazing game, and one I'll be playing off-and-on till the end of time.
Technical Stuff:
Graphics - 8/10
The graphics are much more "curved" compared to the tough characters and rugged landscapes of Skyrim.  However, when it comes to the player animations things begin to take a turn for the worst.  The jump animations are laughable and the swordswing and walk animations feel "claustrophobic" - or, in a better word, "limited."  All that being said, I have got to dock the game for it's poor character animations.  8/10.
Story - 10/10
The entire game has a vast story which, IMO, is the best story in the entire Elder Scrolls universe.  The lore isn't as rich as Morrowind or even Skyrim, but the main questline is exquisite!  The way it blends action in the real-world of Cyrodiil and the hell-world of Oblivion makes it so neither get old (although the way Obliivion is designed is highly repetitive in design; same hallways, same landscape, etc.), and the actual quests, especially the Daedra artifact quests, are amazing and well thought out (THE K'SHARRA IS REAL!!!!  It gets me every time!).
Music/SFX - 8/10
The soundtrack is incredibly atmospheric, and after playing the game every time you hear one of the songs you'll remember that one time you did something really stupid while listening to it.  The SFX can be slightly laggy at times, however, and the voice acting becomes dreadfully annoying after a while, which I have to dock it for.  Overall, though, the game is great for the ears!
Gameplay - 9/10
The controls feel tight and responsive, although the way the attack buttons are mapped (you can change the mapping, though, so don't let this bother you) I sometimes find myself casting a spell when I'm trying to jump!  But, what's worse is the difficulty of quests in relation to other quests in a certain questline.  The first one may be easy whereas the second may be near-impossible, then back to easy on the third.  Overall, 9/10.
Replayability - 10/10
This category is where ALL the Elder Scrolls games excel (if I'm spelling that right. lol).  With over a thousand quests - be it side-quests, side-questlines, or the main quest - the game is extremely replayable!  You can create several characters or just attempt to complete every quest with your massively-overpowered vampire warlord you've strengthened with fifty strength potions! (yes, that's a thing).  The possibilities are endless, and you're the one in control!
Overall - 9/10
Personal Score - 9.9/10
Everything that makes the genre great is all wrapped up in this one awesome package!  Yes it does have a few flaws, but overall:  AMAZING GAME!!!

Great tower defense-styled game. The freeform construction allows for so much more feedom and strategic thinking than other TD games locked into a simple grid. The energy and mining mechanic is very unique; I haven't seen anything like it in another TD game. Four (+sandbox) modes per the 3 maps, Normal, Wave, Rush, and Insane, all have different strategies and require a lot of thought and, in the case of Insane, some . Most tower defense games involve spending a lot of time looking at the screen waiting for stuff to happen. Not in Harvest: Massive Encounter. I have never played a game where I had to spend so much time paused thinking about my next choice of buildings than this game, and it's been a blast. Pretty steep learning curve, but once you get the hang of it, you can reliably get normal mode games to wave 100+.
It doesn't have endless replayability, unfortunately, and updates have long since stopped and the mod support didn't come until the community had been long dead. There's a very clear "best setup" that you get the hang of eventually (don't ruin it for yourself by looking them up), and there are only 3 maps. Despite the shortcomings, it's well worth the price!

I've found myself getting into the 'one more run' mentality about it on more than one occasion.
The only issues I have with the game are that there are only 3 planets (lack of scenary options), and I find at times linking/unlinking towers can be needlessly complicated, especially when I'm trying to get very specific owers to link, unless theres a shortcut command like shift+click that i've been missing all these years.
But those minor gripes aside, it's definatly worth a look, for both casual and hardcore TD fans, and casual gamers in general, the general hardcore crowd might not find it intense enough to start wiith, but it does ramp up later.

If you're a Linux user, don't bother with this game.  In my experience, while the store says it supports Linux, the game refuses to work on most Linux systems you'd ever use.  When you launch a game, a script runs that tries to detect if you have the right libraries installed to run the game, but it just doesn't like 64 bit systems.  The script "runs", but fails to install anything.  Oh, and it relies on apt-get, so good luck getting the script to work at all if you're on a non-Debian system.
Let's say you forget Steam entirely, run the game's executable directly.  NOPE!  If you have the right libraries installed, in my experience, the game will look for the 64-bit library names, meaning you've got a 32-bit game asking for 64-bit libraries.  That just doesn't work.
Why am I posting this as a review, rather than asking for help on the community hub?  Because this problem is not happening just to me, and it has happened throughout the near year I've owned this game.  The reason I have that hour of playtime for a game that supposedly doesn't work?  I accidentally installed a 32-bit version of Ubuntu when I decided to hop distros, so I played this while I waited for the 64-bit version to download.
TL;DR: I can't speak for anyone using Mac or Windows, but on Linux?  Go elsewhere.  There's a reason there is no system requirement tab for Linux.

Dota 2. League of Legends. Smite. Say what you will about MOBA's, but you can't deny their popularity. These games present challenges and commitments that can be enjoyed with friends, so they hold a lot of appeal for a lot of people. Super Monday Night Combat has demonstated that a MOBA playstyle, structure, and map can work in a third person shooter, but Awesomenauts took it one step further.
Awesomenauts is a 2D, platforming, PvP, incredibly fun game, and I would reccomend it to new players interested in playing a MOBA for the first time or old hats in the ring wanting to try a different game. It's fun, well made, with excellent mechanics and a great artstyle. Some stipulations before going in: balance. There is a levelling system and Gnaw is so totally overpowered that having one of THOSE players will ruin the entire game. The sniper, Raelynn, and the tank, Derpl, have some individual issues that are harder to abuse, but still present. One map spawns extra flying bots that make the game longer, and another has a large creep that is somewhat obnoxious. Other than that, I would heartily reccomend the game. Hope to see you ingame sometime.

INFRA, for the most part, is a first person exploration / hidden object / navigation puzzle game, with a hint of, what should I call it, "environmental suspense", maybe?
Your initial task, as the player character, is to survey a number of neglected installations of various purpose in and around a fictional city called Stalburg, and document any damage you manage to spot by taking photos of them. However, exploring these places often requires you to get through various obstacles ranging from closed doors through malfunctioning equipment blocking your way to flooding, fire, toxic gas and various other environmental hazards. To deal with these, you'll need to find items hidden (sometimes way too well to be considered fun) in the environment, figure out how to fix and/or operate certain machines and other devices, or simply find the right path through a complex environment. As you go from location to location, you'll also come across old documents, which shed light on some dark secrets and conspiracies in the past of the city, and give some insight into why all the places you've visited are in such a poor condition in spite of being critical parts of Stalburg's infrastructure.
The puzzle gameplay of INFRA is a bit all over the place, and it was probably the weakest aspect of the game for me. Some of the puzzles are well communicated and fun to figure out, even many of the more complex mechanical/engineering themed ones have a logical flow which helps you clearly unerstand what needs to be done and giving proper hints as to how to achieve that. And then there are the ones which are completely counter-intuitive, way too drawn out for their own good, or you feel at every step of the way how much effort has been put into obfuscating an otherwise simple task into a jumbled mess of unconnected things to do, or making sure that a key element of the puzzle is hidden in the least likely location in the least visible way. As a whole, it will average out to an ok puzzle experience, but there are qute a few frustrating moments temporarily making the game feel less fun than it actually is.
If some of the puzzles were my personal low, then the architectural design of the various environments you encounter over the course of the game is hands down the best aspect of it. Some unavoidable artistic liberty aside here and there, every single place feels as real as anything you can find in any larger city in the world. The layout of the outdoors areas and the floorplan of the buildings make sense from a practical/engineering point of view, the industrial and other installations are not just a bunch of random machinery thrown together for the looks, but actually follow the technical procedures of whatever was supposed to be taking place at that location, and the detailing of each location helps selling it even more as something "real". Another aspect of the level design, especially in the underground and long abandoned locations is how well it can build and maintain a really tense, even frightening atmosphere without crossing the border into "horror territory" or using cheap tricks like jump scares (although if you are really good at exploring every hidden and remote area, making the connections and thinking a bit outside the box, you may encounter things which will come to you as a shock, quite literally ;). The developers have squeezed every bit of performance out of the Source engine, making the game a sight to behold even compared to some of todays more modern game engines, although at the price of extreme memory requirement. (Don't even think about trying the game at max settings unless you have at least 8 GB system memory. I was like "Oh, Source engine, how demanding can this be? Let's crank it all the way up!" Very bad idea; constant paging, 30 seconds freezes, several minutes loading times level bad.)
And while most games that are built on exploration and puzzles offer little reason to play them again after you've figured things out on your first playthrough, INFRA has a certain level of non-linearity, which makes later maps play slightly differently based on what you did and discovered on previous maps. This means that unless you make the exact same choices and do the exact same things during a subsequent playthrough as in a previous one, the game may play slightly differently this time. And based on your deliberate and accidental actions throughout the game, as well as how attentive you've been in spotting the damage you were sent out to survey and discovering the old documents scattered about, you'll get one of several different endings, which might also be a reason to revisit the game a few more times to try to find what you may have missed in the previous playthroughs.
As a whole, if you don't mind slightly (and at times not even just slightly) annoying puzzles while exploring a real-world looking, beautifully realized and detail rich game world, topped off with a story to piece together about how and why a number of corrupt politicians and businessmen almost brought down an entire city in trying to seize more power and money for themselves, INFRA is an ejnoyable game with a somewhat unique gameplay, nice atmosphere, good music (oh, I didn't specifically mention music, let's just say it's good, I really liked it, and the soundtrack is available if you feel like listening to it again after having heard it in the game) used sparingly,  and enough reason to revisit it a few times if you liked your first run.

Let’s face it, on the surface a game about a ‘structural engineer’ doesn’t sound like the most gripping assignment.
It does sound slightly intriguing in the ‘how can this game be of any interest’ stakes and it certainly could be relaxing, but ultimately it’s a structural engineer for chief’s sake.
The blurb tries to sex it up a bit, highlighting a conspiracy and a fight for survival, and while both are technically applicable, they are both secondary and rudimentary.
This is a walking simulator puzzle game at its core, but to limit it to such a label does it an injustice.
While flawed, and rough, Infra is one of the best indie games you’ll ever play and the depth, quality, length and sheer immersion is as good as any AAA game out there.
Infra sees you play Mark, in the fictional German city of Stahlburg, as said structural engineer who is assigned to inspect the Two Gorges Dam which is said to be in structural peril.
After a very enjoyable little foray around the office it’s time to get to work, and there begins an epic journey through the city of Stahlburg, discovering place after place after secret after secret, all the while ensure you get photos of all the damage and problems you see.
At its core, as said, it is a puzzle game – each place you’ll go to will have something wrong and often you’ll have to fix it  - sometimes these puzzles are so logical, brilliant, and ingenius, and others they’re very poor – it’s a very mixed bag on the quality of the teasers.
The visuals are excellent for a 13 year old engine – it’s on Source, so it has the feel of Half Life 2 very much alive, but it is hugely enhanced in scale, scope and benefits tremendously from 4K – but it’s secondly to the sound, which is just some of the best use of audio you’ll hear in a game.
The voice acting is eccentric but enjoyable, the music pretty immersive but that general ambience is outstanding.
As for the locations – the game is divided into three parts – and the second teaches you a thing or two about claustrophobia. It actually gets frustrating – essentially you’re underground the entire time and you have to earn your route back to the surface, but when you do it is one of the great feelings of gaming.
I will say this – the game can be uneven. For every two outstanding sections there’s a less inspired or downright poor one. And the amount of underground can be a hindrance more than anything else.
But the thing is meant to be a long hard day at work and it certainly rewards you for the battles you’ll put in to get to the end of it.
Infra is a game which didn’t get much coverage and few people know about it – when it’s bad it’s really insufferable (some bugs as well as some of the design hurt it) but when it’s good it’s absolutely stunning.
It’s a game without enemies, without people to kill, without anyone to shoot. It’s 30+ hours of you with your torch and camera and lots and lots to do and discover.
Highly recommended.

Seriously fantastic 4x game.
I have always loved the Civ series, and I've played pretty much every turn based strategy game I can get my hands on, but Endless Legend is better than all of them.
It cuts away quite a lot of the bredth of the civ series, there's much less there in terms of espionage, trading, and religion, but that only adds to the experience.
This game is much more simple than most 4x games, but where there is normally 1000 different tech paths to take, there are 1000 different styles of play which are each extremely valid.
If you liked Civ, you'll probably love this. If you couldn't get into civ because it was too complex, you'll defintely love this.

This Game, Dispite being Similar to Civilization V is a much more complex and unique 4X Game than Civ 5. It has may features that build on what Civ 5 Started and improves it. The Map has more complex Terrain Types than Civilization as well as an interesting and unique use of Elevation that has a large effect on Combat. The Technology is the Most Liberating and Dynamic System I have seen with absolutely nothing Linear it adds a unique Mechanic of "Nominal Cost" Which makes it important that you research the proper techs that you need, unlike in Civ where you need to Research Steel even if you have no Iron. The Expasion system is one of the things I love the most as your Borders don't Grow naturally and you must construct "Districts" to Expand your Borders, you will however lose Approval Ratign For doing this so you have to Balance valuable Tiles with your Citizens Happiness. The Most unique thing about the Game is its Amazing Art Style which makes the Game Look Like a Playable peice of Art, and the Fantasy Themed Factions who Build, Trade, Expand, and Fight for Control of the Unstable Planet of Aguria.
The only Major Flaws this game has are a few Bugs that Amplitude are constantly patching, and the AI is a bit Poor at managing Armies and Battles; Which will most Likely be improved on in a Future Expansion or Patch.
If you Like Games Like Civilzation and Enjoy a Fantasy Genre with good Lore this Game is For you.

Before I type anything else, let me preface this review by saying that the thumbs up I give this game is a very, very hesitant one.
Right. Endless Legend is a game by Iceberg Interactive, the strapping folks behind Endless Space. The general consensus for that is while it was a competent 4X with a very good interface, there was very little actual "meat" to be had.
And honestly, that's how it feels here.
The game itself is like any familiar 4X: you start out with a hero (who can settle your first town), along with a few token soldiers to help you explore the world. Bigger cities mean more gold, and more production, and more research.
However, Endless Legend throws a few other things into the mix. Some work, some don't.
First, there's the quest system. Every race has their own unique quests, along with rather generic ones that anyone can get. And honestly, most of the quests are rather dull. Usually some iteration of "go to X". Most of them just feel plain unsatisfying to complete, and feel like a chore.
Second, there's the Empire Plan mechanic. 20 turns into the game, you get to set an Empire Plan, which gives your civilization buffs depending how many infulence points you have to spare towards the investments. Once again, it was good to see Iceberg experiment with something new in a 4X, but implementation was lacking.
The one thing I did really like was the villager system. Villages are small settlements that belong to minor races, and you can recruit their special units through either defeating them in battle or bribing them. It was something that really made me feel like I was building an empire through a foundation of alliances and trade, which is always nice.
The biggest problem this game has, and it's something that's hard to quantify, is that the game just feels *slow*. And not because of its demands on the computer, but just the pace of the game itself. Characters, even on the fastest setting, still take forever to lumber across the map and use up their move points, the battle system is largely the same, and there's just no 'snap' like you'd feel in Civ IV, or Gal Civ II, or hell, even Fallen Enchantress.
And this last one is a personal thing, but I've always hated the "magic is actually forgotten technology" setting. It just leaves a sour taste in my mouth.
You might notice I've said a lot of bad things about this game, but I'm still recommending it. Well, despite its flaws, it's still a rather addictive and competent 4X. It's got its problems, very avoidable ones, but it has a very solid base. If Iceberg's willing to make the effort, they could turn this from a mediocre 4X to one of the greats.
