I have been hearing old, non Bethesda rpg players complaints for years and I always thought that was an exageration and simple "Bethesda hating" by people that don't understand totally how great could be a Open World rpg. As Daggerfall and Darklands fan myself I thought that this Oblivion hate was an overreaction by players who simply prefer a more story guided experience or the back to turn-based combat. I was wrong.
I have zero problems with the infamous potato-heads npcs, I can live with a simplification of character creation, spells, skills and many other features, I read many times about the terrible leveling system as one of the worst flaws of the game, but I didn't need to experience this problem to reject quickly the game. My problem has been basically that silly console typical design, or that's to say, the absolute lack of general planification in world building and gameplay design.
The start is atrocious. The way in what events happen is hardly credible, the emperor and his personal guards reactions are absurd, the ultra-easy tutorial is 100% console decadence ported to PC, the way in what our character level-up many times his skills in this first tutorial dungeon, the over-abbundance of all sort of potions, armor pieces, weapons and tools, wich makes of this first dungeon one of the worst learning process ever, the starting location just in front of Imperial City, all is too much rushed, barely credible, guided and easy.
The game world is generic and bland, the cities are populated by a barely credible but happy mix of every Tamriel people in absurdly equitative proportions -poor Imperials, Cyrodiil isn't cyrodiilic anymore-, the unimaginative architecture, the incredibly  repeated dungeons, the lack of world depth, the tiny npc population, the lack of factions, the small dialogue, the bad and goofy writing, the feeling to be playing "Disneyland the game" and not a TES game.
So TES IV is a simple console game, recommended for 12 years old console players, with a mediocre gameplay and horrible world design. Moreover, Oblivion was the first Bethesda true E-corp product, with all these purchasable little addons, as the marvelous 2,5 $ horse armor and EA level of poor, brainless design. "Creation Club Bethesda" started just with Oblivion...

It's worth checking out if you're curious about it, but I wouldn't really recommend it otherwise.
The game feels more like a proof-of-concept, like testing the development waters with some neat tricks before launching headfirst into a much more challenging project. A bunch of cool first-person puzzles and gimmicks (and I don't use that word in an insulting way here) were just sort of strung together with a really minimal narrative. The game wants to show you some cool stuff, but it's hard to get invested in the "story" of it. There's a lot of banter between the fully-voiced (!) player character and the mysterious shouting man on the other end of the radio, but your questions are never really answered in a meaningful way. The reveal at the end is more of a punchline than a resolution.
Fairly early on, the game branches into two separate paths. One is more surreal, but they both have their moments.
Some of the clues are confusing or easy to misinterpret. Some of the tasks have solutions that you might find by dumb luck, without even knowing what you were looking for in the first place. Some levels make it very easy to die and aren't the most forgiving about how much ground you have to retread as a result.
The visual elements are very nice,  objects and environments look great. Some other games I've played recently have made me more aware of when games (like this one) make an effort to include other characters but never let you see them (I get it; human models are complicated). It becomes a problem when it's clear there are characters talking "just on the other side of this wall/door/etc" but if they walk around to your side, you get killed before you can see them.
It's an interesting game to♥♥♥♥♥♥around with, but it doesn't hold up as a complete game. I want to see what this developer can make when there's a strong story at the foundation.

The game is an interesting Tower Defense idea with wide open map, random enemy spaws and interesting mechanics such as linking laser towers together to increase range and damage and missle silos which can be upgraded twice to either do 4 area of effect chain lightning attacks or 4 long range missle strikes.... Which brings me to the good and bad aspects of this game.
Good
-Unique concept on the normal tower Defense game.
-Very good stratagy use
-No need to waste time on multiple unlockables
Bad
-Laser towers don't link/work 60% of the time even when fully powered, enemy in site and still powered
-Missle silos sometimes lose their 'Area Ring' on upgrade making the radius of which enemies are targeted at is point blank
- Very resource and stratagy heavy to the point one mistep punishes you heavily for it
-Resource gathering is slower then resource need or use
-Minimal bare units (no unlockable towers) make for heavy micromanagement
-No specialized towers with enemeies that are unique (the one that spaws reinforcements will always sit outside of laser tower range and spawn kamakazies) make for difficult planning
-Poor pacing as you barely get your feet wet before you're thrown head first in with the sharks.
That said I do like the game, but it seems to have been released prior to all the bugs being fixed and as I've had this game for only a short time, it seems if they haven't been fixed by now, they never will be. If you can get past the gliches and the tedious game play repitition, this is a great and challenging game. If not then don't even waste your breath.

☺ A different twist on Tower Defence.
☺ Heavy on strategy.
☺ Solid mechanics.
☹ Limited diversity.
☹ Repetitive.
Harvest: Massive Encounter is appropriately named. It's up to you to defend yourself against large waves of enemies that attack from all sides rather than predefined routes as you harvest a finite amount of resources and build up your defences, enabling you to expand your territory to harvest yet more resources and defend against even larger and deadlier waves of enemies.
Unlike a lot of tower defence games, Harvest: Massive Encounter is all about the known variables and a synergy of mechanics. You require resources to build Harvesters, Solar Plants, Laser Towers, Missile Turrets and Link Nodes - no endless stream of unlockable buildings here, just the tools for the job! The Solar Plants produce the power you need to operate the harvesters and fire your turrets and everything needs to be connected via link nodes to allow for a smooth transfer of energy, should a link in the chain break or your layout bottlenecks your supply, you'll be looking at an even tougher fight to survive. It's a very clever mechanic that rewards thoughtful placement and allows you to steadily expand without being constrained to build only area's or a grid system.
It's all about keeping the synergy between your assets allowing you to expand, collect, defend and repeat. For added complexity, Laser Towers can be linked to produce a more powerful beam with a longer range, so it's not just about putting more towers down to stop the flow of enemies, it's also about creating strong defensive points to tackle the harder enemies (of which there are several types with varying strengths, such as speed or the ability to teleport in reinforcements).
It's a tough battle from the start until you're inevitably overwhelmed, victory is not so much about defeating your enemy but simply lasting as long as you can before your defences finally cave in. Maybe you'll fair better on the field, but it'll be tough as thousands of enemy ships close in.
This may all sound rather positive but unfortunately, because the game relies on such closely knit mechanics there isn't that much diversity in what you can do or the enemies you face, its simply about using those limited tools you're given to the best of your abilities. You're also limited to the one, barren map until you can unlock another two after putting quite a few hours into the game and while there are a few game modes available, they offer a similar experience.
While a solid strategy game and a unique tower defence title, I'd only really recommend the game for those patient few that like a challenge, enjoy refining their tactics and can feel a sense of accomplishment in beating their old records. While the game can be satisfying and very rewarding when you defeat a wave with all your turrets still intact, for those looking for a greater sense of progression or some light hearted fun, I feel the game could quickly become repetitive.
Thank you for your time!

I just really wish there would be an option for a "Mixed" review. This one would surely be one of them.
But since this is one of my most favourite games, I rather not hit the "Not recommended" cause that would make me feel bad. Let's say my review is a kind of warning for future players, as I will talk more about the disadvantages rather than the advantages.
This game, as the title already says is really, really Awesome, it has tons of potentials, in my eyes it beats Dota2 and even League of Legends (and I like the latter) just to mention the two most popular MOBAs which are kinda similar to Awesomenauts.
So the task is, you are in a 3v3 match, you with your two teammates have to defend your base on a battle arena which is also protected by 3 or 4 turrets, that's depending on the map. Both teams have 3-3 (or 4-4) turrets. There are various champions, characters, whichever you call them to choose from, and each and one of them has different, unique abilities. From the medic to the assassin, supports, tanks, you can find different classes, and even these little "types" have different selections. The background story is simple yet still enough for this game, the characters all have their own background stories and the design (even the most of the skins) are also amazing. So, everything is set up for a perfect game, what's wrong then?
Pretty much everything else. Sadly.
1 . Let's start with the matchmaking. Catastrophy. Horrific. A complete disaster. The game has no dedicated servers, so you pretty much have to wait until the matchmaking finds players from your region (and this one is preferred, or else you have to deal with laggers, and even with this set up you will probably meet them), sometimes it takes like, 5 minutes or even more. And when you are finally in a game which has not started earlier (and will be a losing match as you will get dropped into the place of angry ragequitters), you will probably have to deal with people who have higher ranks than you. And here comes the second most horrible thing;
2. The ranking system. I can't describe how it works, because I absolutely don't understand it. You can't choose to play or not play ranked matches like in LoL, you will be categorized into leagues, but the way you level up to higher leagues or get dropped back into the former seems to be really, really random. And if you get into higher leagues because out of your 20 matches you luckily won one, you have to deal with the bigger guys. And by bigger, I pretty much say guys with the highest ranks and prestige, becase those are the ones who I get mostly, even if I am in league 6, with prestige 1. I always, and no joke, always get enemies with max prestige, and league 3-4. Maybe even higher. I don't need to mention how do I end up.
3. The last, and probably the worst thing in this game is the "community", if I can call this a community. I have met a few communities before, but this game definitely has the worse, pretty similar to LoL I'd say. Your teammates calling you noob if you die once, your enemies tapping the taunt button more than M1, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s everywhere, trolls, ragequitters who leave you alone with bots, and enemies still taunting you. During this 70 hours I have met like, 1 or 2 nice random helpful players in this game, seriously. And there is no kickvote or ban system either.
4. I also want to mention how I disagree with the content what you have to pay for. Sure, a few skins to buy them, the devs need to eat something of course (no irony), but there are also characters what you can unlock only with using your debit card, pretty strong characters (I'd not call them p2w though) and instead of a few serious fixes or developing, the company seems to put all their efforts into the new skins and into some occasional bugfixes. Oh, and to nerf Voltar to be almost useless.
All in all what I can say about this game is that it is really addicting with its unique humour, gameplay and overall experience, but has so, so many backsides that it might not even be a benefit to play this game. Unless you have nerves made of ropes. I'd suggest the game for people who can be ignorant against trolls, can deal with stress easily, and like this genre.
(Also I am sorry for my grammar errors and typos, my English is not the best, and my typing is even worse.)

I only found out about this game after they released the final version, so I was fortunate enough to play the entire story in one go. The entire game is very polished, I loved it. I always thought I was good at spotting the little details, but after 40+ hours I know I've still got more stuff to go back and find.

The game's biggest problem is when its attention to realism butts heads with the limitations of a video game. Some puzzles I got stuck on and had to go look up a walkthrough, and it turned out that either there was a 'that would work in real life' solution that I hadn't thought would be possible in the game, or vice versa. Plus, my sprite got stuck on doorways a _lot_.
THAT SAID, there is something absolutely satisfying about being able to fix things in the world. This game reminds me most of the quiet city exploration levels from Half Life 2. The environments in Infra are big, detailed, and obviously made by people who do understand architecture. These places feel REAL. More than a few times, I had to take a moment to just marvel that someone had designed every little bit of what I was seeing. And you can do more than just gawk, you can make the world better than you left it.  I was smiling every time Mark said, "That should do it!"
There's a lot of other things I could mention, but other reviwers probably also have. The main points are that it's a little unpolished, but also has unique gameplay and is endlessly inventive. It's in my favorites for a lot of reasons.
....strangely enjoyable experience, it's certainly a game I recommend if you need to take a break from the usual zombie killing stuff!

Probably time to update the front page here.  It’s no secret that I’ve been struggling for the last year and a half or so with the game, mostly financially, but also with the game’s direction. There are a few things in the works that I hope will allow me to return to the game in the near future. And I promise that when time and money permit, development will continue, stronger than ever. I love this game, I have spent hours on it.
In case you are wondering how much, I have played it since it was put on shelf's on one of my favorite stores.
Well anyways, my game was a "non-steam" game, so there is no evidence to as how long as I played that version.
Though I will say it's more addicting than candy-crush, every nation can be player controlled, and each one of them is unique.
It's an inversive game that will keep you hooked, with battle planning, global affairs, and crisises pulling countries into World Wars.
Ranging from 1836 to when the world was still recovering from the likes of Napoleon to 1936 just shy of World War 2.
With over 100 years, you can set the speed for which your country takes.
With Diplomacy and many other things to look after, you'll be kept concentrated on the game. Don't worry, you do not need to micro-manage, the game does that for you, but if you want full control, it's all there.
Then there is colonization.
America and Mexico compete for land, while Britain colonizes Canada.
But you can change this.
You choose the alternate course of history, and you can decide who colonizes what.
The riches of Africa beckon, a Russian or even Austrian Africa is possible.
You guide your country to place itself onto it's rightful place at the top.
This is an excellent game, and I recommend it to people who like playing games where you must control a nation.

The only complaints I have with this game, and the accompanying DLCs, is that the game is not taken far enough in some aspects, and too far in others. Also, the tutorial is rather dull. When it comes to political, social, and diplomatic mechanics, the game has not been taken far enough. Adding several mechanics, like they have in several MODs I have seen and heard about, as well as what Creative Assembly did in EUIV, would improve the game greatly. The Trade tab interface, is rather pointless, and if anything shouldn't be there. If it is retained, it should be further mainstreamed in how it operates, but the amount of goods, should be further expanded. All in all, I am impressed with this game, very, very impressed. I give it a strong 9.25/10, and with the enhancements I mentioned, it would be an immediate 10/10.

Have you seen my review for EUIV? If not, check it out now. Come on, I'll wait.
Have you read it? Yes? Good. Now remember how it looks hard, but is easy to play once you've started? This is the opposite. If you've played EUIV, you expect this to be easy, and then your brain implodes. The amount of micromanagement is kind of scary. This is the game that convinced me that War Games (the movie set in the Cold War about the hacker), if it were ever to happen, would be Paradox's fault, most likely. It's still fun to play, but at some point you have to admit to yourself that you don't understand what half the buttons do, and you're okay with that.

This is like the Advanced course for Paradox spergs like myself (Victoria 1 is the KILL YOURSELF NOW course fyi, fun but impossible to understand). It's the last game Paradox made before they changed their development process for CK2 so it suffers a but from the 'Old Paradox' ways of having the sequential expansions that act as patches. With Heart of Darkness, it's very good, though its one expansion away from really becoming as excellent as EU3 was and CK2 is and EU4 will be. It's based in a fascinating period of history and it's my favorite setting for a Paradox game because you can get the sense of the world shifting massively throughout the time period. From post-Napleonic squabbles over random crap, to the heyday of colonizing Africa and building railroads across the West, to the chaos and horror of the Great War and fascist/communist takeovers, Victoria covers it all. I really wish that we get a Victoria 3 of the same quality as CK2 and EU4 and that it comes with a EU4-V3 converter.

EDIT: re: Joystick/gamepad controls.
One of the classic action RPG experiences that made the genre what it is today, launching many clones (and memes) along the way. This is a single-player action RPG in a fantasy setting, with first-person and third-person view options.
The first thing you encounter after the opening cutscene is a character creation menu, where you can enter your name, choose your race and gender, and customize your appearance. You can change the shape of your face by adjusting a series of sliders, much like some "make a mugshot" police sketch software, or have the game randomize your facial features until you find something you like, and tweak it from there. You can also pick from a variety of hair styles and hair color, adjust age and skin tone, and rotate the camera around. The tech is a bit outdated, but it gets the job done.
You begin the game as a new inmate at the Imperial Prison. Soon, a unique opportunity presents itself: The Emperor is fleeing a coordinated assassination attempt, and the entrance to his secret escape tunnel happens to be in your cell. He pardons you in exchange for your help, having forseen an otherworldly threat to the entire mortal realm in his dreams. Is it merely a stroke of good fortune, or is it your destiny that placed you in his path for a higher purpose? You'll have to ponder that later, because the assassins haven't given up yet, and they apparently don't want to leave any witnesses...
The mouse and keyboard controls are pretty simple and easy to use: Use mouse to look around, left mouse button to attack, right mouse button to block, middle mouse button to switch between first- and third-person view on the fly, mousewheel controls third-person camera distance, WASD to move, and most other functions like spellcasting are near those keys by default. Keyboard and mouse are rebindable and responsive. Switching weapons and spells, and using potions and gems, are done by opening your Journal, which has pages for your stats, map, inventory, abilities, and quest log. Items and spells can also be hotkeyed to the 12345678 keys on the keyboard for quicker access. (I bound spellcasting, use, and grab to mouse buttons for the sake of convenience.) EDIT: Joystick controls are an option, but they didn't work properly with my gamepad's analog sticks, and I'm not sure why.
A short tutorial mission leads you through catacombs and sewers to an exit to the overworld, and from there a wide open world awaits you. You can continue your mission to save the world, or ignore it entirely and go raid some ruins. The main questline will still be there if and when you decide to pursue it, and you'll likely do many sidequests along the way before you tackle the endgame. Finishing the main questline does not end the game, so if you want to get it out of the way early it can be finished at low level. There are also several long questlines attached to various guilds and such.
Your character class is picked during the tutorial mission (someone will even suggest a class based on what skills you've been using, or you can make up a custom class) and this controls your advancement. There are 21 skills in the game, 7 of these will become your class skills. All skills in the game advance individually with repeated use, but you need to gain 10 points in your class skills to gain a level, and others advance more slowly. Levelling raises maximum Health, and lets you raise up to three of your eight attributes, depending on how much you used related skills since your last level up.
You also get to choose one of thirteen birthsigns: Some just give attribute bonuses, others give special powers, like the ability to turn invisible for a minute once per day. These can help you out of some tight squeezes in the early game.
Combat is relatively simple. Your weapon skills and attributes modify how much damage your weapons do, and weapons and armor quickly degrade and need repairs between fights. Armor effectiveness also depends on your skill with that armor type. As your skills improve, and you find gear made of better (and more durable) materials, you become much more effective. Blocking with a shield or weapon reduces damage and interrupts an attack, allowing you to counter. Holding the attack button launches a power attack, which may hit hard enough to stagger even a blocking enemy. Attacks use up your Fatigue meter, which regenerates quickly whenever you're not running or attacking. Attacks made with low Fatigue do less damage, so walking and making your hits count works better than running around and flailing.
Magic spells use up your Magicka bar, which regens much slower than Fatigue (or not at all if you took a certain birthsign) and can be restored quickly by using potions or Welkynd Stones. The Magicka cost of spells drops as your relevant magic skill improves. There are seven schools of magic: Alchemy is used to create custom potions. Destruction spells are mostly elemental attacks. Restoration is mostly healing. Alteration has useful buffs. Conjuration summons creatures. Illusion can charm people, paralyze enemies, or change lighting condtions. Mysticism is a catch-all for things like telekinesis, detecting life (like a "heartbeat sensor") through walls, and trapping souls to recharge magic items.
Stealth options include moving silently, sneak attacks, picking locks, and talking people into trusting you. Stealth mode movement takes into account footstep noise, facing, and line of sight; as well as lighting conditions and magic effects like Chameleon. A target that hasn't detected you can be sneak attacked for extra damage. Lockpicking and speech get their own minigames, which are tricky at first, but once mastered allow even low-skill characters to reliably beat them. The bow and arrow are the signature weaponry of most stealth classes, and can be used for sneak attacks as well.
Every town, including the Imperial City where you start, has a few quests you can get involved in if you talk to the right people. Or you can leave town and wander the wilderness in search of trouble. Some interesting dungeons are in very remote areas of the map, and the Imperial City itself is built over ruins that can be accessed by manholes. The main quest revolves around portals opening to the demonic realm of Oblivion, so these are another type of dungeon to raid.
Any marker on the world map that you've visited can be reached by "fast travel" to save the trouble of backtracking.
The official DLC is of varying quality, mostly different types of homes for the player to improve, but Shivering Isles is like a sequel in itself. The official creation kit is also availble, and the modding scene has done plenty of good work with it.
There's lots of impressive scenery, amusing voice acting, inspiring music, and overall the game builds a lot of atmosphere that gives a "hero's journey" feeling to the whole experience. It's worth relaxing and taking your time to soak it all in.
I have some minor gripes, however. Terrain pop-up is annoyingly common, as are clipping and stability issues. A lot of quests have bugs that can trap you or halt quest progress. Level "scaling" is way overused, it feels wrong that common enemies like bandits and goblins get tougher as you do, and this drags out fights at high level. The level system tends to punish you for sticking to your class skills, as your attribute gains may fall behind, compounding the "scaling" problem. There's an animation bug which will eventually (after 200 hours or so) make your character unplayable, which is bad news for players who just want to develop one character indefinitely instead of starting over. Community mods address many of these issues, but the game was clearly rushed to market, and the final official patch hasn't fixed everything.
Overall, despite its flaws, this game provides a truly engaging single-player experience, and I enjoy playing it to this day.

The premise of
contains mystery, intrigue, terror, and numerous conspiracies. Despite the jolly humour and lighthearted beginnings the core atmosphere of
is filled with dread. Please do not mistake
as being another typical horror game at first glance, instead think of it as being a first-person "walking sim" on steroids. I highly recommend this to fans of puzzle games in a similar vein to
, to those with an appreciation for detail, and to whomever would have the patience to delve into various notes, documentation, and sights in order to slowly extract and piece together this breadcrumb trail of exposition as it balloons into something much larger than anyone could have anticipated.
Based in Finland,
's campaign will see the protagonist, Mark, cross an entire city, trying to save himself, whatever, and whomever else he can whilst everything crumbles down around him. My first playthrough of
offered a playtime of around 30 hours which I can see being doubled in order to discover all the intricacies that this game and its world has to offer.
is an absolutely stellar game where developer, Loiste Interactive, displays an insane attentiveness in regards to the detail and quality of the game and its world: from incredibly complex story lines where each branching narrative and its characters are subtly interwoven and eventually come together in the end; having each chapter's set pieces tastefully hide tonnes of pop-culture references and further important revelations to the story that can easily be overlooked as just another in-game texture; containing puzzles that may require the player to accomplish something seemingly insignificant in the first few hours of gameplay that won't prove its usefulness until the final act; and a masterful handle of the Source Engine with massive, sprawling levels and visual tricks that keeps the adventure interesting and occasionally provoking a sense of true horror.
For fans of point and clicks from the '90s to the present day, for anyone who enjoys puzzles with a logical and methodical solution, and for those who want to experience something completely different and who have an appreciation for detail,
provides all of that and more. There is no doubt in my mind that
is my game of the year for 2017 and one of the best adventure/puzzle games I have ever had the pleasure of playing.

This game made me want to be a structural analyst.
While not traditionally "graphically impressive" (which may be from the choice of engine), INFRA still manages to stun with its environments. The massive open vistas of dilapidated industrial facilities and the winding service tunnels beneath both play in the Source engine's favour. That the game's main focus is on observing the environment says something about how good it looks; it comes under scrutiny far more often here than in other games, and I can't say I saw more odd seams and glitches than in any AAA title.
The puzzles vary in difficulty, and they don't really follow a clear difficulty curve (except for some of the later puzzles having a time limit), which is not really a problem as the focus of the puzzles is more about fitting into the world. They do that amiably.
The humour of the story is typically Finnish, something I really love, and the "ambient narrative" about corruption is told in a really cool way. Any questions about why certain parts of the environment is the way it is can be answered by the scattered notes. They way sidequests have consequences further down the line is also very neat.
I worry that some people may miss important parts if they don't read everything they photograph. I started out thinking that the documents weren't supposed to be read because of the almost-transparent ink colour and the low resolution, but after a while I realized that wasn't the case. That's definitely a point of future improvement, overall texture quality is on the low end, and for the documents it's on the verge of being unacceptable. It is still readable with some effort.
The absolutely worst part of the game is unfortunately the voice acting. I can see that this really was a labour of love and I hate to be negative about such a thing as someone's voice, but the quality overall is low and the main character is just awful. He gets the enunciation wrong in just about every line of the game. I get that he's supposed to be a Finn, but Finns usually speak English a lot better than this. He also doesn't "sound like a surveyor". It's really a nitpick, but it goes a long way to help immersion. Someone like Grady from the Practical Engineering YouTube Channel is more of what I'd select as a voice actor, with proper enunciation and an air of professionalism.
All in all, a top-notch experience with some minor hiccups, which shouldn't be missed by anyone who has even a minor interest in infrastructure. If you can't stand the main character, that's understandable. Fortunately, he speaks relatively little.

Unsung excellence.  Why isn’t this game much better known?
It’s hard to summarise Infra but that’s because it doesn’t fit any obvious genre. It has Myst-like puzzles but it’s not just a puzzle game. Then there are bleak underground areas with a heavy sense of dread in the air but without horror monsters to face. And it's all joined up with huge detailed explorable areas which would grace a AAA blockbuster. It combines these beautifully to give you (in my case) 50 hours’ worth of unhurried playability in the first run through without a single enemy to fight or weapon to fire. And the perfect pacing maintained my enthusiasm to keep going every step of the way.
The jewels in the crown for me though are the fabulously detailed industrial environments. I’ve worked in places which have plant, switch panels, pipelines, ladders, cable trays etc.
like this. The dev team and artists have got this absolutely spot-on; the immersion here is total, right down to the tatty control rooms and abandoned workshops with tools, coffee cups and notes left by long-gone workers. Each one had its own challenge and “Aha!” moment of satisfaction to slowly tease out before you could move on.
Criticism? Well, the logic of some of the switch & valve puzzles can be a little off-piste. There was one in particular which required
. I’d still be there now if it wasn’t for the walk-through. And there are a few timed puzzles which I for one dislike. I’m an older gamer and don’t have a young person’s quick reactions, so I just die dozens of times over before getting through. No fun there, just stress and broken immersion. So that would be my one change request: an “easy mode” option to globally increase the timeout on all timed puzzles to make them more easily achievable for players like me.
But in the end, they all added to the quirkiness of this unique world.  So it’s 10 out of 10 for me, I loved it.

ALL OF THE NOSTALGIA!!! From the very first sounds of the opening sequence and game menu, I was instantly transported back to late 1990's, sitting in my older brother's bedroom, playing this on classic playstation and a tiny, heat-warped telly that we had to use a bit of blue-tac and a screw to keep the switch on AV (occassionally the screw would come loose and we'd suddenly be plunged into static mid-game!). My brother and I would take turns playing, switching every time we got Abe killed (which, on my part, was normally almost instantly), jumping out of our skins at the scarier parts (this game had the best graphics we'd ever seen at the time) and laughing our arses off at all the fart jokes. We had played through Oddysee pretty quickly, so we were excited to have a much longer game this time (TWO whole discs!), with slightly better graphics, and OH THAT REALLY AWESOME QUICKSAVE FUNCTION! Our mum even got in on the action, and played this with us on more than one occassion, helping us out with the more "puzzle-solving" sections that we couldn't work out (plus she is an x-files fanatic and loves everything to do with Aliens and weird♥♥♥♥♥♥like that).
So for me, this game is totally worth playing, even though it definitely wasn't designed to be played with a keyboard, nor on a 27" HD screen. It brings back so many fond memories of the rare moments that my brother and I were working together to keep Abe alive and rescue all of the Mudokons, instead of at each others throats trying to kill each other. I still love the quirky nature of this game/universe - the artwork and landscapes are mind-blowing to me even now that the graphics are incredibly below-par. The characters and creatures of Oddword are so unique and terrifying. I love the 2D platform gameplay - I wish there were more games like this. Some of the levels are pretty easy, and some of them are infuriatingly difficult (for me anyway), which just makes completing them all the more rewarding :) Just don't be a dunce like me and forget that you've only been Quicksaving for the last 3 hours, decide to exit after completing a particularly difficult level and forget to do a proper Save... That♥♥♥♥♥♥is devistating.
So yeah, if you loved playing this game when it first came out, you won't regret playing it again :) It's everything I remember and more.
If you've never played it before, give it a go! It was ahead of it's time when it came out like 15 years ago, and it's still a unique gaming experience in a lot of ways. If nothing else, the story is fantastic. The implications and irony of the story is something you just don't get in many popular games. We sympathize with the Mudokons and their hero, Abe. But most of us, if we took a hard look at ourselves, probably fall into the Glukkon or Slig category... or the kind of Muddokon that just watches it all happen and does nothing.

Well, now you've gone and done it. You've made a remarkably unique Tower Defense game, and that takes some serious effort these days, along with a whole lot of crazy.
Harvest: Massive Encounter is honestly just that: a TD game. If you like TD games, you're going to enjoy it.
So what makes it so unique compared to the others out there on the market, from the starcraft 2 maps to flash games?
First off, resource harvesting. You get nothing for killing enemy units; you're dumped into the middle of an endless field full of minerals. Your job is to mine as many minerals as possible, and survive as long as you can. (With some variations on a theme for different game modes).
The map starts out small, but if you build towards the edge of any one side, it'll stretch out, expanding the minimap further and letting you move farther away from your base. As such, you have pretty much unlimited room to build, but the most dense packs of minerals will be close to where you start off, and the farther from your central base you get, the less efficient mining will become.
The towers provided to you are remarkably few in number for a tower defense game, but they're very carefully fine tuned to be exactly what you need. For example, laser towers have relatively short range themselves, but can be set to focus all of the laser towers in an area to a single, massive beam. This effect can scale to an unlimited degree, and you can chain smaller groups of laser towers together to form an enormous, intricate network of lasers that has immense range and godlike firepower, or break off their power temporarily to wipe out a swarm of smaller enemies that are faster.
You can set your towers to prioritize, deprioritize, or ignore certain enemy types as well, so it's well within your power to tell little lasers to focus fire kill the suicide-bomber style gehenna shuttles, but ignore some of the larger units, while having your eagle class missle launchers ignore the shuttles unless they're the only thing left on the screen, or ignore them entirely, only aiming for bigger game to hunt.
Another really unique feature to H:ME is the energy system. I've seriously seen nothing remotely similar to it in any game before or since. The idea is that you build solar power generators, which create a ball of energy every few seconds. The energy ball bounces randomly between any adjacent point that it can possibly reach, until it comes across something that needs power, and then it rams the target and provides the power required, disappearing from your screen in so doing. This quickly leads to a vast, intricate network of energy lines going all over your base, and energy management becomes vitally important. Having a ton of energy on one side of your base, but not the spot that it's needed, is BAD. Fortunately, you have plenty of very easy to use tools to control your energy flow, such as marking a building as top priority to get any and all energy it needs, or drawing out routing paths to force energy balls to travel along a set path, only being allowed to follow their typical AI programming when they exit the path.
Pretty much everything in H:ME can be summed up this way: it's weird, but in a really good way. It's creative, unique, and it WORKS. It's not just different for the sake of being different, but rather, it's different because it makes the game more interesting and fun.
It'll take awhile to get used to most of the unique aspects that Harvest has to offer, but they're well worth the enjoyment once they've grown on you a bit.
Final Verdict:
Everything Harvest: Massive Encounter does, it does well. The learning curve is really quite steep, however, there's no plot, no multiplayer, and it's really just one big tower defense sandbox. For what it strives to be, it's pretty much perfect at. For what it doesn't try to be, however, it doesn't do at all. If you don't like TD games, this won't be the one to make you a convert, by any means, but it'll be one of the best TD games you've played if you do like them.
Score: About 70%. It does what it does pretty much perfectly, but it completely lacks a few areas that could make it a lot better still.

A deep and sophisticated grand strategy/gommunism simulator from Paradox Interactive, Victoria II poses several fascinating questions, such as:
"Why is Britain such a lazy doucһebag?"
"How can I have 6 million rebels
when I have a population of 5 million?"
"Why does Fascist Tibet have a better economy than me?"
"How is Fascist Tibet even possible?"
"Why is everyone leaving my country?
"Britain, help, Tibet is invading me!"
"How is that a game over?"
In addition to creating endless possibilities for such believable worlds, Victoria II features a robust and realistic world economy that's too complex for any mere mortal to comprehend. Constantly bail out bankrupt factories and watch your country spiral into debt, just like real life!
The political aspect of the game is also breathtakingly realistic. Watch as your pops do the exact opposite of what you want them to, always be upset with your decisions, and rebel at the worst possible time. A basic guide to politics is that just like in the real world, communism is always the answer. With it, the only one you have to blame for your fuϲkups is yourself, not incompetent AI.
Diplomacy is an important part of the game, especially alliances. If a country is even slightly favorable towards a great power, you can expect them to always intervene against you, ruling out any conflict with that country. Your own allies will constantly call on you for aid, but won't have any problems with leaving you on your own when you need help. There's also the great infamy system, which supposedly prevents blobbing but really just creates artificial difficulty.
The game might seem way too complex at first, but after an hour or 50 you'll see that it's just as complex as you thought it was, but at least you sort of understand it now. If you stick with it long enough to git gud, the game will be a lot of fun.
Overall: 10/10, it's decent
P.S. Expect to have fun with massive yearly Jacobin rebellions in the latter half of the game unless if you're the USA or Gutter Germany. Although, if you're Gutter Germany, you should probably just kill yourself.
P.P.S. I forgot to mention the many amazing mods there are for this game, including the infamous Pop Demand Mod, which adds great features such as
, the amazing-and-totally-not-broken Victoria Ultimate which tries to apply 19th century politics and economics to 400 years of history, and vickymod, letting you experience all the epic reddit memes you can fit in your fedora.
Massive learning curve, but awesome game overall. One of the most realistic but still fun games I've played.

Were you one of those disappointed by the dull Civilization 5 reskin earlier this year that was Beyond Earth? Do you crave for a return of personality to the Civ-like 4x genre? Do you want a game that makes you want to start a new game as soon as your last one ended? Well, consider trying out Endless Legend.
Firstly the mechanics of the game: It takes the functional shell of a Civ game but makes subtle tweaks to almost every mechanic so that the game feels very unique among its genre even as it retains the fundamentally strong core of a Civ 4 or 5. I'm not going to go over every smart thing this game does to switch up the formula, but trust me, the changes are mostly very positive and really make it an enjoyable experience. The questing system and the periodic bits of writing you get when doing faction quests are also quite strong and give the setting of the game some interesting 'pop'.
Secondly the presentation: This is a game that looks and sounds impeccable. The game looks amazing with colorful and attractive visuals, the interface is sleek, and the sounds and music are all excellent.
Finally the factions. The factions of Endless Legend are where, I believe, the game is truly special. Each faction is so unique and plays so differently from one another, it's just tremendous. While I've so far only tried out 2 of the 8 unique factions (1 is currently just a reskin of the other, I'm told this will be changed later on), the differences between the two changed my playstyle dramatically. While the nature of these differences generally pigeon-holes some of the factions into specific playstyles (Vaulters are going to necessarily use their bonuses to go for a science victory, the necrophages will probably be gunning for a domination or supremacy victory) I don't consider this a great weakness when the variety on offer is so strong.
There are some weaknesses. No espionage system is a bummer. Imagine how cool it would be if you could hire heroes to work like probe teams from Alpha Centauri. Also it would be good if there were some big projects or wonders you could build like in those games. Some voiced snippets upon research to give the game some more flavor (which it already has a ton of) would be nice too. The tutorial for the game is inadequate and it took a full playthrough for me to really come to terms with all of its mechanics.
With continued support this could be one of the finest 4x games ever made. If you're a fan of the genre, pick it up.

I have to say, i have been playing 4x games for years, all the way back to alpha centauri and civilization: call to power and onward and this is hands down my favorite thus far. Endless Legend brings a lot of innovative new things to the arena that just take what i love so much about complex turn based strategy and bring it to a whole new level.
After taking a long look at Civilaztion: BE and realizing it didnt quite hold up to the sid meiers's name like i wanted it to, i began looking for other 4x games to fill the void. Then i stumbled onto endless legend and was instantly hooked. I havent once regretted the purchase.
Pros-
- The graphics are gorgeous, there is just a huge amount of beautiful detail that they manage to cram into every map all without feeling unnatural, everything feels like it actually belongs there. For a 4x its pretty awesome.
- The UI is simple and easy to use, everything u need is right there and theres no annoying navigating through menus to get what you want. All the info u need is right at ur fingertips.
- The races are all pretty specialized and a lot of thought has been put into making them unique. Im really grateful that so much depth has been given to each race and each one brings something different to the battlefield whether you are playing it or going against it.
- The tech tree is sort of generally divided up into "styles" like military, economy, influence, etc, but the nice thing is that you can research ANY tech in ANY order as long as you have the era unlocked. This gives a refreshing bit of flexibility to how you build your empire.
- I love that the resources in game actually serve a purpose aside from merely profitable trade routes. Depending on which race you play they can be anything from a helpful boost at the right time, to being the entire cornerstone of your empire
- At first i was intruiged but skeptical about the rpg elements of this game but it actually pulls it off nicely. Quests seem to be pretty well thought out and play nicely into the rpg inspired troop and hero customization. There are unique items and each piece of gear has unique benefits. The quests add lore and depth to each race and give a deeper purpose to the game.
- the minor factions are well thought out fill in the gaps left by the somewhat limited racial units. Again depending on what race you play they can be either a helpful benefit or the entire foundation of your empire.
- the combat! OMG THE COMBAT. Contrary to what the first guy said, the combat is hands down the coolest thing about this game. You actually can control precisely what each unit does, whether its kiting a slow but powerful enemy or holding a chokepoint or quickly taking a vital position, etc, and the battles play out on the actual terrain in the actual world. So there is an awesome amount of tactics involved between the terrain, unit composition, weapons, etc. Where you decide to pick your battles makes a real difference in how it plays out. I made the mistake of attacking an enemies city when it happened to be on a peninsula that only had a line 3 hexagons long and 1 wide for the entrance. my units started out stuck in that choke point while they had a pile of calvary and archers at the other end. Cliffs and mountains and forests become legitimate (often beneficial) barriers and this is where the equipment system meets battle and your decisions really make a difference. Do you want slow but tanky units that are powerful but subject to the whims of your faster enemies or do you want super fast, high damage berserker shock troops that can run circles around the enemy, or anything in between. Archers and calvary have a serious tactical purpose instead of just being little icons blankly attacking the enemy. Once you learn how to use it, the combat system will make you weep tears of joy for how much fun it adds to 4x combat.
Cons-
- Diplomacy can be a bit sketchy at times. I spent the better part of a game winning an ai over to an alliance and sharing maps with them so i can watch the super powerful enemy i was facing only to find half way through that the ai will do annoying and irrational things. no matter what i gave him, he would constantly cancel the vision sharing and eventually even cancelled the alliance too so i ended up having to fight two enemies in a 2 front war instead of one.
- Sieging seems just a bit overpowered. There doesnt really seem to be much incentive to attacking cities when you can almost always defeat them without cost by sieging them.
Endless legend is definitely a solid 4x game that offers many features that no one has done before, it'll be sure to give you a unique experience and is worth picking up if you enjoy the 4x genre

This is a serious little jewel of a game. If you like exploration, and long rewarding gameplay I very seriously urge you to check this one out. Despite how there are some dark, even mild tension inducing parts in the game it's overall a very relaxing, chill experience. This isn't one to be rushed! The game is very long - and even so it manages to keep the player interested and immersed. I found no part boring myself. There are some minor, vexing inconveniences; such as the terribly energy hungry camera and flashlight. But to be fair there are plenty of batteries really, and managing them isn't terribly challenging. Some bugs here and there; that is an unfortunate little downside to this game. Nothing that can't be managed though.
There is a very well spun, even a somewhat complex story and plot in the game; but there are also plenty of hidden easter eggs and strategically sprinkled bits of humour to keep it from becoming too serious. I'm a bit conflicted on weather one can call it a walking simulator. On some ways I suppose the term can be partially accurate here - but keep in mind there are plenty of puzzles and exploration to keep you more active than your usual "walking simulator" would. At least in my humble opinion.
If one is a fan of a chill, exploration experience, I seriously urge you to check this little gem out. Even more so if you happen to Finnish like myself; there are plenty of little jokes us Finns will definitely notice and apperciate. (there are even a couple of references to Kummeli; I won't spoil and say what and where they are but they made me laugh when I found them!)
Finally I'd like to just praise the environments. They are absolutely beautiful, even if you find yourself inside a crumbling, rusty decrepit damn or outside in the more foresty, shiny areas. Rust or lush greenery, it's all wonderfully created. I have nothing but respect and love for the devs here!
I DEMAND MOAR.
All in all: Great, fun, long rewarding gameplay, wonderful silly little easter eggs (especially if you're a Finn), enjoyable puzzles and hell, it's just great fun. You also feel sympathy for the poor player character. Really isn't having a very good day :P
Please consider buying this if you like long, rewarding exploration games.

Victoria 2, for those of you reading this who have played other paradox games such as Crusader Kings or Europa Universalis will understand how the game works. If not then I shall give a brief overview. Victoria 2 begins in 1832 and allows you to control any existing nation from Russia to Mexico, France to the Transvaal. Each nation is different and you will have to manage a variety of different aspects of your nation: The economy, Politics, Military ect. You can choose how to run your nation acting as a semi deity. You can put a party in power each with its own policies such as Laissez Faire or State Capitalism. You can influence population demographics, industrialisation.
The scale of the game is impressive with working trade, factories, political parties and economy. The freedom allowed in Victoria 2 gives such an amazing replay value as it will be rare things happen the same way twice, this is further benefit from the sheer number of nations that are playable. While the fact that battles cannot be directly controlled (as a total war fan this can be annoying) veterans of other paradox games will find that similar battle mechanics have crossed over.
The game does have a somewhat steep learning curve and I would reccomend following a guide until you get used to the mechanics of the game. Industrialisation and factory managment can end up feeling like a huge micromanaging project if you follow state capitalism. Diplomacy can also be extremely frustrating at times when nations seem to have no reason for their diplomacy, warfare can also be annoying when forcing a peace on a nation which even though the warscore needed has been achieved the nation will still not accept.
However, despite some drawbacks the qaulity of these grand strategy games has continued over. Not everyone will enjoy these games however if you do, you may find yourself lost in the world of 18th politics and diplomacy.

Now Only If is a free-to-play eight minute demo that is a surreal first-person puzzle with some platformer elements that puts you in role of Anthony Clyde who after a heavy night of partying at his female companion’s house by the name of Sam he passes out.  When he comes to he has no memory of the previous night all Anthony knows is that he needs to find Sam.  Upon his search Anthony comes across a voice on a radio that introduces himself as Vinnie who clearly has it in for the protagonist to point he wants to keep him in the world he created.  And as far as antagonist Vinnie goes the best way to describe him as a twisted version of Jekyll and Hyde type personality.
The world in general in only if likes to trick and toy with you in the environment by implementing riddles, puzzles, choices, observation or combination, while at certain times dealing with obstacles in the environment itself in order to progress which this games does this very well in both creativity and difficulty.  Also the world itself changes as you progress which some of these changes can be settle while other changes can be extreme which result in some trippy moments that will make you wonder all until the end (Is what the protagonist experiencing and hearing is real?  Is it in his head?  Is he dreaming?  Is he even alive?).  Lastly the world in only if doesn’t follow any type of rules especially when it comes to which path/choice is right or wrong (right path/choice = wrong and the wrong path/choice = right, and vice versa.)  Now there is something I should point out here the path/choices are kind of on the linear side and don't really have a impact on the ending which is a little bit on the disappointing side.
Philosophe/Dialogue – Now the game takes in a mixture of serious believable philosophical quotes in the form text, while at the same time adding entertaining is the best way to describe it which comes from…you guess it Vinnie.  The reason this is a strength in only if because not only how it’s set up but also how entertaining and funny hear the dialogue between Anthony and Vinnie, especially Vinnie.
Keyword Typing – Another thing that stood out was this particular feature both in the menu and the main game.  Now how this feature works is by you having to type a word or phrase in order to continue from the level you left off which works fine (note: No need for spacing or upper case letters as far as I can tell.  And providing you remember or wright down the name of the level.)  While keyword typing in only if is interesting and unique idea and I would like to see this feature put into the full game, however I didn’t enjoyed this feature as much that I wanted to which part of the problem is that the even though I typed the correct word in the game wouldn’t register what I typed in which forced me to type the same word multiple times just to progress (thankfully though there is not to many of these in the game/demo).
Replay ability-Now there is some form of replay ability for a game like this in terms of  achievements.
Ending -  In my opinion the ending seems disconnected from the game itself, however does remind me of one of those hilarious/awkward/what?! punch line moments you find in certain movies.
In generally I really enjoyed my time playing "Only If" and I recommend anyone at least give it a try.

Picked this up based on the very positive reviews it had received, there is definitely some merits to the game:
- factions are more unique/different from each other than in other 4X titles
- it's a new entry to the 4X genre, so it's play isn't quite the same as you'd expect
- the random maps seem to be well designed
Some cons though too definitely:
- the factions are not even remotely balanced. Some are much easier to win with than others.
- there are a lot of events that players can do to each other that have immediate impact that cannot be anticipated or countered.
- the auto combat is rather random - it results in draws far too often, and can sometimes result in truly baffling losses.
- the actual turn-by-turn manual combat doesn't really give you much strategic options - unless all of your units get to move first, any positiong you plan out will just wind up making your units stand there and look silly.
There is a substantial time investment to go through a match, and it shares a common weakness with other 4X titles: While the match lasts a long time, usually it's decided within the first 1/3rd of the playthrough, if not earlier. Much like the civilizations franchise, how your starting area is will decide the outcome of at least half the games, proximity to other players/AI will decide about half of what's left, and having some form of plan will decide the final piece of the pie.

Crumbling monoliths of concrete and steel. Valves to turn, buttons to push, levers to pull, a city to save. Government negligence and a corporate conspiracy.  A game with a message? Definitely! More importantly, an epic 25-plus hours ode to the Source engine, virtual urban decay, machine puzzles, and having the final word in all of them. No zombies to kill or simulators to walk here—just puzzle after puzzle after puzzle, elevated to new heights by a mind for what matters, a darkly eccentric comic instinct, and the greatest level design to ever grace the [gracefully-ageing] Source engine. Is it without flaws? Of course not! Prerequisite vehicle sequence #1-too-many, a power-hungry portable image-taking gizmo in constant need of fresh batteries, and a listless middle act will have you itching for less, but the pitch-perfect Part 3 of the whole $25 shebang will drag you back in with a vengeance. The perfect companion to the existential dread of urban collapse hitherto conquered by Condemned: Criminal Origins (minus the bloodthirsty hobos), the precarious navigation of hazardous environments of the Half-Lifeian kind (minus the iffy first-person platforming), and the anxiety-inducing quiet and poke-and-prod puzzling of Myst (minus the impossibly oblique leaps of logic), all brought down to surreal earth. Buy it!

I love puzzle and exploration (myst, the witness, etc), but nowadays 70% this kind of game is horror based, so the setting of this game alone is already a big plus for me.
-
no horror or fantasy element at all, everything is based on modern this day stuff. (there is 1 horror/spooky aspect in the game but it's just an easter egg from the dev so you can completely skip it)
-
the graphic is not nextgen quality, but still more than enough to make you enjoy the  surrounding scenery
- puzzle difficulty is manageable. it start easy and gradually increase it's difficulty and complexity but still enjoyable throughout the game, i played until part 2 and only need guide in 4 specific puzzle
-
one great thing about this game is that the game will often put you on the spot with a lot of pathway which you can  explore at your own leisure. its not open world but its not "corridor" exploring either, the game somehow give you a "false feeling" of freedom to explore, but at the same time still manage to "guide" you as to where to go next.
-
another thing that i like from this game is that you actually explore the building and the surounding area, there is no 'stage clear" or you end up to totally different area in abrupt way. you start from A and slowly progressing to B and C and so forth, it feel serene and very zen like sometimes.
-
there is almost no music in this game, even if it's there it's mostly ambient sound.
-
because the amount of path you can explore, you will miss a lot of thing  like document, letter, object to photo, etc, some of this stuff is lock behind puzzle and well hidden, the game really demand you to explore every nook and cranny if you want to get everything.
-
aside from highlighting stuff you can pick up or interact, there is nothing else. the game give you no waypoint, no objective marker, no inventory, not even a hud, what you see is what you get.
-
you move slow even when you run, also jumping and climbing is very stiff which is bad considering this game is all about exploring.
-

Orange Juice is a zesty and refreshing multiplayer experience if you're weary of the unhealthy toxicity plaguing most titles today.

Victoria 2 is probably the best strategy game I have ever played and is less imposing than you might think.
If you are looking at this game with fascination but feel it looks to imposing, do yourself a favor and purchase it and its two expansion the next time they go on sale. This game is complex, yes, and it will take several hours to get the hang of the mechanics and begin to lead your country to victory, but the process is not as diffucult as your might think.
There are no win conditions or lose conditions (except having your country wiped off the map), while countries are ranked in terms of overall power, some countries will have it much easier than others, and if you start off a small nation you may never hope to pass Germany, France, or Great Britain. The game is open ended and there is no pressure for you to any thing in particular. Instead you can set your own goals for the path of your country.
It's easy to play several games focusing on different aspects of the game's mechanics, and there are several options in game to assist you. For example, if you are still learning how the industry and trade aspect of the games work you can set your economic policies more liberally, and the AI will trade and build factories automatically in your country. Overall, the game can be as complex as you want it to be, and there are numerous tutorials online that you can reference.
As a student of political economics and diplomacy, I have literally used examples from this game on tests. For example, on a test I might be presented with the situation in a country, and the possible paths a country can take from that situation. Thinking in terms of Victoria 2, I answer what I would do in the game and get the question correct. Victoria 2 is a profoundly in depth game and is not only fun to play, but can give you a great perspective on what it's like to manage an imperialistic power.

When I first started playing this game, I thought it was incredibly boring and that it will take hours to finish in one campaign.
After playing couple of hours, I started to get into it and it took me into an amazing journey with couple of countries.
GAMEPLAY:
Victoria II provides you with a great and simple UI that you will easily remember. It's looks beautiful and simple though some things should have been put into the top bar to make it quickly accessible but with DLCs such as A House Divided it will fix it. The game starts at 1836. You get a wide range of countries you can play as. It took me a while to choose which country I should go as and after a while I picked Prussia. Diplomacy is quite important in the game because if you don't have any allies and you start a war, multiple Great Powers might take the chance and annex you. You have a couple of categories in your top bar such as Budget, Diplomacy, Research, Population, Military, Production etc. You're gonna have a lot of fun improving your country's production, doing some research and seeing your country go up on the list of top countries and even one day, becoming a Great Power. Being in war is enjoyable, not like in some games, it can take a lot of years for countries such as Germany vs. France (it took me up to 15 years once) but it still makes you wanna write down the big battles of 100k soldiers dying for your country and your dictatorship. Winning wars, annexing countries, taking their regions, humiliatin etc. is so satisfying that you'll feel great! When I humiliated France and took most of their regions in 50-60 years, it felt amazing. When the game ends, 1935., you might feel sad if you didn't complete your goals but ofcourse Hearts of Iron III is there for you.
MULTIPLAYER:
Multiplayer felt dissapointing when you couldn't connect to any server and play with your friends. After some time I found out that you must use Hamachi or Tunngle to play with your friends which was rather dumb. I tried the multiplayer with my friends and I enjoyed a lot. Having you and your friends plan for massive Great Wars against your enemies is awesome.
THE VERDICT:
Victoria II will take you to an amazing journey that will last dozens of hours and even hundreds of hours. You will enjoy the amount of countries and possibilities, you won't be able to Quit the game. Having no servers for multiplayer was dissapointing but programs as Hamachi and Tunngle will fix it. After playing for some time, you WILL want the DLCs and they won't dissapoint you, they're not like CoD or BF DLCs, they will give you a wide range of NEW possiblities and scenarios.
GOOD:
+ User Interface
+ Possibilities
+ Addictive
+ Long Campaign
+ DLCs
+ Fun Multiplayer
BAD:
- Having to use Third-Party software to make MP playable
OVERALL:
9/10

Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus is a landmark game, and worthy sequel to the original Abe's Oddysee.
Even in its now-limited screen resolution, the strong visual design of Abe's Exoddus shines through. Don't expect to run this game at your native resolution (unless you never upgraded beyond 800x600 - in which case, you're in luck!), but do expect the following: some fantastic and challenging platforming gameplay; a vast number of gorgeous levels interwoven with an interesting, dark and downright odd narrative; some brilliant music which changes dynamically depending on the events taking place; and finally, some fiendish puzzles which make use of Abe's talent for posession and the use of GameSpeak - a system by which you can instruct other characters to whatever ends you desire, be it salvation or something more nefarious.
If you've played it before, there's no better time to return to the original Oddworld titles before enjoying the delights of the HD Remake, New N' Tasty, which recreates the events of the original game in a modern game engine and is "coming soon". If you're new to the series, don't be put off by the age or initial difficulty curve. Exoddus has a quick save system, so you'll never lose progress as long as you're diligent. A must-play!

Only If,
Only if this was a good game I wouldn't have to write a negative review for it.
The good bits about this game.
The developers actually managed to make the Unity engine good, which is pretty shocking due to the nature of Unity the majority of the games that use it as its engine look terrible, however there is quite a rather beautiful park section of the game that looked pretty good even on the lowest settings. The game is also free, which is honestly the right price for this game. There also some short pieces that 'mess with your mind' but that's about it.
You start off in a bedroom, facing a giant poster of some Japanese girl bent over with somebody behind her (not joking) two seconds into the game you see that, it's just stuck there for no reason and pretty much sums up the quality of the rest the game.
You leave that room and are surrounded in darkness with a floating orb of light that you are told to follow. You smash through the door and then some 'internet tough guy' starts shouting at you through a radio. You're told to look for a key, you get it escape that room and then you are told to choose a chess piece. Black or White. The choice you make doesn't really matter you'll end up taking the same path eventually anyway.
I decided to take the black piece and my god was it bad. The game really fell apart quickly. I was thrown into a lake and then told to mash the E key because everybody loves QTE's. Then you aren't given any instructions what to do next, you crawl one direction whilst constantly mashing E and then you get insta-killed and have to watch the cutscene again, after seeing it three times it gets pretty damn annoying. So you do the same thing you just did but crawl ever so slightly to the left and you survive, you then walk along a path and black smoke appears, you turn around to run and then more smoke appears, so you die and get killed and have to watch the cutscene again.
Now the way the save system works on this game is by entering a certain phase or the name of a particular level, so luckily I was able to skip that level. However this is 2014 not the 90's so either they were too lazy or unable due to lack of skill to program a save system, looking at this game it's kind of hard to tell which one it is. After that you're stuck in the darkest house ever, considering the fact that it's midday and the sun is shining outside. You'll bumble around in this mansion for a few levels and finally you'll end up back to the choice you got with the two puzzle pieces. Unfortunately the devs couldn't be bothered to make a model for Vinny 'the angry radio' (the antagonist) he appears in the game as a flashlight.
The game did get a little better on the white puzzle piece, however the game never really tells you where you are supposed to go or what you are supposed to do, It's obvious that they tried to do a similar thing to The Stanley Parable, unfortunately I guess they missed the part where The Stanley Parable had good voice acting and for the most part was obvious what you needed to do. As well as clever writing. This game seems to mistake random swearing for wit.
The voice acting and audio levels are all over in this place. One minute the protagonist is talking loudly to the antagonist and then he'll just start mumbling to himself like the VA forgot to turn his microphone on when he delivered the lines, you could turn your speakers up if you want to run the risk of Vinny blowing both your speakers and ear drums. The voice acting itself is sub-par. The Stanley Parable had a top-notch narrator. The narrator in this game sounds like he was trying to do a Vinnie Gognitti impression from the excellent Max Payne series.
The ending, my god, that ending, I have never seen any game use the subject matter that it did for a surprise twist ending. Not even South Park: The Stick of Truth touched it and that is the most messed up game I've ever played.
This part probably doesn't matter for most of you but man the achievement icons look like they were taken straight from Google Images. Really bad unprofessional images used for the achievement icons.
Overall, unless you are really really bored and/or don't have a great machine to play games on I can't recommend this game. It's free so some of you may be able to overlook it's flaws but so is Unturned and that game is actually being updated for free.

Fun for a game now and again. But if you want to play a moba where the devs pay attention to what the players want, how the game should be balanced, or I don't know, care. This is not the moba for you. With the only thing resembling a competititve scene being dominated by 99c, and the "Prestigious League 1 for the 250 best players" is a total joke. The game isn't hard, the queues and matchmaking are awful to put it lightly. Combine that with very few characters to play, let alone are viable. One of the 'draws' of the game is that it has a very low skill ceiling and a high skill floor, and is supposedly easy for new players to enjoy and play. Again, this is not true. The difference between a good team and a bad team is noticable immediately into the game, and has very little to keep the player playing. The unlock system is completely arbirtary. See, while other mobas like League or SMITE force you to play the game for a while to unlock the things you want, you get to choose what things you want. In Awesomenauts, you have no choice whatsoever about what you unlock. Are you a frog player? Do you see all of these fancy items and great builds that other frogs have? Do you want those items? Well you're going to have to play about 30-35 hours of the game before you can get to that point, oh and I should mention that you can unlock these things faster for winning games, which is near impossible with the disgustingly bad stock items. As for the matchmaking, it's total trash. The matchmaking servers matches you with player within 2 leagues above and below you. Let's take the average League 3 player, not outstandingly good, but still good enough to be about top 8000. You can get matches with anyone from League 5 (roughly top 20000) to League 1 (top 250). If the game can't find anyone within those 5 leagues you can be matched in, it will take literally anyone and put them in your game, for better or for worse. Now this wouldn't be an issue with the game, if it had draws to keep players playing (which it doesnt) achieving League 1 wouldn't be hard if it weren't for the outright broken matchmaking, and even then so few tournaments are held with so small prizes almost always dominated by the same 3 or 4 teams. The devs have absolutely no direction and little involvement with the community, the game is easy with little to no reward for being good, matchmaking and soloqueueing is cancerous beyond description, I haven't even touched on the DLC which for $10 awards players with 4 characters who are absolutely dominant in the current meta (if this game could even be considered as having a meta), the balance is constantly changing with every patch and the devs are putting time into things noone cares about, games are near impossible to win if you're on your backfoot in even the first 5 minutes, everything about this game is maddening to say the least. If you want a good F2P moba, go play Dota 2. If you want a moba thats easy to get into, go back to Call of Duty.
