So I'm generally not going to say what this game
, because I assume you at least know from the Store page, trailers and other places. Suffice to say, it's a fun fast-paced 2D platformer MOBA with an awesome (ha-ha, get it, funny joke, am I right??) aesthetic (artstyle + music + character design).
I've pretty much seen this game go through all sorts of things by now - good patches, bad patches, awful patches, great patches, controversial patches, you name it.
And despite the fact that it's extremely fun at the core, it always had some issues - lag (caused by the peer-to-peer network structure, which is pretty much bound to stay unfortunately), subpar matchmaking (even with the new matchmaking server Galactron in place), wonky balance and a generally awful progression system and a lack of things to really
past a certain point.
I was a
fan of the game for a long period of time (
), but even I lost my faith at some point, thinking the game is forever going to be stuck in limbo until it dies a slow,
death. I stopped playing it for over a year, and only recently started to really care about it again.
But, in comes 4.0, and everything has changed - the new progression system is great - at least compared to the old one we've had. The level of polish and visual improvements the patch itself brings is out of this world, and soon enough the two issues I've mentioned - lag and screwy matchmaking
be fixed by the virtue of the hopeful playercount influx.
So even right now, you can get a taste of things to come - sure, the main course is yet to arrive to this table, and it might just end up tasting horrible, but you can really smell some nice things coming from Ronimo's kitchen here, and I want to congratulate them on taking on this risky (though some could say "desperate") decision.
(I did have a lengthy negative review here before, but honestly I take back everything I said back then - I was somewhat angry and may have said things that I either straight up shouldn't have said, or wouldn't have said knowing what was to come for this game. )
I think Ronimo deserves a praise for their continued effort to keep the game alive, and even if some people might see this shift to F2P as a "desperation move because the game's sales and playercount have been dropping" - like tell me, would you rather have this game be left in the dust to a silent and lonely death? I sure as hell wouldn't, and it's evident that neither do the devs here - it really shows just how long they've been preparing this, and how much heart they've poured into it, and I think they should be rewarded for this. So here's one to you, Ronimo Games.

If you don't like the hunter you probably wont like this game. That's just the way it is! Its not for the cod or bf2 fans. Its not run and gunning and running around without consequences. You have to play it like you are actually hunting or as close to that as you can get in a game. If you run you'll only spook the herbivores and call the predators. You have to place your shots. I see all these videos and almost 90% of the time they shoot for the head. You must go for those body shots, Like real hunting specifically the vitals besides dinos in this game have small brains and the chance of hitting them there is slim if at all. Hit em in the hart or the lungs and their gona go down if not immediately then within a few feet. Your the hunter and the hunted depending on the situation.
Ive only been playing about 7 hours but I haven't died once yet, have no room left to carry anything and I have full camo because im careful and not in any rush. Ive never used the run meter once because you don't even need it if you play the way the game is intended. The metter is also for swinging handheld weapons so conserve it if you like to use it for running. The game is also very beautiful especially when everything is on high.
With all this said, are there issues with the game? Of course. Is the game getting better? I think so and the immersion is really that good especially the thunder and lightening. Dinos do get stuck on cliffs, the t-rex has some issues and yes there is no swimming to name a few. Basically  I think that most of the complaints are from people who expect this game to be something it never was going to be. I also believe the games not the problem here its the people who play it, then complain that its not what THEY expected it to be.
Like I said at the beginning of this review, If you like the hunter than you'll like the the hunter primal. If your looking for run and gun or a swimming simulator then go play something else because this isn't it nor will it ever be. Please also remember, when they say realistic that is also realative! My deffinition of what realistic is, of course is different than yours but as games go this one comes very close. If its not realistic enough for you then I suggest going outside and doing some real hunting!

You've woken up, deep in the wildernes... "How did I get here?" You look around in wonder of the place, a pod just inches from you with a machete and a part for the gps in your hand that shows an icon. You figure you should travel there. You walk as you normally would, knowing nothing of the place and what it holds in store for you, but that's your first mistake!
It isn't long before you hear a roar, followed by a screech... You've heard these sounds once while watching a movie but the name is misplaced at the moment. You shrug it off and continue on walking... But that becomes your next mistake as you hear footsteps running towards you and another screech. You quickly turn around to see something come after you and suddenly the movie pops into mind, "Jurrasic Park!" You shout it aloud for some reason as you stumble over your own feet and the Utahraptor bites into you, killing you. That's only your first adventure...
I thought I'd give a little story in the review xD I'm so proud of the developers!! Every change and fix we request, ends up happening at some point in time.
T-Rex and Utahraptors were left and right, given they were the only two predators of three total dinosaurss. But now there are another two predators but yet still one prey.
It sucked when you were stranded beneath a T-Rex after wasting yoiur ammo and it wouldn't move... So, we reqeusted a knife. We got a machete! Although, the T-Rex and other Dino AI have improved as well.
T-Rex would crash you if it killed you, but that's changed among other death crashes and glitches.
You now get XP for your kills and in-game G.. As you level up, you can purchase things with the G as they unlock after you die, prior to your next adventure such as clothing, guns, or ammo.
They've now released uncommon/rare variations of dinosaurs to make the hunt more interesting.
Things I'd like to see in future, other than the obvious more dinosaurs, especially less harmful ones to hunt.
I would really love some sort of perk system... Right now, it assumes everyone is the same. It'd be nice if people could be better at what they love to do. Stealth, Marksman, Healing, Trapping (traps totally need added too), Vitals (say someone has studied dinosaurs enough through kills and can now detect roughly where a vital sits).
You still find way too many bows with maybe one arrow or so, along with guns that have one or two bullets. It gets painful.. it really does.
Dinosaurs are brutal, even to each other! Thus, it'll be nice if that's ever implemented.
There's a building with three floors that you can climb, but never any dinosaurs there (I waited a couple hours and later restarted and traveled with a friend to only find one Triceratops wayyy off in distance, nothing came) It would be nice if that building (and hopefully there will be more in other places) had more use.
Issues/Cons
Honestly finding it hard to find any problems/cons now... Besides one.
There would be times where I would take things out of a container and push esc.. If I combined that ammo with mine, my ammo would disappear and the items would still remain in the container. I had always used esc to get out of a container I was done with. Please fix!!

During your travels and analysis (primarily on-foot,) you'll want to make use of a flashlight and camera, since many locations are dark and many things are in disarray. While the game had some frustrating areas for me, mainly because I would run out of time to finish, nothing in the game is difficult to the point you'll be wasting hours trying to find the answer-----but if you do, there are videos and guides online to help you through.

It's a bit of an odd game in some ways. There are certainly things about it that will seem strange or quirky about it, and yes there are elements of it that feel a little bit cheap or underdeveloped in the beginning. BUT. Hang in there. At least hang in there until you get out of the office and start exploring the first site.
If you are a fan of Myst-like games that are all about slow-paced and mindful exploration of a detailed 3D environment, manipulating machines, buttons, levers, valves, and other doo-dads to solve puzzles, opening desk drawers and filing cabinets in search of documents or some AA betteries, well then there is going to be plenty enough here for you to like. If you happen to have a thing for abandonment and urban decay, then you're going to have an even better time.
You are also a site inspector of sorts in this game, so there is also a photography aspect to the game where you snap photographic evidence of areas that are damaged, deteriorating, or dangerous. Basically take a photo of anything that looks like some kind of OSHA violation. This part of the game can be a little frustrating because sometimes things look photo-worthy when they're not and vice versa. But if you open your camera, the viewfinder should hint whether a photo should be taken or not. The game also could do more to underscore this aspect of the game or explain what it is for. It is possible to forget about the photography and complete the game without taking any photos, for example, which may lead some players to ignore it if they don't see the purpose.
Another demerit could be the areas in the game where there are environmental hazards that can kill you---especially areas where the player is obligated to perform a specific sequence of actions on a fast time limit or else immediately die. These segments often feel confounding, cheap, or frustrating; but hang in there. It doesn't happen TOO often.
But the real draw of the game is its nostalgic Myst-iness. As a person who craves that type of experience and is sort of sad that we don't see many titles like that, it really does a lot for me. And unlike games from Cyan, it's more friendly to slightly older machines.
It's a pretty solid game, though I am sure the $25 price tag will make some people hesitate--especially if they are not too sure what to expect. If you really really enjoy that slow exploration/puzzle type Myst feel, and if you enjoy abandonment and urban decay, then it should be worth the money for you. As I understand, this game will be updated later with more episodes, which should add even more value to the game.
It's not without its odd rough edges here and there, but on the whole, I feel it was a good buy.

This game was a pretty big surprise to me - I kept my expectations rather low when approaching it, hoping for some decent humor, political and otherwise and a bit of absurd, fun dialogue. And I've found some seriously good writing, appropriately creepy totalitarian undertones and pretty impactful ending that made the whole story much more than just a distasteful joke many people make it out to be.
While not a serious piece of political critique (or a serious romance when we look at that part of the equation), “Stay! Stay! DPRK” both manages to keep you entertained and smuggles a decent amount of information and insight into the reality of North Korea. While not dark enough to truly portray it and not without some factual mistakes, it’s actually decently researched and the storytelling is solid enough that it never feels like just an empty joke, exploiting the controversies it unavoidably creates by the sheer virtue of its setting.
Also, without the 18+ patch (wasn’t interested in it really) even the fanservice seemed mild and rare enough to not make the game feel like an offensive excuse for Hentai scenes, and really those NSFW moments made a tiny fraction of the content presented. It also directly parodied “Go! Go! Nippon” with some of those scenes and they worked more as meta-jokes than actual fanservice for me. While the story is short, both girls were developed just well enough to not feel like empty silhouettes with boobs attaches – I actually liked them quite a lot by the end of the story and cared about what was going to happen to them. Authors of the game joke about it working as porn, but I don’t even think that’s the case, or at least it’s far from being its main focus.
Even the production qualities had me positively surprised for a $10 VN, with the sprites, backgrounds and event-related illustrations being of a very nice quality (even if the very small cast of characters made it rather easy to achieve). Music didn’t catch my attention very much, but also never got in the way. In summary,
Honestly this was probably the best $11 i spent

(you need to get in and close the rifts by doing some dull mini quests into demonic towers etc and it gradually gets more and more boring. So to sum it up these 2 major problems kill this game:
1) The leveling system that is terrible in combination with monster scaling, because the world scales as you level so when you level up also the monsters level up, so if you don't level up optimaly, aka if you don't get the max points into your attributes after some levels the enemies will feel too hard and the only way to proceed will be to lower the difficulty slider which i hate cause it feels like cheating. So the world will get harder and harder unless you level up optimaly. But to level up optimaly you need to repeat boring out of character stuff like jumping under a low bridge for 2 hours etc which kills immersion
2) Constant rift spawn also is a major distraction that forces you to get into a random generated map full of demons and kill them off before proceed to do your story or quests otherwise the rift will spawn demons who may kill friendly NPCs that give quests etc...

I cannot in good concience recommend this game to anyone I like. The game is immensely frustrating. I even tried watching a walkthrough on YouTube but that player got so annoyed that he just stopped the game. I may recommend this game to a few people I dislike, though.
One example of this game-breaking frustration was in an area where you are trapped in a casket and thrown in a lake. You manage to break out and a message pops up on the screen telling you to repeatedly press the spacebar to swim to the surface. If you don't press it fast enough, you have to restart that part. The game then has you on the ground at the edge of the lake and asks you to rapidly press E to keep from passing out. If you manage to crawl down the path you can stand up and see some kind of darkness hovering. If you don't press E fast enough to fight it off, you have to restart this part. I made it past this and there were three patches of darkness blocking the path. No matter what I tried, I was unable to press E fast enough. At one point, I took my hand off the mouse and focused only on pressing that button as fast as I could. It still killed me and made me restart. I hate games that feel the need to test the player's reflexes because I feel it is a cover for poor design.
I'm one of the minority who loves cut scenes in games, but ye gods, at least tell the player when it is their turn to move the camera. At one point, I sat there staring at the screen waiting for something to happen. The cut scene before this had a lull in the action, so I figured it was the same thing. I felt rather stupid when I realised the game was waiting for me to make the next move.
I uninstalled the game and was a bit upset that I wasted my bandwidth to download it.

One of the first MOBA's I've played (unfortunately I've put this game on hiatus for being too addicting for now).  Different from a lot of MOBA's and very creative (also pretty easy to learn if you're just starting to get into MOBA's).  Each character has a unique aspect about them as well as strategies you can devise based on the other team.  I very much enjoyed this game, however there are several things I'd like to nitpick at.
In terms of settings and matches, there are several things to be aware of, especially with older desktops
Older AMD processors and graphics cards will generally get the 1 FPS dip from time to time (mine generally lasted from 30 seconds to 2 minutes, might be a game changer if you're carrying), even at low graphics settings  (anything made around 2009 or older that are pre-built or store bought at a fairly high price).  Though I have upgraded my PC since then, it's still something to be wary of.
Some characters may feel off (not necessarily input lag, but do feel rather slippery).
Lag Priority (who's actions count first when lag strikes) is inevitable, as long as the host isn't laggy, it should be fine for the most part.
Matchmaking sometimes doesn't work properly, though this may be an issue with the number of players geographically.
Some sounds for weapons and effects don't match up in terms of volume (Not sure if it's fixed as of March of 2014), though it's not really noticeable if you're not a nitpicker like myself.
Because I'm nitpicking, it means I don't see any major issues or flaws with the game whatsoever and I would highly recommend this game to anyone that has the time to play it (A LOT of time).

This game is an incredible take on the MOBA genre. Unlike games like DOTA and LoL, Awesomenauts is based on the premise of casual competition. It is designed to be fun. An interesting result of that is the lack of a real consequence when somebody quits your team. He is replaced by a bot that is often more competent than himself and continues to play in his stead. Another player can join mid-game to replace the bot at any time.
Awesomenauts also has a great community (official forum, not Steam). It has a thriving fanart community, a modding one, a tactics one, etc.
This game really opens itself up to modders. It allows creators to modify in-game bots and make their own using an AI editor. Modders can also create gamemodes using this tool. If Ronimo likes a bot, it can find its way into the official game. I have made two of the in-game bots, myself.
Overall, I highly recommend Awesomenauts. It has a thriving community that you should not miss out on. The gameplay is very fun, if less competitive than its other MOBA counterparts. All that is lacking is you.
Not everyone can be MLG like me, but it is a very enjoyable and addictive game once you get to a decent level. LOL

I am a fan of puzzle games with walking simulator elements along with hints of mystery, but this game has just become increasing annoying the longer I have played it.
The environments between crawling the various sewers and maintenance tunnels are varied and pleasing. Some scenes are quite beautiful. The backstory is rather unique and appealing. Some instances are genuinely frightening without involving monsters, jump-scares, and the like. Puzzles are very varied, involving acquiring information or manipulating objects in a combination of rooms or facilites in order to progress the main puzzle; thus, advancing your physical progression through the area. (My particular favorites are the instances where you interact with a computer and manipulate facility functions to get it back in proper running order). The computer interfaces for these puzzles are very satisfiying. I don't know why, but I found the uniformity of the piping that can be seen throughout the game to be very pleasing, especially the color-coded ones. The physics at times where things collapsed or broke were very impressive. I found the way you interact with menus, settings, and saves to be very pleasing. The game is stable, and well optimized.
I ran the game at 4k, so I often found the textures to be adequate in some areas, but the world is very large, involving many assets to texture, so this can be overlooked. Effects, such as from explosions, are subpar. The puzzles are what ultimately got me. I am essentially half way through the game, and I just can't bring myself to play it any longer. The freedom to explore with a lack of direction is welcome to some, but aggravating to others. I fall into the latter category. When you get to a new puzzle involving buttons, switches, and dials some notes, scrap paper, or just some form of direction or information is provided on how to begin solving the puzzle at hand. However, the arrangement and use of these dials, switches, and buttons ends up being used in so many different and new ways throughout the game, that you sometimes don't know how to continue solving the other half of a puzzle without the guidance of a walkthrough, which becomes annoying very quickly. The camera is also a point of contention for me. At first, it was novel and unique, but as time progressed, it just became something I cared less and less about, and finally stopped doing altogether. I had no incentive or way to measure my progress with the pictures I had taken. The flashlight is also a pain. I was almost always getting by, by the skin of my teeth with batteries, which is a pain, because most places don't have sufficent lighting. And, if you want more batteries, you have to use your flashlight to look in tight and obscure places, so it is rather self-defeating. The voice acting is also comical, both for good and for bad. In terms of quality, I would place it at the half way point.
TL;DR:
Overall, the puzzles become increasing annoying, with a few gems of the computer-based puzzles intermingled. The voice acting is adequate. The camera mechanic gives you little sense of purpose or a goal. If you really want it, make the walkthroughs that have been made of it your friend.

Edit: Part 3 of 3 has been released, the game is now totally finished.  Part 3 is as amazing and interesting as the previous parts.  Pick it up if you've been waiting for it to be complete first.  Still worth every penny.  Short review about part 3 below.
-Review-
Honestly, one of the best puzzle adventure games I've played in years.  There is so much to see and find while playing, I never felt once like I was wasting my time by taking the obviously not correct way to go, in fact I felt rewarded most of the time by coming across collectibles and little pieces of lore.
The level design is bloody amazing, everything seems to have a purpose and not once did I feel like an area was empty or meaningless.  The entire game feels so connected and gave me a clear sense of progression as I played the game.
The graphical design of the game, even though its limited by the source engine, is still beautiful.  Standing on top of a large tower and looking out at the horizon and seeing a sprawling town with individual buildings, trees, planes, cars, people, and more, was just breathtaking.
The puzzles for the game are all challenging, but don't fall to the same problems that most adventure games with puzzles seem to have when it comes to logic.  You're always sure what needs to be done to progress and simply need to take some time to understand the problem.
While its a puzzle game where you can mostly work at your own pace, there are still moments in the game where you have to act fast and feel real pressure to figure things out, such as a room collapsing on you while you figure out how to get a door open.
If you're a fan of puzzle games like the witness, you'll like this game.  If you're a fan of linear style adventure games like Half-Life, you'll like this game.  If you're a fan of games with heavy atmosphere and mystery, you'll like this game.
There are also some bugs in the game.  I've found very few, none of which were game breaking for me, but others have experienced some bad ones.  Luckily the devs are very active and communicative with the community and have an active github you can submit bugs too which will be fixed fast.  They are also active on the steam forums.
TL;DR, great game, worth full price easily, third episode should be released soon.
-Part 3 short review-
Part 3 was just released, and introduced some brilliant, and slightly frustrating designs to the game.  If you've played the first 2 parts, then you're probably used to the more enclosed, linear underground areas.  Without going into too much detail, part 3 is a lot more open than the previous parts, which can make figuring out what you're supposed to do a bit more challenging, simply because you have so much more ground to explore to figure things out.
Some of the more annoying and frustrating introductions to the game include finding very small parts scattered along a very open area, with numerous paths to take and very little direction given.  You're going to get lost in part 3 a lot.  If you prefer exploration, you'll love part 3.  If you prefer puzzles however, part 3 might leave a little to be desired.
Part 3 TL;DR:  Great conclusion to the game, lacking slightly with puzzles, mostly exploration.  Little frustrating at time. Still worth 25$ easily.

This is a fantastic game. If you're someone who loves to explore and appreciates small details, you won't be disappointed by this game. Everywhere you look, you can see the care and attention to detail that the developers have taken. Exploration is rewarded. The game gives you a lot of freedom to figure things out on your own, but doesn't just drop you in the middle of a game with no backstory either. Some parts are funny, while others are spooky (DON'T OPEN DOOR B2!)
I had this game on my wishlist for a long time and I'm glad I took the plunge. With the amount of secrets and hidden details in the game, I know i'll be able to enjoy more than one playthrough of the game. The graphics are really impressive coming from such a small indie studio, and I've only come across one bug so far (got stuck between some crates of beer and had to restart - and I noticed on a second playthrough that this issue had been fixed).
At the time of this writing, Parts 1 and 2 have been released, with Part 3 at ~85% completion, according to the devs. This game is rapidly becoming one of my favourites, and I'm pumped for the conclusion.
The price is a little steep but the sale prices have been very good and make it easy to justify buying.
edit: Coming back to this review after playing the final part to say that it was completely worth it. I ended up playing through the entire thing a second time and saw so many things I had missed the first time. The devs were also quite good at coming back and patching issues. The end(s) were satisfying and the achievements actually worth grinding out to see more of the hidden details of the game. Still a solid thumbs up from me.

After playing for some time, it's become clear to me that Cuties is by no means the inherently adorable and family friendly adventure it is marketed as, but rather a relic of Cold War propaganda targeted at the youth. While to those just giving this game a quick glance this may seem to be an unfounded assumption, just give me some time and you too will notice the prevalent pro-communism roots. Basic gameplay consists of the player controlling not one, but two rabbits. Moving one will cause the other to move in the opposite direction. Your goal for each of the increasingly complex levels is to collect each and every carrot on the screen, before reporting to your supervisor, a lazy and rotund pig, who you chuck out of the stage shortly before making love to one another. That is really the basic extent of the game, though everything I've mentioned, when seen in a different light, becomes one huge red flag. For example, you undergo strenuous labor collecting what every rabbit desires, carrots, though you yourself are not allowed a share, despite you and your soulmate clearly doing all of the work. Going a step further, let's revisit your supervisor. A comedically fat, mean, and beyond lazy literal pig who is clearly exploiting you. Now if this isn't the most overdone caricature of a capitalist that I've ever seen, then I truly don't know what is. The rabbits in question are depicted as sad, slender, overworked souls driven by their lust for each other as well as the pursuit of a better tomorrow. They themselves have experienced the dehumanizing aspects of capitalism in their daily lives and desire change in the most radical form, violent revolution. As in any revolution, no one man or woman may accomplish anything on their own, but rather working side by side with a surplus of comrades. The unification of the black male rabbit and the brown female rabbit represent how no amount of injustice will suppress the voices of the many when all races and both genders unite for a common goal. However, capitalism in this day and age has reached a point where it is the expected norm, and any one attempt of changing that would likely go unsuccessful. This is seen by the pig always coming back even after being overthrown each level; capitalists are slimy and will stop at nothing to continue to hurt the working class, demanding "I NEED MORE FOOD" after each level, throwing his workers through even more dangerous labyrinths for personal gain. This does not stop the willpower of the rabbits however, as they will push on because they know the power of the majority will eventually emerge in triumph over the elite few. The main menu screen, with the large word, "Cutties", may appear to be a simple typo or bad translation, this has existed for many months, and I suspect something sinister may be behind this, perhaps even a call to action for kids to use their acquired skills in the real world, sickle in hand and their hatred for the upper class in the other.
EDIT: I have found one last tidbit, perhaps the most revealing of them all. A true bombshell, certain to convert anyone who still isn't quite convinced of this game being communist propaganda. This game is published by "Atriagames", which according to their official Twitter page as well as the fact they often use Russian on official sites (and even have published "Russian Car Driver"), is based out of Russia. Their cleverness was enough to get greenlit by Steam, but I will not allow it to pass through me, and I hope others feel the same. Do not buy this game, who knows what the communist blood money will go to?

Disclaimer: I haven't finished a game yet.
Wow. I mean, just wow. Trust those crazy French guys huh. The ambition of this game is just jaw-dropping. As someone who's been playing strategy games a _long_ time, I didn't expect to see so many changes to the Civilization style 4X format which just work. How do you stop city spam as a strategy? Only allow one city per map region. It just seems ridiculously simple when you put it like that, but game designers have been mucking around with global unrest etc. for years and never really got to the heart of the problem, which is too many cities. Here, they just limit the number of cities per region to one. Job done. Diplomacy: how do you make a cost for declaring war, or stop a player stealing all a losing faction's technology before they kill them? Simple: every diplomatic action requires Influence points, and those Influence points can be used for other things (notably an "Empire plan", which gives faction wide bonuses in various areas). You almost certainly can't steal all their technology just before you kill them, because you don't have enough Influence points. It works really well, and allows additional logical actions such as "Compliment" (makes them like you more and reduces the cost of positive actions) and "Warning" (moves you closer to war and reduces the cost of negative actions).
The artwork is frankly amazing. I just don't expect this level of artwork from a strategy game, certainly not from an independent designer. To be honest the map can be so busy it makes my eyes hurt, especially if you need to have the resource numbers displayed for some reason, but the artwork for the various map features is just beautiful.
The factions, ah the factions. I have never seen a list of eight factions which are so genuinely utterly different in their gameplay. One faction cannot declar war but can move its cities. One faction is forced to only have one city but can upgrade that city further than other factions and gets various benefits when razing enemy cities. One faction ignores food and gets a bonus for Dust production (the money of the game) but needs to use Dust to build population. One faction gets science bonuses and gets to nominate a resource which if it is consuming it gets various benefits, e.g. teleportation between cities. One faction gets less food and cannot make alliances, but gets cheap units and various benefits from killing units (friendly or enemy). One faction gets relatively few bonuses but can impose alliances on other factions.
Can you begin to see the strategic possibilities yet? I certainly can. Every faction will play almost completely differently. And every single faction has a well-written "main quest" to provide some focus as you play through the game.
There are also minor faction villages dotted through each region, which spawn roaming armies, and can be interacted with to provide quests to pacify them (or you can just kill or bribe them). If you "assimilate" a particular minor faction, you can now build units of its type, as well as getting a faction wide bonus to science or life points or building time etc. etc. In my current game I was lucky enough to start next to some Kazanji who I have assimilated, and they give me "Daemon" units, which are every bit as worth having as they sound.
I haven't even talked about Winter yet, where movement is halved and production is greatly reduced. You know roughly how long each season will last, but not precisely, so that means making some calculations (particularly when declaring war) about whether you want to declare war now or wait until you can be sure you will have a long enough summer to take the cities you're targeting.
Is the game perfect? No. Even with a tutorial, a large manual and a Wiki I still struggled to understand certain concepts. Sieges and fortification points spring to mind. Web searches and a certain amount of trial and error have generally cleared up those points though. Tactical combat is not particularly inspired. The most interesting idea is that you actually fight on the terrain from the global map. This can create some mildly interesting possibilities with bottlenecks, forests (give defence bonuses) and high ground (give attack bonuses). I have to say I think Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes does this better. Sieges are a bit of a letdown, basically you get some extra hitpoints and some attack and defence bonuses. My other slight concern is that there are so many strategic possibilities, how good is the AI going to be at understanding how they all interact? I'm playing my first game on Normal difficulty, and although the AI seems ok so far, I do seem to be a long way ahead of every other faction at what I guess is roughly the midpoint of the game. I'm used to playing strategy games on higher difficulty levels, and AI is frequently improved after release as the game designers get feedback from players, so this isn't necessarily a huge problem.
Would I recommend buying this game? Hell yes. I can't remember a game which blew me away with its level of ambition like this, and makes so many design choices which just work.

The reason I feel the need to write this review and to not recommend the game is because of how incredibly overrated it is. It even got the Game of the Year 2014 from RPS! Endless Legend is a solid 6.5, arguably a 7, but not an 8, much less a 9, and certainly not GOTY material.
In brief: there is a thousand decisions and a million clicks to make, but all ultimately amounting to very little. You can potentially have more fun working with an Excel spreadsheet
So, without further ado...
the Pros:
- very nice graphics
- interesting factions/story
- Simultaneous resolution TB combat with a couple of interesting twists
the Cons:
- the AI is terrible, no matter how they try to fix it. On my last game (the second of the 2 games I played till the end), played on hard, by the endgame it was me against a single AI (the rest were dead). The AI had more armies (they had like dozen and I had one and a half), more than twice as many points and in theory could crash me in a single turn. I won. I got a single army next to their capital, waited for their armies to decide to wonder off in completely random directions and made a sneak attack.
- Micromanagement. You may say, "wait, the AI could crash you in a single turn, so how can you say that it's bad?" Well, the reason it got into this advantageous position is because it expanded very quickly and wiped out the other AIs. I could have expanded and crushed the other AIs myself but I didn't because it was literally too boring and grueling to do so. I've not lost a single battle or loaded a game, but the insane amount of micromanagement I was expected to do with every new city and army got me every time. Examples:
*There is around 20 different resources, each of them doing something different and not intuitively obvious, but using them correctly is very important because of the boosts they give.
*Every time you want to expand your city, you need to decide on what tile to expand it to.
*To maximize efficiency you need to assign citizens to different tasks (in a city of 20, there is 20 of them... yay!).
*The units are exactly the same throughout the game (more on this on a separate point), but they have different slots for weapons, armor and special items. All these look more or less the same, but they come in different tiers and different colors (materials), which means that every time you discover a new weapon/armor tech you have to redesign your units and figure out exactly what's the minor advantage between that titanium and glassteel bow.
*etc, etc, etc. This game is a perfect simulation of chartered accountancy.

- Did I mention that the units are exactly the same throughout the game? You see, the interesting part of the story/world is that it's a post apocalypse pre apocalypse with a hint of technology-indistinguishable-from-magic deal. Awesome, right? You would think that your Vaulters, who emerge from the Vault in power armors, but armed with bows and hammers, will progressively wield more powerful technology. I mean, it makes sense that at some point they will learn how to make firearms, right? Nop. No, instead of a replacing your bowmen with riflemen or something like that, your bow tier 1 is replaced by bow tier 2 and so on and so worth... Of course, this is incredibly uncool, but in addition to that it means that there is no visual feedback to allow you to distinguish between units of different tech levels and that upgrading units (which is supposed to be fun) becomes a chore. You are always squinting your eyes to look at the numbers, which are the real protagonists of the game.

Imagine if Civ tried to be a fantasy RPG where you have minor factions (e.g. dwarves, orcs, etc.) instead of barbarians that you can assimilate into your empire and gain their units for production. Then imagine each major faction has a wierd modification that completely changes the way you play the game such as: removing food as a resource and making you buy citizens and repair units with dust (money), forcing you to only have one city that can become a super city, or being able to pick up your cities and walk them over to another tile and plop them down, as well the ability to craft your own faction.
Thats about half of the features of this game.

Before we start, I want to be clear: You're enjoyment (and the relevance of this review) depends entirely on what you're expecting from TheHunter: Primal. If you are expecting a slow-burn, high tension survival title in an alien world of dinosaurs, you may garner a lot of enjoyment from this game.
If you are expecting a immersive, realistic hunting simulator where you pursue and down the greatest creatures to ever walk the land, you will probably be disappointed.
First, the positive: the game is beautiful. The textures are crisp. The dinosaurs are quite colourful and varied looking, yet still manage to blend in enough to require careful spotting. The plantlife is dense and oppressive. The weather is startling to see for the first time. The world is huge and packed with dense forests, open plains, beaches and swampland.
The dinosaur damage model is highly detailed, with careful shot placement required to ensure that Utahraptor goes down in one shot, or at least bleeds out before it runs too far to track the body.
The sound design is also well thought out, as careful listening is needed to pick up approaching predators and tell their mood.
What are the major problems with this game? The largest (in my opinion) is the stamina and running mechanics. I mentioned this game is huge. It truly is, yet you walk with the speed and haste of a high-class Victorian lady visiting the Botanic Gardens on Sunday afternoon. The stamina bar is woefully low and is depleted in 10-15 seconds of running (the running too is far slower than any person with full use of their legs would manage when being pursued by hungry dinos). It refills much slower than it is consumed. I can understand wanting to discourage endless running over kilometres without breaking a sweat, but for the self-proclaimed "most realistic prehistoric survival game ever created", this is extremely tiresome, not to mention immersion breaking. It also makes no sense from a standpoint of offering a challenge to players: most everything can outrun you if it makes a beeline for you, and running already makes extra noise, so why bother adding ANOTHER impediment to your escape? It would have made more sense to add a general "exhaustion" meter that slowly increases the more you run, that slows machete swings and makes aiming more difficult as it fills.It also makes tracking wounded dinos a pain, as they will run far from your position in the time it takes them to bleed out. The choice of stamina bar clashes harshly with the wide open spaces and fast dinos around you, especially considering you are meant to be a fit, strong colonist capable of crafting machetes and bows from scrap.
This brings me to the second major complaint: the predatory dinosaurs. The predators on this island are incredibly numerous, and VERY dangerous. This may sound exactly like a predatory dinosaur should be, but let me ellaborate. These creatures are determined to catch you. VERY determined. Too determined. T-rexs will more often than not just *happen* to wander in a straight line towards you, and once there refuse to leave until you move from hiding. Once again this would not be a problem if it were not for other choices made in development, such as the inability to run for any real length of time, and the limited weaponry or distractions. Just to reiterate, this helps makes the game stressful and tense, effective for survival gamers, but infuriating for hunting enthusiasts who simply want to grab a rifle and track down a triceratops.
Other complaints involve the lack of swimming mechanics to allow lake crossings, or even crossing 10ft wide bays at the beach, the dinosaurs' stilted attack animations (that do fortunately make the machete a viable weapon against solitary raptors), and the absurdly high populations of predators. Arrows are also extremely difficult to track in flight, and hence getting a grip on the shooting mechanics is primarily trial and error (since you can't retrieve arrows from the ground you're discouraged from practicing shooting trees and stones). The predators themselves are too... predatory. Why is it the T-rex's will always go out of their way to catch a bite sized meal like me when a raptor just walked by them. Why can't they ever just not be hungry you know... LIKE REAL ANIMALS. In fact, other than apparently clearing out when a T-rex wanders their way, the other dinos don't come into ANY conflict with each other, limiting your strategies to deal with them.
If the developers DID intend this to be a survival game primarily, then I'm baffled by the lack of food requirements (other than health regenerating eggs and mushrooms), proper shelter (other then some bare concrete walls to hide behind) or other survival staples. The only goals really are to go from landmark to landmark across open ground, avoid the overly numerous Tyrannosaurs, gather some ammo and hunt something for points, before lettting yourself die so you can use those points to buy a better weapon. Survival in this game is too often down to dumb luck. HOPEFULLY a T-rex won't march right up to you just as you got a .44 magnum with no bullets. HOPEFULLY a Quetzacoatls won't grab you as you're lining up a shot on a raptor and drop you 70ft to you're death. HOPEFULLY those raptors won't wander on top of your hiding spot.
If what you were expecting was The Hunter with dinosaurs, where you choose from a variety of weapons a gadgets to track down elusive and deadly creatures in their natural habitat, then you'll probably be disappointed. I appreciate that Expansive Worlds wanted something different for this game. And there is still time to make a strong impression in future updates. But I feel that if they had simply ported the weapons and hunting mechanics from the Hunter, and made this current game mode optional, they would have made a stronger first impression.
Too sum up: Buy if you want to crawl past huge predators, sneak around raptor packs and quietly through herds of triceratops with hair trigger tempers.
Don't buy if you're looking for a hardcore hunting simulator where you can bring you're favourite mauser rifle to bag a velociraptor at 150m.
To each their own I suppose.

Auto-detection of one's internet connection speed would help reduce the instances of lag occurring. These are things a actively supporting developer could see to addressing.
What the game does right is give you feats of prowess to grant XP, and unlocks. It also gives you randomised daily feats to accomplish to gain XP, or a specified number of costume coins. The majority of the costume options are clever approximations of what normal people might use to make their Batz costume or their Jokerz costume. The homemade weapons are rather well thought out, and fit naturally into the arsenal that is available to players. What is there is quite entertaining, even for those who are more Batman fan that a FPS player.
There are 4 game modes, but only traditional Team Deathmatch (TDM) sees action everyday, even though the other modes are all TDM with a special twist that is even more fun that traditional TDM.

Stay! Stay! DPRK is a humoristic anime-styled visual novel. While not very long - it took me 3 hours to complete - the game is pretty decent for what it is; a "Go! Go! Nippon!" parody. A good one at that. Why is it a "Go! Go! Nippon!" Parody? Because the entire game is pretty much the same thing, only that instead of Japan (Nippon) you are in North Korea (True Korea!).
The basic Plotline is the same thing as in "Go! Go! Nippon!". You are an American US Marine in the "Waterdog" unit (which in real life specializes on water treatment) and you know some penpal friends in the DPRK. Upon arriving there, you realize that your 2 male friends are not male, but 2 female soldiers in the Korean People's Army.
As I guess characters tend to be in visual novels, the protagonist is the most blatant, unrelatable and naive character you've ever seen, and the game utilizes this for it's humor and some stereotype-jokes. However, the game doesn't take itself too seriously overall, and 4th wall breaking is a constant thing through the Protagonist's thoughts and almost every character's knowledge of the meta level and the 4th wall.
Besides the humorous storytelling, the inside jokes that an unaware reader might skip, and the hilariously cliche-fueled perspective of North Korea, the game also allows you to actually date the 2 main girls/waifus, Jeong and Eunji. While that doesn't influence the story too much - the story that only really comes into play in the last 15 minutes anyway - it is still a nice aspect that is fun on one hand, as well as another cliche on the huge pile of stereotypes this game reinforces.
Game also features some CGs of the girls besides the normal dialogue artwork, fap potential still limited however.
Overall good game.

After playing
, DEVGRU-P's previous Visual Novel, I kept my expectations quite low for this one. The former game just seemed too rushed, low-budget and not very rewarding at the end of the day.
Turns out I was wrong on this one!
is actually a pretty decent Visual Novel, and a polished one at that. It has a very decent UI, detailed widescreen backgrounds, gorgeous CGs and sprites. Even the music is on-par with some of the professional VNs from Japan, with the catchy main menu theme sticking out. Speaking of that one, why are the lyrics in JAPANESE INVADER PIG-DOG LANGUAGE?
Apart from that expect a standard visual novel with two girl routes. If you already played visual novels before, you know the deal. Focus on one girl, make decisions in favor of her and make her your waifu. Or don't choose any of the two girls like the indecisive wuss you are.
What really makes this game unique is the setting though. No other video game comes into mind where you're able to daytrip North Korea, especially not if we consider the current news headlines regarding the bizarre East-Asian dictatorship.
The game puts you in the shoes of
, an American veteran of the Afghanistan war who's about to visit his two penpals in North Korea. Well, turns out that his penpals
and
are in fact two busty sisters just waiting to put the protagonist in a harem situation and to show him around the country.
While the story is clearly a black comedy with a grain of seriousness, you can definitely sense that the developers or at least the script writers took some effort by studying real-life North Korea. If you already read about stories from travelers who undertook trips to North Korea, you may recognise many details. In fact you may even learn a new thing or two about one of the world's most isolated countries.
To see all of the endings and CGs you'll need about 6 hours. I think that's pretty good considering how well the small team behind this game pulled off this production.
I definitely recommend it if you are into Visual Novels, black humor, memes, military topics and politics. Make sure to install the
from the official website. Once more it's not absolutely necessary, but it makes the experience more complete. Because of reasons, you know.

This is hands down my most favorite game of all time. An independently developed Civil Engineer Puzzle, Thriller, Mystery, Survival game I never knew I wanted! A game like that must sound odd to most, after all, what could be so thrilling about being a game where your job is to go around fixing a city's worth of infrastructural issues? The fact is, everything's been abandoned, built poorly, in extreme disrepair, or just down right broken. Also most of the things in those horrible conditions are not things you want like that. Such as Subway tunnels, sewer tunnels under the city, a whole dam, water treatment plants, power stations, and it all falls under a corruption scandal. The story is still going and the final Part 3 is still on the horizon with no release date in sight, but I have faith an amazing game like this has people working passionately behind the scenes to complete this properly but at their own pace. The one thing I want to point out as the big part of the game I enjoy, it has to be the Engineering puzzles. The story is awesome, the suspenseful almost horror like elements are well done on their own, but my interest is mainly with the Puzzles. I always feel like I accomplished something when I run around a building or a series of tunnels and manage to fix something using only notes and signs left behind by the now unemployed workers or unfortunate explorers, or just my ability as a puzzle solver to find the answer to each puzzle. And they always feel like a pure achievement as you fix a water treatment plant the city needed, or restoring electricity, preventing disasters, correcting the problems like a Civil Engineer would in real life! In fact I'd say the game about meets the definition of engineer: A person who performs precision guess work based on unreliable data provided by those of questionable knowledge. See also Wizard, Sorcerer. I'd say fixing a whole city's infrastructure using sticky notes and ones own wits about sum up the game. This game is a must have!

Despite all that, I really enjoyed this game, and I'm eagerly looking forward to part 3!

In this review, I will not be comparing this game SPECIFICALLY to any other Elder Scrolls games. However, my opinions will be based on this game in comparison to the series, and to other RPG's. I am doing this because I played Skyrim first, then Morrowind, then this. Also, the points I make in this review will be considering the fact that this game was released in 2006, so comparing to games much later isn't entirely fair. Enough rambling, let's get started.
TLDR; Great game, don't compare it to Skyrim solely, and if you keep an open mind you can discover what this game has to offer like I did.
PROS:
+ First and foremost, follows the formula very well for what makes a good Elder Scrolls game, as well as an RPG and open world game.
+ Fantastic world, argued by many to be the best in the series.
+ Almost unlimited player choice when it comes to character creation and progression.
+ Tons of variation in the world, from NPCs to shops to entire towns, you won't see the same thing twice.
+ Most quests in the game are fantastic, and are not like other TES games where you are always fetching item A or killing person B. There are some truly memorable quests from this game, both good and bad.
+ Factions in this game are the strongest and most diverse in the entire series. Most of them are structured differently as well, offering even more variety to your experience.
+ NPCs in the world react to the things you do and the feats you accomplish, making the world feel the most alive and believable it has ever been.
+ Despite what you may read online, there is no specific way you must level your character to remain "efficient." Play as you like.
+ Character progression is well balanced and makes sense.
NEUTRAL:
+- The Main Quest in this game is beloved by many, but for me got tedious and repetitive towards the end.
+- There are several factions in which you can "join," but can't progress your rank in any way.
+- The game, for anyway, requires some basic mods to be playable in 2017 (UI mods, patches, etc.) This is listed as neutral as this is something to be expected a games age, but graphics, content, or gameplay mods aren't something I consider essential for a 2017 playthrough.
CONS:
- Probably the least believable TES game in terms of the player's position in the world. There is absolutely no reason for the player to be in the position they are in at the start of the game.
- No reason the player should be able to be good at so many things. In Morrowind, you were the Nerevarine, and Skyrim the Dragonborn, so at least in those worlds it made sense for you specifically to turn out powerful and amazing at some point. In Oblivion, your character is not anyone special, and thus makes it hard for me to believe that they are just naturally willing to help anyone and everyone they see once they escape the opening level.
- This game practically forces you to follow the main quest. In other games, once you complete the often horrible tutorial levels, you can go anywhere you wish and ignore the main quest if you like. In this game, even though you mean nothing to anyone from the start, you are thrown immediately into the conflict because of a "vision" someone has.
- User interface by default is designed for consoles, even though this game doesn't offer gamepad support.
- The system in which you must use to level up is atrocious, and one can find themselves very easily over or under-leveling their characters if they don't choose appropriate major skills from the start.
- As is TES fashion, the tutorial level is terrible.
I know that my CONS section is almost as long as my PROS section, but don't let that stop you from buying and trying this game. It is an excellent Elder Scrolls game, and has its share of flaws like the others do. I do recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the series, or action RPG's in particular.
Overall Score: 8/10

Ok, so let me start by saying I do enjoy this game a lot, but I (and im sure many others) would like it a lot better if there were more dino's and possibly even more weapons, but I'm not too fussed about it.
GAMEPLAY
theHunter: Primal is a hunting game. So don't go into it expecting to be able to kill the dino's, cook their meat and eat it, or be able to build a shelter. This game is a survival game, but not in the sense like the forest or stranded deep. I haven't played the normal theHunter game so I'm not sure if this game has the same mechanics, but i do enjoy the tracking system, and the ability to use stealth to your advantage to either hunt or get away from a dino. The game has no plot or storyline which does make it a bit boring for those people who expect to have an overall mission. 8/10 for gameplay.
THE MAP
The world that this game is set on is visually stunning (if you have a decent computer) and is actually really big, so you can spend a lot of hours just navigating your way around the map and discovering the different environments which in itself is enjoyable. The addition of settlements is great because they can provide players with a goal or shelter. 10/10 for the map.
MULTIPLAYER
This game is pretty much just a multiplayer game. There is no point even bothering to play singleplayer because you will die. I am yet to play on a PvP server because personally I find it more enjoyable to hunt with others, not against them. This game is meant for friends to actually play together and take down a rex, which is why you can buy it in a 4-pack. You will find people even in PvE servers that will backstab you and take your stuff, but you will find even more people that will help you survive if you are a new player ( I have helped multiple new player get to a settlement and get some gear). 8/10 for multiplayer.
DINO AI, SPAWNRATE AND HITBOXES
Ok, so this is defeniatly the biggest issue that the game has. The AI for most of the dino's is really annoying and is kinda dumb (they are working on improving this though). The spawnrate of dino's is actually reasonably good at the moment, and pretty much all old players will know of the problems created by some updates (When they increased the rex spawn rate so you couldn't walk through a field without seeing 10 rexes, and the Quetz update where you couldn't walk though a field without being dropped to your death). The hitboxes at the moment are terrible and gotta be fixed. I have been picked up by quetz's when i am standing 10 feet on either side of it, and bitten by Utahraptors even when I sidestep them. 6/10 for the AI, spawnrate and hitboxes
OVERALL VERDICT
Overall, i would defeniatly recommend this game for people looking for a game which provides a good teamwork experience, and are looking to make friends while hunting dino's (it's a win-win if you ask me). I would tell people that want a game where they can just jump in and start spraying dino's to look somewhere else.
7/10 rating for the whole game.

Been playing since early access with over 160 hours of exploring the game solo and with groups of up to 6 people. Overall I like the game. I’m not going to go in to the balance and state of the game as of this review because that changes from patch. Instead I am going to cover how I play the game, and some of the notable aspects that struck me. Side note, I have never played any hunting games
and do not have an interest in doing so. I have yet to try any of the PVP but having played the original DAYZ mod for Arma 2… ya I’ll just stick to the PvE where the humans can’t ruin your day.
First off, the visuals started out very decent and just got better over time. Now in April of 2015, the weather effects are absolutely fantastic and wandering around the island is still breathtaking. And it’s not just grand vistas, it’s the attention to detail. The little PDA you use that shows what you are looking at in game is accurate when another player looks at your PDA for example. You can see the world reflect in other players eyes, the leaves from trees blow in a uniform direction to denote wind. It’s little things like that which impressed me.
Another interesting feature of the game is the sound. This is one of the few games where it actually matters. Almost any game I have played, I really could blair music or have a movie playing at the same time and not be affected. In Primal, everything is silenced but the game sounds. Even after you get comfortable with the game, the sounds are essential to knowing what’s coming and what it is. I found that having a nice subwoofer is one of the best early warning T-Rex detection systems available :-).
My third point is the most subjective but you are reading my review so you’re going to get my opinions. In my opinion, the game is beyond my patience and skill to play solo and enjoy; it’s too hard. I found I had much more fun with a small group, even if it was just one other person
. If I did not have friends to play with, I probably would have abandoned the game after a few hours of exploring and being eaten. Not only can you be overwhelmed by dinosaurs but the supplies in the game are relatively scarce. This is not a complaint; I LIKE that things are scarce and that you are often down to a few precious rounds and if those fail, you are likely to die. But because there is that element of chance and that “being in the wrong place at the wrong time” aspect, the few people working with you can avert a total loss into a narrow escape or only a few deaths. Even after you are pimped out in the noble came and have whatever weapons you wanted, you are just as frail as you were when you landed and having the most powerful gun does NOT mean you are safe.
So overall, I am pleased with the game. You need 2-3 hour sections of time to really enjoy it when you hop on so don’t think you are going to play for 20 minute and be fine when you log on next, but I am happy with the time I have got out of it to date.

Warframe scratches my itch for more than one reason. Its' fast-paced combat system (melee, mainly), the fact it's somewhat sci-fi/futuristic and also the fact that I can play this game again, again and again. Having hidden hints of story scattered across the game is just a (great) bonus. As someone, who loves a good chunk of story, I honestly didn't expect much from this game, it being primarily shooter/horde-killing type of game, but it managed to surprise me in more than one way, and continues doing so over the course of almost two years I have been playing.
Add up the fact that the developers behind this game seem to genuinely care for making a fun game, their strong connection with the community; quite unrivalled in the gaming industry. For a first time, in last two decades of my gaming time, this is a game I enjoy not only as a product, but also because of the people, who work on it. With close to 1300 hours played over two accounts I used to love this game. A simplistic side scrolling MOBA that's very easy to get into, what's not to like? A lot of time was spent in the game, I made friends and we had lots of fun. Unfortunately, as time passed the flaws of the game were revealed.
This game actually favors people with poor internet connections and if you don't have a bad internet connection you might as well simulate one to gain unfair advantage over your opponents. How is this possible? Due to Ronimo being a small company they can't really supply dedicated servers so they designed the game for p2p networking. You have the option to queue in different regions, same or nearby would be recommended. It doesn't matter though, if someone feels the need to queue worldwide (maybe because lack of players) they can join you no matter what your settings are. It gets frustrating real fast playing an opponent with over 300 ms of latency. They can actually pick a naut that favours their ping to get the upper hand because it gets impossible to dodge certain skills because you can't anticipate where a projectile might be on their screen and before you know it you've been hit. If someone choose to queue worldwide you'd think it'd be more of a challenge for them because of latency but it's really the other way around.
And if they don't have high latency they might have packet loss and that can actually trigger effects on abilities multiple times. There's a naut that has the ability to pull other nauts to him using his tongue, if the player has packet loss he can actually tongue you multiple times and this is very frustrating. His client registers that he hit his ability but the packet was lost and had to be sent again and maybe a few more times.
The design wouldn't be so awful if both players had a say in the matter and dedicated servers would make it even better and actually favor players playing on the right side of the globe.
Networking issues aside, the matchmaking could also use some work. Solo queuing is ok but can be a terrible experience since players can just leave the game without any ramifications. If the player hosting the game crashes and the host migration fails everyone gets a loss. Some maps end in single lanes which makes a choke point and favors nauts that can turtle and just delay the game for as long as possible.

As you probably might guess by the Awesomnauts' cutesy artstyle and wacky character design this game was built around the idea of creating a casual and arcady 2D MOBA. The idea was executed well: gameplay is indeed largely twitch skill based, yet most of the mechanics familiar from DOTA clones were preserved. Learning curve is pretty mild and the game is satisfying to play right off the bat. There is a sufficient degree of complexity in terms of metagame, so it's not entirely meaningless, but superior platforming skill can definitely elevate even the crappiest of builds to a point where you might be an asset to the team. There is also a pretty varied roster of characters, all with their own style and personality. On top of that, devs are still adding new content, which gives you incentive to come back regularly, as it almost guaranteed to feel fresh again.
The few gripes I have with it are not related to the core gameplay as much as they're basically inevitable problems that this game has to face as a multiplayer game run by a small indie studio and a (sort of) MOBA. One of them would be the occasional toxicity you might encounter in the game. It can be upsetting and annoying, but it's still slightly better than in LOLs and DOTAs. Matchmaking is another problem. The issue here lies in the basic reality that there simply aren't enough concurrent players at any given time  to make the algorithm work well so the result is oftentimes you end up in very lopsided  matches and unequal team members. The best remedium for this is to play with friends, that way it won't affect you nearly as much.  There is also a huge chasm between what the most dedicated part of the community, those who play in League 1 and 2, wants and what all the rest wants  and  sometimes it seems like the devs don't quite know how to deal with these conflicting demands which sometimes leads to some balancing issues. But that's rather a minor complaint as this state never lasts for very long and eventually returns to equilibrium.
With all that said, Awesomenauts still has me going back to it and despite my frustrations I can still say that it's still ton of fun and I recommend it without any hesitation.

I used to own this game retail, and bought the steam version for the small DLC items like horse armour adn those houses (which was cheaper in the sale than buying all those small DLC seperated). I had arround 800 hours in this game already when I bought the Steam version, and at time of writing another 150 have been added. To me Oblivion is in many ways better than Skyrim. Yes, Skyrim gave me 1600+ hours so far, but in all honestly, it's because I like modding and the 64bit engine let me do more in that field. For playing, I open Oblivion way more times.
I'm a huge sucker for older RPGs. Many people tell me certain games are broken, while in truth, I never had a problem, and those people are generally not used to make decision while overthinking long-term consquences, listen to what NPCs say, etc. In all honestly, I'm sad gameplay from games is strating to look more and more like each other, and I often grab my older games for their typical gameplay.
The game has a great, complex, but well working leveling system. You do indeed need to pay attention and think things trough, but thinking about the consequences of each of your actions, both short and long term, is part of a good RPG. If you're on of those kids who has only played newer games, you might come to find older games are less easy, and help you/protect you less. Oblivion is one of the more easy/protective in this (for example, Morrowind would simply tell you you ruined the world if you killed someone important, you was so stupid to randomly kill people after all), but it's not as caretaking as Skyrim and other newer games are. Personally, I love this. When I grew up, children games where as difficult as adult games now, and I think this is a sad development.
The voice-acting, yes it's horrible, and so are the graphics. It was outdated when it started. It's the reason I once started modding years ago. However, with the right set of mods, it looks very decent, and as someone who even loves playing on a Commadore64, or other old computers and consoles, I think the older look and feel has it's charme. It's defiantly not unplayable to a newer generation gamer, especially not with mods like OCOv2 and HGEC arround. That being sad, don't expect your game to run as nice as people have in screen archery. Even tho you can indeed mod it that greatly, you should not forget that Oblivion is a 32bit game, which means it won't use your hardware to it's fulles potential, most noteworthy, it can only uses 4GB ram (with a patch, not even by default!). You might find many bugs and crashes with modding it to look so awesome. However, it will still be able to look very playable and even pretty, even tho it will have an older feel to it.
Story-wise, it's great. Not just the main story, or the side stories (like the Dark Brotherhood, fighters guild, mages guild, thieves guild, arena), but also many sidequests are more than a simple fetchquest, or a simple "go murder [NPC]" quest. Some make you think about what the best result should be. Dialogs become more important, and decisions have to be made. Many side quests are longer, and need a combination of sneaking, talking, fighting, and might offer ways arround them. Sometimes, the skills you have, the disposition, and previous actions, might allow for extra options (or the removal of them). You won't be warned or told. It's up to you to find out. I think this is a great thing!
Another story related things that I love, that many older RPGs have, is these little, useless, but hilarious quests or references, like having a quests about potatoes someone mentioned previously. It makes you smile, and even when it's sometimes stupid, un-immersive, it's also hilarious and it gives a nice feel to the game. After all, you don't play an RPG to be in a world that is just like the real one, and the funny stupidities really brighten my day.
Compared to Skyrim, this game is a thousand times beter. My biggest problem in comparing the two is that Skyrim is too simplified. The quests and storylines where simplefied so you could blindly folow map markers. The gameplay, all the mechanics, where all simplefied so non-rpg fans could jump in without explanation. In Skyrims case, it made the game kinda boring, easy, and after a while, repetative. I sadly see many modern games do this, and it makes me sad. I wish more games where made like this. I miss the time RPGs where popular.
A funny part in the comparison with Skyrim tho, is that I find Oblivions landscapes to be more simular and boring than Skyrim, unlike most people. Skyrim had snowfields, tundra, woods. But in Oblivion, many places are basic grass landscapes, sometimes basic woods. Only towards Bruma I see huge differences.
Imho, Skyrim is great at looking pretty, and for modding and screen archery, or when you feel like something simple you don't need to think too much about (which I also often do), it defiantly wins in those subjects. But for actual gameplay and story, Oblivion is way better than the newer title in the series.
One last thing that does make me sad, is that the Steam version has trouble with loose files when modding. This makes modding a bit more complicated, as I have to make a OBMM compatible file, just to unpack that file (after which, it suddenly works). As someone who has learned manual modding when BOSS and OBMM wasn't a thing yet, and someone who always does everything manually, it's a lot of extra work for nothing.

Full review:

Oh man, Endless Legend is like if Vlaada Chvatil designed Civilization set in Smallworlds.
Now that I've said the board-gaming-nerdiest thing in my life, I mean that it takes that 4X style game, makes some clever and major changes to the systems, makes every system important to the whole play experience, and then makes every choice feel way more important (and, occasionally, bone-wrenchingly painful decisions).
And if you try to play it like Civ, you'll fail spectacularly, like I did. You can't just ignore subsystems you don't normally focus on - you'll have to become familiar with the diplomacy system and upgrade your units manually and consider each of these choices in detail. So if you're used to relying on a automated manager system for some of those mechanics, you'll be in for a rude awakening -- because there either isn't one, or the AI isn't very good -- but one that'll make you a better player even as you're having fun failing.
if you want a fantasy-setting 4X game that's a little leaner and a lot sharper, pick it up. Just be careful, as you'll be one-more-turn-ing long into the night.
Fantastic game. Can't recommend it enough.

It could be that it is a bit early to review a game when only having progressed through the tutorial, but let that stand as a testiment to the quality of this game.
If you are looking for a new 4X game that is at the same time familiar and refreshing, look no further, for this game is tops.
As someone who has played every Civ game ever over these past couple decades, I feel I must classify myself as a "4X fan".  One of my greatest desires over that seemingly endless span  ( ... ) has been a true, quality fantasy 4X game.  Many a whack has been taken at scratching this itch, but it wasn't until I encountered Endless Legend that I feel maybe I have finally hit it.  Fallen Enchantress is quite a good game, but to me it seemed to lack something I couldn't quite define.  Whatever that something is, Endless HAS it.  It is quite possible that I am simply a graphics wh*re and this game is gorgeous.  But I think that what they have managed to do with Endless is make a fantasy 4X that FEELS as complete and refined as the Civ games always have.
There are certainly many similarities with Civ.  You have a cities and armies upon which you expand and improve via a science-based research tree.  You have a social influence metric that plays into your diplomatic relations and your faction's happiness and prestige.  You have minor factions with whom you can gain favor for benefits.  You move your units across a hex-based map to explore, find ruins or initiate combat with other units.  However, each of these things is implemented with a fresh twist, which is where I think Endless wins its biggest points, in my book.
To elaborate:
-The world map is divided into regions.  Unlike Civ or Fallen Enchantress (yes, these are my largest points of comparison here... I feel for good reason) you can't simply pop out new cities wherever you like.  Instead, you can develop on city per region (unless I am mislead by the tutorial).  You can improve upon luxury resources throughout the region, even if they don't fall into your city's immediate "zone of control".  Your city will, however, still only be able to "work" the tiles within it's influence sector.  Said influence sector expands as you buid improvements to your city, which I feel is brilliant and refreshing.
-Minor factions, once encountered, can be made peacable either by force or by lending aid by way of quest completion.  Once the faction is peacable, you can spend your cultural influence currency to assimilate the faction, granting you specialized units based on said faction.  Again, all brilliant!
-Unit-based exploration is, at first glance, again very similar.  However, finding ruins is not simply a "guarantee of random free stuff", but rather can yield nothing at all, various research or financial boons (with improved liklihood of such if you choose to boost your exploration skillz) or can potentially present you with large, ogre-y obsticles.  Units will initiate combat in their map tile, with adjacent enemy units, much as they would in Civ, et al.  However, once combat is initiated, your units deploy to surrounding region either manually or based on a formation you prescribe.  Combat itself has tactical layers, with general per-unit stratigems which can also be predetermined by you or controlled play-by-play if you so choose.  For those less inclined to get into the nitty gritty (or those times when you so vastly overpower your enemy that it hardly matters) combat can be set to auto-resolve as well.  BRILLIANT, I say!
Again, this review may seem wordy or premature considering the nary more than an hour I've spent learning the ropes in the tutorial.  BUT, I feel that was enough time to get a good sense of how this one rolls and I must say, it rolls beautifully.
