Timber and Stone is a City Builder game that combines elements from Real Time Strategy and Sandbox games, the goal of the game is simple, guide your settlers to create a sustainable settlement, and survive for as long as you can. Personaly I love this game, simply because I love City Builders, but the traits that put Timber and Stone above all other City Builders on my list, are its complexity and its micro-management features. I love the fact that the game lets me build anyway I want, to direct my settlers with simple commands, to perform complex tasks, and finally, the dullness is gone!!! that feeling you get when you build your settlement, to unlock better structures or to reach higher population, until eventually you just ask yourself, "now what?" that "dullness" is non-existant in Timber and Stone, because there is always a bigger challenge to overcome. I recomend this game, even though its on early access, its a very good experience as it is, and to think the developers have more in store for us is just outstanding.

For a management sim ala DF and others of the genre, this game is, honestly, pretty bad.  I just don't understand how all these people can review a game in development this long so glowingly, when any veteran of this genre can see within a few hours of playing it is exceedingly clunky and lacking in many ways.
First let's start with the interface.  UI is important for a game like this since so many decisions require querying a usable interface.  This interface is a throwback from more than a decade ago.  No resizable, movable windows, bizarre, clunky interface patterns, poor fonts, a lack of tooltips, and on an on.  Remove a designation?  Alt-Shift and click!  Obviously!  You will buy the game anyway, because you are a sucker for this genre like I am.  And you will say "Well, that dude was right."
Management of the AI is a lesson in frustration.  Each settler may only have one job activated at a time, and if you want to change a job on a settler, it requires a few clicks to manually change.  If you are a veteran of these genres, you certainly are wondering, "Why don't I just set the priorities for my jobs so if no orders are present for a higher priority job, I will fallback to a lower priority one?"  This doesn't exist.  One of the most fundamental concepts for this genre and it is absent.  Be prepared to be pausing and clicking until you have carpal tunnel.  You will be spending hours changing jobs on settlers as priorities shift until enough immigrants have arrived to fill your basic needs without switching them manually. At that point you will just leave your core settlers at their jobs even when they idle, because the idea of switching them manually anymore brings tears to your eyes.
There is no concept of hauling between stockpiles.  All stockpiles appear to be magical entities that transport goods across the map.  So if your farmer puts food in his nearby stockpile, someone else can grab it out of his magical stockpile four levels down immediately.  Who needs stockpile optimization in this type of game anyway?  Sigh.
Combat is god awful.  Since there is not really any military organization whatsoever, when you get attacked by the three or four types of NPC groups that exist, you will need to pause, change the jobs of your settlers to soldiers / archers, and then basically micromanage them by constant moving and pausing until the fight is over.  Things get a bit better once you grow large enough, as you generally have full-time soldiers, but you will still need to micro them for battles of any size.  At that point you just draft any new immigrants into your undead army because there isn't much else for them to do.
Pathfinding and job fulfillment still have fundamental issues.  You will have to constantly manually path settlers so they resume what they were doing.  Want your archer to train?  Sure he will train, for a while, until he wanders off to upgrade or eat, or whatever.  After that, if he is not right next to the training dummies, he will just idle at your meeting hall.  You will need to click on him and move him back manually to his training dummies.  Get used to it - you will spend most of your game doing this in some form or another.  How does a game that has been in development for four years still have fundamental issues with the foundation on which everything else is built?
There is no point to building anything other than walls and doors.  The screenshots from the store page?  Pointless.  There are no prefab buildings and there are no game mechanics that encourage you to build them manually.  These buildings were constructed (very, very slowly and tediously), for absolutely no purpose other than a screenshot.  There is no concept of housing, or rooms, or even sleeping other than recovering from wounds.  Your settlers seem to work 24/7, they have no moods, or desires (other than food), or quirks (meaningful in this context anyway).  There are no socialization, mood, beauty, recreation, weather, seasons, temperature, or any other such mechanics expected from this genre.
I played the game until day 35-40 or so, had almost every profession maxed (except for engineering, which is impossibly slow to level), had a slew of fully kitted soldiers and archers, and frankly found the game quite easy.  Any veteran of these games would find it that way.  As long as you micro combat and retreat wounded settlers, there is really no danger unless you get unlucky in the first few weeks.
I have many, many games in my library, and I have never felt compelled to post a review until now.  I love this genre and wanted to love this game, but it just is not there and I'm not sure it ever will be, early access or not.  Do yourself a favor and grab Rimworld, or Gnomoria, or just re-download DF for the tenth time.  Thank me later.

If you have a hankering for turn based strategy, this will appeal to fantasy and non-fantasy fans alike. The hero units (while capable of soloing) are much better placed in organized battle units. Those battles take place on a hexagonal grid with individual unit control! Ruins and the like are balanced in that they provide different rewards based on your current tech level, and while there is a chance to discover a rediculous weapon, it won't be equippable until you have that resource, preventing random steam rolls. Even better though, is that each player benefits from exploration, regardless if another player already did. Letting you play the game at your own pace rather than be rushed into clearing out 'huts'.
All of the systems are linked together, tech, cities, heroes, units, exploration and the game is adequately paced (incremental research costs, expansion penalties) so that the game isn't immediately decided once a single player has an edge. There are multiple paths to victory, though probably only 4 of those are unique. And the races play differently to one another, at least 3 of which are notably different enough to completely alter your style of play.
The only gripe I have with the game is that the empire editing mechanic is supremely unbalanced. Empire attributes are foolishly priced and empires start with more or less than the starting points they should have. Fortunately this is pretty minor, as effective army and empire design will trump any bonuses you may or may not have.
To summarize if you enjoy turn based strategy, this is a must have for your collection.

Really Unique Take on the 4x genre.  Factions play completely different. Interface is ungodly slick and gorgeous.  Impossible and higher difficulty are some BS, but I think you can find good games on Serious.  Apparently not very well balanced in multiplayer from what I've heard but for singleplayer it is worth a look.  I love a lot of what it does.  Just some examples of some of the factions:
- Bugs who can only make war. Use dead bodies from battles to boost food production in a city.
- Crazy puppet dudes who are only allowed to make one city
- Gypsy like faction who can move cities and isn't allowed to declare war and focused on trade, and mercenaries.
- Diplomatically inclined dragons
Each faction has a main quest (not sure what happens when you beat them but along the way you get cool rewards.).  Minor factions you can assimilate into your army.  There's a fully working stock market esque marketplace although I wish the AI would use it more.
The map is ungodly gorgeous and theres a cool tilt shift effect when you zoom in.  Battles take place with stacks of units meeting and then fighting on the actual hexes of the world for 6 phases.  You can give pretty specific orders to units as far as who to attack and buff and where to move but they are not garuteed to be followed. I get a Heroes of Might and Magic Vibe for some reason from the battles even though they're different mechanics Overall it is an interesting system.  You upgrade your units with gear you aquire through research and moving through the ages if you wish.  I do wish there was an 'ultra' unit for each faction, as each faction only has I believe 3 units (which can be augmented by minor factions you asimiliate, or mercs).  Apparently the lore is pretty deep and all of the Endless games tie in to eachother (Endless Legend, Dungeon Of The Endless, and Endless Space).
Basically a really gorgeous, slick take on the 4x genre which might not be the deepest 4x around but has tons of stuff going for it.  Not to rag on Civ:BE which I don't have anything against, but comparing BE to Endless Legend and the uniqueness of the factions is quite a change of pace.  Civ V is still probably the game to beat for most players, but Endless Legend definitely deserves a look if you are a fan of the genre.
I've addressed the pros.  And seriously, Civ:BE's interface can only fantasize about being as good as Endless Legend.  You right click to back out of ANY screen, it's a beautiful thing.
Cons would be -
-Unit variety (any way you slice it a faction really only has 3 units), the AI has almost always spammed 1 type of unit against me.
- Multiplayer Balance (which is made up for in singleplayer uniqueness)
- Animations are really slow for battle, you need to speed them up in the map options BEFORE you start. Trust me start with the animations turned all the way up or late game battles will drag on for minutes and minutes with not even much happening.
- Really really bad AI cheating on the 2 highest difficulty levels, but what can you do?

Firstly, I would like to thank the 4X-enthusiast group eXplorminate for giving away this game.  I typically don't pay much attention to giveaways, but I actually won something that time.  And that something happened to be a game that seemed somewhat fascinating to me at the time.
As of now, Endless Legend is a whole lot more than "mildly fascinating," and I am shocked I did not know about it sooner.  This is one of the few games that I wish so many more people
know about.  My opinion of this game is from the perspective of a[nother] person stepping into it from Civilization V.  I also have some Total War to be comparing it to, so I have that to reference as well.  That said....
Endless Legend is a beautiful game.  There are few other words that can describe it so aptly.  The presentation of Auriga (the gameworld) from the map anomalies to the tile improvements that match the civilization's stylistic impressions to the special effects during winter to the GUI, everything about the game is beautiful.  The UI deserves a special shout-out, because everything is placed so intuitively, and it's simple, clean, and elegant.  There is no other game that matches the polish of Endless Legend's UI (although vanilla Civ and G+K were both very meticulous through the menus and what-not).  As a turn-based strategy, the gameplay is sufficiently balanced, and the overall war mechanic is somewhat more sophisticated than what you'd find in Civilization, using Total War's army-building model.  The quest functionality provides a lot of deep lore, and it really is amazing how intricate Amplitude's universe is - they have clearly committed a lot of energy to just... being creative here - so I have to mention it even though I really don't care for it much in my playthroughs.  I don't have to, though.  It's there if you want it, but I'm just not an RPG person.  My biggest gripe about the game is how much ALL CAPS ARE USED IN ITEM DESCRIPTIONS. I MEAN, IT'S KIND OF ANNOYING TO READ.
All in all, it's a fantasy version of Civ that is very, very polished, endlessly replayable (see what I did there?), full of character, surprisingly strong on the war/conflict front, and I am recommending it now solely because I want more people to know about it.  I encourage you to pick it up, or at least look into it a little deeper.

I enjoyed playing with this strategy game but I think it suffers from one very annoying flaw...
The Game focuses on the gravity fields surrounding planets in the (imaginary) solar system you are waging war in.
You fire projectiles across the solar system and plot your projectiles paths with the aid of a prediction line,
and this seems to be the games selling point. But...
Unfortunately you find that the most effective weapons are the lasers, - which are not affected by gravity....
This sort of kills the whole fun of plotting trajectories for projectiles or missiles as they become redundant fast.(If you have not built lasers too by researching the right technologies, then you`re going to lose as soon as your opponent does...).
I also found the predicted projectile paths very innacurate as many times I`d have set up several rail guns trajectories and used the targeting paths shown, only to see my shots miss by large margins. The general rule is that the further away the target is from you, the less accurate the prediction is.
Unfortunately the AI seems very accurate when firing back.
It`s quite hard playing against a single opponent in single player mode so can only imagine how fast I`d find myself being obliterated if I start a game with several AI opponents...
I DO like the game  and think that in multiplayer, against human players this will be quite entertaining so I`m recommending it,
but kinda wish you could disable the use of lasers, as this would prolong games and enhance them.
It's not that the game isn't fun. It's just that the game isn't fun for long.

The game starts off promising with interesting environmental puzzles and world-building, but gradually replaces its claustrophobic loneliness and reflections on the banality of corruption and decay with over-the-top action set pieces and overwrought conspiracies that ultimately detract from some of its best charms.
To be honest, the game is downright schizophrenic with its tone and focus. On the one hand, you'll find yourself faced with some intriguing problems, and if you take the time to walk through them you'll find yourself gradually pushing back the inevitable collapse of the city's forgotten infrastructure. But you don't have to. You could just progress onward, building bridges over the rubble of the past never once looking back.
This is a pretty great choice for this game, but it's implemented so poorly you wonder why it was an option at all. As mentioned before, the game loves throwing you into skin-of-your-teeth breakneck action sequences, which would be fine every once in a while but becomes the bread and butter of the last half of the game. As a result, puzzles you were in the middle of solving get swept away in a flood or a pile of rubble and you're simply pushed onward into the next segment leaving your latest project frustratingly half-finished. What's worse, there's never any subtle clue that what you're doing is about to gate you off from any previous content -- you simply walk into a room and suddenly everything hits the fan.
One could almost forgive it if the game was instanced or modular in such a way that you simply can't retrace your steps due to the code. But several times you have complete and unfettered access to massive stretches of territory you casually walked out of, including an entire chapter. Speaking of which, the last half of this game abandons its close-knit and focused puzzle environments for a sprawling, endless city barred off increasingly by artificial gates and doors that you will never be able to open, giving it an awkward sense of padded uselessness.
It's a pretty good game but abandons its own promise to stretch out its length at the end.

Again, the rubber boots thing saves lives.  Anyways I go back down there flip the lever run up hop over a wall instead of just have it locked like another door I had to get the keys for earlier, go into some cabin that's been abandoned for years in the most unlikely way possible (climb a ladder up the roof and fall down on some sort of wood shutter that's held by some string strong enough to hold our weight to climb into the attic) get some guys keys into a mineshaft that for some reason is related to the power system we're inspecting.
That was only a PART of my time with Chapter 2.  3 from what I played involved a switch puzzle that only existed because the lines weren't managed professionally, and something that was literally filp all the switches on, turn it on, then hit reset and you know all this by reading a note placed right next to it all.  It was then I realised that this game is a puzzle game based on cheap tricks that are 'puzzles' only because it takes a minute at most for you to turn something on and it was also based on hiding what you're actually supposed to do, I thought I was only investigating the actual power plant, why am I in a cave now.  I only got more confused by this game as it went on.
Alright now time for the graphics, while they're actually good for an indie game and the price I cant say I enjoyed a lot of the enviorment design, in chapter one the graphics were the poorest some models looked phoned in and textures were sometimes large part solid color, that was the worse of it, chapter 2 the starting area sums it up pretty well.  A lot of green outside, green, green, green making it harder to believe.  And the interior is grey dirty and overall just ugly.  I'm just going to say this ugly is ugly even when intentionally made ugly.  From what I saw of chapter 3 the game was only moving more toward that.
The soundtrack was never played, its odd I remember it badly but going back and listening to it it sounds fine, maybe even good.  I hope for their "Episode 2" they utilize it more because while the tracks are short they're enjoyable and might be good for ambience.
I am actually sad I couldn't enjoy the story it seemed like it had something written but we already know what's going to happen from our surroundings in the very start of the game we're told we were handed this place off FOR A CORRUPTION SCANDAL. I was very pleasantly surprised with the game. It looks great considering the aging engine. (It would be amazing on modern engines) It's very atmospheric and I just love crawling in every place looking for easter eggs and more things to photograph. (and if you're careful you can find plenty of batteries. I had 10/10 for both almost all the time in last episodes)
Some people complaing about the protagonist's voice acting but I find it very fitting for what I imagine the guy is like :) The game has a lot of easter eggs, hidden things, things that only Finnish people understand (+/-) and on top of that extreme attention to small details. I found a phone number in random poster after the cave early in the game and much later I could call the number for some additional fun. Plenty of things like that.
The basic gameplay consists of walking around looking for structural damage / other things that need maintenance or documents exposing corruption and then snapping a photo of them. May not sound very exciting but the beautifully aged environments make if very enjoyable. For me at least. The game really rewards exploration.
There are also a number of puzzles which vary from simple to slightly more complex ones but  you don't have to solve them all (Unless you're looking for 100% completion) Good thing about the puzzles is that usually they are rather logical. There are few places where you have to do some precision jumping but if you've played any fps games it's nothing too difficult.
There is also bigger plot behind the whole thing which slowly unravels as you find new clues and stuff. I have to pay more attention to it on the next playthrough but it seemed interesting enough. Anyway I'm really looking forward to part 2 and want to congratulate the devs for great work so far.
As a sidenote I bought the game for my 70 year old father who enjoys playing Myst type games and he at least seems to have enjoyed the experience even if some areas that require nimble fingers were causing additional grey hairs for him :)
As a final warning I'd like to point out that if you're looking for continuous action and get bored of exploring places just for the sake of exploring you may not enjoy the game as much as I did.

Victoria II is an epic strategy game that trancends the 19th century, in to the dawn of the 20th. It is as neither expansive as Europa Universalis III, nor as in-depth as Hearts of Iron III, yet it manages to capture perfectly a time period of industrializatoin and expansion. The combat system is a hybrid of EU3s simplistic 3 unit-type system, and the depth of HoE3. The government and economy seem to be the focus of this game, as your main difficulties are supplying your citizens with their needs while establishing a powerful industrial economy. This can be easy or difficult depending on your nation of choice, as you can choose to play as any nation in existence on January 1, 1836. If I were to give this game a rating out of 10, I would give it an 8.5. I would recommend this game to any hard-core strategy fan who is looking for an in-depth yet accessible game.
A Great Political, Industrial, Colonial and War simulation.

Perfect stratetey sim that revolves around diplomacy, economic planning and affecting domestic policies. Not the typical warfare game but still holds these elements and pulls it off well. If you want a different kind of strateg game, where the emphasis isn't just about base building or conquering your neighbour, check this out. It's like controlling a virtual economy and anyone who appreciates the subtleties of diplomacy will highly enjoy this game.
Graphically, Victoria II is quite impressive. Like most Paradox games, it won't wow you, but it will highlight a beautiful topographic landscape and implements shiny water reflections. Not for the flashy but those who enjoy staring at a map or globe will love this. Aesthetically, you'll also feel enthralled with the gameplay. Mozart and other classical musicians blasting away in the foreground while you negotiate peace with the Confederates through gunship diplomacy is highly applaudable.

Update 4/11/2015:
They did a MAJOR overhaul on the Quetzalcoatlus and it made the game A LOT more bearable. Quetzalcoatlus aren't EVERYWHERE now (they only spawn near Volcano's and really high lands). This alone made the game so much better. Now you can actually EXPLORE the land without definite insta-death.
However, every other issue I've stated is still a thing.
1) You rarely see dinosaurs in a game about dinosaurs.
2) You travel for LOOOOONG lengths of time (up to 50mins) with absolutely nothing happening.
3) Killing dinosaurs is nigh impossible at the start of the game (i.e. Levels 1 through 5-ish)
4) If you haven't racked up a few kills for exp and money then good luck killing anything after an hour.
Once you get to higher levels (9+) the game becomes a lot more tolerable; but from a gamer point of view: Why would I want to keep playing a game if the start of it is dreadful, boring, and hard (in the sense that you can't really kill anything)? I mean, yes, the survival aspect becomes fun once you're higher level; but with that promise, why would a person new to the game stick around long enough to sift through the bane of this game?
I know I called the game "Garbage" in my original review; but it's not. What it is, is unbearable (at first). And you'll have to put up with that unbearable irritation for a long time because levels aren't easy to gain (since dinos are rare to come across). Once you get past that, however, you could potentially start to enjoy yourself.

Original Review:
This game is a COMPLETE waste of money! Hear me out, because I keep coming back to this game, TRYING to like it, but it's terrible. And here's why:
-There's NOTHING to do:
You spend, I kid you not, 90%+ of this game walking around with absolutely NOTHING eventful happening. NOTHING in this world can really be interacted with except for loot crates and dinos. Your objective for most of the game, survuve. How are you gonna survive? Find camp points that have survival equipment (weapons, camo-clothing, healing supplies, etc). But the map is HUGE and that becomes obvious when you're walking with your GPS for 20 minutes and you've literally only traveled a distance about the size of 1/3 your pinky finger. None of these camps are anywhere NEAR close to each other, either; so if you're at a camp and you try to travel to the next closest one, be prepared to walk in a straight line for about 50 minutes, with NOTHING happening.
-It's nearly impossible to kill dinosaurs in a game about KILLING DINOSAURS:
Game Story - "You're a convict sent to a dino planet to kill as many dinos as possible to pave the future for potential civilizations." Early game, you MAY get lucky enough to find small Raptors. You can kill those with the machete that you get for free when you spawn, and that's where you get experience and money to buy things when you die and have to respawn anew. However, the dinosaurs age within game, and after 30 minutes they're fully grown (your gps tells you the age). Cool mechanic, BUT YOU CAN'T KILL THEM BY THAT POINT! Fighting baby Raptors is likely to yield success, BUT your health is gonna be dried up by that point, so you're going to eventually die. HOWEVER, the timer for the dinos doesn't reset! So now you have ADULT raptors, which you can't kill because as soon as you get close to killing them, they run away; and there is NO catching up to them. You can run, but your stamia is a handicap BEYOND BELIEF! You can track them with your GPS (via blood trail, foot tracks, dung, etc) but you'll be tracking for at least 20 minutes before you catch up to it. The dinos can bleed out and eventually die once you hit them; cool mechanic, HOWEVER, the time for that varies and the odds are, you WONT find the dino that you wounded; but if you do it'll be like I said before, "Tracking them for 20 minutes before you finally catch up". Mind you, this is just the case for the raptors, THE EASIEST THING TO KILL IN THE GAME!
-Quetzalcoatlus... Quetzalcoatlus...
If you can tolerate walking around doing nothing for 90% of the game, and don't mind the fact that after 30 minutes, you wont be able to kill dinosaurs anymore, then I present to you, the one dinosaur, that ruins this entire game. Quetzalcoatlus. This flying dinosaur is the ONE major flaw that was put into this boring, uneventful, over priced, waste of time game! Quetzalcoatlus flys down, picks you up, and carries you around for 10 (Mississippi) seconds. Then he drops you and you die... No questions about it. You WILL die when it drops you. I've survived drops twice (I don't know how) but then it circles around to finish the job... Quetzalcoatlus is the primary reason this game is absolute garbage. You think walking for 50 minutes to reach a camp and get its spoils finally pays off. Nope. Quetzalcoatlus are ALWAYS around these camps. You can go in and get the stuff, yeah, but Quetzalcoatlus WILL catch you while you try to leave, and it WILL kill you. When you die your body becomes a pack of bones that you can come back and loot for your old equipment; but of course Quetzalcoatlus will STILL be in the area; in fact, MORE Quetzalcoatlus will be in the area! Because it seems like every time you die to one, another one spawns in the area! Quetzalcoatlus are only a threat in open areas? Oh ok, so my options in this game are 1) Be safe from them while I walk around the forest areas where's there are no camps to get equipment, little hope of actually seeing a dinosaur, and just endless walking around with absolutely nothing else to do. or 2) Walk out to a camp in hopes of finding things to survive and die to Quetzalcoatlus, walk out into the open in hopes of exploring this huge world and die to Quetzalcoatlus, or try to walk from this forest to another forest and die to Quetzalcoatlus.
-There are very few dinosaur sightings in a game about DINOSAURS!
It's so rare to actually see a dinosaur in this horrible game. You'll find tracks and other signs of them in your area, but they're constantly moving, and they're faster than you and don't have STAMINA ISSUES! You will NOT see dinosaurs often. So you will not kill dinosaurs often. So you will not gain money or experience to buy things that will help you kill dinosaurs... which are rare to find in a game ABOUT dinosaurs! There is one dinosaur that you can easily find though. Quetzalcoatlus! Just look up into the sky and there he is! Walk out of the boring tree's and die! Or stay in the boring uneventful tree's and NOT die! GREAT GAME!

Buyer beware.  This game is NOT Early Access in any shape or form.
Do not buy this game expecting there will be many improvements/features to come because it is EA, it simply is not.   The game is playable (Windows only) but has many frustrating usability issues, but if you can see past these as it currently stands it might be worth a buy.

However the game is already 3+ years old, I bought it a year before the Steam release.  In the past 2 years updates have occurred at about once per 6 months (see the T&S forums). The lack of communication from the main developer of T&S (the one setting the roadmap) is the worst I have ever experienced. On the forums it is almost non-existant, here on Steam, as you can see, there is no news whatsover since release.
The developer needs to move it from Early Access into a release version ASAP.  That way you as a buyer know exactly what you're getting.  Also, as a released game it is quite acceptable for 1 or 2 updates a year (or less) and minimal communication.  As Early Access it is absolutely not.
Pros:
- Great feeling of creative freedom to build whatever style of fortress you want.
- Nicely generated procedural landscapes to play on.
- Ability to override AI temporarily and move people into position for combat or run away (greatly reduces frustration).
- Excellent music soundtrack.
Cons:
- Micro management is fine to some extent, but having to contiinually change professions of people to get anything built is not fun after the hundredth time.  This may be mitigated slightly once you have more people, but getting more people is not easy (see later points).  Regardless, there is no task priority system whatsoever, very poor for a game of this type.
- Very poor communication of key concepts.  The in game tutorial is very basic.  For example it suggests build roads to get more workers but doesn't explain the additional conditions required to get visitors (tip: it seems to depend on your food levels).  How do you remove designations to build/mine etc, (tip: select build/mine , hold down Shift Alt, and drag over the existing designation).  Why is this not mentioned in the game at any point?
- Farming is extremely confusing and counter intuitive.  In order to increase your food level there seems to be some  hidden magic balance between size and number of fields, number of farmers, skill of farmers and possibly crop type.  If you don't get this balance exactly right eg. you have say too many farmers or too large fields, your food levels will actually drop.  As food is so critical to success in this game (getting more immigrants) , this is frustrating and needs much better explanation.  I've even noticed farmers actually removing plants before they yield any food.
- The game often displays quantities as a total of the mass of all items eg. 8 items with 0.5 mass each is displayed as 4.  In many screens however it often has no indication whether a number indicates mass or straight quantity.  This is ridiculously confusing. How hard is it to add just a 'mass' suffix to all relevant fields?
- Road system is tedious.  You have to manually build roads to the very edge of the map, adjusting the height level for every hill you come across.  This adds nothing to the gameplay, visitors should be able to find their own way to your hall like almost every other similar game.
- Mouse and keyboard view controls are unintuitive.  You scroll the view using the WASD keys with Shift to move faster.  (Default scroll is too slow so I  continually have to use Shift which is painful after a while). You rotate the view by right clicking and moving the mouse.  An improvement would be scrolling via right click on the world/drag and rotate via Q/E keys.  This is simpler,  more accurate and less tiring.
- Mouse wheel zooming is also very flaky, sometimes gentle zooming-in jumps you 10 levels below the surface, zooming out puts you way out above the map.
- New textures are ok for stone, rocks etc but grass is quite ugly in my opinion.  I also have to turn off shadows, not for performance but so I can more easily see elevation changes etc.
I'll revise this if/when any updates occur that address any of these issues.  It's a game with plenty of potential, but it's been in "early access" for about 3 years now (way before coming to steam) and the development team seem to just disappear for months at a time.

Maybe not if you're a newbie to the concept of 4X as it can be a bit information overload for a while, but overall, I would definitely recommend.

700+ hours across nearly four years of playing this game, in a time where dedicated developers are few and far between with AAA $60 titles getting little more than a year's worth of content updates, while most of these "content updates" hardly improve the overall quality of the game. I'm looking at you "The Division". Warframe is a game that has constantly brought me back time and again with its devoted developers, who actively try to improve existing mechanics while adding new ones to increase the depth and longevity of the game, showing just how much they truly care about their game. Looking back at just how different Warframe looked and played on launch compared to today is akin to watching a completely different game in nearly every aspect, while the moniker "Ninjas Play Free" has remained the same throughout its lifecycle. But even with the frequent updates, practically the biggest thing impacting players enjoyment,  that has remained the same for as long as I've been playing is its own playerbase, they are some of the kindest and most dedicated people I have ever seen devote their time to a single title, with the amount of unpleasent experiences I've had being counted on one hand.
Where the majority of the industry has pushed more toward competition and being "the best" at shooting other people, Warframe hones a sense of cooperation among all players to achieve a common end-goal, and I am happy to say that I am one of them. I've recommended the game to countless people and while the game is certainly not for everyone, if you are someone that enjoys the "looter-shooter" esque genre, it is a treat. Starting in Warframe has pretty much always been difficult, even with DE making moves to make the transition easier for newcomers, I feel that the learning curve is still pretty steep in some regards as the initial grind can be too much for some people. But if you can make it over the hump, you'll find a vast network of things to do and to accomplish with total strangers actively willing to help new players get started.

If you are still not sure if you should check out this game or not, first a very easy information: It is free to play and therefore the only thing you need to check out this game is a bit of free time.
Which brings me to what this game is. It is a cooperative (you can play solo if you want, but this is only half as fun) looter game, similar to maybe Diablo or Destiny. However where these games offer a relatively shallow build variety, you can do so much more in this game - if you invest the time, because gathering all mods (these will be the items you need to create your builds) and building/leveling up the equipment you want does not happen instantly, especially if you are new.
You can choose to spend money to accelerate this part, but be aware that this is basically the game: Get loot, become stronger, get more loot faster to become even stronger, repeat ad infinitum.
If this basic principle is not for you you should maybe check out more story-driven games?
If you like the basic principle, you will love this game - the grind is carefully balanced to never feel too harsh while also giving people who choose to spend money a sizable shortcut. Personally I have only spent money here once when I started (keep your eyes open for platinum discounts 50% or better) and now support the developers by buying things I don't really need.
There are more Weapons than you can count and many different playstyles. Everyone should be able to find something they like. Finally, slaying hordes of enemies is insanely fun in this game and so far has not lost any appeal, even though I have probably played this a bit too much.
There is a lot more to talk about, but you will discover this if you give this game a try.
If you are looking for a list of pros and cons, here is is:
Pro:
+ free to play with a fair model where it is easy to get by with spending only minor amounts or nothing at all
+ huge diversity in playstyles, deep build customization and game mechanics
+ large arsenal of weapons with different look and feel
+ many different game systems will keep you occupied for many many hours
+ very fun to play with friends and good clan system with actual rewards
+ easy matchmaking
+ quick response to bugs and other issues, very frequent patches
+ one of the best online communities, frequent dev interaction
Cons:
- not for casuals; you need time to enjoy this game
- the better parts of the lore and story only appear later into the game
- steep learning curve; best play with friends who know the game or find a clan
- PvP exists but is generally regarded as a separate experience not played by many
- auto matchmaking sometimes means poor host performance (missions in this games do not run on dedicated servers, but are hosted by individual players)
I fully recommend this game and hope you will have as much fun playing it as I have.

Bernackels’ Shoggoth:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Do you remember the game we used to play in a group when we were kids? Several of your friends were sheep while a few others were wolves. The aim of the game was that the children who were sheep had to reach a specific location (within a house) without being seen or caught by the wolves. Well, let’s change the scenario a little bit . . . instead of sheep and wolves, you have small dragons. Some of them can breathe fire while the others can morph themselves into items to hide. The location is a combination of a dark subway and a mansion.  If you are one of the dragons that can breathe fire, you have to eliminate the ones who can’t before they find the keys to unlock the exit door. If you are the other dragons, well get on with it, find the keys and exit the dungeon before getting roasted! Let’s play Bernackel’ Shoggoth.
Bernackel’s Shoggoth is an action / stealth / online multiplayer game where you take control of one of six dragons (one dragon per player, up to six players) and your goal is to either eliminate the other dragons, or to escape the underground facility, depending on whether you are the hunters or the hunted!
On the main menu, you have the option to select either the intro, which is a small tutorial, or to find a game online. I must point out that the player base is rather small at this stage and it might take you some time to find an online game.
Personally, I had a couple of sessions with a few of my friends and moderators to give me a bit of an idea about this game.
As I mentioned above, you can have up to six players per session, and each of you controls a small dragon. If you are one of the hunted dragons, you are basically defenceless at the start of the game and must familiarise yourself first with the dark environment. All dragons have the ability to throw light balls so that you can see around you and find items and new chambers. As you fly around, make sure to check every corner of every room, and to open every single piece of furniture to see if there is anything interesting to pick up and place in your inventory. You can only place five objects in your inventory at any given time. What type of objects can be found? Weapons such as sword, axes, lances or shields, to mention a few. You can also pick up books, which are basically spells. There are coins you can collect and each time you do so, you’ll earn experience points.
In regards to the gameplay, it’s actually pretty good! Regardless of whether you play the hunted or the hunter dragons, it’s all about stealth. You can hear the wings of your opponent flapping when they approach you. Flying your dragon around is not hard at all, but be careful not to touch objects that can fall on the floor; that will give your position away. You can morph your dragon into a commonly-used object (if you have it in your inventory) for a few seconds, if you don’t have somewhere to hide.  This decision could mean the difference between life and death.  The other move you can execute is to throw an attacking spell or a weapon to your opponent, with the hope of killing him. If you are the hunter, as I mentioned above, you also have the luxury of breathing fire on your enemies.
If you manage to escape or kill all the remaining dragons, you’ll be awarded experience points.
Graphically the game looks good and the controls work very well.  However, this game really needs more players; I think it would be great fun to play against five opponents.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Interesting concept
-	Plenty of items to pick up and use
-	Easy to play
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Needs more players
-	No achievements
-	No trading cards at this stage
A nice combination of action and stealth in control of small dragons.
6/10

You CAN skip it though if you prefer to learn on your own, but id advise against it.
The 3D movements are very cool but kind of remind me of a few of the convoluted 3D modeling software controls I've learned. You don't have to play in that mode though as I typically spend my time on the 2D tactical map, but the 3D view is cool to watch a battle or check out an incoming ship you might want to steal.
You dont actually control the ships though, just their behavior. (which you can customize too). The AI can be trusted in some of the trickier dogfights though I'd still keep on eye on them from the tactial map.

O.R.B or Off-World Resource Base, is the best spaceflight strategy warfare game that I have EVER played.
The story behind this is just as gripping as the gameplay, you play as the Malus, and then after - as the Alyssians. Both races are "children" of a lost species that spanned an entire universe - moons upon planets upon systems upon galaxies, known as the Aldar.
All that is known of the Aldar is through a "bible" if you will known as the Torumin, which is posessed by both species.
The Aldar came to extinction due to an unknown species known only as The Great Betrayer.
After searching and discovering the remains of the Aldar, the great betrayer shows his face.
The Elathen, and their slaves, the Kyulek.
It is up to only you - to defend Alyssia and the Aldus system from the Elathen - destroyers of matter.
Can you find and harness the lost and ancient Aldar technology and use it to your advantage, or will all the great work of the ancient intergalactic Aldar be lost as floating, frozen relics in an endless wasteland of death.
This game is not forthright in its secrets...but each mission has a secret trigger event that will unlock a hidden mission later in the campaign, new unseen units, or reveal a hidden storyline.
This game was going to be much bigger than it turned out to be - there is enough content inside to fuel several spin-offs, but sadly, none of this occurred.
O.R.B is a game to which I have never been bored of, or have ever seen an end to the unique gameplay. And although I wish it had server support, the Singleplayer experience is absolutely tremendous, and the graphics are extremely appealing for a game made in 2002.
Good job, Strategy First!

Having played both Skyrim and Morrowind, I can say that Oblivion falls in the sweat middle ground not just chronologically, but gameplay-wise, too. In many cases, other TES games I've mentioned do the exact same thing in completely opposite ways, pushing them to the extreme. Just a few examples:
Item durability? Morrowind armor breaks like it's made of crisps, Skyrim Leather withstands sword hits, dragon fire and prolonged exposure to angry archers indefinitely long.
Faction quests? Morrowind will have you pick mushrooms for hours, Skyrim requires you to do a total of 2 quests and 3 mouse clicks to become the grandmaster of everything. Oblivion retains a feeling of progression from Morrowind, but shortens the questlines a bit so you still feel LIEK A HERO.
Melee combat? Morrowind offers you an exciting chance to play invisible dice instead of combat. Skyrim combat consists of one attack and several nonsensical gimmicks that waste your time preparing them. Oblivion leaves you a limited set of useful moves and tactics.
Oblivion, due to having voiced dialogue, is much more immersive than Morrowind while still retaining its complexity. NPCs still offer generic topics, which contain useful information as well as immersion-reinforcing chatter. Skyrim, in comparison, loves adding NPCs which will talk to you about potatoes and nothing else, ever.
There are several things you should explicitly avoid using not to ruin the experience (such as teleporting to yet undiscovered locations through your map). More so than Morrowind, Oblivion offers you things to do (and things to stare at in amazement) while travelling through the world, and fast-travel is guaranteed to remove a huge chunk of content from your playthrough.
"Are you saying this game is perfect?", I hear you ask. No, I'm not. Quite the opposite, in fact.
Firstly, it's a Bethesda game. It's as free of bugs as a tanker full of bugs, and some of them can break your game in one way or another. As with any Bethesda game, pimping it up to enjoyable state may require you a few minutes of research and mod installation.
Secondly, the aforementioned dialogue system isn't actually perfect. Saving HDD space resulted in some NPCs sharing lines from several different voice actors - not once will you hear a beggar thank you in one voice, and tell you about mudcrabs with another.
All NPCs without exception have the worst faces imaginable. There's no evident reason why they didn't employ that same framework to generate something that doesn't look like a victim of crippling genome-wide mutation - especially since we the players can do that with their face editor right in the tutorial.
Not sure who decided that NPCs most stare at you dead-eyed when talking to you. The random flailing of eyes also doesn't help. If you pick the game up, I beg you to mod it so that these freaky faces don't gaze at you from your entire screen.
Speaking of mudcrabs, the way random NPC-to-NPC conversations work will also rise your eyebrows with frightening stability. While sometimes it selects replies adequately, and generates quite a beliavable exchange, more often than not this IMMERSIVE INNOVATIVE SYSTEM will generate conversations such as
- Hey there!
- Any news from other provinces?
- Don't wanna talk about it.
- Ok. Any news from other provinces?
- I hate mudcrabs!
...
Another questionable thing in this system is the list of topics NPCs discuss. Talking about frightening mudcrabs seems like an OK joke the first time you hear it, but 10000 levels later people wearing full Daedric will still be afraid of them, even though they could probably kill crabs just by having them in peripheral vision.
There are three categories of people I can recommend Oblivion to:
1) You've liked Morrowind. These games share some key features that will render you familliar with the world and its rules, and it's a whole new enjoyable story.
2) You've felt like Skyrim is too dumbed down. In such case, leave it to the console crowd and switch to a game that just allows you to do more things in more entertaining and challenging ways.
3) You're new to TES. Starting here will most likely get you interested in the world and core mechanics of TES without boring with walls of text Morrowind proudly features, or rudimentary gameplay of Skyrim.

I never expected to enjoy Crusader Kings 2 (CK2) as much as I have. This game is an historical dynasty simulator. You control a dynasty set roughly in the middle ages. The world is made up a realistic depiction of the patchwork of kingdoms and lesser states that populated Europe and western Asia. Populating that kingdom are thousands of characters, each with numerous attributes and personalities. You will spend much of the time either staring at a map screeen or otherwise interacting with the characters who populate the world. The strength of the character system makes these actors seem to have real personalities, and your actions feel more consequential as a result.
CK2's defining feature is one of constant choice and freedom, while at the same time responding to events outside of your control. Your character is your own, and where you choose to lead your dynasty yours to make. Along the way, you will face literally thousands of events and choices, some to your benfit, others to your considerable detriment. Random chance can srike down your nemesis, prompting a sucession crisis to be exploited, or disease can claim your children, leaving you with no male heirs. Learning to sail these winds of fortune is a huge part of the game.
While there are many strategic simulators out there, none are so devoted to having those decisions carried out by simulations of people. France isn't just a faceless kingdom; it is embodied by a simulation of a ruler, with his own whims and caprices.
Having read a fair amount of history on this period, I'm extremely impressed by how a simulation represents both the realities of the time: a rough approximation of feudalism, inheritance law, and giving even relatively obscure historical figures an appropriate representation in the game. You will learn how dynasties rise and fall over roughly 700 years of history. This is a great game to kindle interest in the history of the time.
The learning curve is deep, but not steep. The tutorial is enough to figure out the principles of the game: using marriage for alliances/gaining land, going to war, plotting against kings or vassals, and manging your kingdom. Underneath that, though, is an enormous amount of depth that rewards players who are ruthless in exploiting the ability to use plots, succession law, and claims on landed titles to advance their own interests.
The game has been updated for over 5 years, and each update improves the game even more. I've played this for over 1000 hours, and I absolutely recommend it.

Kind of a one trick pony, and that trick doesn't make a damn bit of sense in the context of the game. The core of the game is aiming a projectile through multi-planetary orbital mechanics. I realize it's just a game, but it just defies even the most forgiving of logic to believe that a planet which can build interplanetary missiles and rail guns can't accurately do the math to figure out how far you have to lead the planet you're targeting.
Other than the orbital mechanics shooting gallery stuff, it's a totally generic build-and-attack strategy game. If you like the shooting mechanic, then pay the few bucks and get this on sale.

Think of it like the old turn-based board game "Battleship", just on an interplanetary scale of course!
-Strategy:
+Intel- Provides you with locations of certain structures on another's planet, the more you get the different types of structures you reveal.
+Counter intel- The more you have than the enemy does intel on you, well you counter them and limit their intel on yourself.
+Cities- Your main source of growth, and essentially the "battleships", don't let them all be destroyed. To avoid that you can "hide" them with certain structures.
+Defenses- Build shields to protect your cities or important structures from attacks.
+Structures-Your basics; Power, materials, intel, science, defense, offense.
+Upgrades- Increase power, enhance weaponry, science/material intake etc.
-Battles:
+Weapons- Placement is important since the planets spin on an axis, making timing important.
+Physics- Timing and "leading" the target is important here since everything is spinning on an axis and orbiting the sun. Catching the gravity of one planet to redirect a projectile is also possible, as well as throwing off your shots!
-Gametypes:
+Single Player- Vs AI, you can battle many and tweak the system as you like.
+Multiplayer- Not a big croud to play with here, mostly just your friends.
-Content:
+Not too much of that here, just your basics and some upgrades for those basic structures.
-Price:
+ At $15 I would say it is $5 too much, it's a fun game but bare and "plain" really. Wait for a 50% sale.

A fun turn based strategy game where you build railguns, missiles, and lasers to destroy enemy planets. It is very satisfying to line up your shot, using the gravity of other planets to help your railgun/missile hit another planet and blow up their buildings. It is also possible to accidently hit yourself with your own weapon, which I have done several times. Unfortunately theres not usually anyone online to play with, which sucks because its such a great game.

Short take:
Initially fun game, with potential for strategic depth. But very little of either after a first or second playthrough.
Premise:
Build your railguns and missile silos and fire them at everyone else in the solar system; it's a deathmatch. Don't forget to pick something to research!
The deal:
The fun dries up quickly though. The reason it does is actually the ultimate failure of the game. The part of the game that should be joyful and exciting, the aiming and fire controls, are poorly done. It comes down to nudging your mouse one more pixel to the left to get the wacky flightpath indicator to fart out a viable firing solution. Also, rather than group firing all your weapons, you must repeat this tedious process FOR EVERY SINGLE WEAPON YOU BUILT ON THE PLANET. That's right, if you built 10 missile silos, you must use the awful mouse-nudge to trajectorize and fire each single weapon separately, every time, every turn.
Then, the resulting destruction isn't at all satisfying. It can be fun to line up a curving shot with an (unguided) railgun slug on a target planet. But the result is just a sad pop sound. Comically, the only real confirmation that you have succeeded in destroying a city with over 40 million presumably human inhabitants, is a little skull icon in the screenside combat log. Do this a few more times to win the game. Yes, that is the bulk of the gameplay, and yes, it's pretty much that simplistic.
This might lead you to think that there's some sort of nuanced underlying depth going on that makes for great PvP or something. Unfortunately, that is not the case. WYSIWYG.
Side note on some design flaws:
My overall feeling is that certain things were included in a derivative (I know "Cargo Cult" is cliche now) way without the real understanding of how those game elements impact the the whole. Example, a research tree is included so cities can generate science points and unlock new upgrades, just like every other game that has this tech tree element.
But here it seems to just be there as a thing to do. At no point does it feel like focusing on one section of the tree while neglecting another has a major strategic consequence the way it would in well-designed games that include this feature for an actual reason... So, I'm left with the feeling that it's there 'coz that other game has it.  Any other tiered-tech per-structure system might have made the game more strategically interesting. Perhaps small tech trees for each building, forcing the player to choose to upgrade now for more instantly gratifying damaging shots, or hold off to expand the structure later for higher potential outcomes but a higher potential loss if the building gets destroyed. There are other examples of this throughout but that one stands out.
Because there's good potential, I could go on for a long time about similar relatively simple and meaningful ways the game could've been improved.
Should I buy it?:
Wait for a major price drop, or sale. I suggest not spending more than $5 as, optimistically, you might get 5 hours out of it; unless it strikes some kind of chord with you.

I was very, very surprised to see that this game was released to soon after entering early access. A name like Avalanche Studios carries weight with me, and that's mostly the reason I bought this game a few days after it came out on early access. It didn't have much content, but it was in early access, so I has expecting that they'd add more. I was so very much hoping that I'd able to return to this game after a few months of development. I was wrong.
First of all, this is not a bad game. It's a good game, don't get me wrong. The graphics are amazing, the sound design is probably the best of any game I've ever played, the dinosaurs are well designed and the terrain is well crafted. The world is massive and will take you at least an hour to walk from one side to the other on foot.
With that being said, mechanically, this game is sound, more or less. The new flying dinos broke the game with their bugs, (thankfully, the worst one was fixed) they fly through terrain, are sometimes impossible to see or hear, and make you unable to reclaim your gear after you become dino-chow. There are a few more bugs related to the dinosaurs, but thankfully I've never encountered a crash.
The game (to my knowledge) advertised this to be a survival game, but, don't be fooled: there is anything that remotely has to do with the "survival" genre that we've come to know and love within games like The Forest and Stranded Deep. The only type of "survival" to be found here is the kind where you avoid not being killed. This IS "survival", per se, as surviving literally means "not dying", but hey, semantics. I was really looking forward to the kind of survival that I thought was being advertised, and I suppose that it could be said that it was my misinterpretation of what I read that lead to my disappointment. I was so excited to make a base, look for food, water and weapons, make medicines and then go hunting for some large extraterrestrial lizards. (Yes, in case you didn't know, this game takes place on an alien planet.) I do know for sure that this game labels itself as "realistic". This is probably where my misconception originated from:
"Hunt - Explore - Survive The most realistic prehistoric survival game ever created." theHunter: Primal, 2014.
There's nothing realistic about hunting dinosaurs on an alien planet. Trust me. I know my♥♥♥♥♥♥ But do I care about that? No, of course not. I get to hunt dinosaurs realistically, of course. All sillyness aside, and to summarize what I've just said, I'm sad I can't have a real dino-hunting/survival game.
This leads me to me largest and most bitter gripe with this game: there's no content. There's nothing. Literally. Well, not literally... there's a few gigs of space being taken up by this on my C: drive, but it's substance is lacking quite a lot. There are a total of 5 dinosaurs to hunt. 5 dinosaurs in total.This is a dinosaur hunting game with only 5 dinosaurs. Why? There are only a few weapons too. These are what I can think of: Magnum, Rifle, Shotgun, .50 cal Sniper Rifle, Machete, Bow. The bow is REALLY buggy too, and I've never found the .50 cal Sniper Rifle. While there are some cool attachments you can put on your weapons, there is no excusing the lack of content here. Sure the world is big, but what good is it if there's nothing to do.
The game is thirsty, it's STARVING, its emaciated; just begging---"Please, please, give me sustenance! Food, water!" And we're here, kneeling beside this sad mess of skin and bones, screaming, "Yes! Please! Feed it, FEED IT! WE BEG OF YOU!"
The developer answered our cries for more content by saying, "Hmm... maybe. If it sold more copies, we might."
(I can provide a link to the discussion thread where a dev said this, if anyone wants it. Assuming they don't delete it, of course. The thread is titled "Post-release heads up.)
Uhh. I paid $20 dollars for this game. For some unimaginable reason, the devs think that the small, bare-bones amount of content they added within the few short months of early access somehow, and unexplainably, warrented a 50% increase to the price of the game. It's insulting, really. I never would have bought this game in early access if I knew that they wouldn't add anything to it. That's the risk we take when we buy early access games and technically it is our fault for making a bad purchase, but still, it makes me feel sh*tty. Most of this review was written after playing part 1, but main issues are still present in part 2. As such, I can't really recommend this game. The game seems to have not been playtested with people coming into the game completely blind.

If I'd have to sum up INFRA in one word, it would be confusion. Most of my playtime was spent backtracking, trying to search every corner for something to interact with or take with me, staring at panels and walls for numbers, trying a route and dying, only to figure out that the last save was 5 minutes ago, retrying a solution only to fail because of the controls, figuring out there's a path that has been deadly in other instances, but now all of a sudden it's safe to traverse etc.
Games like Portal and Braid can have moments of simply staring at the puzzle, but in those situations you know what the goal is, and thinking about the problem takes you closer to the solution. In INFRA, there were plenty of times where I had no idea what I was supposed to do or where I was supposed to go. Many of the puzzles in INFRA take the form of overly complicated machinery that needs certain switches and buttons in certain positions, or certain pipes need to be either opened or closed via slowly turning valves somewhere, or sometimes you need to find the valve itself somewhere and find where to stick that valve. If there are any locked doors, you bet there are easy to miss keys and keycards somewhere. The same puzzle types get very old very quickly.
It's kind of sad to write this kind of review, as INFRA was one of the first games I witnessed in Steam Greenlight, and it seemed like a fresh idea with plenty of potential. Now INFRA seems more like a TC mod for Half-Life 2 rather than a fully fledged game in it's own right, and things haven't improved in part 2.

I don't usually do this but I'll lay out a few pros and cons for this game as there are a few things I feel could use some polish to really put the cherry on this tasty Dino-cake;
Pros:
1) Huge, lush, GORGEOUS environment with varied lighting and weather.
2) Intelligent, smoothly animated Dinos with unique features and weak points.
3) Easy to use inventory system
4) Feathered, (almost) accurate dinosaurs! At last!
5) Raptor selfies! (Trophy shot option)
Cons and nitpicks:
1) Some dodgy sound transitions, especially when approaching the beach. The ocean sounds don't fade in very well.
2) Online features could be better implemented. Not a huge problem for me though as I prefer to play solo anyway!
3) NOT ENOUGH DINOSAUR SPECIES!! Come on guys, this is my main complaint.
I love this experience as it is but seriously; ONE herbivore type? Hell just stick some un-killable Sauropods in there if you must but please add some more to the roster. T-rex and two types of Raptor is challenging and cool but again a bit more variety would be nice.
So, in conclusion:
This is a great survival game if you can cope with its tough difficulty curve. It's a genuine pleasure to master it but time and patience is required; for tough-guy shooty action, look elsewhere.
I can't think of a better single player Dinosaur experience on Steam at the moment and my only reall issue is with the severely limited variety of Dinosaurs in the game.
Add some more herbivores and perhaps one new mid-sized carnivore and this would be a must -have.
[EDIT] With reguards to 'Game breaking bugs' people have found so far, it's poor form for a dev to have left so many in there at release. However, my review doesn't mention them as I have had the good fortune not to have encountered any of them in my playthroughs!
This review is my opinion based on my experiences playing the game, if you don't like it, that's cool. You'll have to excuse my ''Glass half full'' attitude.

INFRA is a different type of game – a first-person exploratory puzzler. No guns – the only things you'll be shooting are pictures; minimal inventory – just your camera, flashlight, batteries for both, and whatever random bit of the environment you're lugging around at the moment, whether that be a fuse that belongs in a fusebox somewhere, a crate you'll need to cross a pool of electrified water, or an empty beer bottle that's just lying around, waiting to be smashed.

Infrastructure Isn’t Sexy
You play an engineer who works for a fictional Baltic country's infrastructure inspection service (in case you're wondering, the developers are based in Finland). Your job is to go out to inspect dams, highways, bridges – all the little things that make life easier, but could cause disasters if they break. And boy, do they ever break.
In a nice nod to just how things work in the real world (channeling John Oliver here), the nation's infrastructure – and the agency itself – is pretty blatantly underfunded. Even your starting office area is badly in need of repair, and only sparsely staffed. The workers hanging around complain about unsafe – but heavily used – tunnels that they refuse to drive through because they know just how bad they are.
The plot of the game kicks off with a typical, monotone office meeting (which, mercifully, you can skip), explaining where to go (a local abandoned dam system) so that you can gather photographic evidence of the repairs that need to be done, as well as doing patch jobs on whatever you can. Using your camera (or flashlight) drains batteries like crazy, but you can find plenty of them as you go along. The only downside is that there is no real way to tell how many batteries of each type you have left, aside from your character's comments when picking up fresh packs or installing a new set. The digital camera – which helpfully adjusts its viewfinder whenever you point it at something you need to photograph, has a battery meter; the flashlight just grows dimmer and dimmer to the point of uselessness, as its way of saying “Feed me!” The whole short battery lifespan thing is par for the course for a video game – but, obviously, they only drain when they are active (this includes looking around with the camera out).
Your secondary purpose, along the way, is to figure out why the place was abandoned in the first place – and you can even find some evidence pointing to this in your home office if you explore it thoroughly enough. It looks like a profound lack of funding might not be the only problem with this country.

Dam It
INFRA uses standard WASD for movement controls, E to interact, R to reload batteries, F to toggle the flashlight; jump, crouch, pickup/drop/throw – you know the drill. All fairly standard FPS-type controls. Spinning the mouse wheel toggles the camera, and clicking it zooms in or out. For better or for worse, there’s no HUD, and no inventory screen.
If you don't quite make a jump, you just get kicked back a few seconds of gameplay. They want you to play the game, not re-do ten minutes of running around every time you miss a jump by a few pixels. There are no enemies save for the environment itself – a few feet of water, most falls, etc. will one-shot kill you if you're not careful, along with the more obvious deathtraps such as the aforementioned electrified pools of water. For certain scripted, survivable falls, your character will have something to say about that, complete with some colorful language.

Graphics and Sound
The game is simply gorgeous at maxed visuals, even on a mid-range graphics card (GeForce 660). Old crumbling bricks and concrete, rust-covered metal, faded glass, and flowing water all contribute nicely to the atmosphere of the game, while providing an effective contrast to the relative sterility of your equally-in-need-of-repair home office. The dam and its environs feel abandoned and empty, even if most of the vehicles you find look brand new, and have been polished to a mirror shine!
The ambient noises that comprise much of the soundtrack accompany the visuals well – birds chirping out in the wilderness, winds rushing down deserted corridors, water dripping off of rusty pipes, etc.
[Eric Kei]
Summary
INFRA is a nice break from the run-of-the-mill first person games. They take a topic that most people find exceedingly dull, but with a touch of mystery, some entertaining gameplay mechanics, and excellent visuals, turn it into something worth sinking several hours into – and it's longer than you might think. A true exploration game.

I just got T&S a few days ago and I have been enjoying it to the most part (more about what I didn't enjoy, below)... up until now. But this is not the (main) reason why I give my positive / negative recommendation (I will come back to this review and change that if necessary and also edit / add to my written part, as new editions come out).
I'll post what I found out (and my own thoughts, but based on facts) as bullet points next, take them as positive or negative, that's up to everyone's taste (at least to some part).
First off, some general info:
This game project has originally started as a Kickstarter (Sep 26 2012 - Oct 26 2012) - 3,368 backers pledged $88,577
of $50,000 goal.
This is a one-person project ("Robert"), who says (on the Kickstarter "about the creator" page) that he is a self-taught artist / programmer with no formal education in those areas.
The screenshots of the game on the Kickstarter page show very blocky graphics (trees and terrain) - this has improved drastically since then, overall I like the graphics very much (although I have all settings on their highest levels with so far no major performance issues, and that running on three monitors AKA triple-head - however, I have a high-end gaming system - latest Intel CPU, 32 GB RAM, ROG mobo and a GTX Titan X).
The dev's stance is to not post any timeline of milestones and in general is vague / unsure when and what new features will be implemented.
The dev's overall stance is that the project / game will never be finished as such, which means that either he'll continue working on it for as long as his health allows him to, or that he will just stop working on it whenever he feels like it - this was supposedly a commend he made, plus "Robert"'s signature slogan on the forum is "Art is never finished, only abandoned. -Leonardo da Vinci".
Which by itself is not necessarily something that should raise concern, however it took six (6) months for the latest update (v1.7), despite that the majority has requested in a poll made mid-2013 to receive updates every two to three weeks.
There's an outdated "dev roadmap" from Aug this year (2015) posted on the website's forum (again, not on Steam, as the dev, "Robert", refuses to interact with "the Steam community" / to post on Steam) for up to v1.7 (the current release). The last post from someone was made in mid-October asking for what's next and when, with no response almost a month later.
Posting on the forum at
requires creating an account, which requires email verification that is sent to the email address entered during registration - I, for my part, never received that email. Trying to log in only displays that I need to contact the forum administrator, but no link / email address is displayed and as a result I can not do.
As a result, reading posts is possible without log-in to an active account on the site's forum, but posting there is not possible.
Game mechanics related:
However, blocks and "float" and as such, there is no physics (at least no gravity) in the game - all moving objects (creatures) are bound to the ground (or swim in water), but trees, if dug underneath, can "float", AKA "minecraft experience".
From what I could gather, the "end game" mechanics have changed from version to version (at least from the previous 1.6 to this latest one, 1.7) - right now, and this seems to be the stance of the dev "Robert", is that, due to more and more enemies and stronger ones spawn as in-game time passes, eventually all your virtual people in the game will get killed and you will have to start all over again.
I have read that there is a mod out that can change that (or at least it has difficulty settings), but AFAIK that mod is not maintained by the dev and as such might not work anymore when a newer version of the game is released and if the mod dev ceases to update the mod to keep it working with newer versions of the game.
The path-finding is quite good, and you can have events displayed to various degrees that you can define, also you can have the thoughts / responses  of your virtual displayed, to help you understand and react to if something doesn't work or if there's something you need to change, according to a situation.
You select what every few of the virtual person should focus on (their profession) but you don't have to (but you can, to a certain level but it works well) what every single one should actually be doing at any given point in time. Yet even though, you have to switch around professions quite often, to satisfy supply and demand of resources and tools required. Which in the end does result in quite a bit of micro-management (note: the dev stated that the professions will be replaced with a skills system, to reduce / eliminate micro-management - which was supposed to have happened already in this current version, 1.7).
You can manually set a location for a virtual person to move to and then, if set correctly / accordingly, will perform its actions there (they perform actions as per their set profession and closest to their current location). That way you have quite a high amount of control, if needed, to prioritize where work should be performed.
There is a few things here and there, but this is overall what the game is about.
Verdict:
Overall, if you're looking for a game where you can temporarily build a virtual civilization and design somewhat interesting structures via A LOT OF micro-managing, no physics (AKA floating in mid-air of trees and other resources) and time-pressure due to getting attacked in steady intervals and by increasingly stronger opponents (some have complained that they get too strong too soon, AKA the game has a too high of a difficulty level - but again, there's currently a working mod for that) to the point of where they will overwhelm and extinguish your virtual civilization and you then have to start all over again - then this is the game for you.
So basically, if you don't mind restarting over again after a few hours (but that is dependent on how long you pause the game) and overall a fairly steep difficulty (at least without mod) then this is a game for you. If you look for something where you don't have to do that, then this is not the game for you.
However, if you want to focus on designing block-by-block and manually building interesting virtual structures and keep those as long as you wish, but you lack the ability to build a virtual civilization and as such you are doing all the work yourself, in first-person - and, AFAIK, no physics (AKA floating trees and parts of trees and terrain) - then you're better off with something like Minecraft. Or "7 Days to Die" (which has physics but that can be buggy, yet so far not game-breaking and still gives hours and hours of fun).
So my recommendation (or lack of it) is based on all of the above - again, this might change from version-to-version.

I really wanted to like this game. Falling colored blocks, what's not to love? Unfortunately this game has major problems.
The first thing you notice is everything is slow. This makes the facts that key input is unresponsive even harder to understand. If you hit the right key the blocks should move right, right? They might eventually move right. They often move right twice even though you hit the key once. I'd think this is basic. But if the input is so slow they're obviously not responding in time with a slow moving game to start with, that's bad.
The next major thing you notice is that nothing works right. The rules say, for example, that if you match four colored blocks in a row that the adjacent blocks of the same color would also disappear. But they don't. Well, sometimes they do. But it's random which ones do. And falling blocks either make four in a row with blocks as they fall (but before they hit bottom) or they don't, not sometimes if they feel like it. Shift + Tab to get the Steam interface got it but didn't pause the game, just made it difficult to see. And I somehow rotated blocks off the side of the grid? How?
The graphics are fairly decent to good. Sound was repetitive but OK. The how to play screen was too small (and only semi-accurate anyway due to the poor programming). Meh.
Basically, the blocks just don't do what they're supposed to do in any consistent manner. If that's your game's one job, it better do it. Any advancement in the game felt like it was not you being skillful over the game's challenges but prevailing over a poorly responding user interface. And considering how slow it is there's little reason to want to fight it. I'll get my cards and go, thanks.
