I love this game, though I've only played it for roughly 18 hours since it has been released on steam I've spent countless of hours playing it before.
The game is fairly difficult and it takes some time to get used to in my opinion but once you figure out how everything works it becomes quite easy to set up a thriving settlement. (that is until you encounter a necromancer who keeps summoning skeletons inside your walls)
A few things I love about this game are.
- A fair diversity, there are quite some classes yet not that many,
the easier tools break and better tools that won't, require resources,which can be hard to get by or scarce,  and professions at certain levels meaning some professions are still a worthwhile investment even later on in game,
- Freedom to build/create/destroy/design as I desire
- Enemy difficulty progresses compared to how wel your settlement fares
- The new fog of war-ish, making enemies invisible unless one of your settlers can actually see them (even though they have a 360 degree sight radius) making it a bit more difficult to prepare for enemies, and in my opinion thus more interesting,
- Enemies not being allies with eachother, this compared with the previous point can however suprise me with suddenly finding piles of corpses on the map when looking around. (this was not the case before T&s got released to steam and made it really annoying when I got several types of enemies attacking my settlement at once)
- Siege weapon(s).. though there is only one for now, it's still awesome to have ballistas guarding your gate
- Inventory management (speaks for itself, though it can be a bit buggy at moments when one does take the items yet won't use them when they should)
There are a few things I'm personally disappointed with which are.
-The fact they turned sleeping into a thing to do when wounded instead of, whenever the settles were fatigued or scheduled to sleep,
-That they took out the adventurer class, even though this one did not have such a great purpose and it did not work that great, (not certain if they just took it out to be fixed or not to be completely honest) but it was great to walk through my settlement as one of my settlers.
- Archers, when set to train using a  practise target, tend to shoot the moment they can see the target, thus hitting fellow settlers or constructions if said archer moved for a bit to gather new equipment/food
- Archers quickly losing too much morale if there are too many enemies in sight when alone, even if enemies arent pursuing and could easily be picked off one by one from a distance
As for other things, I'm glad to see they added a few tips on how the game works, though from the reviews I read people still seem to miss a few things, hence I figure I'll mention a few things that might be good to know.
- '[' & ']'  should help you cycle through your settlers rather easily
- 'U' should give you an overview of your settlement & settlers and quickly assign roles.

One of the best 'Not-quite Dwarf Fortress' games I've played to date. Highly recommend you grab this gem.

Pros:
Micro-management heaven: You're not just expected to point click and wait...you will need to literally 'pause, grab unit, unpause, click away, pause, repeat'. Sounds like a pain in the buttocks but when you survive 12 wolves trying to eat your face and no one dies; you'll feel like a pro
Building Freedom: Design your settlement so you can protect it
Easy to pickup; Difficult to master
Difficulty Scaling: By far the best scaling game I've played of this type that I can remember. Game gets harder the longer you play but never more than you should be able to handle (this is really hard to do)
Cons
Random Mouse actions caused by Path-finding during a crisis will have you swearing! Take the 12 wolves scenario spoken of earlier, clicking on a nearly dead unit trying to pull them out of combat; you click and click and the mouse random moves to the middle of the screen and your command click was ignored...ouchie~
Path-finding: Major work needed here. Not really noticeable at the beginning of the game but reach day 50 odd on a large map and your frame-rate will have gone from XXX to XX and no one can seem to do anything without bumping into each other and stopping. Mining/Building path-finding will comically often trap the settler on a single block in mid-air. Funny at day 10, not so much by day 90
Frame-rate: Start of the game, I was at triple figures. I am now on my second map (I died horribly at day 22 on the first map, RIP Rugolas; you died a Spartan) at day 93 and it's struggling to stay above 50 - assuming path-finding is the cause.
Particle effects cause discos; this has to be seen to be understood...
------
As this is early access, I would expect these cons to be fixed but hell, adding more content (blocks, décor, workshops, tech) and I wouldn't even care. There part of the charm, pick it up and see for yourself.

I've been playing Timber and Stone for what seems like years now, through many big changes, long before it made it to Steam. The Dev team has been dedicated, and consistently interacting with the community (on their website forum): taking feedback, adding content, polishing, squashing bugs, everything you want out of a good early access project.
The game improves in every update. Do note that updates take a while, but that's only because they're always substantial. There's a lot of content and depth to the game already, though a bit more in terms of crafting and professions would be welcome.
The only three issues I have:
1) the game should have a built-in difficulty-level option. Vanilla, especially in the most recent update, it's tough. Which is great! But sometimes I just want to build, as that's a lot of fun--relaxing fun--too. My ideal case: give several options. Give an option to turn off monster spawning entirely, but allow it to be turned on later in the game (test out those defenses you've built!); give an option to have a very slow buildup; give the current difficulty level, which is tough but achievable (for a while!); give something ridiculously tough.
NOTE: There is a mod, which can be found on their website forum, that turns off the waves of monsters so that you can build. It would just be nice to have this natively.
Devs: consider something like Rimworld's various difficulty options.
2) Once you have quite a few settlers (15+) in a big map, it starts to get sluggish, and the pathing algos stars to struggle. I don't have the newest setup, but an i7-920 + 16GB DDR3 + Radeon 280x isn't terrible. Smaller maps do a lot better. I'm sure that performance will improve as the project goes on.
3) Picking the exact sort of landing site you want for your map is a pain in the butt. There NEEDS to be a search option, a-la Dwarf Fortress.
But again: highly recommended. And as I've already said twice: if you just want to build/expand, get the no-monster mod from their forum!

You can roll out the big guns, create a massive army and wreck everyone to win, you could instead expand your empire by building cities and then conquering other people's cities until 80% of all lands on the map belong to you.
You can achieve a diplomatic victory by keeping your relations with other countries at peace or in alliance for a long enough amount of time (you get peace points, 1 for any country in the game, 2 for any country at peace with you and 4 for any country in an alliance. You can win by being the most technologically advanced country (research 5 of the 6 most advanced technologies)
Or you can play a bit more strategically than just kicking everyone's♥♥♥♥♥ and capture all your opposing player's capital cities which will give you the Supremacy victory.
All of these are viable ways to win, besides maybe expansion victory (80% is a lot) but this sums up what the game is about. It's difficulty level is somewhere right between Heroes and Civilization, but the fun I'm getting here is a lot more than in either one of these other two classics. This game rocks! and if you're any sort of fan of turn based strategy, you should give it a try!

With a good base game and some really wonderful expansion packs, Victoria 2 is such a neat game, with a variety of things to do, ways to challenge yourself,  as well as semi-consistent updates to help keep the game fresh. There's a huge variety of mods which do a huge variety of things, and the base game itself is pretty much as complicated as you make it out to be- Newer players can test the waters in the safer areas of the world, while more advanced players can play as a greater power competing for influence, micromanage the markets of its land, and play politics to ensure the right party gets (and stays) in power, all in their attempt to achieve the status of #1 in the world, to either oust the damned British or let old Queen Victoria keep her spot on the throne of nations.
Your quest to become the empire on which the sun never sets will not go without adversity- the AI presents a fair challenge to any player and often makes cunning moves to protect its own power and hegemony in the status quo, while weaker powers opportunistically enroach on greater nations through diplomacy or sword to attempt to make themselves a name and put themselves on the map. Finally, internal strife hampers many prospective nations of Europe, as German and Italian states squabble amongst themselves to try and become the best. The world needs a great leader, and that person could very well be you.
If I had to give any downsides, it'd be the fact that the Infamy system is still a little imbalanced (the 2 province Luang Prabang kingdom being annexed by you is just as costly as finishing off the respected kingdom of Egypt, perhaps even moreso), the fact that there are a lot of prospective time period countries not represented (Which has been dealt with), and the fact that the tutorial is sort of outdated and not very helpful (WHICH I MANNED UP AND DEALT WITH MYSELF).
Overall, I would highly recommend the Victoria 2 complete edition, or at the very least, as much as you can get out of it. It's a great introduction to grand strategy and one that's kept me interested for a very long time.

I like how the game is presented. I like the tech tree, the visuals, and the music. However, the main aspect of this game is trajectory warfare (pick a flight path and anticipate orbital movement of your target). Now while the idea of trajectory warfare is a novelty it is executed rather poorly in this game. Not only do you have to deal with poor camera controls, but even if you hit the target it provides no satisfaction. The strategy aspect of this game is too deeply impacted by chance. Simple build up of counter-intelligence makes this a rule rather than an exception. If you're playing this game on multiplayer, know this: The outermost and inner most planets have a severe edge over the middle ones, as there are less angles of attack on them.
Overall, I applaud the design team for thinking outside of the box, and creating a truly unique experience, however I cannot recommend this game for anything more than a quick bout of curiosity.

Crusader kings 2 is a medieval grand strategy game. It focuses on relationships and individual people within in the game, rather that many other strategy games which focus on world domination. However, for people who would rather take over the world, it offers that possibility as well. Some people hate the DLC policy, but unlike EU4 it is perfectly playable without any DLC.

For $40 dollars over 400 hours.
I had lot of fun managing my family dynasty and setting a certain goal (uniting all of Scandivian as a Viking for example).
Along the way you can encounter some surprises such as wife wishing to kill you after being married barely 6 month in.
A boy growing up to have "Culture of Horse" instead of Norse or something more typical.
Having to kill a fellow King because if he become your lord. He would strip your title just because you pray to the wrong god.
Crusade and Warband invading and create an enclave of wrong religious people in someone's else land.
Having a brother of your successing at something you never dream he would be able to.
Having a realm-wide tournament and looking forward to see who won. Only to release that the winner is an "idiot at combat" and cowardly. You begin to wonder if the tournament was rigged after all!
In additional to having fun witnessing or "creating your own story". Developer are always hard at work to create new content so even if you don't buy any of the extra DLC. It is still a good deal. Even better when on sale.
I would not trade my time spend on Crusader Kings 2 for anything else!

This last year has been a sizeable disappointment. Plenty in the way of terrible events, losses, general bad news, and to top it all off an election that will put someone in the white house for the next four years, and no one is particularly excited for any of the candidates.
This game is a cathartic bit of satire built into a 'dumb phsyics' game. It's kind of like Postal 2 meets Goat Simulator while being neither of those things. You have to use a barely functional(please note, that's not an insult, it's just the best description) physics system to either hurl your bodyguard character into the path of danger or knock "Ronald Rump" to safety. There is also a side-game of sorts where you have to unleash dope wrasslin' moves on Rump, but it's clearly not the focus of the game.
The satire is the most standout part of this game, with the level designs going from tongue-in-cheek references to cutthroat political crucifixion, eventually reaching to a bleak representation of the state of the world in four years.
The weakest part of the game is the controls, which is to be expected from a dumb physics game. There are a variety of 'secret' controls tied to keys on the keyboard that aren't listed, you just have to press buttons to get the bodyguard to do stuff. Some of it is useful, like a front flip that helps maintain some momentum, or a quick scurry forward on hands and knees to get under low obstacles, and some of it is just elaborate fluff like a ten-second victory animation that if hit prematurely ensures you will not complete the level. There were several points where an obstacle was seemingly unsurmountable was passed again the next time round without changing the approach strategy in the slightest. If that is something that is a deal-breaker, you should probably steer clear.
So if you like satire and enjoy dumb physics games, check it out; there are far less-entertaining ways to spend five bucks.
And if you want to enjoy the thoughts of people who don't really understand what the first amendment means, feel free to check out the community page; it's pretty magical.

Let me start by saying I really enjoyed INFRA, it wasnt what I was expecting (I dont really know what you could expect after reading you get to be a structural analyst in the first line of text but yeah...) but I felt it was a really rewarding and relaxing journey.
So what actually is it?
INFRA is a kind of mix between a game like Amnesia and Dear Esther, you get the puzzle elements from one, and the story elements/walking from the other (mostly the walking). I thought the puzzles were extremely well done personally, they dont have a sort of mad science feel that some other games like this have, its mostly about you controlling stuff to progress on and complete your job (which is to monitor how bad the spot is wrecked so you can begin fixing it).
I've noticed it had the tag of horror but I wouldn't really agree with that, I didnt come across anything that made me feel uneasy at all, it was just quite atmospheric throughout. By the way you dont get attacked by anything like in a survival horror game. I felt that was something I should mention because I was concerned about that throughout.
The story is pretty decent to, the game tells the tale of an economic collapse of an entire region, and you get to experience how it progressed to where it was by looking through notes and areas that you experience when going through the game. I began by not really careing all too much and didnt pay that much attention to the newspaper articles littered through the world, but then towards the end I started to read through them and found them to be quite interesting, so my recommendation was if you get it do that from the start :).
This game has a great atmosphere too, in particular theres a section where you go into an abandoned steel factory and lose connection with the outside world, and it feels really earie which I guess explains the horror tag. The sound was done really well in this area too, mostly silent with a low bassy hum of I guess the old poweplant?
Speaking about sound, I really liked the soundtrack for the game and I felt that it fit well with each section, so if you have a few extra pennies I'd say its worth buying it.
My time played shows roughly how long the game lasts, and I'd say its not bad for a small indie game, infact quite good. Theres also multiple collectables and stuff you can go back and do for the achievements giving you a reason to play it again, which you know, its always a positive.
Bad Bits:
Although I really enjoyed my experience with INFRA theres a few points I think you should know:
1. The voice acting at the start was pretty bad, the characters other than your own didnt feel genuine at all and the animations of the people were lacking quite a bit (but this goes away after about the first 15 mins or so, so dont worry about that too much).
2. Its got quite a walking simulator feel to it, aside from the puzzles, and is more of a relaxing experience than an intense one. So thats something to watch out for if you don't really like those types of games.
Anyway to sum this up, I also had a crack at making a video review which you may want to check out to see what the gameplay is like and get my full view on it before you buy it:

Now, essentially this game is Civ V, but in a fantasy setting and faster paced.  There are just a few suggestions I have for features that would be nice:
1. Turn rotation/Hotseat option.  Having a way to set it so that players take turns in rotation instead of playing each turn simultaneously would be nice, mostly because it would add the potential option for hotseat gameplay.
2. More units.  Having just three units per faction is... kind of lame.  Having more variety in each faction would be nice, and while having unique factions is cool, having only one or two viable options for victory for each faction seems kind of limiting.  Having more units for each faction would definitely improve the replayability of this game, by making more viable options for strategies to use.
3. Single player campaign mode.  The current version of "campaign", which is doing class quests in the game, while unique, kind of just leaves me wanting even more of the faction's lore.  Having a way to play that in a classic campaign mode would be great, making the game feel even more in depth than it already is.
And that's it!  since they fixed the frequent crashes (and various other bugs) a while ago, that's all I would really add to this game.

BugZy's Review: INFRA - Debris, debris everywhere
The following is my opinion.
In INFRA, you enter the world of a structural analyst, just another day at the extremely large and detailed office - and I say large and detailed because that is completely the case. About half of the building is unavailable to explore, but you can see through the many big windows that more than a lot of time and effort has gone into this building alone. The building is only a fraction of the game and it would already make up one of the best maps for an online FPS.
Anyway, your job turns from bad to worse when you go to visit and report deteriorating infrastructure. I will avoid spoiling any more of the game so you can experience it for yourself. Just expect to spend a lot of time exploring places that the people at Loiste didn't need to add, but added anyway, which made the game just that little bit more detailed and affected the overall amenity of the game in the long run.
The game can be compared to a not-so-scary version of Outlast, in that you are navigating dark areas with a camera. Unfortunately your camera doesn't have a built-in flashlight, so you carry one seperate (which if the developers had thought through, you would be able to smack some stuff with.) The camera and flashlight both have batteries that drain unbelievably fast though, so you must find some new ones lying around in convenient places. Not to worry, there are more than enough lying around!
As you can see, I am so far, very impressed with INFRA. It has some very meticulous developers and the environmental graphics are brilliant (the humans could use some more detail though, but the environment makes up for that.) The sound effects in the game make the game a bit eerie and - although it is a completely non-violent game - it does get a bit spooky (especially when you take a picture of something out of the ordinary, that sound caught me off guard a few times.)
The game plays nicely once you manage to load it up without crashing, Sometimes it crashes on launch, sometimes mid-game, sometimes when I'm trying to quit. No game is without problems, though.
Overall, the game is awesome and I would recommend it to anyone who likes exploration, attention to detail and/or taking photos.

I'm giving this a careful recommendation.
Countless Rooms of Death is not a high production value game and I'm not sure it counts as horror either. Instead, it is a decently made randomized puzzle game, which uses strange object placements in its rooms and discomforting music and sound cues to keep you feeling tense.
There are no cheap deaths or scares, but a lot of frustration as the game doesn't hold your hand in the slightest and relies on you to figure out what to do in each puzzle room.
Essentially it is a maze of interconnected cubes, with each room being either empty or holding some form of puzzle. Occasionally you will come across documents or specific occurences which advance the cryptic story. Most of the time the room is empty though and there are a lot of dead paths requiring you to backtrack -- at least each room has at least something in it so you can keep them apart, and occasionally something weird happens when you first enter.
If you like SCP games, Countless Rooms of Death is worth a try. Just remember that it is not a particularly good looking or all that well designed game.
And do play it with headphones on and crank up the sound to at least setting '2' in the in-game settings room before playing. Playing it in the dark can help as well.
(Updated: upon further replays I'm pretty sure it's not procedurally generated, but randomized. As in a specific room will always be the same but where it's placed and what doors are active will change across games.)

Color Syndrome might seem  at a brief first sight as a Tetris clone. You couldn’t be more wrong. This title managed to take the basics of an already established game within its genre and add a new flavor to it. That is indeed something you don’t expect from an indie dev, on its 2nd published game on Steam. And yet Color Syndrome blends the old & the new thus creating a casual title which can’t go wrong, whether you’re into slower paced, more strategic approaches to Tetris or more alert modes of it. The brightly colored visual style is well complemented by certain effects which break away any signs of monotony. The sounds might have deserved some more diversity but that is about the only con I could honestly find in ths game. Even if I wasn’t nostalgic about the “good ol’ days” when a bootleg Tetris handheld knockoff, was the best cure to boredom, I still feel like Color Syndrome achieved its goal and provided me with a few good hours of strategic fun. Add to that, Leaderboards, Trading Cards & Achievements, all for a more than decent price tag and you got yourself a contender to one of this year’s best casual games.
+ Balanced mix of gameplay innovation and homage to the classics.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.

There are some good things about this game, like the interesting concepts and the artwork/asthetics. But there are some major problems:
- Most of the player's time is spent doing tedious and annoying things that feel like chores. Iterating through every single building one by one to apply an upgrade, or painstakingly aiming every single missile one by one through a series of twists and turns across the solar system... only to have them all miss the target. Even navigating through the different views sucks up time, because you have to wait for the camera to finish spazzing out every single time.
- Secondly, there aren't a lot of meaningful choices for the player to make. There's no real incentive to focus on offense, which makes the game drag on for even longer.  A lot of the items in the tech tree are pointless, the same goes for a lot of projects. Play one game, or at the very most two, and you'll see how a large portion of the game can mostly be ignored. There are too many tiny, meaningless details that take up time I'd like to spend strategizing.
The game was interesting for a couple of playthroughs. I think this game could be great if the actual mechanics were made less tedious.

While seemingly very simple to begin with, this twin-stick is actually quite lovely and has a lot more depth than it appears to.
The main draw for me to this game is the sheer, arcade-level replayability. Despite being a (relatively) modern twin-stick with a shooting style most easily compared to The Binding of Isaac, its shining feature is the style. With infinite replayability and a certain degree of variety throughout each unique playthrough, it really feels like it belongs in an arcade cabinet.
The only problem I have with this game right now is the competition, which SHOULD be one of the main features of an arcade style game. I'm #2 at the time of posting this, but my score is so close to #1 that I should be able to beat it with a few more tries. This #1 score is a developer! I wish the playerbase would be just a little bit larger, so I could have something to try for.
But that's why I'm writing this review! I've supported this game since its alpha phase back on Desura, and the devs have done nothing but lather it with love. And I'm sure they won't stop now!

This is one of several ways to survive at start and for a long time: (unless you f-up)
What you need to do is choose a LARGE map size and then find a RIVER (the map is randomly generated so you can enter the same spot every time and get a different map).
What you are looking for is an Island with trees, once you've found one you need to settle down there and start building a wall around it.
This way you won't need to worry that much about enemies easily killing your settlers at the start of the game, and that island could become your very own fortress. Just build a bridge to main land whenever you're ready to expand.
It's also good to start with whatever food farms you've got and expand them, to prevent starvation. (Your food supplies will be very short at start but you'll eventually end up with an abundance of food)
The rest is up to you, good luck and have fun! :)

To be honest, when I bought INFRA, I really didn't know what would be involved.
Now, I know, And I can tell you, INFRA is more than a game. It's a real experience to master, an unexpected journey, a precious one.
I had no particular expectations when I started to play and very quickly I've been really impressed.
From the office, that warm cocoon you have to leave with your only "friends", your flashligh and your camera, to the very last dark tunnel you have to escape to.
The game brilliantly alternates between the great outdoors and shabby interiors, between quiet moments and those more agitated, between easy puzzles and those which will lead you gently but steadily to madness.
There's also the purpose to deeply involved the player, not only to follow a path, but to make it your own way.
The more you'll explore the faster you'll understand what, why and how you need to do it.
From here, the only usefull advice I can give to you : Keep your eyes fully opened and your brain fully prepared to really appreciate it.
Yes, INFRA is a masterpiece. Unique and scarce one.
Thanks Loiste Interactive for being more than just a company that wants to make money.

I had to rewrite this review, since the time has passed, the game now is fully released (my previous review was for pre-release), and all the bugs I've witnessed in the pre-release, are there - and even more.
Games like Color Syndrome usually gets descriptions such as "Tetris with a twist". Only "twist" is bigger than basic Tetris game this time. Obviously, we still have blocks falling in the well, so yeah, it looks like Pajitnov's thing. However, while original Tetris mechanic is based on the old (maybe ancient) puzzles with polyominoes - geometric figures shaping each other - Color Syndrome is something of another breed. The closest relative I can think of is the old NES game Dr. Mario... Just as the name of the game prompting, the colours, and not the shapes will be the primes for "writing off the lines". Construct the lines with same color by 4 in the row - and try to not get yourself buried under blocks, okay?
The main question: Do I like the game? Maybe. It should have been a decent piece of work, with all those modes and trials... In a Tetris/Color Assemblers/Connect4/Dr.Mario type of the game. It has trading cards, achievements AND good price... and yet it is still full of the same bugs I've witnessed when the game was in pre-release state.  The most recent thing still - is the freeze of dropping figure just when it Could scrape smth, no matter if it actually can be moved to another side freely - sorry, but no more, figure is falling, hands off, no buttons will work now. This bug is getting really annoying after some time, when your well is half full already. This freezing still occurs quite recently. Also I have witnessed strange things when some figure is stacking at 1/2 of grid line - in between. Some figures might stuck somewhere "in the air", creating a distraction for any new figures next to it... And the list of bugs is not over there, it could be much longer!
My mark is 5/10. The game had potential, yet, alas, as many indie-projects with a single man behind it, it was forgotten on the half-way, without cleaning up the code. Potentially fun game - in its narrow subgenre - but broken code-work, which leaves no hopes for a good time.

You have a decent amount of weaponry and utility available and at first, it is quite interesting to see where the projectiles travel depending on nearby planets.
Scrolling through the tiny tech tree, you make up your mind on what to boost first and later on just go straight for the super weapons. It's pretty straight forward, yet not always tactically very decisive or interesting. Good luck finding all the buildings for your newly gained upgrade, though.
After a while you find yourself annoyed from needing ridiculous amounts of power plants (nuclear ones!) just for putting one extra utility building. This is not because of energy consumption, it is because of a maximum amount of links each station can host.
Another thing that gets annoying after a while is trying to make the projectiles actually shoot an angle you want since they only accept relatively small angles. You are literally moving the mouse pixel by pixel, hoping that the projectile's way shows up properly.
Clicking through lasers and missiles, you spend an enormous amount of time waiting for the constant zoom in- zoom out animations, leaving you confused on where that building was you wanted to focus.
The user-friendlyness clearly needs to be raised with proper displays of available shooting arcs, proper selection for planetary targets and maybe the option to build just one weapon and support it with clusters of ammo for less clicks and the same amount of projectiles.
Relatively small amounts of projectiles kill your fps here which is another argument to reduce the amount of projectiles and guns and add spreading effects on impact and such.

This'll be my first Steam review, so bear with me if it's not quite up-to-snuff, but this was a really unique game. Hopefully this can be helpful for possible players as well as the designer, because while interesting, it has room for serious improvement.
On the plus side, the game has nice visuals, some catchy audio, and a quasi-Silent Hill tendency to manipulate puzzles/environments against you. As soon as the game opens up, you open the only possible door and are swallowed by darkness. Upon escaping, you wind up in a room with no door at all. The puzzles are generally simple--if you listen closely to the dialogue--and the fact that you can walk into the same dead end hallway three times and see a blank wall, a mirror, and a door, respectively, is really disorienting and interesting. Some even require actual typing, which was cool, despite me failing and getting killed when that one came up.
On the negative, this game also embodies everything that was wrong with gaming in the 90s. Entire levels that rely exclusively on platforming generally don't need to appear in a 2014 game, especially when the edges of platforms are apparently slippery, resulting in a lack of jumping and an untimely death. This isn't helped by the pointless and cliche use of a revolver that breaks green jars, allowing you to collect a magic-like substance that allows you to jump high. The continue system requires passwords rather than save files, so if you'd like to continue, you have to remember the level title--and be willing to start that level over upon returning.
As far as the writing goes, there seems to be some potential, but it's obscured by two major issues: One, there are no scenes and no actual conversation, aside from Vinny, the antagonist, yelling at Anthony, the protagonist; and two, Anthony starts off as a shy, awkward, potentially likable college student who quickly degrades into a hateful, repulsive moron. That may sound harsh, but I can't count the number of times he described Vinny as a c**t, and when he started shouting for Vinny to "man up and stop hiding," I couldn't help but think, "You just got eaten alive by darkness and then a room turned upside down. You walked across the ceiling and leapt into a void to chase a talking ball of blue light... and you have nothing to say to that? Not even 'Holy crap, Vinny, how did you just turn off gravity?'"
All in all, the opening levels are neat, and the fact that this is free helps a long way, but the 'plot twists' (so emphasized because there really is no plot) are contrived and the execution to this nice idea is deeply flawed. I sincerely hope the developer takes the ideas behind levels like Parlor and Park and creates a whole new game--ditch the crappy characters and shock-value ending, try again, and there will be quality gaming hours in store.

This review used to be a recommendation, with words of caution added later on. It's been a while since then, and I feel I have to change this review to "not recommended", if only to balance out the people who recommend it after a couple of hours of play. Don't get me wrong: discovering how the game works is fun, but after that it just falls flat and the grinding quickly becomes unbearable (to me at least). If you're the type of gamer that goes "well I got 20 hrs of play out of a €10,- game, so excellent value", you might still want to buy this. But with games like these, I'm looking for an interesting sandbox experience with a lot of replayability, and that's just not the case yet with Timber & Stone.
Since the release on Steam, the devs have fallen almost completely silent, and everything points to development being halted indefinitely. Player complaints (either about the game itself or the lack of communication) are ignored (except by a few diehard fans who attack people for being critical) and that's basically two of the biggest sins for an "early access" title.
So. Unless you don't mind "wasting" a bit of money for a couple of hours of fun (and aftert that, likely disappointment), avoid this title in favor of early access builders that DO have an active developer behind it.
(1.7 Steam release review)
My most recent settlement, called "False New Hope" (it seemed appropriate after the first few settlements I started got wiped before I even managed to build a decent town hall), fell to a horde of goblins that almost thanked me for building so many nice gates to smash through. Next time, I'm building a citadel with just one gate, and it will be heavily defended.
If you like games that mercilessly ramp up the difficulty with every small accomplishment you make, that require you to plan ahead for threats you don't even know about yet, that give you quite a lot of options to do so but don't hold your hand at any time, Timber & Stone is for you.
At this point, the interface is still quite clunky and unintuitive (well, to me at least) and there seem to be some balancing issues that could lead to frustration. Be prepared to do a lot of reading up to get started properly. On the plus side, the forums and developers seem to be very active, so I'm sure things will improve in the future. The devs also seem to have plenty more new features up their sleeve, so I don't expect to get bored with this anytime soon.
Just be careful that your archers don't shoot their friends.
EDIT: after more playing, and following the forums for a bit, I feel like I need to update this review:
- development actually seems to be halted now, with very little communication from the developers on the forums, except for vague and slightly defensive posts indicating it's "temporary". No plans for the future have been announced since releasing the game on Steam, aside from a few remarks on feature requests (either to dismiss them, or to confirm that they're planned, whatever that means when nothing seems to be happening development-wise)
- once you figure out the mechanics and get a handle on the clunky controls, the game isn't very deep yet. A few tech levels and a handful of enemies that become increasingly numerous and a bit tougher as your settlement grows and becomes richer/more advanced
- I spent a good amount of time on it, while having fun, but a lot of it was getting to grips with the game's weirdness and grindyness ("teching up" is largely dependend on finding enough appropriate ores or repeatedly building the same objects over and over again)
- now that it looks like I won't be encountering fresh challenges, my urge to play is largely absent because of poor controls (both for building and for managing large numbers of settlers/soldiers), low fps and general annoyances (i.e. archers shooting their infantry buddies half the time, having to manually click individual enemies to target them and then again to loot their corpses)
- judging by the people running "old" settlements with intricate, large builds and big populations, some gamers will obviously still find it worth their time despite the aforementioned shortcomings. I guess it depends on how much time you're willing to spend, whether you're a hardcore builder or not, etc.
- in short: this game will probably still entertain you for a few good days if you're into survival/crafting/base building, but there's a good chance it'll start to disappoint further down the line, with little in the way of a development plan (even one without specific promises and deadlines) to keep you interested
I'm saying NO only because this game needs TONS of polish before I feel like it's really playable. I like the concept and graphics, but the implementation just isn't there yet.

Interesting concept, horrendous execution.
Projectile combat is just a guessing game, one that can simply be reduced to "attack when you're ahead of the enemy's orbit and there are zero obstacles in your way." The only way to reliably get hits is to let your attacks fall into the target's gravity well. There's zero room for interesting maneuvers because you can't see or reliably guess where the future positions of the planets will be, and you can't adjust any its trajectory mid-flight.
Lasers trump everything. The only thing balancing it is that it has a small radius and that you need to have intel to really make use of it, but intel/counterintel is just a resource sink, i.e. can I build Telescope Arrays faster than the enemy builds Data Security Hubs?
Strategy-wise this game sucks, especially if you have more than two players. The innermost and outermost players inherently have a strategic advantage compared to the ones in the middle because there are fewer attack approaches. City placement is random and it's much better to have cities that are relatively closer for shielding purposes.
It's not in your best interest to shoot first because that draws away energy that could be used for defense/construction. Since you can't loot enemies for resources, the only strategic advantage that you get from it is that you remove a threat, which quickly dwindles to nothing the more players there are. Thus it favors defensive strategies over offensive ones, i.e. just keep building until you strip the planet dry before making a move. Also, a 3+ player free-for-all becomes a Mexican standoff, which disincentivizes attacking even further.
Honestly the game is just a one-trick pony that actually kinda fails on its selling gimmick. The physics simulation in the game is ridiculously simplified: it's all in the 2D plane and it's no more complicated than eyeballing it. Approach vectors don't matter; the only thing the game cares about is that the shot connects. Which makes no sense for, well, a freaking railgun whose projectiles are governed by orbital mechanics. For instance, tripling the impact velocity should increase the damage by roughly an order of magnitude, which would also be nice because it would reward more difficult (i.e. moving, not falling) shots.
Also, the interface is clunky but at least that can be fixed.

Not knowing really what to expect, the premise immediately hooked me in that I genuinely cared about my job as a structural engineer going out into the countryside and city of Stalburg.  I was welcomed with beautiful hiking, urban exploration, nature, and fascinating infrastructure and overall care taken by the designers, programmers, and artists of this wonderful Finnish gem.
All that would have been enough, but included are elements of intrigue, intense enviromental action, and a sense that my presence in the world is having long-lasting effects for its infrastructure!
The ending of Part 1 was very abrupt for me, but Part 1 is certainly lengthy and quite varied! I simply can't wait for more of this game and more similar games to come from Loiste Interactive!

First of all, the game is beautiful, yet it doesn't rquire a high-end machine to max out. Dont get me wrong, the graphics arent photorealistic - they are just very well crafted in terms of level design and setting an ambience. Its not just a couple of very detailed setpieces with bland areas in between, all environments in INFRA have been crafted with the same attention to detail. INFRA is truly a level designer's game.
The puzzles are truly challenging if you want to do them properly, but the game also allows you to progress without finishing them. This creates a very rewarding game that, at the same time, can be completed by nearly anyone.
The story isnt really that deep, in fact sometimes it feels like a portal rip-off, but everything is made up by the phenomenal atmosphere the game offers. Even with the shortcomings regarding the main story, I found the game very immersive.
Is INFRA a walking simulator? Not really. The environment interaction in infra is deep, and always conected with the core puzzle gameplay. This means the walking around and enjoying the visuals isnt its own goal, but rather forms a solid puzzle solving experience with plenty of eye candy.
All in all, a very enjoyable experience.

I was expecting a 4-hour game at best, but instead I got 18 hours of enjoyable exploration and puzzle solving set entirely in Finland, as it should be used more as a setting and not just for sports games. And that's just Part 1. I can't imagine how many more locations are in store in Part 2, which will be a free update, when I've already experienced the length of at least two modern FPS games for €15. Not only is it a refreshing change of setting from your usual New Yorks or what have you, though any city would work here, it's also inspired by a documentary about deteriorating infrastructure. That fact alone fills me with confidence that games as an art form is in safe hands. It's a fascinating choice of subject matter for a developer's first game and not in any way presented through a prism of science fiction or a military conflict, which is usually the choice for first-person games set in crumbling cities.
Instead of having a decaying city as a backdrop, it's a character of the story. A victim of neglect, rivaling companies and corruption. You're tasked with surveying the structural damage of the city of Stalburg by taking photos of the damage. Finding documents and tapes people have left behind, you start to piece together where it all went haywire. You work your way through a maze of different locations, each of them detailed to the point of being believable, but not impressive by standards available to those with a huge budget. This being a crowd-funded game however, the scope and level of detail achieved here is shocking for a team of just 6 people, according to the credits.
INFRA removes the guns, the aliens or bad guys with guns and you're left with elements that every great FPS relies on: exploration, environmental storytelling, quiet moments, puzzle solving, dealing with obstacles, etc. It's a game of valves, switches, key cards, buttons, turning it off, turning it on, reading notes and instructions to operate machinery and I loved every minute of it. You can find most of these in every notable FPS since the days of DOOM. The reason I'm emphasizing these is because the devs have honestly described what their game is about. It's not overburdened by pointless distractions that only create the illusion of immediacy and importance. What you're doing here is important in and of itself. The game sends a strong message of being responsible with the world around you, which is, among all these hugely expensive and ultimately pointless games, thoroughly heartwarming and commendable. Not to mention rare.
Couple of moments where I couldn't figure out how to progress, so I consulted a video walkthrough, but I'm more bummed about the the stuff I didn't know how to repair. You're stuck between analyzing and trying to leave a place in a better shape than it was, but many of the bigger puzzles tied to achievements I just couldn't figure out, so grudgingly I had to move on. Thankfully there are no easy-to-use guides out there yet, so you can actually enjoy the puzzles as opposed to following a step-by-step guide on how to restore the functions of all these different facilities. There is damage, or scripted moments, that's unavoidable, but instinctively you try to be responsible where you can. These places have been abandoned, reminiscent of Pripyat, but the machinery still has life left in it, which continue to do damage.
The overall aesthetic reminded me of STALKER meets Half-Life 2, so a big thank you for Loiste Interactive in filling a gap that certain developers have failed to do for too long. To crawl through vents and solve puzzles is not to be underestimated, guns or no guns. While I eventually gave up on reading newspapers or longer notes, towards the end, I'm very much interested in how the story will progress in Part 2 and I look forward to taking more photos and solving puzzles. Somehow I've managed to ignore the elephant in the room. The voice acting of the player character is atrocious, but it steadily grows on you at a snail's pace, cos it's just so bad that it becomes almost cute. There is a lack of polish here, but that didn't stop Shadow of Chernobyl in becoming one of the best games of all time. You have to let a few things slide in order to get something special out there and that's fine, cos it's important that we get to play this in its current form than not at all.

INFRA is a linear, story-driven adventure with an impressively well-realized world and engaging puzzles that are esoteric but not aggravatingly so.
Let's start with the world. INFRA is packed full of little details. It definitely rewards you for exploring and being observant. These rewards range from simple easter eggs to shortcuts. Puzzles in INFRA can have multiple solutions. You can get to the other side of a door by cunning navigation or clever circumventing. Because of these multiple routes, there are many offshoots (not complete branches because they connect back to the trunk quickly) that make the game feel organic and immersive. This game is definitely replayable as you will miss things the first time through.
Let's talk about the bad a little bit. So while on the whole, I thoroughly enjoy the puzzles in this game, they don't scale well. What I mean by this is that rather than having puzzles that get trickier as you progress through the game, the puzzles get harder to solve because the pieces become hidden. My favorite part of putting together a puzzle isn't the part where I have to dig in the couch cushions because I think I lost a piece. So while this can make simple things take longer it does have the upside of forcing you to explore the world more and none of the pieces were ever hidden in a way that I thought was unfair.
On the balance, the experience and mystery of this game significantly outweighs the frustrations of having wasted an hour because you didn't look behind a door or in a box.

I've really been looking forward to this game, and I bought it as soon as it was released. It still has a way to go but im looking forward to when the glitches are fixed. Here are some of the things that need to be changed:
-It takes WAY too long for the next piece to come out. Once your current piece lands, there is a large delay between when it lands and when your turn stops. This would be okay if you could still move, but you can't. The piece just sits there until it thinks that turn is over.
-The pieces fall too fast. It would be a big help if you could change the fall speed, difficulty, etc.
-The pieces fall like they are affected by gravity. This wouldn't be a problem except that the physics are buggy. Every once in a while a piece will bounce and go flying off, sometimes out of the boundaries.
-The white pieces are glitchy. Occasionally you will be able to control the white piece, but most of the time it just goes back and forth, left and right. This sometimes messes up lines that are set up.
-We need two rotate buttons. One clockwise, the other counter-clockwise. It would also be nice if the pieces stayed in place when rotating instead of moving around.
That's about all I can think of at the moment. I hope these get fixed soon.
Thank you for your time!

Although my PC account is low leveled as of December 2017, I have over 400 hours spent in Warframe on Xbox and I am mastery rank 14. As being a sort of "veteran" or "experienced player" I feel that I am eligible to review warframe, and that it is one of the best games I have ever played. Warframe has it all. Hundreds of warframes (or combat suits), weapons, customization, and things to do. Warframe has many storylines, and all of them are playable. You can do missions with your friends, and it really offers a great and fun alien-killing, shooting, and exploration experience.
Now to wrap up this review, let me adress the 2 most persuing complaints about Warframe.
1-The grind. Yes, warframe requires a lot of grinding. As it is a ftp, Warframe makes you work for your items. Of course, you can always just buy items in the menu, but you aren't forced to! I find gridning fun, and if it is too much for you then find a differnet game.
2-"Pay to Win". As mentioned before, everything in warframe is farmable. There is no forcing, and it is free-to-play, so the developers have to make money somehow! If you find warframe pay to win, then you are not dedicated or competitve enough to farm. And while that's fine, you shouldn't bring your gaming flaws to batter a perfectly good game.
In conclusion, Warframe is great. One of the most played ftp games of all time. If you want a free game, or something to grind and farm with your friends, or a fun shooting and exploration experience, come get Warframe. You won't regret it.

Endless Legend innovates on the 4X genre in ways similar to how Warcraft 3 brought forward RTS into a new era. They do it in the same way: with hero units that can lead your armies (and here, cities), gain levels, use equipment, etc. This adds a ton of new possibilities. Combat is also different and more interesting, with armies moving as one and then breaking up into their component parts when a fight starts. So rather than just click to attack, there is a 6-round battle that requires strategy and tactics.
There's a lot of other things to recommend as well. The game is simply gorgeous. It's a pleasure just to watch the map rise out of the fog. The lore and factions are all interesting, with diverse playstyles and quests to shape your goals.  I have played thousands of hours of civ over my life, and this game now makes it all seem new again. I am loving it already and can tell I will be playing for many hundreds of hours.

Each playable Race has a very own style to play and even its very own game mechanics. Each Race tells it own story and shows the player its very personla view of the world.
There are very few bugs and the developers are constantly working on solutions  for the bugs and ways to enhance the game experience.
Over all id give the game extremly enjoyble 9 out of 10 points.

So much THIS. I got this and Endless Space (and Dungeon of the Endless) all in the Amp pack, and so far this is my favorite of the three amazing games.
At first, this looks just like a Civ, or other turn-based-startegy game clone. Well, it doesn't, actually. The UI is strange and beautiful, and it takes a while to get past the breathy style the Endless games all have. But once you do you think "Oh, it's just like all those other spreadsheet war simulations."
But it isn't. It seems like the games are designed to make you think like the empire you're playing. I didn't play on easy, just went with "Normal" mode out of the box (and then went back and played the tutorial for the cheese, and ended up learning a thing or two. Don't skip it, it's on the first menu somewhere), and got soundly thrashed when I tried to play it like any other strategy game.
Anyway, I could blather on about it for a  bit, but instead I'll try to make some comparisons to things you may have played thata re sort of similar:
If you liked:
Civ (natch)
Master of (Magic/Space)
Age of Wonders
Turn based strategy in general
You'll probably get at least 24 hours of entertainment out of this (about how long it takes to really get a handle on the mechanics in general and beat the slightly-stupid AI into the paste it deserves to be).

This is a very good looking 4x game.
But :

- the AI is inexistent, making the game way too easy. This is quite common among 4X games but for endless legend, upgrading your army weapons means turning on God Mode as NPC factions don't do it.
- In the end it is more a contemplative experience of a marvelously good looking game (Firaxis, be ashamed of your Civilizations) than any kind of challenge.
The lack of challenge from NPC opponents is something common in 4X games, as the use of the words "artificial intelligence' is just marketing (there is no such thing). But for Endless Legend, there is just no challenge and I got bored on my first game, despite the interesting idea of faction quests.
I feel really let down by the reviews, specially the one from RPS whom I used to trust but have become over the last year yet another mediocrity celebrating gaming website.
You could like this game, just accept beforehand that just as in Civilization, you won't encounter any challenge from the faction NPCs. This is really too bad.

My only major complaint is with the crafting system, which feels unnecessary except for a few valuable recipes. I like it and want to see more of it in the next game, but it's not perfect here. Luckily, you can completely ignore it if you want to. There are also a few head-scratching design decisions IMO (why is Pet Pal a talent and not a Huntsman/Summoner ability?) but these are all minor complaints and there are plenty of mods to tweak the rules to adjust. The modding scene seems extremely robust - I'm running about 40 mods for co-op, for example, a few of which are very well-executed.
This game is a unilateral improvement over its predecessor - I found it much more engaging and polished. The voice acting and character-centric writing really elevate this game. I wasn't a huge fan of D:OS 1 but I'm completely sucked into this one.
If you like CRPGs, you don't have a good excuse not to play this game. 10/10, a masterpiece.

INFRA is not my usual type of game - I normally stick to RTS titles. Yet the concept of walking through dilapadated ruins looking for dangerous cracks and things out of place sucked me in, and I'm very glad it did! Having played through Part 1 (Part 2 is due later and will not be DLC but an integral part of the game, which will rise in price when it is released, so buying now may save you!) I would say that my favourite part of INFRA is the incredible atmosphere the game manages to create. An effective mix of impressive visuals and ambient effects bring to life the game's juxtaposition of the natural and artificial landscapes - so you'll emerge from a tunnel to see the decaying entrace behind is encrusted in trees and plants just as a slightly haunting tune plays, giving a pleasantly melancholy feeling.
The game puzzles are nice and varied, with clever use of the same elements to prevent everything from feeling too 'samey'. The game plot appears threadbare at first, but as the game progresses you can find out a lot more - nothing is presented explicitly, but if you piece together the scattered documents you find along the game you can put it all together, culminating in the final setpiece which sets the game up nicely for Part 2. The game has pretty good replay value, with a good mix of hidden achievements and collectibles (e.g. when going off the game path to some inaccessible place you'll sometimes find a geocache). After finishing my first playthrough I really want to go through again and find every little detail! Overall, INFRA is a steal for its price - I'd thoroughly recommend it

AN EXCELLENT ARTILLERY SPACE GAME
I’ve been a fan of artillery games for many many years. I’ve played most of the Worms games and loved them (most of them), and I loved playing a game called Tanks way back in the early 90s. Yes I’m old. I had to break out of the retirement home just to write this review for you guys so please give it a thumbs up.
Anyway, Interplanetary differs from all of the other artillery games I’ve played in that the developers have taken the genre into outer space. Boy does it work wonderfully in this new playground! Because planets are continually orbiting their host stars you have to predict where you think the enemy planet will be by the time your projectile will have reached it after having traversed the star system - very much like leading a target with a sniper rifle in a first-person shooter game.
Not only do you have to take into account the movement of your target planet as it performs its orbit, you also have to consider the movement of other orbiting bodies, their gravity wells, and the fact that they may move in to the way of your otherwise well-aimed shot. I’ve often been saved from the onslaught of incoming enemy fire by an uninhabited planet “heroically” diving in the way to bear the full brunt of the barrage. Thank you, physics! :D
Moreover, you have to take into consideration the rotation of your planet and that of the target planet too. If you’ve built a laser and it’s on the opposite side of your planet facing away from the enemy then it’ll be completely useless for that targeting turn until your planet has rotated to face the correct direction. Likewise, if you’re aiming for a particular enemy city and it’s currently on the opposite side of the planet, from your point of view, then it’ll make it a lot more difficult to hit, and you may even have to wait until the planet’s rotation has put it on the side that’s facing you to score a successful attack.
Very basically, in each turn you can build, undertake research, and shoot at your enemies. You have to plan this carefully because firing lots of weapons in one turn may not leave you with any energy remaining to begin contruction projects that round. This is true the other way around: too much building and you'll have no energy left to fire your weapons. So it's best to go on the offensive when you've got easy shots lined up, and build up your planet when the targets are far away and with lots of celestial bodies obstructing the path.
You then win the game by destroying all of the enemy's cities and massacring the millions of civilians who, hitherto, inhabited it.
PROS
- Single player and multiplayer with up to 7 enemies in both cases. This can provide some very interesting and challenging matches, especially when one player's shot misses the intended target and hits someone else instead :D
- Buildings and cities are upgradeable e.g. power plants can produce even more energy, satellite arrays have improved detection of enemy structures, HP increase...
- Weapons are upgradeable e.g. increased damage, reduced power consumption,
- Lots of great upgrades to research and unlock via the tech tree.
- Great orchestral soundtrack that adds wonderfully to the atmosphere.
- Firing a shot around the sun only to have it slung-shot back in your direction, hit your own planet, and destroy your own buildings is surprisingly good fun. There’s even a Steam achievement if you manage to do that! :D
CONS
- Relatively few weapons: rain gun, missile, laser, solar laser, asteroid diversion... That’s it, sadly.
- The computer AI has pretty much perfect aim. In my experience the AI shots almost never miss.
- All of the matches are played in just unary star systems (i.e. just one sun). I know it would make aiming interplanetary projectiles a lot more difficult in binary or ternary solar systems (2 or 3 stars respectively), what with all of the extra gravity wells, but it would be a great challenge for those who want a ‘hardcore’ game mode.
- (as an extension of the last point) All of the host stars are just main sequence stars like our Sun. It would have been great to have had different star types like blue super giants and white dwarfs. With their differing sizes (and different mass) firing projectiles through the planetary system would require very different trajectories and velocities with such different stars. Also, their very different masses, and therfore gravity, would greatly affect the angular velocities of the orbiting planets - another factor that would influence how you’d have to plan your trajectory paths during the targeting phase.
I’d easily give Interplanetary an 8 or 8.5 out of 10. It would instantly get an extra point if the developer added the “missing content” outlined in my cons section.
If you like turn-based strategy games, with excellent artillery action which requires precise planning, and also involves base building with research then Interplanetary should be an insta-buy for you.

Happy mass-murdering!

Very enjoyable strategy game. Worth trying even if you didn't like Endless Space (which I did not.)
There's a great deal of depth in the mechanics. Unit selection is somewhat disappointing, but it doesn't detract from the gameplay. Graphics are very unusual and I'd rate them the best in any 4X I've played. There's alot of personality in the world, with tons of flavor text. City building is satisfyingly deep but can require some micromanagement if you have alot of cities. There's a governor for that though I haven't tried it. The research tree isn't a tree exactly as you can research anything in a given tier at a time. It also forces real choices since you can't realistically get them all. I've read that some people don't like the combat but I find it enjoyable. It takes place on actual game hexes, rather than some arbitrary battleground. You can assign units to attack a particular unit or (if available) heal/buff a friendly unit instead. There's not a ton of movement involved. There's no flanking that I'm aware of, or penalties for moving into or out of hexes adjacent to enemies.
My one complaint is that the game crashes to desktop on me frequently. I'm late into a game and it's crashing every single time I end a turn. Luckily it's a clean crash and the game boots right back up but it can be very frustrating.

I have to review this a little: the strategy, both strategic and tactical, can prove challenging depending on the factions you are in... My original review was based mostly on the Wild Walkers faction. Consider it a "start up" faction. For *that* faction the decision of what to do is really a no-brainer: build archers, fast... But then there are many interesting decisions to make: I'm playing Vaulters nowadays, and there are some scrutiating decisions:  you have an strategic resource that is also a "luxury" resource, the "holy resource". Do I expand, and let my cities suffer in unhappiness? Do I use the holy resource as it's bonus?
And now we have "wonders": achievements that are a district, and that can be upgraded. And also field achievements. All this shows the developers attempts to give a full assortment of strategy options.
I still think that the AI kind of sucks, but there is an active community and an attemptive development crew, that is taking a good effort on improving it... The strongest suit of Amplitude Studios... I'm looking forward on what they will show in the next months.
ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Is it a good strategy game? No. Is it fun? Yes. There is something of a compelling history inside it, and an unique universe. It have many features to explore. And I like very much the developers' attention, where they actually stimulate the flow of ideas.
Why I don't consider it a good strategy game (yet): there seems to be balancing issues that makes one way of winning easier than the others. So, if you play on singleplayer to win, you don't fully explore the available options. The decision on how to build your armies seems almost a no-brainer.
Why I consider it fun: the ambient, the universe, the history, building cities , exploration, the quest system, the minor factions... Even the way the tech tree works, where you have many optional techs to explore.

(sigh...) Lets be clear about this: I loved this game, I still do. But I cannot recommend this to anyone at all just because it is extremely unfinished. When the Pre-alpha started in December I had really high hopes for this game. But I quickly realized that a really buggy pre-alpha really hurt the publicity of this game, so much that I feared that this game would be scrapped. It seems as if my fears have come true.
As a $30 dollar game it is alright. The objective of the game is to survive long enough so that you can gear up and hunt dinosaurs. It follows the basic structure of thehunter in that the OBJECTIVE is hunting. This confused allot of people at the beginning, they thought it was a DayZ with dino's which it is not. With a large Island and a 5 species of dinosaurs you can have alot of fun. Running from Raptors, hunting Triceratops, and teaming up to kill T-Rexes is essentially what you will be doing. Most of this game revolves around teamwork to take down the biggest and baddest of dinosaurs. This is really what made this game stand out. It fostered a teambuilding enviroment without holding your hand. But as with most pre-alpha's it had its downsides.
It started with only 3 types of dinosaurs (which grew to 5 types) which really wasn't that great. The weapons were lacking, the AI was terrible and it was all around a buggy game. Over the past 3 months the developers had been working really hard to polish up the pre-alpha and so it seemed as if everything was going just fine. Alas that was not the case...
Currently the game still feels like its stuck in pre-alpha, there are still bugs, a low amount of content, AI STILL SUCKS, there are only a few weapons in game, and in general it is unfinished all around. This really sucks as it had alot of potential to ge a GREAT game but in its current iteration I WOULD GIVE IT A 5/10 AT BEST.
Will I still play it, Yeah. But I would not advise you to buy it. Hopefully the devs will continue to produce more content and this jewel of a game can be saved. If they do fix it I will revisit this revew but for now, save your money and buy any of the other great indie games out there. It will be a much better use of your time and money.

At its core, Timber and Stone is a base-building, survival sim game. You control your guys, have them craft and build and survive against enemies and starvation. Plenty of games like it, right?
However, Timber and Stone does something wonderfully different; it does it enjoyably (something many games of this genre fail to do) but most importantly, it does it consistently.
The game is fun from beginning to end; it is insanely hard to come to grips with at first, but that challenge never quite reaches the level of frustration. As you get stronger, you start to be entranced by the desire to build the perfect castle, or town or whatever you're building, as well as fending off attacks from horrible Goblins and a myriad of Undead. When you lose your first settler... trust me, you'll feel it.
The game has been in development for a few years now, going through several iterations, but the developers have never been anything but completely transparent in their development process. We've been clued in from the start, and most of our feedback has been listened to. This is a dev team that is wholly intent on keeping their playerbase happy.
Timber and Stone is both as simple as its name, yet also wonderfully complex and interesting. It's hard, it hurts you emotionally, but it's so damn rewarding to see your town grow and your settlers progress. You do require a certain self-motivation to play, as there is very, VERY little hand-holding, but you will damn well enjoy yourself.
Also, don't let my hours played fool you; I have played... just so many hours of this wonderful game, before it was released to Steam. The developers have been putting off Steam release until it was in a good enough state.

is a first person puzzle adventure game with a very mysterious tone to it. While some may call it a “walking simulator”, I personally disagree, most of all due to the fact that INFRA allows you to take different routes and solve puzzles in different ways.
First off, it is necessary to say that at the moment only Part 1 of the game is available. The developers are already hard at work on Part 2 but, as of now, there is no estimated release date and the first part ends somewhat abruptly.
I was really surprised as I began to play this, that right from the start the game doesn’t hold your hand. Even though it is a linear game, you are able to explore your surroundings within certain limits. The game also doesn’t give you an objective so sometimes you might have a hard time figuring out what exactly you have to do or where you need to go. That said, even though you’ll encounter multiple puzzles, they are not mandatory but they might give you access to documents that can provide you with some background information on certain events that could potentially shed some light on the mystery you’re trying to solve.
You play as Mark, a structural analyst that is sent on a job to survey some old structures for potential degradation. What begins as just another day at work, quickly turns into a series of events that test his dexterity and resilience.
At the beginning you’ll most likely find yourself lost and with no idea of what is going on but slowly throughout the game you’ll find clues that will reveal why these events are taking place and who is responsible for them. This was one of the reasons why I ended up exploring a lot and looking for as many documents and audio logs as I could. The world surrounding you seems so mysterious at first but you’ll gradually get to know the city past, its history, how it became an industrial power and what led to its demise.
INFRA mechanics will be explained to you very early on and they are really simple but yet, they add a whole other layer to the game. The most important one is your camera. You can use it to photograph evidence of structural damage and documents that contain information relevant to your case. Assuming you’re actually interested and immersed in the world, this mechanic adds a lot to the game. I often found myself looking at every single structure I came across looking for damage, and still, I only found around 50% of the evidence in the game.
One other mechanic that also plays a huge role is climbing. You can climb any object, assuming it is not very high, by just getting closer to it and jumping. Of course you can also jump in the “normal way” like in most first person games and this will also allow you to overcome some of the deadly traps that await you.
The puzzles in INFRA are varied but most of them involve activating switches or finding missing electrical components. Some of them are very easy and its answer will be obvious you right from the start. Others however, left me going back and forth on the level looking for hints and activating several switches in order to get them right which sometimes was rather tedious, especially on larger levels.
One thing that became pretty clear for me since the very start, was the fact that the voice acting is very subpar. This kind of voice acting combined with the lack of dialogue didn’t leave a lot of room to get attached to the main character.
Still, the game has great sound design with background noises and overall the music is pretty great as well. While the graphics close on are somewhat dated, from a reasonable distance they allow for quite the scenery. You’ll be exploring gorgeous open door environments, dark tunnels and abandoned buildings. Each of these places has its own unique markings, either it’s an old dam, an ancient tunnel or an abandoned industrial complex from the early 1900’s which make the game world feel a lot more real. All these aspects combined, provide for an amazing and relaxing experience
- Loading times can take up to 30-40 seconds
- I experienced some framerate variations (even though I’m way above the recommended system specs), one second I’d have over 100 fps and the next moment it would dip down to the 40s and sometimes even lower
- The game auto-saves but there is also an option for manual saving. The problem I have with this is that you have 4 different save slots but it easily gets very confusing which save is which because the game gives you no indication other than “Save Slot 1”, “Save Slot 2”, etc.
Even though only Part 1 is available, INFRA is well worth your time. It is a mysterious and engaging experience that conveys the story by narrative means other than dialogue. It has its relaxing and tense moments and, most importantly, it lets the player choose if they just want to storm through the scenarios or explore them meticulously looking for clues of the towns past and the whole mystery surrounding this structural degradation. I highly recommend INFRA to any fans of adventure or mystery games or to people who are looking to enjoy a nice and relaxing scenery.
