Within the opening thirty minutes of "Max: An Autistic Journey", the titular character failed to understand a simple knock-knock joke, had a melt down over which bathroom to use and repeated a verbal tic a dozen times.  As the father of a child with ASD, it felt immediately familiar albeit from a different perspective.  "Max" tries to carry the player though a day in the life of a ten year old high-functioning autistic child and help you see things from his side.  Along the way, the game is carried by fairly simple RPG elements where, through Max's imagination, the player does battle with obstacles as varied as houseplants, zombie ants, dinosaurs and manifestations of anger.  The game uses pictographs at each stage of Max's day to help explain Max's particular challenges and how he has learned to cope with them the best he can.  Despite being the protagonist of the story, Max isn't above reproach, sometimes making a joke about a fellow student's disability or causing a scene.  By its broad strokes, Max's story seems true to life: he's not a Hollywood-style autistic savant nor is he sainted because of his disability, he's just a kid with his own unique struggles.
As a game, "Max" sometimes falters.  There is a tricky line to walk between making a game challenging for the player and having a ten year old boy lose an imaginary fight with a toy dinosaur and "Max" tends to play it safe which means that combat soon becomes rote.  Likewise, the minigames are designed more around evoking a sense of imagination or whimsy than compelling game play.  I understand that they wanted some "game" in their game rather than a walking simulator PSA but it could benefit from some reworking.
Ultimately though, I felt that "Max" was successful in what it sets out to accomplish: giving the player an alternate perspective into the challenges of an ASD child without being overly preachy.  I don't know if it holds up on its own as a gaming experience but I did feel like it had something honest to share.
Internet jokes aside, this game just isn't fun to play at all. A subpar RPG maker tier game that feels very rough and missing some basic RPG elements.

As someone diagnosed with ADHD as a child, and with several friends who have Asperger's, I can related to this game. You play Max, a 10 year old child with high functioning autism. Your job is to get through the day's challenges, such as getting dressed, making it through school, playing with friends, doing homework, and weathering a thunderstorm.
The gameplay is standard for games made with RPG Maker. You have turn-based combat, items, spells, and experience levels. The real charm of the game is not the gameplay, but how you see the world through an autistic child's eyes. For that reason alone, this game is worth the investment.

Awesomenauts is a 2D platformer/side-scroller MOBA that pits players against each other in 3v3 arenas. It uses a very rich and creative formula that supports a distinctive MOBA experience.
The basics of the game are very simple, every character class has two abilities, each assigned to a button of your choice, aside from the basic attack. Your objective, like in most games of this genre, is to destroy the enemy base, and to reach that base you need to get past turrets, which requires creep management and strategy. Killing other players and creeps awards you with Solar, the currency needed to purchase upgrades for your abilities. The gameplay is, therefore, very easy to learn and incredibly hard to master (which keeps things interesting).
The similarities with other MOBAs end there. Character classes differ vastly from each other, not only in the abilities they possess, but also in their complex movement traits (some are fast, some are slow, some can jump high, some can hover in the air, others can fly). There is an enourmous variety as each ability's effects and the possible upgrades for each, which can lead to a lot of different possible strategies for a single class.
Map design is clever. Currently there are not a lot of them, but clearly each and every map available was well thought of to allow for resourceful use of its elements both offensively and defensively. The map selected for a match can have a very high influence in its outcome, as you may excel in a certain map with a certain class and play poorly in another.
The basic game options available are four: The quick match, which randomly selects players based on their League, the Practice mode, that allows you to practice with and against bots, Battle, which allows you invite friends to be your teammates, and Custom Game, which is available only for Starstorm DLC owners, and allows players to create a completely custom match, defining settings like starting solar, creep spawn rate, maximum number of bots allowed, and several other modifiers. Custom Games have two different game modes, aside from the classic mode (destroy the base): Team Deathmatch, which takes the bases away and the ultimate objective of the match itself is scoring kills, and Randomnauts, which is exactly like the classic mode, but each time a player spawns it gets a random awesomenaut with a random build (upgrades are randomly and automatically purchased as Solar is acquired).
The audio in this game is superb. Every map has a background music that is slightly different depending on the class you're playing and every character has a theme song, a killstreak song, and a lot of fine voice acting lines. The SFX is also very, very well done. There is a handful of custom announcers available for purchase, as well.
Cosmetically, this game features a lot of character skins (premium ones come with custom voice acting) which helps add visual variability to the experience, the only downside being the price (but if you like the game it is a nice way to support the developers!)
My general impression is that this game is a must-play, even if you do not like the genre. It is almost guaranteed that you will like it, and even if you don't like, it is certainly worth the try.
EDIT: The new party system and matchmaking are, in my opinion, great improvements for what was previously marked by me as downsides of this game, so I have removed those. I feel that the developers have even put quite some effort into tackling the balancing issue, and currently I have really no general complaints.
EDIT (2): The much-needed F2P turn was for the better and fixed the matchmaking problems, among other problems this game had. We now have a fully fixed experience that continually gets improved with new content. I loved the weekly brawls!

Autism is a mental disorder that affects the central nervous system of all individuals who are affected. It is characterized by high levels of anxiety, distress based on sensory perception and following a set routine in order to stay organized and together emotionally. Rather, it is best defined as a cognitive-emotional disorder that affects most people emotionally with anger, anxiety, fear and sometimes guilt. A relatively common misconception of people who are autistic is that some lack the motor skills to speak. The majority of people with autism have no speech disorders and actually tend to be some of the smartest individuals you will encounter. I knew one guy at my high school that was autistic; he was very intelligent in subjects and areas that many people in school wouldn't be. He knew history very well, had an incredible memory bank he could draw from and would interact with others well socially.
In large crowds, many people with autism tend to withdraw from large social groups because it makes many feel awkward. Any type of awkwardness would leave them with increased stress and anxiety, so it is best to minimize it. He had limited ways in which he would approach people. Many approach people directly instead of indirectly. However, they follow certain rules based on every activity that they do.
Max is an autistic kid that you play throughout this game. The game's presentation is in a first-person view where you get to directly experience what it feels like, the experience that one case of autism in a person is like day to day. Max is a fairly lovable ten-year-old kid at the beginning of the game trying his best to survive in a normal world but with minor setbacks. Max has Attention Deficit Disorder; he takes his medicine once every morning to help him concentrate in school. I actually have General Anxiety Disorder myself so I know what being on a concentration pill does to you. It will suppress the anxiety all day, for a long period of time yet eventually long-term it takes over your mind blocking you from full cognitive and emotional expression. It blocks you from being able to think rationally to the point of shielding from your inner self your gifts and talents in life.

This is one of my favorite alpha games ever to hit Steam.. And It's a damn shame I have to stomp it into the ground because during the estimated 1-2 years of work I expected this game to take before beginning to reach a finished state, the developers had a stroke of genius and decided that it would be a good idea to call this HEAVY ALPHA GAME a FULLY RELEASED TITLE after being on Steam for only 5-6 months. Doing so, Avalanche Studios have yet again showed the world that they do not give a damn about actually delivering a polished product to customers and fans alike and instead falsely advertise & release yet another unfinished glitch-fest onto Steam like a big, flaccid díck onto your dinner table, expecting a price-tag of 30€ for an experience you can expect out of a glitchy tech demo.
I mean holy hell. They JUST spewed out a new dinosaur with this "release update".. AND IT HAS NO TESTING DONE TO IT WHATSOEVER. If you still insist on buying this garbage, kindly make note of the following issues the game currently has:
------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Animations for both dinosaurs and players are on a "Proof of Concept" level at most, and when combined with point 2, It makes for a disgusting game-play experience as far as immersion is concerned.
2. The AI is absolutely atrocious. All dinosaurs can get extremely stuck on certain hills, get seizures or freeze up indefinitely if you decide to go up on a rock, the T-Rex can use you as a surf-board and stand ontop of you indefinitely without being able to attack if you go prone and have him not see and "aggro" you directly (Realistic, right?), The smallest of dinosaurs can take 10+ shotgun slugs to the head (and smash their skulls to thousand pieces) and still be alive & charge your person endlessly with no difficulty or signs of being stunned whatsoever, T-Rexes can with a 100% accuracy pinpoint your location If they hear you, say, walk at a steady pace 500 meters away, they WILL rush your location and insta-gib you unless you log out. Fun fun fun!
3. The game has a disgusting lack of realism. Building on the previous statement of the dinosaurs having nonexistant AI in regards to stun or reactions overall, the game does not allow you to do VERY basic things like jumping while also having an absolutely broken "Hit-detection" system whereas you can know the exact angle and 3d space of say, a raptor's heart, shoot it with a shotgun slug.. And have the bullet either go through him completely, missing all organs or hit another bodypart. It's disgustingly random and sometimes, you can even get one-shot-kills without hitting any organs - and have no damage show up in the dino death re-cap window. There are also another giant design problem and that is the way that foilage works in this game. Dinosaurs do not say, leave grass bent or otherwise moved when they pass through it. It's like they're ghosts, so every time you chase or otherwise look for a dino where foilage is thick - you WILL NOT BE ABLE TO SEE IT. EVEN IF YOU KNOW IT'S RIGHT INFRONT OF YOU IN THE GRASS. It is one of these GIANT design issues that force you to avoid grassy areas all-together and it really brings light on how much of an alpha game this shít of a title really is.
4. The game is very unoptimized. Most PC's struggle to run this game and while I didn't have any particular big problems myself, the forums speak for themselves though and following the numerous complaints I saw, I made a closer inspection and did infact see that my G-Card had a tendency to being extremely hot when playing.
5. The developers do not take advice or read the forums. Ditto. It took them literally 3-4 months to notice a typo in the forum section called "Thoughts & Suggtesions" or something like that and that's just a depressing realization as there are literally hundreds of posts made - Not ONE of them has seen their ideas/suggestions been implemented into the game.
6. There is legitimately no goal in this game. You roam around like an idiot (sometimes for a whole hour or more if you're unlucky), looking for dinosaurs with a shoddy bow and If you want to have different weapons, you HAVE TO <-- go to a pre-defined location and rummage through larger crates... Or die and go to the store that have rétárded level restrictions on all weapons & ammo that can sometimes require you to kill literally hundreds of dinos before having THE OPTION <-- to spend your own points to spawn with the gun you want next time you die. Crafting? End-game? Goals? Plot? Story? What's that?
7. Sounds are downright broken and extremely confusing. Your own footsteps can make stomping noises with that of a T-Rex if you take small steps and listen carefully while certain raptors simply have no sounds to them at all except the standard "chop" attack bits while others have loud yelping calls, aggro noises, etc etc. While It certainly has jump-scared me a few times to get my buttocks suddenly chewed on by something that didn't make even the tiniest of noise, having some raptors suddenly become Batman in the Jungle while the rest are akin with that of howler monkeys is not a good as far as gameplay consistency is concerned.
------------------------------------------------------------------
Avoid this game and for the love of god, avoid the developers just as much. unless you enjoy being ripped off.

A thoroughly enjoyable, beautiful exploration game with plenty of great ideas only lacking in polish and general quality assurance. Some of the puzzles throughout the game are brilliant, but others are really not that good (I'm looking at you, raft section and all the elecrified floor jumpathons). I like the scandinavian aesthetic as I am a Finn myself (really brought me back to my heydays in Kontula with the above ground segments) and I really loved the nature segments as well.
Above all, the game really needs some solid hints. I got through most of the game without a hitch, but some solutions are not so obvious and could use for example the player's voice to guide through them. I think there should be a prelude "routine infrastructure case" before coming to the office, a small tutorial course where you need to photograph, flashlight and get used to the mazelike urbex gameplay of INFRA. The game could really use one where you learn some not-so-obvious things like stacking crates and such. I really loved the office, but only in hindsight as it's a bit too good at showcasing the gameplay elements...it's just too much too fast and might scare more casual players away.
I gotta hand it to you Oskutin & friends, the level design is phenomenal. There are some really amazing vistas and you managed to squeeze everything out of Source. I loved the blast furnace tower. I really really loved the little landscapes near the dam and the little suburban canal section. Top marks on the hacker den too - that place was fun as hell to go through. The waterfalls, the dam, everything is so peaceful, serene yet manage to get the atmospheric 'spooky' factor to the max.
The unpolishness is making this a bit of a tough sell. There's a LOT of spelling errors, confusing sentences and overall weirdness going about. In my playthrough, none of the audiologs worked so I didn't get much out of the storyline. I'll play it through again when part 2 is out (lovely cliffhanger by the way). You really need someone to fix those quirks in text and script when you get around finishing the entire experience.
There are also quite a few bugs. Physics glitches, sound issues and such were thankfully quite fast patched, but there are some lingering issues that almost all pertain to the engine itself. There's a crane that can detach its load in late chapter 5 that can kill your playthrough unless you reload a checkpoint, if you do things in wrong order with a certain forklift. There's some inconsistencies in level design where that cool area you found might not go anywhere at all. There's the infuriating pixel-perfect-or-you're-dead raft section that makes me want to skewer the one who okay'd that through QA. I hope these gets fixed after part 2 is out, since these really destroy the immersion and experience.
And boy, what an experience it is. I'm almost inclined to go romping around abandoned factories and facilities in real life after having so much fun exploring these urban ruins. The camera mechanic is genius, if only you'd give more batteries to play around with. The puzzles are creative and the nice crisis scenes you get from time to time are well thought out and executed. A phenomenal title focused solely on urbex and puzzling, beautifully laid out in an urban yet natural scandinavian wonderland. Few more spit shine polish elements and I'd give this a solid 10/10, but I'll have to go with 8/10, with one point out for repeated 'electrified water' and 'stack the boxes' gags and the second one for unpolishness and the infuriating raft section. Did I mention how I hated that part yet? Seriously, it is beyond terrible.
Overall, 8/10, would heavily recommend. Hyvää työtä Suomen pojat! :D

This is not a bad game, it's rather nice, but it is unfinished.
I hope I will rewrite this review when the game gets patched a few more times, and hope to change my recommendation to thumbs up. Currently the game is a drag, and that's a shame, because I really want to like this game. It has a unique atmosphere and does (tries to do) something different from most games today. I wouldn't have bothered to write this review if I didn't like this game, but in it's current state I cannot recommend it.
My main issue is that it feels very much like an alpha release, and definitely should still be in Early Access. But as that is not the case, I fear some of the weird design features will not be rectified. I will list a few issues I have with the game below.
The game world is not logical. It appears to be, but is far from it. Abandoned places still have electric lights on, and every place is generally too well lit; makes me wonder why do I even have a torch with me. People have left notes lying around which are obviously there to help me, but would make no sense in a real world. Usually these notes are right next to the puzzle and basically tell you how to solve it, so it's not really a puzzle but "follow instructions" type of a problem. I got stuck at the sawmill for several hours because I didn't notice an attic window, which for some unnatural reason had a plank protruding from it, and I was supposed to go through there. Never in my life I've seen something like that in real life, so I didn't think to look for it. It makes sense in game, kinda, but I've never liked puzzles which do not rely on real world logic but impose their own on the player. There are other kind of logical problems which break the immersion, like finding a dead body but not reporting it to anyone immediately, and halting a train but not communicating to the crew in any way, etc.
There are several places in the game world where you can get stuck, like falling between some rocks. Otherwise the character can climb low obstacles, but apparently 50 cm of rock is too much for him. This wouldn't be a problem, as most of these places are off the beaten path, but the game suggests that it rewards exploration. And I like that, it's nice that there are places you can walk around, which are there just for the atmosphere, but as it is, it's way too easy to get stuck or fall into water (instadeath, naturally). This is all made worse by the save game system, which doesn't tell you which save slot you used last (nor name the saves), and doesn't ask if you want to overwrite your last save. Additionally you can also get to areas from which you cannot go back, so saves are somewhat important, yeah.
The voice acting is pretty bad, but okay I guess for an indie developers budjet. The English used in the notes found in game is rather awful, with a lot of typos and poor grammar. Almost every note found has some mistakes in it. Another thing related to this is the weird nation the game takes place in, as it seems to be some sort of strange hybrid of Finland, USA, UK and some East European countries. The main character speaks like he's Slavish, but still speaks in (very broken) English, and most of the names are English as well, yet there are some Finnish products and words here and there. Pontikka is moonshine in English, so why would the characters in game use the Finnish word? This would've worked so much better if the whole game was set in Finland, or if the protagonist or another major character was Finnish living in whatever country this is supposed to be set in. Being a Finn myself, I'd love to see a pretty game like this set in Finland.
The main character's camera uses AA batteries and runs out of them after a couple of shots, doesn't zoom or record video, and you cannot look at what pictures you have taken. I guess the state of decay extends to the city officials equipment as well. The protagonist should know his camera is a POS, and pack extra batteries, but no, he prefers to rely on luck, finding fresh batteries in buildings abandoned for years or decades. Feels like a producer told the dev team that if there aren't any guns, there still should be reloading and ammo pickups. Please. Hunting for batteries adds nothing to the game and is just plain irritating. The fact that you can't look at the pictures you've taken is also a missed opportunity, as taking a picture of a found schematic and checking it from the camera later when you actually have to solve a puzzle would make much more immersive gameplay than finding the instructions right next to every puzzle.
The good? As I stated above, the game is unique in atmosphere. Mix of slow paced exploration and puzzle solving is a great idea, and at times works very well. The game looks good enough, but runs very unevenly, freezing sometimes for no reason for a second or two, and having other graphical glitches like doorways that are nothing but bright white light until you walk through them. The sounds are good and the sparsely used music fits the game well. The environments are somewhat unusual for games, as there are areas which seem to offer nothing but places to walk around. I like that, makes the world feel all the more real. Many of the puzzles are fun enough and most of the locations look like they could actually exist. This is by no definition a bad game, but it could be so much better than it currently is.
I haven't finished the game yet, so maybe there are more things I'll like later in the game, I don't know. Had to stop playing because it got so annoying to deal with everything above that I had to write this review. Loiste Interactive: INFRA is the Steam debut for Loiste Interactive a small gaming development and self-publishing firm located in Finland. The game had humble beginnings as a Source Engine mod project  that eventually grew large enough to become its own fully fledged title.  The game drew a rabid fan base whilst it was in the Steam Greenlight program attracting more than 45,000 votes and peaking at #4 on the Greenlight Charts. It wasn’t until the developers understood just how popular their title was that they ultimately decided to create the company from that – until this point it was a group of friends who were working on their mod together. Soon thereafter thanks to some investment into the company the group were able to commit themselves to their project on a permanent full time basis.
Pre-Steam Release Acclaim: To show just how popular INFRA had become the game received a number of nominations and awards during its development cycle beginning in 2011 with selection to the top one hundred “Mod of the Year” list by ModDB, earning Greenlit status the following year on Steam and peaking with a nod from IndieDB as a top one hundred selection to “2014 Indie of the Year Awards.”
A grand beginning: The first episode in the INFRA episodic adventure, part two will be free for purchasers of the first part, averages about ten hours in play. You play the role of a structural analyst whose tasked with the job of navigating, and hopefully surviving, a brutal labyrinth. As it says in the Steam Description, it is a gun-free puzzle adventure. Intelligence and strategy are awarded as you work your way through some of the most rewarding interactive puzzles to be seen in gaming in recent times. It’s an ambitious opening act that offers highly rewarding gameplay.
Large maps that truly inspire you to explore: Almost from the very beginning you will be surprised at just how large the maps in the game are. Although I found the office section to be more than a little tedious  – it’s main purpose  is to serve as a tutorial – I was surprised at just how large the area was. This continues right throughout the episode. They are all highly detailed featuring a number of different potential routes and offered a feeling of an open world better than some true open world games. Each area is filled with puzzles and unique game play that really does make you feel that you’re not repeating the same things over and over again. The game design has been very well thought out. The maps provide you ample opportunities to explore and to try different ideas with all of this feeling very rewarding. I quite enjoyed the distinct looks and sounds of the various areas. The environments are lush and beautiful. It genuinely feels as though Loiste Interactive thought of everything to create an immersive experience for the players.
It’s not perfect: There are a number of flaws in the game. However, I believe that this can be explained by the availability of resources for development and the relative inexperience of the development team. Overall, I believe that these flaws can be overlooked but they are notable. First, I was worried that I couldn’t even start the game. I don’t necessarily put games straight onto my SSD. Consequently, I put INFRA onto my HDD and it stayed there. When I first loaded up the game I got long periods of black screens to the point where I quit the game multiple times believing that the game had crashed on me. I believe on the third or fourth attempt I just said to hell with it and got myself a drink. I soon heard the game begin – so if this happens to you please wait. Secondly, the voice acting is poor. However, thankfully once you get out of the office there isn’t a lot of it and what little of it there is is bearable. That office seen, though, felt as though the voice actors didn’t particularly care for the job that they were doing. Not a good beginning. There are also grammatical errors in the English within the game but not to the point where you are dumbfounded at what is being said.
INFRA is one of the best new Indie games on Steam. It offers significant gameplay value at its current cost and is perfect for those of you who enjoy good adventure puzzle games with some horror thrown in for good measure. If you don’t buy it now because you’re waiting for the second part of the game to be released then you should at the very least put it on your wishlist.

If you have an interest in urban exploration or have ever wondered what's behind those locked gates, inside those buildings full of blinkenlight panels and machinery that keep a city running, here is your chance to find out, and push some of the buttons along the way.
Visually gorgeous and dripping with atmosphere, INFRA is a solitary exploration / environmental puzzle game. A highly unique and enjoyable experience that really tickled the right spot for me with its attention to detail and atmosphere.
Some puzzles seem to be avoidable or optional and the reason for using the camera is not well explained. Several times I questioned my mental map of things to do, thinking about those locked doors or unpushed buttons that I'd promised to return to, then somehow managing to progress to the next section unable to return, wondering if I had maybe cheated the game. Perhaps this is an intentional design choice, I feel that the multiple paths and player choice elements could've been made clearer to avoid anxiety about fully exploring before moving on. Some kind of labelling/inventory system for keys/doors might've helped in that regard.
Voice acting is cheesily bad but thankfully sparse, and I did encounter some bugs (graphical glitches, had to reload saves to progress, achievements only earned if online in Steam).
Wishing the best success for Loiste Interactive and looking forward to Part 2 and any future projects.

INFRA is possibly the best puzzle/exploration game I've played-and I've played them all. I've played through part 1 about five times now and I keep finding new secrets, puzzles and alternative routes.
Urban exploration or infrastructure enthusiasts will especially love it, but I'd recommend it for anyone who likes good settings or atmosphere.
A note on horror: INFRA gets its scares from the oppressive atmosphere of abandoned industrial settings, and its danger from industral hazards and accidents. There are no dogs leaping through windows or posessed pizza parlor animatronics to be found- no jump scares or bleeding walls, either. If you favor that kind of horror, best to look elsewhere- or better yet, try this game for a subtler flavor of fright!

Very fun strategy game, that offers many hundreds of hours of gameplay.  It looks very difficult at first, but once you play for a while, or look at a few let's play or how to videos on the internet, than you will realise it is very easy to control and play the game, but you will still spend a lot of time thinking about your next move, be it starting a war, marrying someone for an alliance or inheritance, or starting a plot against a rival or where to spend your gold.
There are many different stiles of play to choose from (eg. be a catholic ruler, play as a viking raider, a muslim ruler, merchant republic) different difficulty (start as an emperor, or a count at a very bad spot).
There are lot's of random events that influence your game (both in positive or negative way), but none of them are so serious, that will ruin your entire gameplay.
You can also play differently, like roleplay your character based on his/her traits. Which can lead to interesting in game events, if you choose not to go for the best strategical option, but choose a funnier one, or one that mathes the personality of your character.
Lot's of DLC-s are available, that change the base game significantly, but you can choose to play with or without them.
You can also export you realm to EUIV via an official mod.

Gotham City Impostors is a first-person shooter multiplayer-only video game set in the universe of DC Comics' Batman. Developed by Monolith Productions and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment, the downloadable game is played from the perspective of two teams each trying to kill the other: one with people dressed like Batman and the other with people dressed like his archenemy, The Joker.
It was released on Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade, PlayStation 3 via the PlayStation Network and Microsoft Windows via Games for Windows – Live in February 2012. The game was re-released on Microsoft Windows as a free-to-play title in August 30, 2012 via Steam using Steamworks. The game is a six versus six first person shooter multiplayer game featuring customizable characters. Players take on the role of either amateur vigilantes (the Bats) or villians (the Jokerz). The game features a range of both traditional and imagined weapons.

世界の中心で「自閉症」を叫んだけもの
Drawing heavily from Evangelion, MaAJ is the story of a young boy’s quest to find not only his place in the world, but also to attempt to understand the hearts and minds of others. However, where immense care was put into making Shinji’s struggles feel relatable and his mindset coherent, the creators of MaAJ forgo this effort by simply giving the protagonist autism. Thus, any of Max’s actions can simply be handwaved away by his disability: Max flipped over a table and started screaming? Oh, well he’s autistic. Shinji flipped over a table and started screaming? Well, it’s related to his feelings towards Asuka and how he feels as though she refuses to be understood by him and… (from here the viewer would continue to think about Shinji and his identity, and whether Asuka is truly at fault in this case)
In the end, Max is a flat and uninteresting character, and MaAJ fails in its efforts at presenting us with a compelling story. Perhaps the game is aware of this: roughly two-thirds in, Max becomes trapped within a strange womb-like enclosure in a scene highly reminiscent of Shinji’s own entrapment within the angel Leliel. Guided by his inner self in the form of a dinosaur, Max attempts to reconcile his own identity with his mental problem and the world around him. Where Shinji’s internal struggle ends happily, for Max there are no congratulations, and when the scene ends he finds himself locked within a room of isolation. Indeed, Max’s life appears to be one of eternal torture, trapped in a world that refuses to change in much the same way that the creators do not allow him to change. Despite this moment of likely accidental genius I cannot recommend the game due to, again, the otherwise uninteresting nature of Max’s character and his lack of any serious development. My hope is that the developers learn from this experience as I believe that they have the potential to create something truly meaningful; they just need to avoid such silly cop-outs as autism when writing their characters next time.
Taster’s score: C-

EDIT:  A shmup needs excellent and precise controls, otherwise any and all potential for fun has been wasted.  Keep reading for more detailed reasons why this game has failed, even at it's low price point.
First off, I should mention that this is a sequel to Crazy Steam Bros. which you can find and play for free over on Kongregate.   It's a simple yet fun horizontal shoot'em up, or shmup, that has a number of interesting weapons and enemies to keep fans of the genre occupied.  It's not quite like your typical bullet hell shooter, but the games style is what sets it apart from the pack.  I enjoyed the original, although us players were stuck using just the keyboard and there were very few additional options to choose from or adjust in game.
Crazy Steam Bros. 2 feels a bit like the original and looks slightly sharper.  In fact, the graphics are quite charming given the era that the game is supposed to take place in.  The visuals won't blow you away but they work quite well for the theme of the game.  Unfortunately, I can't recommend Crazy Steam Bros 2 because of how it controls.  It says on the steam store page that Crazy Steam Bros 2 includes full controller support, and although I could get my wired Xbox 360 controller to work, it felt quite wonky and my plain "floated" all over even after I had let go of the analog stick or the D-pad.  Shooters need to be smooth and precise, and while the Keyboard controls work better than the controller, I can't recommend the game considering how unintuitive the controls feel while playing with a gamepad.
It's very obvious that this is a game that could be played on a tablet or mobile device (there's even an option that allows you to hide or show touchscreen controls while you play - although I can't see why anyone would want to play this using touch screen controls even if you do own a smart monitor!).  Even mouse input would have been a nice option, but the controls really do need to be more precise.  I'm sad to say that It almost feels like a rushed port, which it very well might be.  I really wanted to like Crazy Steam Bros 2 especially since I found the original to be novel idea with some entertaining gameplay, even though it was free and the game wasn't very long.   The sequel unfortunately doesn't provide enough options, or precision in its control schemes that should be found in any and all good Shmups.
Crazy Steam Bros 2 isn't a bad game, it just controls badly, and until these rudimentary features are fixed, it isn't worth your money, not even at the low price it's selling for.  It should also be mentioned that there are no Steam Leaderboards either, even though it is listed as a feature on the Steam store page.
Be patient and wait to see if the game is updated anytime soon.  If it is, then I'll update my review as well.

All the other reviews lay out the general pros and cons well, so I just wanted to reiterate one main point with this review.
Atmosphere.
This game has it... lots of it. INFRA is on par with some of the greats in terms of atmosphere, like S.T.A.L.K.E.R, Metro, Half-Life, Bioshock, old school Silent Hill, or even the more recent Soma. The world is beautifully designed. The detail is incredible, and every building/area seems to be meticulously designed and unique in it's own way. Visually, the game is quite appealing, and impressive for a game running on Source. The environment strikes a nice balance; it is realistic and believable, yet remains imaginative throughout the story.
Really, if you took away the poor voice acting and sometimes poorly written notes, you would be left with a game that doesn't look or feel Indie.
My main complaint is that it is far too short and ended quite abruptly, though the price reflects that. I very much look forward to the second part.
Edit: Nearly 2 years later, and I finally got around to playing all three parts consecutively. It was hard to tell where the story was going to go after part 1, but I love the direction it went.
I still adore the meticulous & realstic detail of the levels, with the final level really taking the cake. Overall, it's a game unlike no other, and while I understand it isn't for everybody, I wish it would get more credit. It's definitely the best under-the-radar game I've played, and a game I will never forget. Look forward to Loiste's future projects.

Fantastic game. Currently I don't know if it's worth $15, but the developers are going to add further parts for no cost to those who own it, so it will be worth it in time.
Plot: The story feels a bit forced, but it is interesting, and fits very well with the concept of the game. It has a lot of potential for advancement, and is left on a cliffhanger that does work. I'm looking forward to the continuation with the updates.
Puzzles: The puzzles are Portal-style; built into the level, completing them is the only way to get through. There's a mix of physics puzzles, jumping puzzles, and others that incorporate many different concepts and features into them. Some are easy, some are very hard, but I was able to get through all of them except one without having to look on the discussion forums, and in that case, it was because the instructions were poorly worded. Here's a tip; remember to always look at EVERYTHING in the area. There are a few puzzles that I feel are unnecessarily hard, and one or two instances where the instructions themselves are unclear (water treatment plant...) but you can work past them, and the developers are very active on the forums answering questions if it comes to that.
Graphics: The game is gorgeous. There are some incredible locations, both outdoors and indoors. Some of the locations remind me of the coastal area in Half Life 2, but much more beautiful. So while the game produces plenty of great outdoor scenes, the indoor locations also do not fall to the tendency that games have to make their indoor locations boring and dark. The indoor locations feel varied but familiar, with new visuals every time.
Sounds: The sound design is pretty good, nothing to phone home about. There isn't much you can do with this kind of a game, but it feels atmospheric, which is about all is needed, I guess. Voice acting could use some work, particularly the main character, but it is far from game-breaking. The music is pretty average throughout, but there are a few points where
the right piece starts playing at
the right moment, creating a fantastic feeling.
Overall, if you like puzzles, I would recommend this game. The first part of the story took me about 9.3 hours to complete, with a pretty average amount of struggling, so with the updates, there will be enough content to make it worth it. If you've always wanted to be able to explore infrastructure (like me), this will be a blast. I can't vouch for its accuracy, but it feels realistic, and that's pretty much all I care about. I'm looking forward to what kind of new locations I'll get to explore in the next chapter.

What a game. I usually have no interest in these puzzle games but INFRA is an exeption as I've followed the development for many years. And I also love games using the Source engine so of course I had to give it a go.
I don't want to bore you with a long review where I point out every single thing that I liked or disliked so I'll keep it short. I also hope one of the developers read this review as I think that I make some interesting points.
INFRA is a game based around puzzle solving and exploration. It's based in modern times but you spend the majority of your time in abandoned buildings/areas. You encounter some puzzles along the way that you have to solve. Some are easy, some.. not so much.
The level design is absolutely amazing. To see how much they managed to squeeze out of the good old Source engine is beyond what I could have imagined.
There's an interesting story to it which encourages you to progress and explore further.
There's a good amount of puzzles to keep you occupied throughout the game.
And then there's multiple approaches to pretty much everything.
The developers are showing great interest in the people who are playing it and are helping them out here on Steam!
I'd like to mention first of all that I got stuck twice in my first playthrough due to crashes and bugs. Most of this has already been fixed though.
The game is confusing at times. There's not much guidance for what you're doing so you keep asking yourself if this is the right thing. There are notes throughout the game that can help you solve the puzzles but you're not guaranteed to find them due to the multiple approaches.
The multiple approaches makes you wonder if you've missed something. Would I have found a key to this door if I had gone the other way? Am I even supposed to go this way?
The voice acting is not great. I don't mind the accent, it just gets annoying at times, especially the player's voice. He keeps pointing out the obvious. "Somebody should fix this","I'm pretty sure that's not meant to be like that", "A pack of spare batteries for the flashlight", "A pack of spare batteries for the camera", "I should have brought my other boots","Fascinating", "Interesting", and so on. You really don't need to point out the obvious, after all, I did make you pick up those batteries.
Why not use the player's voice to help out the player? Something like "I wonder if I could get up there" or "Maybe if I can find a way to smash this". There's a bit of this towards the end of the game but I really would have liked it earlier on. (And it certainly could have helped me) I don't want it to give it away but maybe if you can tell that the player is struggling, help them out?
All in all, a very solid game and I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a bit of puzzle solving and/or exploration! If you want to avoid getting stuck because of bugs, wait a few weeks before buying and then I'm sure they've been fixed.
And a shoutout to one of the developers, Oskutin, for helping me out! ( I broke the game :D )

Well, when , what I reached for instead was a different 4x game that was recommended to me: Endless Legend. This is a Civ-like set in a fantasy universe, similar to a Masters of Magic. And man, does it scratch the Civ itch in ways I find new and different for a Civ-like. Endless Legend's fantasy setting means that the game still has emotional resonance, even though the tech trees still have magic and other non-realistic advances. They lean on fantasy tropes quite a bit, but manage to stretch the lore in some new and interesting ways, particularly in the creation of their alternate races, many of which play almost entirely different games due to the nature of their mechanics. The exploration aspect of the game is ramped up - similar to what you see in CBE. Military is both viable (i.e. it doesn't drag the game too much) and (in many games) somewhat dodgeable if you prefer to turtle and just build a great society. Rather than freeform city placement, the map is divided into a series of states or territories, each of which can hold one city in it. This makes for a much nicer, cleaner political map, and also creates a much more interesting race to snag resources - first one to build a city in a territory will control all resources in that territory, no matter how large or misshapen the territory is. This has the nice benefit of allowing players to not let resource placement force them to build a godforsaken desert city that will always struggle, for example. The city can always be built on the best squares in the territory. And for what it's worth, the city placement and expansion part of the game is what I love the most. It's something I felt I didn't pay much attention to in Civs 4 and 5, but in Endless Legend, I'm back to fanatically comparing where the ideal hex to place a dude is, and identifying where expansion can go. Unlike recent Civs, city shape expansion is done manually by the player (with the 'create boroughs' action), and the designers did a good job of putting in competing desires - you can spread like a virus if you want to grab better resource tiles, but you also get rewarded with greater reputation and glory if you build a compact city. Basically, any city hex that borders 4 other city hexes 'levels up' to be more profitable - this is a very neat feature that is also criminally underdocumented. The game is not perfect - it is, to be blunt, very indie in its levels and production values. Major systems are undocumented: I've played the game for hours, and am still not sure how trade works, or how about half of the victory conditions are initiated. The game could desperately use some GUI love - the game would be massively more approachable if you could mouseover data that currently only exists in tooltips, for example. The game does have some bugs that are inexplicable, and crashes enough to make you appreciate the annual autosave. Some oft-used functions that really should have hotkeys simply do not seem to. There are also some design ideas that are undercooked. About a third of the time, the game will plunge into winter months, which stalls out production and slows movement. This is a neat idea, but in practice is mostly just miserable gameplay time. Of particular frustration is that winter pretty much hoses any time-limited quests the game may grant you, making them impossible to complete for reasons utterly outside of your control. The art is WAY too busy - you'll find yourself zooming out a lot to look at the purely tactical map to be able to easily find units that otherwise get lost in the busy landscape. Unit customization is somewhat TOO fiddly. And lastly, the tactical combat just mostly sucks. I could go into the litany of details I found frustrating here, but suffice it to say - if the summary of combat shows that you'll likely win in autocombat, just do it, you'll thank me later. None of these derail the fact that this is a tidy new entry into the Civlike genre that, in my opinion, cements the dev team as serious contenders in the genre. The game is fun, constantly brings back that 'one more turn' vibe from the old Civs, and at the same time, breathes some new life into the format, largely by the virtue of a solid and fun city building model. If you like Civlikes, give this one a try.

Although the initial idea of a Mario Party Steam game is pretty thrilling to some, the game is way too long. The way the objectives are set makes it take a really long time for the game to end. In real Mario Party, the game ends after a certain amount of turns, and you can always modify the amount of shorten game length. But in Orange Juice, the game doesn't end until someone wins.
Generally, the board game itself is boring. Your objective is to round the board and reach your flag or another players (by landing on it) and achieve your goal of either collecting enough stars or killing enough enemies beforehand. Sure, sounds simple at first. But when you realize that there's so many ways you can screw up or get destroyed by your enemies that it almost becomes ANNOYING. If you miss your pole, you have to round the board again. It's long and frusterating to have to go through the same cycle every time (which you have to do SIX TIMES to win, by the way), especially knowing that you're always subject to being at the recieving end of an enemy card.
Fighting may be by far the most fun aspect of the game. It's a one-on-one battle between you and either an opponent, a simple ai, or a boss. However, every different type of foe you face is complete BS, because the ENTIRE battle system is randomly-generated! You fight and dodge by rolling dice. There's two ways to avoid getting beaten the hell out of: either defending or evading. Evading is useful but risky, and defending is slightly harmful but safe. These are interesting tactics you can use, and I do like them, but whether you're a defender or an offender, the whole fight is completely random, so in the end its just a fight between luck and no luck. The worst part is that losing makes you hand over a bunch of stars to the winner of the fight, AND you're KO'd for up to 5 turns if you're still not lucky enough to roll your way out. This makes the tables turn like CRAZY - and it's not the only way tables can turn either.

If you have the money to spare for a game that's a funny, difficult and ridiculous time-killer, you should try spending it on Mr. President! If you're looking for story or innovative gameplay, not the place to be spending your money, but if you're bored and you're looking for a fun and easy way to spend time even with a bad computer, buy this game. It is a puzzle ragdoll physics game where you're a bodyguard, tasked with defending "Ronald Rump" from various threats, from snipers to Scorpion from Mortal Kombat lookalikes.  Clearly referencing the presidential candidate Donald Trump, you may think at first glance, that since you have to save him all the time, it was made for people who like the man. You'd be wrong. Dead wrong. As the game progresses you'll witness progressively worse nightmare scenarios based on Trump's quotes and controversies.
Silly and disturbing at times, the ragdoll physics provide some funny moments. Thing is, the physics themselves allow for some really frustrating moments as your character may flail about in the exact wrong direction even though you had the right intention. Besides, I didn't even laugh that hard at any point during the game. Your mileage may vary here.
A big issue I have with the game is where it resets your entire progress in the story mode when you finish it. Which is awful because I don't want to have to endure 3 or 4 frustratingly bad puzzles to replay one or two levels I may have found amusing.
Update: With the new update, you're once again in control of Donald Rump, where you now have to wrestle, roundhouse kick those "bad hombres", the immigrants and refugees.
I have to admit, I actually laughed out loud quite a few times with the absurdity of a fat orange wig man rotating like a ballerina as random people, even kid characters, are being projected to oblivion.
Should the game continue to be updated as Trump's presidency goes on, this could turn out to be quite a fun little game, and I now recommend this game, seeing as it manages to still be relevant after the election, unlike all the other Trump games out there. Pleasantly surprised.

As an man with autism it was only natural that I'd play this game and heavily relate to it.  It's easy to see myself in the 10 year old main character from his desire to not be autistic to how he was bullied, it brings back so many memories.  It even gets deeply emotional like when he's first diagnosed and his parents promise to give him the best life they can.  I haven't cried like that since the end of Metal Gear Solid 3.
As for the gameplay itself it's standard RPG fare from the mid 90s, turn based like many of the games from that era.  Since the game was made in one of the RPG maker series you can see a few things that weren't changed but for the most part it's very original.  What is left over from RPG maker is used properly so it's not a problem.  Additionally there are many different minigames which serves to provide some variety so it's not just battle after battle.  Speaking of battles, there are no random battles.  You won't be surprised by baddies, you will decide if you want to fight them.
Overall while the game isn't going to standout for it's gameplay (which is above average) but rather for it's subject matter which provides a good mix of gameplay and education.  When dealing with a subject like a neurological difference it's hard to find the balance, keeping the game fun while also informing the player on the subject.  This game found that balance which is about as tight as walking a cable over the Grand Canyon.  I would like to thank everyone involved it making it and getting it on Steam, you did an amazing job.

All truth out I bought this game years ago, before it even became part of greenlight.
Do I reccommend this game?  Yes.  But with fair warning!
A:  This is in early access and by no means finished.  Is it playable now?  Yes, but be prepared because there is no tutorial, no explanation of any of the mechanics, and it can be hard to learn what you are doing.     EDIT!!  In truth there is a VERY basic tutorial that simply includes tips that explain some of the mechanics when you create a new game, but you have to make sure you select it.
B: The learning curve can be quite steep.  A note to all new players: Stockpiles are important.  Make sure you try to build at least the masonry and wood piles ASAP before your current ones fill up.  It is very easy to begin mining dirt and have no stone to build the stockpile with, leaving you with no space on your miner(s) for the stone they need to build the stockpile and nowhere to put it.
Other than that this game is great fun.  You start out with a few settlers who are usually experienced in different things and with them you need to build a bustling town.  With the constant threat of wild animals, goblins, and skeletons attacking at night you need to balance the need for food with protection.  Hopefully after a while you can have a nicely defended castle/fort/wood hut/hole-in-the-ground/whatever you want to build, as long as you have the materials.
This game can take a while to get used to, and it will certainly take a while to build a massive town, but in my opinion it is worth it, as long as you can find a tutorial or something on Youtube or elsewhere on the internet.

Imagine when you were a kid and how awesome it would have been if your Lego came to life – that’s kind of what this game is.  You get the freedom to place each block how you want it (with decent tools for creating larger buildings).  Sometimes you have to give orders to your guys one at a time, but part of the charm is the slow burn of starting with a wagon full of goods, a few settlers and getting everything set up the way you want.
The Good:
- Nearly unlimited creativity with a great variety of resources and building materials.
- Enough uniqueness to each villager that you are invested in their wellbeing and frustrated if they die.
- All characters and professions are important, this isn’t just a matter of getting some max level troops and laughing as enemies break against your defenses.
The Neutral:
This game is tough.  Part of the fun is that it is not a pushover, but it’s worth mentioning so you know what you’re getting.  Realize that you will have some settlements wiped out as you learn how to survive.  The difficulty plus a casual pace of play means that at some point a pack of wolves or goblins will tear apart a settlement that you have really grown to like.  There will be little you can do with the frustration other than start over.
The Bad:
- At some point you will probably get frustrated that your soldiers don’t behave like a true RTS game.  Even as you develop a large settlement, the game is still based of a group of villagers surviving and thriving in the wild, not an Age of Empires style battle of armies and the controls reflect this.
- Surprisingly taxing on my system given the graphics level.

My favorite 4x strategy game. Period.
The aesthetics are wonderful, and I personally love the fantasy setting more than historical, or sci-fi (civ:BE), although I'm looking forward to trying Endless Space 2.
Your towns are easy to manage, and fun to build, since you physically build the town with burroughs.
Combat is really sweet, and large engagements can resolve faster than in Civ 5. Armies are stacked into a unit with a size limit, that has a hero for a leader. Combat is similar to Heroes of Might and Magic, with reinforcements entering battle from neighboring armies/cities, and with a 6 turn limit until the battle is drawn.
The heroes can level up, equip new stuff, and spend skillpoints in trees unique to their class/faction. You can customize your units with equipment, and you can add neutral faction units to your roster by assimilating their villages.
All the factions are very unique, and only share common technologies and buildings. Civ does not have unique factions compared to this game.
Really great game, and I recommend it for playing with/against a group of friends on a weekly basis or so. Civ 5 broke multiplayer with a patch in January, so there's really no choice.

Cons first!
This game still bears the scars of being an early access game, and being developed on Unity. The 64-bit version is crashy (likely due to Unity), it has unnecessarily high system requirements (also Unity), there's some bits of the game that are still broken like a bunch of the text with the events and quests, and there's a weird sort of general feeling that the game is still not 100% complete. Unity is an awful engine and anyone reading this would be wise to avoid it if they're developing a game. On that note, I'm amazed at how well the devs of Endless Legend managed to polish that turd of an engine. Great effort.
Now for the good stuff, and there are a surprising amount of good things about this game!
The art direction is simply fantastic. I absolutely love the art in this game, and the artists who worked on it are the best I've seen on any video game. Forget all those pretentious indie games whose main goal is to be art. This game is art, it knows it, and it feels no need to draw undue attention towards it. It's confident in what it is. It even helps the gameplay, and even though the game is hex-based, the landscape art simultaneously removes any jarring inter-hex transitions while also making a hex-grid helper overlay unnecessary. Simply amazing.
The gameplay reflects the care and attention they put on the art. It's solid 4X gameplay, every single faction plays very differently, and there's the option to make custom factions to play with and play against. The FIDSI mechanic and the way this game treats land grabbing and city/land improvements is a surprisingly good innovation on the old tired Civ-like mechanics. All strategic and luxury resources are produced on a per-turn basis with different modifiers depending on your faction and any events or quests. Very nice since it avoids the civ-style limited resource wars to prevent being locked out of certain buildings and units, but it also requires you to practice effective resource management.
The combat! I saw a lot of grumbling on reviews of this game and it made me hesitant to get it. Originally it seemed as if it was going to have combat like Endless Space, mostly just rock-paper-scissors doomstack-pushing. It was surprisingly different! On combat, armies spread throughout the surrounding landscape and it plays very much like a hex tactics game. Each unit type has different abilities, different strengths, different weaknesses, and these are all modified by your faction type, your technology, your heroes, and your customizable equipment. Equipment and heroes are customizable and you have to pay either production per unit or gold per hero, so you can have cheapo combat troops pushing forward while your expensive combat troops stay behind to finish them off. There's a surprising amount of flexibility here and it's better than most 4X games.
The quest system and the minor factions are locked together in terms of mechanics, and overall their random spread gives you something to worry about in the early-game. Not as completely horrendous and violent as pirates or barbarians or aliens in other 4X games, their pacification through quests, bribes, or destruction gives you direct bonuses if you colonize that region, and killing someone else's minor faction villages removes their bonuses from your enemy. They're another interesting strategic facet of the game.
The victory conditions are quite odd in that there's 8 of them and they cover almost every possible way you could think of winning a game like this. There's the requisite kill everything, love everything, research everything, and discover everything victories, but there's also a few odd ones like having loads of money and doing your faction's questline. Generally you'll be doing the faction questline or research victories, or an economic victory might sneak out of nowhere and win the game for you. Sometimes the AI will suddenly win an economic victory or pull a diplomatic victory off if you stop watching it. It's all very fun and has a lot of replayability compared to the conquest-dominated or research-dominated victories of Endless Space, or the conquest-dominated victories of the Civ series.
Overall this is a very very solid game made by developers who have clearly shown that they can and have improved. Vastly better than Endless Space, much better than pretty much any 4X made in recent years, and overall a very good game. That's coming from someone who liked the civ series (even 4 and V), BE, and Distant Worlds. Endless Legend is a better and more solid game than any of these. Less flashy, perhaps, but excellent in its gameplay and unified direction.
If Endless Space was any indication, there will be tons of free DLC packs and patches coming out in the next year or two, followed by an expansion or two, followed by more free DLC packs and patches for people who got the expansions. A very hearty recommend! Get this game if you enjoy 4X games!

Overall, pretty fun game, I like it.
That said, it's far from a flawless experience:
Has some interface problems:
Tab should move between GUI fields. It does not.
Cancelling targeting should be as easy as right-clicking once, not a dozen times and pressing random buttons hoping targeting aborts,
Selecting planets with guided weapons should be far less nitpicky about accuracy of clicking.
Tutorial needs some fixing(Spelling and grammatical errors, incorrect information "Press End Turn"->there is no End Turn button->It's "Next Player".).
Scrolling with WASD in an otherwise mouse-oriented game is ridiculous.
And some glaring issues:
The occasional inexplicable crash during a multi-hour game sucks.
No ability to play games with other players + AIs, it's just one or the other.
A tech tree that's kind of small, leading to most players having most of it by the end of the game.
While it's nice that the game tells you how many of your own buildings have been destroyed or damaged, it would be nice if it showed you which ones specifically, or told you which had been destroyed, rather than having to remember or guess at it.
Some performance concerns:
Running on a decent computer the game performs fine. It's more that it should be fine on a piece of crap too.
Really, really, really long loading times for under-spec-but-still-capable-of-playing computers(On the level of 5-10 minutes.).
The system requirements are ridiculously demanding for what the game is. I'd expect something like this to run fine on an early Pentium with a VooDoo 2. (It is not impressive visually, nor is it doing especially demanding calculations to my knowledge.)
Seriously, if an older machine can comfortably run something like Supreme Commander or Mass Effect, it should laugh at Interplanetary. It weeps instead.
It'd be nice if some sort of ship/fleet/satellite  combat was implemented, rather than pure artillery. Having a few little mobile or semi-mobile units around to do things would be a nice addition.
This is a great game. The ever shifting gravity can be a bit frustrating at times, but that moment when your shot makes contact feels so good.

Ok, here's the quick and dirty on INFRA: It's a first-person, non-combat puzzle game (much like Portal 2 or The Talos Principle). You'll follow an interesting and mysterious story, explore fantastic urban environments and solve environmental puzzles to progress.
The game has some flaws, which mainly come from a lack of time/money: the voice acting is dodgy at best, the character models are hilarious (and not in a good way) and even the written English texts have the occasional grammar error and misspelling (the devs are Finnish so that explains it somewhat).
But none of that matters. After the first level, voice acting is scarce and there's no hideous characters models to look at, only the amazing environments (look at those screenshots!).
If you like exploring atmospheric worlds and solve clever and logical puzzles don't even think twice. Buy it.
THE DREADED "VALUE" QUESTION:
It's a known fact that most indie games nowadays don't offer much in terms of length and sometimes ask a hefty price. INFRA is the exact opposite. The game costs just 15€ and the first part alone can last you over 10 hours. The second part is coming later this year and it'll be FREE if you already own part 1. That's a lot of high-quality gaming for just 15€ and more devs should follow this example.

To start - you start with nothing but a machete, and you're supposed to go around finding better gear, but there is NO GOOD WAY TO STAY IN STEALTH AROUND DINOS. I can't hardly find my way up the freakin' volcano to the research center to get better gear without being killed by a dino that shouldn't of seen me. Prone does nothing, crouch does nothing, moving slow does, guess what? NOTHING
Then there's the 'store' to unlock and buy better starting gear. There is nothing telling you how to level, there is nothing telling you how to earn the stuff to purchase things (such as the bow) from the store. I can only assume that you have to kill dinos and get the trophy ones to gain xp and coins, but again, if found it IMPOSSIBLE to do this without the proper gear, which I found IMPOSSIBLE to gain.
There's also the fact that this is labeled as a survival game, which I indeed am in love with as a genre. Here's the thing, this isn't a survival game. This is a 'run around like a chicken with it's head cut off, falling off a cliff and dieing multiple time as you attempt to get gear to kill stuff' game. There is no crafting, there is no 'good' way to get the improved gear, you can't build a camp of any sort for any kind of protection. It's run, kill, run, kill, loot if you can, and try to SURVIVE the dinos, but there is no way to actually do this. It's not a survival game because you have to survive, it's a survival game if you have to survive WITH THE MEANS TO DO SO.
Lastly, maybe this game isn't just for me. I'll be honest here and admit that. I think I would enjoy it with the ability to craft better items, maybe some resource gathering? BUilding up a base camp for protection, make me need to eat and drink, or at the very least, GIVE ME GEAR AT THE START THAT WILL ACTUALLY HELP.
With these things being said, I'm giving it a down vote for the time. I understand it is still in development, and I understand that it's probably got a long way to go. The thing is that at this stage, I don't see an appeal to it, and don't recommend it to anyone that's looking for a fun game that they can acomplish something with. I'll revisit it in the future some time and see how it's going then, but for now, I'm deleting it, and not planning on checking in for a few months, hopefully it becomes worth the 20$ soon!

I think "environmental puzzler" best describes Infra. As a structural analyst, you venture deep into the infrastructure of a city, gradually making your way through various factories, tunnels and facilities. Traversal problems are the main meat of the game - You need to figure out, repair and operate decrepit machinery to progress, pushing and turning dozens of buttons and valves.
Some of the contraptions are rather complex, and combined with the fact that the levels in the game can get quite expansive, patience and perception are required. Be prepared to run around in circles every once in a while, since the game isn't in the habit of holding your hand at all.
Other than your wits, nothing much else is required. There's absolutely no shooting or enemies of any kind, but you can easily die to a multitude of enrivonmental hazards. There are some sections that require precision jumping and swift actions, but they are relatively far and between. For the most part, you can take as long as you want to explore.
Some of the industrial levels are quite good-looking especially considering that the game is running on Source, but Infra definitely doesn't put its best foot forward and the game begins by bombarding the player with some extremely dubious character models and seriously weak voice acting. Fortunately these are the only attempts at human interaction you'll have to endure during the playthrough, and things quickly get into the groove once you're alone in the rural areas.
I was pleasanly suprised by the length of the game and the toughness of the puzzles - Infra took me nearly ten hours, which is a lot considering the low price of the game. You'll have to look past a lot of rough edges though; The game crashed on multiple occasions, and I even had to momentarily swap into windowed mode to get past a particularly nasty level-loading crash. More than that, there are a few map glitches that forced me to revert to a previous checkpoint because I got hopelessly stuck. Oh, and the achievements seem to work very sporadically.
Anyhow, despite of its shortcomings, I enjoyed my time with Infra a lot. The environments of the game tell a way better story than the various memos sprinkled around, and there's a promise of Part Two coming in the future. I'll play that one as well for sure.

Ever since I was a kid I've always dreamed of that fantasy video game that was the most epic of adventures, and one I could embark on with friends. An unforgettable tale full of twists and turns, one we could immerse ourselves in and that would even try our own trust in each other as decisions present themselves. One where we're the great heroes we were always meant to be.
This is that video game.
I'll admit, DOS2 has its shortcomings for sure. Mostly graphics and various other nitpicks. The customization is limited, causing for a lot of NPCs to look nearly identical to others. Some armor combinations leave see-through spots in characters, primarily the lizards, and some lizard horns don't even connect to their heads. This, however, is (mostly) mitigated by the fact that you'll rarely be looking at someone up close. The controller support is also pretty crummy (this is honestly my biggest issue with the game, some things, like toggling helmet visibility, flat out can't be done unless you're using keyboard and mouse), and sometimes, I have to select a skill multiple times before the game even registers it.
But the gameplay is fantastic, the story is very engaging and full of twists, the voice acting is remarkable, and don't even get me started on the impeccable soundtrack. Often I've found myself questioning my choices in the game, and the line between good and evil keeps getting smeared. Also, this game has a great sense of humor. There's a lot of great comedy spread throughout the game, but not so much that it keeps you from being able to take things seriously. It's just the right balance.
One thing to note though is this game is LONG. Some people love that, others hate it. And I suspect just about nobody is going to see all the dialogue in the game. So make of that what you will.
This game certainly isn't cheap, and had a friend not gifted it to me I likely never would have played this. But here I am, and this has quickly become one of my favorite games of all time. It's definitely worth the price.
So yeah, I definitely recommend this game.

The first Original Sin blew me away and when I heard that a second was in the making via kickstarter, my excitement couldn't be contained. To put it simply, I was not dissapointed. Pros:
+ Graphics have improved greatly from the first original sin
+ Many secrets and tons of optional choices for situations
+ Combat is simple, yet complex at the same time
+ Character customization is much better, including more races (All hail the undead race and lizards)
+ You can talk to animals and ghosts.
+ 4 player Coop
+ Good story and sidequests
+ Has hilarious moments and dialog while maintaining dark undertones and creepy factors. (Watching an alligator teleport around because of a magic glove it ate Vs. A man who ripped out a womens eyes and chewed on them and kills children.)
+ GM mode
Cons:
- There are a decent amount of bugs, most not that impactful
- Wonky vision at times
- Gamepad controls aren't that refined, often leading to the controls spazzing for a short moment
- Elves are only playable as undead, since their living forms are absolutely vile.
- Hit chance RNG and AI can be rage inducing at times
All in all, the cons can't stack up to the pros which can go on forever. This is definitely a must play if you are an RPG fan or strategy fan, and has easily made its way to my top 10 (maybe even top 5) games of all time.
