Hello Guys! TeoXD here to give you guys a short, but fruitful review of Timber and Stone. I have put in three years as a tester and player, if you want to descredit me that is. Now to get on to the point, "is this game worth the price? Do you reccomend it? "
Yes, this game is worth the price, and I reccomend it whole-heartedly. If you love rimworld, dwarf fortress, gnomoria, then I would also give you the go on buying this game because it will feel just like home.
- This game is a rogue-like game that has a steep learning curve for new players. It will be challenging, and will punish you when you neglect your people. It pulls at your abiltiy to strategize, to care for your units, and make all your effort and decision meaningful. The game aims to createa story for your own settlement. You as the leader, the governor, the mayor, will decide if your story will live long, or end in a wall of flames. It is precisely becuase of this, that makes this game really interesting.
- The game features:
*Free control of constructing your base
*Training/leveling your units through profession managament
*Faction wars between monsters, and also against you.
*Herding, weapons, armors, etc.
*Bosses, trading, and more!
Now, like I've said, this game has a steep learning curve, but with every mistake, you will improve, make better choices, and help your settlers survive in the hellish world they were randomly thrown into. Also, I fairly warn you, this game is created in the image Robert, the lead developer and creator, imagine it to be. This is a well-known quote around the forums from Robert:  “Deal with it, plan better, start over.” <--- This is reality encased in a game. Your choices and decision matters, and this will also include the way you fight, and survive.
Like before, I highly reccomend this game, and it is worth the cost to buy. You will spend over thousands of hours playing this game, and will never notice it.
Here's a screenshot of what you can do in the game (From my current project):
However, I have to warn new players that it is still in developement. As a tester myself, we strive to make the game playable to before releasing it to the public. This can be agreed upon by the developer of the game. Now I digress.
Also a fair warning: This game is of yet not optimized for low-spec desktops and laptops alike. You will need a strong, or relatively new computer.

I have owned timber and stone since about a year and a half ago, and have followed its development throughout that time. I can safely say that this game is shaping up to be one of the best castle-defence games. I highly reccomend you get it at its 40% off pricepoint, If of course you take into account that it is an alpha and is unstable.
Many people have compared this to Stonehearth and think its either choose one or the other. I completely disagree with that. Here's why:  Timber & Stone is a Defence and Castle building management game. It is great for having a large castle with small groups of people defending, and others creating the resources and mining/foresting, farming, even creating seige weapons such as a ballista to defend from ever - increasing hordes of monsters looking to destroy your quaint palace of death and destruction... and crops. it is also worth mentioning that getting new villagers or 'migrants' to join on this game is a bit harder, and overall you will often have less people to manage.
Stonehearth on the other hand is a city builder, handling large amounts of villagers to quickly create sprawling towns, with a much more relaxed feel to it in terms of combat and resource management. In other words, this game is far less punishing and challenging from this perspective.
These games are similar, but only in a few aspects. I would easily reccomend both, but if the idea of a huge castle of your exact design fending off seiges of necromancers, skeletons and goblins excites you, this is definately the game for you.
My only gripes come from it being in alpha, so the usuals apply. Go into it knowing there will be bugs! Don't judge the final game off of an early view of it!
And remember... Dying is fun!!! ;)

Edit: i had to change my recommendation to a negative because the game appears to be abandoned. The dev has never once updated or communicated since it was released on steam and now the website is offline - seems abandoned, another EA fail.
However! The rest of my original review is below and it still holds true. The game is great as it is, but it will likely not get any more updates, so I HAVE to thumbs down in good concience.
I have somewhere between 200-3oo hours into T&S over the last few months, and i really do love to play the game. It's one of those games I should set an alarm because 5 hours can go by and i will not even notice until I am parched and my stomach is growling.
Currently it is very playable and stable. The systems are all there and work quite well, as an EA game, it's in great shape technically and gameplay-wise.
Mod friendly - install mods if you want no enemies, kill enemies, permanent daylight, you name it. Copy a .dll to your save folder and that's it to install mods.
So you juggle professions, resources, defences, weapons, walls, increasingly dangerous hostiles in the wild who want to slaughter you all. A trader comes by now and then randomly, and depending on a bunch of factors (food, wealth etc) a new migrant may show up and join the town if you let them.
Settlers have random traits both good and bad (strong back, bad vision, etc) that make them a little better for certain jobs. You mine, farm, craft, build structures and walls, herd animals, all while keeping a sharp eye on the surroundings
Protip: Game start; make sure your miners mine stone very first thing, not dirt. Make the Stonemason build pick axes very first thing. reason is the picks will break randomly, and if you haven't got more, you're screwed somewhat. Get stone, make several picks, then make stone tools or storage or whatever you want.
Pros:
-Planning is key
-Massive replayablility & restarting is fun to try new ideas.
-Surviving a nasty Necromancer attack is a great feeling!
-Soundtrack is beautiful; sounds of chopping, hoeing, digging, combat etc all sound great.
-How each game plays out is really up to the player. Fortify and turtle? Go underground for a network of caves? Build in the sky? You can go nuts with creativity, check screenshots tab above!
-Each game you can do a little better as you fail, adapt and try again with what you learn, it's great.
-There is a definite learning curve, some people like this (I do)
Cons:
-Still needs optimization, late game the fps can suffer with many settlers
-Occasional bugs here and there that may require a reload, but nothing major/gamebreaking type.
-There is a definite learning curve, some people like this (I do), but the learning curve is a part of the game, you learn and do better next time.
-An entire day can disappear while you play (yep one of those games that can eat a whole Saturday no problem ;)

on to the actual review:
I think this is the first time I've ever seen a civ clone that significantly improves on the formula. Let that sink in. Endless legend takes the classic Civ formula, strips it down to it's bare bones, and fixes a lot of it's problems. Mechanically the game is stellar, but also has clear flaws in its execution. Primarily it doesn't do a good job of explaining its mechanics or displaying information concisely, especially bad where some quest and technology explanations were clearly written by a someone who's primary language was not english making the sentances hard to parse.
Still, Endless Legend's design shines through its flaws, and its lore is refreshing and blurs the line between Sci Fi and Fantasy in a way that puts one in mind of legendary writers like Michael Moorcock.

I was sitting at home with a few buddies contemplating an evening of good old fashioned bellysticks when one of my buddies Bobo asked me if I had ever heard of a game called Genital Jousting.  I said, "Are you talking about that thing I do where I trot into a room full of unsuspecting people riding the Libman Wonder Mop, making Horsey noises, wearing Only a Natty Ice box on my head and a hot pink towel shoved into my butt crack so I have a pretty tail?"  I could not have been further from the reality of the situation if I had wanted to be there.  Well my friend Boboso graciously gifted me this game knowing that I am constantly questing for the rarely seen and somewhat twisted side of life. Upon download and install of this gem you are greeted with an intro screen that is like getting blindsided in the face with a 14 inch kielbasa, slathered in horseradish and mayonnaise and for some reason you enjoy the nearly unbearable sting that is now violating your eyes.  I knew in an instant that this work of art was going to allow me to reconnect with my inner 12 year old.  We started off in party mode online which is actually a cleverly disguised learning tool that teaches common sense principles to young and old alike. Topics like car maintenance, pet care, astronomy, enviromental survival, centering oneself, and blood born pathogens are frequently discussed in this mode.  To my absolute delight, the culturally diverse and somewhat taboo subject of B u k k a k e is delicately and artfully discussed in all of its prizmatic glistening glory.  I am truely excited to see what other educational and mind expanding topics that this "game" will offer in the future.  The Sound effects of this game made me instantly reminiscent of that one life changing summer as a Boy Scout, camping in the woods with my fellow Scouts.  When you have to take your tent to the car wash to steam clean it in the aftermath, you know a whole lot of learning happened.  Out Scoutmaster was a true leader.  Ladies,  do not be shy. At first this game may be a little confusing to you because a lot of what is going on can only be understood after a weekend with the boys and your weekend with the boys is a lot different than what ours is. Fret not.  You can be docking with the best of us in no time if you just open your mind. Freelives are obviously pioneers of the "How friggen far can we really push this?" genre and to you, I tip my hat.

This game is by far the best cycling game in the world. There are two main modes that are commonly played throughout the community (Career, and Pro Cyclist Mode)
Career-
The career mode is great if you like to control a whole team. The pros about this mode are it is easy to understand. You can change every aspect about your team and can master the manager part. It is always hard to choose which team you want to choose at the beginning of a career, and this game helps your choices. You can choose between any of the three   divisions to select your team (Cya World Tour, Contintental Pro, and Continental) You can filter alphabetically or by the amount of stars they possess (Overall Rating) The cons about this mode are, when selecting a team, they should also give you sponsor details (i.e. Sponsor Budget and Length of contract) Also in this mode there are no major advancements from pcm 2014. Overall this game mode is adicting and very fun. I would recommend this mode to anyone who likes a team and realistic aspect.
Pro Cyclist Mode-
This mode is amazing. You can control everything about your rider during the race and out of race (Height, Weight, Complexion, Nationality, you can even change the picture of your rider) The gameplay of this mode is outstanding. There are no downsides to this mode except you should be able to do something with the money you earn. I would reccoment this game to anyone who likes fantasy due to the fake Cyanide Cups at the beginning and the fact that you are not a real pro cyclist.

Interplanetary is a lot like those tank and artillery flash games that you would play against your friend or the ai, but with the quality of a full game.
As far as the shooting goes, it is very fun to attempt to line up shots across the solar system using several different constantly moving gravity wells. Definitely an improvement over the old flash games.
The tech tree is fairly simplistic, and you have to select a new tech to work towards each time you finish researching (you can queue techs, but only if they form a continuous path). This gets very annoying later on when you have to pick a new tech each turn.
The intelligence system is also very basic. You build scanners and data encryption centers, and in order to see other people's buildings, you need to have more scanners than they have data encryption centers. Its not a simple 1 scanner = 1 data encryption building kind of equation, but there isn't much complexity to it either.
Overall, its a great game if you are really craving some turn-based space artillery, especially if you want to play with friends either locally or online. However, there is not very much complexity here outside of the physics.

It is difficult to say if this is a good or bad game. At first it is a lot of fun. It is also great to find the best way to attack another planet especially when it is far away. I was always very happy when I hit a planet on the other side the solar system.
However, there are two big problems in this game:
- So far, you can not rebuild a city (or at least I don't know how). If you lose a city, it is gone. The problem is that if someone has a lucky strike (close to your planet, game stops his planet on the right side), he can wipe our some or all of our cities very early in the game. This means that you lose a lot of resources which creates the second problem...
- Superweapons! they are awesome, they look great but they are also overpowered (my opinion). If you are not getting attacked by other players (lucky you) and can rush trough the research you can build yourself a fortress and wipe out the other players in a few turns especially if he is good in using them.
So, is it a good game?
Yes, if you like these kind of games and if you accept its design flaws.
No, if you expect more options and if you want it perfectly balanced.

INFRA is definitely one of the best indie games I have played that have come out of the source engine. It takes wondrous care in it's level design and mechanics that topple many of the other games out there. It scares you with every day things, nothing supernatural except you own imagination. Even though I do recomend this to anyone with any interest in puzzle, exploration, story or even real-life urban exploring there are a few major problems that this game have that are purely to do with immersiveness, user learning and user preferences.
First off, there is no options menu in-game. You can save, load and all that but no options to find keybindings, change mouse sensitivity, or any of the normal stuff. This is really quite irritating especially when there is no information given during the game as to what buttons to press for the flashlight and camera. That said, there is a pop up telling you to press R for switching batteries when you have to. This needs to be implemented for when you get the devices. tutorials are important, especially without an in-game keybindings screen.
Secondly, it is very annoying to me when I find this many grammatical and spelling errors everywhere in the game. In a discoverable office early on there are some logs that are written with many spelling mistakes and general sloppiness like "close of bankcrupty" and "waiting receiving the funds". These errors really take away from the immersiveness of this lovely game for me. Not saying that these errors can't be good if done right, but there are just so many and the game offers no lore-friendly explanation for them.
Finally, the voice acting is really quite bad in some areas, with much of the scripting following the errors in the writing. I actually feel like I am in The Room (movie) with everything combined. Something I think also ties in with this is when you talk to the office workers at the beginning. They have voices, but no animations.
All that in consideration, this is still an amazing game with even more amazing potential in the future. I am judging this at the same level I would judge games by EA and Valve, which is saying a heck of a lot for an indie title. If you read all this and are still considering whether or not to buy the game, do it. The gameplay is unique in so many ways it just doesn't compare. Fantastic job devs, keep it up!

Timber and Stone, in short, is a great but slow game.
Guide your settlers in the steps it takes to build your castle/town/underground refuge/etc.
The game is a balancing act between harvesting resources, training soldiers, and building your defenses. Fail at any of these and watch in horror as something simple like a wolf pack kills off all your settlers, or something as extreme as a horde of skeletons following an evil magician burns your world to the ground.
Its a slow process of mining rock, shaping it and building it into your massive castle, training settlers to be knights outfited with the best armor and weapons, setting up an economy to trade for resources you dont have, and finally reaching a level of safety and refuge for your lazy/weak/overeating, worthless settlers. Its your choice whether to feed them to wolves, or let them stay in the hopes that maybe they will contribute at some point.
The game has a steep learning curve, you will be playing along thinking that your doing fine, then get destroyed because you didnt realize how important feathers were, or maybe you do know how important they are (key ingredient for arrows) but the damn chickens didnt want to shed any. . . either way you can invest a few hours into it, and get wrecked. But if you stick with it (meaning start over and over) for a bit, you will start to feel the satisfaction of successfully raising an army, filling your battlements with archers, polishing up your castle, and building a thriving town. Then let the hordes come, let the goblins chop the forest down, for when they approach your walls, hell will rain down from your archers. And when they charge your gates, greet them with the points of a dozen lances. When the spider monarch shruggs off your arrows, fire balistas at her until she is nothing but crumpled remains.
The game is still a work in progress, there are lots of little things that can irritate the crap out of you, but its worth grinding your teeth and working around them.
The game is very playable as is, but will only be getting better. The devs have proven their loyalty and dedication to the game and Im very excited for the finished product one day far far from now.

If exploration and unique environments are up your alley, you'll spend countless hours exploring the expansive levels looking for every bit of detail. The game is also exceptionally beautiful, years of craftsmanship and practice have gone into extracting every inch of beauty possible out of the source engine. The game smacks heavily of Portal 2 in terms of quality and scope, however this game is much less linear and provides a heavy emphasis on expansive environments and exploration.
The game is a little rough around the edges sometimes, and the puzzle solutions may get a little obscure from time to time, but I required no external assistance and I'm not exactly a brainiac. The game's developers are also actively correcting and repairing bugs as they are reported on the tracker.
The game, although technically incomplete, has given me over 8 hours of gameplay so far, and I'm still not finished. The value is well worth what you'll receive.

Oblivion, oh the memories. Successor to Morrowind, predecessor to Skyrim, a brilliantly awesome Elder Scrolls game with the by far worst main quest, infamous for the abysmally outrageous horse DLC, which started DLC content in the entire gaming industry in the first place.
Oblivion is gaming history, that much is sure, but the more important question is, whether it is still up to speed by today's RPG standards. The short answer is: Yes and no. Oblivion does indeed have quite a lot of the comfort functions we players today are accustomed to, but it also feels very outdated from a design perspective. For example Oblivion was the first Elder Scrolls title which was focused on console releases (Morrowind having been available on the first XBox, as one user felt the primal urge of pointing out) and therefore butchered its entire interface to make it as console friendly as possible, something which Morrowind was not back when it released. This meant drastically reduced tooltips, completely absurd item descriptions and names in all but the English localization (Potion of inferior Invisibility = "Ptn. o. inf. Inv." etc.) and very undescriptive info boxes to make every font large enough to be readable from 2-3 meters away on screen. It was an outrage back then, it still is bad interface design today.
Interface wise, Morrowind was ahead of it's time and considering console layouts today, from a design perspective regarding a heavily complex RPG universe, it still is.
I wouldn't really recommend Oblivion to anyone currently anymore, if it wasn't for the Shimmering Isles expansion which entirely made up for the bland main plot of the base game and had extremely memorable and mindbogglingly insane quests. Do you remember the Quest in Skyrim where you wake up naked without all your gear after a night of drinking and embark on a quest to get uncursed by a Daedra prince and get your stuff back? Imagine an entire Addon which solely consists of quests like that. Shimmering Isles is probably the best Addon Bethesda ever made and it is solely playable by playing Oblivion. Therefore I still do recommend Oblivion, although I personally would rather recommend Morrowind and / or Skyrim to people who'd want to get introduced the the Elder Scrolls series.

Picking up Endless Legend, I wasn't quite sure what to expect from a fantasy-based 4X developed by a studio whose other main foray into the genre was a crowdsourced space empire-builder thick with science-fantasy lore. A quick look at Endless Legend's functions and features reveals the same bones as Amplitude's other 4x, Endless Space, but everything that wraps those bones up is unique while still feeling familiar. Where Endless Space clearly takes inspiration from classic 4X games like Master of Orion, Endless Legend hearkens back to fantasy empire-builders like Master of Magic and Age of Wonders. The game's major factions are just as weird and wonderful as those featured by its predecessor - each one has a unique theme, a distinct look and feel, and a plethora of strange and interesting faction features. All of these factors combine to give every faction a completely different feel and a unique strategy that is required for success with each one. Certain combinations of factions can affect gameplay in unexpected ways, perhaps forcing players to deal with their opponents differently - the nomadic Roving Clans, for example, can literally ban others from utilizing the inter-faction marketplace...providing a potentially devastating economic weapon against an opposing faction, particularly, perhaps, the Broken Lords, who rely on the Dust (currency) resource for just about everything.
The hex-based game map is fantastically well-done, and a huge range of game setup options allows a player to customize each game world to a splendid degree. A colorful variety of sprawling plains, towering mountains, glittering rivers and lakes, treasure-laded ancient ruins and weird, fantastical terrain features compels you to push against the edges of the map each turn, driving an urge to explore that is rare in many games of this kind. The game has a robust quest system, with each major faction having its own unique main quest line; in addition, a wide range of side quests is randomly available as you delve into the abandoned temple sites scattered across the landscape.
The way in which the game handles your empire's cities is novel. Every region on the map can support only a single city, regardless of its size - a feature that I thought was a bit of a drag at first, as some of the larger regions could easily support two or three small to medium-sized cities. Since each region may sport a range of terrain types and various useful anomalies, deciding exactly where to plant each potential metropolis poses a strategic challenge. However, as a city's population grows, it unlocks the ability to construct new districts, allowing you to directly plan the expansion and pick specifically which new map tiles you want it to exploit. The ability to direct a city's growth towards the resources that you want helps to mitigate the downsides of having only one in a region.
As you expand from region to region, there is the opportunity to take advantage of the dozen or so of the game's minor factions. Ranging from avians and insects to ogres and orcs, their roving warbands can pose a threat to your settling parties and newly-minted cities. Through conquest, bribery, or diplomacy, each village can be pacified, adding to the number of available workers in that region. Minor factions can also be assimilated into your empire, giving you global bonuses that increase with the number of villages under your control. Assimilated factions make each faction's signature unit available for training in your cities, allowing you to diversify your armies with troops that can help to shore up the weaknesses of your main faction units.
Those units, by the way - of which each faction has only four types - are one of the key features of the game, as you move them around the map like elaborately detailed chess pieces. Your troops (as well as the heroes that command them) can be outfitted with various types of weapons, armor, and relics as you research new technology and unlock better grades of metal. The game keeps the size of armies under control throughout the game as you progress to higher research levels, by increasing their cost in exchange for having them start at a higher level of experience right off the bat - a novel (if potentially controversial) design choice that prevents zerg rushes at all stages of the game. Even with a large city with a fully upgraded set of industrial structures during the endgame, training new military units will still require a substantial investment of time or money. While armies move in stacks, combat sees them spreading out onto individual hexes of the main map, where factors like terrain, elevation, and positioning matter just as much as relative experience and gear levels.
Endless Legend is definitely the kind of game that can provide 'endless' replay. With eight unique factions, the ability to customize any of those factions, a fully-randomized and customizable map, and amazing strategic options, this is a game whose various ingredients combine to create a recipe for truly addictive gameplay. It is one of those kinds of games that I haven't been able to stop playing since I got it, and I believe it to be one of those games that fantasy/strategy fans owe it to themselves to pick up and play for hours on end.

A very absorbing MMO where you fill the shoes of a Warframe, some kind of space ninja robot.
+ Melee combat is really satisfying. So is the gunplay at times.
+ Free-to-Play, with a vast majority of the equipment being craftable.
+ A story and theme that is quite well-developed, despite being a f2p. Not the best, but I was pleasantly surprised by its depth.
+ Fills my personal hunger of wanting to play a cyborg ninja. Metal Gear Rising was so long ago......
+ Missions have quite a bit of variety in them (Several types e.g. Sabotage, Spying, Defense, Assassination).
= Microtransaction model can be seen as "Pay-to-progress-faster". They have to earn their money in some way.
- Story sometimes doesn't make sense. Requires some looking up.
- Incredibly grindy. Gear drops are very RNG-based.
- For a game that focuses on being a fast space ninja, some of the game's later elements detracts from that focus. Not gonna elaborate, as it is a massive spoiler.
I honestly can't believe that a free-to-play game manages to be more engaging in every way compared to some AAA games ( *cough* Destiny *cough*).

I LOOOOOOVE this game. However, if you are just looking at this please read this review.
I know it looks like I have not played that much but I actually got this game about 6 or 7 years ago. Over that time, I started with the launcher that you download off of the internet, not steam. I spent at least 300 hours on that. Then I got it on my old steam account and spent around 350 hours there and now I have spent 101.3 hours on my personal account as of writing this review. I have spent around 751 hours total over this game. I must say that along the whole way, this was a very fun game, however, if you are new, there are a couple things you need to know
First off, you will start on Earth, this means that you will get access to the plains of Eidolon pretty quickly, my suggestion, do not mess with it that much. It may look interesting but as a new player, I have heard it is a bit overwhelming. You can mess with it a bit because it can give you some good mods but I would not try to mess with the terralysts,Eidolons, or even the vomvalysts and stuff until you have more knowledge of what you are doing(Partially because you do not have the abilities to fight the terralysts and vomvalysts effectively.
At first, do the Vor's Prize quest and just keep doing quests as you go along. You FIRST GOAL OF THE GAME is to unlock the planets. As you go along, more planets means more stuff and more quests. Along with more lore. Over time you will find that the player base and the wiki are your best friends when figuring things out.
I am not going to just be saying this because it is funny but also because it is true. The actual lore and meaning to the game kicks in late. It is odd but the hook of the game really appears late game. Here comes the joke, you ready? Everything kicks up around Uranus. I know it is technically spoken as ur-uh-nis but it is funnier if you say it like yur-a-nis because... come on. You start to discover more about what you are and how you got where you are after that point because that really starts the main quest line.
After all that, it is now time for the pros and cons.
Pros:
-The player base is large but not to large, you can usually find a group for anything and their are enough new players around that you are not the only newbie
-The gameplay has some decent variation with missions like hijack, capture, extermination, spy, defense, mobile defense, and several others.
-The amount of weapons and frames(content), from the level of small to large, it ends around the OMG MY BRAIN IS ABOUT TO EXPLODE. This is a pro in that, there is variety, but a con for new players because it can be overwhelming, my word of advice, don't be too ambitious and just TAKE... IT... SLOOOOOOW.
-The quest line, once you get to it, is very enticing with some mind-blowing moments where you can't help but smile or gawk, wide eyed, at the computer.
-The variety in the game is very nice, you like shooting and killing everything around you with firey hatred, you can do that mutliple ways, you like sneaking around everywhere and making the enemies look like idiots, you can do that multiple ways, you like sitting around petting a dog or cat like thing all day, YOU CAN DO THAT!!!
-The game's areas are procedurally generated, basically the rooms are always in a different order, so their is always a level of something new in every match, even if it is just the rooms you see. It never has felt old to me.
-The Devs of this game, you may not believe me when I tell you this, they listen to the playerbase. I am not kidding, they listen to what we want and they are very active, this game, gets a new warframe every couple months, I believe around 3 a year. That is pretty big, you will understand when you see the warframe.
-It is free to play. This game, and this is not an overstatement, is MASSIVE for a free to play game. I am still unlocking and finding new stuff and I have played for ages.However, this is in part with the active dev team. You can spend money in this game but you still get the whole experience when not paying money, yes you can speed up the gameplay with money but a person who doesn't spend a single penny on this game can still become as powerful as someone who has spent 2000 dollars on the game, it will just take a little more time. You can even still get platinum by trading, platinum is the in game currency, and this can help speed you up,l and in the trading method, speed you up for free.
I could go on all day with pros but we need some cons too
Cons-
-The variety is great unless you try to take it in all at once, like I said, take it slow.
-There will be a couple times when you don't know what to do, however you can USUALLY fix this by consulting the players or the wiki.
-time, this game takes time to understand and time is something people do not always have. However, I do still recommend getting it because even an hour a day could get you pretty far eventually, plus it is a decently fun game.
So, in conclusion, I believe this is a great game and it is free to play, so seriously, why don't you scroll back up and download it, if you are worried about data limits, I live out in the country and use hughesnet, I have limited data, however, this game still works perfectly fine with it, the actual playing of the game may take about .1 megabytes per month, that is just for signing in and seeing the deals on the market, the only other data usage is for update but all games have those nowadays, unless they are dead. So, go up there and click the download button. It will be a fun experience.
I realise I may be about to kill myself in the fire of 100's of supporters but, this game is BY FAR, better than destiny in a lot of aspects. There are some ways where destiny is better but there are a h*** of a lot more ways where warframe is better. Then again, remember this is my personal opinion(casually slides papers of evidence and statistics off my desk and into a drawer).
If you get in the game and ever need any help, then please, message me or send me a friend request to help you out whenever we are both on, my username is Voltz118 and I want to help newbies become pros at this game.
I hope I will see you on the battlefield Tenno
And as always, happy hunting.

I have played almsot every pro cycling game for the last 8 years. I really like the 1st player career mode, only a few weeks into the season but it is a great addition to a game that over the last few years hasn't added much. Which is why typically I don't suggest buying the new game until it has been out a while. As always with a new game it will crash occastionally and I'm sure they will put out patches soon as the game as only been out 2 days now.
1st person career mode:
You determine what type of cyclist you want to be (sprinter, climber, stage races, et cetera).
Then pick your team, typically a contentional or contentional pro team.
You have a race director or tell you want he would like you do during the race (just like in old career modes you used to give to your riders). So he declares you the leader, or free element, or teammate, and gives specific instructions like don't attack, ride in the breakaway, follow counter attacks, et cetera.
You have a small number of points that you are allowed to use to adjust your race schedule during the year, which is nice when you want to get more training in.
You select how much workload for your training, which in effect hurts your freshness for when races come up, so you need to decide how many rest days you want.
Overall just a great addition, and as always if you like the career mode as a manager that has changed a little, they do R&D now on equipment, but quickly other than that I didn't see any major changes from previous version of the game.
So far I highly recommend this game if you like cycling. I will update if any major issues arise.

Well, to cut it short, PCM 2015 is... an unexpected step behind :(.
There are two main problems that plague PCM 2015
The new Cyclist mode is great, it's a nice idea, but the AI seems weird. Whenever I simulate, I always get near last position, despite my cyclist being already decent stat-wise.
The second thing is... the UI. It's a disaster, I don't know what the devs were thinking. PCM's 2014 UI was perfect, it had a nice graphics, nice buttons, smart placements, everything.
Now:
- the menus are a mess.
- there are tons of UI bugs everywhere, going from buttons that can't be clicked on because there are UI elements over them, to scrolling pads not working.
- the new icons are ugly. And believe me, that's stuff that I usually can't care less about. But these look like they were made by a photoshop beginner, while last year's were pretty damn cool.
- the fonts are simply unreadable. Again, I just cannot understand why there was a need to change things. It was perfect in PCM 2014 but now everything is barely readable, and I'm mostly speaking - unfortunately - about the in-game races.
There's an option to expand the interface but if you do that, it'll lose focus, so it's still ugly to see.
I really hope that the patches will fix a few things but unfortunately I doubt that a complete overhaul of the UI will be considered, so this year is done. Sigh. I still can't go back to the old PCM simply because of the new Pro Cyclist mode. However, the reality is that, if it wasn't for that, last year's version is currently better.
That said, the perfomance of the game has improved, the loading is faster and the races are smoother. There are also some nice little new touches that make the experience in itself a bit better, but so far it's not enough.

This review only covers the new Pro Cyclist Mode.
Pro Cyclist Mode is a new game mode in Pro Cycling Manager 2015. You create your own rider, where you can choose your riders nationality, age, height and weight. You can also choose skin colour and a profile picture for your rider.
All in all you don't get a lot of customization options.
The big decision is in choosing your focus in your career; are you going to be a climber competing with Vroome and Contador or are you competing for the green jersey with Sagan.
Your starting stats are decided from what you chose as your focus, and the age of your rider.
As you start the game, you get the choice of 3 teams, usually from the country you chose. You can choose the worst team, and become the captain, or choose a higher ranking team, get access to bigger races, but having to ride for your captain.
When entering your main hub after choosing your team, you get into the familiar career menu. Only here you have less options. The only thing you can really adjust is your training schedule.
If you toughen up your training schedule, you will level up at a faster race, but of course you will suffer from more fatigue.
Leveling up increases your stats in what ever area you are trying to improve your rider in. If you are trying to win the Tour de France, you will quickly get improved Mountain, Time Trial and Restitution.
To level up, you can gain XP by training, finishing races in top positions and getting in the early breakaway.
In the races you can control your rider with 4 and 8 on the numpad to move him right and left. Or using 5 and 8 to increase or decrease his effort.
Unlike career mode, in Pro Cyclist mode you can't look at other groups other than the group, your rider is currently in, which means if you are in a breakaway, you can't see who is leading the chase in the peloton, and instead have to use other means to figure out how much of a chance you have of winning.
All in all this game mode is a great improvement to a game franchise which desperately needed a new game mode.

The White Pawn path of Only If is reason enough to recommend this game to others.  The White Pawn path features interesting puzzles along with trippy dreamlike visuals.  The Black Pawn path has less interesting puzzles and for the majority of that path you will be stuck in a monotone building.  The only thing I really liked about the Black Pawn path is what it added to the story.  This is because game seems to assume you'll follow the Black Pawn path first before going the White Pawn path. One thing both paths have is great dialogue and voice acting.
A problem is that you might not be able to hear all of the dialogue because the game audio tends to suddenly get quieter before becoming very loud again (so I don't recommend turning up your volume to hear quieter pieces of dialogue).  This is a problem that could be easily fixed if subtitles are ever added to the game.  Another problem that some people appear to have with the game is the fact that there is a good amount of profanity.  Given the situation the main character is in I found that for the most part the cussing was belieavable, although it did at points start to seem a little too excessive to be a realistic response.
That said if you don't mind profanity and you're willing to overlook a less than stellar beginning segement then this is a pretty well made and entertaining game.  Also it's free, so the only thing you'll be wasting is a couple minutes of your time if you find you don't like it.

This is my first review so I'll keep it "short" and try to get to the nitty gritty. I bought this game on a whim after seeing a friend of mine had it on his wishlist and couldn't figure out what to get off the store. I wanted something immersive, with serious replay value becuase I (like most people) don't care to drop $40 to $60 on a game you play for 20 hours and never touch agian.
Knowing nothing about this series I went ahead and bought it totally blind to what I was in store for, and I'll go on record saying I have ZERO love in my heart for turn-based combat.
This game has literally changed the way I feel about videogames in many way, including turn-based combat. I have never played a game that literally ran off an element I didn't like and still love to play the game, yet I'm drawn back to this title agian and again. In what time I have played it I've barely scratched the surface and I'm constantly wanting to know more. The world is BEYOND immersive, nearly every single NPC has some quest or bit of lore that you can soak up anytime you want, making you run from NPC to NPC trying to figure out the current task or quest you happen to be focusing on at the time.
It is not an easy game, but the drive to learn and lose yourself in this world is so great the challenging combat becomes less about a challenge and more about a the actual world itself. I became less driven about the loot as I normally would and was solely driven by want to know more of the story. No game has done that to me since the original God of War.
Basically if you want a game that you can totally lose yourself in, this is THE game for you.

Infra is not your average game. There are no guns here, but there are still bad guys and monsters. There are no soldiers, spies or saboteurs, but there is a battle taking place. There are no jump scares, creeping horrors, or panicked flights from hordes of undead, but Infra can still scare, unnerve, and frighten you. Just not in the ways that you would expect.
You take the role of Mark Siltanen an industrial engineer from a firm who has just taken over the maintenance contract for the city of Stahlberg, and you are about to have the bad day to end all others, and maybe everybody else's day toboot.
You could use the words 'Walking Simulator' to describe Infra, but that definition barely scratches the surface of what's going on here. You could say that Infra is a puzzle game, but you'd only be talking about the tip of the iceberg. You could say that Infra is a job simulator, but you'd still be missing the real point of what is going on.
Yes, Infra is an Indie Game, and a bit of a klunky one at times. With a smattering of wooden character sprites and voice acting recorded on what sounds like half a dozen different setups that needs better post production. But that's not why you should buy it. The chewy chocolate-fudge centre of this game may take some of us a little while to get to, but when we do, it should give everyone pause.
If you've ever worked in one of those big, Star-Wars-scale industrial environments where a moment's inattention in the wrong place can end your life without so much as slowing down the machinery that just turned you into paste then Infra won't take long to get under your skin. The cracks in the walls, the leaky pipes and barely functional equipment. . . If you've ever worked in heavy industry and had to find a new workaround to each successive problem, and/or deal with OHS and get management to take things like this seriously, then the reaction will be instinctive. Like me you'll be thinking about all the dominoes that could be toppled by that half-flooded generator room or tainted water pipe. I realised that the game had me completely immersed when I found myself backtracking time and again to keep turning off the generators in said half-flooded room only to find out I wasn't yet past the point where I needed to have them running.
At its brilliantly mundane heart, Infra is an interactive cautionary tale, and one that hits close to home for all of us. All around us we are surrounded by tecnologies and systems that we take for granted and that is the spot where Infra builds the edifice of tension that makes up the game's core. Because despite the cinematic license with which Infra's story is presented, the Bad guys and monsters are entirely human, perfectly possible. The horrific scenarios that play out have happened in our world before and they are doing so right now, even as we sit here unaware of their unravelling beneath our feet. Perhaps what is more horrifying is that it doesn't take corporate malfesance and corruption on a grand scale for those little scenarios to play out time and again in the real world. All it takes is a moment's distraction for one person at one step along the long process of getting water from the city dam to your kitchen sink.
Games like Infra should be made, they NEED to be made, and in greater numbers (and yes a little extra polish would be nice too), about things other than psychotically emotionless Space Marines turning the seemingly endless ranks of disposable mooks into hamburger (or some minor variation thereof). Because if Infra can give you pause the next time you take a ride on the subway, the next time you flick a light switch, or turn on a tap, then it has succeeded in a way that few other games can, because you don't have to suspend your disbelief very far at all for Infra to work its magic.

INFRA is a game that I first saw on Greenlight about a year ago. I was getting worried with the time it was taking to deliver BUT now that I have seen what they delivered I am blown away. The puzzles are great. They almost reming me of Myst in some regards. And the enviroments are amazing. I wasn't even aware the Source Engine could look this good and run so well. There are a few bugs at the time of this review (launch day) but I have confidence that they will be quickly attended to. The price of 14.99 USD is a very fair asking price for this game.  If you decide to purchase make sure you spend time to explore each area to it's fullest. There are little goodies hidden all around the map.  The subject of the game really is interesting. I found myself wondering about what sort of underground cities are beneath the city I live in and how much effort it must take to keep it running. When walking around INFRA I feel less like I am walking around river controls and steel mills and more like I am walking through an ancient tomb that has become overgrown and has started to decay. I can't wait to see what else these developers have in store for us.
EDIT: This game has no real horror elements. It is more of a puzzle game. That being said  there were several points where I had a chill run down my spine or a feeling that something was not right was felt mostly due to walking through the decaying areas alone with nothing but the sound of wind and the structure creaking around me. It is no walking simulator with the amount of puzzles and a few fast paced scenes. There are no zombies or slendermen or Nazis but the enviroment and the structures are working against you.

- Dinosaur's are highly detailed,fitting Sound and movement animations ( since last patch)
-Terrain is absolutely beautiful (set to max resolution)
-The majority of the community is friendly, and willing to help out a hunter in need of assistance.
-The Terrain is large and comfortable size, your stamina recovery rate is just perfect to make sure you can run and keep an eye out for predators.
- Weapon sound and animation's are spot on
- gives you a customizable option to wear selected camo such as Merc Spec - Ops, Noble Gear, Settler gear etc.
They've included feathers on the dinosaurs (which personally i have really enjoyed as it gives them such a unique look like no other dinosaur game has done, like the Utahraptor has an amazing look thanks to the Feather pattern.
- Have encountered a few pesky,annoying bugs.
-If you fall in the water, you cant swim out and you have to helplessly watch yourself drown...
-Game has crashing issues, however they are working towards fixing that and so far there has been a drastic improvement.
-Some dinosaur spawn point's are glitched - Take for example i joined a game and had three T - Rex's in the area, I did not survive as expected.
-inventory space is quite small, hence you will have to be very careful as to what you keep in your inventory because take for example if a t rex is charging at you from a distance you will want to start shooting at it with your scope, but when he gets closer you would like to switch to iron sight but you may have a full inventory space so you would have had to drop it..
-Some dinosaurs get stuck in the terrain, which is rather unfortunate in my opinion.
i am going to write from an honest point here, i think the game is absolutely brilliant, The Dev's love the community and are willing to help the community in any way. Playing with other hunters is a must do, because sometimes you can get yourself into a really sticky situation it's always best to have someone watch your back.Some situations can be so intense for example hiding under a bush when a T Rex is standing right next to you.
Or the absolutely wonderful feeling you get when you find a .700, or noble gear for example.Even walking halfway across the map to meet up with your fellow hunter just gives you this great feeling of relief and joy.
For an early access game, i say this is a MUST PLAY! so go on, get the game - support the devs they really do deserve the support!

This is an excellent strategy game. You build various weapons, power plants and defense grids on your planet, research tech, and sling missiles and railgun rounds at neighboring planets in an attempt to wipe out the competition. I tend to favor massive defense grids, which require huge amounts of energy, so I usually beeline for kinetic defense followed by nuclear power research. Then I build as many nuclear power plants and mines as my planet will hold and squeeze a lot of guns in throughout the network. My entire planet is secure, and I can safely fire at enemies. Others will take a more offensive apporach, immediately speccing into the weapons tree, and beeline for railgun and missile upgrades with intel mixed in to hammer foes into submission before they can even get off the ground. Both strategies have merit. But watch out for the superweapons! If you're taking an offensive approach, make sure you have the energy required to fire them. If taking a defensive approach, best to just build up massive amounts of counterintelligence (so people can't see structures on your planet)... because nothing can actually defend against a superweapon. Thankfully the last update let you place gamewide limits on how many of these can be build on both sides.

The game assumes perfectly circular orbits, too. I'd
to see this kind of thing with some deviated orbits, like a
star system. Now THAT would be a great game!

I was torn on how to rate this game. On the one hand, it is an interesting game, it's certainly unique, it's fun to play, and kept me occupied for a bunch of hours. But it's so frustratingly shallow! There's no diplomacy, so no reason not to attack absolutely everyone all the time. So combat isn't a strategic choice, it's just something you do, and something other people do to you.
There's no way to plan movement (your planet just always goes around the sun), so there's really no need for forward planning, or to watch what others are doing and react. The only interesting choices are in which buildings to construct, and if other people happen to blow your bases up along the way, you cope with it. And once you've figured out your favourite tech tree and building progression, you just do that every time.
It's a shame, because it's all built on a solid foundation and an interesting mechanic - it just feels like it needs more depth.

Before CK2, my historical strategy game experience was limited to the Civilization series. Then one day a friend of mine complained that her boyfriend really loved, what she described as, "spreadsheets, the game."
Needless to say after a bit more info I thought it actually looked fantastic and I dived in.
It's hard to get into. Playing through the tutorial and learning what ALL the info boxes actually mean felt like studying for an exam. But after an hour or two, and after having my tutorial character kill his brother to inherit his kingdom, start believing he was possessed, and reunite Spain, I felt like I had a decent understanding.
I've had a few playthroughs. I set my own ambitions when I start. Eg. "As an Irish count, I am going to form the British Empire" or "Let me see how far the moors could have advanced into Europe if I controlled them."
There is this whole huge map to play around in and you can choose any place or time and set whatever ambitions you want for yourself.
Honestly, I can't go back to Civilization after this because the world in CK2 just feels so full.
Some people hate the DLC policy. That's their opinion. For me, after a playthrough, I uninstall the game and then play other games for a few months until my itch for a historical strategy game returns and I reinstall. And with a new DLC or two having come out, the game itself just feels slightly different, slightly better - even though I don't buy the DLC. During a sale I'll grab one or two if I feel like the next playthrough I want to do involves it. That's what's nice - the DLC's give vastly different playthrough abilities. Want to play as a norse pagan, raiding and pillaging and maybe resisting Christianity or adopting it? Old Gods DLC. Want to be the most terrifying force eastern Europe has ever seen? Horse Lords DLC.
You don't even have to pay for the DLC to enjoy the benefits of an updated and well-maintained game. And for that, I love paradox's policy.
Anyway, it's time for my next playthrough... should I try to learn more about Indian history, or shall I try to rebuild the Roman Empire?

I'm a huge fan of Marble Blast Gold and Marble Blast Ultra, and while I didn't expect this to be the exact same game, I hoped it would evoke the same feeling. Sadly it did not; it seems a bit too rough and unpolished, the lighting effects aren't too great, the backgrounds can at times be so bright they make the level itself hard to see, and the mixture of different texture styles are a bit jarring to the eyes.
When you make a game based around trial and error for solving the levels, a lives-system is infuriatingly aggravating and adds an extra level of frustration to the game. The timer for the puzzles also includes all your previous attempts as well, which makes the solve-timer seem somewhat skewed. My biggest gripe with the controls is the fact that you can't turn the camera around, but rather tilt it left and right in an odd fashion, which makes precision jumping an absolute nightmare. Now I don't mind difficulty, Marble Blast could drive my patience into the ground and grind on it and not let up until I decided to GIT GUD, but compounded with a limited number of lives (although it doesn't take many coins to buy 100 lives) takes away from the experience.
The physics seem a bit wonky at times as well, there's a sequence of falling platforms that you have to get across in one of the earlier levels, and if you're on the platform when it starts falling, the direction you'll be sent bouncing off into is seemingly completely random.
I feel there is so much potential in this game, but the menus look like they're straight out of the 90's, the aestethics rub me the wrong way (the textures gives me the cheap low-key indie vibe in some levels), and the fact that precision jumping is a total ♥♥♥♥♥ when you can't tell if your jump will be straight or not, and it just makes me long back to Marble Blast Gold and its sprawly levels of creative and sunny look and feel.
In its current state I cannot with good conscience give this game anything but a thumbs down; the game isn't strictly speaking BAD; while I didn't expect it to be Marble Blast, and I expected to be let down on at least a few points, the fact that it let me down on nearly all points means the game doesn't get my recommendation. I applaud the developer and hope they can take it to heart and make either updates to the current game, or a new one with improved controls, a little face-lift, and perhaps some more cheery backgrounds (that perhaps also wouldn't be so taxing on lower end machines as well), then they can have a new review and perhaps a recommendation from me too.
TL:DR; there is a lot of potential in here, but the games' controls are too restrictive to deliver a good experience. Bad camera controls make precision jumping a pain, and the backgrounds can be too demanding for low-end computers without choosing a very low resolution.

Endless Legend is a well built 4X game that has a unique flavor of its own, and does a lot of things that keep the game interesting at all stages. This is the initial draw for me, as other games (Civ, Endless Space) have a tendency to devolve into a click End Turn fest towards the end of the game.
First off, the factions of the game not only are different in terms of advatages and disadvantages, they each have a wildly different playstyle. My first game was as the Necrophages, and I felt like I was literally devouring the minor tribes and faction cities that I encountered. I produced little food on my own, but pacifying vilages gave me a boost, and I could feed my slain foes to a city for a growth boost.
The second thing I like about the game is how it forces the player to think long term and also consider his opponents when decided tech choices. Each level of tech has several choices, but every 9 techs researched opens the next level, forcing you to consider stay at the lower level to reseach those magic swords you need, or going up to the next level to research the wonders of the next age. Furthermore, the overall cost of technology increases with each researched, so any time spent on low level tech beyond the necessary gain slow your progression into later technologies.
Thirdly, I enjoyed the game's use of resources. Endless Legend has a resource system that I feel is much better done than Civ. All tiles immediatly surrounding your city are gathered, and you can expand your city to talk advantage of strange and unusual tiles. Also, as your city grows you can assign workers who can be focused on any of the 5 major resources. This means that you can found a city where you know you will make money and use workers to compensate for the food shortage. The game also sports 6 strategic resources that are used for building unique buildings and producing advanced armor and weapons for your troops, as well as 10 luxury resources that can be gathered and then activated for empire wide bonuses.  This means that you will rarely find a resource and not be able to make use of it.
Endless Legend is a run and well designed game that I will probably play long after I have beaten it as all the major factions. It sports the expected unit and faction customization, so the possibilties are limited only by your imagination. I have not yet tried multiplayer, but I hear the experience is improving. This is a solid game I can easily recommend.

The sounds are amazing on headphones and really immerse you into the game.  I know there are still tweaks to the sounds as some pings on containers are not correct and you get sound drops during rain storms.
Utahraptors, velociraptors, and tri's all interact and react well  when attacking and being shot.  The T-Rex I have not figured out yet.  I have killed several throughout the changes and thank goodness the population was decreased some; however, I am still finding multiple in a common areas, which really makes it tough to escape or hunt.  Their vision is incredible (too good) and I do not see them fleeing when shot. They seem to continue to attack you until they are finally dead.
I like the tweaks to the weapons and the opportunity to purchase a weapon at the start upon reaching the right level.  The Bow can be effective it just takes some time on learning to aim it properly based on distance to target.
I would like to see more interaction between the dino's especially when there are multiple T-Rex. Interaction between Triceratops and T-Rex, Pack of Utahs and T-Rex, and Utah's vs Utahs when in different packs.  They should be more territorial areas to develop this interaction. I am still looking forward to more dinos being introduced.
Additional Game play comments:
I don't like that you can only see 250 m with marksman scope, past that range the humans, dinos disappear but all the vegetation and land looks the same.    If it's due to a range issue with the gun you should just show the shot dropping and hitting before the animal.  I often use it to scan a valley to search for dinos before proceeding but then when I think it is clear a T-Rex will suddenly appear.
Equipment could include a tree stand, however, the height allowed would have to be limited keeping you vulnerable to Utahs and T-Rex.
Instead of a red screen at your death, you could show a more animated death from the attacker in a 3rd person view.  And while you wait your 10 seconds you could watch them eat your body.
Really Enjoying the game!   Keep up the development, the price is a steal at the early release price, when finished it surely will increase and still be well worth the cost.

I honestly wanted to be able to recommend this game, but I just can't. Not as it is right now.
The level system is an interesting concept, even though it's only a means of artificial prolongation, however... You need to be level 10 before you can even buy a pistol, which means you're stuck with a bow until then, and I had enough money to buy 15 pistols by the time I was ALLOWED to buy one (even though I also feel the pistol is over priced for what it offers). "But you can find guns in crates and sparse ammo" True, that is something you can do, but as it stands right now over almost 12 hours I've encountered more T-rex than ANY, OTHER, SPECIES, PERIOD. (And 90% of the time there's been one OR TWO T-rex in one of the limited areas where a gun is likely to spawn.) Currently, the rex tanks bullets from anything like a massive sponge. Shoot it in the brain, heart, lungs, intestines, doesn't matter; takes 30 or more shots to bring it down. Add with that the extremely clunky mechanics or firing and it does nothing but frustrate the hell out of you.
They also camp on your body after killing you and if you're close enough to hear their footsteps then they're already walking towards you. They haven't noticed you, yet, but they will. Even walking they move faster than you, try to run and they'll see you, lay still and they'll walk up and stomp you to death; so you can forget about going back to your body to get your gear.
- The level system needs to be rebalanced, badly.
- T-rex are entirely too hard to kill, a dozen 12 gauge slugs to the chest, at least half to the lungs and heart, doesn't even phase it. Same with buck shot and .308, currently they just soak whatever you throw at them and refuse to die until you've emptied clip after clip into their organs. (Though I will admit I haven't tried the .700 or .50 cal yet, mainly because I'm not allowed to even buy one...)
-There are only 4 species currently, and of those expect to see more T-rex than any other species hands down. In order of frequency, from most to least, I encountered: T-rex, Utah raptors, Triceratops, Velociraptors. They both need more variance and need to rebalance how many there are. I've run into 2 T-rex in one place at least 5 times; that's just silly.
- You move so slow. SOOOOOOOOO slow. Stamina runs out very fast, regenerates rather slowly, takes you forever to get where you want to go only to run into a T-rex and die instantly. Well, not instantly, it SEES you instantly, then you empty every single round you have into it, face, chest, intestines, whatever tickles your fancy; then it eats you.
- Audio, especially the rain, cuts in and out frequently. Textures also act very weird, mainly trees when they're on the edge of rendering distance. Trees looking like they're made out of netting is the best way I can describe it. Once you get close it fixes but during play it's no bueno.
There are a lot of negatives about this game right now, it's glaringly obvious how unfinished it is, and that's fine. It's early access, that's what you should come to expect, but it is NOT worth buying in its current state unless you are an incredibly patient person. The game looks pretty good, it might give you some feelings of nostalgia if you played Carnivores when you were younger, but that's about it. (There's also no trophy room, like we had in Carnivores, and I feel like that would be a great addition.) I've tried really hard to like it, and been nothing but frustrated the entire time. Most of this stuff can be fixed, and hopefully it will, but like any early access game it's a gamble. It feels like a pre-alpha at the moment with the horrendous balancing and lack of content. If you like the game as it stands and think I'm being too harsh, I'm happy for you, you're a more patient person than I am, but I experienced 11 hours of frustration and maybe 30 minutes of enjoyment.
TL;DR: As it is now, I strongly feel it's not worth buying. Wait until it's more polished, if it ever is, and since you don't know if it will be that's why it's not wise to buy into it now. It's extremely frustrating and there's a distinct lack of anything resembling entertaining content at the moment. Save your money for when it's more polished (again, if it ever is) or go spend it on a game which won't make you want to throw things out the window.

Interplanetary is a quite some Fun, if you play it with Friends. I grabed it during a Sale and bought the 4pack, shared it among my friends and we soon started Annihilating each other. I try to keep it simple and compact.
The Graphics:
Nothing superb but not bad either. It does the job. There isnt much to show basicly. A few planets, a skybox, the Sun and then the few effects for shooting and hitting each other.
Story:
Not there. There is no Campaign or whatsoever. You can play vs the AI if you like but its kindah like the Worms AI. Not much fun imho. Stick to the Multiplayer and you´ll have some fun while shouting at each other.
Gameplay:
Very minimalistic basicly. You start with a planet with 5 cities, you then start building a couple of Mines and Powerplants. Then build teh guns and shoot at each other. If all of your cities are destroyed, you´re done for.
You got some dumb projectiles that randomly disdributes the Hits on the planet and ofc, you got some Smart weapons like missiles where you set the Impact point on the Planet. Not to forget the Lasers, wich are somewhat super accurat but only can hit the side of the planet that is Facing to you.
The Balance:
As far as I´m aware, there wasnt a Single balance update since launch, only a few stability patches that where desperatly needed at Launch, but thats got nothing to do with the Balance.
Some weapons feel Overpowered. In "our" first few rounds Laser became quickly popular, since they dont got a balistic flight. They hit instant in a straight line. Ofc there is a soft counter, to name them Shields, but if you aim them clever you can work around them. Same for basicly all Defensesystems. You only got a few weapons to choose from:
-railgun, basic balistic gun
-Missiles, advanced balistic weapon
-Lasers, point and click weapon
And the 2 "superweapons"
-Solarlaser, wich is basicly a Ray that is fired from the sun, not from your Planet and 1 hits basicly everything
-Asteroid Diversion, a Load of clusterf*ck aimed at your opponents... and somethings coming back to you
So, including the superweapons you only got 5 different Weapons wich lets room for improvement. And since the Laserweapons are point and click, they are pretty much the strongest. Our group Disables them in most of our Games, because of Obvious Reasons.
This game features a Techtree that is quite big but nonetheless allmost useless. We tried different tactics but straight rushing the Superweapons and going for Ecoboost tech afterwards, seems like the only competive way to play.
Summit:
I really enjoyed the Game so far BUT there are quite some things I would like to see adressed since the games is a bit expensive with 17€ without any discounts.
The games doesnt feature an Observer Mode, wich means if you play with like 4-5 of your Bud´s and you´re out first, you sit there and wait for them to Finish since you cant watch them anymore.
The tech and weapons needs rebalance, nothing big but little adjustments would be lovely. Like increasing the needed Techpower get the Superweapons. Be aware that the Game runs fine but still gets Server timeout errors once in a While. Around every 10th game or so.
Do I recommend it?
Yes, if you got some Friends to play it with and if it is on Sale.
Thanks for Reading.

This is personally my favorite strategic game that paradox made.  Its one of those rare golden strat game.
The game says it, its Crusader kings  you get to be a king and manage your country that you chose in the medieval era. The game starts at the year 1066 and ends at the year 1453. You can start earlier if you get some of the DLC'S, which its worth to buy it. Honestly the game is really accurate with the history, not that I know a lot of history but I do know enough to notice if there is some mistakes in it. It also has A LOT of replay value so much that I just hit 550 hours of playing and I didn't even scratched the surface of the game, and yet I still enjoy as much of the game as I did when I first started. If you are fairly new to strategic games just make sure to research how to play, since the tutorial is not that good and its never fun to play when you don't know what you're doing.
What I also liked about this game is how the fighting works if compared to other strategic games. A lot of the strategy games just throws in number, and whoever has the bigger number wins. It could be the same thing with CK2 but it also counts the geography and the leadership. For example if you have an army of 500 men's against an army of 1200 men's. Depending on where your men's are standing (Hills, Rivers, Mountains) or you have good and capable commanders, you could easily defend and win against the 1200.
If you would compare the game with other strategic games, this one would most definitely be one of the best one for political, family, assassination, religion strategic games out there. And its the main reasons why this game stands out the most comparing the other strategic games. You can start playing as a some unknown and least powerful count, and just by making a marriage proposal at the right time to some other noble's daughter, you can jump to a king.
One of the only cons I can think of is that you have to spend quite a bit of cash on this game.
Let me clarify this, if you expect to buy this game, you need to buy some of the DLC's with it. It just makes the game way better and enjoyable. I definitely do not regret buying some DLC'S. If you don't have the money to buy most of the good DLC'S you can wait until paradox makes their sales, you can save a lot by those sales.
Now honestly for the price of the game (Including the DLC's) I personally think its worth it, this game is too much good of a strategic game, and personally my favorite..
It has taken me a long time, but I can finally recommend this classic.  The replay value is extraordinary, although there are still some quirks after all these years.  Enjoy!

Atum Games developed this game in Unreal Engine 4 and it’s quite obvious that there’s a lot of effect work going on which is sometimes very nice to look at, but on many occasions also very blinding me while cruising along those tracks.
It’s and interesting spin on a classic idea, yet the execution of it shows some severe problems. Let’s begin with the obvious, the UI of the game does not scale properly, in fact, the font and information shown on screen are sometimes hard to read. I recommend a thicker font maybe and an adjustment of the underlying shadow effect.
But my complains won’t stop there, ooooh no, there are some logical flaws with the game I just can’t understand. For example, why do we have different currencies with money and score? In classic Jump ‘n Runs the money value stands for a progress until we unlock a bonus life. For example 100 coins turn into one extra life and so on. Here we just collect… for the sake of collecting. I guessed that there would be a shop, as seen in the small menu screen between levels, but whenever I try to open said shop with the prompt of the shown button, only the next level loads. Is this some leftover artifact? Is this game not even finished yet but thrown on the steam market to make some quick money? Those questions are sadly coming while playing more and more of this game.
Good thing I waited a few days to review this game, because now there are at least some improvements placed into the game. So now with 50 scorepoints, you gain 1 live, the shop is finally reachable so you can use your coins to buy more lifes and different skins for your marble. You also see now a small statistic at the end of your run showing you the seconds down to the millisecond that you needed to finish a level and how many coins you got from the total amount in the level. So yeah, at least some stuff had been fixed. But the rest? Let’s continue.
See I don’t have proof of those accusations, so I tend not to make them, but I still think that some things haven’t even checked properly before posting this to Steam. For example if I set the resolution to fullscreen 1080p, the options menu background is not filling the entire screen. Then the options itself are very limited,  even though the game was running on a stable framerate at all times. Then there’s an input bug, when I get from the game over screen to the main menu and then use the continue function, no controls work, neither from the keyboard input nor from the controller. Somebody had to use this function at least once to check if there is no problem. This bug is reproduceable, so I expect that to be seen from the devs.
So… is this game even any good? Well… I have to say, when the game is working properly, it is fun. The level design looks good and gives us various settings with different soundtracks, while not being too annoying after a while. I would love to have a better input control on the ball. Because from my perspective, it is more fun to have control over the height of the jump by pressing the jump button for a different amount of time. In this game you can quickly push the jump button or hold it, the height is always the same, making those jumps on the Z axis more difficult as we can not see how far the distance between two tiles is sometimes and we have to adjust our speed in order to get the correct length to jump. I suggest something like a marker, poles for example, would give a visual help to see how far different tiles are apart from each other on different axis.
At least the gamepad control in this game works, as long as your are on a track. The main menu itself has sadly no controller support and you have to take your hand from the gamepad to use the mouse. This should not be a thing, if I chose at the beginning of the game to play with the controller, I should not switch between different options of inputs to continue the game. A PC game with lacking controller support where the game hugely benefits from a gamepad with sticks to control the player sphere, is not an option, this has to be fixed.
There is one final thing I want to address before I leave my final comment on this game: Why is the continue function after a game over so useless? There are to major things why failing is not a risk or even restricting our progress. First, when you depleted all your lifes you get an way too long game over screen, from which you can continue with one life left, but also with all your money and score. This does not make sense, why should you be able to continue endlessly after you have eaten all your lifes without any consequences? Again I point out to the classic jump and run games: Reset the money and score, and maybe give us 3 lifes instead of one single life.
But to be honest, you don’t even need to get to the game over screen, which is technically not even a proper game over screen as NOTHING is over after reaching that phase, because you can restart the level if you press options quick enough. Seriously, just cheese your way through levels, because if you miss the track, just restart the level and you’re good to go. You lose your money and score which you have earned from the beginning of the level until your failure, but your lifes stay the exact same. There is not logical reason why to restart the level, if it does not have any meaningful consequences for the player.
The only real consequence for the player is the few seconds it takes for the game to reload the level which is not only annoying, but from my perspective a bad design of the game mechanic. With the Unreal Engine 4 it has to be possible that if your ball is lost, you don’t have to reload the complete level, causing the music to stop and the player to be left without control for a few seconds. The proper way is to reset the camera, spawn a new ball and all the collectible objects in the level, without the music to stop or the player being left frustrated because of a small error in his calculations. It can be so easy to make a failure not frustrating, when you can easily retry again and again and again. Take a look at the new Trackmania Turbo or any Trackmania game for example. Every time you miss a jump or hit an object which causes you to lose time, just restart and retry immediately. This is how you can remain the game controls as it is, but give the player no additional frustration other than leaving him in his own fault of giving the wrong input.
I can not recommend this game in this state.
