Okay. So this game is free, obviously. So, you are free to try it. And you should, so you can formulate an opinion of the game yourself.
The thing is, this game has a great idea. It's very surreal with narration and dialogue playing a heavy role in the game. It reminds me much of the Stanley Parable in some ways, and then "Anna" in others.
The *problem* is this game has a lousy setup with controls and gameplay. God, I beat it so quickly but it was so f*cking frustrating. Basically, much of the game includes button-mashing quick-time sequences, but these are botched. You can try button-mashing, which seems to always fail. Trying to time each sequence right also fails, because you have to reach a certain amount of timed hits before death. You can time it just right, but the cue for the next sequence might take too long to appear, OR it can just be downright buggy in that it doesn't matter how you do it, you will fail.
Unlike Stanley Parable, which had humor, clever dialogue, and no player dialogue (thus giving the player the sense he is communicating with the *vocal* narrator through his choices), this game lacks humor and clever dialogue, and instead uses excessive language and sexual innuendos.
While I am a fan of excessive language and sexual innuendos, this game uses them rather crudely. They're not effective and it's like the game is trying to overdo itself with them. The player himself has dialogue, which takes away part of the surreal feeling.
Would I recommend it if was a paid game? No. Would I recommend it when it's free? No. Unless you have taken a serious interest in the game already, I would not reccomend it.

I'll give you the tl;dr version upfront:
Quite fun. Way too grindy. Really obtuse for new players. Story is serviceable, but mostly non-existant. Has some really good bits towards the end. The game is packed with content, but most of it is rng-generated and repetitive. Feel free to try it, but requires a lot of investment (grind and IRL research) to fully enjoy.
Now for the In-depth review:
Warframe is like a flawed masterpiece - it does a few things very, VERY well, but they come with some real major downsides.
By far, its most distinguishable feature is its combat, the real meat of the game: Warframe is a fast-paced, third person shooter/hack-n-slash/platformer/looter with a heavy enphasis on dextrous movement with an enourmously high skill ceiling, unlike any other game on the market. The freedom of 3D movement and speed of the player character is by far unmatched by any game I have ever played. The controls take a while to learn, but soon you will be flying through the maps at lightspeed, doing ninja flips while shooting and slashing at 10 different enemies before landing you feet, all with seamless ease and fluidity.
The controls are great (after a little customization), the matchmaking works wonderfully, the loading times are short and the melee combat is okay. There is even a stealth system you can use every once in a while
However, the enemies themselves, have very little variety and, for the most part, have a very limited moveset and are all dumb as a rock. Melee enemies rush you, ranged enemies move into range and shoot you. That's it. That is the exntent of enemy AI. No tactics, no special moves, no fancy mechanics. To kill them efficiently, you just shoot them in the weak spot till they are dead. Works on 95% enemies. The other 5% are proper bosses and the occasional miniboss.
Make no mistake, the combat is REALLY fun and has an enormous skill cap. But enemy variety is  quite limited, so it eventually devolves into brainless shooting and gets dull after a while.
Mission variety is also a major issue. Every single level in the game is one of a handful of mission types, like exterminate (kill all enemies), rescue (save a npc), capture (kill a specific enemy), etc, which play, for the most part, exactly the same, with nearly no varity except the map layout, which is procedurally generated. So you end up playing the same missions over, and over, and over, until you finally  unlock a new map type with reskinned enemies with higher stats. Rinse and repeat.
What breaks up the monotony is actually the loot, weapons and character you use. In each mission, you gain resources and currency, which you can use to create new weapons and unlock other characters Gathering said resources and currency usually takes a hefty amount of time, especially for powerful weapons and new freames (characters). After you DO get the resources it takes from 12 to 72 hours for them to be available for use. Yes, you red this right, 3 days for a new character. And the wait isn't even the biggest issue, it's the resources themselves:
The game has systems upon systems of mechanics and resources to manage and does a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor job of telling you how they all work together and what you need to progress. The weapons available range from useless peashooters to overpowered death machines and they all look the same in the store. It demands an unreal amount of outside research to understand how this all works, like Phd level reserach.
The real problem now is, even when you do finally understand how to unlock all the content (missions and planets), know which characters (frames) and weapons to get and how to upgrade them you will come to realise the enormous amount of grind it will require to get them up to notch for endgame content.
Alternatively, and much more feasibly, you can buy stuff from other playerswith premium currency - plat. Yes, there is a very active, player-to-player trading market in this game, regulated only by offer and demand. Rather than hoping for that 1 in a million loot drop from an enemy, you can just sell stuff you don't need and use the plat to buy what you want. There is a limit to how many trades you can make per day, but a smart and/or patient investor can make all the plat necessary to progress for free. It does takes a lot of time, research and keeping up with the metagame to know what to buy and sell. So most people just buy a few bucks worth of plat with the occasional 75% discount and make it last a while.
So, in a nutshell, this is a game with fantastic combat, plagued by very poorly explained and streamlined progression, with a severe lack of enemy variety and competent, with a handful of very good story arcs you must search for in the wiki and a volatile marketplace you must understand and use to tackle endgame content.
Is it fun? Every once in a while. Try it, play a bit and move on.
Tips to get the most enjoyment:
Don't binge on this game, or it gets really frustrating really fast.
The wiki is your friend.
Join a clan asap.
Use the warframe.market - sell what you don't need and buy what you do.
Ask for help from other players. They will tell you how things work

Despite how simple this game looks, it's a shockingly deep and polished bullet hell smup. While, if your a fan of the genre, you're probably not going to encounter many
mechanics, what you will find is a large range of ways to approach a familiar formula. Unlike many bullet hell games, where defensive play is essential, in this the majority of bullets are produced by low health minions, and since bullets are transformed into points on death, aggressive strategies are shockingly valid. The game also allows you to customize your bullet patterns (although most need to be unlocked) and switch between three of them on the fly (either with a direct bind and/or with cycling if your prefer). While most are fairly simple, some are complex and can be affected by the direction of your movement, your location when you switched to them or the use of slow move (the essential bullet hell feature reduces your speed and displays your hit dot for precise dodging).
The only complaint I have is that some of the menus are less intuitive than I'd like them to be. For example if you don't have enough points to buy a bullet pattern, you're not able to see a display of it. There also isn't a fully functional stage select function; you can either play arcade mode which allows you to set all your options but always starts you from stage 1, or conquest mode which allows you to select previously beaten stages but saves your lives and doesn't let your alter your bullet patterns without creating a new file (starting from stage 1).
If you're new to the bullet hell genre and interested in trying it out, this game is probably a fantastic starting point. Easy is challenging enough to be satisfying and since conquest mode allows you to save progress between stages, the game is relatively forgiving. If you're an experienced smup player, this game is certainly worth having in your library. If you're only a casual smup player, this probably isn't a must own unless you're a fan of the cute/derpy aesthetic. The screenshots and video paint a rather accurate picture of the game, so it should be rather obvious if this is something that might appeal to you.

Imagine a mad Soviet-monkey who flies a jetpack that can manipulate time and space fighting a squid-admiral who tries to slam him with his anchor. If you burst into laughter while you tried to do this, this game is for you. And if you didn't you should try it as well, because Awesomenauts offers some really slick gameplay behind it's silly façade.
Awesomenauts is a match-based MMO that is best described as the child of a SNES-era Mario title and League of Legends. Don't go away yet, my fellow LoL-hater! The only elements this game borrows from LoL (and other MOBA's, such as Dota) are that you have to destroy enemy turrets behind the cover of your minions and that you win by destroying the enemy's nexus, or the drilling core as it's called in Awesomenauts. The Mario-element would be it's cartoony style and ofcourse the fact that it has only two dimensions.
Well, now you've got an idea of what to expect from this game, I will proceed to the actual review. The presentation is pretty damn neat. While the cartoony style might not be for anyone (I don't know what to think about it myself), you have to be a downright madman to call it ugly. Oh, have I mentioned the humour? I think this game is the funniest I've ever played. The music is great as well: all 16 characters have their own, unique theme in the character selection-screen and the in-game music is pretty neat, too. I do believe that the character themes are a bit of a wasted effort, though, as I think the devs could have spend the time and money better by fixing some of the issues I will address later.
The gameplay is almost as fancy as the presentation. It's pretty neat to jump around the map and shoot your enemies. You can also upgrade your character as the match progresses, in a similiar fashion to LoL. However, the upgrade system is much more simplistic. I consider this positive, as LoL's system requires quite some time to dive into and Awesomenauts's absolutely doesn't. You'll fully understand it by the time you complete your first match.
However, not everything of Awesomenauts is as beautiful as the butterfly spirit (yep, that deity can actually be summoned by a certain character). Although it isn't critical, the game suffers from some balancing issues. Some characters are quite a lot stronger than others and easier to play, too. This means that you'll find a few characters constantly dominating the match. While it is entirely possible to counter them for an able player I think the devs should pay some more attention to this problem.
A much more major issue are the servers, or rather their absence. Each match is hosted by one of the players. This means that when the host has ♥♥♥♥♥♥ internet, you're screwed. Things become even worse when the host decides to quit. The game will go black for a few seconds as it attempts to find a new host. Don't be scared away by this fact, however, as it's really the only major issue I can think of.
All in all, you should really buy this game, even when it's not on sale (;

Picture yourself as a ball around on a thin platform (unfortunately no Monkey in the ball)...avoiding obstacles, making precise jumps from platform to platform....and cursing at your inability to make the marble move the way you want. Then picture yourself doing that 100 more times. It's actually quite fun, until it isn't.
Before I get into it: I'd give the game a 4/10. You'll probably play it once and put it away. But for less than $3, it's not much of a gamble. And yes, I did beat the game.
Pros:
-The mable mechanic is really intersting. It takes some getting used to, but it is really nice once you have adapted.
-The level variety is pretty interesting, ranging from slow platforming stages, to racing down the strip as fast as you can, to avoiding obstacles that will push you out of the way.
-Some of the music is good.
-The level designs are interesting, but get a little repetitive.
Cons:
-There is no incentive for anything. The items are pretty useless. You can only use your coins for lives and slightly different skins. Points...Are just points.
-Because items mean essentially nothing, there are many levels where you say screw it, move forward as fast as possible and jump until you reach the goal. This is further enhanced with the first bug I list below.
-There are items that seem to serve zero purpose.
-No timer of any kind. This would cause some stress and make me feel like I'm playing a game. Add some speedrunning aspect or a countdown timer to make it more interesting.
-The first 50 or so levels are varied and somewhat interesting. After 50 you end up seeing previous levels with small differences. The last 10 levels or so...just a straight line with a bunch of 1 obstacle. Oh..and screw level 82.
-Some of the music stinks.
-Not sure if this is on purpose, but in some of the levels  the end of the platforms are not flush, causing a really awkward stall in flow. For instance, on the ginat ball rails you'll be fine until the end..where you hit the platform and get launched out of bounds.
Bugs:
-Low on lives? No worries, just press start and restart level before you die...no lives lost.
-Music stops looping on certain stages, so you're stuck with the sounds of the level, which is typically one 2-3 second sound that constantly repeats.
-Some levels have no music.
-Some levels are broken. You'll see messages along the lines of "Lighting needs to reinitialize. <X objects did not appear>"
All in all, give it a try if you want. If you've played games like this...you'll realize right away that it's not the quality of other ball platformers, but it's alright to waste some time.

I'm no newbie to stragegy games, 4X or otherwise, back from the original Master of Orion up through Endless Space, which I really like. I bought this expecting the same level of awesomeness as Endless Space... and was thoroughly disappointed.
Pros :
It's pretty, which isn't really a selling point for strategy games, but it's there.
The setup of resources is pretty self-explanatory - Food, Industry, Science, and Dust (money). It's basically the same as Endless Space. Sure there are other resources, but I like the simplicity here. If I wanted something more complex I would go back to the Hearts of Iron series.
Having seasons actually affect the game was pretty nifty. As far as innovation goes, this is a good one. I wish it was more controllable in the game setup, but maybe that'll come later.
Design your own faction and play against them is pretty great. I've loved this feature ever since GalCiv II.
Cons : (this might take a while)
AI is immune to the approval penalty for expanding AND building burroughs. Sure, human players are ALWAYS gonna be smarter than a video game's AI, but handicapping me in this way kinda made me feel like they took the "eXpand" out of the "4X," which is my primary problem with the game. You get penalized for expanding while the AI doesn't, and since the AI likes to just burrough their cities in whatever random direction they want, if you capture that city, your approval rating plummets. Again sure I understand the need to beef the AI so it's a challenge, but this kind of handicap makes me feel like I'm playing a 3X game instead of a 4X one. I'm certain there are other, better ways to handle this. OR the other option is to not advertise it as a 4X game, which I'd also be ok with. On a side note, GalCiv III is out and they're always seeking new ways to tweak the AI so it's a challenge and thus doesn't really need these weird buffs.
UI is completely WTF. Some elements are good, but I shouldn't have to search for stuff like "how long do I have on this siege?" Also had to dig for how to activate buffs.
Combat is clunky. as. hell. Go play Fallen Enchantress or Master of Magic to see how it's done. Seriously, everyone wants to be Master of Magic. The concept is so simple, but somehow everyone misses the target.
Immersion is meh. The seasons were nice, but nothing else was compelling about the storyline or the gameplay. For good immersion, go study Emperor of the Fading Suns - while it's a terrible wargame, it does an amazing job of immersing the player in said terrible wargame. Even Endless Space sucked me in - I would play for hours and not realize that it's past midnight. What happened here guys?
Difficulty. It's pretty standard that I play the tutorial, which was moooostly good, though it left out some key info. Then my first game I pretty much always set on "easy," or whatever's just below "normal." Learning curve. That said, and the fact that I'm not a newbie to strategy games, I still get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me. Like it's not even a contest. This isn't my first time juggling villagers between production and food, nor is is my first time moving armies around. On easy the game claims that "the French could win Agincourt." Still, the AI wipes the floor with me. Did I maybe miss something crucial in the tutorial?
Slooooooooooooooooooooow animations. Even if you win / lose a combat, you have to sit through watching the surviving units on the board do a little shuffle. Moving around the map is pretty slow too. Maybe a speed slider for that? I mean I don't want to feel like I'm watching something in fast-forward, but being able to kick it up one notch would be pretty great.
Pathing is a complete crapshoot, and when certain spaces or actions cost you ALL the remaining movement, this is a BIG deal. Also if I mis-click an area, no matter how fast I click to correct it, there's no going back. On a side note breaking sieges is pretty wtf too. I had to path clear around my entire city, which took a while during winter, to break a siege. If the attacking army is only on one side of the city, that's not really a "siege." That's "hey let's everyone sneak out the back where it's unguarded."
So yeah, if you want a good 4X fantasy, go give Fallen Enchantress a shot. Or if you're an actual wizard and can get Master of Magic running, play that - it's the original "weird races + FIDS + fantasy strategy." If you want a good space 4X, Endless Space is good. For some reason though, they really extra failed with this one. It turned me off enough that I'm proooooobably not gonna buy from Amplitude again.

Only played one match so far but I like the idea of taking shots at distant planets that affect the trajectory with their gravity. Aiming is pretty weak. I find that hard to believe. Also, the laying down of the flight path is imprecise. It would be nice if you could have sort of a sniper feature to get the precise trajectoy you're going for. I think later in the game you get some kind of homing device that fixes this problem.

The quick start didn't tell me about being able to fix or upgrade buildings but mostly aiming takes a lot of time and then everything gets fired at once and very quickly impacts with a teeny "biff" sound that is about the most unimpressive noise in gaming. SOASE has it right. "BAADUNG" and a huge cloud of dust goes up into the atmosphere. You can't follow these projectiles or slow them down so its very undramatic. Aiming is tedious and the whole game seems to be about aiming and upgrading things. You don't build any ships. You put up buildings and then try to maintain them. Think how crazy that is. You're making war with these distant planets but you have no way to invade and steal their stuff. The whole point of war is to beat them up and take over but in this game you can't. All you can do is destroy.
When you research something there's no progress bar. They do give you a ratio like 212 of 450 but they didn't have enough money to put in the universally accepted and easily visible, moveable progress bars. It is also hard to see the slight change in border color when you select a thing to research.
When you're rounds impact the planet you will not get zoomed in automatically to see the shells spectacularly impacting, destroying buildings and throwing cars around. This would have been a nice reward after all that tedious fiddling with the aiming system but its not included in this game. You will also not be rewarded with numbers popping up out of the destruction to tell you you've actually had some hits. All you get is a little "pft" or "pft, pft, pft. pft" if you hit with four rounds.
No dog pops up to laugh at you if you miss.

The AI in this game isn't good, though that's not peculiar in a grand-strategy game. The game does have some unique 'dumb AI' moments.
-Continuously wandering it's smaller army around where you're seiging one of it's castles; allowing you to finish the seige and then go stomp the army at your leisure.
-Starting murder or usurpation plots that never pick up traction and just sit at, say, 20% for years at a time, meaning you can hold it over them all that time and move to arrest them at just the right moment.
Anyway, most strategy games compensate for AI shortcomings by letting the computer-players cheat or having the other factions blatantly gang up on the player. This game does neither and other than some period-realistic FU moments (your get sick and die at the ripe-old age of 21, have fun playing as a baby) the game feels fair. Instead, the systems are just so rich and unique that you can learn something new almost every time you play. I've put in 255 hours at this point and I'm still learning little tricks and quirks buried within the game's rules. And all that in a presentation that looks good with barely any loading times. Maybe the game I've had the most fun with over the past several years.

This is personally my favorite strategic game that paradox made.  Its one of those rare golden strat game.
The game says it, its Crusader kings  you get to be a king and manage your country that you chose in the medieval era. The game starts at the year 1066 and ends at the year 1453. You can start earlier if you get some of the DLC'S, which its worth to buy it. Honestly the game is really accurate with the history, not that I know a lot of history but I do know enough to notice if there is some mistakes in it. It also has A LOT of replay value so much that I just hit 550 hours of playing and I didn't even scratched the surface of the game, and yet I still enjoy as much of the game as I did when I first started. If you are fairly new to strategic games just make sure to research how to play, since the tutorial is not that good and its never fun to play when you don't know what you're doing.
What I also liked about this game is how the fighting works if compared to other strategic games. A lot of the strategy games just throws in number, and whoever has the bigger number wins. It could be the same thing with CK2 but it also counts the geography and the leadership. For example if you have an army of 500 men's against an army of 1200 men's. Depending on where your men's are standing (Hills, Rivers, Mountains) or you have good and capable commanders, you could easily defend and win against the 1200.
If you would compare the game with other strategic games, this one would most definitely be one of the best one for political, family, assassination, religion strategic games out there. And its the main reasons why this game stands out the most comparing the other strategic games. You can start playing as a some unknown and least powerful count, and just by making a marriage proposal at the right time to some other noble's daughter, you can jump to a king.
One of the only cons I can think of is that you have to spend quite a bit of cash on this game.
Let me clarify this, if you expect to buy this game, you need to buy some of the DLC's with it. It just makes the game way better and enjoyable. I definitely do not regret buying some DLC'S. If you don't have the money to buy most of the good DLC'S you can wait until paradox makes their sales, you can save a lot by those sales.
Now honestly for the price of the game (Including the DLC's) I personally think its worth it, this game is too much good of a strategic game, and personally my favorite..

As a complete newcomer to MotoGP as a sport and a game I was very surprised at how fun it is. The riding aids help a lot at the beginning and can be disabled step by step as you become more comfortable with the controls. Riding in general feels great, there is a special thrill to be had from riding at the very limit of your bike's abilites and shaving fractions of seconds off lap times. Other than trainings and qualifyings, the races pose a different challenge as you don't just battle with the track, but with other riders too. On most difficulty settings you can just ride off and win by a landslide, but on the higher difficulties the opponents can become quite hard to beat and the occasional duels that can last multiple laps are some of the high points of this game. Also it's worth noting that the opponent AI is surprisingly solid as they're reasonably good at avoiding crashes and giving eachother (and the player) space where needed. The graphics hold up pretty well, the tracks have their own distinct looks and there are some nice little details here and there. Some parts of the game lack a little depth, like the commentary at the end of sessions that repeats itself a lot or the rather repetitive and unimportant social feeds, but no part of this game is actually broken or dysfunctional and the underdeveloped parts are limited in a kind of charming way instead of being annoying.
This gets an easy recommendation from me if you like no-frills bike racing or racing in general.

This is one of those games that is full of itself. It's full of itself because it believes it innovates. It's full of itself because it believes the game has a good cast of characters. It's full of itself because it believes it has a great writer. It's full of itself because it's indie, and it's free.
Only If is a game where you are potentially set into a world of hallucination and fantasy beyond comprehension, yet while all this is going on, you are stuck in the real world where bizarre people are trying to kill you, Anthony.
I care not for Anthony. I care not for the Radio Man, nor his accomplice. I. Don't. Care.
A few hours into the game and I just couldn't take it anymore. It is evident that the Radio Man is played by either one of the developers or one of the developer's friends. It is so obvious that his voice actor is a 20 something year old man trying to impersonate someone in their 40's or 50's, and it is simply terrible. I hate that his accent is nonexistant at some points, but most of all, I hate this game's writing. It is so poorly thought out and poorly done that I just couldn't help but drone out the useless noise spewing out of that Radio Man's mouth. It was nothing but cussing and esoteric "philisophical" dialogue that anybody can make up. It is obnoxious and frankly, really boring. Just because your main antagonist is yelling at me and saying profound and vulgar things at me DOESN'T make me scared of him or threatened by him.
Anthony is also not very interesting, and as soon as he opens his mouth, my brain shuts down. He's an average white male trying to escape this very average hellhole. Amazing.
But now that I've talked about the story and dialogue, I think I should also mention the gameplay, because after all, story means nothing if the game is entertaining. Sadly, it is not. It is shallow and heartless and it makes me feel like a robot. I am going through the motions while simultaneously being flashed by pretty colors. It feels all so generic, and the puzzles didn't surprise me at all. In fact, they bore me to tears. I also found certain places where I just couldn't progress because the game wasn't designed in a way to prevent me from leaving the boundary of progression. I found myself wandering a valley of nothingness because I left the viscinity of the game's influence, and so I had to restart and try again many, many times because of the games less than distinctive path of progression.
Oh, speaking of which, there is no save function in this game. Only a password system. We live in the year 2014, and I still have to put passwords in my game?
Overall, what I found in Only If was simply an indie game. A pretentious, self-loving, poorly written, horribly designed, boring-as-hell, indie game. I have no respect for this game.

Endless Legend is an amazing game, although very deceptive - at a glance it looks like yet another Civilization-like 4X turn-based strategy, but upon closer inspection it reveals numerous differences. Territory management, army management, research, even diplomacy, all these things work in a novel way, still intuitive, but very different from what various 4X games taught us.
Driving the change are the factions - all of them unique and distinct, toeing the line between science fiction and fantasy, with their own strengths and weaknesses in all areas, and their own unit designs. Unlike Civilization, the differences amount to more than just a single trait yielding more food or gold from trade routes - they affect the gameplay much more heavily, e.g. by removing the dependency on food or being unable to declare war.
The soundtrack itself deserves a mention. In Endless Space, it was very good. In Endless Legend, it's spectacular. Over one hour of stunning music for all races and situations, Excellent background music that perfectly balances calm and energetic tunes depending on the situation.

+ Solid, consistent 4x game in the vein of the Endless Universe.
+ Different factions play completely differently thanks to wise application of characteristic mechanics unique to the faction, from one that is wholly dedicated to Dust production for both "food" and "money, to another that cannot directly wage wars, to another that can leverage strategic resources for faction-wide benefit.
+ Hauntingly beautiful art direction that seemingly lifts from the concept art right into the game assets wonderfully, as if the game itself is made out of the art on a Magic: The Gathering card.
+ Rest of the game looks, flows, and works very cleanly, from UI to graphical fidelity to stability and performance, and actually plays on IGP (read: Intel HD Graphics) hardware when my GPU died at acceptable levels (with everything turned down).
+ Endless Universe is a large, deeply engrossing lore-universe to dig into if you are into lore, which spans 3 games as of this review.
- Combat is a weak point as with all of Amplitude's offerings so far, with obscure mechanics, number crunching and uninspired and wooden animations, which is a shame since the rest of the game looks and flows wonderfully regardless.
I won't rehash what others have said, but, if you enjoy a good strategy game, you'll like this.

Action platforming MOBA at it's finest
I have been a fan of MOBAs for most of the year now. My work doesn't take me near human contact for most of the day. So when I get home and look for some qualifications of the games I want to play, multiplayer is a definite attractor. Thus, MOBA is a natural genre for me to ease into and get some much needed human contact, no matter how venomous the comments.
Honestly though, I was suprised when I picked up Awesomenauts by Ronimo I jumped right into a game after lightly reviewing the mechanics and controls. The game lends itself to a fast learning curve at least at first. Much of the game is fast and twitch reflexes are necessary, but a basic knowledge of MOBAs and action platforming are all the basis you need to have fun in your first games.
During my first game, I felt as though I wasn't even playing with humans. You are constantly moving and jumping, controls which take both your hands, and every second counts since the arena is much smaller than most MOBAs. So there wasn't much time to type, and as far as I could tell there wasn't voice activated from allies mics. It is quite a different experience to play with the basic communications that are provided by the game. Each of the several number different buttons that are quickly accessible allow you to communicate ideas that are basic to every MOBA. Retreat, attack, help, and the like are all communicated through generic terms to your teammates instantly. Fortunately there aren't sarcastic or abrasive comments that can be communicated so quickly so the entire thing turns out often to be relaxing and fun, even if you end up losing. There is of course a chat option, but I found it unnecessary and not often used by others either.
The mechanics of battle remind me of platforming action akin to Smash Brothers. Though unlike that genre, special abilities have cooldowns. So you can use them as they come available, but are disabled for some time after their use and you are left with just a simple attack button. Fusing the two concepts actually works very well. The most important aspect to combat then is positioning and timing. This allows for a very gradual learning curve after beginning to learn the game, eventually breaking into the concept of meta and having to change your tactics based on the current trends of combat and the game. So even though the game might be more simple than say DOTA, it still has a sense of depth.
I will thank the creators for breaking down the timing of modern MOBAs because the constant stress of being put against other humans, and having to remain evasive for more than 20 minutes in an action platformer can be very strenuous on my hands. Luckily, rarely did a match extend beyond that time. It seems to be the median time that you can spend in a game, many ended before that as pushing strategies were involved.
Other great things that I enjoyed about the game: The reduced dependance on items (though there are some tactical choices in your purchases), faster respawn times, unique characters, and a great system for cosmetics. Cosmetics are a big attractor to me for a MOBA, as they are a way to customize the game to your preferences. I think the art style is very appropriate, and many of the cosmetics are either comical or very well constructed for the character type. Some immersion is broken for some of the cosmetics, like the minecraft model for one of the characters. However this is a game that never takes itself so seriously as to not allow for such concessions.
I enjoyed my time with Awesomenauts and I will be glad to come back to it as a game that has a lot of replayability. Not only that but the development team are still working on creating new and interesting characters and cosmetics. Even developing the AI to be better on a consistent basis. So even if you purchase this game now, you won't be disappointed with the future prospects. This is definitely something to look into if you enjoy MOBAs but need a break from the seriously competitive play that pervades the attitudes of their populations.
You'll like this game if: you're tired of more serious MOBAs but don't to leave the genre entirely behind. Great gameplay, fun characters, and quick matches are the star qualities of this game.

The reason I'm giving QP Shooting - Dangerous a negative review is because it is
too flashy to be a practical and playable bullet hell game. I've played many danmaku shooters - Touhou 2~14 (several of which I've 1cc'd on Hard Difficulty), Bullet Heaven 2, Suguri, and Murasaki, to name a few - and in every one of those games, it was very clear what on-screen was safe to collect and what enemies and bullets you need to avoid. In QP Shooting, however, everything on screen looks like it just blends in with itself (due to the lack of high-contrast borders on everything), making it extremely difficult to discern what's safe and what isn't.
QP Shooting's difficulty comes mostly from visual-effects distraction and pointless screen clutter rather than actual curtain-fire bullet patterns; many times, it's very difficult to determine what is a bullet and what's a harmless visual special effect on-screen because the special effects get way too cluttered when combined with the flurry of things you're trying to avoid. When you kill an enemy, it (and the bullets it shot) all turn to semi-transparent stars that quickly home in on your character; said stars are the same size and color as the very bullets you need to avoid. The rotating flashy greenish circle that's constantly around QP only serves to let brigher-colored bullets (especially the green ones) blend right in, making them more difficult to see. When anything on-screen is destroyed, it goes up in a poof, obscuring vision in that area briefly and making it hard to anticipate anything going through it, especially if you're getting swarmed at a closer range.
This game feels like the equivalent of playing a driving game where you have to avoid obstacles, and several holograms of said obstacles clutter the path around what you actually have to avoid.
If you don't care for the bullet hell gameplay and just want it for the silly story and cute protagonist, or you just want the 100% Orange Juice DLC that comes with it, then I'd say this game is just right for you. If you want a playable bullet hell game, there's a vast number of better alternatives than this.

Now I can't give a full review as I've only had about 7 hours into this game and my time with the game has been off and on for short periods of time. What I can tell you is that from the beginning, this isn't your average hunting game, but you know that right? You've already seen the clips from YouTubers and watched the videos here on Steam. So you know its a dinosaur hunting game, its in early alpha so theres bugs, and its a bare bones game. You got dinosaurs who act weird sometimes, although everyone is raving about how they look like what dinosaurs are supposed to look like (they've got feathers hurr durr). What I can tell you is that I've seen all of them, hunted them all (and been hunted by them, mostly this part) and its always an intense situation especially when you are alone. I'm a lone wolf so thats kind of what I do, but the game is about taking down the big buck of the land, the T-Rex. This is something I can only assume you'd need friends, lots of friends, and a lot of firepower to accomplish because T-Rex lives up to his reputation in this game. He can take a beating and still keep coming at you and only your buddies and your trusty .308 will help bring him/her down. As a loner though you don't have those luxuries, well you might have been lucky to stumble across a .308 and some ammo,  but I wouldn't suggest trying it alone unless you are certain you are a great shot. Also, like a proper hunting game, this game relies on target boxes that you must hit in order to maximize damage and bring down the beasts. And, much as you may have heard in science class all those years ago (or yesterday, whatever age you are), most of these creatures have a brain the size of a walnut, so your Call of Duty, 360, No scoping sniper skills won't get you anywhere in this game except in the digestive tract of a very appreciative carnivore. Instead you must rely on lung and heart shots, not saying a brain shot isn't possible (I've seen the videos of a guy take down a pack of raptors with only a bow and head shots, this guy was a pro... you probably aren't) so keep it safe, conserve your arrows/rounds and breathe and train your sights on the heart. Ok I got off track there, moving along. The dinosaur AI isn't the greatest here, before a recent patch (and I haven't confirmed its fix) but you would have moments where you were hauling♥♥♥♥♥across a field from a pack of raptors cause you didn't take your time with your shots and now you're out and along comes a might T-Rex to swoop in and save you like he did in Jurassic Park, right? Nope... they'd team up and chase you down together, probably resulting in a nice picnic between the two species as they discuss why your taste didn't live up to their expectations. Or, as I've observed, you can watch as a triceratops grazes on the grass when suddenly a T-Rex emerges and you finally get to see the epic battle you played out as a child with your toys, two titans clashing, who will win? Definitely not you, because the Rex would rather eat you in your 170lb boney frame than deal with the triceratops as it continues to eat in peace. Now, again, its alpha, there are bugs and they'll be fixed. But sometimes the AI gets it right and when it does, it adds soo much to the experience. For example, you can be travelling along, and you hear the roll of distant thunder, and you look out and see the clouds rolling in. It starts raining, gently at first then it picks up and the sounds of nature slightly wash out over the sounds of the pats of thousands of dropplets hitting the ground and lightening starts its dance across the sky (I don't mean to paint such a picture, but the atmosphere alone is worth the price. Watching a storm roll in while I was on the side of a volcanoe literally brought me to tears with its beauty, not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you) and all of a sudden you hear what sounds like monkeys chattering, only you know well that those aren't monkeys and its not background noise as they always, always make different sounds instead of repeating in a loop. Then you slowly crouch/walk your way up to high ground and you peer out into the forest and its hard to see because of the mixture of rain and darkness from the clouds and thats when you spot the first utahraptor. Then another and they slowly begin making their way up the hill in your direction. So panic quickly sets in as you only have a bow with a few arrows, so you ease back off the rock and keep your eyes in the direction you last saw them and thats when it happens... while the two were heading towards you while you were focusing on them, another two were coming up from the other side and started closing in a little faster. They screech and every single one of them zeros in for the kill and you never stood a chance. It could have just been my experience, it could be the way the game does it for everyone, but these moments get seared into your memory and give you a healthy appreciation that these things no longer exist. As for the big guys, triceratops is a bit of a wimp unless you corner him, then he will instantly kill you by trampling you. T-Rex, why not save the best for last? I've been killed a few times by them and its always a moment filled with heavy, heart pounding excitement. You absolutely can't win on your own (at least I never have), so when you see one, you immediately go prone and hope to god Dr. Alan Grant was right about his vision being based on movement. And as it turns out, while you back pedal slowly across the ground with the big creature closing in, you may just stand a chance as he isn't immediately attacking you but just smelling the area you were in. So you hold still for a few minutes, hoping he looses interest and that is when it happens. T-Rex adorns his troll face mask and immediately bites you in half, because he knew you were there the whole time. It may sound like I'm mocking this game, but I swear the bugs only get to you if you focus on them and let the deaths get you down. But if you take a moment to take in the atmosphere and the beautiful creatures that inhabit the island, you will realize that by the time the game gets flushed out (and they add the rest of the dinosaurs and weapons) that it was worth the price all along.

They essentially are the same concept, one person trying to escape a place while being subjected to the games of an omnicient being who hates you, except, without the cake that is. In short this game was truly a joy to play and I would reccomend it to anyone who i a fan of the puzzle genre of games.

RADical ROACH Review – Raymond KT
Summary: RADical ROACH is a fast paced shoot em’ up, set minutes after nuclear hell falls from the sky engulfing all but a few tough little bugs.
Well, finally you get to play as a bug. And no, I do not mean Battlefield 4. Radical Roach makes you play a..Roach, and this game is typical shoot-em-up - you fly from one side of the screen, to another, obliterating your enemies. The game itself reminded me a lot of Flying Hamster from PS Vita, just in a bit less-cutish version. Radical Roach seems filthy and ugly, just like The Bindings of Isaac. The game mechanics are so simply, that even your momma could play it, but the game itself is hard, challenging, and often frustrating, but that's the general idea behind the genre. I've played the game for good few hours on Desure, before it was put on Steam, so my review is based on that version of the game - the Steam version may have some additional polish.
I love when developers put a lot of humour in their games, even if it isn't a comedy game but simply, like Radical Roach, shoot-em-up game. What's that made me laugh? First of all thing - idea. Like, I don't think there are any other shmup game that allow you to play as cockroach. I'm not sure how many people noticed that mouse icon is a little cockroach as well. As for difficult settings, there are 3 to choose from: hard, hard and, of course, hard. Little things like that makes me to think better of this game. About gameplay, there isn't much to say about Radical Roach. It's typical shoot-em-up game, that is in my opinion a little too easy. Also, there are not many options to customise, such as volume of music, effects etc. You can't either skip cut-scenes, even if they aren't long, it's just somehow annoying to watch them over and over again, if you replay some levels. Get it if you are fan of shmups and you are looking for different experience.

Radical Roach feels like a Newgrounds free flash game. There’s not much depth to the game and it relies on being difficult. No power-ups, no score, no pausing, no recovery time between hits, no control re-map, no in-game sound volume adjustment. I feel like only the most hardcore horizontal shooter players would enjoy this. Perhaps that’s what the devs were going for, I’m not sure.
I got through the first two levels before giving up on the third one. It’s just a massive amount of enemies thrown at you for a certain period of time until the next level begins. I wouldn’t say it’s in bullet-hell territory though. There are no patters, etc. usually associated with those games.
One positive is that I did like the art style.
+60fps
+Neat art style
+Too difficult for the wrong reasons (also no difficulty adjustment)
+No power-ups
+No scoring
+No pausing
+No recovery time after being hit
+No remapping controls
+No sound settings in-game
+Can only use D-pad to move on 360 controller
Overall it’s a pretty barebones game with no elements to keep things fresh.

I have put in just shy of 20 hours playtime in the past two days and I cannot get enough!  The movement is so fluid and the combat so fast paced that it just pulls you in for one hell of a ride.  The sheer amount of content and complex game mechanics is very intimidating but do not worry about learning everything right off the bat.  Work on getting all the various types of movement down first and have fun jumping around and exploring the maps you end up on.  As you do that the combat skills will naturally fall into place without to much effort.  All the complex systems like mods and such will slowly begin to make more sense as you accumulate them.  The game does not really hold your hand when it comes to teaching you all but the basics (which is probably my only "mild" complaint) but I found a very experienced player on youtube named iFlynn who has a huge series of videos breaking down the all the various systems and mechanics for new players that is extremely helpful.
Overall, this is an outstanding free to play game that puts many Triple-A titles to shame.

This game countains what people probably expected of Spiral Knights, a fun game where you are rewarded for acquiring something new, and not thrown s*** in the face for using it, there is no complicated way of getting your equipment stronger, you just have to level it to then be able to equip mods that changes what your equipment has to offer, your character even acquires masteries when levels up the equipments, which unlocks some stuff alongside new possibilities of equipments.
Besides this item doesn't have a drop of equipments, sometimes enemies drops the recipes of the weapons they are using, and If you don't want to try dropping a recipe, you may browse the game market for recipes for weapons, warframes and other things. I don't really remember, but I guess I found some things that aren't offered as recipes there too that are bought with in-game money. The recipes you acquire, require items that are found on certain planets to be able to craft them, some planets offers a high number of certain item, while others offers scarce numbers of the item.
Not only that, but every planet you visit, have a lot of different missions, and each mission, has a different objective to achieve the goal, so you most likelly will have to change your way of cleaning up the stage, aswell as possibily checking for hidden loot. The planets also often have multiple paths, and sometimes may even lead to different planets which are filled of more missions, aswell as the levels from each mission increases the farther you go from the starting stage, but the increment is not fast, so you have enough time to pick up the gameplay.
And there's the best, you may even have a pet, or a sentinel, to aid you in combat! They even have their own levels and mods that you can equip on them.
Now, to the downsides.
During my gameplay, at least of around 7 or 8 planets, I've found only 3 types of enemies, the Grineers, the Corpus and the Infested, being that I'm not even counting the "Corrupted", since they are a golden version of the Grineers and/or Corpus, beside depending on the planet level appears new types of enemies to rise the challenge, playing stages over and over may make you tired of seeying the same enemies over and over.
The crafting system involves letting the game craft the item for real day time, beside you don't need to be online to progress on the items crafting, and can do multiple crafts at the same time, some crafts are quite unfair to do, like the ones to create new Warframes, I'll take Rhino warframe for example, beside having to find and crafting the 3 parts of it, each with their own recipes, and taking around 12 hours to be fully crafted, to create the warframe itself, needs 3 days to finish the crafting, that is quite insane, isn't? But at least is bearable.
There is a limit on how many weapons/warframes you can have, but It seems like the only way of increasing the limit, is through cash shop. Aswell as some warframes and items are only acquired that way, since I didn't found their recipes for sale, unless they are acquired from some other way I didn't found out.
I don't know If I'm paranoid, but everytime I play this game, I bump into bugs and glitches, either certain interfaces locking, misplaced text/animation, missing environment object, or even other issues. Hardly those issues were detrimental to the gameplay, but a good number of times I could take a good laugh out of that.
The archwing probably is the worst part, the control is slippery, and you most likelly will end up hitting something on your way, no, not something, everything in your way you will hit, and the way you are introduced to it, is in a mission where you have to flee while avoiding a giant ducking spaceship of turning your character into spacedust. The rush mission of it is the best part, since you'll end up hitting the wall often, aswell as being hit by everything in the way, since If you slow down to deal with the enemies, means you will fail the mission.
And the best part, is that the Archwing has It's own equipments, so If you enjoyed the gameplay of your character with the weapons It uses on ground, then forget it because you'll be getting a new set of weapons, alongside skills, which you will probably not know what each skill do when you enter in action.
And If you miss the Archwing during land missions, no worry, there are some stages where your character will use it when enters the water, that is, If you find out what planets allows you to enter water, since most of them makes you respawn upon contact, anyway, If you got inside the water, congratulations, now have fun trying to get out of water.
I'm enjoying so far the game, but the gameplay starts to wear out after some time, but that mostly happens when you play alone, so be sure to play with other people, or else you might not play this game for too long.

This game is brilliant. And I do mean absolutely brilliant.
It's not often a game comes along that both manages to be incredibly simple and yet so magnificently complex. And that's the true beauty of Interplanetary.
Despite being a strategy game, despite having tech trees and build units and economy etc. Interplanetary, threw virtue of an intuitive interface, tooltips that tell you exactly what you need to know, and combat that centres around a simple yet unique mechanic, manages to be a game anyone could pick up and within minutes understand everything they need to know in order to enjoy playing.
What is that central mechanic you might ask? Well to put it simply, gravity. Interplanetary is a game were you construct weapons, defences, and resource buildings in order to fling tiny little projectiles of mass destruction. During each turn you lock in your trajectories, cross your fingers, and watch as your planets death balls of destruction fly across the screen. "Did you guess the orbits properly? Will that planets gravity be enough to align the shot? What if the turn accelerates the missile too fast?" These questions and more will be ricocheting across your head as you cross your fingers and pray your little shots hit. And the ones coming towards you don't.
And that's just what's so wonderful about interplanetary. Even with such simplistic gameplay it will have you on the edge of your seat nervously waiting between each and every turn, completely absorbed in the interactions of these little planets and their annoying to predict orbits. It lands perfectly in that "easy to learn, hard to master" spot. And stands as a game I can recommend not only to strategy lovers, or space nuts, but to anyone looking to have a good time.
Seriously, if you think you might like this game, get it. You won't be disappointed.

I've always loved turn-based artillery action, and Interplanetary is a welcome addition to the genre. Less "Worms" and more "Scorched Earth" with some strategic building mixed in. Online play is where the game shines, although curiously online AI players are not yet supported.
I would like to see a few additions/changes made, if possible.
1) Persistent projectiles: Currently, if projectiles miss their targets, they explode before the next round starts. It would be nice if they remained until they hit something. This would add some much needed chaos and open up the possibility of new strategy elements (flood the solar system with cheap railgun slugs and hope for the best!).
2) Balance for orbit positions: Some may disagree, but the players on the outer orbits are definitely at an advantage. Players on the inner orbits are guaranteed to get chewed up first, and the outer rim planets are free to build up and attain superweapons. Perhaps the method of balancing this would be my third suggestion...
3) Planet speed: It seems that all of the planets move at the same speed, but the outer ones should move slower. This would make them easier to hit, perhaps?
The developer seems to be actively updating the game, so hopefully they can consider these suggestions. All in all though, an amazing game! I highly recommend it!

This game has a great concept, interacting with orbits and gravity to wage interplanetary war, but could use better execution.
Unfortunately I found the interface not to my liking.
- The building placement interface was decent, but there is no obvious way to change your plans if you accidentally click.
- Shifting angle and perspective of the universe works well most of the time, but it is too easy to end up with what you want to see off screen on a smaller monitor resolution.
- Aiming was too "jumpy". I really wish I could specify my aim using a text box for angle degrees as opposed to moving the mouse.
- The event notifications could be handled better, particularly if there are multiple of the same,
- I wish the event notifications said which of your buildings were destroyed instead of just showing where they were.
If the UI was more friendly I would enjoy this game a LOT more and probably change my recommendation.

This is a good game with quite a lot of potential, but several things annoy me to the point where I've stopped playing:
1: THE GAME HAS A HUGE MEMORY LEAK.
Now I don't normally type in all caps, but I haven't been able to finish a game yet due to the memory leak growing to eventually 3 gigs+ and causing all sorts of bad behavior, then crashing.  I'd expect this in a pre-alpha, but for $15?  Really?  I feel like a Kickstarter idiot lately as the amount of half-baked not ready for release games lately is amazing.
You know it's about to crash when the interface starts glitching.  But then the save function usually doesn't work.  I guess I could save religiously every ten turns or so, but when playing vs other players?  "sorry - have to save" - Give me a few minutes and re-join...
2: The cheating AI aside, the interface is atrocious.  You want to be able to plan ahead, but there is no overlay to see your positions on your planet from a distance ( ie - red dots as it rotates), so you are never sure if your planet will rotate enough to get a shot off the next turn.  Also, when you are going to take damage, you don't SEE it hit.  Most of the fun in these types of games is seeing the shot and what it damages in real time.  You might as well skip the animation in this one - fire, come back, zoom into your planet to see what was hit.
In a typical artillery type of game, you can see your shots, where they flew, and how to adjust to hit the enemy.
To add insult to injury, the cities are the most hidden/first to be made not visible items???  And if the enemy has enough stealth, you simply forget their location?  You can't even remember what you saw last turn?
3: Playing with the AI is useless unless you turtle for 40 turns or just build 10-20 ( not joking ) railguns and idiot-spam them.
PVP:
Now, it is good playing hotseat, which is fun, but the time required to do so is hugely prohibitive.  The issue is that playing versus humans nets a 3-4 hour stalemate due to the only way to really do damage are superweapons.  If they make a grid of defenses over each city, and start building some stealth, you're going to waste the next few hours doing nothing. (ie - turn 40+)  Your railguns are not aimable, your missiles can't get through the kinetic defenses ( can't aim them unless you have a visual target), and lasers are the only thing that can consistently hit cities.  Until they get laser shielding.  Maybe you get lucky and take out one city with railgun spamming, but it takes all five dead to win.  You can take out a few things, but the cities are the only thing that matters.  Once those have 2-3 defenses on top of them, you're into the endgame:
A: lob an asteroid and hope it hits something useful and critical/not fixable as it's random.
B: Fire your one super laser and take out a single building or damage part of a city.
C: wish the interface would stop forcing you to do your research queue when all you want to do is fire and get on to the next round.
As it is, my son and I have played for 4 hours and still not finished a game before it crashed one of our two systems.
Two copies, $30 wasted.  I should have just bought a game for my console instead.

After playing Skyrim for countless hours (maybe over 200?) on a console, I was well acquainted with some of the lore of the Elder Scrolls series. I highly enjoyed skyrim but felt like some game mechanics were poorly explained and I had to stumble in the dark for many hours before I learned the tricks to playing. Examples are not knowing how to recharge enchanted items, not knowing what to spend perks on,  and even struggling with potion making.
Seeing this game on steam and thinking it looked quite similar but with different enemies, I tought I would give it a try since all of the dlc was included anyway. Oblivion shows its age from the begining, but it is quite fun to play if you know what you are doing. Character building seems to be a deeper and more engaging process here than in Skyrim, and there are more spells. The shivering isles expansion was just gorgeous and a blast to explore, with a great story. However, the vanilla map seems too sparse. You can run for several minutes in one direction and still find nothing, or useless abandoned mines with virtually nothing in them. Lockpicking is harder in Oblivion than it is in Skyrim, and your success with it has almost nothing to do with your level in that skill. In fact, speechcraft and security skills seem relatively useless to me, which is disapointing because I was primarily playing as thief/bard. There are many ways to circumvent the issue of low skill. Some skills take way too long to level up like mercantile and restoration, which are very important. Many of the good spells are still out of my reach to cast and I am at level 50 on most magic related skills. Yeah...
There are some things to be disappointed by, but the good news is I have thoroughly enjoyed building my character even more so than in Skyrim (where I was a mixture of everything and a master at nothing). The oblivion gates are exciting at first but get drab after the 5th or 6th one. They also suck all of your potions, enchanted items, arrows, etc.. down the drain from overuse. Towns are decent in size and there are guild halls in most of them where you can join. There are great perks to being in the guilds. The combat is kinda nice but the animations SUCK. They are so stiff looking and unrealistic. Also, after a while combat just feels like a chore. This problem coupled with the drabness of the environment and lack of variation, kills the game a little bit :( I'm sorry but charging into a cave or ruin that looks exactly like all the others with almost exactly the same enemies just sucks the life out of you. After striking 100 hours I don't know how much longer I will play. I feel as though I have seen most of what the game has to offer and I haven't even completed the main questline. Don't get me wrong, this is a great roleplaying game (some would disagree), but the action is lacking.
I suppose since I didn't play this before Skyrim, that the nostalgia factor really doesn't do it for me. Buy it, it's fairly cheap. It's probably my favorite of the two ES games Ive played, but age does not do it a favor. Also mod the character faces with Character Overhaul mod, please for the love of Tamriel! They are god awful ugly in the vanilla version.

This is the first Moto GP game I've bought for a while, I've had most of the early games 07 being my favourite with Moto GP 4 on PS2 my second favourite.
The newest one I had previously was Moto GP 10 on the 360 which was way too arcady and required less skill to play properly than previous games so I lost interest in the series.
As this game was on offer for £2.24 I thought I would give it a go.  Straight away I set everything to realistic and difficulty on max removing racing lines etc.  I started a Moto 3 career as myself and with the difficulty being so high the rewind button is a definate help as you won't get back in touch with riders once you fall off.  Limiting it to 6 rewinds in fair, I usually do 25% race distance so have the option of one per lap.
So far 10 ten races into my first season I've had a 5th place best finish, nobody lets you win which I like.   Setting the bike up takes a bit of thought, the technical adviser will undo good settings if you use him too much so best to sort it yourself and save the data as it will get altered when you come to the next session sometimes.
I like the way you can switch teams mid season and set targets of certain riders to beat so even if you are not battling for the win it's worth playing.  You can also adjust traction control setting while riding which is handy as conditions sometimes change during the race.

That said I've not played a racing game for 2 years so am re learning the tracks as I go so maybe my qualifying will improve next season and I'm just picking the best lines from following in the races.

Moto GP 4 - PS2
Moto GP 06 - Xbox 360
Moto GP 3 - PS2
Moto GP - Xbox

My review from Larian forums (there are spoilers below):
To start with the positive, this game very nearly is a masterpiece that’s chiefly let down by a rushed Act 3, weak characterisations and an over ambitious agenda that could have benefited from shedding some of its larger promises that it obviously couldn’t uniformly deliver in the time it was given.
The visuals are easily the best I’ve seen in any game. And here I don’t mean the technical bells and whistles, which are no doubt excellent in themselves, but specifically the art direction. The storytelling, hugely improved over D:OS 1, can’t live up to the imagination that went into the environments, or the creature design. Take the Harbinger of Doom that stops on occasion to neurotically chew on its own arm – this is a vividly wretched creation that sticks out in memory. And the kraken is, I think, the most original, and convincingly warped invention since Giger’s mind-bending human-machine hybrids – it definitely needed more show time than it was given.
There’s an expanse of thousands of candles the quietly opens up in a demon’s lair that was so simple, evocative and well-played that it trumped the entire narrative efforts of Act 3 combined. The timing of the lashes of rain during what is, for me anyway, the game’s second best battle – The Drillworm and Alexander – makes for some great visual drama.
I could go on about the visuals – but long story short, the artists are doing their job, and doing it better than most.
Narrative-wise, the game starts strong, and is infinitely improved over the goofery and cartoonishness that made D:OS 1’s story seem so slight and forgettable. But the foundation starts to tremble somewhere during Act 2 – and by Act 3, it has completely lost the plot, almost as though the writers suffered some kind of artistic crisis and couldn’t pull it all together at the last minute.
Characters like Dallis, Alexander and the mysterious ‘Cloaked Figure’ disappear for massive stretches, only to show up so abruptly that they might be characters from another game. Somehow, Braccus Rex is unmasked as the main antagonist during the daftly unbalanced final battle. Didn’t he die in the first game? Never mind: I don’t want to know the hokum that’s shoehorned in to make this plot twist viable. He’s fighting alongside another character who’s also had no development (read: appears as a relatable person, with lines of dialogue) whatsoever throughout the game. I’m talking, here, about Lucian the Something, who I think had a few waypoint statues made in his honour, and was mentioned fleetingly in dialogues here and there.
Because these characters scarcely appear in the scenarios leading to the climax, there’s no investment on the part of the player. No big payoff in watching them live or die through what follows.
The weak characterisation is problematic across the board, however. In a story full of largely well-written, if underdeveloped, female characters, all of the males, bar Ifan, get the short end of the narrative stick, and end up snarling lines like the zingers our man Braccus flings at Lucian – ‘you babbling buffoon!’. It schlocky stuff, I’m afraid, and there’s a lot of it.
There’s no Jon Irenicus or Master Mirror from The Witcher 3 that the game badly needs to give it some edge in the villain department.
Act 1 is, for me, the strongest part of the game, with a sturdy if somewhat bloated Act 2 following close behind. Ultimately it’s the slapdash Act 3 that lets the game down the most. Everything about it seems hurried. There are technical slowdowns witnessed nowhere else in the game that tell a story of developers who didn’t have enough time to optimise code. There are paintings that actually have the name ‘placeholder’.
There’s a passable fantasy city, full of a couple of named merchants and dozens upon dozens of anonymous ‘cizilian this’ and ‘paladin that’ types. The village areas of Driftwood and Fort Joy had more personality and life. They were more organic, more lived in – more populated with people than walking placeholders. The quests in Arx are maddeningly designed, culminating in a pipe puzzle that makes you wonder what on earth the designers were smoking at this point.
The game becomes the equivalent of that really great, nearly five star movie that gets four stars because it was ‘30min too long’. Except here that 30min is exploded tenfold into hours upon hours of messy, badly designed Act 3 quests that pale in comparison to the quests that preceded them. I would have been happy if they’d just ditched Arx completely, took its best elements and turned them into an epic final few hours that consisted of 10% of the time you otherwise have to waste in Arx.
The best battles in the game are the ones where randomness was allowed to create its own drama. The highlight for me is still the brilliant Blackpits oil field battle with the slugs. It just so happens to be the best fight I’ve ever played in a game. Simply genius design, full of deviously unexpected moments. The rest of the game’s battles are unfortunately the same thing over and over. The same number of enemies, the same enemy types reskinned to look like monsters but that are really just variations of the standard classes you’ll encounter throughout the rest of the game.
If only they’d thought of more enemies like the revenants that respawn in cursed fire (although some of these, with infinite cursed arrows, are clearly broken). Now that’s what adds tactics to the game, not inflated HP and armour bars.
The boring tactician mode could really benefit from the few more randomised encounters seen elsewhere but are sadly limited in number.
Level progression also becomes a problem, when nothing ever really changes, bar the health bars. The same set of skills used in Act 1 will still be used in Act 3, alongside ridiculously overpowered ‘source skills’ that really should just belong to a few boss type enemies and not be available to the player. The problem is that the base skills don’t evolve beyond damage boosts and the like, so very little seems to change, beyond the length of time it takes to end a fight.
The environmental eruptions of poison, ice, fire and so on, once one of the great innovations of the game, degenerate later on into cursed variations (inevitably cursed fire) that are immune to the more interesting clean ups and mutations available to their earthly counterparts. It’s either tornado or bless, which is dull and limited and the very opposite of what this mechanic offered in D:OS 1.
All of that being said, it still manages to be a fantastic game. The visual artwork, in particular, is exceptional. The story, though flawed, is far better than that of most other games, and the writing, though occasionally hockey, is nonetheless solid enough that it never completely embarrasses itself. The actors appear to enjoy delivering their lines, at least in Act 1, where the writing affords the characters some personality and variety. But by Act 3, it sounds like even the voice actors gave up and are just going through the motions.
Thanks for the entertainment anyway, Larian. It was well worth taking a trip around this remarkable, flawed, inventive creation. And I’ll be glad of long break from it all as well!! Best of luck with your future projects. Cheers.

Were you as disappointed as I was by Civ 5? Because this is what that game could have been. With an oddly satisfying scifi/fantasy setting, this is the first TBS since Civ 4 that recreates that "one more turn" craving. Each faction plays differently enough as to be it's own expansion pack, and the game mechanics are different enough to be a change of pace, but still firmly grounded in normal Turn-Based Strategy fare. You'll notice it bears a striking resemblance to Endless Space but (as someone who couldn't stand that game for more than 10 turns at a time) it's vastly different. Not even mentioning the quest/hero system that hearkens back to Warcraft III. I highly recommend this game for any fan of turn based strategy, and anyone turned off by what Firaxis did with a hex-based map.
The civilizations feel unique. Many of the basic features are new and refreshing. I've enjoyed this much more than I did Civ BE.
Probably one of the best 4X games I have ever played. Looking forward to many more hours playing with each faction.

Love this. Its a game that's simple to learn, but you probably never master. I opened my first game and it gave me a tutorial that unlike so many game tutorials these days didn't leave me either constantly checking back (the UI is so simple that I read the tutorial (all 7 screens of it, most of which were images showing what you're looking for, which shows you how simple it is)) or getting to a point where something new is developed or unlocked but I have no idea how to use it.
But despite the fact that I learned the game in about 10 minutes, the actual playing is a great challenge. You want to hit a target? Ok, so you go to targeting, pick your nice laser (a relatively late unlock but simplest to target) out of your weapons... but your laser is on the wrong side of the planet. So you switch to your railguns. Its on the wrong side too, but that doesn't matter. You get a nice red line that shows the path your projectile will take through the gravity wells of the planets and star (though not the odd little asteroids that might randomly jig it mid flight) and line it up on the planet. You lock on and proceed to resolve the turn. Your projectile flies off and misses the planet by just enough to swing around it and career into the star because you didn't factor in the movements of all those planets you slingshotted around and the movement of the target itself. My first few shots missed by half a solar system as I got use to it. Plus, its a very different animal targeting a planet if your projectile is chasing the target compared to if the planet and projectile are coming together head on (for me, the chase shots are much harder as the projectile takes longer to catch the planet so there's more time for error).
All in all a great romp, and a step in the direction of something I've wanted to see for a long time (space combat between fleets using the actual physics of a solar system where everything is orbiting the star rather than the games like Star Trek Armada or Sins of a Solar Empire (both of which I love) where you just fly in a straight line toward where you want to go).

This game is the love child of Worms and the tabletop game Battleship ... but in space!! ><
It is simply awesome ... play it, you won't regret it.
In more detail, 3 pro's and 3 con's for balance:
Pro's:
1) it has the addictive charm of both the above mentioned games; as it utilizes the artillery style of worms with the damage style of Battleship. To win you have to eliminate your opponents cities, and in a few multiplayer games I've had opponents yelling ''i sunk your battleship'' ... which continues to make me smile.
2) it is very simple to pick up, as the general mechanics and the buildings should make sense to you very quickly, and games are also relatively quick, so it's great for short bursts of fun - though mastering the game is not easy. There is also no story or general context, or diplomacy, other than to 'sink' those cities. That sounds bad but it is not, it is refreshing and the game excels at providing focused strategic fun.
3) it is satisfying - hitting an opponent on a near impossible shot, or having your planet just escape a major hit ... it just feels good.
Con's:
1) not much information feedback from the game. it would be nice to know how much damage I did, or how many shots got through, or, well, anything really ... there is also no information at the end of the game either. I guess I could just be spoilt by other games, as this does not detract from the enjoyment or mechanics. However, even though I can understand that limited information is best at the end of each turn (that the intelligence system should give you what you need), there could be something at the very end (even a simplistic score based on damage or population or something).
2) a bit buggy, had a few crashes here and there and the AI takes a while to make a turn.
3) no quick save feature (as far as I can tell). Given the occasional crashes it is useful to save after each turn, which means going into the menu each time and selecting a save ... not a hassle you say? It gets really annoying after a while.
Overall: just buy it and love it. My hopes are this game will continue to get developed, as I would love to see a few extra buildings, a bigger tech tree and all new features. It is addictive fun :)
p.s: though the game is best played with other people, the AI seems fine to me. I've only played on easy and normal but the AI seems to generally hit well enough and miss well enough on both of those settings ... the AI is not obviously overpowered or underpowered to me, though they don't really use telescopes to spy on the player much.
