I am a huge fan of racing games and rarely are there ever good ones, let alone motorcycle ones. I'm certainly glad I purchased this game (on sale may I add)! I've also rode a motorcycle so you can count on me being judgemental on this one.
None the less great game. The user interface is easy to use with many options available. Options to change resolution can be configured before the game boots. There is a launch menu that appears with different settings. Changing controller buttons is easy and the game is very controller friendly. Some of the game mode options are instant race, grand prix, championship, career (which I'm really enjoying at the moment), multiplayer and YES!!! SPLIT SCREEN!!! <---- :) .... seriously, need more games like this on steam.
is pretty immaculate on this one. Need for Speed Shift 2 was one of my favorite racing games until I stumbled upon this. Shift gives a challenge, I feel this one does too. The AI will give you a challenge certainly when you first start, but getting a hold of the gameplay/controls  will eventually put you up front (unless you make a mistake... in which they added a feature to rewind. I've used this feature a few times watching me demolish a race because I cut a few people off). Added features are the options to have assisted steering, traction control and all that hooplah but I really like the feature where you tuck your rider into the bike. With the press of the Y button on the x-box controller, the rider tucks in obviously (too much work? Just turn it off in options and make it automatic). When taking a turn though this tiny modification can make your turn ever so smoother, and definitely a more enjoyable experience. Ever seen the guys out there racing put their knee to the ground? Well having a first person view (and even option to add a helmet HUD) delivers that experience. The friciton system also feels accurate when taking turns.  I like the controls, I like the steering, I like doing wheelees, I like being able to do stoppies, and I like to be able to drive in reverse backwards on the track and collide with other players to watch the physics system. The crash effects are pretty neat on this one, especially when you don't break enough and send another rider flying. Of course this isn't ideall; it is fun to watch the reply. All in all, the racing aspect is very apparent. My only complaint is touching the joystick ever so slightly sometimes makes the bike look like it "jerks", as in it's sort of quick or choppy to move a bike like that.
The
of course are as nice as they are shown. 1980X1080 is an option with this game. The bikes look appealing and the riders are as good as they get. I'd like however a little more ability for customization when it comes to the bike or the racing suit. I'm not sure if it's only my computer (and I haven't done my research on this yet ... may edit later) but I'm having issues with cut scenes. The screen plays the scene but sometimes it does a bunch of pixelation stuff then goes back to normal. This is NOT an issue while playing the game though. I have yet to have a problem with the gameplay aspect. Side note on first person view, there are stickers on your windshield. Personally I'd like the choice to have them off. It bugs me! Seeing riders bump into one another and then react is quite neat as well. Changing gears and seeing the clutch being pulled is also a mentionable feature for motogp 13.
... well the sound is good because usually I keep my music on while I play games. However I find that listening to the motor while playing is helpful at least to me. In this game you have to be quite attentive or get ready to wipe out. Although the sound is decent, that's all it is. I think the sounds could have been a lot more authentic (especially from the motorcycles).
I would have to highly recommend this game to anyone and would say it is a great addition to a steam library.
***I would recommend for future motogp games perhaps add a stunt bike section? I know it's not quite GP but it would add an extra depth and a few more challenges to the game. Not the mention the handling of stunt bikes would be different***. Also... for goodness sakes please make the replay interface better. Also, adding some more tracks for local co-op would be greatly appreciated!

Crusader Kings II is probably one of the greatest strategy games I ever played. While the many features this game offers may seem overwhelming at first one quickly gets the basics that are enough to play. And after that, the player slowly learns more and more. Even after over 70 hours I still consider myself a noob and have a lot to learn and many features to fully understand. But this is in my opinion one of the things that make this game so charming.
What's also great is how diverse different campaigns can be because of different random events and the fact that there is no predertemined goal. Whether you plan to convert the whole world to your religion, control the biggest empire in history or just live a happy life with a big loving dynasty, the possibilities are endless.
Still there are two things I want to criticize: First of all, as mentioned, getting into the game can be hard at first and one might lose interest quickly. However, once you get basics you have access to one of the greatest strategy games with RPG elements that there is.
Second is Paradox's DLC policy. This isn't just a problem with CKII but also with other Paradox games. If you want to own all DLC packs that there are you have to pay multiple hundred bucks, even on sale. My advice: Get the game and some DLC on sale (google will help you find out which DLC are the best) and skip stuff like the content packs entirely.
Once you get into this game, there's no getting out...

Hard to fairly review an early access game.  As it stands, the game needs more.  And not more dinosaurs, it needs more layers of strategy, more training up of the hunter you play, etc.  If it doesn't gain more depth, I'd give it a bad review because the replay value isn't there like the standard "theHunter" game.
But I'm not sure why some people are calling for more dinosaurs.  It's a hunting game, not a shoot-the-fish-in-the-barrel game.  And when one of the dinosaurs starts hunting YOU, you'll be more than a little grateful for the low population count.
The concept of a hunting game where sometimes the prey hunts you in a semi-realistic setting (doesn't the most recent research indicate that dinosaurs had feathers?) is a wonderful concept.  This game oozes potential through every pore, and nothing about the game's development indicates to me the development is headed in the wrong direction.  That's reason enough for a positive rating for me.

Awesomenauts is fun casual take on the MOBA scene. It is a wacky but secretly complex at the same time. Matches are around 20 minutes long at most and theres over 2 dozen unique characters to play as. The game is easy to pick up and start playing but there's still lots to learn about each character and how to use them to optimal potential. The game supports gamepads but its suggested you stick with mouse and keyboard as it is easier to aim attacks that way.
My only complaints are the lack of more supports like VOltarr who turn the tide of battle for whichever team they are playing on. It is also annoying how quickly you will move up in rank in just a few games and suddenly be playing against prestiged pros who will completely cream you and your team. I also don't love that you have to pay extra to unlock any new characters but at the same time i only paid 3 dollars for the game when it was on sale and currently it is at a dollar so i guess it's fair.
Overall Awesomenauts is definitely worth checking out and playing occasionally with buds.

Fun, easy to learn MOBA. Better community than that of Dota 2 or League, though there are some undesirable people. With a smaller cast of 'Nauts (Champions/Heroes), it's much easier to get into and learn the strategies. Each 'Naut has their own 2 abilities, with 6 upgrades that you can choose 3 of. All 'Naut abilities are unique, except for the bottom row, which features increased health, regen, instant cash and other nice abilities. Real talk. This plays like Civ. You start with nothing, you end up with spaceships. Not literally, but you know what I mean. But it flips the script because you don't pick a nation with minor benefits, you pick an entire race that is completely different from the others. And these races tend to lean towards a certain playstyle, so you can choose the one you that suits how you want to play for that game.
As an example, there is a market in the game where, with the right research, you can buy the resources you don't have for that next city improvement. One of the races controls this market, and gets a cut of all the sales that go through it, and they can even ban you from it as a diplomatic tool.
The even crazier thing is you can just mix and match parts of races you like and make your own, because why not? And this gameg handles combat very interestingly. Each race has its own set of 3 units that you keep for the entire game after you research them, but you keep them upgraded with new items and you can have multiple versions ready at any time. Got a type that you made three hours ago that suck but can be pumped out in a turn? Keep it. Then make a new version that has a sword that can kill that weaker guy in one hit. Anything is possible.
Its a good game, its got a lot of concepts that I haven't even touched on here, but for a short list:
Its a great game. Especially half off. Just buy it.

It's an amazing fantasy 4X with fantastic visuals and LOTS of ways to play. The tutorial only explains the basics, though, and there's a lot of complexity that it doesn't go into, so play your first game on the lowest difficulty as a learning game.

Amongst the many 4x fantasy strategy games, this is the one that for me mostly re-creates Masters of Magic, even though there is no magic. The kind of troop management, and the variety of troops, villages, natives and vastness of the world is commendable.
These people seem to like this "endless" setting, having done a 4x fantasy, a 4x sci-fi and even a sci-fi dungeon crawler. Next i'm expecting a visual novel just to round up the genres. XD
Seriously, though. The only problem that i find in this game is that it seems very forgiving. I mean i have a race  that by design is limited to >A SINGLE CITY< which i took just to see how screwed i could get in a single playthrough, yet i'm in the third era (out of 4) an i yet have to be obliterated into oblivion. And i only have the 4 troops (plus 3 militia) that you are allowed to keep in the city (plus a few roaming ones). And yes, it's the first time i'm playing this game.
So... yes, a tad too easy. But if you can forgive this thing the game itself is strangely enough full of lore to explore and full of strange sights, resources and friends to meet. It even has (weirdly enough for a 4x title) a quest system that allows you to pacifically annex neutral cities. It's weird but i dig it.

I love this game and has been playing it for 100+ hours.
I would like to recommend this game to those that love good RPG Maker games with an excellent storyline.
You can play this game as a Warrior, Paladin or Summoner. In this game the Summoner is the most interesting character which also enables you to unlock a lot more achievements. The combat mechanics is interesting as you play with different form of elemental damages (fire, water, air, earth)  which are resisted by different degrees by different monsters. You also alternate between real and dream worlds.
Unlike most other RPGs, you do not gain skill points as you gain more experiences and levels. You need to explore every nook and cranny to look for skill upgrade points. You also need to talk to every character and do every quests to get skill upgrade and unlock points as well as better gears. As a summoner, you can also unlock different creatures to summon through various quests as well.
There is also an excellent crafting mechanism in this game as well. The best armors in this game, called Relic Armors cannot be bought or received as drops from monsters. They need to be crafted using various crafting items, as well as some very difficult to get monsters drop. Furthermore you need to keep your very first set of armor for all 4 characters as well, because you need to use them to craft Relic armors at the very end.
You can buy better weapons from differnet vendors in this game, but the very best weapons, called Ultimate Weapons can only be receive through quests too. Hence this elevate the importance of doing all quests.
To get all achievements, you will need to play this game twice, and hence giving it more replay value. This is because there is a New Journey+ mode which can only be unlocked when you finished the game. Furthermore there are quest that are started during your first game which can only be completed during the New Journey+ as well. So the achievements associated with these quests can only be received if you play the game twice.
The second time you play this game, you get a lot of benefits, including new skill sets which can only be unlocked in New Journey+ You can also get better creatures to summon and start of with certain crafting recipes which are not present in the first game. I have started on my New Journey+ and this game is still sustaining my interests even though I am playing it a second time.
This is a great game. The only shortcoming I can think of is that the graphics are OK, but not top-notched. However, considering that I got the game on sale at about $10, this game is defintely worth its weight in gold, in terms of the enjoyment value and the time played.

I really tried to like this game, but I've given up on it.
Battles are pretty unavoidable and very monotonous (I am no stranger to RPGs, but with only 2 kinds of enemies per map, this gets old).  Leveling up also doesn't seem to do much for your character except increase HP.
Maps are very mazelike and there will be a LOT of backtracking (especially since there is no map).  They can also be hard to maneuver around (a stick in the road that I can't walk over or around? yeah ok, guess I'll go back and look for another way to get over there -.-; ).

Here's what I liked:
-Great art direction
-Good music and sound
-The turn-based combat was fun and streamlined
Here's what I didn't like:
-Battles could get repetitive
-The crafting system isn't very well-explained and the skill tree doesn't let you look ahead to plan
-Some design pitfalls like making some objects impassible even though it's not clear why + invisible walls
-Characters are flat, with attempts at nuanced backgrounds but...
-the writing is all over the place, and it felt like it was written by somebody very young.
That being said, if this game was the result of somebody's first effort or that of somebody young, this is great work.
I would recommend it for those who are interested in game design, as a good case study, but only if deeply discounted

If you know that Whisper of a Rose was made by one person, it's a remarkable achievement. You can't expect triple A quality here, but what you will find is a love-letter to RPGs of the old days.
The Good:
- Graphics are top notch and have a lot of personality

- Several music tracks
- The world with interesting lore
The Bad
- The story means well but is a bit messy. All over the place at times. Could've used a bit more focus.
- The dialogues are of average quality. It's really hard to write compelling dialogue. So, with that in mind, the game still holds up pretty well.
- Some strange bugs like selecting "fast" for battle speed makes the battles slower and selecting "slow" makes the battles faster (try it!) or being able to walk on place where you shouldn't be able to walk. (even on the final beach this happens).
Overall I would recommend this game to players who really like 16-bit RPGs. This is not Final Fantasy VI quality, but there is enough to like here. Give it a try with an open mind!

*Take the time to develop a claim on some else's title, try to enforce that claim throught war.  (Good luck with that one.  lol)
*Try to be a good religious servant and get granted titles through wars on heathens.  (Good luck with that too. lol)

I have played and enjoyed a bit of The WItcher: WIld Hunt, but the combat in that game was not to my liking. I also put some time into the most recent Fallout game, but the progression and story never interested me enough to keep playing on a regular basis. At the time writing this I've played Divinity Original Sin II for just over ten hours, and I think I finally understand the allure of RPGs. I am playing with a friend as an assasin and a ranger, both with the Lone Wolf perk, and I am throughly enjoying every aspect of this game. The quest system is brilliant. Hardly anything is handed to the player, but I have never felt stuck. The impeccably well written story and dialogue have been enough to nudge me in the right direction. Graphically this game is no anomaly, and my laptop equipped with a Gtx 1060 6gb, an i7 (not sure of the model number), and 16gb of ram is able to easily push 60 frames on high settings. The audio is superb. Birds and crickets chirp while you progress through forests and marshes, waves gently roll against the sand when you're near a beach, drops of water echo through caves, all adding up to a thoroughly interesting atmosphere. The enchanting soundtrack is also worth mentioning, and all of the dialogue is voice acted. I have actually listened to what the NPCs have to say, which I don't often feel the need to do in other titles. Combat is strategic and challenging with the "Classic" difficulty selected, but never overwhelming. My partner and I do primarily physical damage, limiting our creativitiy in combat to positioning and buffing eachother strategically rather than combining spells, but in one example of a fight our enemies created a pool of oil at my feet, set it on fire, and then doused the flames with a summoned rain storm to creat a cloud of blinding fog. These combos keep the combat fresh and exciting, with even the easiest of encounters providing opportunities for creativity. I might look up a build guide if I ever feel the need to bump up the difficulty, but at the default setting almost any build seems viable (at least in the first act of the game). Keep in mind that, although my friend and I chose to adventure alone, you can have up to four unique members in your party. If you prefer to talk your way out of conflict, the talent Pet Pal allows you to converse with the wildlife you encounter. Five hours into the game I grabbed this talent, and it got me out of some serious trouble. I picked up Divinity Original Sin II during the winter sale for $40 and found a game with more depth than any "full price" AAA title I've played. This game is worth every penny, and there's something in it for everyone. (Especially if you play with friends.)

Love this game!  I keep thinking "I haven't liked a motorcycle game this much since Superbike 2000".  I just realized the two games had the same developer.  I'm sure there are a lot of different people at the company now, but still, it seems like there's some similar DNA between the games.
I don't really understand some of people's  negativity towards this game.  I guess maybe it doesn't feel simmy enough for the sim enthusiasts, and not arcadey enough for the GRID and MX vs ATV crowd.  I, however, love the balance.  The menus are beautiful, lots of good multimedia content that gives it more life, lots of game modes, love the Moto2 and Moto3 options because MotoGP is pretty intense for a starter.  Great control/realism options (I like joint-braking and auto-tucking because I don't need THAT level of simulation).  I think the graphics are great personally.  The player models are particularly good I think, and the tracks have a lot of spectators and a good lively feel to them, although they don't quite have that GRID polish and detail, but I don't really care for that look.  This game is clean to look at and not cluttered.
People have complained about the controls being unrealistic, but I don't see what the problem is.  I loved MotoGP 07 which actually felt a little too arcade-like to me, but I like this game much more now that I've tried it.  The camera is more stable and improves gameplay, and I like the way the bike responds to over-throttling it.  High-sides and low sides seem to occur reasonably, and if it were any harder or sim-like, it would be a pain to play (using a controller with joysticks will never perfectly reproduce the feel of a real motorcycle and people need to accept that.  So why not make a game reasonably PLAYABLE?  I think this game is, yet isn't a silly arcade game either).
The wreck physics are a litte silly though.  You can bump into the back of people and flail around over the handlebars and easily recover.  It's easy to maliciously wreck other people too.  But reasonably trying to race among a large pack isn't impossibly difficult.  But it's a challenge.  I think the wet conditions LOOK nice in this game, but they don't seem to affect control very much at all, so that seems a little unrealistic.
I tried MotoGP 14 first and my video card struggled, and it seemed glitchy as hell.  I actually prefer the cleaner look of MotoGP 13 anyway.
I think Milestone did a admirable job with this game and I'm happy with my purchase.

This game... This game is an absolute masterpiece in the rpg series. While I do believe that Morrowind is the best Elder Scrolls game, my heart still goes out to Oblivion. It was the first game I had played in the Elder Scrolls series, and after Skyrim, I wished it was the only one I played. Well, I atleast wish I didn't play Skyrim, since Morrowind exists too. But, Oblivion has an amazing story that revolves around your world's other-worldly neighbors, the Daedra, as they invade Tamriel in hopes of destroying it for their ruler, Mehrunes Dagon. Your character (whose background and race are entirely up to your imagination) is put in charge of stopping this invasion by finding the late Emperor's last son. You'll go on an adventure like you've never seen before in Cyrodiil. Make this game one of your Must-Plays, and close shut the Jaws of Oblivion.

Going back to Oblivion was Interesting to say the least.  I forgot most things about it until playing those aspects.  Except for a vague recollection,I even forgot the dungeon I used to farm skills with; Doznot (or something) on the west side of the Imperial City.   Sometimes coming back to a game you feel a warm recollection because you either understand and empathize with the main character or the computer is responsive to whom you have made the character to be.  With this game, it treats you exactly the same no matter who you are.   You can make choices in conversation that will make people mad at you but there is no impetus or reward to do so past just trying to stir things up.  Then they look at you all spooky eyed straight like everyone has got♥♥♥♥♥♥face.

There are a lot of fun quests to do.  There are some annoying quests like 'Tears of the Savior'.  Alchemy isn't as easy as it is in Skyrim; there are no recorded recipes; get out a pad and paper and write down combinations that work unless you like to search your entire inventory each time.  Leveling is quite intersting and, by that I mean fun but kind of messed up.  You never want to use a standard character because primary skills level you up (and almost everything opposing you levels with you).   Attributes will not significantly rise unless you use skills that are directly related to them.  Consequently, the most efficient way to play is to manage your levelling process.  You will find yourself jumping off roofs or with a shield holding block for like half an hour against a rodent that just won't quit just to level your speed and endurance respectively.  My advice?  Don't do it.  Life is too short to me sitting for half an hour vegging at a screen holding the right mouse button.  Mod that s!@# out.  The Character doesn't look too good and no amount of messing with the face editor seems to change it?  Mod that s#$% out.  I did.  2 less things to worry about.  Now I can choose whatever character I want.

I like Skyrim but there is definately something to this  game.  It seems Skyrim threw the baby out with the bathwater.  I don't want to start as a big special muckety much.  I like being the guy that was in a cell and spent most of the game making  a name for himself from the ground up.  You don't often have too much money in Oblivion...which is a good thing.  There is always something to buy even if it is a particularly annoying to upgrade skill.  Training isn't terribly unaffordable and if you are a hybrid character like a Battlemage or a Spellsword it just is a regular expense.

This game can be very hard at times...and it will force you to think about alternate strategies and whatnot.  There is one mission where you are trying to defend a farm with a couple of brothers.  You get swarmed by goblins and in a straight slugging match it always seems that at least one of the brothers die.   I pulled out a calm spell and cast it on two of the three charging goblins in each wave.   I never thought to do that before.  Skyrim doesn't force you to think like this too often...you don't have to...it's generally pretty easy.   What else?  Most Light armor is useless in a fight.  Heavy armor weighs too much (and looting is a big part of the game).  You may find yourself going into a farming dungeon with no armor but with an idea of how to get through it.  Once again, challenging the player.

Group battles are more annoying than they are fun.  All Npc's seem to move from side to side like they can teleport at will and you are as likely to strike a friendly NPC as an enemy.   Mostly the battles are good versus bad...unlike Skyrim where it's two philosophies; neither of which you can quite agree with and you generally think anyone who does is kind of thick.

This is a fantastic cutesy SHMUP starring characters you'd find in 100% Orange Juice. You play as QP and have to find out who took all the pudding from the world. You have a variety of options for your weapon patterns, some more useful than others, and can choose between three play styles, one with more offensive power but less time in "hyper" mode, a defensive mode, with less power but longer time in hyper mode, and a normal mode.
The game is pretty neat in having a chaining system, which basically tries to have you kill enemies and keep collecting stars to get a high chain for more points and so on. It can get pretty challenging trying to keep your chain, and often might mess up because of that, but is a fantastic feature.
This game is HARD. Don't let the cute graphics fool you. You will end up restarting a lot, but the game never gets boring. the graphics are nice and crisp and the music is adorable. The characters are fun and overall it's an incredibly polished game.
There are two modes of play, arcade mode, which lets you just play through the game straight, or a mode which lets you save progress between levels.

I was going to write a full review of this game after I finished playing all the way through, but considering that I've been stuck for a couple of months, I figured I might as well write it now.
Let's get the positive aspects out of the way. Every single map, dungeon, and town has its own unique look, with what I think is an original soundtrack to back it up. The battles work well, with quite a bit of strategy involved. The pixel art is good, and the custom face graphics add a nice touch.
However, I still rate this game negatively. Why? For several reasons...
First off, this game's plot can't decide what it wants to be: a psychological exploration into dreams (which is what the trailer made me think this was), a government conspiracy (which comes out of nowhere after a few hours in), a horror story (which they really lay on in the first section of the game), or a girl-gets-sucked-into-another-world story (present almost throughout). It took four good ideas and put them together into one game. In theory, this sounds really good, but what results is a very bipolar story that doesn't focus on any of these points long enough to develop any of them. I don't even know what genre this game fits into.
Second, Melrose is a Mary Sue. Not the worst I've come across, but all the symptoms are there. It starts off with her being bullied in school by 2 dimensional bullies (who bully her like elementary schoolers would, even though they're supposed to be older than that), then goes home to abusive, 2 dimensional parents, who beat her up for coming home late from school, and then she cries and wishes that her life was better. The writers are trying too hard to make us pity her, it makes it downright impossible to. Even if you disagree with me on that sentiment, Mary-Rose is a character just as bipolar as the story she stars in. They want to write her as the tortured girl who has distanced herself from others because she either doesn't wanna get hurt or just doesn't know how to interact with others. But then they need her to be a clueless outsider who's curious about everything at the same time. Have one or the other--you can't have both. Also, she's kind of a terrible person too. She tricks the one person who gives her sympathy so she can steal something extremely expensive, and treats arguably her only friend like dirt. Melrose...Melthorn is more like it.
Third...the dungeons... While they all look unique and have a different score, there are just too many of them. I found myself on more than one occasion wading through three consecutive dungeons to get the plot to advance. However, whenever I DID get through them, I was rewarded with only a sliver of plot before I had to go back and wade through three more. And while there are no random encounters, most of the enemies run towards you in corridors that are only one square thick, making 95% of the battles mandatory. This really doesn't help when you find yourself low on health and supplies and need to make a quick run back to the nearest town (which I would find myself doing a LOT, since I would have to go through three dungeons in a row). The result was me hating every dungeon, despite how atomspheric and beautiful it looked.
(The main reason I'm hopelessly stuck right now is because I did do what the game required me to do, but nothing happened. I thought this was a glitch, but then I recalled that the characters mentioned prior that there would be one part of the game that would require me to go into the heart of a dungeon, and then backtrack outside again. Considering that getting INTO the heart of the dungeon drained me of all my resources, going back would certainly kill me. So, yeah. I'm not continuing, because that is just ridiculous.)
Fourth...the characters were disappointments. (I'm excluding Mary Rose, since I already dedicated a paragraph to her.) The first party member you get was described as a "girl with black and green hair". Naturally, I assumed she was a cool, no nonsense Goth chick. Instead, she's mild mannered and demure, who Melrose pushes around most of the time (Melrose is bullied all the time, yet she so readily bullies others...?). Later, not-goth-girl's mom shows up out of the blue and puts a curse on the main character for no reason other than to drag out the plot some more. Then there's this lady bug guy who I seriously thought was a part-time party member until he refused to leave after several hours. The only two characters I liked were this mysterious blonde dude (who I hoped would join the party, but turned out to be evil), and this redheaded secret agent chick that doesn't show up until much later on (she almost makes it worth it, though). Apart from those two, I was sitting through a story about an unlikable girl and her bland "friends", bored out of my skull.
Fifth, which kinda ties into the fourth, none of the townsfolk are interesting. I get it, it's an RPG and programming all of these individuals to be unique is challenging, and I know this is a nitpick... But, like, 95% of the dialogue from the people I talked to was generic town stuff. Do none of these people have lives? The only town I liked was a town called Valentown (I think; it's been a while), because the entire town is powered by a love device, and somebody shut it off, making everyone really crabby. It was mildly hilarious and a good change of pace. I expected the townsfolk's dialogue to shift to ultra-lovey-dovey sap when I turned the machine back on, but it made the dialogue turn back to just the same old generic stuff. Kinda wish I didn't have to turn the machine on...
Lastly, how the game discouraged and didn't account for exploration drove me CRAZY! Example, there was this one time where I encountered a fork in the road and thought "sweet! Optional areas to explore", only to find out much later that the areas I thought were optional were all mandatory. I seriously spent hours looking for a key item in one area only to find it was in Valentown. Why? Why can't the world have extra areas optional to explore that aren't directly linked to the plot in any way? It would, you know, make it feel more like an actual WORLD. Another example I want to mention is that early on in the game, an Inn Mary Rose was staying in caught fire. When I backtracked there, days or weeks later in game, I found the Inn still in the process of burning to the ground. Really? I just...GAH!
There are other things, like the complicated crafting system which I never used, and an overpowered boss or two, but I think anyone who is considering getting this game gets the picture. Even though I got this game for free, I had to force myself to play on several occasions; usually while listening to Game Grumps. Is this game the worst thing ever? No; I've come across much worse, and this game does have its highlights. But I still wouldn't recommend it to anyone.
Look how many hours I have put into this game, Over half a day's worth. I'm trying, But this game just isn't worth it.

Disclosure: Played this game all the way to the end. Have not completed all sidequests. Have not started New Journey+ at the time of writing this review.
Potential spoilers in my review.
Pros:
- Good artwork and animation
- Good combat mechanics for an RPG
- Hard to recognize it as an RPG Maker game aside from the stock sounds and effects it provided.
Cons:
- Normal battles get too long, tedious, and repetitive at the later part of the game. I found myself actively trying to get rid of these enemies as fast as possible, as they constantly come around repeatedly, and it gets boring after a while.
- Very easy to get lost sometimes. A main storyline quest is a bit vague.
- Sometimes the plot can get a bit dull at times, but there's plenty of good stuff in between.
- Could use a bit more portals for fast travel mechanics.
- Noticeable bugs. Avoidable, but noticeable.
Bug 1: Before fighting Lisetrix, you are offered a chance to save the game as well as heal up, as it brings up the menu. If you go to the "New Skills" area while at this point, you will be taken to the fight WHILE in the skill selection area. Results in you fighting Lisetrix in what looks to be a simple, beta fighting background, while the skillpoints are still visible. Not sure what happens if you defeat her as I didn't kill her the first time, but I imagine it might result in something gamebreaking, knowing RPG Maker.
Bug 2: At the volcano, there is a simple jumping puzzle that you have to leap through. It's possible to wound up jumping into the lava, and end up getting stuck in it if you take a certain path.
Overall, this is a game that took some excellent advantage of RPG Maker's mechanics. One of a kind.

This is an old-school RPG Maker game, for better and worse. The game has a good story, a lot of areas to explore, chests to find for items and equipment, fighting enemies with solid combat, skill trees, crafting, many side-quests and a great soundtrack. Although all these elements are good for themselves, the biggest problem with this game it's the pacing: you'll have to backtrack a lot and fighting the same enemies over and over gets saturated. The 1.08 patch helps to skip random encounters, but you'll still need to gain EXP to be able to progress. And the side-quests are generic: talk to NPC, go there and there (more backtrack), complete task, and return for reward. But if you can overlook these issues, i think that this is an enjoyable game. The characters are likable and the story gripping, besides the pacing.

Whisper of a Rose is a very well done RPG Maker game about a girl named Melrose who has a pretty awful life and very much wants to find some way to escape it.  She finds a device called the iDream and uses that to escape into her Dream World.
But she ends up finding out that the Dream World isn't as nice as she thinks it is.  After all, not all our dreams are nice and happy, there are plenty of nightmares as well.
Whisper of a Rose takes us on Melrose's trip through the Dream World.  Everything in the game is based on things that happened to Melrose and her own fears and wishes.  Even her own repressed memories show up at times.  The settings range from rolling hills to unpleasant forests and swamps.  And all Melrose wants to do is find a way home.
Overall pros:
+Lengthy game, it took me just under 30 hours to beat it, though that included having to redo some stuff when I was defeated.
+Gorgeous settings, you can barely even tell it's RPG Maker
+Wonderful soundtrack.  All the music fits great with the scenes and the battle themes are just amazing.  You can get the soundtrack for free at the dev's website too.
+Very responsive dev which is always a good thing.
Overall cons:
-Never thought I'd say I wanted random encounters in a game, but this game really would have been better off with them.  Visible encounters just don't work here with how difficult it is to avoid enemies and how they immediately respawn with no chance for immunity to avoid the encounter.  Monsters also don't stop while you grab treasure which leads to encounters you may not want.  (Edit: This has been improved upon as well with a short delay between respawn and an item to avoid encounters.  New Game+ mode gets an important item to allow unlimited avoiding of encounters)
-Regular battles can get lengthy and tedious.  (Edit: This has been improved upon and they are much shorter as long as you aren't avoiding everything and not upgrading equipment)
-While there is a quick means of travel, it only covers limited areas and you'll be backtracking a bit for sidequests, which makes the encounter annoyances even greater because you'll get stuck fighting some monsters when you just wanted to make a quick run to grab an item.
Achievement wise, it's not an easy 100%.  You'll need two full playthroughs to 100% the game and there are a few missables.  It's about 30 hours per playthrough from the looks of things if you want to be sure to miss nothing.  There is some replay value though since you get some new stuff on a second run and there's one sidequest that can only be finished on the second playthrough and it nets you the best summon in the game.
Still, it's a very good game and I do recommend it.  It's not exactly short and sweet, but it's worth playing all the way through.
Also a little tip for anyone playing it: don't sell your initial armor for any characters.  You'll need that later if you want to get the best stuff in the game.  It's doable to beat the game without it, but more difficult.

I am so impressed with Divinity: Original Sin 2. I have been playing RPGs for 20 years now and with the 20 hours I have spent in game, I can tell that Divinity: Original Sin 2 will be one of my all time favorites.
Where to begin... there's just so many things to say about this game. The game itself is not particularly original, what is so impressive however, is how much passion and effort was put into creating the game. It is easy to see that Larian Studios wanted to create a living breathing world, an unadulterated RPG experience. The music is some of the best I've heard in gaming. The stories are wonderfully written. Character arcs are interesting. And the world is full of surprises and mystery. And there are many many ways you can interact with and manipulate the world around you. Larian Studios understands that an immersive and organic feeling world, is just as, if not MORE important than a game's story.
Playing this game, you feel no rush to complete story arcs. You just want to explore and experience the world. In my opinion, this is an early sign of a masterpiece.
As adults, it can be hard for us to find something that evokes a sense of wonder. Divinity: Original Sin 2 has done this. I spent 15 hours in the starting island alone. One could say this is a bad thing as the game might be mechanically convoluted and tedious. But I spent EVERY minute of that time immersed.
It's been said many times. But Divinity: Original Sin 2 takes great effort in putting importance on the player's decision making. Your interactions with NPCs can have a minimal to a colossal impact on the future. I haven't seen a game where the player's decisions hold so much weight. And you are invested throughout; thanks to the wonderfully written characters, immersive world, and beautiful music. And of course, the fun and strategic combat system.
Some frustration may also arise from the amount of freedom given to you. Quests and story arcs may be solved and end in different ways; very rare is there a linear progression. These leads to times of being utterly lost or even confused of what to do or where to go. I imagine this is a polarizing aspect of the game. It's been some years since I've played a game like this, so I was admittedly frustrated, but grew to love it after some time. This was the nature of many old RPGs.
In my mind, the only viable excuse to NOT enjoy this game is: you're not a fan of turn based combat, or the game is a little too old-school by design. The game's foundation lies in older RPGs, so the prime demographic are the older gamers. Younger players will have some getting used to. Otherwise, in all respects, Divinity: Original Sin 2 is an instant classic. A masterpiece.

***This review was written using a Press key provided by the Developer for review purposes***
Interplanetary is a turn-based strategy game set in Space that is currently available through Steam Early Access. In Interplanetary you wage war against AI or human players across an entire solar system which is randomly generated each time you play so you'll never play the same game twice.
A word of warning, if you want this game purely for a singleplayer experience I'd suggest holding out on it but if you're looking for a great multiplayer strategy experience you have found it.
+The graphics are quite nice and even when you zoom in very close to the planets they look great
+Nice visual effects when enemy planets or your own planet gets hit by enemy fire
+The game has fantastic projectile physics but I'll come back to physics later
+Thanks to the turn-based nature of the game you can really take your time with choosing what to build and where to attack to maximise your power
+Despite the tutorial being several intimidating pages of text explaining core mechanics this game is relatively simple to understand and once you have a basic understanding of it you'll quickly improve and figure out how everything works
+Buildings can be upgraded to improve them in a way which suits the building, for example extra damage for railguns, and each building can only have two upgrades which prevents AI and players alike from developing overpowered buildings
+The resource management is very simple in Interplanetary and there are only two resources in the game so you often have to make simple but difficult decisions regarding what to build next
+Trying to figure out the right trajectory for your attacks is incredibly challenging but also a whole load of fun though I did feel that it was too difficult at times especially when firing across the solar system with other planets in your way as the game gives you no indication of their speed so you have to guess where they'll be to avoid entering their gravitational fields
+Even at this relatively early stage in development the tech tree is already quite good and it contains boosts to material, power etc. as well as the expected unlockable buildings
+Even just loading up an empty game and shooting at nearby planets is fun
+Good variety of weapons
+The game's calculations take place impressively quickly
-AI are overpowered and have no levels of difficulty. In my time playing this against AI I never once saw them miss a shot and as far as I can tell they also build much faster than you can, as I was struggling to build a second weapon I was already being bombarded by three weapons
-Of course it is in Early Access and allowances should be made but it isn't overly realistic. First off not all of the planets orbit in the same direction. Secondly, and this is me perhaps being a little too critical, the type of planets you'll find in a solar system often don't match what should be found where they are orbiting, for example Earth-like planets orbiting very close to suns and barren Mars-like planets in outer orbits towards the edge of the solar system
-There aren't many people playing this game so if you don't have friends who own it or you can't play local multiplayer you might struggle to find any matches
-The defensive buildings in the game are almost entirely useless, particularly against AI
-You can't save your progress
Worth a mention:
-The predicted paths that the game provides when you are choosing trajectories become entirely incorrect as soon as your weapon fires
Verdict:
8
Despite the lack of a good AI this game is a fantastic strategy game and can be enjoyed in more than just the usual ways, I'd strongly recommend getting this to play with friends.

After having played a decent amount of hours I had like to say that Warframe is a game which isn't beginner friendly. If you want to play the game, be prepared to do quite a lot of research yourself or ask others. In the beginning you can do whatever you want, but as you progress through the planets the difficulty will ramp up a bit and those who dont know what they should do will be left clueless.
In terms of content Warframe has a lot to offer for new players, but as you play more and more you will get the feeling that there isn't much to do anymore. The game does get updates pretty often, introducing new gear and content, but in the end you will always grind. If you dislike grinding don't start with Warframe!
Some people might label Warframe as P2W, but that isn't the case. By paying you actaully speed up the grind, and eventually will make you stop earlier. Everything in the game is obtainable through playing. If you want something specific you will always be able to get it within a day as long as you are prepared to grind. I have never spend any money on this game in order to buy the premium currency. However, I did spend quite a lot of money on cosmetics, and that is also an issue which I will adress. A lot of fashion items can only be bought directly with money instead of the premium currency. If you dont like to spend money, there is still a lot of fashion options available which doesnt require you to pay money.
Last but not least I had like to point out the community of Warframe. Since the game is centered around Co-op I have noticed that a lot of people (especially those who have played more) are always willing to help out newer players to the point of doing super low missions or taking low level players on high level missions. The community is really great and you will always find someone who wants to help you out when you are in a pinch.

Warframe is one of those games where you have to stick around to see the good potential this game has to offer. for starters, this is completely free to play so money isn't necessary to progress. Warframe offers a variety of different playstyles to choose from whether you want tank out dealing heavy damage or be supportive by helping out your teamates. With a ton of features to choose from including different game modes, different places to explore, and lore to unravel, this game will have you lost for hours.

I received this game for free during a giveaway from Indie Gala this past summer. Had no idea what to expect from RADical Roach, and thought the titular character looked charming. But the game hardly matches the decent aesthetic that RAD has going for the little roach.
The graphics are amongst the best Decaying Logic has done, outside of Pixel Puzzles: Japan (but those are actual photos). This is saying a lot, considering how garish or sometimes horrendous the games look. (I was stubborn and needed to finish PP: Zombies even with the awful picture art.) The gameplay though? Totally misses the mark on the genre it's trying to be, and as a result I've found it to be the worst of their games.
It's a side-scrolling shoot 'em up. How do you screw that up? Well...
Even with all of that, I was still enjoying it and continued right up until I hit the brick wall that is 2-2. Instant death spikes covering walls, flea soldiers with horrendously tiny bullets sprayed everywhere, no super laser, a joke of a shield... all of this turns into a formula for cheap, frustrating failure. Hard to gauge exactly how close you can get to the microscopic bullets, barely touching a direction sends you flying (relative to how you WANT to move), you have very little room for error and the game punishes you for the slightest mistake.
Honestly I don't mind not having score, or having a hard shmup, and I was really digging the aesthetic. Too many shooters now are anime / danmaku / etc, some harken back to good ol' spaceships, but barely any go in a different direction like insects. But I had to draw the line at the unfair difficulty. There's a fine line between being "fun but hard as hell" and "frustratingly difficult for blatantly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reasons". Ikaruga, G Darius, Satazius, Jamestown, Jets'n'Guns... these are fun but hard as hell.
And RAD? It's a shame that the charm was only skin deep. I'm a mite upset I won't be able to see the rest of it.

Radical Roach is one of my favourite game types, side scrolling shooter and has an extremely cool concept with awesome cartoon style graphics. However, the Developers have failed to output the concept and gamemode into anything worth playing and here's why.
Pros:
♦ Cartoon Style Graphics (This style of graphics will always appeal to me, as someone who has grown up reading comic books)
♦ Sound was decent (Wasn't repetitive or annoying)
♦ Many Free Steam Trading Cards (This is the best part about it)
♦ Controls seem to just work and be in an easy to use place (They seem to just work but you can't remap them)
Cons:
♦ Steam Achievements added a year late (Achievements were added 1 year after the game was made, which is annoying as people have already played the game and now have to replay it just to unlock achievements, which they should've got first time through if they were added)
♦ No Difficulty Mode (In options there are difficulty settings but all are set to hard. Should be difficulty settings for those that just want to play without having a ridiculous almost impossible feeling to the game)
♦ Some of the earlier levels you can easily just camp the top or bottom of the map to win (This shouldn't happen in any game)
♦ Bosses seemingly have random attack cycles every time you die and have undodgeble attacks as you can't tell what type of attack they are going to fire so you can dodge them (This is terrible as you can't plan a course of attack and never know when to dodge or not)
♦ Storyline is weird (I say this as you’re randomly fighting things and then the boss comes and next thing you know you’re fighting a Chameleon for no reason at all...)
♦ No Points or Highscores (As a Side-Scrolling Shooter... the main reason to play this type of game genre is for the highscores/points to see who can get the highest... not having any sense of score or points ruins the Side-Scrolling Shooter Genre for me)
♦ Can't pause levels (Pressing escape in the middle of a level brings up level select making you have to start the whole level over again)
♦ Can't Skip Cutscenes (Really annoying having to watch cutscenes over and over again every time you close the game and want to come back and play)
♦ One hit kill objects no matter how many lives you have or if your shield is on (This is annoying as the hitbox on the one hit kill objects such as the tyre seems really out and nothing is more annoying than getting so far and hitting a one hit kill object and having to restart from the beginning)
♦ No Recovery Period after you get hit and lose a life (This is annoying as, as soon as you get hit and lose a life, you can get hit and lose another life instantly. There should be some sort of recovery period to give you time to adjust to being hurt and get back into the game)
♦ Can't remap Controls (There is no reason why we shouldn't be able to remap controls)
♦ Only has three really dodgy graphic options, v-sync on or off, Fullscreen on or off and HD on or off (This is really poor as there is nothing to justify what HD is in a PC game and there really should be resolution settings, not just Fullscreen on or off)
♦ No Sound Settings (This is annoying as multiple people like to be able to control volume from within a game)
♦ Price is relatively expensive for what it is (It would be a decent price if the game was worth playing)
Overall, the game has an amazing concept and a good Side Scrolling Shooter Genre but the Devs have lacked in output of the genre, concept and gameplay making me not be able to recommend this in any case. Also as there is way more Cons than Pros, I'd recommend only picking this up on sale if you want a lot of free trading cards.

Imagine if all of history was laid out before you. It's all going to roughly play out exactly as it always has, but as a player you have a choice: pick one of the world powers of the era and see if you can keep them afloat with all the resources available to them or pick one of the other nations and see if you can survive next to the big boys.
The point of the game is that you see how long a family line you can keep. The best way to do this is by having as much territory as possible, have a large family and let them prosper. Unfortunately, dark plots and random events are set out to ensure they end up on top. While you'll start as a king, it won't be long before a envious family member eyes the throne and takes you out. If you had children, you continue play as them and try to keep the family line going.
It is. Crusader Kings II (and all so called "Grand Strategy" games) have a steep learning curve. Added to that confusion is the fact that everything uses names and terminology of the ages, so you'll undoubtedly be confused when you want to attack a neighbor for their land and the game tells you that you can't without casus belli. Of course, that's one reason the game is so addictive, while you play you also end up learning.
Of course, the genre isn't for everyone so I highly recommend checking out a few people playing on YouTube to see if it's interesting. At the end of the day, it's little more than a strategy game where you never directly control combat, politics are more important than fighting and your life is basically a choose your own adventure game.
If you're into the idea of Civilization, but the combat feels rote or boring, Crusader Kings II might be worth a look. If you like historical simulation, then the game is certainly up your alley. However if the idea of a game where years can pass and nothing really happens, or if you want a game with balance, you'll probably want to look elsewhere. There's admittedly a lot of challenge in trying to take a small country and change history, but there is a reason they never actually changed history. You can just pick one of the kingdoms that was successful, but then the game is much easier.

TheHunter: PRIMAL
OVERVIEW
OK.... So theHunter: Primal is very very similar to theHunter (obviously) however the main difference are the fact that you cannot purchase anything and then equip them when you first start because it is not a hunting expedition, it's survival... However they have just added an in-game money system, where everytime you harvest a dino, you get money and when you level up, you unlock something in the shop, so when you die, you get taken to a shop where you can purchase weapons and whatnot before you spawn...
But it's not like other survival games... you can't build stuff... you basically just gotta scavenge containers and bags and/or kill other players and take their stuff... if it's set to PVP of course...
The graphics are a little better than the hunter in my opinion and who can ever forget the beautiful sunrise and sunset water colours... and choice scenery!
As far as gameplay, the mechanics are buggy, but can only get better with time. The player movements are different from the Hunter the walking and running are faster, but they have introduced a sprint system which uses stamina and is extremely loud to attract dinosaurs. (Only use in emergency) The hunter mate (although called settler mate) works exactly the same way, spotting and tracking works the same but there isn’t tracking or spotting skill levels, and of course trophy shots and harvesting work the same way also. You don't get experience for weapon use in this game either...
There is also a new tracking feature in which I really like... when you wound an animal and you track it's blood, it tells you in percentage how injured it is... for eg.... after shooting a T-Rex 6 times with a shotgun, after scanning it's blood it told me that it had 45-60% health left and the next time I shot it once... it said 30-48% (as well as body/intestine shot etc)
THE GOOD
- Great graphics
- Excellent immersion (especially when the t-rex is nearby or when a raptor knows you're there and he/she calls out to the pack to help look for you)
- Cool map with central volcano (no dinosaur game is complete without a volcano to set the mood)
- Has major potential for many wonderful things
- No pay to win, no money at all (except in-game currency from harvesting)
- Injury percentage for prey
- When you die, you can retrieve your goods from your old backpack... as long as no-one else has pillaged it!!
- Thunderstorms :D
- Mean looking dinosaurs
THE BAD
- Lots of gameplay bugs and a rushed full release from Early Access
- Only five dinosaurs... T-Rex, Utahraptors, Triceratops, Velociraptors and Quetzalcoatlus (Dino-birds)
- Scavenging gets boring and old really quickly - needs traditional ‘the Hunter’ mode
- Controls are very stiff and sometimes sluggish
- Bad framerates in high detailed areas such as swamps and dense jungle regions
- Faulty hit register, (shoot the 6,000kg T-Rex in the heart with a .700 while it's standing still and it registers as only a body hit, where sometimes I can drop a 10,000kg Triceratops on the run with one .308 round to the heart, where the bullet hole is on the leg... Can be quite frustrating at times... as you die from not dropping them or you run out of ammo...
- Quetzalcoatlus seem to be able to swoop through hilly terrain and through metal spikes and grab you, even though you shot them in the head...
- Sound is a little buggy crossing from biome to biome
- The Quetzalcoatlus, although remarkable are very annoying and frustrating to deal with at times...
WHAT IT NEEDS
- Need to be able to craft something, to build defences to stand a chance killing dinosaurs without dying
- Needs more dinosaur species (especially herbivores) and less of the current ones for a nice balanced game
- Need to see the Dinosaurs attacking each other... raptors attacking T-rex and Triceratops, Velociraptors getting taken by Quetzalcoatlus and the traditional T-Rex versus triceratops battle...
- Maybe a 4 wheeler would be good as usually the game spawns you on the other side of the map as your friends
- The T-rex needs to have a bigger roar like on Jurassic Park... to really make your hairs stand on end.
- A traditional ‘the Hunter’ mode, to create expeditions instead of scrounging around...

Whisper of the Rose is a slightly more mature version of Sweet Lily Dreams (also done by Rose Portal Games). The story revolves around Melrose who is in a harsh relationship with her (supposed) parents and rough school life. She thrives in happiness through her dreams and imagination. This ends up leading her to steal a device that allows one person to enter a dream world that may or may not be better for them.
The story is common among many people and may even connect with those who might be in a similar state (or were). The game play is a little different than SLD, but is still an RPG Maker Game with simple RPG elements. The game has some great music and you can even get through it with little grinding if you are decent with these kinds of games. The variety of sidequests also help to make the game a little more interesting when you start getting tired of the main story events.
Some of the game's plot can be a little too dull and may lead some people to give up early, but it ramps up the further you get into the game, making most people wanting to continue. The Skill Tree almost seems like a real tree. It has giant branches and is not the easiest to navigate, but once you get use to it, it is not that problematic. There is not a large variety of enemies, but each enemy  has different weaknesses no matter what type it is.
There are other good ideas and bad moments in this game, but I will not spoil too much to give anyone interested in the game a chance to experience the game for themselves. There is a free guide online if you ever get lost or need some kind of help and exploration is always recommended. You may find things that you didn't know you could get early on that will help with your game play. All in All, the game is decent for an RPG Maker game and is definetly worth trying.

I want to like this game a lot. There are a few key problems that keep me from doing so. Primarily the balance of weapons and defences is very far off. When your planet is hit with a railgun round, the round splits in atmo into 5 or so chunks that cause quite a bit of damage. Your kinetic defences that you've hopefully deployed cover a very small area... and guess what, railgun rounds have a large area of effect, so when a round hits even just outside of your defences, it causes damage everywhere. If you possess the power to hurtle cannon rounds across your solar system, you should have the ability to build defences that cover a much larger area of your planet. Another smaller issue I have is that when going up against more than one AI player, they are practically unbeatable. They build faster, and are far more accurate than you will ever be.
TLDR: kinetic defences are almost useless, and shouldn't be. And the AI is very powerful. Like Matrix level.

There are 5 areas (forest, dungeon, etc) each having increasingly tougher and more enemies. The levels are procedurally generated but you can retry a floor until you beat it which I felt was nice. The later levels actually were easier since you can buy guns and health upgrades.
A couple negative points: 1) the game is short as you can see my playtime is just under 2 hours and 2) the final boss was a little simpler/easier than I would have liked.
A couple positive points: 1) weapons variety is good (each has its own feel) 2) there is a bit of replayability via an arcade mode if that's you thing.
Some closing thoughts: I imagine a lot of people will pass on this just given that it doesn't drop cards but honestly this is truly a gem at this price point. Hope this helps.

Interplanetary is a very different game, that has a ton of potential. The devs have pushed out this physics heavy turn based space strategy game that is working great. I've had this game long enough that i now feel comfortable to write a review about it. I've seen the devs update the game with a lot of new depth and mechanics, e.g. building upgrades.
Despite being in early access, it seems as though it is already done. It looks polished and has a very nice (AND THREATENING) weapons system, a tech tree that can be built upon, super weapons, and some very nice physics implemented.
The single player can be pretty fun, but in the end you know the bots are just missing on purpose. The game gets high stakes and interesting when you play online or with friends. I've had plenty of moments where a friend and I are slowly watching our planets revolve towars one another, to where we broadside eachother in a "fire everything" moment of mutual destruction.
Negotiation and begging other players to not shoot is also fun as well.
TL;DR Pro/Con list:
Pros:
-Great Gameplay (balanced)
-Gorgeous Graphics (liking this alliteration?)
-Fun and inviting multiplayer
-Tech tree
-Many weapon paths
-Structure upgrades
-Attentive devs
Cons:
-More diversity wanted
-Minor camera issues or annoyances
-Small community
Overall, I think that Interplanetary is a great game for its' price, and even if that's an issue just grab it on sale. The devs continue to implement new things, and I assume theres more to come. 7/10

The real problem with the game is that you only have three options (or a mix of them) for playing: local multi, online, AI.
For a new player like myself, the AI is insanely overpowered, and I get demolished without being able to do anything effective against them. As for local multi, that's not really an option for me. So online seems like it would be the way to go, but there's not really many people playing the game. I sat in the lobby for quite a while occasionally opening rooms, but it seems like there's 8 or 9 people that just want to play in private rooms all day and ignore me.
Pity, really.
In any case, the game itself is good, and I hope it continues to progress, but if something isn't done to facilitate matchmaking and adjust the AI difficulty then it could actually destroy this game.
I'm choosing to be optimistic here and vote positive, but think carefully about it before buying this one.

in Green Hill was cool and the chemical plant

Awful game. Employs a few aspects I absolutely hate. Instead of letting you know what to do in the slightest it's just a trial and error until you get it right. How about you tell us what to do? This is supposed to be a game after all. I'm playing this for fun, not to work hard for no reason.
Instead of zone walls and restarting where you leave off if you fail you to accomplish some arbitrary task you go all the way back to the beggining of a level to repititously and boringly replay the same inane bits over and over again for no good reason. Also it's glitchy and the reasons you die have no bearing on anything.
You don't find a hidden key fast enough: Restart the same level and keep looking. Why? What's the point of an arbitrary time limit? Why don't you put up some shiny pointers if the point is to grab it quickly and move on?
So you move the wrong way: Glitch, purposefully kill yourself to restart the level. Why not put up a zone wall?
Move the wrong way again: Someone shoots you for no reason. Not like you could've gone anywhere that way. Restart the level again. Why?
I tried to give it a chance but replaying the same level from the start 10 times for no good reason has a way of ruining things.
That's a trap that poor game designers fall into. Just because you know everything, where everything is and what to do with it all in every situation doesn't mean that we, the players, do.
Now I'm all for opening up side-roads. Another big thing I hate in games is having this huge open looking world you're gaming in only to be locked into small set paths where every turn is an avalanche or a fence. The problem here is you have these paths open just to go down them and die - restarting the level over and over again. That's a huge step backwards. That's some throw-back NES stuff right there. The improvement to that was just blocking the way off. The improvement to blocking it off is to put things there you can do or find. Something games figured out back in SNES days.
Why does it constantly seem like 2 steps forward 1 step back with video gaming since SNES days when it was all leaps forward?

An overrated game, exaggerated for it's prettiness and puzzle-like nature. This review does contain minor spoilers. I would also like to add that I played this game on a different account before this one, so don't be fooled by the time played.
The first thing I notice, right at the get go, is the confusing menu. "Click to start" or "Space to continue"... Clicking will automatically start a new game for you, while pressing space will bring you to a screen saying "What was the name of the last area you were in", or something along those lines. So, assuming it was something that would be added to over time, I started the game. After making a bit of progress, I decided to exit the game to try pressing Space. But according to the game, on the pause menu, you must remember the name of the location you were last at. So i'm presuming this is a game you have to either play all at once or have a very boring life to remember such a small detail.
Anyway, digressing. Back on the menu, I press Space, and it brings me to the screen where there are no new options. Now, being a first time user of this game, I have no clue what to do so I spray my fingers across my keyboard. Nothing appears at all. I then remember the name of the area I was in, typing it into the invisible format and then being randomly put at the start of it, even though I had already completed it. Excuse me if it is me just being blind, but it doesn't even show what you typed in and it doesn't take you to where you were. This is literally the laziest thing I have seen in a game in a long while.
The gameplay is smooth yet buggy in some places, with little to no clues given about what you need to do. Especially in the second area where you're put in a white room with two doors. The radio says some inaudible babble about fire and a "tiny♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;, then cuts off without a single hint. Luckily, sprinting around the room and spamming E (and let's be real, E is not the most desirable key for doing an action when you're using WASD) helped me out. I understand that it's a puzzle game, but when the "narrator" is just spewing out garbage metaphors etc., then it becomes a little too impossible to play.
One bug I did find is the instant FPS loss when you jump on a chair and try to move off. This also, occasionaly, teleported me across the room for no reason. And to put the cherry on the cake, if you tried to jump off the side of said chair, you will sometimes glitch out and be stuck in it, twitching every now and then.
The actual characters are dull, groaning and boring throughout. The person you play as, Anthony, seems really calm and sarcastic about the situation, even though there is an apparent mad man torturing him. They just don't seem worth listening to, in all honesty, since they don't help you and only talk to eachother almost casually.
So overall, I view this game as more of a multiple-try spammer instead of a puzzle game. You can click around every room to get your solution, and it'll help alot more than the game itself. Another attempt at a mind-boggling mystery, with confusing rooms and drab gameplay until conflict. The whole "look away, and suddenly it's there!" cliché gets annoying very quickly as it wastes your time completely. I mean, for example, the timed room at the start could have easily just shown the door and not the pointless mirror, and hidden the key a bit nicer (such as under a book or in a drawer). However, the game altogether is nicely strung together but just not something for people with weak attention spans or common sense.

Going back to Oblivion was Interesting to say the least.  I forgot most things about it until playing those aspects.  Except for a vague recollection,I even forgot the dungeon I used to farm skills with; Doznot (or something) on the west side of the Imperial City.   Sometimes coming back to a game you feel a warm recollection because you either understand and empathize with the main character or the computer is responsive to whom you have made the character to be.  With this game, it treats you exactly the same no matter who you are.   You can make choices in conversation that will make people mad at you but there is no impetus or reward to do so past just trying to stir things up.  Then they look at you all spooky eyed straight like everyone has got♥♥♥♥♥♥face.

There are a lot of fun quests to do.  There are some annoying quests like 'Tears of the Savior'.  Alchemy isn't as easy as it is in Skyrim; there are no recorded recipes; get out a pad and paper and write down combinations that work unless you like to search your entire inventory each time.  Leveling is quite intersting and, by that I mean fun but kind of messed up.  You never want to use a standard character because primary skills level you up (and almost everything opposing you levels with you).   Attributes will not significantly rise unless you use skills that are directly related to them.  Consequently, the most efficient way to play is to manage your levelling process.  You will find yourself jumping off roofs or with a shield holding block for like half an hour against a rodent that just won't quit just to level your speed and endurance respectively.  My advice?  Don't do it.  Life is too short to me sitting for half an hour vegging at a screen holding the right mouse button.  Mod that s!@# out.  The Character doesn't look too good and no amount of messing with the face editor seems to change it?  Mod that s#$% out.  I did.  2 less things to worry about.  Now I can choose whatever character I want.

I like Skyrim but there is definately something to this  game.  It seems Skyrim threw the baby out with the bathwater.  I don't want to start as a big special muckety much.  I like being the guy that was in a cell and spent most of the game making  a name for himself from the ground up.  You don't often have too much money in Oblivion...which is a good thing.  There is always something to buy even if it is a particularly annoying to upgrade skill.  Training isn't terribly unaffordable and if you are a hybrid character like a Battlemage or a Spellsword it just is a regular expense.

This game can be very hard at times...and it will force you to think about alternate strategies and whatnot.  There is one mission where you are trying to defend a farm with a couple of brothers.  You get swarmed by goblins and in a straight slugging match it always seems that at least one of the brothers die.   I pulled out a calm spell and cast it on two of the three charging goblins in each wave.   I never thought to do that before.  Skyrim doesn't force you to think like this too often...you don't have to...it's generally pretty easy.   What else?  Most Light armor is useless in a fight.  Heavy armor weighs too much (and looting is a big part of the game).  You may find yourself going into a farming dungeon with no armor but with an idea of how to get through it.  Once again, challenging the player.

Group battles are more annoying than they are fun.  All Npc's seem to move from side to side like they can teleport at will and you are as likely to strike a friendly NPC as an enemy.   Mostly the battles are good versus bad...unlike Skyrim where it's two philosophies; neither of which you can quite agree with and you generally think anyone who does is kind of thick.

I used to enjoy this more back in the day when I felt that I had more time on my hands to spend.  I will still recommend it though.
