Endless Legend is the 4x game I have always wanted.
It has the complexities of a standard 4x, but it presents them in a very user-friendly way. And while there is a learning curve involved, it feels natural. Unlike other 4x titles, every new game I play I feel a new sense of understanding and I make better choices. I'm not stuck trying to memorize some obscure tech-tree/web, and I don't have to figure out the perfect build order for a particular faction. That is quite a change, as most similar titles end up with a skill-wall that you hit almost immediately - only defeated through sheer grinding and studying of the various tech paths/faction properties.
That isn't to say such things are entirely absent here. There are certainly build orders better than others, and tech choices better than others, but because of how everything is presented, you aren't punished as a user trying to figure those choices out. As long as you have some general 4x background, you'll be able to make good decisions from the very first game, and you won't find yourself being held back because you forgot to research some early-game tech.
City management is also fantastic. It is so easy to manage your city output via the workers, and keeping track of cities as your empire grows is also very well thought-out. There's still a bit of click-grinding in the mid/late game, but that's inevitable in any true 4x.
Combat is a reinvinted a bit here as well. Each battle can become it's own little game of chess (or you can just automate it if you want). I think this is one of the greatest elements of the game. Combat has so much more depth that it really changes how you play. With good micro and a bit of luck, you can survive or even win battles that would typically be lost if it was just up to attack/defense/terrain dice rolling. Instead, you can use your surrounding terrain, or unique abilities, to make much stronger stands, or much stronger attacks. Since both sides have the expanded capabilities, balance is maintained while the skill-ceiling gets raised (always a good thing for a competitive game).
The addition of heroes rounds off everything, providing a chance to benefit armies or cities with unique perks and skills. The heroes provide a nice RPG element, even going so far as to have unique drops of weapons/armor/trinkits around the map to bolster their usefulness. I like that heroes play a big role, but I also appreciate that they don't overtake the game. You'll definitely want to use heroes and distribute them wisely throughout your empire, but it's not a thing that needs constant grinding to level up, and a hero won't win the game alone. They provide just enough benefit to be worth while, and lack just enough impact to keep from becoming a turn-based DOTA game.
The addition of optional quests is a nice feature. Other 4x titles have started following this route as well, and I think it's a good trend. The quests help provide some guidance if you have no idea what to do (you will always have a main quest line that, if followed, will keep your empire growing), and rewards earned can vary from luxury resources to specialty items for your heroes.
Overall, this is the longest review I've ever written for a game - and I think that alone says quite a bit. There are still some quirks here and there, but the game is obviously built on a solid foundation. The UI, the graphics, and the gameplay all work together beautifully to provide an enthralling and captivating experience. I've barely scratched the surface, and I'm already excited to see what they do in terms of expansions/sequels. For now though, I'm happy to keep playing this for one... more... turn...

QP Dangerous is an entertaining shooter with a surprising amount of depth. You start out choosing one of three different styles: Aggressive, Orthodox, or Defensive. Aggressive gives you more attack power but takes longer to charge up hyper mode, Orthodox is the middle ground, and Defensive charges your hyper mode faster but reduces your attack power.
The Hyper Mode is important because when activated you erase all bullets on screen and gain points based on how many you destroyed. This is important because in QP Dangerous you will be overwhelmed with way more bullets than you can dodge. Bullets disappear when you kill the enemy that created them so can't take too much time. Also in Hyper Mode your combo meter stops decreasing for the duration, allowing you to keep building your score through sections where you can't constantly eliminate enemies. Most importantly though, you're allowed to take one hit in hyper mode without losing a life. This resets your combo counter completely but is a very useful panic button. Hyper mode immediately ends but you can erase a difficult pattern's bullets and have insurance in case you happen to get hit in the next few seconds. Killing a boss while Hyper Mode is active nets you a huge bonus.
Aside from the Hyper Mode mechanics, we also have formations that affect how your own bullets work. The bullets you shoot spawn from the R-Bits flying alongside you, and the formations affect how they are positioned. There are over 20 in total, with all of them aside from the default available for purchase with points earned from playing the game. Some of them even increase the score you get in exchange for being more challenging to use well. Every time you start a new game you pick 3 separate formations out of the ones you've unlocked to use and can swap between them at any time during gameplay. I've had a lot of fun experimenting whenever I unlock a new one and quite a few of them have really interesting gimmicks that require completely different strategies to use effectively.
Last off the story is rather simple but the dialogue is entertaining and the whole concept of saving the world's pudding is taken to the comedic extreme. It takes a turn for the epic towards the end that's hard to take seriously, and I found myself laughing at the absurdity of it. The focus is definitely on the gameplay though, and they've built an extremely solid shooter out of it. Pick this one up if you enjoy the genre. It's one of my favorites.

Having put a few hours into this game with a group from 2 to 5 people, I have mixed feelings about this game. I love the concept, but in it's current state, the game mechanics make it near impossible to survive for any prolonged amount of time.
One very large issue is with running and (the lack of) jumping. I understand the point of the game is slow movement and tracking, but that doesn't always work. Particularly when a T-Rex comes wandering by. Maybe I haven't figured out what draws their attention yet, but at this point, it seems like merely being in their presence brings them right to you no matter your actions. And once they are onto you, it's nearly impossible to get away thanks to the movement mechanics. Being able to run in something like 15-second burts, and otherwise having to walk everywhere is not realistic in any sense, and makes evasion impossible. Even someone massivly out of shape can run for longer than 15 seconds before being winded, so there's no reason why a group of fit looking hunters shouldn't. I'm all for stamina, and having prolongued running affect your ability to shoot or something would be great. But basically not being able to run as a means of evasion when you end up in a fight you cannot win, that makes the game seriously fustrating.
Also, the T-Rex seems to sort of have a homing ability. In several instances with multiple players, a T-Rex has killed one of us, only to ingore the other players and instead head in a straight path directly where the player respawned, sometimes several hundred meters away. I don't know if this is a glitch or not (I really hope so), but it is also fustrating to spawn into the game with a T-Rex already zoned in to come find you and kill you.
Those two issues aside, the game really is very tense, and a lot of fun. I see a lot of potential here. I hope that the two issues above are a result of bugs or experimentation, and not perminant gameplay mechnanics.

A brilliant Open World RPG. Oblivion is one of those games that set the bar high for future titles in the genre and has had a massive influence on many open world games since its release. So many creative and imaginative quests which are so much fun to play through. The lore of the elder scrolls series are so in-depth that you can just spend hours just reading through the hundreds of books that are in this world.
The problems are the graphics, combat and the levelling system have not aged well due to massive advances in these areas in other games since Oblivion but they are still good enough not to put most people off.
If you love open world games, a medieval setting or a fantasy setting you need to play this game.

NOTE: I only have 60 hours on here, but I bought the game when it was new and before Steam existed. I must have at least 1000 hours into this game, and I bought it three times.
This is one of the most awesome games and at the same time one of the most broken games I have ever played.
Broken, not in the sence that it is buggy. In fact it runs almost perfectly, especially this edition with all the release bugs worked out.
What I mean is that while playing the game "normally" is loads of fun, the objectively best, most effective way is to play it totally wrong.
This was the first time Bethesda pioneered an adaptive level system, meaning that enemies are always as powerful as you. That means that if you choose all the spells as class skills but make your main attribute strength and endurance, then focus only on swords, you will only face imps and goblins your entire game.
Funny exploits like this are everywhere in Oblivion, but in the end if you want it to be easy just turn the "difficulty" slider all the way down. That way it will be easy without you making a fool of your character. :)
One thing I truly love is that you can choose to not start the main story. In fact, Oblivion is almost two games:
Play the main story, and Gates pop up everywhere, demons swarm out, and you get challenging dungeons filled with gore and epic loot.
Don't start the story, and no Gates, no Demons, but instead the landscape is unscarred and you see Cyrodiil in all it's perfect beauty.
You can even complete all the side quests, buy a bunch of houses, become master of all guilds, and only THEN start the main quest. If you do that, it will be very different indeed since the enemies match your level.
This is JUST the story, I'm not even getting into the many ways to play the game itself.
You can be a sword-master without peer, an bow-wielding stealthy assassin, even beat enemies with your fists.
Focus on one element to defeat your foes, or focus on all three. Or use magic in a more subtle way to enhance your abilities, convince people to fight you in crowded areas to avoid getting charged, turn invisible to walk right past a cave full of bandits, even goad enemies into fighting each other so you don't have to!
And best of all, you will probably end up doing ALL OF THE ABOVE since there are no classes. Given enough time, you can be a master of all things.
All paths lead to victory, in the amazingly weird world of Oblivion!

I want to start off by saying that I REALLY like Whisper of a Rose, when it isn't making me tear my hair out, but I have a hard time recommending it to anyone who wants a stroll down memory lane. Especially those that come from generation 4/5/6 Final Fantasy. Realizing this is a debut title and is going to have issues, being a fan of this type of game I plan to throw the book at it. Not out of malice, but because I really hope to see this game and future games improved from constructive criticism, rather than take on a holding pattern as a result of unwarranted praise.
In Whisper of a Rose, you are Melrose, a schoolgirl from a broken home with social issues at school who steals an iDream, an experimental device which allows you to live your dreams, from a museum in which it is to be showcased. In using it, however, she becomes trapped in an inhospitable dream world with no clear way to escape.
The story itself is well written and functional, and the characters diverse (if archetypal) but I find my relationship with Melrose to be an emotional rollercoaster. I seem to alternate between sympathizing with her plight and wanting to punch her in the face, because there are situations in which she has violent outbursts and behaves like a total b!tch on an irrational level. I mostly settle on indifference to her entirely.
The visuals, taking into account that the game was built in RPG Maker XP are very good, and I have thus far encountered no bugs or glitches that spring to mind, and experienced no crashes. However the way the interface is designed, while functional could definitely use improvement. When it is an allied character's turn, there are two visual prompts to assist in this - their 'wait bar' fills and turns red, and they flash white. Now, this is usually fine in areas with good colour contrast but in bright areas with really low colour saturation it is really difficult to tell whose turn it is, especially if two characters' wait bars fill simulatenously. Similarly, you are notified that an enemy is charging up an ability to use by the same white flash, which again is not readily apparent in low saturation areas with bright colours. I have little knowledge of the limitations of the RPG Maker interface, but in this regard I feel the battle interface could have been built better.
That said, the battle animations and particle effects for spells and abilities play out smoothly and are well done, and the diverse beastiary of enemies encountered are appropriately thematic for where they are found and the more cleverly named of them are aptly so. The game maintains an acceptable framerate, and apart from periodic pauses in isolated instances where the game informs me it is 'loading' there is no graphical stuttering.
Spells are learned inorganically and the screen on which they are learned is better described as a dark cave than a tree. It is needlessly large, and the little amount of the map that is visible on screen gives no clues as to which spells are in which direction until you stumble onto them, wandering aimlessly through it. I honestly would have rather had a cascade menu with each spell, a button press to unlock and branching menus to power up each attribute (Speed, Power, Mana Cost) than this... mess. The way in which Skill Unlock points are obtained makes some semblance of sense, however. Each one is obtained by completing a story segment, usually through defeating a boss. Though gaining Skill Upgrade points is frustrating and nonsensical to say the least, as they are loot objects in dungeons or obtained through talking to NPCs, rather than leveling up. However, the variety of spells and abilities available are fairly vast, each with different effects and power levels, and are unique to each character. I would have preferred a more heuristic approach to learning them, though.
Which brings me to the next point - magic is WAY overvalued in this game, especially during bosses with adds. At my current playtime I have 3 characters unlocked - the main character, Melrose (summoner), a mage and an archer. Melrose and the archer do little damage of any consequence with their basic attacks, and don't have enough mana to reliably use their spells to deal and recover damage. Whereas the mage, while having really high mana costs can usually wipe the field clean in one area of effect cast, and continue to do this reliably for many battles consecutively as long as the archer feeds her mana with his own abilities. A very big contrast to most other RPGs comparable to this.
The puzzles present in this game are generally very good, reaching and even exceeding complexity found in games like The Legend of Zelda. I have scratched my head for a while trying to work out exactly what to do with them, and even had to ask for help on one occasion. In this regard I give the game a very high grade.
The maps are generally well laid out, if sometimes needlessly large and complicated. I felt as if some of the areas were built to have complex routes to navigate through and multiple dead ends for complexity's sake, rather than to actually serve a purpose. Sure, some of them have treasure at the end, but others are just... there. Add to that random collision objects that pepper some of the maps and navigating them can be somewhat frustrating at times, but this is only an issue in very isolated instances and doesn't permeate the entire game. There are also frequently really long distances that need to be travelled through the world map, with no random encounters or treasure to discover to break up the monotony of trekking around the world looking for the next area entrance.
The crafting available in the game is somewhat esoteric. Recipes are found throughout the game in various places, but the materials required are often not that common without grinding and the interface for crafting is clunky at best. It's often easier to grind currency to buy items at shops and ignore crafting altogether until much later in the game, where crafting seems to be required to create relic quality equipment.
The music is okay, and what little voice acting is present is well done. I haven't encountered any audio stuttering, glitches or any other annoyances with it. The game has good KBM and gamepad support, though it seems notably easier to play with a gamepad than KBM, but that may just be me and not a rule.
My understanding is that a playthrough should take 30-40 hours, and with my 9-10 hours into it so far I believe that approximation to be accurate.
Overall, it's a decent little RPG. Though if you came hoping for something to rival titans like Final Fantasy, Legend of Dragoon, Star Ocean or Phantasy Star and take a walk down memory lane, you're probably better off spending the couple of extra dollars and getting an actual Final Fantasy game. If you just want a nice little RPG to get your turn-based fix, Whisper of a Rose is for you.

The old Sonic the Hedgehog trilogy (& Knuckles, also Sonic CD) are some of the finest gems of gaming from the early 90s during the 16bit era. Considering how beloved these games are, and how Sega's newer takes on Sonic games have been...a mixed bag, perhaps a return to the basics was in order. Hiring Christian Whitehead, PagodaWest Games and Headcannon to take care of the development was probably for the best, and the result shows.
You can probably guess what I think by now. Sonic Mania is a fantastic game overall! It plays almost exactly like the old 16bit classics, but refined for a modern audience. Everything is here, the gorgerous 2D environments, the platforming,
, the absolutely amazing music and the speed.
In fact, my only point of criticism is that I feel there are too many old zones present and not enough new ones (from what I understand that was a corporate decision on Sega's part, so I won't really hold it against the developers). But at least the older zones do bring something new to the table, especially during the second act, whether it be the bouncy goo in Chemical Plant Zone or the "cleanse the air to not lose rings" gimmick in Oil Ocean Zone.
While the game as a whole is praiseworthy, there are some things that are annoying. Instant-death crushing is quite common especially in the later stages due to the way the hitboxes work, and on more than one occassion it felt like a real cheap way to die (I'm pretty sure I was standing next to that platform moving up and down, as opposed to under it, thank you very much!). It's not something that detracts significantly, but it's a bit of a pace-breaker and a general nuisance.
Also, some of the bosses are a pain, namely Mirage Saloon Zone Act 1 (depth perception in a 2D sprite-based environment is pretty iffy) and Oil Ocean Zone Act 2 (That robotic squid is just a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥overall).
One final note, the soundtrack is breathtakingly amazing.  Kudos to composer Tee Lopes for creating what has become my favorite 2D Sonic soundtrack. From start to finish, the music really helps immersing the player into the game, and is just an absolute joy to listen to in general.
Pros:
- Amazing throwback to the old 2D Sonic games.
- Fun and varied level design.
- Absolutely wonderful music.
- A plethora of Easter Eggs and stuff to unlock.
Cons:
- Too many old zones, I would have loved to see what the developers could have done with more entirely new zones.
- Death by crushing is a bit too common for my tastes, and a few of the bosses are a pain to deal with

With the distance of time and many updates later, I played this game again and a lot of the things which frustrated me have been fixed. I enjoyed the game. The thing to note about this and most 4X games is that it takes several days to play through one game, so I generally don't have time anymore to pickup and play this game casually. The factions have some interesting variety to their play styles as well, so unlike most 4X games, choosing a faction to play is more than just an aesthetic skin change and slight tweak in abilities: It actually feels different and unique in a good way.

After finally passing 600 hours of playtime in this game, I think its time I left a review on it. Since I bought this game I've watched empires collapse, formed my own, failed horribly, and suceeded against all odds, and still there are things that keep bringing me back to it.
The micromanagement of your realm is just enough that it's fun and actually impacts how your game plays. The grand scope part of the game is a lot like managing an empire in real life (I assume) in the fact that it's difficult, but can be mastered through some good effort. For me though, it's better to be a vassal rather than a ruler, because you can focus on your dynasty. There's something really satisfying about having distant relatives in Russia, Africa, and the Middle East without you ever leaving England yourself. Having a huge, branching dynsaty tree is something I go for every game. It's diffcult, but fun when it pays off. You can join factions and defensive pacts, force your liege to give you a county, or even your own country, or wage a multi-front war against the Holy Roman Empire because the Kaiser wanted Ulm.
There are a few drawbacks like the fact that some content that should have been in the base game is locked away in DLC, or the combat system that is essentially Quantity over Quality (usually). Your characters can just randomly contract diseases without there being any disease in your province, which I suppose is possible, but when my King contracts Leprosy for no reason, dies at 24, and hands my kingdom to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ relative, for the 5th time, it starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Also, I'm pretty sure that there is some sort of code in place to keep the number of Men in the world down. Since men pass on their bloodline, they create more characters when they have children, which slows the game down after a while since it has to keep track of all of the people. More than once have I had an heir who produced 6 daughters, but not a single time have I had someone crank out a bunch of sons, not to mention the shorter lifespan for males.
Honestly though, if you're willing to pay for all of the DLC as well (It's practically required for a true experience) CK2 is an amazingly amazing game. It's like playing through a story book. I still remember forming the Kingdom of Ireland over the course of a few real-life weeks, only for it to dissolve before my eyes due to a run in of a bunch of bad luck;
My only son died of Pnuemonia, my daughters died when they were infants, my wife was possessed, the King of England (who was a Nordic Pagan) was gearing up for a holy conquest of my land, my brother was plotting my death with numerous backers, and I was climbing up to age 70 with my brother-in-law (not the one plotting my death) set up as the one to inherit, and because he wasn't of my dynasty, I would lose the game if my character died before producing a male heir.
100 reloads later and all I managed to do was lose the English-Irish holy war 37 times, die of old age 29 times, get assassinated 17 times, give birth to a half-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥/half-dead girl 13 times, have a son die a month after child birth 3 times, and finally, after gaining the "depressed" trait (which I don't blame my guy for at all), I killed myself and watched the end screen tick along after two weeks of hard work, going from a count, to a king, to a corpse. Such is the way of CK2, and that is the reason I play it; you never know how it's gonna end.

Oblivion seems to be the least appreciated of the contemporary Elder Scrolls games; somewhere between the incredibly simplistic design of Skyrim and the sprawling web of Morrowind, in my opinon Oblivion is better than either for the person who wants to play a solid RPG and enjoy being immersed in it without having to practically live in the game. Since pretty much everyone has played Skyrim, I'll use it as a reference point for comparison in this review.
This would be a really long review if I wrote down all the unique facets of Oblivion that i love, but I'll list a few of the major ones.
- Firstly, IMO the rolling, forested hills of Cyrodiill are much prettier and more enjoyable to wander around in than the rugged landscapes of both Morrowind and Skyrim. Plus, whereas 3/4s of the quests in Skyrim take you into some underground ruin for half an hour, you actually get to enjoy the surface detail throughout most of Oblivion, which is nice.
- The cities in Oblivion are larger and generally more unique than the cities and towns in Skyrim.
- Being able to enchant armor and trinkets with spell effects like chameleon, detect life, water walking, and water breathing is a nice feature that was unfortunately removed from Skyrim (many spell effects were removed entirely).
- Creating custom spells with whatever spell effects you desire via spellmaking altars is a cool feature, and adds a level of experimentation and customization to magic-based characters that Skyrim fails to match.
- Many of the faction quest lines are more unique and enjoyable in Oblivion than their counterparts in Skyrim. The Dark Brotherhood, for instance, offers some very intriguing contracts that involve more than just slipping a dagger into someone's back. I also enjoy the Fighter's Guild line better than the Companions in Skyrim as well. The main quest isn't quite as interesting, but the game does well enough without it.
- The Shivering Isles, Oblivion's large expansion, adds a TON of extra content, and the island seems larger and more detaied than Solstheim from the Dragonborn DLC. The Knights of the Nine also introduces a pretty neat quest line, although it pales in comparison to Skyrim's Dawnguard DLC.
Although the game has aged a little over the past decade, it's fairly easy to slip into and provides countless hours of entertainment, no matter what kind of character you choose to play. I wholeheartedly reccommend Oblivion to anyone who has an interest in open world RPGs.

Endless Legend is like Civ, which is fantastic because Civ is a great, sturdy game, with some flaws though. There are some differences between the two.
In Endless Legend, you have 9 aysmmetrical (completely different) factions to choose from (with the exception of 2 as far as I know), each have their own ways of obtaining victory in an easier way, much like Civ, there's Expansion, Elimination, Science, Diplomatic, and so on...
Unlike most RTS's and TBS's/4Xs (Turn-Based Strategies), In Endless Legend, each faction only has 3 different military units.
Now, I know what you're thinking: Where's the diversity?!?! BUT, the COOLEST thing about your armies is that you can change what weapons, armour, and trinkets they can have equipped, depending on what you have researched at the time, and then retrofit your current armies to have the newest equipment, adding in an RPG-like element! Also, better equipment made from different alloys you research have special properties to each of them that add damage to certain enemies (flying, infantry, etc...) or that buffs your unit or army (regen, health boost, etc...). Same goes for heroes, in which you start out with one hero, then can buy more via in-game marketplace you have to research to unlock first. Also, all armies and heros level up over time, making them more powerful, and for heros, have a skill tree.
ALSO, so that just 3 units doesn't discourage you; There are what's called "minor" factions that are basically neutral camps all over the different regions. If you have a city in that region, and destroy the minor faction's little base, you can assimilate them, thereby being able to produce the combat units that they create as well, so there's a lot more to it than just the 3 base units you have!
Personally, just having 3 units is so much better, so you don't have to build a crap ton of different units and worry about "what is strong/weak against what" and have a huge ordeal over it.
The combat is supremely better than Civ, being that, there's actually combat (lol sarcasm...sorta). The combat is completely tactical, meaning once you initiate a battle, you get to organize your force on the board, and then take turns targeting and attacking/defending attacks, it actually takes some tactical knowledge to win a battle! Unlike Civ, where you just send a gajillion people into one square/hexagon and hope for the best.  But if you know you're going to win a battle without any casualities (in which the game gives you statistics before you go into battle), you can auto sim the fight so you don't waste time on your turn.
There's a lot more that I would like to say, but most people won't read this far anyway.... SO:
Pros
___________
-Beautiful Graphics
-Aysmmetrical Factions
- Very, Very Solid Gameplay
- Fantastic Combat System
- The "Endless" Universe, which is freaking sweet
- Simple Army System (3 diff military) With Awesome Equipment Interchangeability
Cons
____________
- If you haven't played Civ, it's going to take a little bit to get used to the interface and everything....but that's common sense. No turn-based game is easy the first time around.
-There's only one faction that is preferred to win by elimination, which is perfectly fine, but they can't go to peace, an alliance, or even trade things with other factions. If you're using that faction and playing with friends you want to ally with, you're not going to be able to, unless you can pre-organize teams in the menu before starting the game (whether you can or not, i'm not sure, haven't had much time to play to find that out yet).
- I can't think of anything else.
Other Thoughts
____________
In the past, I would've totally recommended Civ and I have played it a lot with a bunch of friends over time. But, Endless Legend changes everything. Don't buy Civ, buy this game, it's just better. I highly recommend it.

Endless Legend is the best 4X game I have played.  I really liked Civilization V and was kind of expecting Endless Legend to be like that but rough around the edges.  Part of this is because I thought Endless Space was a really good game at its core, but had some major problems, especially with late-game combat.  Instead I got a game that significantly better than Civliization in some aspects and on par with it in most others.  It has a few problems that I'll talk about below, but they don't stop it from being my favorite new game for 2014.
====== PROS ======
Part of what makes this game so good is the UI.  Everything is incredibly clean and consistent.  For instance, right clicking on any menu anywhere brings you back a menu, so if you get lost you can easily get back to the normal map screen.  Battles take place directly on the overworld map (more on that later).  Most of the UI doesn't change when this happens, and you can freely swap between the battle and city, hero, or technology management without a loading screen or any extra UI lag.  Highlighting over any of your resource counts shows you whether your income is due to a hero skill, city, trade route, etc.  All of the UI elements like this are very concise but also show you more information when you need it.  Endless Legend is very complicated like most 4X games, so having such a clean and consistent UI helps it a lot.
If you've played Endless Space, you'll find many elements of this game to be familiar.  Many of the luxury and strategic resources have the same names, the FIDS and approval systems are pretty much identical, max army size is identical to max fleet size except that all units count for one capacity.  You start with one hero and there's no cap on how many you can have, but otherwise heroes work the same.  They also count as units during strategic battles.
The thing that makes Endless Legend so much better than its sibling is the strategic battles.  When two armies fight each other (army size is usually 4-8 units, depending on game era), any tiles on the main map within 3-4 tiles of the main armies are part of the battleground.  Other armies on both sides join the battle as reinforcements.  This is similar to the system Age of Wonders uses, except since armies don't need to be immediately adjacent, it doesn't have the problem where an attacker can surround a fringe army instead of the center one to get a more favorable engagement.  If a defender has five armies near a city, they will all take part in all battles for the city until they are dead or have moved away.
Before the first turn, the battlefield is split in half and players can arrange their units in the main attacking and defending army however they would like.  Then, on every turn of the actual battle, two new units from reinforcing armies join the battle on each side.  It's not uncommon to see battles with 12 units on a single side during the later phases.  The battle ends when one side and its reinforcements are all dead, or after six turns have passed.  In the latter case, the armies can sometimes re-engage or reposition that same turn.  If they've both used all their movement and attack points, then the battle will have to continue on the next turn.  One thing to note is that you don't have total control over your units during battle; instead you provide attack or defend orders at the beginning of each turn and can select a unit to prioritize.  Your units will mostly do the right thing when their turn comes, but sometimes this can have unexpected results, and learning to deal with the combat AI is a thing you'll need to learn.  That said, you can almost always get your units to do what you want, so this is only a minor annoyance.
Each faction only has four different units it can build, one starting and one that can be unlocked in each of the first three eras.  For the rest of the game, you instead unlock new kinds of weapons, armor, and accessories to equip them with.  Weapons and armor tend to be simple number bonuses that give a strength advantage to armies with a tech lead, while accessories provide meaningful tactical choices, such as extra movement (incredibly helpful on slower units), health regeneration, or bonus initiative.  In general this is one thing I feel that Endless Legend does well.  Many types of items, skills, and researches in the game provide upgrades to a very specific thing, which makes your choices feel very meaningful.
There are a bunch of other things that are really nice and polished about this game, but the last one I'll talk about is the faction selection.  The game has eight factions (you get a ninth if you buy the collector's edition of Dungeon of the Endless, but it's just a reskin of another faction).  The vaulters are probably the most "normal" faction, and are the easiest to play if you're used to something like Civilization.  The other factions are very different, and range from different types of bonuses to breaking the core rules of the game.  For instance, the Cultists are not allowed to expand and must immediately raze any cities they capture.  In return, their city grows much faster and better than other factions, and they periodically get free units from the minor factions they've encountered.  The Roving Clans are not allowed to declare war on other factions, but their trade route bonuses are massive and they can impose pretty big diplomatic restrictions on other factions.  Using these factions requires a different playstyle and I'm still pretty bad at them, even though the vaulters feel very natural to me.
====== CONS ======
The game is usually over part-way through, but the victory conditions are all pretty hard to reach so the game just keeps going.  This is a common problem in 4X games so most of you won't be surprised, but Endless Legend doesn't really do anything to fix it.  Games can easily last 10-12 hours, even when one team has a huge advantage at the 4-hour mark.  For instance, you can get the Conquest victory by controlling 80% of the regions.  I realize there are some factions like the Cultists that don't need to expand much and could still be in the game at that point, but 80% requires something like 50 cities on a standard-sized map, which takes forever and means you'll have destroyed and seriously hampered most of the enemy factions.  I don't know lowering the victory conditions would ruin the game, if the games I played were just really lopsided, or if this is a fundamental issue with the game.
There's a fair amount of RNG involved at the beginning of the game, especially with respect to which minor faction quests you get.  I had a game where I was playing the cultists, and all of the minor faction quests required me to have strategic resources that weren't in my area.  The cultists rely heavily on pacifying minor factions, since their base units are awful at fighting, and this is doable with impossible quests but quite a bit harder.  Regions also vary wildly in quality, and while late-game researches can turn a bad region into a good one, your cities' growth and production heavily depends on favorable anomalies in the early game because the bonuses they provide are rather large.  That said, this is always going to be a factor in a game with random elements that lets you make meaningful choices; sometimes you get stuck with only bad choices, and learning to play well means learning how to deal with them.
Overall this game is fantastic.  If you like 4X games then you should definitely get it.  I'm not sure if it would make a non-4X player like the genre, as I came into it having played many of them.

This should be a good game, but it's not because it is horrendously unstable. The reason it autosaves every turn is because it crashes constantly, especially on a long game. According to the forums this is a chronic problem and the developers admit it has a serious memory leak but they can't find it. It typically uses over 2.5GB (I have 8) of memory. And asking players to submit crash reports in a popup without telling them HOW or WHERE is just stupid.
After getting used to the speed of the game and the quirks of the mechanics (it has some traits that will really throw experienced Civ players) the actual gameplay is very enjoyable and a nice challenge.
However, the stability issues are so bad that they really shouldn't  have released it yet. If you like long games and choose the "Endless" option, which lasts 600 turns, then once you get past ~300 the game might go a dozen turns at a time without crashing, or it might crash EVERY SINGLE TURN until the end of the game. Even if you choose a shorter game length it will still crash so often as to be infuriating.
I would only buy this game if you can get it on sale, because you may give up on it pretty quickly if you can't stand it crashing all the time.
Despite the enjoyable gameplay, I really can't recommend this game because the instability makes it seem like a very amateurish effort, which is a shame because I really liked Endless Space and was hoping to like this game too.

Imagine if all of history was laid out before you. It's all going to roughly play out exactly as it always has, but as a player you have a choice: pick one of the world powers of the era and see if you can keep them afloat with all the resources available to them or pick one of the other nations and see if you can survive next to the big boys.
The point of the game is that you see how long a family line you can keep. The best way to do this is by having as much territory as possible, have a large family and let them prosper. Unfortunately, dark plots and random events are set out to ensure they end up on top. While you'll start as a king, it won't be long before a envious family member eyes the throne and takes you out. If you had children, you continue play as them and try to keep the family line going.
It is. Crusader Kings II (and all so called "Grand Strategy" games) have a steep learning curve. Added to that confusion is the fact that everything uses names and terminology of the ages, so you'll undoubtedly be confused when you want to attack a neighbor for their land and the game tells you that you can't without casus belli. Of course, that's one reason the game is so addictive, while you play you also end up learning.
Of course, the genre isn't for everyone so I highly recommend checking out a few people playing on YouTube to see if it's interesting. At the end of the day, it's little more than a strategy game where you never directly control combat, politics are more important than fighting and your life is basically a choose your own adventure game.
If you're into the idea of Civilization, but the combat feels rote or boring, Crusader Kings II might be worth a look. If you like historical simulation, then the game is certainly up your alley. However if the idea of a game where years can pass and nothing really happens, or if you want a game with balance, you'll probably want to look elsewhere. There's admittedly a lot of challenge in trying to take a small country and change history, but there is a reason they never actually changed history. You can just pick one of the kingdoms that was successful, but then the game is much easier.

Whipser of a Rose is great, until you actually start playing it.
In the opening scenes, I was immediately drawn into the game. Whisper of a Rose has an immersive narrative pulling from the real world into a fantasy one with a played out but fitting transition. Everything in the game is quite symbolic of the paralells between the real world and the dream world you enter. Melrose is a unique character to follow around as far as RPG worlds go, and the cast that was starting to form as I played through seemed at least not totally cheesy (but if the super powerful person who can't control their powers! trope bothers you, red flag). Unfortunately, once the opening scenes end and you actually start existing in the game world, the reality sets in that this not an exciting adventure, it's a typical JPRG grindquest without the tension relievers most of them typically throw in.
I have to state before I get too far into this review, that I only played 5 hours of the gameplay. Maybe after the 5 hours I played, the game would magically become 200% better, but I find it doubtful. It's obvious from the get-go that the game was not very well play tested early on in the development process. If it was, the obvious feedback would have been that The areas within the game are far too large. How often do you hear people complaining about that in an RPG game? Typically when RPGs have large areas, when you go well off the beaten path, you are rewarded. This is something WoaR attempts to do, but fails miserably at.
Let me paint the picture. You are going through the dungeons with your party, spamming the attack button on small groups of enemies because it literally takes less time to do that than to cast a spell that would kill the enemies in one hit (in addition to your turns refilling, your spells have their own cast bar. You also have to wait for every other characters turn to end before your spells go off). So you're going through the area, killing off the exact same enemies over and over and over and over and over again, trying to see if the path you're traveling on is the main one or a little detour. When you get to a dead end, you see a chest. "Ah, this isn't the right way, but maybe I'll get something cool!" you may think. But no, what you'll get is a weapon or armor piece that literally increases a stat by one, or memory orbs. Memory orbs are the currency of the game. So imagine spending literally 30 minutes going through a dead end path (I'm not exaggerating, the game is that poorly planned) only to end up at a chest that gives you more of the same money that you're already frustrated of seeing... and that's it. YOu have to backtrack all the way back to the beginning of that path and find a new one.
This is all the game is in the first 4 real hours of playing it. A mindless treck through bats to find very small upgrades or useless money. That's it. I didn't even encounter a TOWN in the first 4 hours of gameplay. The game is a constant motion forward through dungeons. There was one point where I found an inn, but there was nothing to do or explore there, and there were no NPCs worth talking to (about 3 total anyways). Typically in JRPGs, towns offer a kind of tension relief their repetitive nature can sometimes cause. It gives the player a chance to relax, plan, and become immersed in the world they are exploring. Whisper of a rose ingnoring this convention in an otherwise convetional game becomes one of its greatest flaws.
I'm sad that I quit the game so soon into it. The environments are gorgeous and inventive, the story, while a bit cliche, is rather interesting and makes sense with the surroundings you find yourself in... but the gameplay is just... boring. That's all there is to it. Perhaps at some point, the game does a complete 180 and the paths becomes more linear and the combat becomes more complex, but I personally couldn't force myself to sit through any more of it after the sidequest boss I spent an hour and a half trying to find died in about three turns.... and then I realized I would have to backtrack all the way back to a teleporter just to get back into the story (would probably take at least 20 minutes to do). I didn't want to hate this game, but unfortunately Whisper of a Rose stands as a perfect example of how a great story and world can be hindered by the actual gameplay of a poorly planned JRPG.

Immensely game-deprived at a certain point in time, I found Whisper of a Rose on Steam. My first thought was "It looks very pretty. Immensely pretty, in fact. Whoever made the art for this game was very good." Honestly, the trailer and blurb sounded so mundane and cliché ridden that I considered not giving this the time of day but I thought, maybe advertising the game was just harder than writing it? So I sat down and started playing it.
Four hours later, I regret this decision. The writing the bland and cliché as it gets with only the slightest hint of self-awareness (which, I will not be afraid to admit, shows promise but I don't care enough to pursue it), the combat never gets anywhere, and it takes about three hours just to get the ability to upgrade your skills.
But the WORST of it comes when you're going through Butterfly Forest. At one point, you're impeded by a group of butterflies that you're not allowed to touch else you get cursed. So what you have to do? BACKTRACK TO THE LAST LEVEL to get an item that will let you pass! Uggggggggggh... Fine, whatever. So I go back but the game misdirects me; I get dragonfly eggs instead of dragonfly droppings. Or maybe those WERE the dragonfly droppings but I'm not using them right. Either way, I don't know how to proceed.
I can tell you now that, even if your JRPG well is so dry that your tears are literally the only things that allow it to hold any sort of liquid, Whisper of a Rose is not worth it. The art is pretty, though. Whoever made the art assets for this game, if you're reading this, you are fantastic. Sadly, good aesthetics does not a good game make and thus this game has effectively stolen $7.50 of mine that I'm never getting back.

When I first saw the trailer I was immediately reminded of Alice in Wonderland and had to get it! I haven't played far yet (and apparently the game is over 25 hours so I still have a long way to go) but here are my thoughts so far:
Story: Very interesting and bittersweet. I feel like the story was written by a 17 year old girl, but in a good way, because it makes the story and dialogue believable. You also see the story behind the other characters, and it seems like the villains are heroes in their own way. It's very good, I almost teared up at a certain scene in the beginning (no spoilers).
Graphics: Beautiful! It has a nice old school look. It doesn't look perfect and modern, but that's good, because it fits in with the entire game's "retro" feeling. I've only played a little bit and have already seen SO many different areas with a lot of variation! There's a candy land, sewers, a museum, a dark school, etc.
Music: Sounds great. Some songs are just "OK". They fit the mood but are nothing special. Other tracks (like when you fight the first boss) are absolutely amazing. I wish I could fight that boss over and over just to listen to the track!
Gameplay: The most important part! I really like that Melrose can summon a helper. It makes the beginning of the game more fun and strategic before you get the other main characters in your party. The battles are also real time so you can time your actions with the enemy! It's a lot of fun!
Conclusion: It's a really amazing game. It's right up to par with To The Moon and Skyborn for me. Actually, as a game it's WAY better! But I still have to finish it so I can't say for sure yet which of the three is best.

I've played this game for a few years now, bought the first DLC pack and one skin, and I feel like the investments towards the developers was worth it. People who rate this game negatively because it's going free to play are simply seflish because they bought a game 4 years ago for maybe $5 and played at most 10 games. Now there are a few cons to this game, but my month of playing makes me feel like this game is definitely worth a shot (once it goes free to play).
Pros:
-The graphics are simple, yet detailed. It doesn't feel in your face.
-The sound and music is great. One of my favorite soundtracks.
-The gameplay is simple, yet there is good strategy involved. All characters have 3 attacks (some have more than 3 abilities when including their attacks) but the range of characters in the game requires you to think about what is appropriate to do for your team.
-The devs seem to be very understanding. Now it's an online competitive game, so no one is going to like the devs. Hell, most of the time I don't like the devs, but in reality they are pretty kind and respond accordingly to the communities desires typically. Recently they went back on their decision against offline games when the community lashed against it.
-The game is not very demanding. I have a terrible computer and it runs just fine on it.
Cons:
-Small map pool.
this is most likely due to the fact that it's a 2D MOBA with only 3 players on each team and there is only so much variety you can get out of that, so this is excusable. The only real differences between the maps as well are the mids.
-You will usually have your character-of-the-month that gets a big buff during an update and everybody plays them. This is inevitable in almost every competitive online game, sadly.
I feel like the game has made some big improvements, despite its dying playerbase which will hopefully be fixed by the Free To Play update. Characters such as Ayla don't bully low ranking players that hard anymore. The community seems to be much less toxic. More games seem to be fair now than they used to.
Wait until the Free To Play update and give this game a try. No harm if it's free. If you enjoy it, I definitely recommend buying a skin for your favorite character so you can support the devs.

QP Shooting - Dangerous!! is the story of a dog girl named QP trying to reclaim her pudding and find out why no one remembers pudding.
The game is easy to pick up and hard to master, and provides a challenge to players of all skill level with multiple difficulties, and two game modes: A classic arcade mode, where once you run out of lives, you have to start out, and a conquest mode, where you can save inbetween each stage, and even go back and beat previous stages, which isn't as useless as one would think! By going back and re-beating stages and doing better than you did before, you have the chance to finish with more lives, which means you start the next stage with more lives!
QP Shooting - Dangerous features R-Bits as QP's main method of attacking. During each playthrough of arcade or one save of conquest, you can set 3 different formations of R-Bits. R-Bit formations can be bought at the in game store, featuring the bunny girl Aru. R-Bit formations can do many things, such as sit in front of you, sit behind you, form a shell around you, or even rotate around you.
The music is very catchy, the art is appealing, and features a fun story. The game doesn't take itself very seriously, which is nice. Sadly the original QP isn't on steam, so QP's relations with the characters in the story isn't very well known to us. There is also the mysterious Kyupita, a character mentioned in game, but never seen.
Bonus: If you own 100% Orange Juice, another game created by Orange_Juice and translated by Fruit Bat Factory, you unlock a character in the game.
I highly recommend buying this game. Very well made bullet hell from Orange_Juice.

If you have the choice of buying CIV Beyond Earth or Endless Legend, buy Endless Legend.
The combat is entertaining to watch, as well as more intuitive and responsive. The graphic style of the game is gorgeous, and the sound design is very nice as well. The factions have unique personalities to them (unlike Beyond Earth) and each race plays significantly differently (vaulters choosing a holy resource that buffs their economy vs. Drakken who can force diplomatic decisions). The region system is an interesting addition to the game and adds an element of significance to each city you own. Minor factions can be integrated into your empire, providing powerful and useful units to build your armies with. The unit customization is intuitive, and relies on you as the player to make sure your units remain effective on the battlefield. The hero units can change the tide of a battle by healing or using range attacks against enemies.
If you want a solid 4x strategy game that is new and exciting to play, pick up this game.

Pros:

-AI are actually good at avoiding you, unlike some sims

Cons:
-Sound feels a little dated

Overall its an above average sim for me, and its actually fun to play. Note: There is a huge glitch in this game that should be forwarned before buying. If you use Steam Cloud and have more than one computer, using this game on a second computer will stop your career mode from saving -ever- again on either computer. The fix is simple enough, you just don't use Steam Cloud for this game.
Challenging and aggressive AI makes for enjoyable offline play. The tracks have a somewhat dated look, but the bikes are beautifully modeled.

Oblivion, oh the memories. Successor to Morrowind, predecessor to Skyrim, a brilliantly awesome Elder Scrolls game with the by far worst main quest, infamous for the abysmally outrageous horse DLC, which started DLC content in the entire gaming industry in the first place.
Oblivion is gaming history, that much is sure, but the more important question is, whether it is still up to speed by today's RPG standards. The short answer is: Yes and no. Oblivion does indeed have quite a lot of the comfort functions we players today are accustomed to, but it also feels very outdated from a design perspective. For example Oblivion was the first Elder Scrolls title which was focused on console releases (Morrowind having been available on the first XBox, as one user felt the primal urge of pointing out) and therefore butchered its entire interface to make it as console friendly as possible, something which Morrowind was not back when it released. This meant drastically reduced tooltips, completely absurd item descriptions and names in all but the English localization (Potion of inferior Invisibility = "Ptn. o. inf. Inv." etc.) and very undescriptive info boxes to make every font large enough to be readable from 2-3 meters away on screen. It was an outrage back then, it still is bad interface design today.
Interface wise, Morrowind was ahead of it's time and considering console layouts today, from a design perspective regarding a heavily complex RPG universe, it still is.
I wouldn't really recommend Oblivion to anyone currently anymore, if it wasn't for the Shimmering Isles expansion which entirely made up for the bland main plot of the base game and had extremely memorable and mindbogglingly insane quests. Do you remember the Quest in Skyrim where you wake up naked without all your gear after a night of drinking and embark on a quest to get uncursed by a Daedra prince and get your stuff back? Imagine an entire Addon which solely consists of quests like that. Shimmering Isles is probably the best Addon Bethesda ever made and it is solely playable by playing Oblivion. Therefore I still do recommend Oblivion, although I personally would rather recommend Morrowind and / or Skyrim to people who'd want to get introduced the the Elder Scrolls series.

, the debut production of
, is perhaps the most often updated title in their catalogue, with each new edition boasting additional content and a myriad of fixes and other updates. It's hard not to see the love for the game and its players in the actions of the developer, who despite working on two completely new titles, never forgot about the fans of the original game from 2009 that can safely be called a cult classic now.
As with most RPG titles, the vital part of
's charm and appeal is its storyline and setting. Set several years into the future, the story features a college student by the name of Melrose, who's struggling to keep her life from completely falling apart. Not only she comes from a poor and pathological family (both parents abusive towards her), but she also faces the everyday problems of school bullies targeting her and most of the other students simply not bothering to even notice her. Eventually, when she finds out about a device that would allow her to travel into a happy and colorful Dreamworld, she immediately decides to get it and use it on herself - ignoring the warning that the iDream is a mere prototype and thus there are certain risks involved with using it.
And so she ventures forth into the Dreamworld but quickly discovers that it's not the peaceful, happy place it was supposed to be. As opposed to her wishes, it's more often shaped by her fears, both those she well knows of and those residing in her subconsciousness. She is instructed to find a way out of there... and despite her understandable reservations in the beginning, she eventually realizes that she must do so.
Thus begins her journey, full of sudden twists and mortal dangers.
The synopsis above may have reminded you about
, or Carroll's
- and while it may be bearing many similarities to those, it's also quite original, especially in comparison to many other indie jRPG titles which feature a destined-to-save-the-world protagonist in a fantasy setting, with most of the events being quite easy to predict. Melrose's role isn't to save everyone in the Dreamworld, she's merely a bypasser who's trying to leave. Whether or not she helps some of the NPCs (there's an extensive array of tasks the player is nowhere near being forced to complete in order to progress further) is entirely up to her... or to you. It's a very interesting spectacle of how a young woman matures, with being a self-centered teenager with multiple personal issues in the beginning and becoming a decent and brave young woman not hesitating to do the right thing in the end.
This is primarily Melrose's story, and via interactions with two of her Dreamworld-born teammates, the player will soon realize that they both serve to show
character depth, however not for a moment losing any of their own. However, with the appearance of the last party member, things become even darker than before. Christina may seem like a generic tsundere deadpan snarker at first, but she is also just as well developed a character despite not being the main star of the show. Her fears are much darker than Melrose's and when they are revealed, it becomes fully clear how tragic a past she had.
If you are a sensitive person and can invest yourself emotionally into the game, you'll find many scenes genuinely moving. I did shed a tear or two while baring witness to the no holds barred beatdown Melrose's deadbeat dad gave her very early in the game, just as I did when at one point her memories were in large part erased and everything looked hopeless. I genuinely felt bad for Christina when the horror of her past became known... and it's a lot from me because I don't cry a whole lot. In fact, almost not at all.
As far as the visuals go, the game is just as awesome. It takes time (or looking into the game's file structure) to realize that this is RPG Maker XP, due to a variety of reasons: first off, there's barely any stock material left in, mostly limited to spell effects during battles and a few leftover tiles in the areas - the entire remainder of the graphic resources is completely new and fresh. And much more detailed than the RPG Maker stock resources -
the main characters. For pixel art, this is outstandingly realistic - visible limbs, proper body proportions and vivid animation of movement - something previously unseen in RPG Maker based titles. Here's how this looks from the technical perspective: RPG Maker VX and VX Ace titles usually have their chibi characters with heads doubling the size of the rest of the body on a single tile, whereas their predecessor engine RPG Maker XP has them a bit more realistic, utilizing two tiles - out of which one is usually for the face and another for the body.
uses
for a character in total. Go figure. That's not all - the enemies have been given the same treatment as well, being incredibly detailed and fully animated. After this game, I found it hard to readjust to XP standard-size humans, while VX ones became a sight absolutely unbearable for me. That's right:
is downright beautiful and will steal your heart...
(as would a certain witch say) Not for any other game, not after this.
That's not all in terms of graphics - did I mention, there's barely any stock resource in the game? I think I did. Now imagine the fact that there's
unique locations I've lost count! We have a modern city, a bare, cloudy dreamworld area, a child's dream candy-filled land, a school - both real-life and nightmarishly twisted, mountain hills, a forest, several different cave systems, a valentine-themed town and an actually unsettling marionette factory.
There's also character avatars - something not available in the regular RPG Maker XP featureset (it was introduced as a stock feature in VX), and there's a lot of those, with more being promised in a future update. They've gotten a redesign since the original release of the game and both versions are equally beautiful. Each of the main characters has several of these avatars at their disposal, allowing them to fully show you the scope of emotions they're going through.
As for the musical score, it's very extensive and varied. Almost every location has its own main theme and many of the events have special tunes written for them as well. The musical styles are varied, but surprisingly consistent - that includes the new tunes written for this re-release. The music is mostly fresh, with a very small number of tracks being remixes of RPG Maker stocks (I think in the re-release there's just one such track left), or freely available on the internet (of those I think I know two). I've gotten the soundtrack album in the past and every once in a while I give it another whirl because even outside of the game, the enchanting soundtrack stands firm as a smash hit.

This game is really amazing, because it's beautiful in its imperfection. You can tell it wasn't made with a high budget, but everything is so detailed and original. The scenery varies greatly: there's a Candy Mountain, an underwater city, a fire city, a dark museum. I love the dark areas the most, they are actually quite creepy!
I played the earlier version of the game and purchased it immediately when I found out a new version was coming to Steam. The face graphics are completely new (I love them!), the dialogue has been re-written, the whole game feels more polished now.
The only downside to the game is that the beginning is a little bit slow, but it also allows you to sit back and take in the atmosphere and relax. Then later when more main characters are introduced the pace increases and battles become very strategic and exciting. The whole game feels like a build-up to the amazing climax (small spoiler: there's a huge battle on a sky scraper), but there are also a lot of interesting side-plots that get resolved.
What I love the most about the game is the symbolism. The whole game takes place inside the main character's "dream world" and everything there (even the quests!) are symbolic of a part of her personality, past and a part of human nature. The parent-child relationship is also an important theme that is explored throughout the game. At the beginning Melrose, the main character, seems a bit bratty and snotty but through her dream world the subject goes a lot deeper and you see her transition into a better person.
Concluding, I would definitely recommend this game! I'm going back to playing it again. :D Love that I can choose Summoner on first playthrough this time!

You know what really makes me sad? having to edit a review. This game is effectively abandonware at this point. It's satisfying enough, but it's just at a standstill and assuming the devs will be forever.
: I really normally don't plug early access games because I've been irritated by them in the past, but as of this moment this game is a whole lot of fun. It's one of those 'survival sandbox' types, except.. streamlined? You have health, stamina, your only way of regaining health is rare-ish healing items and rare as crap mushrooms. You start with a bow and 10 arrows, bright friggin orange jumpsuit, and your trusty PDA map thingy. You pick your way through the landscape trying not to die and also find weapons/clothing/equipment at various ruined resource caches throughout the map. It's made with the engine of the prolific hunting game by the name of: TheHunter that i've played years off steam.
: 'The hunter has become the hunted, hurrdurr'
: Bloodsplats, you see your impacts and arrows sticking out of stuff.
: You are on a giant subtropical island, swamps, beaches, mountains, and volcanic terrain
: TheHunter devs have been updating that game for years, and as satisfying as this is right now, wow!
: You basically have to make a solo multiplayer game to play, even if by yourself. As of this moment the only multiplayer games joinable are from folks who bothered to forward ports and all that. I hope that changes down the road as someone that enjoys multiplayer but also has a somewhat unstable connection.
: While by no means impossible, it so far has taken a long time to walk away from an encounter with raptors alive 50% of the time, not to mention with only a bow. I consider this game to be a DayZ lite, in that regard.
: Despite my adoration of the game, as of this moment there isn't an awful lot in terms of weaponry/dinos to hunt/be hunted. 4 guns, I think 4 different outfits (counting hats and glasses and so on) 1 bow, 3 healing items, misc hunting gear, T-rex, Utahraptors, Triceratops.
This game has a ton of potential and I would definitely recommend it. But it has serious connection issues and drops games constantly, so be ready for that. Otherwise it is a very good game.

If you have the choice of buying CIV Beyond Earth or Endless Legend, buy Endless Legend.
The combat is entertaining to watch, as well as more intuitive and responsive. The graphic style of the game is gorgeous, and the sound design is very nice as well. The factions have unique personalities to them (unlike Beyond Earth) and each race plays significantly differently (vaulters choosing a holy resource that buffs their economy vs. Drakken who can force diplomatic decisions). The region system is an interesting addition to the game and adds an element of significance to each city you own. Minor factions can be integrated into your empire, providing powerful and useful units to build your armies with. The unit customization is intuitive, and relies on you as the player to make sure your units remain effective on the battlefield. The hero units can change the tide of a battle by healing or using range attacks against enemies.
If you want a solid 4x strategy game that is new and exciting to play, pick up this game.

A great Turn based strategy that has a backstory that goes deeper than it appears. Using the already well built setting Endless Space, Endless Legend is a satisfying 4X game that actually allows you to steer away from the eXterminate portion that most 4X games end up being.

If you are on the fence about buying this game I'm going to say a couple things first. 1. Check to see if your computer meets the requirements. Double check and triple check it even. I neglected to thinking my computer could run it since it can run a lot of more demanding stuff but turns out it can't so the game crashes a lot at random. I can still play the game but it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to have to watch for crashes and restart the game. 2. You'll get much more enjoyment out of this game if you are already familiar with the Endless Space universe and lore. It's still a fine 4X strategy game but it's not too special if you don't appreciate the Endless Space lore.
That being said here's some pro con action.
Pros: Excellent soundtrack, keeping in tradition with Endless Space the game is has a very comfy atmosphere with it's music
It's damn pretty for a 4X game even on low end settings I'm impressed, I'm not sure there's another game out there that compares to this game on the graphics level in the same genre.
The AI is challenging but fair, it tends to make some really petty decisions though like "oh I see your army has visited my lands! you're banned from the market now lol" but each enemy empire has unique personalities a la the civilzation games
As mentioned earlier the lore and universe of Endless Space is important here and if you can appreciate it you'll get more out of the individual faction quests. The quests overall add something unique to the 4X genre and even though all of the sidequests tend to be random the main quests for each faction adds something cool to do when you're not doing other 4X activities.
Also keeping in tradition with Endless Space each of your units are completely customizable, well as far as weapons,  armor and accesories affecting unit stats goes.
The cons: AI is basically cheating at higher difficulties, this could be considered a pro depending on how you look at it but I don't really like it.
The combat, when you aren't auto-resolving, is a bit shallow. It basically boils down to changing positioning and firing orders each turn and watching two armies' numbers roll against eachother. Also if you build ranged units with maxed out initiative you can't lose really it's kind of disappointing. A fascinating take on 4x games that's too poorly documented and fiddly to recommend.
--Pros--
Some of the most specialized factions I've ever seen in a 4X game. They each get unique units (different classes of units, not just stat modifications) and have dramatic civilization modifiers, such as the roving clans faction that get significant economic benefits but cannot declare war.
Cities are limited to 1 per (fairly large)province, which prevents overcrowding while still giving a lot of freedom in city placement.
On top the usual forest/grassland/river tiles you would expect, there are also a plethora of "anomaly" tiles, which give powerful and unique bonuses. Each province usually has 1-3, which coupled with terrain + resources contributes to each province having its own flavor.
Interesting and varied quests.
Almost all heroes and units can be customized.
You can integrate a wide variety of minor factions (each which their own bonus and unique unit) into your empire. However, you can only do this with 1-3 minor factions, so this choice is nice way to further customize your faction.
--Cons--
Extremely poor tutorial and in-game documentation. Unlike the Civilization games, there's no help menu or in game tips. You're just kinda thrown in to flail.
Finding and reading the 60-page manual (an online pdf) helps, but lots of important mechanical details (especial faction-specific) are still not explained and need to be uncovered by coincidence / trial and error.
Examples: The cost of a technology scales based on the amount of technologies you have, INCLUDING those acquired from quests or trade, meaning you can accidentally sabotage all your future research by completely a quest for a technology you didn't need (PS: It's impossible to cancel quests.)
Even though cultists only have one main city, they get 10% of the strategic/luxury resources from a province where they have a converted village IF they have the appropriate mining technology (technology which you would never research unless you knew this rule).
As an additional frustration, this game was in early access for a while and it can be hard to tell which wikis or forum posts have outdated information about how the game's systems work.
The battle system is really bad. It's hex based like HoMM or King's Bounty, but instead of specifying moves, you specify intent. However, after 40+ godd*mn hours, I'm still not sure how to get my archers to just attack something convenient without suicidally charging into the fray. Additionally, when attacked, a unit must counterattack, consuming it's action. It's an interesting way to make initiative matter, but now you have imprecise commands which are ignored half the time anyway, and the combat frequently feels like a comedy of errors.
Additionally, combat takes place on the geography of the world map (but with cities and uninvolved units removed). Even leaving aside coastal battles (where you might not even be able to deploy most of your army because you had a sea at your back) the geography complications can play havoc with your units' AI.
There's a bunch of other minor inconveniences, like being unable to see a unit's abilities at various points where that information's important. Or being given a settler when razing a city, and being unable to sell him (meaning you just pay upkeep the rest of the game, unless you want to expand or suicide him.)
--Conclusion--
For all the cool ideas the game brings, I was too frequently frustrated with the lack of information or the fiddly mechanics. That said, if you're a very patient person who's interested in the unique elements of this game, I could see you having fun with it.

Oblivion, oh the memories. Successor to Morrowind, predecessor to Skyrim, a brilliantly awesome Elder Scrolls game with the by far worst main quest, infamous for the abysmally outrageous horse DLC, which started DLC content in the entire gaming industry in the first place.
Oblivion is gaming history, that much is sure, but the more important question is, whether it is still up to speed by today's RPG standards. The short answer is: Yes and no. Oblivion does indeed have quite a lot of the comfort functions we players today are accustomed to, but it also feels very outdated from a design perspective. For example Oblivion was the first Elder Scrolls title which was focused on console releases (Morrowind having been available on the first XBox, as one user felt the primal urge of pointing out) and therefore butchered its entire interface to make it as console friendly as possible, something which Morrowind was not back when it released. This meant drastically reduced tooltips, completely absurd item descriptions and names in all but the English localization (Potion of inferior Invisibility = "Ptn. o. inf. Inv." etc.) and very undescriptive info boxes to make every font large enough to be readable from 2-3 meters away on screen. It was an outrage back then, it still is bad interface design today.
Interface wise, Morrowind was ahead of it's time and considering console layouts today, from a design perspective regarding a heavily complex RPG universe, it still is.
I wouldn't really recommend Oblivion to anyone currently anymore, if it wasn't for the Shimmering Isles expansion which entirely made up for the bland main plot of the base game and had extremely memorable and mindbogglingly insane quests. Do you remember the Quest in Skyrim where you wake up naked without all your gear after a night of drinking and embark on a quest to get uncursed by a Daedra prince and get your stuff back? Imagine an entire Addon which solely consists of quests like that. Shimmering Isles is probably the best Addon Bethesda ever made and it is solely playable by playing Oblivion. Therefore I still do recommend Oblivion, although I personally would rather recommend Morrowind and / or Skyrim to people who'd want to get introduced the the Elder Scrolls series.
